en: The Five-Part Vinaya (Pañcavargika-vinaya) of the Mahīśāsaka School, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Jibin,
together with Zhu Daosheng and others, during the Song Dynasty.

The First Division: The Pārājika Dharmas. In the first part of the first division, regarding the Pārājika Dharmas: The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Sūrpāraka together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus; he went to the village of Veḷudvāra and dwelt beneath the trees of a forest.

In that town there was a brahmin named Vairaṇya, to whom King Prasenajit had granted this territory as a fief. Having heard that the Buddha—born of the Śākya clan, who had left the home life to study the Way and had become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān; one who universally knows all the mental activities of the world;
and who for the sake of others preaches the True Dharma, which is good in the beginning, middle, and end, excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing;
and which is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy Brahma-conduct—had arrived in this town together with his disciples, he went there.
He exclaimed:
"Excellent! I wish to see the Buddha!"

He was then surrounded by five hundred attendants, preceding and following him, as he went forth to the place where the Buddha was. Seeing the World-Honored One from afar beneath the trees, his faculties serene and composed, his radiance extraordinary, he leaped for joy. He alighted from his carriage and proceeded on foot; standing before the Buddha, he exchanged greetings and withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the sublime Dharma for him, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him.
Having heard the Dharma, he was filled with joy and immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will accept my offerings for the three-month period of the rains retreat!"
The Buddha said, “I have many followers here, yet you have different faiths, different views, and different inclinations; those whom you serve are different.
He addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Although my faith, views, and inclinations differ from yours, I do not consider this assembly of the World-Honored One to be large.
Thus he spoke three times, and only then did the Buddha accept him.
He immediately rose from his seat, circumambulated [the Buddha] to the right, and departed. Returning home, he prepared the requisites for the summer retreat (*varṣā*) and made offerings.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"Now this brāhmaṇa has invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha for a three-month summer retreat; I shall cast a spell (*gūḍha*) to bewilder and confuse his mind."
Having thought this, he immediately came and possessed him.
Possessed by Māra, that brahmin entered the inner palace to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses and commanded the gatekeepers:
"I shall now entertain myself within for three months; regarding external matters, whether good or bad, not a single word shall be reported!"
He no longer remembered having invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha.

At that time, that country followed false paths, and there were no monasteries or lecture halls in the villages. To the north of the city was a mountain with pure forests and streams; the Buddha and the great assembly settled there for the rains retreat.
At that time, there was a famine in the world, and it was difficult to obtain food through begging; entering the village for alms, they received nothing at all.

At that time, there was a horse merchant from the country of Pāri who was driving five hundred horses and had arrived at the beginning of summer. When the heat of the season set in, he saw that this town was cool and refreshing, with abundant water and grass, so he halted there together with his men to feed and tend the horses.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to the horse trainer's place and stood there in silence.
The horse trainer, having faith in the Buddha and a pure heart, felt compassion for the bhikṣus who had come to beg but obtained nothing. He then spoke these words:

"I have only horse-barley; if you can eat it, I shall reduce my own portion by half a measure—one *śoṇa*—and give it to you. This will suffice to sustain your bodies so that you may practice the Path."
The bhikṣus said, "The Buddha has not yet permitted us to eat the horse's portion.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, in various ways, praised having few desires and knowing contentment. He addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit you to eat the horse's portion."
Then Ānanda took the Buddha’s portion and asked someone to grind it into flour to offer to the World-Honored One; the assembly of bhikṣus pounded and boiled it for their meal.
At that time, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana was in a secluded place and had this thought:
“At present, alms-food is difficult to obtain in this country. I should now go with those who have attained supernatural powers to Uttarakuru and eat the naturally produced non-glutinous rice.”
Having reflected thus, he immediately rose from his seat, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I then had this thought:
"Now, it is difficult to obtain alms-food in this country; I should go with those who have attained supernatural powers to Uttarakuru to eat the naturally grown non-glutinous rice."
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"If you may do so, what should ordinary bhikṣus do?
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha:
"I shall receive him by means of my supernormal powers.
The Buddha said, "Stop, stop!
"Although you possess such supernormal powers, by reason of past karmic conditions, where would you wish to place him?
Furthermore, what can be done for all the ordinary beings of the future?
Having received these instructions, Maudgalyāyana remained silent and ceased his efforts.
At that time, while dwelling in seclusion, the Venerable Śāriputra had this thought:
"Among the Buddhas of the past, which Buddha’s holy life did not endure for long?
Which Buddha’s holy life endured for a long time?"
Having reflected thus, he immediately rose from his seat, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Just now, I had this thought:
Among the Buddhas of the past, which Buddha’s holy life did not endure for long?”
"Which Buddha’s Brahma-faring will endure for a long time?
At that time, the Buddha praised Śāriputra, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"What you have thought is good, and what you have asked is also good. Śāriputra!

The holy life (brahmacarya) of the Buddhas Vipaśyin, Śikhin, and Viśvabhū did not endure for long; however, the holy life of the Buddhas Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa endured for a long time."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions do the holy life (brahmacarya) of three Buddhas not endure for long, while the holy life of [the other] three Buddhas endures for a long time?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“The three Buddhas did not extensively teach the Dharma to their disciples, nor did they establish the precepts or proclaim the Prātimokṣa. After those Buddhas and their disciples entered parinirvāṇa, disciples from various names and clans went forth, and the holy life quickly perished.”
It is like loose flowers placed in a bowl set at a crossroads; when winds blow from the four directions, they are carried away and fall as they drift with the wind.
Why is this? Because there is no thread to hold them together.
In this way, Śāriputra,

it was because those three Buddhas did not extensively teach the Dharma to their disciples, did not establish the precepts, and did not proclaim the Prātimokṣa that the holy life (brahmacarya) could not endure for long.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Buddha Kṣemadharśin was traveling with a thousand disciples through the Forest of Terrors (Bhairavavana). As for why it is called the Forest of Terrors: when those who have not yet abandoned desire enter this forest, the hair on their bodies stands on end; therefore, it is named the Forest of Terrors."
That Buddha taught the Dharma to his disciples by means of their mental recollection, with no words spoken from his mouth:
"O Bhikṣus! You should contemplate this; you should not contemplate that."
"One should contemplate this and not that;
one should abandon this and cultivate this; one should practice in reliance upon this!
When the bhikṣus understood this in their hearts, their outflows were exhausted, their minds were liberated, and they attained the path of arhatship.
“Śāriputra! The Buddha Krakucchanda, the Buddha Kanakamuni, and the Buddha Kāśyapa extensively taught the Dharma to their disciples without weariness or fatigue. That is to say:
sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, nidāna, avadāna, itivṛttaka, jātaka, vaipulya, adbhutadharma, upadeśa; as well as the formulation of precepts and the exposition of the Prātimokṣa.”

After the Buddha and his disciples have entered *parinirvāṇa*, although the various disciples who have left the household life come from diverse names and clans, they will not cause the holy life (*brahmacarya*) to perish quickly.
It is like various flowers strung together with thread and placed at a crossroads; even if winds blow from the four directions, they cannot cause them to scatter.
Why is this? Because it is supported by the thread. Thus it is, Śāriputra!
The three Buddhas extensively taught the Dharma as described above to their disciples; for this reason, the holy life (brahmacarya) has long endured.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"If the holy life were not to endure for long because the Dharma is not taught extensively, the precepts are not codified, and the Prātimokṣa is not recited, we pray that the World-Honored One will teach the Dharma extensively for the sake of his disciples, codify the precepts, and recite the Prātimokṣa!"
"Now is precisely the right time.
The Buddha said, "Cease; I myself know the proper time."
Śāriputra! This assembly of mine is pure; there has never been, nor will there ever be, such a phenomenon. Even the least among this assembly of mine has attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not establish precepts for their disciples based on phenomena that have not yet arisen as outflows (āsrava).
Because there is no one among this assembly of mine who relies on their great learning, no outflows arise;
because there is no gain or fame, no one of excessive desire, and no one who has manifested supernormal powers to be known by gods and humans, no outflows arise.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had completed the three-month rains retreat, he addressed Ānanda: "Come, Ānanda!
Let us go together to the place of Pileyyaka."
Ānanda, having received these instructions, adjusted his robes and followed the Buddha to the entrance of the house.

At that time, the Brahmin was on a high tower, amusing himself with the five desires; seeing the World-Honored One from afar, he immediately recalled his duty and descended in haste. He wiped out the seat for the Buddha, invited him to sit, and prostrated himself before the Buddha with his five limbs touching the ground.
He repented and reproached himself, saying: "I am a foolish man; having invited the Buddha for the summer retreat, I failed to provide any offerings."
It was not that I felt remorse for something insentient, nor was it that there was no object at all; rather, I was simply deluded and forgetful, and could no longer recall it.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept my confession of transgression!
The Buddha said:
"You are truly foolish!
Having invited the Buddha and the Sangha, you failed to provide them with offerings; you ought to repent for this transgression!"
"I shall now, together with the assembly, accept your repentance!
He further addressed the brahmin:
"In my noble Dharma, those who know how to repent cause wholesome qualities to increase."
That brahmin spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will remain for one month to accept my offerings!
The Buddha did not accept this, and said:
“You, O Brahmin, have different faiths and different views; yet that you have been able to invite the Buddha is already a great matter.
Thus he spoke up to three times, but the Buddha again did not accept, saying:
“I have already completed my three-month summer retreat here; now I must travel on and cannot remain any longer.”
That brahmin spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will accept my offering of a farewell meal tomorrow.
The Buddha then accepted it by remaining silent.
At that time, the brahmin prepared various kinds of delicacies throughout the night; when the time for the meal arrived at dawn, he spread out the seats.
When the hour had come, the World-Honored One went with his assembly of disciples and took their places.

That brahmin then prepared the offerings; serving them with his own hands, he provided water for rinsing after the meal was finished. He then presented four pieces of *karpāsa* cotton cloth and a pair of leather sandals to the World-Honored One, and two pieces of cloth and a pair of sandals each to the members of the Saṃgha as an offering for the summer retreat.
The bhikṣus said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept offerings for the rainy season retreat.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
After the Buddha had praised in various ways having few desires and being content, as well as praising the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Because of Vairaṇyā, from this day forward, I permit you to accept offerings for the rainy season retreat."
They all accepted them.
Thereupon, the brahmin was greatly delighted in heart; he took a small seat and sat before the Buddha, and the Buddha further recited for him these verses of sympathetic joy:
"Among all the celestial shrines, The service of the sacrificial fire is supreme;..."
Among all heterodox teachers, Sarvārtasiddhi is the foremost;
among all people, the Wheel-Turning King is the foremost;
among all flowing waters, the water of the great ocean is the foremost.
"Among all illuminations, the light of the sun and moon is supreme;
among all that is above and below heaven, the Buddha’s field of merit is supreme.

When the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, he further preached the Dharma for them, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them. He then rose from his seat and set out toward the kingdom of Saṃkāśya.

Traveling by stages, he later arrived at Vaiśālī and stayed in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall by the Monkey River, where he was provided with offerings, honored, respected, and praised by the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, as well as by kings, ministers, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas.

At that time, the elders of the town of Kalandaka had business that took them into the city. Hearing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall, they all went to where the Buddha was; there they saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, surrounded by an immeasurable multitude as he preached the Dharma.
At that time, among the assembly was a householder named Sūdena, the son of Kalandaka. Hearing the Dharma, he rejoiced and immediately thought:
"As I understand what the Buddha has taught, one who lives as a householder is bound by affection and cannot cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya) extensively for the duration of their life;
but one who has left home is unattached, like space."
"I shall now rather rely on the faith of my household and leave the home life to practice the Way.
Having each returned from the assembly, they went before the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
Having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, I had this thought:
"As I understand what the Buddha has taught, those who live at home are bound by affection and cannot practice the pure conduct (brahmacarya) extensively throughout their entire lives;
those who have left the home life are unattached, like space."
"I now think it would be better for me to leave my home with faith and go forth to practice the Way.
"World-Honored One!
I have had this thought and now wish to go forth; I only pray that you will grant me ordination!"
The Buddha said,
"Excellent! Have your parents given their permission?"
He replied, “I have not yet heard it.
The Buddha said:
"All the Buddha-dharmas cannot be practiced for the sake of the Way if one's parents do not permit it.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I shall now return home to inform my parents."
The Buddha said,
"Now is precisely the right time.
Thereupon, Sudinna rose from his seat, circumambulated [the Buddha] three times to the right, returned home, and addressed his parents, saying:
"I have heard the Buddha's Dharma; being bound and attached as a householder, I now wish to leave the home life and extensively cultivate the holy life.
His parents replied, "Stop, Sūdena! Do not speak such words!"
I previously had no son; having prayed and made offerings to the gods and spirits, I have finally obtained you.
My affection for this one child is truly deep; that we should not be far apart even in death—how can I bear to be separated from you while still alive?
"Your family is wealthy; gold, silver, and precious treasures are at your disposal for you to cultivate virtue and enjoy happiness in this present life.
Why must you leave the home-life and deprive us of our hearts' desires?
Though he entreated them as many as three times with earnest pleas, his parents would not permit it.
He then rose from his seat, went to a separate place, and made this vow:
"If I do not attain renunciation, I shall never eat again; I will die right here—for what use is it to live in vain!"
He immediately ceased eating, and this continued for six days.
When his relatives heard of this, they all came to comfort him, saying, "Your parents have only you, their one son;
their affection for you is profound. They would not survive even if you were dead, let alone hear that you are living apart from them."
"Your family is immensely wealthy and well-suited for cultivating virtue. The Way depends upon the mind; it does not reside in outward appearance or dress.
Why must you harm your life and painfully oppose your parents?
He spoke thus up to three times, yet [the youth] remained silent and did not accept his advice.
Furthermore, his friends and companions also came to admonish him with the same earnest words as before, but he remained just as he was.
Each of them gave up and departed, going to where his parents were and all said:
"As we see it, he cannot be turned back."
If you permit him to leave home and become a monk, he may still be seen from time to time;
if he does not delight in the Way, there will be a set date for his return.

Having gone without food for six days, his remaining life is but a matter of moments; within a few days, he shall be cast into the middle of the wilds to be pecked at by hawks and crows, and vied over as food by tigers and wolves.
"O father and mother, how can you bear to witness this?
Having heard this, the parents shed tears and replied,
"We grant your son permission to leave the household life and practice the holy life."
"However, for our mutual agreement, we shall meet again at the appointed time.

Having heard this, his friends were all greatly delighted; they went back to him and said, "Your parents have already granted you permission to leave home [to become a monk]. As long as you do not forget to return at the appointed time, you may go!"
Sudinna was filled with great joy; he went to his parents and said, "I shall now go to the Buddha to leave the household life and practice the Way.
His parents wept sorrowfully and replied:
"I grant you permission to leave the household life and extensively cultivate the pure conduct;
however, do not forget our essential agreement, and return to see me at the proper time.
Thereupon, Sudinna bowed in farewell to his parents, circumambulated them three times, and departed.
Returning to the place where the Buddha was, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
My parents have granted their permission; I only pray that you will allow me to leave the household life and receive the precepts!”
The Buddha said:
“Welcome, bhikṣu! Practice the various holy life.
I have well-expounded the Dharma to sever all suffering.”

When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, Sudinna’s hair and beard fell away of their own accord; the saṃghāṭī robe was upon his body and the alms bowl was in his hand; he immediately became a śramaṇa and attained full ordination.
Not long after he had gone forth, a famine occurred in the world. When the bhikṣus entered the city to beg for alms, they obtained nothing at all.
While staying in a secluded place, Sūdena thought to himself:
"At this time of famine, it is difficult to obtain food through begging; however, the place where I was born is abundant in food and pleasant."
"I shall now return these bhikṣus to my own city so that they may receive offerings, and thereby bring merit and deliverance to them.
He then rose from his seat and, accompanied by the bhikṣus, returned to his native city, where he stayed beneath the trees of a forest.
When the parents heard this, they instructed their wife, saying:
"You should adorn yourself with the garments and ornaments that my son enjoyed while at home.
Once she had finished adorning herself, the parents took her and went together to that forest.
At that time, Sudinna saw his parents approaching; he rose to greet them and inquire after their well-being.
His parents said to him, "Why have you disfigured yourself and taken up residence among the trees and forests?"
"You may as well return to abandon the Way and cultivate goodness while living at home.
He replied to his parents, saying,
"I cannot abandon the Way to return to a lowly and base life."
Thus it was repeated up to three times, yet his resolve remained even firmer.
His parents wept and, letting him go, returned home.
Within a few days, Sudinna’s wife experienced her menses and informed her mother-in-law, who spoke with joy:
"This is the mark of one who has a son.
He then ordered him to be adorned with the same attire as before, and his parents once again took him together to that forest.
At that time, Sudinna greeted them as previously described, and his parents spoke again:
"Why do you disfigure yourself, enduring the hardships of wind, dew, hunger, and cold amidst these forest trees?

Your family wealth is known throughout the world; as for my private treasures, they are so vast they could submerge a man's head, let alone the property of your parents—how could one possibly measure it?"
"You may return home and cultivate merit as you please; you shall enjoy happiness in this life and receive blessings and prosperity in the future.
He said to his parents:

"As I have perceived, the five desires damage one's virtue; pleasures are like lightning, while sorrow and suffering endure for a long time. I shall never, on account of these things, abandon the cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya)."
Thus it was repeated three times, and his reply remained firm and resolute.
His parents spoke again:
"Though you are our son, you have now become a member of the Śākya clan; since you have opposed us for the sake of the Way, what more is there to say?"

"However, the ancestral sacrifices have been suspended; the bonds of human relations are profound. When Wang Xian’s lineage perishes, his property shall be confiscated by the state—I have prepared for this!
Do you not know that my remaining wish is for you to continue the family line? You must reflect upon this; my words are now at an end!"

At that time, Śuddhodana heard these instructions and wept with grief; he silently accepted the command and returned home with his wife. While they were in their own chamber, they engaged in sexual intercourse three times, whereupon a deity descended:
at that moment, a deva from Tuṣita Heaven of great majesty and virtue passed away and entered the womb.
At that time, the Earth Deity addressed the Space Deity, saying:
"The son of Kalandaka has performed an unprecedented act among the Sangha.
The Space Deity informed the Four Great Kings; the Four Great Kings informed the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; thus they informed one another in succession until it reached the Brahmā Heaven.
When his wife’s term was full, she gave birth to a son who was intelligent and discerning; he was named Jāti-caraka. When he grew up, he left the household life and became an Arhat.
At that time, after Sudinna had committed this evil deed, he immediately reproached himself:
"I have now lost my advantage; how is it that, having gone forth in the True Dharma of the Buddha, I have not brought the holy life (brahmacarya) to its ultimate fulfillment?"
He was emaciated and haggard, barely possessing breath.
When the bhikṣus saw him, they asked, "Formerly you had a fine complexion; why are you so haggard now?"
“Is it not the case that you did not delight in the holy life and committed evil offenses?
He replied, “I have indeed committed evil offenses; that is precisely why it is so!”
He then asked, "What offense have you committed? He replied:
“I have engaged in impure conduct with my former wife.
The bhikṣus said: “What you have done is unwholesome;
it is not pure conduct, it is not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, and it does not accord with the Path!”
Having rebuked him in various ways as the Buddha had instructed, they led him to the Buddha's presence and reported the matter to him.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. It is the constant law of all Buddhas:
to ask even though they know [the answer], or not to ask even though they know.
One asks at the proper time and does not ask at an improper time;
one asks what is beneficial and does not ask what is not beneficial.
This is the constant law of all Buddhas:
There were five hundred Vajrapāṇi spirits standing guard on his left and right; if he did not answer truthfully when the Buddha questioned him three times, his head would split into seven pieces.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"What do you wish to say?"
The bhikṣus reported this again to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Sūdena,
“Is it true that you did this?”
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said: "You foolish person! What you have done is unwholesome;
it is not a pure practice, it is not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, and it does not accord with the Path!"
This cannot cause those who have no faith to believe, nor does it cause those who already have faith to fall away.
Have you not heard how I have in various ways rebuked sensual desire, the perception of desire, thoughts of desire, and the fever of desire;
and how I have praised the abandoning of desire, the detachment from the perception of desire, the removal of thoughts of desire, and the extinction of the fever of desire?

I have always said that desire is like a heap of bleached bones, like a great pit of fire, like a sharp blade, like a sharp arrow, like a venomous snake, like poison, and like an illusion or a dream that deceives people; why do you now commit such a great evil?

Have you not heard the Dharma I have taught: it enables those who have not yet abandoned desire to abandon desire; it causes those who are already negligent to become diligent; it can sever craving and bring about detachment from conditioned phenomena; it leads the seeker beyond training who has abandoned desire toward the unconditioned path; and it reveals to people the essential right way for ultimate Nirvana!
Do you not fear the suffering of the three evil realms?
Had you not committed this great evil, you would have surely attained immeasurable wholesome merits within the Buddha’s True Dharma.

"You have first opened the gate of outflows and committed this great evil; Pāpīyān constantly watches for the shortcomings of the bhikṣus, and you have now opened a path for Māra, toppled the banner of the Dharma, and raised the standard of Māra."
"Śuddhodana! It would be better to cast this body into a great pit of fire or into the mouth of a venomous snake than to touch the body of a woman with it!
The evil you have committed will cause you to sink forever into birth and death; you shall never again be able to cultivate wholesome dharmas!"
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. What are these ten? [1] To harmonize the Saṃgha; [2] to bring peace to the Saṃgha; [3] to cause the Saṃgha to dwell in comfort; [4] to restrain those who have not yet entered the path; [5] to encourage those who have already entered the path; [6] to honor the True Dharma; [7] to uphold the Vinaya; [8] to benefit the lay followers; [9] to prevent evil persons from entering the order; and [10] to ensure that those who have already entered the order may easily abide therein."

That is to say: for the sake of harmony within the Saṃgha; for the sake of gathering the Saṃgha; for the sake of subduing wicked people; for the sake of providing peace and happiness to those with a sense of shame and remorse; for the sake of severing the outflows (*āsrava*) of the present life; for the sake of extinguishing the outflows of future lives; for the sake of inspiring faith in those who have not yet believed; for the sake of increasing and expanding the faith of those who already believe; for the sake of ensuring the long endurance of the Dharma; and for the sake of ensuring the long endurance of the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) through the analysis of the Vinaya.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse, he commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
There was an *āraṇyaka* bhikṣu dwelling in a secluded place, where a troop of monkeys lived nearby.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu became lustful for a female monkey; he lured her with food and subsequently engaged in sexual intercourse with her.

Later, when many bhikṣus were inspecting the bedding and furniture, they arrived at that dwelling; at that time, the bhikṣu had entered the city for alms, and a female macaque came and displayed signs of sexual desire.
The bhikṣus spoke among themselves: "Observe this monkey;
there must surely be a reason for it. Let us watch closely together, and its true nature will certainly be revealed.

A bhikṣu who had been staying there previously returned after a short while. The monkey immediately went to him and manifested the signs of desiring sexual intercourse; at that time, the bhikṣu then engaged in sexual desire with it.
The bhikṣus saw him and said, "Have you not heard that the Buddha has established this precept: that a bhikṣu who commits sexual misconduct incurs a pārājika offense? He replied:
“The Buddha has prohibited [sexual relations with] human women, but not with animals. The bhikṣus said:
“What difference is there between a human woman and an animal?”
"What you have done is unwholesome, not a pure practice, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, and does not accord with the Path!
This cannot inspire faith in those who lack it, and it causes those who already have faith to fall away."
"Have you not heard how the World-Honored One has in various ways rebuked desire, the characteristics of desire, thoughts of desire, and the fever of desire?
He recounted everything as above.
Having finished his rebuke, he led [the youth] to the Buddha's presence and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked them:
"Is it true that you did so?
They replied: [Yes].
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
"You foolish person! What you have done is contrary to the Dharma.
He rebuked him in various ways, as described above.
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse, even with an animal, he commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.'"
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus took no pleasure in practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and spoke among themselves as follows:
"To leave the home life according to the Buddha’s Dharma is a very great hardship. We should together practice the customs of laypeople and the customs of non-Buddhist outsiders."
They engaged in the affairs of laypeople and the affairs of non-Buddhists;
they entered villages at the proper time and at improper times;
and they practiced killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, drinking alcohol, and eating meat.
Day and night they watched performances, amusing themselves with songs and chants.

Having spoken these words repeatedly without any sense of shame or remorse, at that time certain bhikṣus who maintained the precepts, were of few desires, and were content, rebuked them in various ways. They then led them to the Buddha’s presence and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked them:
"Is it true that you did so? They replied: [Yes, it is true.]
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"You should not speak these words together:
'We practice the rituals and laws of non-Buddhists' or 'We practice the rituals and laws of laypeople.
If you say, 'We practice the rituals and laws of non-Buddhists,' for every such utterance, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense."
"To practice the ritual observances of a white-robed layperson is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu from the Vṛji country named Sundarananda, who was well-known and venerated by the community. He took no pleasure in cultivating the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and instead adopted the ritual observances of non-Buddhist practitioners and the ritual observances of white-robed laypeople.
They committed various evil deeds such as killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
Those householders who did not have faith in or delight in the Buddha-dharma rebuked them, saying:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, commit such evils?"
In every place, people said:
"The bhikṣu Sunda also enjoys the pleasures of the five desires; these bhikṣus have neither the conduct of śramaṇas nor the conduct of brāhmaṇas;
they do not follow the dharma of śramaṇas, nor do they follow the dharma of brāhmaṇas."
"In all those places where these bhikṣus do not travel, one shall obtain excellent benefit!
Thus a foul reputation spread and was heard throughout the world.
At that time, Sundarī returned to the assembly and spoke these words:
"Grant me the going forth and the precepts.
The bhikṣus said, "We must inform the World-Honored One."
He immediately reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:

"Sundarī is no longer a bhikṣu; if she had already received the precepts, she should have been subjected to the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) for expulsion."
If the senior monk, or one equal to a senior monk, who is learned in the Dharma and Vinaya, should make the following motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu Sundara, while his precepts were weak and he had not renounced them, committed the act of sexual intercourse."
The Sangha now proceeds to carry out the formal act of banishment against the bhikṣu Sundara.
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent and listen.
This is the motion.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu Sundara, though his precepts were weak, did not relinquish them, yet he committed the act of sexual intercourse.
Now the Saṃgha shall carry out a formal act of banishment against the bhikṣu Sundara."
"Whichever elders approve, remain silent;
whoever does not approve, speak.
A second and third time it was said in the same manner.
“The Saṃgha has completed the act of formal suspension (pravāsanīya-karman) against the bhikṣu Sunda;
the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu acts according to the customs of laypeople or the customs of non-Buddhists, this is not called 'renouncing the precepts.
However, if he says with his own mouth, 'I renounce the precepts,' this is called 'renouncing the precepts.'"
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

"If a bhikṣu, while training together with other bhikṣus in the rules of the Dharma, engages in sexual intercourse—even with an animal—without relinquishing his feeble commitment to the precepts, that bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion."

“Bhikṣu” refers to: a bhikṣu by begging; a bhikṣu who wears robes of dyed, cut pieces; a bhikṣu who has destroyed evil; a bhikṣu in reality; a steadfast bhikṣu; a bhikṣu who perceives his faults; a bhikṣu ordained with one utterance; a bhikṣu ordained with two utterances; a bhikṣu ordained with three utterances; a bhikṣu ordained by the “Come hither” formula; and a bhikṣu ordained through a formal ritual of motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman) in accordance with the Dharma—these are called bhikṣus.
Regarding "training together":
as the Buddha has said,
"To refrain from transgression for as long as life lasts— this is training together."
This is called "practicing together.
As for the precepts and dharmas:

they are the precepts received without deficiency, the precepts that do not give rise to unwholesome dharmas, the precepts that accomplish wholesome dharmas, and the precepts concurrent with meditative concentration.
Regarding "one who is weak in the precepts but does not relinquish them":

if one relinquishes the precepts while asleep, or relinquishes the precepts toward a person who is asleep, it is not called relinquishing the precepts. If one relinquishes the precepts while intoxicated, or relinquishes the precepts toward a person who is intoxicated; [it is likewise not called relinquishing the precepts].
One who is insane relinquishes the precepts by relinquishing them to another who is insane;
one with a distracted mind relinquishes the precepts by relinquishing them to another with a distracted mind;
one whose mind is impaired by illness relinquishes the precepts by relinquishing them to another whose mind is impaired by illness.
Renouncing the precepts by addressing a non-sentient being, a non-human, or an animal;
renouncing the precepts by dispatching a messenger or sending a letter;
renouncing the precepts by making gestures, by moving the hands, or by using ambiguous speech;

If one renounces the precepts while alone yet perceives oneself as alone; or if one renounces the precepts while alone yet perceives oneself as not alone; or if one renounces the precepts while not alone yet perceives oneself as alone;
if one renounces the precepts by speaking the language of the Central Kingdom to a person from a borderland, or by speaking the language of a borderland to a person from the Central Kingdom;
if one renounces the precepts in jest; if one renounces the precepts with indistinct speech; if one renounces the precepts with a mind of anger; or if one renounces the precepts under duress.
If one does not intend to relinquish the precepts yet proceeds to relinquish them, none of these instances are termed "relinquishing the precepts.
If one does not speak the words of relinquishing the precepts, it is not termed "relinquishing the precepts"; this is called "not relinquishing the precepts."
The opposite of the aforementioned constitutes the relinquishment of the precepts.

There are cases where the precepts are weakened but not relinquished; cases where they are relinquished but not weakened; cases where they are both weakened and relinquished; and cases where they are neither weakened nor relinquished.
What is meant by "the weakening of the precepts but not the abandonment of the precepts"?

It refers to a bhikṣu who no longer delights in practicing the holy life; yet, having ceased to delight in practicing the holy life, he still respects the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; he respects the precepts, respects the dharmas of a śramaṇa, respects the dharmas of a bhikṣu, respects the Vinaya, respects the Prātimokṣa, respects his upādhyāya and ācārya as well as their fellow disciples, respects his fellow practitioners of the holy life, and does not slander the Triple Gem.
However, he still remembers his native land, gardens and pavilions, bathing pools, mountain forests, trees, parents, brothers, sisters, sons, daughters, and even his male and female servants.

Recalling this, one feels sorrow and discontent, yet throughout one's entire life refrains from violating the holy life (*brahmacarya*); this is called "weakness of morality" (*śīla-kaśāya*) but not "abandoning the precepts.
What is "abandoning the precepts" but not "weakness of morality"?

If a bhikkhu does not delight in practicing the holy life, and having ceased to delight in practicing the holy life, he still respects the Buddha, up to and including his fellow practitioners of the holy life, he thinks to himself:
"I wish to become a śrāmaṇera, or an upāsaka, or even an outsider brahmin; I am no longer a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya."
Again, he had this thought:

"I now wish to abandon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha; I wish to abandon the precepts, abandon the Vinaya, abandon the Prātimokṣa; I wish to abandon my upādhyāya and ācāryas, as well as those who share the same upādhyāya and ācāryas; and I wish to abandon my fellow practitioners of the holy life."
He then spoke these words:
"I now abandon the Buddha; what use have I for a Buddha?
What meaning does 'Buddha' possess?"
"I have now attained liberation from the Buddha," he said, continuing,
"I have now attained liberation from my fellow practitioners of the holy life."

He further said: "I am one who maintains what is not the practice of a śramaṇa or a son of the Śākya; I thus slander the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, even slandering my fellow practitioners of the holy life."
To form such thoughts and speak such words, and then declare them to others, is called "renouncing the precepts" (śikṣā-nirākaraṇa), not "the weakness of the precepts" (śīla-daurbalya).
What, then, is "the weakness of the precepts," which also constitutes renouncing the precepts?

If a bhikṣu does not delight in practicing the holy life, and has little respect for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, even down to having little respect for his fellow practitioners of the holy life;
if he recollects his native land, even down to his slaves and servants, and forms this thought:
"I now wish to abandon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, even down to abandoning my fellow practitioners of the holy life."
He then spoke these words:
“I now renounce the Buddha; what use have I for a Buddha?
What meaning does ‘Buddha’ possess?”
"I have now attained liberation from the Buddha, and even from my fellow practitioners of the holy life.

He further said: "I am one who maintains what is not the practice of a śramaṇa or a son of the Śākya; I have thus slandered the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and even slandered my fellow practitioners of the holy life."
To form such thoughts and speak such words, and then declare them to others, is called "weakening of the precepts" as well as "renouncing the precepts.
What, then, is neither weakening of the precepts nor renouncing the precepts?
If a bhikṣu firmly maintains the precepts he has received without abandoning them, remaining unshakable and unwavering, this is called "neither being weak in morality nor relinquishing the precepts.
Regarding "practicing the act of sexual intercourse":

the term "sexual intercourse" refers to the practice of non-celibacy, the practice of indolence, the practice of dogs, and the loathsome practice; the mutual union of two bodies resulting in the emission of impurity—this is called practicing the act of sexual intercourse.
*Pārājika*: This is called "falling from the Dharma," called "an evil dharma," called "the dharma of severed heads," and called "not the dharma of a śramaṇa.
"Not to live together" means:
Just as when one was formerly a layperson, one does not share the same training, equal training, unequal training, or alternative training with the bhikṣus;
one does not share the same *karma*, equal *karma*, unequal *karma*, or alternative *karma* with the bhikṣus;

and one does not share the same recitation of the precepts, equal recitation of the precepts, unequal recitation of the precepts, or alternative recitation of the precepts with the bhikṣus—this is called "not living together."
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, skillfully expound the True Dharma and also skillfully employ parables.
They say that one who commits sexual misconduct is like a needle with its eye broken, which can no longer be used;
they are like a human life at its end, which cannot be restored.
Just as a stone once shattered cannot be joined back together,
and just as the heart of a tāla tree once cut off cannot grow again, so too,
a bhikṣu who engages in sexual intercourse with three kinds of sentient beings commits a pārājika offense: [the text continues with the specific categories].
Humans, non-humans, and animals.
If a bhikṣu engages in sexual intercourse with women of these three types—
human women, non-human women, or animal females— he commits a pārājika offense.
With three kinds of males:
human males, non-human males, and male animals;
and three kinds of eunuchs:
Human eunuchs, non-human eunuchs, and animal eunuchs;
three types of those without sexual organs:
human beings without sexual organs, non-humans without sexual organs, and animals without sexual organs.
There are three types of those with two sexual organs:
humans with two organs, non-humans with two organs, and animals with two organs; engaging in sexual intercourse with them is likewise [an offense].
A bhikṣu may engage in sexual intercourse with a human female, a non-human female, or an animal female in three places: [the anus, the mouth, and the vagina].
In the large or small orifices, or in the mouth;
during sleep, intoxication, insanity, mental distraction, impairment of the mind due to illness, death, or when [the body] is half-eaten—these constitute a *pārājika*.
When it is more than half-eaten, or when only bones remain, if semen is emitted, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if no semen is emitted, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
The same applies to women without sexual organs and those with both sexual organs.
A bhikṣu commits sexual misconduct with a human male, a non-human male, or a male animal in two places:
the great path (anus) and the mouth.
If it occurs while sleeping, or even during the first half of the time spent eating, it is a *pārājika*;
if it occurs after the half-time has passed or when only bones remain, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* if semen is emitted, and a *sthūlātyaya* if no semen is emitted.
The same applies to those who are rootless males (*aṇḍaja*) or eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*).
If one engages in sexual intercourse with any of the aforementioned parts, whether by external means with internal emission of semen,
or by internal means with external emission of semen, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense, even if it occurs while the person is asleep or during the time it takes to eat half a meal.
If it exceeds half [the length], it is the time of bone; if impurity is emitted, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if impurity is not emitted, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If a bhikṣu, being coerced by force, engages in sexual intercourse in any of the aforementioned places: if he experiences pleasure upon entry but not during emission or staying, or if he experiences pleasure upon emission but not during entry or staying; [it is a *sthūlātyaya*].
When dwelling, one experiences pleasure, but not when exiting or entering;
when exiting or entering, one experiences pleasure, but not when dwelling;
when entering or dwelling, one experiences pleasure, but not when exiting.
If one experiences pleasure during emission, but not while entering;
or if one experiences pleasure during emission, entry, and remaining, yet not while sleeping—even up until the point of consuming half [of the semen]—it is a *pārājika*.
If more than half has been consumed, or when it is in the stage of bone, and impurity is emitted, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; if impurity is not emitted, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If, during the acts of entering, exiting, or remaining [within], one does not experience pleasure, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, inserts even a single part of his male organ into any of the aforementioned orifices, it is a pārājika;
if he inserts a finger or any other external object into any of the aforementioned orifices, it is a sthūlātyaya.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is also a pārājika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta, and they are to be expelled.
There is no offense in the following cases:
If one acts with a deranged mind, a distracted mind, a mind impaired by illness, or when first undertaking the training, these four cases do not constitute an offense.
This applies to all subsequent precepts as well; they need not be repeated here.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Daṇḍaka, the son of a potter, who lived in a grass hut on Mount Vaidehaka.
When the time came, he took his bowl and entered the city to beg for food. While he was away, some wood-gatherers suddenly destroyed his hut and carried off the timber.
After he returned from his meal, he repaired it once again.
When this had been repeated three times, his heart was filled with resentment, and he thought to himself:
"I am fortunately skilled at mixing mud; why should I not build a finished tile-roofed house to relieve myself of this affliction?"
He then had it built accordingly.
The rafters, ridgepoles, capitals, beams, purlins, columns, joists, and main beams, as well as the ornate latticed windows and doors, were so exquisitely crafted that they seemed divine.
When stacked with firewood and burned, the resulting color was a magnificent crimson; when a great wind blew, it produced a sound like that of a *kōṇḍohu* lute.
While on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, the Buddha saw from afar that house, which was adorned with various carvings and was magnificent,
being red in color. He asked Ānanda, "What house is that?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“This was performed by the physical strength of Daṇḍakī.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This is an unrighteous act committed by Dhanika!
How can one who has gone forth engage in such evil karma as harming living beings without compassion?
Previously, I have taught various dharmas of loving-kindness and patience; how is it that this bhikṣu lacks such a heart of mercy?"
After the World-Honored One had thus rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Go there yourselves and demolish what he has built.
Having received these instructions, the bhikṣus immediately went to the site of the house.
Then Dhanika came out from inside the house and asked the bhikṣus, "I have done you no wrong;
why do you form a faction to destroy my house?
The bhikṣus replied:
"It was by the command of the World-Honored One; it was not our own intention.
Dhanika said, "When the Dharma King has brought about this destruction, what more can I say?"
The bhikṣus immediately broke it together and took Dhanika back to where the Buddha was, reporting the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Dhanika:
"Did you actually do this?"
He replied, “I truly did,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways as described above, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, if a bhikṣu builds a house of fired bricks, it is a sthūlātyaya;
if he displays his own craftsmanship, it is a duṣkṛta."
At that time, Daṇḍaka again thought to himself:
"Previously, when I constructed a grass hut, it was immediately destroyed by woodcutters;
later, when I built a tile-roofed house, it violated the character of one who has gone forth under a Dharma-king."
"Now it would be better to seek out superior timber and construct a large house; then we shall surely dwell there for a long time, free from further suffering and distress.
He then thought again:
"The Superintendent of Timber in Rājagṛha is my acquaintance; I should go to him and ask for it."
Having thought this, he went to him and said, "I require timber; you may give some to me.
The Superintendent of Timber replied:
"I have no freedom regarding the timber. He asked, "By whom?"
He replied, "It was by the king. Dhanika said:
"The King has already given it to me," said the Director of Timber.
"If the King has already granted it to you, take it as you please."
Daṇḍakīna then took large timbers used for city fortifications, cut them into pieces, and carried them away.
At that time, the minister Vāsava was inspecting various places when he encountered him on the road and immediately asked the Superintendent of Timber:
"Why have you taken these large timbers used for city fortifications and given them to that bhikṣu?"
He replied, "It was not I who gave it.
He asked again:
"Who is it? He replied, "It is the king."
Vṛṣaśarman then asked:
"I do not understand, Great King, why have you given the great timber for the city's defenses to Daṇḍakin?
The King replied:
"Who said I gave it? Vāsava replied,
"It was the Director of Timber."
The king immediately commanded his attendants to arrest the Superintendent of Timber.
Having received the order, they arrested him and led him to the king's presence.
At that time, Dhanika entered the city to beg for alms; seeing [the Superintendent] on the road, he asked him:
"What offense have you committed that you are bound so tightly?
He replied, "It is because of the Venerable One that I have incurred this great transgression."
"We pray that you will grant us your protection and spare our lives!
Dhanika said, "You go on ahead; I shall follow shortly."
When the Superintendent of Timber arrived at the king’s residence, the king asked,
“Why have you brought these large timbers for the city’s defenses to Daṇḍakī? He replied:
"Great King! I did not dare to act on my own authority.
Daṇḍaka said that it was by Your Majesty's command that he was made to give it."
The king then issued an order to summon him.
At that time, Daṇḍakī was already outside the gate; the king ordered him to come forward, and he immediately approached and saw the king.
The king asked:
“When did I give timber to the bhikṣus? Daṇḍaka replied,
“Does Your Majesty not recall that upon first ascending the throne, You bestowed all the grass, wood, and water within Your realm as a gift to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas?”
The king said,
"My original intention in giving was not to reach those who have owners.
How strange!"
"The bhikṣu has employed such a stratagem to take another's property.
He spoke further, saying, "I am a consecrated king; how could I imprison or kill a śramaṇa?"
"You may now return at once to the Buddha; the Dharma King himself shall surely govern you according to the Dharma.
At that time, those who heard this were all struck with astonishment and said, "Dhaniya has committed a crime worthy of death!"
"How can one scold someone and then simply release them?
If one can escape in this manner, who would not commit theft?
He further spoke with derision and reproach:
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, personally receive the king’s offerings and yet steal the king’s timber;
how much more so should we be granted fearlessness!
These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, constantly praise non-stealing and teach people to practice generosity.”
"How can you now personally practice the dharma of thieves?
These people possess no conduct of a śramaṇa; they destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!
Thus did this evil reputation spread from one person to another.

The elders, householders, and brahmins within the kingdom who did not have faith in or delight in the Buddha-dharma would immediately revile the śramaṇas with various insults whenever they saw them from afar.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they asked one another,
"Who has stolen the king’s timber, causing such ill repute?"
Daṇḍaka said, "It was my doing.
Then the bhikṣus rebuked him in various ways.
"What you have done is contrary to the Dharma and does not accord with the Path!
The World-Honored One has in various ways censured taking what is not given and praised refraining from theft.
How is it that you now personally practice the way of a thief?"
After the bhikṣus had thus rebuked him, they led him to the Buddha’s presence and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Daṇḍaka:
“Is it true that you did this?”
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked Sūpannaddha in various ways.
At that time, a high minister from Magadha had left the household life to practice the Way and was attending upon the Buddha.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
“King Ajātaśatru, at what amount does a person become guilty of a capital offense for theft?
A bhikṣu said to the Buddha:
“If it is five coins or more, one incurs the death penalty.”
After the Buddha had further rebuked him with this, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu steals property worth five māsakas or more, he commits a pārājika offense and is no longer to live in communion.'"
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus spoke thus:
"The precepts established by the Buddha concern things within a village; they do not refer to open ground."
Furthermore, there were monks who spoke thus:
"Whether it is an offense or not an offense, whether it is prescribed by the rule or not, one should simply take them without concern.
They then each, with a thieving mind, took property belonging to others from vacant land, whether it had an owner or not.
Having taken [the robes], they each felt doubt and regret, went to Ānanda, and questioned him; Ānanda then reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"What difference is there between a village and an open space?
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, with the intent to steal, takes what is not given from a village or an open space—
whether a king or a high minister should seize him, bind him, kill him, or banish him, saying:'"
“You thief! You child! You fool!”
"Such a bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and shall not dwell in communion.
Whether it be a city with moats or a village surrounded on all sides by fences for three yojanas down to a single house, this is called a "village."
Outside the village, excluding the area frequented by the village, is called "open space.
The area outside the village extending for the distance of one arrow-shot, where those with a sense of shame perform their bodily functions, is called "the area frequented by the village."
To take what belongs to another, which is protected by another, without it being given—this is called the mind of theft.
Furthermore, to take the property of others with a deceitful mind, a crooked mind, a mind of malice, or a mind of fear is also called the mind of theft.
Whether one takes it oneself or causes another to take it, once the object has been moved from its original place, this is called taking what is not given.
A sovereign of a nation, a leader of a village, an anointed king, or a wheel-turning monarch is termed a "king."
Those who preside over state affairs are called great ministers (*mahāmātya*).
To seize someone by the hand or the hair is called "seizing.
Shackles, fetters, stocks, and manacles are called "binding."
To sever one's life by means of weapons, staves, and the like is called "killing.
To expel one from a dwelling place, even as far as an entire kingdom, is called "banishment.
To cause one to depart from wholesome and neutral states and fall into an unwholesome state is called "robbery."
Lack of discernment is called "smallness.
Entering into darkness is called "delusion.
Regarding the transgressions therein:

Objects on the ground, objects above the ground, objects in the air; villages and village property; mounds and mound property; fields and field property; groves and grove property; houses and house property; vehicles and vehicle property; loads and load property; boats and boat property; ponds and pond property; entrusted items; blocking the road; waiting at the road; indicating a place; guiding the way; teaching how to take; taking together; and not paying taxes.
Regarding objects within the earth:
if there is an object within the earth, a bhikṣu forms the thought,
"I shall steal this object."
To resolve upon [the act] and to employ the means are both *duṣkṛta*;
to dig the earth is a *pāyattika*;
to seize an object is a *duṣkṛta*.
Regarding animals, it is a sthūlātyaya;
if the value of the object removed from its original place is five kārṣāpaṇas or more, it is a pārājika;
if less than five kārṣāpaṇas, it is a sthūlātyaya.

"Objects on the ground" refers to items situated upon the ground, such as bed frames, tables, stools, door lintels, beams, rafters, and so forth, up to those on rooftops or trees; all such things are termed "objects on the ground."
If a bhikṣu forms the thought,
"I shall steal this object," the initial resolve,
the preparatory effort, and even the act of seizing the object all constitute *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Regarding animals, it is a sthūlātyaya;
if the value of moving them from their original place is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is a pārājika;
if less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a sthūlātyaya.
Regarding objects found in space:
if one places an object in the air through supernormal power, or if it is brought there by a bird carrying it, or blown there by the wind,
the bhikṣu should form this thought:
"I shall steal this object.
The initial resolve and the preparatory effort both constitute *duṣkṛta*;
if the object is animate, it is *sthūlātyaya*.
If one moves [an object] from its original place and its value is exactly five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika* offense;
if it is less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
As for "a village":
Within a radius of three yojanas, even down to a single dwelling,
a bhikṣu thinks to himself:
"I shall steal this village."
To resolve to commit [the offense] and to employ the means thereto constitutes a *duṣkṛta*;
to drive in a stake constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*;
to measure with a cord and obtain a value of five *māsakas* or more constitutes a *pārājika*.
If it is less than five *māṣakas*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
"Village property" refers to whatever items exist within the village.
If a bhikṣu forms the thought,
"I shall steal this object," and obtains it,
he commits a pārājika offense.
Regarding the *diana* (a storage shelf): the bhikṣu forms the thought,
"I shall steal this *diana*."
To form the intention and employ the means [of measurement] constitutes a *duṣkṛta*;
to drive in stakes constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*;
to measure with a cord and obtain the land through dispute constitutes a *pārājika*.
Regarding "the objects on the stand":
it refers to whatever objects are present within the stand.
The bhikṣu should form this thought:
“I shall steal this object.
If he obtains it, it is a *pārājika*.
Regarding “a field”:
Regarding fields in water or on land,
a bhikṣu forms the thought:
"I shall steal this field."
To form the intention and employ the means [of measurement] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense;
to drive in stakes constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*;
to measure with a cord and obtain the disputed land constitutes a *pārājika*.
Regarding "field produce":
it refers to the various grains and goods produced within a field.
A bhikṣu should form this thought:
"I shall steal this object.
If he obtains it, it is a *pārājika*.
"Garden" means:
Regarding orchards and vegetable gardens,
a bhikṣu forms the thought:
"I shall steal these gardens."
To form the intention and employ the means [of measurement] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense;
to drive in stakes constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*;
to measure with a cord and obtain it through dispute constitutes a *pārājika*.
Regarding "garden items":
these are whatever items are produced within the garden.
The bhikṣu forms the thought:
"I shall steal this object.
If he obtains it, it is a *pārājika*.
"House" means:
Regarding a house inhabited by laypeople or monastics, or a multi-storied building,
a bhikṣu forms the intention:
"I shall steal this house."
To form the intention and employ the means [of measurement] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense;
to drive in stakes constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*;
to measure with a cord and thereby obtain the object of dispute constitutes a *pārājika*.
"Household goods" refers to whatever items are contained within the house.
A bhikṣu forms the thought:
"I shall steal this object.
If he obtains it, it is a *pārājika*.
As for "riding":
Regarding elephants, horses, chariots, and various vehicles,
a bhikṣu forms the thought:
"I shall steal these vehicles."
From the initial resolution and the preparatory efforts up until the moment of seizing it, all constitute a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing);
regarding a living being, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense);
if it is removed from its original place and its value is five *māṣakas*, it is a *pārājika* (defeat).
If it is less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding "the goods on a vehicle":
it refers to whatever goods are upon the vehicle.
If a bhikṣu forms the thought,
"I shall steal this object," and obtains it,
he commits a pārājika offense.
"Carrying" (*bhāra*) refers to wearing on the head, carrying on the shoulder, bearing on the back, or holding in the hand— all these are termed "carrying.
A bhikṣu should form this thought:
"I shall steal this carrying-pole.
The initial resolve and the preparatory effort both constitute *duṣkṛta*;
when one begins to move it, it is *sthūlātyaya*.
If one moves an object from its original place and its value is exactly five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika* offense;
if it is less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding "one who carries an object":
Regarding whatever items are within the eaves,
the bhikṣu forms the thought:
"I shall steal these items."
If she obtains it, it is a *pārājika* offense.
As for "boat":
a leather boat, a bottle-gourd boat, a wooden boat, or a raft—all such things are termed "boats."
If a bhikṣu forms the thought,
"I shall steal this boat," both the initial resolve and the preparatory effort constitute *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If he moves it, it is a sthūlātyaya;
if he removes it from its original place and its value is five kārṣāpaṇas or more, it is a pārājika;
if it is less than five kārṣāpaṇas, it is a sthūlātyaya.
"Vessels" refers to all items whatsoever on board the ship.
A bhikṣu forms the thought:
"I shall steal this object.
If he obtains it, it is a *pārājika*.
Regarding "a pond":
All embankments, lakes, and various bodies of water are termed "pools.
A bhikṣu forms the thought:
"I shall steal this pool."
To resolve to commit [the offense] and to employ the means thereto constitutes a *duṣkṛta*;
to drive in a stake constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*;
to measure with a cord and obtain a value of five *kārsāpaṇas* or more constitutes a *pārājika*.
If it is less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
"Things from a pond" refers to whatever items are produced by that pond.
If a bhikṣu forms the thought,
"I shall steal this object," and obtains it,
he commits a pārājika offense.
Regarding "entrusting":
if a person entrusts an object to a bhikṣu and, with a thieving mind, does not return the object,
and the owner relinquishes their claim to it, and its value is five *māṣakas* or more, it is a *pārājika*.
If it is less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding "returning what was entrusted":
if a bhikṣu receives an object entrusted by another and, with a thieving mind, does not give it back to that person, and its value is five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika*.
If it is less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding "obstructing the road":
a bhikṣu obstructs the road for thieves so that other people are not permitted to come through.
The scout: one who waits in ambush to see a person and then goes to inform the bandits. The guide:
[one who indicates the location].
"A bhikṣu showing the way to a thief" refers to a bhikṣu acting as a guide for a thief, leading them along the path.
"Teaching to take" means teaching a thief the method for taking property.
"Taking together" means:
Regarding "taking goods with thieves and not paying taxes":
it refers to a bhikṣu who ought to pay taxes but does not pay them.
Regarding the taking of objects as described above, if the value is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is a *pārājika*;
if less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one takes the property of another person without it being given, and the value is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, for both bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, it is a *pārājika*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense; they are to be expelled.
Regarding taking what is not given from a non-human being: for a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, it is a sthūlātyaya offense;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
Taking the property of animals without it being given constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense in all cases.
There are four ways of taking another's heavy object that do not constitute an offense:
taking while perceiving it as one’s own, taking with the owner’s consent, taking for temporary use, and taking without the intent to steal.
The Five-Part Vinaya, Scroll One;
The Five-Part Vinaya, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kasmira during the Song Dynasty.
Translated together with Zhu Daosheng and others.

Part One, Section Three: When the Buddha was at Vaiśālī, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "By practicing the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), one attains great fruits and benefits."
Then all the bhikṣus immediately began their practice, entering deeply into a state of revulsion and feeling shame and remorse for this body.

It was as if a young man, fond of cleanliness, who had bathed, anointed his body, and put on fresh, clean clothes, were suddenly to have three corpses draped around his neck, with pus and blood pressing against him and worms crawling over his entire body.
That person is so tormented by suffering that they have no other thought but this:
"When shall I be freed from this disgrace?
In the same way, the bhikṣus loathe their bodies; some among them commit suicide, others harm one another, some seek out knives or ropes, and others consume poison.
There was a bhikṣu who, having become weary of his own body, went to where the caṇḍāla Mili was and said to him:
"Take my life for me; I shall give you my robes and bowl."
At that time, for the sake of the robe and bowl, the caṇḍāla immediately took a sharp blade and ended his life.
With the blade stained with blood, he carried it to the Pākmala River to wash it, whereupon he immediately gave rise to a mind of remorse and thought:
"I have now done what is unwholesome."
"How is it that for the sake of a small profit, one cuts off the life of a śramaṇa who upholds the precepts, thereby incurring immeasurable sin?

At that time, the Māra Pāpīyān, knowing his thoughts, came before him in the time it takes a strong man to extend or contract his arm; emerging from the water, he stood upon the surface and praised him, saying: "Excellent!"
"You have attained great benefit; by ending the life of this śramaṇa who clings to his precepts, you have delivered those not yet delivered, and your merit and blessings shall be immeasurable.
The celestial deities have recorded this, and therefore they have come to inform you."
At that time, the caṇḍāla conceived a wicked and heterodox view, and his heart was filled with great joy, thinking:
"I shall now further deliver those who have not yet been delivered.
That caṇḍāla was well-versed in discerning the signs of one who has grown weary of the body and one who has not yet grown weary of the body.

"If this ordinary bhikṣu has not yet abandoned desire, and his mind is filled with terror when I raise my sword toward him, it means he has not yet grown weary of his body; if I were to kill him, the merit I would obtain would be very slight."
"I shall now seek those who have already attained the fruit of the Way and are free from fear.
Thereupon, grasping a long sword in his hand, he went from room to room and from walkway to walkway, crying out in a loud voice:
"To those who wish for parinirvāṇa, I shall deliver them!"
At that time, those bhikṣus who were weary of the body all went out to him and immediately took his life.
Within a single day, they killed ten, twenty, and even up to sixty; because of these causes and conditions, the number of monks decreased, and the great virtuous śrāvakas no longer appeared.
At that time, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and sat in an open space, surrounded by a great assembly.
Surveying the community of monks, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
"For what reason has the assembly of monks diminished today?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha:

“World-Honored One, at one time you taught the contemplation of impurity to the bhikṣus. As the bhikṣus practiced it, they became weary of and loathed their own bodies and suffering, and they began to harm and kill one another. Even Mālinī, in a single day, injured sixty fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacarya). For this reason, the Saṃgha has diminished today.”
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We only pray that you will further explain other dharmas of the wholesome path, so that the bhikṣus may dwell in peace and happiness.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You must now issue a proclamation to all the bhikṣus residing in Vaiśālī, commanding them to assemble at the Mahāpariṣad Hall.
Ānanda received these instructions and immediately called for them to assemble.
When they had assembled, they said:
"Venerable Sir, you alone know the proper time.
The World-Honored One rose from his seat, went to the lecture hall, took his place upon the seat, and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it truly as you say? He replied, "It is indeed so."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked them in various ways:
“You are foolish! What you have done is contrary to the Dharma!”
"Have you not heard the compassion and patience I have taught for the sake of protecting and mindful of sentient beings?
Why then do you now fail to remember this Dharma?
Having thus rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one kills oneself, one incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
He further instructed:

"From this day forward, you should practice mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), take delight in the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), and take delight in the contemplation of joy (*muditā-bhāvanā*)."
Having observed this, he was able to eliminate the evil and unwholesome states that had arisen.
For ten reasons, he established a precept for the bhikṣus: from now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu kills a person with his own hand and takes its life, that bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in communion."
At that time, many bhikṣus were afflicted with serious illnesses. Some bhikṣus came to inquire after them, saying:
"Venerable sirs, has your illness lessened? Is the suffering bearable?"
The sick bhikṣu said, "My illness has not yet abated; the suffering is unbearable.
He then spoke to the other bhikṣus:
"Give me a knife, give me a rope, give me poison, give me food that increases illness, and lead me to the edge of a high precipice.
At that time, the bhikṣus all complied and gave them these things.
A sick bhikṣu might pierce himself with a blade, or hang himself with a rope, or take poison, or consume food that aggravates his illness, or throw himself from a high precipice to end his own life.
When the bhikṣus saw that he had died, they felt remorse and reported the matter to Ānanda.
Ānanda took them to the Buddha’s presence and informed the Buddha of what had occurred.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: [Yes].
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
“You foolish ones, what difference is there between taking one’s own life and giving a knife to someone so that they die?
From this day forward, this precept shall be stated as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu takes his own life or hands a knife to another, he commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.’”
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who fell gravely ill. When various bhikṣus came to inquire after him, he spoke to them as before:
“Give me a knife, a rope, or poison.”
The bhikṣus said, "The Buddha does not permit us to provide others with the means for suicide;
however, we have an acquaintance who is a hunter, whom we shall summon for you to end your life."
The sick bhikṣu said,
"Call for me quickly!
That bhikṣu ran and spoke to the hunter, saying:
“There is a bhikṣu here who has fallen gravely ill and no longer desires to live.
If you were to take his life for him, you would gain great merit. The hunter said:
"If killing living beings were to yield great merit, would butchers and slaughterers also obtain great merit?
You bhikṣus claim to possess a heart of compassion, yet now you teach others to kill."
"What difference is there between instructing another to kill and killing by one's own hand?
At that time, all the bhikṣus felt remorse and went to inform Ānanda.
Ānanda led them to the Buddha’s dwelling and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so? They replied: [Yes, it is true.]
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"What difference is there between committing suicide and inciting another to kill?
From this day forward, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu kills himself or incites another to kill, he commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in community.'"
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who fell gravely ill. The other bhikṣus visited him as described above and said to the sick man:
"Your conduct regarding the precepts is complete; you ought to receive celestial blessings. If you were to take your own life, you would surely be reborn in heaven."
