"What is the use of suffering thus for so long?
The sick bhikṣu replied, "Even if it were as you say,
though I have this suffering, I cannot take my own life."
Why is this? If one were to take one's own life, one would commit a sthūlātyaya offense;
furthermore, one would be unable to extensively cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya).
He rebuked him again, saying:
"What difference is there between killing a person with one’s own hands and inciting another to commit suicide?
Yet you, a bhikṣu, have committed such an evil deed!"
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they rebuked him in various ways and brought him to the Buddha’s presence to report the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked them:
“Is it true that you did so?”
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked them in various ways:
"You fools! What difference is there between killing a person with one's own hands and inciting another to commit suicide?
From this day forward, this precept should be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu kills a person with his own hand, or instructs another to commit suicide, he commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in community.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who fell gravely ill; the other bhikṣus visited him as described above and also said to the sick man:
"Your holy life has been established; upon death, you will enjoy celestial bliss."
"Why endure such suffering from illness for so long without taking one's own life?
The sick bhikṣus replied,
"Although we are in this state, we cannot take our own lives."
Why is this? Because the Buddha has prohibited suicide, which constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense;
furthermore, once my illness has been cured, I shall be able to cultivate the holy life.
At that time, there was also a threat of bandits in that country, causing the separation of flesh and bone among the laypeople and bringing them manifold suffering and affliction.
A bhikṣu said to them:
"You have already cultivated the meritorious karma for rebirth in heaven; why do you undergo this sorrow and grief of being separated from your own kin, rather than committing suicide?"
He replied, "Although I am filled with grief and sorrow, I cannot take my own life. Why is this?"
"Having encountered suffering while in the world, one knows how to cultivate the path and its practices.
He further rebuked him, saying,
"The way of the śramaṇa is to practice compassion and patience toward all sentient beings."
"Why do you praise death, desiring people to commit suicide?
What difference is there between committing suicide oneself and praising death?
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked him in various ways and led him to the Buddha's presence to report the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: [Yes].
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"What you have done is contrary to the Dharma; what difference is there between taking one's own life and praising death?
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

'If a bhikṣu, whether regarding a human being or one resembling a human being, kills them himself, or provides a weapon or poison to kill them, or instructs another to kill them, or instructs them to commit suicide, or praises death and extols death:'"
"Alas! What is the use of living a life of evil?
Death is better than life."
Having formed such a thought, he kills according to that intention;
through various causes and conditions such as these, the other dies because of him. This bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and is no longer to live in community.
After entering the mother’s womb until the forty-ninth day, it is called "resembling a human.
After this period has passed, it is entirely called a "human.
To kill by means of one's own hands, feet, knives, staves, poisons, and so forth, is called "killing by oneself."
If one seeks to commit suicide and provides the means for it, this is called "killing by providing weapons or poison.
If one causes another person to kill, this is called "inciting others to kill.
If one instructs another to seek death, this is called "inciting suicide."
To say that death is superior to life is to praise death and extol death.
To dispatch various spirits and deities to kill according to one's own mind is called "forming such a thought" and "killing according to the mind."

Regarding the offenses herein: killing by one's own hand; sending an emissary; sending through a series of intermediaries; sending a messenger with further instructions; indicating by gesture; speaking aloud; speaking while asleep; speaking toward one who is asleep; speaking while intoxicated; speaking toward one who is intoxicated; speaking while insane; speaking toward one who is insane; speaking while mentally deranged; speaking toward one who is mentally deranged; speaking while afflicted by illness; speaking toward one who is afflicted by illness; sending a letter; making signs; using hand gestures; using ambiguous speech;
being alone and perceiving oneself as alone; not being alone but perceiving oneself as alone; being alone and perceiving oneself as not alone.
Idle talk; forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles; *upādāna*, *upāsā*, and *upaghāta*.
As for killing by oneself:
killing with one's own hands, feet, knives, staves, and so forth.
If that person dies, it is a *pārājika* offense.
"Sending a messenger" means sending a messenger to kill that person.
If that person dies, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding the indirect messenger:
having dispatched "A" to kill, if "A" does not kill him personally but instead dispatches "B" to kill him; [the same applies].
If the person dies, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding "sending again":
the messenger first received the order but was unable to kill; he returned to report to the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu sent another messenger to kill him.
If [the person] dies, it is a *pārājika*. As for "indicating":
it means indicating the sun, moon, or constellations, and saying to another person:
"You possess the merit to be reborn there; you may take your own life.
If, as a result of these words, the person dies, it is a *pārājika* offense. Regarding "speaking": [this refers to the aforementioned statement].
To speak of the evils of birth and to praise the excellence of death;
if one dies as a result of this, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
This applies even if spoken while asleep.
While asleep, the bhikṣu spoke the words he had previously been thinking:
"Your merit is now complete; you ought to take your own life.
Having heard this, the man waited for him to wake and asked:
"Why do you say this? He replied, "While I was asleep, I spoke these words to you for the sake of benefiting you."
If, having now become aware [of this], he also speaks these words,
saying, "You may die according to my word," and the other dies because of this, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding "speaking to one who is sleeping":
it refers to addressing a person who is asleep with these words:
"Your merit has been perfected; you may take your own life with a blade or similar means."
A spirit caused him to hear this while he was asleep; upon waking, he asked, "Why did you say that? He replied:
"When you were asleep, I spoke these words for the sake of benefiting you;
now that you have awakened, I speak them again.
You should die according to my words."
If one dies as a result of this, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding "speaking while intoxicated":
it refers to speaking words previously intended while in a state of intoxication.
"Your merit has been fulfilled; you ought to take your own life with a blade or similar means.
Having heard this, the man waited until he had regained consciousness and asked, "Why did you say such a thing?"
He replied, "When I was intoxicated, I spoke these words for the sake of benefiting you;
now that I am sober, I likewise speak these words."
"You may die according to my words.
If one dies because of this, it is a *pārājika*.
As for speaking to one who is intoxicated:
He spoke these words:
"Your merit has been perfected; you may take your own life with a blade or similar means.
Once the intoxication had subsided, he asked:
"Why do you say this? He replied,
"It is because I wish to benefit you that you spoke these words while intoxicated."
"If you are now awake, speak likewise.
You may die according to my words.
If one dies because of this, it is a *pārājika* offense.

The same applies to speaking when one is insane, speaking to one who is insane, speaking with a deranged mind, speaking to one with a deranged mind, speaking with a mind impaired by illness, and speaking to one whose mind is impaired by illness.
Regarding the one who dispatches a letter:
if a bhikṣu dispatches a letter ordering a killing,
for every word written in that letter, it is a sthūlātyaya.
When the letter reaches that person, they kill him because of it;
for the one who dies, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding "making a sign":
A bhikṣu says to a person:
"Watch my sitting and rising, my raising and lowering of my hands, and when I speak of cold or heat; then you shall kill him.
Seeing these signs, he kills him.
If the person dies, it is a *pārājika* offense.
"Hand gestures" means:
making hand gestures to instruct another to kill, and that person kills accordingly.
If the person dies, it is a *pārājika*.
Regarding "similar speech":
if a bhikṣu uses similar speech to instruct another to kill, and that person kills accordingly;
If the person has died, it is a *pārājika*.
If one is alone and perceives oneself as alone, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if one is not alone but perceives oneself as alone, or if one is alone but does not perceive oneself as alone, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding "jesting speech":
a bhikṣu speaks with joking laughter, saying, "Your merit is already accomplished; you ought to commit suicide."
That person asked, "For what reason do you say this?
The bhikṣu replied:
"Although what I said previously was merely in jest, my present intention is indeed so;
you may take your own life.
If she dies because of this, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding "form" (rūpa):
if a bhikṣu performs incantations to summon malevolent spirits of hideous form and causes them to terrify people,
and someone dies as a result of this, it is a pārājika offense.
Regarding "words": if a bhikṣu speaks thus:
"Your parents, children, and grandchildren have already died; your wealth and property have been scattered and lost."
Having spoken these words, he intended to cause [the other] distress so that they would commit suicide;
if they die as a result of this, it is a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding "incense": it refers to mixing various perfumes with poison such that the person dies from inhaling them.
If one dies as a result of this, it is a *pārājika* offense.
As for "poisoning": it means placing poison in food to cause someone to eat it.
If one dies because of this, it is a *pārājika* offense.
"Touching" refers to killing by smearing the body with *kāviṣa* poison.
If one dies as a result of this, it is a *pārājika*.
Regarding "a pitfall" (*upakrama*):
to set a trap for all sentient beings so that if a person falls into it and dies, it is a *pārājika*.
If a non-human dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if an animal dies, it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the term "upāsaka":
If one constructs a weak bed with a thin covering over it and places a lethal device beneath it,
causing a person to sit upon it and die as a result, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding "indirect killing" (*upaghāta*):
If one kills by means of a *gū* (poisonous charm),
and a person dies as a result of this, it is a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣu forms this thought:
When one gives rise to the thought, "I shall kill that person," it is a *duṣkṛta*;
when one employs the preparatory means, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If [the victim] dies, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one kills a non-human being, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one kills an animal, it is a *pāyattika*.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense. There is no offense in the following cases:
The third matter concerning the mind of loving-kindness and the absence of intent to kill is concluded.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī.
It was a season of famine, and alms were difficult to obtain; when the bhikṣus entered the city to beg for food, they received nothing at all.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Each of you should go to dwell in retreat according to your acquaintances.
Do not remain here and suffer the hardships of famine."
The bhikṣus received the instruction; some went to the kingdom of Magadha, while others went to the village on the banks of the Bhagīrathī River.
The bhikṣus who had gone to the riverbanks gathered together and deliberated, saying:
"Now it is difficult to obtain almsfood. There are those in this village who have faith and devotion; we should praise one another in turn, saying:"
“Such-and-such a person has attained the first dhyāna, and I too have attained it;
such-and-such a person has attained the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless attainments, and I am likewise;
such-and-such a person has attained the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path and the three gates of liberation, and I am likewise.”
"Such-and-such has attained the eight liberations, the nine successive attainments, the ten totalities, and the ten paths of right action; I am likewise so.
Such-and-such has attained firm faith, firm Dharma, the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, and the three knowledges and six supernormal powers; I am likewise so."
When the laypeople hear this, they will surely give rise to a sense of rare wonder and say:
"We have gained a great benefit, for such noble sages who have attained the Way are now dwelling in our village."
"You should then prepare various delicacies to offer us; we shall have no lack and dwell in peace and happiness.
Having deliberated thus, they immediately entered the city and went to the households of the wealthy, praising them as described above, saying:
"You have gained great benefit, for the Noble Assembly, a field of merit, relies upon your village."
When the laypeople heard this, they were struck with wonder and marveled that such a thing had never before been encountered.
They all reduced their own portions, ceased making sacrificial offerings, and stopped giving to others, diverting it instead to provide for [the monks].
It is the constant custom of the Buddhas to hold two great assemblies during the final months of spring and summer, when monks from all quarters come to pay their respects.
When the monks of the Magadha country had finished their rains retreat, they approached the Buddha—emaciated and haggard—and having prostrated at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas to offer greetings to visiting bhikṣus, asking:
"Was your rainy-season retreat harmonious? Was alms-food easy to obtain? And were you not fatigued by the journey?"
The bhikṣus said, “We have completed the rains retreat in harmony; we were not fatigued by the journey, but almsfood was difficult to obtain.
Then the Buddha taught them various sublime dharmas, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening them, before allowing them to remain wherever they wished to dwell.
The bhikṣus from the Pāṅkavatī River, their bodies refreshed and joyful, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha likewise comforted them as before, and the bhikṣus said to him:
“We have spent the rainy season retreat in harmony; alms were easily obtained, and we were not fatigued on the road.”
The Buddha then asked:
"In this present age of famine, it is difficult to obtain alms through begging.
Why do you alone say it is easy?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“While we were there, because almsfood was difficult to obtain, we praised one another.
They related everything as described above.
The Buddha then asked,
"Is your praise true or false? The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
“There is truth and there is falsehood.
The Buddha rebuked those who were false in various ways:
“Your conduct is contrary to the Dharma and does not accord with the Path; this is what those who have left the household life ought not to do!”
"I would rather eat burning stones or swallow molten copper than, out of falsehood, consume the faithful offerings of others.
Have you not heard how I have condemned the sin of lying and praised in various ways the virtue of not lying?"
"Now, how can you, for the sake of gain and offerings, speak falsely and claim to have attained superhuman states?
He further rebuked them, saying: "O Bhikṣus!"
In the world there are five great thieves:
first, those who act as leaders of a hundred or even a thousand men, destroying cities and villages, harming people, and seizing their property;
second, wicked bhikṣus who travel through the human world with other bhikṣus, preaching the Dharma for the sake of a wrong livelihood.
Third, there are wicked bhikṣus who, regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, claim it was composed by themselves;
fourth, there are wicked bhikṣus who do not cultivate the holy life, yet say, "I cultivate the holy life";
fifth, there are wicked bhikṣus who, for the sake of gain and offerings, falsely claim to have attained superhuman states that they actually lack.
This fifth thief is named the greatest thief among all those in the world—gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas.
"How can you, for the sake of such trifling gain, act as the greatest thieves?
Having thus rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, not knowing and not seeing the superhuman states, the noble benefits, and the fulfillment, claims of himself: 'I know thus; I see thus.'"
At a later time, whether questioned or not, for the sake of purifying oneself from the offense, one says:
"I spoke what I did not know as if I knew it, and saw what I did not see as if I had seen it; this was a false and deceptive lie."
"Such a bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in communion.

While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī, there were many bhikṣus of little learning who, without studying or inquiring, lacked any superhuman qualities (uttarimanussadhamma) yet claimed: "I know, I see, I have realized."
At a later time, hearing the bhikṣus discuss the characteristics of those who have attained the Way and those who have not, he realized that what he had followed was not the true Way.
A sense of shame and remorse arose within him, and he thought:
"Previously, before we had attained it, we claimed to have attained it; could we not have committed a pārājika offense?"
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu of little learning who neither studies nor inquires; lacking any superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussadhamma*), he claims, "I know, I see, I have realized."
At a later time, he studied the various sutras extensively and gave rise to a sense of shame and remorse, thinking to himself:

"According to my current understanding of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, my previous claim that I had attained what I had not attained was an overweening pride; could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?"
Furthermore, there are some bhikṣus of little learning who do not study nor inquire; lacking any superhuman qualities, they nevertheless claim: "I know, I see, I have realized."
At a later time, he extensively practiced the holy life and attained the fruits of the Path;
feeling shame and remorse, he thought:
"Previously, when I had not yet attained it, I claimed to have attained it—this was overweening pride. Could it be that I have committed a pārājika offense?"
After the bhikṣus had reflected thus, they each went to Ānanda and questioned him about these matters.
Ānanda led them to the place where the Buddha was and reported everything to the Buddha in detail.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned them individually regarding their respective cases:
"Is it truly so? He replied, "It is truly so."
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are five kinds of manifest superhuman states (uttari-manussa-dhamma):"
First, ignorance; second, a distracted mind;
third, following evil.
Fourth, overweening pride;
fifth, actual existence.

If one who is ignorant, deranged, overweeningly proud, or actually possessing [the attainment] were to say of themselves, "I have attained it," and yet commit a *pārājika* offense, such a thing is impossible.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, without knowing or seeing the superhuman state (uttarimanussa-dhamma), the noble benefit and fulfillment, should claim of himself: 'I know thus; I see thus.'"
At a later time, whether questioned or not, that bhikṣu, in order to emerge from his offense and seek purification, speaks thus:
"I spoke what I did not know as if I knew it; I spoke what I had not seen as if I saw it; it was a false and deceptive lie."
"Excepting one who acts out of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), this bhikṣu has committed a *pārājika* offense and shall not live in communion.
"Not knowing and not seeing" means:
not knowing and not seeing superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*).

All dharmas that lead to transcendence—namely, the various dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and meditative attainments, as well as the fruits of the noble paths—are called "dharmas surpassing the human."

Regarding the Buddha’s teaching on suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, one has already accomplished and fulfilled them, having nothing further to seek; this is called the fulfillment of noble benefit.
One declares of oneself:
"I know and see the Dharma in this way, and the Dharma also knows and sees me"; this is called claiming for oneself: "I know thus, I see thus."
If, after one month or even up to one year, one asks:
"How did you obtain it? Where did you obtain it?"
"From whom did you receive it?
By what dharma did you receive it?
If one does not ask this, but instead voluntarily discloses the offense committed, seeking purity of precept, purity of mind, purity of view, and purity from doubt, saying:
"I did not know and did not see the noble truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; yet I claimed to know and to see them—this was a false and deceptive lie.
Even though one confesses in this manner, one still incurs a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding the offenses herein,
there are two ways one incurs a *pārājika*:
first, by previously forming this thought:
First, "I shall falsely claim to have attained superhuman states.
Second, at the time of speaking, one thinks:
"I am now falsely claiming to have attained superhuman states."
Furthermore, there are three ways of incurring a *pārājika* offense:
two are as described above;
the third is when one forms this thought:
"I have falsely claimed to have attained superhuman states.
Furthermore, there are four ways of incurring a *pārājika* offense;
three are as described above.
Fourth, falsely claiming to have attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) through heterodox views.
Furthermore, there are five ways one incurs a *pārājika* offense:
four are as described above; [the fifth is]...
Fifth, to speak of having attained superhuman states with a false intention.
Furthermore, there are six ways of incurring a *pārājika* offense:
five are as described above; [the sixth is]...
Sixth, falsely claiming to have attained superhuman states through a different kind of patience.
Furthermore, there are seven ways of incurring a *pārājika* offense:
six are as described above; [the seventh is]...
Seventh, to falsely claim to have attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) out of a desire for gain.
Furthermore, there are eight grounds for committing a *pārājika* offense:
seven are as described above; [the eighth is as follows:]...
Eighth, not answering questions by speaking of superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
There are four kinds of non-noble speech and four kinds of noble speech.
As for non-noble speech:

To say one has seen when one has not seen, to say one has heard when one has not heard, to say one has sensed when one has not sensed, and to say one knows when one does not know— this is called un-noble speech. Noble speech, however,
is to say one has seen when one has seen, to say one has heard when one has heard, to say one has sensed when one has sensed, and to say one knows when one knows.
Furthermore, there are eight kinds of non-noble speech and eight kinds of noble speech.

As for non-noble speech: to say one has seen what one has not seen; to say one has not seen what one has seen; to say one has heard what one has not heard; to say one has not heard what one has heard; to say one has cognized what one has not cognized; to say one has not cognized what one has cognized; to say one has known what one has not known; and to say one has not known what one has known.
The opposites of the above are called the eight noble modes of speech (*ārya-vāk*).
Furthermore, there are sixteen non-noble modes of speech and sixteen noble modes of speech.
As for the non-noble modes of speech:

To say one has seen when one has not seen; to say one has heard when one has not heard; to say one has sensed when one has not sensed; to say one has known when one has not known; to say one has not seen when one has seen; to say one has not heard when one has heard; to say one has not sensed when one has sensed; to say one has not known when one has known; to say there is doubt regarding what one has seen when there is no doubt; to say there is doubt regarding what one has heard when there is no doubt; to say there is doubt regarding what one has sensed when there is no doubt; to say there is doubt regarding what one has known when there is no doubt; to say there is no doubt regarding what one has seen when there is doubt; to say there is no doubt regarding what one has heard when there is doubt; to say there is no doubt regarding what one has sensed when there is doubt;
to say there is no doubt regarding what one has known when there is doubt—the opposites of these are called the sixteen noble utterances (*ārya-vāk*).
If a bhikṣu claims to one person that he has attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), it is a *pārājika* offense if the listener understands;
it is a *thullaccaya* offense if the listener does not understand.
To speak thus to a non-human being is a *thullaccaya* offense.
To speak thus to an animal is a *duṣkṛta*.
It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Non-offenses: This concludes the fourth precept on truthful speech.
2. Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas. The First Part of the Five-Part Vinaya, Section Two: Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Udāyin was consumed by the fire of desire; his body was so emaciated that he had barely any breath remaining.
By discharging impurity with his hand, he attained a state of ease and dwelt in comfort.
There was another bhikṣu who was likewise emaciated.
Udāyin asked him,
"For what reason are you like this?"
He replied, "Elder!
I am being consumed by the fire of desire; that is why I am thus."
Udāyin said: "I was also like this before;
by discharging impurity with my hand, I attained a state of ease and well-being.
If you would follow my example, you too should do so."
That bhikṣu said: "What you have done is contrary to the Dharma, not a pure practice; it violates the law of the śramaṇas and does not accord with the Path!
The World-Honored One has in various ways rebuked desire, the perception of desire, thoughts of desire, and the fever of desire."
One must sever the perception of desire, eliminate thoughts of desire, and extinguish the fever of desire;
one should speak of desire as being like a skeleton or like poison.
How can you now, with these hands that have produced impurity, receive the offerings of the faithful and furthermore teach others to do so?
Having rebuked him, he brought him to the Buddha's presence and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Udāyin:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied: "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!"
After the Buddha had likewise rebuked him in various ways as described above, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu intentionally emits semen, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.'"
At that time, some bhikṣus were not one-pointed in mind; they emitted impurity in their dreams, and upon waking, they thought:
"In my dream, there was also a mind, and I also moved my body, resulting in the emission of impurity."
"Could it be that I have committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?
Some confessed their transgressions, some practiced *mānatva*, some underwent the purification of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna*), and some went directly before the Buddha to report the matter.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so? They replied: [Yes, it is true.]
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"You should not sleep with a distracted mind; if you sleep with a distracted mind, you commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There are five faults in sleeping with a distracted mind:
first, having bad dreams;"
Second, they are not protected by benevolent deities;
third, they do not attain clear perception;
fourth, they lack a mind that awakens to the Dharma.
Fifth, the non-emission of impurity.
Sleeping with an undistracted mind possesses five virtues:
one has no evil dreams, is protected by benevolent deities, attains clear perception, maintains a mind mindful of the Dharma, and does not emit impurity.
There are five causes and conditions by which the body arises [in dreams] while one is sleeping:
first, the abundance of feces;
second, the abundance of urine; [and so forth].
Third, the predominance of wind;
fourth, being bitten by insects;
fifth, the predominance of desire.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one has not yet abandoned desire, hatred, and delusion, and falls asleep with a distracted mind, one will inevitably discharge impurity;
however, even if one has not yet abandoned them, there is no such fault if one sleeps with a mind focused on mindfulness."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu intentionally emits semen, except during a dream, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
"Intentionally emitting semen" means:
To "arouse the mind" and move the body so as to emit impurity constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
This offense has a remainder; it still possesses the conditions for treatment and has recourse, such that one may remain within the Saṃgha to seek its purification.
There are ten kinds of impurity:
first, the blueish color;
second, the yellowish color;
Third, red; fourth, black; fifth, crimson.
Sixth, the color of white;
seventh, the color of milk;
eighth, the color of clarified butter;
Ninth, the color of oil;
tenth, the color of honey.

If one resolves [to emit semen], moves the body, and intends to emit it in a greenish-blue color, yet yellow or even honey-colored fluid is emitted, in all such cases it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If one forms the intention and moves the body with the desire to emit yellow or even honey-colored [semen], yet another color is emitted, it is likewise.
There are ten types of instances where one forms the intention, moves the body, and emits impurity, all of which constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense:
first, testing oneself;...
Second, to eliminate illness;
third, for the sake of complexion;
fourth, for the sake of strength.
Fifth, for the sake of pleasure;
sixth, for the sake of giving;
seventh, for the sake of rebirth in heaven.
Eighth, for the sake of non-Buddhist (tīrthika) sacrifices to the gods;
ninth, for the sake of seeds;
tenth, for the sake of fire sacrifices.
There are five types of intentional emission of semen through physical movement that constitute *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses:
[emission caused by] internal form, external form, space, wind, and water.
Internal form refers to one's own body;
external form refers to the bodies of others;
space refers to moving the body within open space.
Regarding "wind," it means moving against the wind.
Regarding "water," it means moving against the current.
Furthermore, there are five types of intentional emission involving bodily movement that constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense: [the emission of semen].
If there is an abundance of feces, an abundance of urine, an excess of wind, the biting of worms, or an excess of desire;
if one arouses the intention but the body does not move and no impurity is discharged;
or if one arouses the intention and the body does not move yet impurity is discharged—in all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one has the intention, moves the body, but does not emit impurity, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one does not have the intention, moves the body, but does not emit impurity;
or if one does not have the intention, moves the body, and emits impurity.
If one does not give rise to the thought, the body does not move, and the impurity is emitted, there is no offense in any case.
If the impurity is emitted while asleep, but the thought arises and the body moves upon waking, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if the body moves while asleep, but the thought arises and the impurity is emitted upon waking, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one arouses the intention while asleep, but the body does not move upon waking and no impurity is emitted, there is no offense.
For a śrāmaṇera, this constitutes a duṣkṛta. The first precept is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Udāyin, consumed by the fire of desire, thought to himself:
"The Blessed One has already prohibited the intentional emission of semen; now I shall employ a skillful means to touch a woman and experience the pleasure of her smoothness."
He then swept and sprinkled the interior of the room, prepared fine bedding and seats, and took a small stool to sit upon in the open air.
Several women came along to visit and look around, and they said to Udāyin:
"We have come specifically wishing to see the quarters."
He replied, "Sisters! Look at it as you please."

He then led her into the room, closed the door, and opened the window; he touched her in various ways—sometimes grasping her, sometimes embracing her, sometimes pressing her, sometimes rubbing her, sometimes lifting her up, sometimes lowering her, sometimes mounting her, and sometimes leaping over her.
Among them, those who were joyful spoke to him, saying:
"Why do you not simply practice [the path] correctly?
What is the use of doing this? Udāyin replied:
"The Buddha does not permit me to perform my fundamental duties.
Those who were displeased spoke with anger:
"We originally thought this place was peaceful, but now it has instead become a land of terror; fire burning within water is not even an adequate metaphor for this."
"Even laypeople in white robes feel shame over such matters; how can a bhikṣu commit such an evil deed?
She then returned to her home and proclaimed these words to everyone.
Those who did not have faith in or delight in the Buddha-dharma reviled him in various ways, saying:
"We laypeople touch the bodies of women, and these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do the same."
"To merely shave this head, how is it different from me?
You lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have violated the dharma of a śramaṇa!
Thus, his ill repute spread throughout the world.
Furthermore, there was a brahmin who, accompanied by his wife, went sightseeing and arrived at the room of Udāyin, saying:
"I wish to view the quarters together with my wife."
Udāyin said, "They cannot enter at the same time; they may enter one after the other. The brāhmaṇa said:
"If they cannot enter together, it is permitted for the wife to enter first.
Once the wife had entered the room, Udāyin again, as before, touched her in various ways, remaining there for a long time before finally departing.
The husband said to his wife, "Why have you been so long? Do you no longer wish to see the other rooms?
The wife replied:
"Stop, stop! Do not speak such words.
You merely entered a single room and, though on the verge of death, have escaped."
"Why should one go on looking at other dwellings?
When the husband asked for the reason, the wife answered him in full detail.
At that time, the brahmin immediately spoke in reproach:
"How can these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, commit such an evil deed?
Entering the city of Śrāvastī, he cried out at every crossroads, street, lane, and marketplace:
"The śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, have touched my wife!"
Those who did not believe in the Buddha’s Dharma reviled him in various ways, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, commit such evil deeds; how can they claim to be pure cultivators of the brahma-faring?"
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they censured him in various ways and reported the matter in full to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Udāyin:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied: “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, with a mind agitated by lust, makes physical contact with the body of a woman.'"

"If one takes hold of the hand, or takes hold of the hair, or takes hold of any individual part of the body, and rubs or touches it against something smooth and slippery, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
"One whose mind is transformed by the intensity of desire" means:
toward the mind of desire, having deeply aroused the intention, the act is nearly completed.
It transforms wholesome and neutral dharmas so that they fall into the realm of the unwholesome.
"Woman" refers to a human female,
from the time of birth onwards.
"Touching" means:
various kinds of physical contact with any part of the body, even as much as a single hair.
If a bhikṣu touches a woman in five ways, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Regarding a woman, with the perception of a woman, a human woman, a living woman, and with a defiled mind, if one touches her with intimate intent and experiences it consciously—
even down to touching a single hair— it is likewise [an offense].
There are five factors that constitute the offense of *sthūlātyaya* for touching a woman:

[the object must be] a woman, the perception of her as a woman, she must be a human female, she must be alive, and there must be a defiled mind; furthermore, it must not be done out of affectionate intimacy, but rather with conscious intent, and one must experience the sensation.
This applies even down to the touching of her hair.
It is the same when a woman touches a bhikṣu. There are five circumstances under which touching a woman does not constitute an offense:
[the person is] a woman, one perceives her as a woman, she is a human female, she is a living female, and one’s mind is free from lustful intent; it is not done out of a sense of intimacy.
If a woman grasps a bhikṣu and the bhikṣu employs skillful means to seek release, although he perceives the contact, he does not experience it.
This applies even when she touches his hair; it is the same.

Furthermore, if there is a woman, and one perceives her as a woman, or is doubtful about her being a woman, or perceives her as lacking sexual organs, or perceives her as having both sets of sexual organs, and then makes physical contact, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If there is a woman, and one perceives her as a man, or perceives her as a female hermaphrodite (*paṇḍaka*), and then makes physical contact, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (*thullaccaya*).
If it is a man, and one perceives him as a man, suspects him to be a man, or perceives him as a eunuch, and makes physical contact, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

If it is a man, and one perceives him as a woman, perceives him as being without sexual organs, or perceives him as having two sexual organs, and makes physical contact, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
The same applies to eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*).

If there is no root [organ], and one perceives it as having no root, suspects it has no root, perceives it as having two roots when it has no root, or perceives it as female when it has no root, and makes physical contact, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one perceives it as male when it has no root, or perceives it as a eunuch when it has no root, and makes physical contact, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
The same applies to both genders.
If a bhikṣu makes physical contact with a naked woman, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa;
if he makes physical contact with a clothed woman, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If a woman takes hold of a monk who is naked, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if she takes hold of a monk who is clothed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a monk and a woman both have clothes on and they touch one another, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu takes hold of a woman’s garment and the woman relinquishes the garment to the bhikṣu, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If a woman takes hold of a bhikṣu’s garment and the bhikṣu does not relinquish the garment to the woman, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣu touches the corpse of a human female or a non-human female, it is a sthūlātyaya;
if he touches the female of an animal, it is a duṣkṛta.
For a śrāmaṇera, it is likewise a duṣkṛta.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Udāyin was consumed by the fire of desire and thought to himself:
"The Blessed One has already prohibited the intentional emission of semen and touching the body of a woman. [What shall I do?]"
"Now I shall employ another expedient: I will address the women with coarse and vulgar speech to gratify their sensual desires.
He then swept and sprinkled the room and sat upon the open ground. When the women came to look at him, he led them inside and closed the door; everything occurred as previously described.
He then engaged in various kinds of coarse and vulgar speech with the woman inside the room, asking her such questions as:
"What are your hands, feet, thighs, upper arms, waist, belly, neck, breasts, head, face, nails, hair, and the organs for excrement and urine like?"
He spoke again:
"Sister! Your hands, feet, and even your private parts are foul."
He spoke again:
"Sister! Your hands, feet, and even your private parts are beautiful."
He asked again:
"When your husband was near you, what did he do?
He then instructed her further:
"If you comply with my wishes, I shall give you precious treasures.
He further entreated him, saying:
"Serve me; all the celestial deities bear witness to my heart."
When the women heard this, some were pleased and others were not, as described above.
When the elder bhikṣus heard of it, they censured her in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Udāyin:
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, with a mind agitated by lust, addresses a woman with coarse and wicked words, speaking according to the ways of sexual desire, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.'"
Regarding the offenses therein:
disparaging, praising, begging, making a vow, questioning, counter-questioning, and instructing.
There are five matters in which a bhikṣu engages in coarse and evil speech with a woman:

Regarding a woman, with the perception of her being a woman, a human woman, a living woman, and with a defiled mind, if through intimacy—from flattery or disparagement up to instruction—one understands her meaning, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if one does not understand her meaning, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
To disparage means to criticize a woman’s three places, whether they are small or large, or if their color and shape are unattractive.
To praise means:
Praising a woman for having three parts that are neither too small nor too large, and are well-formed in shape and color.
To beg from a woman means to solicit her regarding these three parts.
"If you can grant these to me, I shall comply with your wishes. The petitioner said:
"I pray that I may obtain three things from you; to obtain these three things from you would be a person of merit and happiness."
The questioner asked:
"In how many of the three ways does your husband engage in sexual desire?"
"When will it be made?
This is the counter-question. "Question: [This indicates the start of the inquiry.]
"Did your husband not act in this way regarding the three points?
The instructor says: "Instructor, speak thus:"
“If you comply with the man’s wishes in three respects, you will be respected and loved by him.
The case of a woman perceiving a woman, and so forth, up to the case of two sexual organs and the perception of two sexual organs, is all as explained above.
Furthermore, there are five types:
sending a messenger, writing a letter, making gestures, hand movements, and speaking in a disguised manner.
If the recipient understands [the intent], it is a sthūlātyaya.
If she does not understand, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu speaks coarse and wicked words to a human woman face-to-face, if she understands, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if she does not understand, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
To speak harsh words to a non-human female constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*;
to speak harsh words to a female animal constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *śrāmaṇera*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The three precepts are concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Udāyin was consumed by the fire of desire and thought to himself:
"The Buddha has already prohibited the intentional emission of semen, the touching of a woman’s body, and speaking coarse or wicked words to women."
"I shall now offer my own body to this woman in self-praise as an act of worship, so that she may find pleasure and satisfaction.
He then swept and sprinkled the room in various ways as described above,
and spoke to the woman within the room, saying:

"Sisters! Your making offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, even to the point of entering meditative concentration and attaining the fruits of the four paths, is not equal to making an offering of sexual desire to one who upholds the precepts."
When the women heard this, some were pleased and others were not. The Buddha then rebuked them in various ways, as described above.
Having rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, his mind transformed by the intensity of lust, should offer himself for the sake of sexual gratification to a woman, saying: 'Sister!
Sexual gratification is the foremost offering.'"
"Saṃghāvaśeṣa. If one utters various words praising [the recipient] with the intent of making offerings to their person, for each word it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if one says:
"It would be better to offer sexual desire as an act of worship.
For every such utterance, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if he says:
“Sexual gratification as an offering is the foremost offering.
This constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
One praises oneself through five matters as an offering of one’s person:
Regarding a woman, perceiving her as a woman, a human woman, a living woman, and being moved by defiled thoughts, one approaches her with affection and says:
"The offering of sexual desire is the foremost offering."
If she understands, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if she does not understand, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Whether it be a woman perceived as a woman, or even one with two sexual organs perceived as such; whether by sending a messenger, or even by using indirect speech, or speaking face-to-face with a woman, or toward a non-human female or a female animal—in all these cases, it is as explained above.
The four precepts on the *śrāmaṇera*’s *duṣkṛta* offenses are concluded.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

There was a householder named Kāla, who was intelligent and of keen faculties, and skilled at resolving the doubts of others. Whatever the people of Śrāvastī had to do—even matters such as marriages—they would all consult him; if he said it should be done, they would do it.
If they do not give, he simply does not take.
When he obtains something excellent, he says:
"It is because of Kāliya that I have obtained this excellence; I shall cause Kāliya also to obtain such happiness."
Those who received the ill repute said,
"It is because of Kāliya that we have incurred this evil, and it is Kāliya who must also undergo such severe suffering.
In this way, both foul reputations and good fame filled the entire kingdom.

Later, Kāla left the household life out of faith; those who came to consult him increased day by day, until even King Prasenajit personally visited to inquire about matters of state, such that the sounds of joy and anger became twice as great as before.
At that time, there was a widow whose daughter’s beauty and appearance were foremost in the village. Many sought her hand in marriage, but she refused them all, replying:
"If you come to live in my household according to the manner of a son, then I shall give you [my daughter]."
At that time, there was a brahmin of immeasurable wealth who said to the widow:
"If you give your daughter in marriage to my son, she shall enjoy long-lasting peace and happiness."
The reply was the same as before.
Thereupon, the brahmin went among the people to inquire who frequented this man's household.
Someone said to him:
"The śramaṇa Kātyāyana is well-acquainted with this family.
He immediately invited Kātyāyana to provide long-term support for them; once they had become familiar with one another, he presented his request:
"I wish to seek a certain girl as a wife for my son. I pray that you, Great Virtue, would deign to speak on my behalf."
Kātyāyana then put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went to that house. The widow came out, paid her respects, and inquired after his well-being.
Kātyāyana said to her, "You should give your daughter in marriage to such-and-such a man; his family is wealthy and prosperous, and she will surely find peace and happiness."
The answer was as before.
Kāḷudāyin spoke again:
"If you do not give her to me, when this girl grows up, she will surely desert you."
"What is the point of losing your daughter and further parting from such a fine son-in-law?
Upon hearing this, the widow reluctantly gave her consent.
Kāla returned to report this, and the marriage was immediately finalized.
Thereafter, her husband’s family treated her with great severity, so she sent a messenger to inform her mother:
"I pray you will speak to my husband's family so that I may find a little leisure and happiness.
Her mother replied to her daughter, saying:
“Suka will arrive; you must speak to him.
Later, Suka went to the widow’s house, where the widow detailed her daughter’s hardships, saying:
“Our marriage was originally arranged between our families; I pray that you will speak to him on my behalf.”
Kātyāyana replied: "This woman lacks merit, which has brought her such intense suffering.
If she possessed merit, for what reason would she have come to this state?"
"It is not the way of our śramaṇa dharma to concern ourselves with such worldly affairs of others.
The widow rebuked him, saying, "Previously you were well-acquainted with people's business; now you say it is improper."
"Such an evil person will surely bring misfortune!
Thus he uttered various curses, his words bitter and cutting.
Hearing this, the neighbors all came to admonish him, saying:
"You, daughter, have meager merit, which has brought you such intense suffering.
Why involve yourself with the śramaṇas, that you should so bitterly curse and revile them? The widow replied:
"Do you not know that it is because of this śramaṇa that my young daughter has been brought to such extreme suffering?
At that time, those who did not have faith in the Buddha's Dharma all spoke thus:
"You believe in the śramaṇa, and so your daughter suffers this pain."
"If we were to follow their words, it would be even more severe than this.
He further rebuked them, saying:
"We laypeople practice the methods of matchmaking; the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do exactly the same."
"You merely shave this head and wear robes of dyed color!
Since your conduct is such as this, how are you any different from me?
Thereupon, his ill repute spread far and wide.
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they censured him in various ways and brought him to the Buddha’s presence to report the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Kāla:
“Is it true that you did so?”
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu acts as a go-between, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.’”
At that time, various prominent families in the city of Śrāvastī wished to have illicit relations with young maidens of marriageable age;
however, they were ashamed to express their intentions themselves and, finding no intermediaries, spoke to the group of six bhikṣus:
"You may convey this message for us."
"If you require these things, for how long—whether for one day, one night, or even for a single meeting—do you need them?
The group of six bhikṣus then went to the women and asked them about their intentions in full detail.
When people saw this, they all joined in criticizing him, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, purify themselves by practicing the Brahma-faring; how is it that they now commit such evil deeds?
To concoct such perverse and improper acts is something that laypeople would find shameful!"
"These śramaṇas have neither shame nor remorse!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked them in various ways, led them to the Buddha's presence, and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?
They replied: "It is true."
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

'If a bhikṣu acts as a go-between, whether for the purpose of illicit intercourse, taking the intention of a man to a woman or the intention of a woman to a man, even to the extent of a single act of sexual union, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.'"
There are ten kinds of women and ten kinds of men. As for the ten kinds of women:

those protected by their parents, those protected by their elder brothers or sisters, those protected by their relatives, those who protect themselves, those protected by the Dharma, those who have taken responsibility for themselves, those who are protected by their clothing and ornaments, those bound by a mutual agreement, those who have a husband, and those who have given a token of betrothal.
Regarding those protected by parents:
a woman who has parents; her parents can give her away or take her back.
It is the same for elder brothers, elder sisters, and relatives.
Self-protection means having mastery over one's body, such that one may give it away or take it back at will.
Protection by the Dharma means:
Having gone forth in the True Dharma, one practices the holy life.
"Taking charge for oneself" means acting according to one's own inclination.
"Robes" refers to receiving robes from another.
"Common vow" refers to:
Regarding the making of pacts with people,
those who have a master:
a woman belongs to her husband.
One who makes a pledge:
having received a small gift from another, one pledges for a period of one day, one month, or even until the next sexual encounter.
The same applies to the ten types of men.
If a bhikṣu receives a message from a man protected by his parents, it is a duṣkṛta;
if he speaks with a woman protected by her parents, or even with a female messenger (*śraddhā-dūtī*), it is a sthūlātyaya;
if she does not grant permission and he reports back [to the sender], it is a sthūlātyaya.
If he consents and sends back a reply, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If a bhikṣu, having received a message from a man protected by his parents, speaks to a woman protected by her parents, and the woman says:
"You may speak to my parents."
If a bhikṣu returns with this message, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If he causes the bhikṣu to speak to the parents of that girl who is protected by her parents, and they receive this message, it is a duṣkṛta.
If he speaks to the parents of that girl and they do not consent, and he returns with this report, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If she consents and returns a reply, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
It is likewise if one receives the words of a man protected by his parents and speaks them to a woman protected by her brothers, sisters, or relatives.

This applies even when one receives the words of a man acting as a messenger from a woman protected by her parents, or when one speaks to a woman protected by her parents, or even to a woman acting as a messenger;

it is the same for all such cases. If a bhikṣu receives the words of a woman protected by her parents, or even of a woman acting as a messenger, and speaks them to a man protected by his parents, or even to a man acting as a messenger, it is likewise the same.
There are six kinds of communication:
one’s own speech, sending a messenger, writing, sending a messenger with a message, similar speech, and signs.
If a bhikṣu receives a message in his own speech, delivers it in his own speech to the other person, and receives a reply in his own speech, it constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a message from someone and sends it to another person, then returns with a reply himself;
or if he receives a message from someone, delivers it to that person himself, and then has another person return with a reply;
or if he receives a message from someone, sends it to another person, and then has that person return with a reply—in all these cases, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If one receives a verbal message from a person and conveys it to another by means of signs,
and that person likewise returns the message by means of signs, it is the same. If a bhikṣu,
for the sake of a man or a woman, acts as a go-between even by receiving a message through signs, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If one acts as a matchmaker for a human male with respect to a non-human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one acts as a matchmaker for a human male with respect to an animal female, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
It is the same for one who acts as a matchmaker for a human female.
If one acts as a matchmaker for a non-human male with respect to a human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one acts as a matchmaker for an animal male with respect to a human female, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one acts as a go-between for a eunuch on behalf of a woman, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu acts as a go-between for a man on behalf of a woman, or for a woman on behalf of a man, to employ them for long-term labor, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense. There is no offense in the following cases:
The section on the Five Precepts for the sake of harmony is concluded.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

Then, the bhikṣus of the village of Aṭṭhapiṇḍika built dwellings by begging for them themselves; they requested carts from the laypeople, requested the price for carts, requested laborers, and requested wages for laborers; they likewise sought timber, wood, grass, and bamboo from them all.
The laypeople grew weary of this and all fled upon seeing them.
The bhikṣus were no longer able to obtain alms through begging, so they began to cut down grasses and trees themselves and dig up the earth.
There was a virtuous bhikṣu who cut down a sacred tree. A tree spirit, who used to play among the branches when it was a small child, had one of its fingers severed by the blow.
In its agony and distress, the spirit conceived an evil intent and intended to come and strike him;
however, it then thought again:
"This one of great majesty—if I were to strike him, he might even die, causing me to suffer various afflictions for a long night. He further thought:
"The World-Honored One is now in this city; I shall go and inform him, and whatever instructions the Buddha gives, I shall carry out."
He immediately went to the Jetavana and reported everything in detail to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the tree deity:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"What you have thought is virtuous!
This bhikṣu truly possesses majestic power; had you struck him, you would surely have received a painful retribution.
He then addressed the tree spirit again:
"There is a great tree in a certain place that belongs to no one; you may rely upon it.
Having received these instructions, he went there immediately.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One traveled by stages until he arrived at the town of Aṭṭhapiṇḍika.
In the early morning, the Elder Mahākāśyapa donned his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food; when the laypeople saw him, they all fled.
Mahākāśyapa, finding this strange, questioned the passersby.
The traveler replied,
"These bhikṣus are building dwellings and begging without satiety.
The people of the village are distressed by this, which is why they all fled upon seeing you."
After his meal, Kāśyapa returned to where the Buddha was and informed the Buddha of these matters.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked them in various ways:
"You should cultivate few desires and contentment; you ought not to be preoccupied with many affairs or to beg insatiably.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
“In a past age, by the banks of the Ganges River, there was a rishi dwelling in a stone cave.
At that time, the dragon king would emerge from the water daily, encircle the rishi seven times with his body, extend his head above him, and look down upon him with reverence.”

Later, when the rishi was traveling through the human world, his disciple remained to guard the cave. The nāga also came as before to pay his respects, and the disciple, being terrified, immediately became extremely emaciated.

At that time, while I was practicing the bodhisattva path, I was traveling along the banks of the Ganges River. Seeing him in such a state, I asked him the reason for it, and he answered me fully in this way.
I then asked again:
"Do you now wish not to see the nāga anymore?"
He replied, "Yes. He asked again:
"What do you see hanging from the dragon's throat?
He replied, "There is a maṇi jewel."
I spoke again, saying:
"When the nāga comes, you should join your palms toward him and say these words:
'I now require the maṇi from beneath your throat.'"
"I pray that you grant me this!
At that time, having heard my words, the dragon emerged from the water and the seer’s disciple demanded it from him.
Upon hearing the request for the pearl, the dragon neither advanced nor retreated, but remained there in silence.
Then the disciple of the rishi spoke these verses again to the dragon king:
“O Dragon King, you are needed now; The *maṇi* jewel within your throat— Your mind holds it with great affection and delight; Why do you remain silent and say nothing?”
The dragon then replied with a verse:
"All that I require Is obtained through this jewel;
Since you now beg it from me, I shall sever our ties forever and never come back again."
“Like the sudden roar of a fire’s explosion, it causes the heart to tremble with fear.
Having now heard your words, my terror exceeds even that.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One cited an ancient verse:
"A beggar is not loved by people; frequent begging leads to resentment and hatred.
When the Dragon King hears the sound of begging, he departs once and never returns.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
"Even the Dragon Kings, who receive the natural retribution of their karma, do not take pleasure in hearing the sound of begging.
Now, these householders labor diligently and obtain their gains through hardship; how can you repeatedly beg from them?"
Again he addressed the bhikṣus:
“Once in the past, when I was in Śrāvastī, there was a bhikṣu who, having completed his summer retreat, came to where I was.
At that time, I asked him:”
"In what place do you dwell during the retreat? Is your dwelling peaceful and secure? Is almsfood easy to obtain?
Are you not fatigued by the journey? He replied to me, saying:
"I dwell during the retreat beneath the forest on the slopes of the Snowy Mountains; my dwelling is peaceful and secure, almsfood is easy to obtain, and I am not fatigued by traveling."
"I only worry that the birds will disturb me with their nighttime cries, preventing me from practicing meditation and contemplation with single-minded focus.
I then asked the bhikṣus:
"Do you still find pleasure in that forest?"
He replied, "I am very happy! I said:
"You should return there; when the birds come together at dusk, join your palms and say to them:
'I now require your feathers and plumage; you may give them to me.
Do the same during the middle watch and the last watch of the night."
The bhikṣu accepted the instruction and went to beg from them as commanded.
Thereupon, the birds deliberated together during the night, saying:
"Now this bhikṣu is begging from us; should we give it to him or not?"
They all said, "We cannot," and they flew away, never to return again.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If even birds do not delight in hearing the sound of begging, how much more so must it be for humans?"
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, there was a king of Kāśī who delighted in practicing generosity and provided for all those in poverty.
At that time, there was a brahmin whom the king held in great esteem; he had never before made any request of the king."
At that time, the king spoke these verses for him:
"All people come from afar, And beg of me in every way;
Yet you are here now, What is the meaning of not seeking?"
The brahmin then replied with a verse:
"A beggar brings no joy to people; Refusing to give leads to resentment.
Therefore I remain silent and do not ask, Fearing it would sever my bonds of affection."
The King spoke again in verse:
"The wise do not detest begging; they welcome the sound of those who come to seek.
How much more so for one as dear to you as this—how could you possibly harbor a heart of stinginess!"
To maintain poverty while feeling shame at having to beg is to fail to take what one ought to receive;
this ruins a person’s virtue and their fortune, leaving them only to distress themselves.
To live in poverty without shame at begging is to take what one ought to receive.
Having already perfected the virtues of a human being, one naturally grows in peace and joy.
If one does not damage virtuous conduct, nor commit transgressions of body or speech,
then by replacing what is deficient with what is complete, why would one not seek [this state]?
The brahmin replied again in verse:
"A worthy person does not speak of begging; one who speaks of begging is certainly not worthy.
To remain silent and have no desire for anything— this is what is called a Great Man."
When the king heard these verses spoken by the worthy man, his heart was filled with great joy; he immediately bestowed upon him one bull-king and an additional thousand cattle as a gift.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Even though the king and the brahmin hold each other in high esteem, it is still difficult for them to grant what is requested;
how much more so for the householders, who have no affection for you yet demand much?"
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a son of noble family named Rāṣṭrapāla, whom his parents loved dearly;
yet, because he had left the household life, he did not seek anything from his parents."
At that time, his parents also questioned him in verse:
"All people come from afar, And there is no one who begs from us.
You are our own flesh and blood, our beloved son; If you do not ask for anything, what is your intention?"
Ratthapāla replied with a verse:
“Beggars are not pleasing to people, And failing to give them leads to resentment.
Since I have already gone forth from the household life, I should no longer have any seeking.”
“Monks! Even Rāṣṭrapāla’s parents, who cherished him deeply, did not seek him out when he had gone forth and did not return;
how much less would laypeople, who have no kinship with you, make many demands?”
Having thus rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, seeking it himself, builds a dwelling that has no owner and is for his own use, he should build it according to the prescribed measure.'"
It shall be twelve spans long and seven spans wide according to the Buddha’s span.
One should seek a site for its construction with the bhikṣus; the bhikṣus should indicate a site that is free from difficulties and has sufficient space for movement.
"If one does not seek out a site from the bhikṣus, or if it exceeds the proper measure, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
"To beg for oneself" means:
a bhikṣu begs from another for his own sake.
A "dwelling" (layana) is that within which one may perform walking, standing, sitting, and reclining— the four modes of deportment.
"Without an owner" means:
"Having no donor for one's own sake" means acting for oneself, not for others, nor for the Saṃgha.
Regarding the instruction that one should lead those bhikṣus who seek a place for construction:
one should lead knowledgeable and discipline-holding bhikṣus to show them the site of their own construction.
Those bhikṣus should indicate a site for construction that is free from obstacles and possesses sufficient space for movement.

"Dangerous places" refers to locations such as crossroads where many people gather for amusement, brothels, marketplaces, cattle-pasture grounds, areas inhabited by lions, tigers, wolves, and other predatory beasts, precipitous cliffs, deep pools of water, sites of community shrines or large trees, beautiful gardens and fields, and burial grounds;
or places that border a village or are far from one, where the roads are treacherous—these are called dangerous places.
The absence of these various obstacles is called a place free from difficulties (*anupadrava*).
Regarding "having a space for movement":
being able to pass through on all four sides with a carriage is called having a space for movement.
If there are various difficult places above and no place to walk, the bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣu:
"Do not take this place.
If there are no various difficult places above but there is a place to walk, the bhikṣus should say to this bhikṣu:
"You take this place.

That bhikṣu should request the Saṃgha to designate the site for construction; he should bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], am personally begging for materials to build a hut for myself; it shall have no owner. I now request the Saṃgha to designate a site for its construction.
May the Saṃgha present before me designate a site for me!
Thus he requests three times.
One person among the Saṃgha should then announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is personally begging for materials to build a dwelling for himself; it has no owner. He has requested the Saṃgha to designate a site for its construction.
Now the Saṃgha shall designate a site for so-and-so—a site free from difficulties and with sufficient space for movement.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus as a formal motion:
'Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!'"
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is personally begging for materials to build a hut for himself; it has no owner.
He has requested the Saṃgha to designate a site for its construction.
Now the Saṃgha shall designate a site for so-and-so that is free from difficulties and possesses a path of access.
"Whichever elders approve, let them remain silent;
whoever does not approve, let them speak.
The Sangha has already designated the site for [the construction] for so-and-so; it is free from difficulties and possesses sufficient space for passage."
"Because the Saṃgha remains silent,
this matter is thus upheld.
If the Saṃgha points out a difficult place or a place where there is no path, it is a duṣkṛta offense for the Saṃgha.
If one acts in this location, it is likewise.
If one does not point out the site of construction to the bhikṣus, from the initial resolution and the preparation of the ground up to the application of coarse plaster, it is all a duṣkṛta;
for fine plaster, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If the construction is finished, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If it is constructed using gold, silver, or precious gems; if it is a completed earthen house; or if it is constructed upon land belonging to the Saṃgha—in all such cases, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
The śrāmaṇera commits a duṣkṛta; the six precepts are concluded.
*Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, Fascicle II [end]; *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, Fascicle III.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Song Dynasty, together with Zhu Daosheng and others.
Part One, Section Two, Seventh Matter. The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the bhikṣu Chanda frequently entered and left various households, preaching the Dharma for them, attending to their official affairs, and treating their various ailments;
there were no kings, ministers, elders, or householders who did not hold him in personal esteem and respect.

There were several people who came together to pay their respects; encountering him at his place of walking meditation, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet. He preached the sublime Dharma for them, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, after which they each returned to their own homes.
Candana returned, but the senior monk had already taken his room; this process continued in succession until even the small rooms were likewise occupied.
Finding no place to stay, he then wandered among the people.
Later, when other people came again to pay their respects, they saw the bhikṣus walking in meditation in the open air and asked,
"Where is our teacher Chanda now?"
The bhikṣus said, "We do not know.
Having searched everywhere without success, they each returned to their own quarters.
Cchanda returned from his alms-round; having put on his robes and taken up his bowl, he went to that house. All came out to greet him, saying:
"Venerable One! We recently went to the monastery and did not have the opportunity to see you; from where have you come now?"
He replied, "I am the lowest-ranking seat-holder; all the other rooms have already been filled by senior monks. Therefore, I was traveling about, which led to this disagreement.
The people said to him:
“We shall seek out a dwelling place, and we will build it for the Elder.
Having thus seen the merit [of this act], we shall enable the Elder to dwell in peace and security, and furthermore, we shall ensure that our inquiries after his well-being do not fall into neglect.”
Chanda replied, "I cannot do it myself so as to neglect my practice of the Path; when I am older, I shall naturally receive it in due order.
The others spoke again:
"I am fortunate indeed to possess both material goods and a virtuous mind;
yet material wealth is impermanent, and a virtuous mind is difficult to maintain.
I pray that you will seek out a suitable place for me, for I am determined to build it."

Seeing his earnestness and finding it difficult to refuse him, Chanda immediately went about seeking a site for a dwelling; seeing that the location of a sacred tree was most suitable for construction, he cut it down at once.
This tree has a deity who is venerated by the people of the kingdom, and those who offer prayers there mostly obtain their wishes;
when they suddenly saw it being cut down, all were struck with astonishment and wonder. Those who did not believe in or delight in the Buddha-dharma all reviled them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are exceedingly devoid of the Way; seeking only their own self-interest, they harm both devas and humans."
Those who had faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma then said:
"This tree possesses a deity; all people revere it and worship it with devotion day and night, never daring to be negligent.

Yet these bhikṣus cut it down without hesitation, while their physical appearance and mental state remain as tranquil and composed as before. It may truly be called a great deity, one of great nobility and worthy of honor."
The sounds of both slander and praise filled the country.
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they rebuked him in various ways, led him to the Buddha’s presence, and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Chanda:
"Is it true that you did so?
He replied: "It is true."
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, having a patron, builds a dwelling for himself, he must seek out a suitable location with the assistance of the other bhikṣus.'"
The monks should indicate a place for construction that is free from difficulties and has sufficient space for movement.
If they do not seek such a place with the monks, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"With an owner" means there is a donor (*dānapati*).
The rest is as explained above regarding "without an owner. The seven precepts are concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, King Bimbisāra invited five hundred monks for a meal every day in succession, and the ministers and citizens within the city did likewise.
Meanwhile, the bhikṣus were each practicing the Path individually; there was yet no one specifically designated to manage the order of these invitations.
The group of six bhikṣus constantly frequented excellent locations.
People asked them, "We have prepared food for the Saṃgha in its proper order; why is it that you elders always come, while we do not see the others?"
Though he was thus rebuked, he still did not desist.
