At that time, the son of the Malla Dabba, fourteen years of age, had gone forth to follow the path; while staying in a quiet place, he thought to himself:
"Now King Bimbisāra invites five hundred monks for their daily meals, and the ministers and citizens within the city do likewise."

Since there was no one among the Sangha to assign the seating arrangements for the assemblies, the group of six monks selected the best locations; this caused them to lose the public's esteem and ruined the donors' intention to give.

"If I were to receive full ordination at twenty years of age, attain arhatship, and acquire the six supernormal powers, I would serve as the assigner of seating and the distributor of bedding for the Sangha."
When he reached the age of sixteen, he immediately became an arhat and attained the six supernormal powers; at twenty, having received full ordination, he thought to himself:
"I previously vowed to serve as the assigner of meals and the distributor of bedding for the Sangha. Now that the time has come, I should fulfill this duty."
He then went to where the bhikṣus were in Rājagṛha and related his previous aspiration.
The bhikṣus immediately informed the Buddha about this matter. The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Dabba:
"Is it true that you wish to serve as the assigner of duties and the distributor of bedding for the Saṃgha?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had praised fewness of desires and contentment in various ways, and had praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now authorize Dabba to serve as the assigner of duties and the distributor of bedding for the Saṃgha."
The Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) and appoint one bhikṣu to announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Dhava now wishes to serve as the person appointed by the Saṃgha to organize assemblies and distribute bedding."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience.
This is the motion. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
"This bhikṣu, Dhaṣa, wishes to serve as the assigner of duties and the distributor of bedding for the Saṃgha.
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak."
The Sangha has already authorized the monk Dova to serve as the assigner of duties and the distributor of bedding;
the Sangha consents, as it remains silent.
Thus shall this matter be upheld.
Thereupon, Dabba immediately acted as the assigner of duties for the Saṅgha and the distributor of bedding.

When distributing the bedding, those who were of few desires and contented were assigned together with those of few desires and contented; those who delighted in solitude were assigned with those who delighted in solitude; those who recited the Sūtras were assigned with those who recited the Sūtras; those who upheld the Vinaya were assigned with those who upheld the Vinaya; Dharma-preachers were assigned with Dharma-preachers; chanters were assigned with chanters; forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*) were assigned with forest-dwellers; alms-seekers (*piṇḍapātika*) were assigned with alms-seekers; and meditators (*dhyāyin*) were assigned with meditators.
Thus, those of various different practices each obtained their appropriate kind, being guided according to what was suitable for them.
In all the various rooms and dwellings, every bhikṣu found peace and comfort.

Whenever bhikṣus from various regions arrived at dusk, they would go directly to Dabba to seek a place to stay; Dabba would immediately enter the *tejodhātu-samādhi*, emitting light from his left hand while pointing with his right hand to the location of the bedding, so that there was never a single instance where their needs were not perfectly met.

At that time, those from distant regions, having heard that the bhikṣu Dabba was appointed by the Saṃgha of Rājagṛha to oversee assemblies and distribute bedding, and knowing he possessed such virtues, all thought to themselves:
"I shall go there to pay my respects to the World-Honored One, and at the same time see Dabba and witness his supernormal powers."
Thereupon they set out and arrived at the city at dusk; they went to where Dhava was and requested a place to stay.
Dhava accommodated them all according to the Dharma;
he likewise assigned them to the assembly in the same manner.
At that time, there was an elder named Supātra in the city of Rājagṛha who had seen the Dharma and attained the fruit.
Every day he prepared excellent food for two bhikṣus and came in person to invite them.

The brothers Maitreya and Maitrībala were both of meager merit; when bedding was distributed and assemblies were assigned, they always received coarse and inferior allotments. By good fortune, it so happened that the turn for distribution fell upon their own home.
Having understood this, Supriya (Sudan) thought to himself:
"These are evil men who lack pure conduct; how can they accept my superior and exquisite offerings?
He then returned home and said to his wife:
"You should prepare coarse and unpalatable food; when Maitrībala and the others arrive, arrange seats outside the gate and have a maidservant serve it to them.
The wife immediately followed these instructions and prepared the coarse food.

When the time arrived, the brothers Maitrībala and Maitreya took their bowls and went to the house of Sudāna, where they sat down upon the seats. Thereupon, the maidservants brought out coarse food; seeing this, Maitrībala asked them: "Sisters!..."
"In your household you always prepared fine food; why is it coarse today?
The maidservant replied, "I am but a lowly servant; I do not know the reason."
Having finished his meal, he returned; on the way back, he spoke with abuse:
"Dhava, son of a Malla, I shall certainly cause you to suffer even more intensely than I have!
Upon reaching his residence, he addressed the senior monks:
“The son of the Malla Dabba acts according to desire, hatred, delusion, and fear; if he fears you, he gives you what is good, but if he does not fear you, he gives you what is bad.
The bhikṣus said: “Do not speak such words:”
“The bhikṣu Dabba follows after desire, hatred, delusion, and fear.
Why is this? It is impossible for the bhikṣu Dabba—who has attained arhatship and is endowed with the six supernormal powers—to follow after desire, hatred, delusion, and fear.
Maitrībala said: "It is precisely because I have attained supernormal powers that I can perceive which families are well-off and which are poor;
when they give to others who are well-off, they invariably send me to those who are poor. For this reason, I said:..."
"Driven by desire, hatred, delusion, and fear.
Having spoken these words, he departed for another place; first he spread an evil reputation concerning Dabba, and subsequently arrived at Rājagṛha, going to his sister Nandā Mittākālikā.
When Mithilā saw her two elder brothers approaching, she went out to greet them, pay her respects, and inquire after their well-being; however, neither Cīra nor his brother would speak with her.
Mithilā said, "I do not recall having committed any offense; why are you acting like this, my brothers?"
Maitrāyanī replied,
"Because you did not assist me, it has caused Dabba to torment me in this way. Mithilā said:
“Brother, how do you wish for me to assist you?
He replied, “If you would assist me, you may go to the Buddha’s presence and say:”
“World-Honored One!
In that which is free from fear, I have instead encountered terror; I now have no place where I may find peace and security.
I originally thought that Dabba was one who practices the holy life (brahmacārin), yet he has suddenly come to defile me, causing me to commit a pārājika offense.”
Mitrā said: “Dhava is pure;
if I were to slander him, the Saṃgha would certainly carry out a *pratyāyanīya-karma* (act of self-accusation) against me.
Once I have been expelled from the community, upon what shall I rely?”
Maitrāyaṇīputra and the others said:
"We shall bear witness for you to exclude Dabba.
For what reason would you need to have yourself excluded by your own word?"
Mitrā said, "If the Saṃgha expels Dhava, how could I possibly be spared?
Cīrā and the others said:
"If only the World-Honored One would expel Dabba and grant us the formal act of suspension (*pravāsanīya-karman*), what hardship would there be?
We ourselves shall find a suitable place for him to dwell.
Out of reverence for her brother, the sister did not dare disobey his command; she went to the Buddha's presence and reported everything to him as described above.
At that time, Dabba and Rāhula were standing by the Buddha's side.
The Buddha asked Dabba, "Did you hear what Mithilā said? He replied:
"I have heard it.
The Buddha knows it himself.
Thus he asked three times, and the answer was likewise each time.
Thereupon Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
why was it necessary to ask Dabba three times?"
"You should simply expel this bhikṣuṇī.
The Buddha said,
"If Mithilā were to slander you in this way, what would you do?"
He replied, "One should say that the Buddha himself knows this matter.
The Buddha said:
"Is it thus for you, and is it likewise for Dabba?
The Buddha said to Dabba, "Arise and speak for yourself; now is not the time for silence."
"You should bear this in mind: that which exists, you should say exists; that which does not exist, you should say does not exist.
You must not simply say, 'The Buddha knows it himself!
Thereupon, Dabba rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since my birth, I have never even in a dream had such a thought; how could I possibly possess recollection or knowledge of it now?
The Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! You have clearly understood for yourself; those who wish to understand for themselves should do so in this way!
Thus the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus.
“Dhava should be granted the *smṛtivinaya*; the bhikṣu should not be subjected to formal charges.
Mithila should be granted the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for self-accusation and subsequent banishment.”
A bhikṣu proclaimed: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyāṇī herself says:..."
“Dhova has defiled me. The Saṃgha now grants him a *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karma* (act of reconciliation) based on his own confession.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen.
The motion is thus stated.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣuṇī Mettiyā says of herself:
“Dhova has defiled me. The Saṃgha now grants him *pratyāśrava-parivāsa* (expulsion by his own confession).
Those elders who consent, remain silent; [those who do not, speak].
"If you do not approve, please speak.
Thus a second and third time.
"The Saṃgha has already completed the formal act of *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) against the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyāṇī based on her own confession."
The Saṃgha has granted forbearance, as they remained silent;
this matter is thus upheld.
After the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyāṇī had been expelled, she went forth to wander among the people, while the brothers Mātṛceṭa and Kalyāṇabhadrika continued to speak thus to the bhikṣus:
“Dhava-putra has violated my sister’s celibacy, which is why she has become like this.
The bhikṣus reported this matter again to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
“You should interrogate Maitrāyaṇī.”
“You have said that Dabba has violated your sister’s brahmacarya; is this true or false?
Following these instructions, the bhikṣus questioned Māluṅkyāputra, who replied:
“What I have said is true.”
The Saṃgha asked again:
"Where did you see him? When did you see him?"
"How did you see it? He replied,
"I saw it at such-and-such a place, at such-and-such a time, and in such-and-such a manner."
The monk next in order asked Dabba,
"Where were you at that time? He replied:
"I am at such-and-such a place," the monk replied to Maitreya.
"That place is inconsistent; that time is inconsistent."
"How can you say that you saw such things at such a place and at such a time?
He then spoke again to Maitrībala:
"If one speaks a falsehood before a single bhikṣu of firm faith, the sin is heavier than that of killing countless sentient beings."
Regarding one instance of a firm dharma, the offense incurred exceeds that of a hundred firm believers;
likewise, by successively engaging in false speech before the Sangha, the offense is more grave than that of a hundred Arhats.
He further said to Maitrāyaṇīputra:
"The Saṃgha has now assembled; it does not follow after desire, hatred, delusion, or fear.
You may speak again: is this true or false?"
Maitrāyanī said, "I spoke those words because Dabba was driven by desire, hatred, delusion, and fear.
The bhikṣus rebuked him in various ways and led him to the Buddha’s presence, reporting the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Maitrāyaṇīputra:
"Is it true that you baselessly accused Dabba of a pārājika offense? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"You foolish man! How can you, with groundless charges of a *pārājika* offense, slander a bhikṣu of pure conduct?
Have you not heard that three kinds of people fall into hell?"
First, they violate the precepts and lack the qualities of a śramaṇa, yet claim to possess them;
they do not cultivate the holy life, yet claim to have cultivated it; within the Buddha-dharma, they are like rotten seeds.
Second, they hold such a view and speak thus:
"Sexual desire is not evil," and thereby become heedless.
Third, to slander a bhikṣu of pure brahmacarya with groundless charges of a pārājika offense—these three kinds of people will inevitably fall into hell. Why have you now committed such an evil deed?
After the Buddha had further rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣu, being himself unrighteous and out of malice, slanders a bhikṣu who is free from pārājika offenses with groundless charges of a pārājika offense, desiring to destroy that person's holy life (brahmacarya).'"
If, at a later time, whether questioned or not, that bhikṣu says:
"This matter of mine was groundless; I slandered out of malice," it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
"One who is personally unrighteous" means that one's own actions in every matter are contrary to the Dharma.
"One who is evil and wrathful" means:
These are the nine grounds for resentment. "Groundless" means:
not having seen, not having heard, and not having suspected.
"Without an *āpatti* of defeat" means:
not having committed any one of the four *āpattis* of defeat.
"Desiring to destroy that holy life" means:
If one wishes to cause [a person] to return to lay life or become a non-Buddhist ascetic,
then later— whether they are questioned or not— one shall investigate:
at what place, at what time, and in what manner was it seen?
There are four kinds of legal matters:
disputes concerning speech, disputes concerning instruction, disputes concerning offenses, and disputes concerning legal procedures.
If a bhikṣu, without having seen, heard, or suspected another to have committed a pārājika offense, should defame them on that basis, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.

If one slanders another with groundless charges based on what was seen but doubted, heard but doubted, or doubted about the doubt itself; or based on what was seen but forgotten, heard but forgotten, or the doubt itself forgotten, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If one slanders another face-to-face and the person understands, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if they do not understand, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one slanders by means of a letter, a messenger, signs, indirect speech, or hand gestures, and the person understands, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one does not understand, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one slanders a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣuṇī slanders another bhikṣuṇī, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa;
if she slanders a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika;
if she slanders a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī slanders any of the five groups [of practitioners], it is all a duṣkṛta. The eight matters are concluded.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

At that time, because the bhikṣuṇī Sthūlanandā held the bhikṣu Dharmadatta in high regard for his great spiritual power and virtue, she frequently came to inquire after his well-being, sitting together with him in one place to listen to and receive the teachings of the Dharma.
Maitrībala saw this and again desired to slander him. Later, as he was descending from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, he saw two monkeys engaged in sexual union; he then thought to himself:
"I shall now give those two monkeys false names: the male shall be named Dabba, and the female shall be named Thullanandā."
Having had this thought, he spoke to the elder bhikṣus, saying:
"Previously, I slandered Dabba with groundless charges; now I have personally seen him engaging in unchaste conduct with Thullanandā."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should assemble the Saṃgha and interrogate Maitrāyaṇī:
'Did you previously slander Dabba with groundless charges, and now say that you have personally seen him engage in unchaste conduct with Thullanandā? Is this true or false?'"
The bhikṣus accepted the instruction, assembled the Saṃgha, and questioned Cidi, [asking] up to: “You may speak further: is this real or is it false?
He replied in all respects as previously stated.
When he had asked this, Maitrāyaṇī said:
"I truly did not see Dabba committing an act of impurity; however, I saw Sthūlanandā frequently coming and going to Dabba's place, and it was with the intent of slandering him that I spoke."

Descending from Vulture Peak, I saw a male and female monkey mating; I then provisionally named the male "Dabba" and the female "Thullanandā," and thus said that I had personally witnessed them engaging in unchaste conduct!
The bhikṣus rebuked him in various ways:
“How could you, taking a portion from a different category, or something resembling a portion, bring a *pārājika* charge against a bhikṣu who has not committed a *pārājika* offense?”
Upon arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, they reported the matter to him.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Maitrībala:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied: "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!"
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣu, being himself unrighteous and out of malice and anger, takes a portion or something resembling a portion from a different category [of offense] and, with the intent to destroy another's holy life (brahmacarya), accuses a bhikṣu who is free of pārājika offenses of having committed a pārājika offense.'"
At a later time, whether questioned or not, that bhikṣu says:
"In this matter, I took a fragment or something resembling a fragment from a different category of facts; I slandered him because I was dwelling in anger."
“Saṃghāvaśeṣa. As for the matters:
they are disputes concerning speech, disputes concerning instruction, disputes concerning offenses, and disputes concerning legal issues.
If a bhikṣu sees another commit a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and definitely forms the perception that it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense,
yet out of malice seizes upon a fragment from a different category or something resembling a fragment to slander a bhikṣu who has not committed a pārājika offense, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
The same applies to what has been heard, suspected, or seen.

If one slanders another who has committed a *sthūlātyaya*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta* offense by accusing them of a *pārājika* offense based on what was seen, heard, or suspected, it is likewise so.
The remainder is as explained above; thus ends the ninth precept.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the Āmra grove in the village of Miṇā.
Many sons of the Śākya clan from noble families had gone forth under the Buddha to study the Path.
Then Śreṇika Bimbisāra’s son, Mānava, said to Aniruddha:
“Now that all these nobles have renounced the world to cultivate the holy life, why do we brothers alone not do so?”
"If I renounce the household life, you shall manage the family affairs;
if you renounce the household life, I shall take charge of them. Anuruddha said:
"I pray that you, elder brother, will renounce the household life, so that I may manage the family affairs.
Śreṇika Bimbisāra said:
"Previously, you enjoyed yourself at home under my care and did not know the hardships; [how then can you do this now?]"
"However, leaving the household life to practice the Way is likewise arduous.
Since you now remain at home, I shall tell you the methods for managing a household.
He then spoke to him in various ways:
"It should be so by day; it should be so by night.
He explained to him entirely the methods for agriculture, commerce, trade, and the management of laborers. Aniruddha said:
"If one manages a household in this manner, it can indeed be successfully maintained; yet I am unable to do so for even a single day.
I pray that you remain at home while I shall practice the Way."
Śreṇika Mānava said:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not permit one to practice the Way if their parents do not give their consent.
You should now personally inform your mother."
Aniruddha then went to inform her, saying,
"I wish to leave the household life and study the Path within the Buddha-dharma.
His mother said:
"I have only you and your brother as my two children; our affection for one another is deep. How can we part?
Your family is very wealthy; make full use of it to cultivate merit."
"Why must you leave the household life and take away this intention of mine?
He pleaded thus up to three times, and his mother finally replied,
"If King Bimbisāra leaves the household life, I shall also permit you."

At that time, King Bimbisāra was deeply affectionate toward and held in high esteem by Anuruddha, Ānanda, Nandiya, Devadatta, Bhadra, and Kapphiṇa; whatever they had to do, they vowed never to act against one another’s wishes.
Thereupon, Aniruddha went to King Bimbisāra and said, "I have a small request;
I pray that you will surely grant it.
The king replied:
"Our original intent was that we should never go against one another;
should we do so, our heads shall split into seven pieces.
However, let your wish be made, and it shall surely be granted!"
Aniruddha then reported his mother’s words to the king.
The king said,
“Regarding this wish of yours, I am unable to grant it.”
Why is this? My wish to become a king has finally borne fruit today; my kinsmen are wealthy and noble, and I have no external anxieties.
How could I abandon this and leave the home life to study the Way?
Aniruddha said: "If the King renounces the world, my wish will be fulfilled;
if he remains attached to favor and glory, I shall sink forever."
"I pray that Your Majesty will reflect three times and not violate your former vow! The King said,
"I shall grant your wish."
"Forgive me for seven years; after that, we shall go forth together to study the Way.
Anuruddha said, "In seven years' time, it is not certain that the Buddha will still be here."
"Furthermore, my life is fragile and difficult to preserve; how can Your Majesty set this as the deadline?
The King spoke again:
"If seven years is too long, would six years be acceptable?"
The answer was as above.
[He did this] for five, four, three, and two years, down to one year; for seven months down to one month; and for seven days down to a single day, all of which were likewise so.
The king said, "We elders—how could we simply depart so abruptly?
We must devise a skillful means and set out on a journey with our carriages fully prepared; only by traveling thus in disguise can we do so."
"You should now inform Ānanda and the others so that they may understand this intention.
Anuruddha then proclaimed these words to the five men; the five were delighted, with no dissent in their hearts.
They immediately spent the entire night preparing the fourfold army and adorning them with the finest worldly finery, setting out on their excursion at dawn.

Having finished his sightseeing, he took the barber Upāli in secret, left behind all his attendants, and went to a secluded place; there he gave him his precious robes, had him shave his hair, and departed after changing his attire.
Not long after he had departed, Upāli thought to himself:
"The Śākyas are powerful; if they learn that I shaved the hair of these men, they will surely kill me.
Since even such noble clansmen as these were able to renounce their homes, why should I not now cast aside my barber’s tools and precious robes and follow them?"
He immediately shaved his own head, hung his various precious robes upon a tree, and thought to himself:
"Let whoever needs them take them.
Thereupon he hurried on, and in a short while they caught up with him; he spoke to the seven men, saying:
"I now also wish to follow you and leave the household life.
The seven men immediately accepted [his proposal] and went together to the place where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and said:
"World-Honored One!..."
"We now wish to leave the household life to purely cultivate the holy life;
however, Upāli is our servant. We pray that the Buddha will first confer the full ordination upon him, and only then admit us;
thus shall we and the Śākya clan have our great pride shattered before this man."
The Buddha then ordained the seven men first, and ordained them later himself.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Kapilavastu is not far from here; if the Śākyas find out, they may create obstacles."
He then took the eight men to the city of Vādiśā and stayed beneath a tree in Jālinīvana, where he preached the sublime Dharma to them:
"The eye is impermanent; forms are impermanent. Eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling born of the causal condition of eye-contact are impermanent.
This extends up to: the mind is impermanent; mental phenomena are impermanent. Mind-consciousness, mind-contact, and the feeling born of the causal condition of mind-contact are impermanent."
"You, noble disciple!
You should practice this contemplation, giving rise to a mind of weary detachment, attaining the wisdom of liberation,
completing what was to be done, establishing the holy life, and no longer undergoing future existence."
When this Dharma was being taught, six people were freed from outflows and attained arhatship.
Ānanda, who attended upon the Buddha, did not exhaust all his outflows.
Devadatta alone gained nothing at all.
Once King Bādi had attained arhatship, his mind was pure and fearless; whether sitting exposed beneath a tree or walking in meditation, he would always exclaim in self-congratulation:
"How joyful! How joyful!"
Upon hearing these words, another bhikṣu thought to himself:
"The bhikṣu Bhadrika must be recollecting worldly pleasures and no longer delights in the holy life."
He immediately went to inform the Buddha, saying: "Just now, I heard Vaddha say:
'How wonderful! How wonderful!'"
"He must surely be remembering the pleasures of his time as a king and find no joy in the holy life.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu, "You may call him here!"
He then went and said,
"The Great Master calls for you!
Bhadrika immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha asked Bāḍhi:
"Is it true that you spoke those words so eloquently? He replied:
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
He then asked Bāḍhi:
"What meaning do you perceive that you say, 'How wonderful! Vāṣpa replied:

"In the past, when I lived at home within sevenfold layers of city walls and moats, surrounded by four divisions of the army—seven rows of elephants, seven rows of horses, seven rows of chariots, and seven rows of infantry—I was suddenly startled by an extraordinary sound; my heart trembled and my hair stood on end."
"Now, here beneath a tree in the open air, he is at ease and free from sorrow; for this reason, he is said to be 'joyful.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"It is impossible that Bādi, having already attained arhatship, would not delight in the holy life."
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of Bāḍhi, spoke these verses:
"How wonderful is the Arhat! No longer bound by affection and love, Having already shattered desire, hatred, and delusion, He is free from the net of all fetters."
Having reached nirvana, they possess no defiled mind;
unstained by the world, they are liberated and free from all outflows.
Thoroughly understanding the five aggregates, they roam within the grove of the seven dharmas.
Where the Great Dragon travels, all terrors have been subdued;
having accomplished the tenfold divisions, he possesses the dragon-virtue samādhi and dhyāna.
With all outflows extinguished, he is the foremost in the world.
Unshakable and fearless, no longer receiving further rebirths,
having attained the state of cessation and tranquility, forever free from the retribution of suffering or pleasure;
abiding in the wisdom of one beyond training, this body is the very last.
The holy life is firmly established, free from all that is untrustworthy;
among the heavens and upon the earth, there are no further sensual pleasures.
This is called the lion’s roar: there is no one who can surpass the Buddha.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One and the great virtuous śrāvakas accepted the invitation of the Dragon King Anavatapta;
however, Devadatta, not yet having attained supernormal powers, was unable to go and felt his shame grow even deeper. He then thought to himself:
"I must now inquire about the way to cultivate the path of supernormal powers."
He then went to inform the Buddha, saying, "I pray that the Buddha will explain to me the method for cultivating supernatural powers.
The Buddha immediately explained it for him; Devadatta accepted the instruction and, during the summer retreat, attained supernatural powers.
Having attained the supernormal powers, he reflected thus:
"Who should be transformed first?
He then thought again:
"The Crown Prince of King Bimbisāra is named Saṃjaya; I shall first convert and guide him, and only thereafter will others follow my teaching.
Having formed this thought, he immediately vanished from beneath the Jālinī tree and appeared upon the prince’s couch, manifesting as a small child sucking his finger and lying on his back.
Upon seeing this, the Prince was immediately seized with great terror and asked, "Are you a deva,
or are you a ghost or spirit?"
He replied, "I am Devadatta; do not be afraid, do not be terrified!
The Prince said to him:
"If you are indeed Devadatta, restore yourself to your original form.
He immediately transformed himself back, his dignified demeanor becoming as it was before.
The Prince rejoiced and took him as his teacher.

At sunrise, he went to pay his respects, riding in five hundred chariots. Devadatta further manifested himself as five hundred young children, lying on their backs atop the chariots and sucking their fingers;
he also provided offerings of various delicacies and fine foods, loaded upon another five hundred chariots.
At that time, the people of the various kingdoms conceived a sense of wonder and said:

"Devadatta possesses great supernatural power; he has performed such a transformation as to cause the Prince to come out daily to inquire after his health and to provide him with all manner of delicacies as offerings."
Thereupon, Devadatta, failing to exercise self-restraint, sought to attract and gather a following of disciples.
At that time, the World-Honored One emerged from Jālinīvana and traveled among the people, arriving at the kingdom of Kauśāmbī and staying in the Ghosira Park.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana was staying in a separate location.
Previously, there had been a son of Kauṇḍinya in this country named Kātyāyana, who had purified his brahmacarya practice and attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin, being reborn in the Brahma Heaven.

During the tranquility of the middle watch of the night, he descended from heaven, emitting a great radiance, and approached Maudgalyāyana; bowing his head at the Master’s feet, he addressed him, saying:

“Devadatta is now converting the assembly and delighting the Crown Prince, manifesting various supernatural transformations; I fear he intends to attract followers and break the harmony of the Saṃgha.
Having spoken these words, he suddenly vanished.
Thereupon, at dawn, Maudgalyāyana adjusted his robes and went to where the Buddha was, reporting Kṣemaka’s words in full to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Maudgalyāyana,
"What do you think?"
"Should one say that it is indeed as Ke-xiu has stated? He replied,
"I believe it to be so."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"Do not speak these words! Why is that?
"In the heavens above and the world below, I see no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, or brahmā who is able to lead the assembly of my disciples.
He further addressed Maudgalyāyana:
"There are five kinds of teachers in the world, all of whom are currently present:
First, his precepts are not pure, yet he claims his precepts are pure; his disciples know this as it truly is, yet they conceal his transgressions out of a desire for gain and offerings.
Second, he maintains a wrong livelihood through flattery and crookedness, yet he claims to be upright; his disciples likewise conceal these faults.
Third, what he teaches is unwholesome, yet he claims it is well-spoken; his disciples praise it as being excellent.
Fourth, his views are impure, yet he claims they are pure, and his disciples likewise proclaim his views to be pure;
fifth, he teaches what is not the Dharma or the Vinaya, yet claims it is the Dharma and the Vinaya, and his disciples also say it is the Dharma.
Yet they cannot cause the wise to believe and accept them.
Maudgalyāyana!

The Tathāgata’s precepts are pure; he is without guile or crookedness, his speech is never unwholesome, and his knowledge and vision are pure. The Dharma he teaches is believed and accepted by the wise without the need for disciples to corroborate or vouch for it.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who, having completed the rains retreat at Rājagṛha, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and approached the Buddha, saying to him:
“World-Honored One!
Devadatta transformed the assembly to delight the Crown Prince; he manifested as a young child and even provided various delicacies as offerings.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“Do not envy Devadatta for performing such transformations to obtain gain and offerings.”
If there are those who show them respect and make offerings, it will cause them to endure various sufferings and pains for a long night.
It is just like striking a vicious dog with a staff; it only increases its malice further.
"Devadatta was thus; having received much供养 (pūjā), his afflictions increased all the more.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The fool increases his evil, Because he gives rise to craving for profit."
Having severed the pure and white dharmas through delusion, as if body and head were divided;
without cultivating pure conduct, yet aspiring to gather disciples,
wishing to stand above the masses and hoping that all would take him as their patriarch.
Some seek gain and offerings, while others seek nirvāṇa;
gain and offerings wound one’s purity, whereas tranquility dispels stinginess and greed.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
"The plantain, the bamboo, and the reed perish because of their fruit;
the mule likewise loses its life when it conceives.
Now, Devadatta’s greedy pursuit of gain and offerings is exactly like this."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The plantain dies because of its fruit; The same is true for the bamboo and the reed.
The mule dies because of pregnancy; The man ruins himself through greed."

Thereupon, the World-Honored One traveled gradually from the kingdom of Kauśāmbī toward Rājagṛha, where he stayed on Vulture Peak Mountain. He was offered support, veneration, respect, and praise by monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, kings, ministers, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, brahmins, and householders;
yet regarding food, clothing, bedding, and various medicines, he remained unstained, like a lotus flower.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an immeasurable great assembly as he preached the Dharma. Devadatta then rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, knelt on his right knee with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"May you remain in peace!
I shall now personally take charge of managing the Saṃgha.
The Buddha said to Devadatta:
“Even Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana cannot lead my assembly of disciples; how much less can you, who are ignorant and eat only saliva?
Thereupon, Devadatta gave rise to a heart of resentment and anger, thinking:
“How is it that the World-Honored One, before this great assembly, has thus humiliated me with such base reproaches?”
Because he gave rise to an evil mind toward the Buddha, his supernormal powers were first impaired.
He then thought further:
"The Buddha praises Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, yet he reviles me!"
Again, he conceived an evil mind toward Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; this was the second time his supernormal powers were impaired.
He then returned to his dwelling and preached the Dharma while surrounded by kings and a great multitude.
Among that assembly, there was a bhikṣu who came and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now Devadatta is preaching the Dharma, surrounded by the king and a great multitude.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“Devadatta did not only obtain this great assembly in the present life; in past lives as well, he once possessed these bhikṣus.
Long ago, in times of yore, there was a young brahmin who was reciting the Kṣatriya scriptures within a mountain cave.”
There was a wild fox dwelling nearby who listened intently as [the lion] recited his books; having understood their meaning, he thought to himself:
"According to my understanding of the words of these books, I am fit to be the king among all beasts."
Having formed this thought, he rose and went wandering; encountering a gaunt wild fox, he intended to kill it.
The fox said, "For what reason do you wish to kill me?"
He replied, "I am the king of beasts; you did not submit to me, and for that reason I killed you. He said:
"Please do not kill me; I shall follow you.
Thereupon, the two foxes traveled together.
They encountered another fox, and he too was about to be killed; the questions and answers were as before, and he likewise said:

"Follow me. Thus, by successive stages, he subdued all the foxes; then, using the pack of foxes, he subdued all the elephants; further, using the multitude of elephants, he subdued all the tigers; and finally, using the multitude of tigers, he subdued all the lions, whereby he was temporarily able to become the king among beasts.
Having become king, he further thought:
"Now that I am the king of beasts, I ought not to take a beast as my wife.
He then mounted a white elephant and led an incalculable multitude of various beasts, surrounding the city of Kāśī hundreds of thousands of times.
The king sent a messenger to ask:
"You various beasts, for what reason are you like this?
The wild fox replied:
"I am the king of beasts; you ought to give me your daughter! It would be well if you grant her to me;
if you do not, I shall destroy your kingdom!
When he returned and reported this, the king assembled his ministers to deliberate. With the exception of one minister, they all said:
"You should grant it! For what reason?
The state relies solely upon its elephants and horses."

I have elephants and horses, while they have lions; when the elephants and horses catch the scent, they crouch on the ground in terror. In battle, we will certainly not prevail, for we shall be destroyed by those beasts.
"Why begrudge a single daughter and thereby lose an entire kingdom?
At that time, a great minister, wise and possessed of far-reaching strategy, addressed the king, saying:
"In my observation of past and present, I have never heard of nor seen such a thing as a king’s daughter consorting with a lowly beast."
"Though I am weak and dull-witted, I must kill this fox so that all the various beasts may scatter in different directions.
The king then asked, "What plan do you propose?"
The minister replied:
"Your Majesty, simply dispatch a messenger and set a date for the day of battle; first, you must request one boon from him:
'I pray that the lion shall roar only after he has fought.'"
"He said, 'He thinks me afraid; he will surely have the lion roar first before the battle.
When the day of battle arrives, Your Majesty should order everyone within the city to plug their ears.
The king followed his advice, dispatched a messenger to set a date, and requested that this supreme boon be granted.
When the day of battle arrived, he sent a messenger again to request [the lion's presence], and only then did the army set forth.

As the vanguard of the forces were about to engage, the wild fox indeed commanded the lion to roar first. Upon hearing it, the wild fox’s heart was shattered into seven pieces; he then tumbled from his elephant onto the ground, whereupon the host of beasts scattered and fled all at once.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, spoke in verse: "The wild fox,
filled with intense arrogance, Desiring to seek a retinue,
Went to the city of Kāśī And proclaimed himself the King of Beasts."
The arrogance of men is likewise thus: he who governs a multitude of followers in the kingdom of Magadha shall style himself the "Lord of Dharma.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the King of Kāśī was I myself; the wise minister was Śāriputra; and the king of the wild foxes was Devadatta. O bhikṣus!"
Devadatta formerly falsely gained followers, and now it is just the same. "Śāriputra!
Go among Devadatta’s assembly and proclaim these words:"
"If anyone accepts the fivefold teaching of Devadatta, they shall not see the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha.
Śāriputra said, "In the past, I already praised Devadatta; how can I now again revile him?"
The Buddha asked,
"Was what you previously praised truly so? He replied:
"It is true! the Buddha said.
"Now, one should disparage; yet even this disparagement is likewise true."
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now, a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) should be performed to appoint Śāriputra to go among the assembly of Devadatta and revile him.
A bhikṣu then made the proclamation:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
We now appoint Śāriputra to go among the assembly of Devadatta and say these words:
'If you accept the fivefold teaching of Devadatta, you shall not see the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.'"
"If the time has come for the Sangha, may the Sangha listen with patience.
This is the formal motion:
'Venerable Sangha, listen!'"
Now, Śāriputra shall be dispatched to the assembly of Devadatta to say these words:
"If anyone accepts the teaching of Devadatta’s five points, they do not see the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha."
"Those elders who approve, let them remain silent;
those who do not approve, let them speak.
The Sangha has already appointed Śāriputra."
"The Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.
Thereupon, Śāriputra went into the assembly of Devadatta and proclaimed in a loud voice:
"If one accepts the fivefold teaching of Devadatta, they shall not see the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha.
At that time, the entire assembly cried out:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, harbor mutual hatred and jealousy; seeing that Devadatta receives much alms and offerings, they speak these words."
At that time, King Bimbisāra, being in that assembly, immediately issued this proclamation:
"Do not speak such words. Why is this so?"
"The Buddha and his assembly are pure, for they are free from hatred and envy.
Thereupon, Devadatta spoke to the multitude:
"Do you wish to see the *mandārava* flowers of the heavens?"
They all said, "We wish to see him.
Devadatta then vanished from before the assembly and went to the edge of a flower pond; just as he was about to pluck a flower, he lost his supernormal power and returned to his original seat.
Having lost his supernormal powers, Devadatta conceived an evil intent to harm the Buddha and said to the Crown Prince:
"Now your father, the King, governs the world with the True Dharma; as I see it, there is no end to its decline.
Human life is impermanent and cannot be guaranteed for even the blink of an eye. Why must you hold onto this royal throne for so many years?"
"You may plot against him yourself and soon possess the four seas.
I shall harm the Buddha and act as the Dharma Lord in his stead.
Would it not be excellent for the new king and the new Buddha to together propagate the transformative teachings in the kingdom of Magadha?"
The Prince replied:
"The kindness of my parents exceeds that of Heaven and Earth; they cared for and raised me, and I wish to repay them infinitely.
Why do you now lead me toward such rebellion?"
Upon hearing this, Devadatta felt no sense of shame or remorse; instead, he continued to use clever words to entice his mind.
Consequently, he became deluded and lost himself, accepting and delighting in those words.

At a later time, the Crown Prince secretly girded himself with a sharp sword and approached the royal gate; harboring treacherous intent within, he was overcome by involuntary trembling and fear, falling prostrate before the gate and then rising again.
When the gatekeeper saw him, he thought to himself:
"The Crown Prince always comes with such dignified and composed deportment; that he is like this today must surely be due to some cause."
He immediately went to question him.
The prince replied, "I wish to kill the king; that is why I am acting thus."
He asked again:
“Prince! Under whose instruction do you practice?”
He replied, "Devadatta. The gatekeepers deliberated together:
"What should be done? The first counselor said:
"All śramaṇas and the multitude of princes who take pleasure [in them] should all be killed."
The second counselor said:
"The Buddha has already sent Śāriputra to proclaim his wicked rebellion.
Why then do you wish to indiscriminately kill the śramaṇas?"
"The offense should properly fall upon only the Crown Prince and Devadatta!
The third proposal stated:
"We should not pass judgment on this offense rashly; we must report it to the King."
"The King has issued a command; we must carry it out.
Having deliberated thus, they reported this to the King.
The King asked:
"What are the opinions of you ministers?
They then answered him in full as above.
The king immediately banished the first counselor and dismissed the second from his office, while he honored the third counselor by increasing his rank and position.
He further commanded his ministers to deliberate together on this matter.

All the ministers said, "The first and second proposals are both deemed appropriate; yet the King has relinquished his own position, for we observe that His Majesty’s holy heart cannot bear to cause harm."
Since the administration of justice has already become lax, we should follow the lower plan:

the King established the Crown Prince as the heir to the state specifically so that he would quickly ascend the throne; because the Prince harbors this rebellious intent for the sake of hastening his own accession, if the King abdicates the throne to him, his evil will surely cease.
The proposal accorded with the king’s mind, and he immediately abdicated his throne, consecrating him as king and bestowing upon him the title Ajātaśatru.
Upon first ascending the throne, he indulged in the pleasures of the five senses, and his rebellious intent to kill subsided for a time;
yet after a short while, he took the life of his father without cause.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru possessed a great and wicked elephant. Devadatta went secretly to the elephant trainer and said to him: "Tomorrow Gautama shall travel this road;

you should, for my sake, intoxicate the elephant with drink and let it loose upon the path. The Buddha has much pride and will surely not avoid it; by means of this, trample and kill him, and I shall generously reward you with wealth."

On the following day at mealtime, the World-Honored One donned his robes and took up his bowl, entering the city with five hundred disciples to beg for food. The elephant trainer had previously given the elephant wine to intoxicate it; seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, he immediately released it.
Those who had faith and delight in the Buddha’s Dharma, seeing the intoxicated elephant being released, all went to inform the Buddha:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One may take another path!
The five hundred disciples and Ānanda also made this request in the same manner.
The Buddha answered him three times with these words: "Do not grieve!
The dragon will not harm me!"
The assembly of disciples all departed from the Buddha without realizing it, taking other routes;
only Ānanda followed behind alone.
At that time, spectators crowded in from all sides, each of them discussing:
"Now these two dragons are fighting; let us see who shall be victorious.
The followers of the external paths said, "The elephant-dragon possesses great strength and will surely defeat the human."
The Buddha’s disciple said, “The Way of the Human Dragon is honored; the elephant will surely be subdued.
Since the debate in the void offered no proof, they then gathered gold coins and wagered on who would win.
Thereupon, seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, the intoxicated elephant flared its ears and trumpeted through its trunk, charging directly toward him.
Ānanda, seized with terror, fell into a daze and unconsciously slipped beneath the Buddha’s arm.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"You have heard three times:
'There is no suffering.'"
"How is it that you do not believe, yet still harbor such fear?
Seeing the elephant approaching, the Buddha entered the Samādhi of Loving-kindness and spoke this verse:
"Do not harm the Great Dragon; the appearance of a Great Dragon in the world is rare."
"If one harms a great dragon, one will fall into the evil realms in a future life.

Having heard this verse, the elephant spread its trunk upon the ground and embraced the World-Honored One’s feet; for a moment it looked up and down at the Buddha three times, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then departed walking backward.
From that time forth, it became a virtuous elephant, and all marveled at its noble character, praising it with one voice:
“The śramaṇa Gautama has subdued these wicked elephants without using sword or staff; the people of the kingdom shall no longer have cause for fear.
How wonderful this is!
All the followers of the non-Buddhist paths were filled with shame, while the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples leaped for joy. They collected more than seven hundred thousand gold coins.
Once the Buddha had subdued the elephant, he further spoke these verses:
"The elephant, intoxicated and filled with rage, advanced toward the God among Gods.
The common people all came to watch, betting money on who would win."
His form is like Mount Tai; his strength surpasses that of sixty elephants.
His voice resounds, shaking the hearts of men; a single roar shatters the enemy ranks.
The Greatly Powerful One, God among Gods, has appeared in the world out of compassion for all beings.
Desiring to tame the wicked elephant, he stood directly before it;
as the elephant bowed down, all the people beheld it, and both monastics and laypeople leaped for joy.
They praised the Buddha for subduing the wicked elephant, just like a lion king.
When Devadatta saw this, he thought to himself:
"I cannot harm the Buddha by this means; I must seek out a wicked man who does not recognize the Buddha and entice him with generous bribes to go and kill him."
He immediately went out in the four directions to search for someone; seeing a strong man, he spoke to him, saying, "Kill the Buddha for me, and I shall reward you handsomely.
That man, coveting the wealth, accepted the commission and departed.

At that time, the World-Honored One was walking in meditation in the open air. Seeing that man from afar, he suffused his body with the samādhi of loving-kindness and raised his hand to call out to him.
Thereupon, the man unconsciously cast aside his blade and hurried toward the Buddha; bowing his head at the Buddha’s feet, he said to him:
"I was now deluded and mad, wishing to harm the World-Honored One."
"Realizing my own transgression is grave, I pray that you will grant me absolution through repentance!
The Buddha said,
"You are truly foolish!"
"How can you wish to harm the Tathāgata with wealth?
Within my Dharma, if one recognizes their transgressions and repents, their roots of goodness will increase.

He then preached the Dharma for him, namely: discourse on giving, discourse on morality, and discourse on rebirth in heaven; he spoke of the defilements and burdens of the household life, and how the path of renunciation is true happiness.
That person was inwardly joyful, and the Buddha, knowing his intention, further expounded the Dharma for him—namely, the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Upon hearing the Dharma, he attained understanding; amidst all phenomena, he became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Having seen the Dharma and attained the fruit, he took refuge in the Triple Gem and undertook the five precepts.
The World-Honored One dismissed him, and he returned by a different path.
Devadatta then recruited two more men, ordering them to kill the former man in order to silence the ill repute.
He again dispatched four men, and in this manner they proceeded in succession until thirty-two men had all gone before the Buddha.
The Buddha likewise preached the Dharma to them in successive order as before, and they all attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
When the bhikṣus heard that Devadatta had sent men to harm the Buddha, they all took up weapons to protect the World-Honored One; they formed divisions and took positions, each stationed on one side.

It is the constant practice of all Buddhas to emerge from their quarters twice a day; emerging in the early morning, he saw that the bhikṣus were all gathered to his left and right, and he asked them:
"For what reason do you stand here holding staves?"
The bhikṣus said:
"We have heard that Devadatta has sent men intending to harm the World-Honored One; unable to find peace ourselves, this is why we remain here.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If it were for the Tathāgata to die an untimely death, such a thing is impossible.
You five teachers of the world must simply guard yourselves!
I have no need of you; each of you may go wherever you please and protect your own minds!"
Having understood this, Devadatta thought again:
"I am still unable to harm the Buddha by this means; I shall seek out others and go with them myself, so that my purpose will surely be accomplished."
He immediately found one man who agreed to go up Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa with him.

At that time, the World-Honored One was walking up and down upon a rock at the foot of the mountain; Devadatta then sent that man to push the rock to harm the Buddha. When the man resolved to push the rock, his four limbs became unable to lift;
but because he had brought to mind the greatness of the Buddha’s merit, his hands and feet were restored.
Upon seeing this, Devadatta became even more enraged and said, "How can you be so clumsy? Disappear quickly!
He then personally seized a large rock and pushed it down to kill the Buddha.
There was a deity on the mountain named Kumbhīra who caught [the stone] and cast it far away; a fragment splintered and struck the Buddha, wounding his big toe.
Having seen this, the World-Honored One said to Devadatta:
"You have now incurred the karma of an immediate retribution."
"If one sheds the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind, one will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell of Uninterrupted Suffering.
Devadatta then thought again:
"Since I cannot harm the Buddha, I shall at least break his harmonious Saṃgha!"
"The Buddha possesses great supernormal power; if I can cause his Saṃgha to split, my fame will surely spread far and wide.
The Buddha, knowing his intention, said to Devadatta:
"Do not cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha!"
If the Sangha has already been split and one is able to reconcile them, that person will be reborn in heaven for one kalpa and experience joy;
if the Sangha is in harmony and one causes it to be split, they will fall into hell for one kalpa and experience suffering.
Having heard this, Devadatta temporarily abandoned that thought, but shortly thereafter he again gave rise to the same reflections as before.
The Buddha restrained him as previously, and then spoke these verses:
“The assembly rejoices in harmony; In harmony there is constant peace and security.”
If one causes a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha, one will suffer in hell for an eon;
When the assembly gathers in harmony, there is joy, and through harmony there is constant peace and security.
If one brings about harmony within a divided Saṃgha, one will experience the bliss of rebirth in heaven for an eon.
If one creates schisms through divisive speech, constantly uttering unwholesome words to break the harmony of the Saṃgha,
one will suffer the pains of hell for an eon; if one does not create schisms through divisive speech,
but is always able to speak the wholesome Dharma, [one will attain liberation].
"By causing a schism in the Saṃgha through conciliation, one will experience the bliss of rebirth in heaven for an eon.
Having heard this, Devadatta again temporarily abandoned this intention, but it soon arose once more, and his skillful means became even greater than before.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard that Devadatta intended to split the harmonious Saṃgha, went at once to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus; after reprimanding Devadatta from afar in various ways, he said to the bhikṣus:
"A single bhikṣu who is close and intimate with Devadatta should be appointed to go and admonish him, saying:"
"Do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not engage in acts that split the Saṃgha.

You should instead live in harmony with the Saṃgha; for when the Saṃgha is in harmony, it dwells in joy and without dispute, being of one mind and one training, like water and milk mixed together, so as to jointly propagate the Teacher’s instruction and practice in peace and happiness."
"If they accept it, that is well;
if they do not accept it, many bhikṣus should be sent;
if they still do not accept it, the Saṃgha should go to admonish them."
The bhikṣus received the instruction, yet after three such repetitions, none of them accepted it.
Having rebuked them in various ways, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. After reprimanding Devadatta at length in various ways from afar, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu exerts himself with skillful means to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, and the other bhikṣus say to that bhikṣu:'"

"Do not strive with skillful means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; you should instead be in harmony with the Saṃgha. Because the Saṃgha is in harmony, there will be joy and no contention; with one mind and one training, like water and milk blending together, you shall jointly propagate the Teacher’s instruction and dwell in peace and happiness."
If, despite being admonished in this manner, he persists and does not relinquish it, he should be admonished a second and a third time.
If, after the second and third admonitions, he relinquishes this matter, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"To cause a schism" means to seek the causes and conditions for a schism in the Saṃgha.
"To reconcile" means:
The same applies to the regular procedures of the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*,
and the *karmavācanā*.
"The Saṃgha" refers to a group of four or more persons.
If that bhikṣu desires to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, and the other monks see, hear, or know of it, they shall appoint one bhikṣu who is on friendly terms with him to go and admonish him;
if he then desists, he should perform one *duṣkṛta* confession.
If he does not relinquish it, many bhikṣus should be sent to admonish him;
if he relinquishes it, he should repent for two duṣkṛta offenses.
If he still does not relinquish it, the Saṃgha should go to admonish him.
If he relinquishes it, he should confess three *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If he does not relinquish it, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) should be performed to admonish him, with one bhikṣu declaring:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
"This bhikṣu, [name], has been diligently applying expedients to break up the harmonious Saṃgha; the Saṃgha has already admonished him, saying:
'Do not diligently apply expedients to break up the harmonious Saṃgha!'"
"Having been thus admonished, he persists and does not relinquish [his position].
The Saṃgha now proceeds with the formal act of admonition (karmavācanā).
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen."
"Thus it is announced.
Having made this announcement, one should say to that bhikṣu:
"The Saṃgha has finished the announcement; three karmas remain. You should relinquish this matter; do not commit a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
If he relinquishes it, he should confess three *duṣkṛta* offenses and one *sthūlātyaya*.
If he does not relinquish it, one should again proclaim:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is diligently applying expedient means to break the harmony of the Saṃgha; therefore, the Saṃgha now performs the formal act of admonition.
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
Furthermore, you should say to that bhikṣu:
"The Saṃgha has already completed one *karmavācanā*; two remain. You should relinquish this matter; do not commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
If he should relinquish [the matter], he must confess three *duṣkṛta* offenses and two *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If he does not relinquish it, one must again perform the second *karmavācanā* as above; once the second *karmavācanā* is completed, one must again speak as above.
If he relinquishes [the offense], he must confess three *duṣkṛta* and three *sthūlātyaya* offenses.

If he does not relinquish it, the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the second proclamation (*dvitīya-karman*) are to be performed again as above; if he relinquishes it before the third proclamation is completed, he must confess three *duṣkṛta* and three *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
Once the third proclamation is completed, whether he relinquishes it or not, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If the motion (jñapti) is not validly performed, all three karmavācanas are likewise invalid.
If one performs other *karmans*, obstructive *karmans*, or illegal *karmans*;
or if one does not admonish [the offender] but they relinquish [the offense] of their own accord—in all such cases, there is no violation. The ten matters are concluded.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣus who supported Devadatta said to the other bhikṣus:
"What Devadatta has spoken was spoken with knowledge, not without knowledge;
he spoke the Dharma, not what is not Dharma."
"We speak of what is the Vinaya and do not speak of what is not the Vinaya; all this is what our hearts accept and delight in.
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked them in various ways:
"How can you say:..."
"What Devadatta has spoken is spoken with knowledge, not without knowledge;
he speaks the Dharma, not what is non-Dharma;
he speaks the Vinaya, not what is non-Vinaya; all of this is what our hearts accept and delight in."
Having rebuked him, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. After he had censured the bhikṣu who supported Devadatta in various ways from afar, he said to the bhikṣus:
"A single bhikṣu who is intimate with the bhikṣu supporting Devadatta should be appointed to go and admonish him."
"Do not say: 'What Devadatta has spoken is spoken with knowledge, not without knowledge;
he speaks the Dharma, not what is not the Dharma;'"
"To speak of what is in accordance with the Vinaya and not to speak of what is contrary to the Vinaya—this is precisely what our hearts accept and delight in. Why is this?
Because Devadatta does not speak with knowledge, does not speak the Dharma, and does not speak the Vinaya.
"You all must not assist in breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha; you should instead assist in bringing about its harmony.

Because the Saṃgha is harmonious, it is joyful and free from strife; with one mind and one training, like water and milk blending together, you shall collectively propagate the Teacher’s instruction and dwell in peace and happiness."
"If they accept it, that is well;
if they do not accept it, you should dispatch many bhikṣus and the Saṃgha to go and admonish them.
The bhikṣus received these instructions and acted accordingly three times, yet the bhikṣu Devadatta and his supporters all refused to comply.
After the bhikṣus had rebuked him in various ways, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus; having further rebuked the bhikṣu who supported Devadatta from afar in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows: [The precept text follows]"
"If a bhikṣu assists in the schism of a harmonious Saṃgha—whether it be one, two, or many—and says to the other bhikṣus:
'What this bhikṣu speaks is spoken with knowledge, not without knowledge;
he speaks the Dharma, not what is not Dharma;'"
"To speak of what is in accordance with the Vinaya and not to speak of what is contrary to the Vinaya—all this is what our hearts accept and delight in.
Then those bhikṣus said to the other bhikṣus:
"Do not speak such words as these:"
"What this bhikṣu has spoken is spoken with knowledge, not without knowledge;
he speaks the Dharma, not what is non-Dharma;
he speaks the Vinaya, not what is non-Vinaya—all of which is approved and welcomed by our own minds."
Why is this? This bhikṣu does not speak with knowledge, nor does he speak the Dharma, nor does he speak the Vinaya.
You must not take pleasure in assisting in the breaking of the harmony of the Saṃgha; you should instead take pleasure in assisting in the reconciliation of the Saṃgha.

"Because the Saṃgha is in harmony, it is joyful and free from strife; with one mind and one training, they are like water and milk mixed together, jointly propagating the Teacher’s instruction and practicing in peace and happiness.
If, despite being admonished in this way, he persists and does not relinquish his position, a second and third admonition should be given.
If, after a second and third admonition, he abandons this matter, it is well;
if he does not abandon it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"One who assists in causing a schism" refers to:
This assists in forming the conditions for causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
"Harmony" refers to performing the Poṣadha and the Pravāraṇā together.
If one sends a close and trustworthy person to offer counsel, and [the offender] relinquishes [the offense], there is one *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for the act of regretting.
This continues up to the case where they relinquish it on their own without being counseled; all these cases are as explained above, ending with the eleventh.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the bhikṣu Chanda repeatedly committed offenses:

he entered the houses of laypeople, mounting and dismounting from his bed in an improper manner; he ate separately from the community, ate at frequent intervals, and entered villages at inappropriate times without informing the virtuous bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus saw him and said to him:
“You have committed such and such an offense; you should recognize your fault and repent.
Do not remain impure, for if you do not cultivate the holy life, you will suffer various afflictions for a long night.”
"Do not cause the donor to lose great merit.
He replied, "Venerable Sir!"
"You should not instruct me; rather, I should instruct you. Why is this?
The Noble Teacher, the Dharma King, is my master; the Dharma originates from me, and there is no need for the Venerable Ones to interfere."
It is like a great wind that blows various weeds and filth together into one place.
So it is with you, Venerable Ones, who have gone forth from various lineages, various families, and various countries; how can you wish to instruct me?
"Venerable sirs!
Do not speak to me of what is good or bad;
nor shall I speak to you, venerable sirs, of what is good or bad."
The bhikṣus spoke again to Chanda:
"Do not act as one who is self-centered and refuses to converse with others!
You ought to speak to the bhikṣus whether it be good or bad;..."
The bhikṣus should also speak to you regarding what is wholesome or unwholesome.
In this way, by instructing one another and successively helping each other emerge from offenses, the Saṃgha of the Tathāgata is formed.
When the bhikṣus had admonished him in this way, he remained obstinate and would not relinquish his position. They took him to the Buddha’s presence and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Chanda:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways: "You foolish man!

You should not engage in such speech that makes one unfit for communal discourse. When the bhikṣus see you commit an offense, they wish to exclude you from the common practices of the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, and the *karmavācanā* ceremonies."
"Out of compassion for you, I have rebuked and admonished you.
Why do you now refuse to believe and accept [my words]?
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus: "A single bhikṣu who is on friendly terms with Chanda should be appointed to go and admonish him as previously described."
Next, many bhikṣus [were instructed], and next the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus received the instruction three times, yet they did not accept it; they reported this matter to the Buddha.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus. After having further rebuked Chanda from afar in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu is of evil character and difficult to speak with, and having studied the sūtras and vinaya together with the other bhikṣus, repeatedly commits offenses.'"
When the bhikṣus admonish him for his transgression in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, he replies:
"Venerable sirs!
Do not speak to me of what is good or what is evil;..."
"I shall not address you with either pleasant or unpleasant words.
The bhikṣus spoke to him again, saying:
"Do not act as if you are someone with whom we cannot converse!"
"You should speak in accordance with the Dharma for the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus should also speak in accordance with the Dharma for you;
in this way, through mutual instruction and mutual purification from offenses, you shall constitute the Saṃgha of the Tathāgata."
If, after being admonished in this manner, he persists and does not relinquish it, he should be admonished a second and a third time.
If, after the second and third admonitions, he relinquishes this matter, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"Of evil disposition and difficult to converse with" means:
they do not accept instruction, lack a heart of reverence,
and consider themselves right while deeming others wrong.
Regarding "those who study the sūtras and precepts together":
"sūtra" refers to all the Buddha's teachings;
"precept" refers to the Prātimokṣa.
If one sends a close and trusted person to offer admonition, and [the offender] relinquishes [the offense], there is one *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for the regret.
This continues up to the case where they relinquish it on their own without being admonished; all is as explained above. [Section 12 ends.]
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there were two bhikṣus in the village of Killa: one named Aṭṭhika and the other named Puṇṇa. They frequently committed evil deeds and defiled the families of others, engaging in various forms of improper conduct:
they themselves wove flower garlands and also taught others how to weave them.
They wear [ornaments] themselves and teach others to wear them;
they sit on the same bed with women and eat from the same plate as them;
they drink alcohol, eat meat, and engage in singing, dancing, and music.
They produce the various cries of birds and beasts, and even manifest the appearances of birds and beasts quarreling;
they gamble, play, walk backward, leap about, snap their fingers, and wink;

they contort their faces toward women, protrude their tongues, and gape their mouths—performing such evils of body, speech, and mind, thereby violating their precepts, views, deportment, and right livelihood.

At that time, five hundred bhikṣus, fully endowed with dignified deportment, came from the kingdom of Kāśī to this town. When it was time, they took their bowls and entered the village to beg for food.
Upon seeing them, the lay devotees all said:
"From where have these bhikṣus come?"
He bowed his head in silence, appearing like a filial son, not knowing how to engage others in conversation.
"I have here two worthy bhikṣus who are versatile and skilled in many arts, capable of delighting the hearts of men."
"What use have we for these people lingering in this village?
They gave them no food at all, and they departed with empty bowls.
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were also traveling from Kāśī toward this village.
Upon hearing this, Aṭṭhi and the others thought to themselves:
"These two men have come; they will surely bring ill repute upon us and cut off our offerings.
They then went to the lay devotees and said:
"In a moment, two bhikṣus will arrive: one named Maudgalyāyana, who is skilled in the arts of illusion and manifests various transformations;
the other named Śāriputra, who is skilled in the methods of incantations and uses clever speech to delude people."
"If you are of one mind and are not deluded by them, I shall remain here;
if you cannot do so, I shall depart this very moment.
The householders said:
"Elder Anurādha, I shall never again be deluded by him.
When the two had arrived, all the lay devotees, both young and old, went out to meet them, exchanged greetings, prostrated themselves at their feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Thereupon Maudgalyāyana manifested his supernatural powers:
he divided his body into hundreds and thousands, then merged them back into one;
he passed through stone walls as if they were open space, and walked upon water as if it were solid ground.
Sitting or reclining in mid-air like a bird in flight;
reaching the Brahma Heaven with his body and touching the sun and moon with his hand;
emitting fire from the upper part of his body and water from the lower part of his body.
Water issued from his upper body and fire issued from his lower body;
he manifested either half his body or his entire body;
he leaped up in the east and sank down in the west, or leaped up in the west and sank down in the east.
He rose in the south and sank in the north; he rose in the north and sank in the south;
he rose in the center and sank at the edges; he rose at the edges and sank in the center.
Having manifested these miraculous transformations, he returned to his original seat.
At that time, the lay devotees whispered among themselves, saying, "Maudgalyāyana is skilled in the arts of illusion; this must indeed be so!

Thereupon, Śāriputra expounded for them the sublime Dharma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing, perfectly pure, the very character of the holy life (brahmacarya).
Having spoken this Dharma, he remained silent.
At that time, the lay devotees also said to one another:
"Śāriputra truly knows the methods of incantation, and they have also proven effective!"
Thereupon, the multitude did not believe or accept [his words], and none made offerings.
At that time, there were two upāsakas in that town:

one named Puṣya and the other named Uruvilvā. They had faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma, had seen the Truth and attained the fruit, and always delighted in practicing charity and making offerings to śramaṇas.
