The Three Indeterminate Rules (A-ni-ting-fa), Part One, Section Three: The Indeterminate Rules. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, Upananda frequently visited the home of a certain lay devotee. In the morning, having dressed and taken his bowl, he went to the house, spread out his sitting mat, and sat alone in a secluded spot with the laywoman, speaking coarse and vulgar words concerning sexual desire.
At that time, Visākhā Migāramātā heard that Upananda was sitting alone in a secluded place with the wife of a householder, speaking coarse and vulgar words regarding sexual desire.
She thought to herself: "If the householder returns and sees this, he will surely conceive ill-will toward other bhikṣus, causing them to suffer various pains for a long night;
I should send someone to inform the World-Honored One."
He then said to the brahmin Nalinda, who had been his constant attendant:
"Go to the Buddha, prostrate yourself at his feet, and report this matter in detail."
The brahmin immediately went to inform the Buddha; after the Buddha had preached various sublime dharmas for him, he sent him back.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways as described in the section on sexual misconduct, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish an *aniyata-dharma* for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded place, a place suitable for sexual intercourse.'"
If a trustworthy female lay follower sees [an offense] among the three categories of dharma, she shall state each specific dharma:
whether it is a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu says,
"It is as the upāsikā has said," he should be dealt with according to the rule among the three dharmas that corresponds to what she has said.
This is called an indeterminate rule (*aniyata-dharma*). "Alone" means:
one bhikṣu and one woman, with no third person present.
"A secluded place" means a place where one cannot be seen by the eyes.
"Trustworthy" means:
Having seen the Four Noble Truths, one does not utter false speech for the sake of oneself, for others, or for gain.
An upāsikā is one who has received the three refuges and has severed the path of heterodoxy.
Regarding the indeterminate cases:
if, among three matters, one matter is mentioned, the senior bhikṣus should ask that bhikṣu:
"Did you go to that house?"
If he says, "I shall go," one should not yet administer the disciplinary action.
Furthermore, one should ask with gentle words:
"Did you sit alone in a secluded place with a woman, speak coarse and wicked words, or engage in sexual intercourse? If he says:
"No! The senior and junior bhikṣus should question him with urgent words:
"Speak the truth; do not speak falsely!"
"Is it as the upāsikā has said? If he says,
"It is as the upāsikā has said."
Thereafter, one should deal with him according to the rule as prescribed.
For a śrāmaṇera, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
The second indeterminate rule: sitting with a woman in an exposed place; except for the case of a pārājika offense, all else is as explained above.
"Exposed place" means a place visible to the eye. 4.
The Rules on Forfeiture (Naiḥsargika-pāyattika-dharma). The *Pañcavargīya-vinaya*, First Division, Part Four: The Rules on Forfeiture. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the World-Honored One instructed the bhikṣus to possess only three robes; yet the group of six bhikṣus wore different robes before meals, after meals, and in the late afternoon.
The bhikṣus saw them and asked,
"Did you not hear that the World-Honored One has prohibited the keeping of extra robes?
They replied:

"I have also heard this; however, these robes of mine were obtained either from among the Sangha, or from lay devotees, or they were discarded rags (pāṃsukūla). Because they gave them to me for the purpose of wearing them, they did not originally intend for me to keep them as property for the five families."
The bhikṣus rebuked them in various ways and led them to the Buddha’s presence, reporting the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
“Is it true that you did so?”
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked them in various ways:
"Have you not heard that I have previously praised having few desires and being content, wearing robes only to cover the body and eating only enough to sustain life?"
"Just as the feathers and plumage of various birds follow them wherever they go, so it is with a bhikṣu: his three robes are always with him.
Why do you now amass things that are contrary to the Dharma?"
Having rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu keeps an extra robe for more than one night, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.'"
At that time, if any of the bhikṣus required a single robe, the Saṃgha would perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) and give them the portion of goods they were entitled to.
At that time, Aniruddha’s robes were coarse, worn out, and tattered. The bhikṣus said to him, “Your robes are worn out;
why do you not take some from the Saṃgha to have them made, so that they may be finished in a single day?”
Aniruddha said, “I dare not accept it,
for I fear that it will not be completed in a single day, which would lead me to commit an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
At that time, the bhikṣus of the city of Pāṭaliputra came to Śrāvastī, intending to enter the later retreat (*paścimavarṣā*).
The time had passed and he was unable to arrive; thus, he took up residence for the rains retreat at the village of Sāvatthī.

When the retreat was concluded, on the sixteenth day he proceeded toward the Buddha’s location. On the way, he encountered muddy water, and his three robes were heavy and cumbersome, leaving him utterly exhausted.
Upon arrival, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Were you in harmony during the retreat? Was there no lack of almsfood? And were you not fatigued by the journey? They replied:
"The rains retreat was harmonious, and we had no lack of almsfood.

We previously resided in the village of Pāṭalī and wished to come here for the retreat; however, because many of our acquaintances were unable to depart early, we intended to join the later session but failed to do so. Consequently, we remained at Sāvatthī and entered the retreat there."
"When the rains retreat was concluded, he came on the sixteenth day; having traveled through muddy waters, his three robes were heavy and coarse, and he was utterly exhausted.
Because of this, the bhikṣus reported Āniruddha’s situation to the Buddha in full detail.

On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having praised fewness of desires and contentment, and having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit the acceptance of the kaṭhina robe; by doing so, one shall not incur offenses regarding five matters:
first, eating in a separate group;..."
Second, eating repeatedly;
third, going to other households before or after a meal without informing the other bhikṣus;
fourth, keeping extra robes.
"Fifth, one may stay apart from one's lodgings without losing the three robes.
At that time, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Since the Buddha has permitted the keeping of extra robes upon accepting the kaṭhina cloth, for how long is this allowed?"
Having reflected thus, he informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to keep [the robe] when the kaṭhina cloth is being received."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, having finished making his three robes and having relinquished the kaṭhina cloth, keeps an extra robe for more than one night, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika."
At that time, Ānanda received two pieces of kappāsa cloth for the sake of Śāriputra.
Since Śāriputra was staying in another location, Ānanda thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One does not permit the keeping of extra robes beyond one night; yet Śāriputra is not here now—what should be done with this?"
Having reflected thus, he addressed the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"In how many days will Śāriputra return?"
He replied, "Either ten days, or less than ten days.

For this reason, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus; having praised fewness of desires and contentment in various ways, and having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, having finished his three robes and having relinquished the kaṭhina cloth, keeps an extra robe for up to ten days;
if he exceeds that limit, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).'"
"Having finished the three robes" means having finished washing, dyeing, and sewing them.
"Relinquishing the kaṭhina robe" means:
It is relinquished through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation).
"Long" refers to anything other than the three robes; all such items are termed "long."
"Garments" refers to:
cotton garments, *kambala* garments, wild silk garments, *śāṇa* (hemp) garments, and flaxen garments.
"Ten days" means:
If one obtains a robe on a certain day, it should be relinquished on that very day—either by formally accepting it, giving it to another, or making it a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*).
If it is not relinquished on that day, and one obtains another robe on the second day, both should be relinquished on this [second] day.
If they are not relinquished on this day, and one obtains further robes on the third day up to the tenth day, all of them must likewise be relinquished on this [tenth] day.
If one does not relinquish it by this day, then when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, all robes obtained during the ten days constitute *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses.

If one possesses a robe that has been kept for more than ten days, it should be relinquished to the community of bhikṣus, or to one, two, or three bhikṣus; it must not be relinquished to others or to non-humans.
Only after it has been relinquished may one then perform the confession of the transgression.
If one does not relinquish [the extra robe] but merely confesses the transgression, the offense becomes even more grave.
With the exception of the three long robes, if one keeps any other extra robes—even down to a hand-towel—beyond ten days, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) in all cases.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If it is a pure gift (viśuddha-dāna), there is no offense in any of these cases. Thus ends the section.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, after the seventeen groups of bhikṣus had completed their summer retreat, they wished to travel abroad and thought to themselves:
"We shall return here soon; one robe will suffice for us—why do we need many?"
Having had this thought, he immediately wrapped his remaining robes in a bundle, placed them on a rack, entrusted them to the resident bhikṣu, and departed.
Later, when the group of six bhikṣus returned from another place, they said to the resident bhikṣu:
"Assign us a room."

At that time, the resident bhikṣus assigned the robe-closets that the group of seventeen had set up to them. When the group of six bhikṣus saw the robes upon the racks, they asked, "For what reason do you keep these extra robes?"

He replied, “These belong to the group of seventeen bhikṣus who, having completed their summer retreat, were traveling through the countryside; they were unable to carry them with them and left them as a deposit with me!”
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of seventeen bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked them in various ways:
"You are foolish! Have you not heard what I have said?
"Should a bhikṣu not be accompanied by his three robes and alms bowl?
Is it as when a bird flies, its feathers and wings follow along of their own accord?
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣu, having finished his three robes and having relinquished the kaṭhina cloth, should remain separated from any one of his three robes for even one night, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.'"

At that time, there was a pāṃśukūlika bhikṣu who wished to go toward the town of Sāketa; however, his robes were so heavy that he could not carry them away. Wishing to discard them, he did not know what to do, and thus he informed the bhikṣus of this matter.
The bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was and reported the matter to him.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:

"If a bhikṣu possesses heavy discarded robes (pāṃśukūla) and wishes to travel to another region but is unable to carry them, that bhikṣu should request from the Saṃgha the formal act of 'not losing the robes' (acīvarāsaṃsarga-karman)."
He removed his leather sandals, prostrated with his head at [the monk's] feet, knelt on his right knee with palms joined, and spoke these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], wish to travel to such-and-such a place; however, my refuse-rag robe is too heavy to carry, and I wish to leave it behind."
"I now request from the Saṃgha the *karmavācanā* for not losing one's robe.
Having thus requested a second and third time, a single bhikṣu within the Saṃgha proclaims:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, wishes to travel to such-and-such a place; however, his refuse-rag robes are heavy and he cannot carry them with him, so he wishes to leave them behind.
He now requests from the Saṃgha the *akopya-cīvara-karman* (the formal act of not losing one's robe).
Now the Sangha shall perform the *akopya-cīvara-karman* (the formal act of not losing one's robe) for him.
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha listen with patience.
The motion is as follows.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, wishes to travel to such-and-such a place; however, his robes made of discarded rags are heavy and he cannot carry them with him, so he wishes to leave them behind.
He now requests from the Saṃgha the *akopyacīvara-kamma* (the formal act of not losing one's robe)."
Now the Sangha shall perform the *akopya-cīvara-karman* (the formal act of not losing one's robe) for [the monk].
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has already completed the *akopya-cīvara-karman* for the bhikṣu so-and-so;
the Sangha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.

At that time, when the bhikṣus saw that the World-Honored One had permitted the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of being separated from one’s robes, they constantly performed the formal act to remain apart from their robes overnight; they even performed the formal act to be entirely separated from their three robes, traveling about wearing only tattered and worn-out garments.
An elder bhikṣu saw him and asked,
"For what reason are you walking about wearing such tattered and worn-out robes? He replied:

"The Buddha has permitted the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of being separated from one's robes; therefore, we constantly perform the formal act of staying overnight apart from our robes, and we even perform the formal act of being entirely separated from all three robes.
The bhikṣus rebuked them in various ways and led them to the presence of the Buddha, reporting the matter to him.
The Buddha said:

"You should not, by means of a formal act (karmavācanā), habitually stay overnight separated from your robes, nor should you, by means of a formal act, completely separate yourselves from the three robes.
These two are illegal formal acts; for both the bhikṣu and the Saṃgha, they constitute two *duṣkṛta* offenses."
By means of this formal act (*karmavācanā*), one may stay apart from one's robes overnight; however, for each robe and each night so spent, one incurs the offense of losing the robe.

Now, it is permitted for the bhikṣus to perform a formal act to retain their robes: those who enter the earlier retreat (*pūrvavarṣā*) may do so for nine months, and those who enter the later retreat (*paścimavarṣā*) for eight months.
One is not permitted to perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) to retain the *saṃghāṭī* or the *antarvāsaka*; however, it is permitted to perform a formal ritual to retain the *uttarāsaṅga*.

In places where there is the danger of bandits, whichever of the three robes is made of cut-and-sewn cloth (*khaṇḍika*) and is most excellent, it is permitted to retain it according to the circumstances.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

"If a bhikṣu, having finished making his three robes and having relinquished the *kaṭhina* robe, should be separated from any one of the three robes for even one night, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha (*saṃgha-karman*), it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

Regarding "being separated from one's robe": there are common boundaries and distinct boundaries for gardens; common boundaries and distinct boundaries for houses; common boundaries and distinct boundaries for bhikṣuṇī-vihāras; common boundaries and distinct boundaries for villages; common boundaries and distinct boundaries for multi-storied buildings; common boundaries and distinct boundaries for vehicles; common boundaries and distinct boundaries for boats; common boundaries and distinct boundaries for threshing floors; common boundaries and distinct boundaries for areas under trees; and common boundaries and distinct boundaries for open spaces or walking paths.
Regarding those within the same boundary:
when the Saṃgha has performed a *karmavācanā* to establish a "boundary for not losing one's robe," one may move freely back and forth within it.
Regarding those in different boundaries:
The Saṃgha does not perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to establish a "boundary for not losing robes" (*acīvarāpattisīmā*);
even if such an act were performed, one would not be permitted to come and go within it at will.
The same applies to houses, bhikṣuṇī-vihāras, villages, and multi-storied buildings.
Regarding those belonging to the same realm:
one attains mastery over them, whether in taking them up or setting them down.
Regarding those belonging to a different realm:
Within it, one does not have mastery over taking up or lifting [objects].
A boat is also like this. Regarding "the same boundary" for a threshing floor:
In places where one treads upon grain or barley, one may take them at will;
in other realms, one may not take them at will.
"Under the same boundary among trees" refers to the area covered by the shade of the tree.
"Different boundaries" refers to:
Regarding "a place not covered by tree shade" and "the same boundary on open ground":
when sitting cross-legged, the face is seven feet away [from the edge].
"Another realm" refers to beyond seven feet.
"Practicing the Way within the same realm" refers to:
The face is seven bow-lengths from the body.
"A different realm" means beyond those seven bow-lengths.
When the dawn light appears, if a bhikṣu returns to the boundary—even if only one foot has entered the boundary—he does not lose his robe.
If he says with his mouth:
"I relinquish this robe."
Nor does he lose the robe;
however, if he does not formally relinquish it and the dawn appears, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
For a monk, apart from his three robes, to stay overnight separated from any other garment he uses constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense. These two matters are concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had finished preparing their three robes and had relinquished the kaṭhina cloth, they obtained out-of-season robes (akālacīvara).
The bhikṣus felt ashamed and said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept out-of-season robes."
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you received out-of-season robes and felt ashamed, saying:..."
"Has the Buddha not yet permitted us to accept out-of-season robes?
They replied, "That is indeed so."
"World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had praised having few desires and being content, praised the precepts, and praised the upholding of the precepts in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit you to accept out-of-season robes."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus thought to themselves:
“The World-Honored One has permitted us to accept out-of-season robes.
Thereupon, they accepted many, yet they did not maintain them, nor did they give them away, nor did they perform the ritual of formal dedication.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they asked,
"Have you not heard that the World-Honored One has established a precept forbidding the keeping of extra robes?
They replied:
"Although the Buddha has prohibited the keeping of extra robes, he has permitted the acceptance of out-of-season robes.
He asked again,
"Do you all keep out-of-season robes at all times without formally receiving them, without giving them to others, and without performing the ritual of pure donation?"
He replied, "It is so!
The elder bhikṣus rebuked him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: "It is true."
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"You foolish person! You should not seek much or have many desires.
In the teachings of the non-Buddhists, the recipient never tires of receiving, while the donor calculates [the cost]."
"In my True Dharma, one should have few desires and be content; though the giver may never tire of giving, the receiver should take but little.
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu obtains an out-of-season robe and does not accept it for his own use, nor give it to another, nor perform a formal act of dedication (pariṇāmanā), even for a single night, it is a duṣkṛta offense."

At that time, at a certain residence, the monks obtained a great quantity of robes; they accepted them, gave some away to others, made formal dedications (*pariṇāmana*), and offered the remaining pieces to the other monks.
The bhikṣus did not accept it, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept incomplete robes. They said:
"Accept it for now; we shall make it sufficient.
At that time, the Elder Gavī obtained a narrow and short garment, which he stretched and pulled every day, wishing to make it wide and long.
The Buddha was in the habit of inspecting the various rooms every five days. Seeing Gavī pulling at his robe, he asked, "What are you doing? He replied:
"This robe you have obtained is small; you may not accept and keep it.
The Buddha asked again, "Do you still expect to obtain more robes?"
He replied, "There is. He asked again:
"When can it be obtained? He replied,
"In one month, or less than a month."
The Buddha, having praised fewness of desires and contentment in various ways, and having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit you to keep out-of-season robes."
"If it is insufficient, we hope it will suffice until the end of one month.
Once the Buddha had permitted the keeping of non-seasonal robes that were insufficient, the bhikṣus took these robes and traveled about for more than a month.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they asked,
"The Buddha has not permitted the keeping of extra robes that are not sufficient for one's needs beyond one month.
Why do you carry these robes about while traveling for more than a month?"
Having rebuked him in various ways, they brought him to the presence of the Buddha and reported the matter to him.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

"If a bhikṣu, having finished the three robes and having relinquished the kaṭhina cloth, obtains an out-of-season robe, he should accept it if he needs it, and quickly make it into a robe to be worn."
If it is sufficient, that is well;
if it is insufficient, one may look for further means to obtain more so as to complete it, even for up to one month.
If this period is exceeded, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Out-of-season robe-cloth" refers to any robe-cloth obtained after the kaṭhina has been relinquished; all such items are termed out-of-season robe-cloth.
"In need" means:
If any of the three robes is worn out, it must be mended or replaced.
Regarding the hope of obtaining more:
one may have further places from which to obtain robes, hoping to receive them within one day or even up to one month.

If a bhikṣu obtains an incomplete robe on one day and has hope that it will be completed by that same day, he should accept it, give it away, or perform a formal act of purification (pariṇāmana) if it is obtained;
if he does not accept it, does not give it away, and does not perform the formal act of purification, then when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The same applies for two days, up to ten days. On the eleventh day, there is still hope;
if it is obtained, one should complete the requisite on that very day by receiving and keeping it, giving it to another, or performing a formal purification (*pariṣkāra-dāna*).

If one does not accept it, does not give it to another, or does not perform a formal relinquishment (*viśuddhi-dāna*), until the appearance of the dawn light on the twelfth day, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
This applies likewise up to the thirtieth day.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. [The third section ends.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, in the town of Ujjayinī, there was a young householder who went out for recreation and saw a woman named Utpalavarṇā, whose complexion was like the color of a peach blossom and who was endowed with all feminine graces;
feeling mutual respect and affection, he immediately took her as his wife.
A short while later, his wife became pregnant; he sent her back to her own home, and when the months were complete, she gave birth to a daughter.
Because his wife was in confinement following childbirth, he could not approach her, so he subsequently engaged in illicit relations with his mother-in-law.

Utpalavarṇā, having realized this, wished to entrust her to others and sever the bonds of marriage; yet, fearing she would bring trouble upon her parents and out of compassion for the infant, she swallowed her shame and returned to her husband’s home.
She raised the girl for eight years before finally departing.
Upon arriving at Vārāṇasī, he sat by the water’s edge, utterly exhausted by hunger and thirst.

At that time, a certain elder was out on an excursion and, seeing him, felt a profound affection. He immediately asked about his native place, his parents, and his clan, and why he was now here alone, belonging to no one?
Utpalavarṇā said, "I am a woman of such-and-such a family; at present, I belong to no one.
The elder asked again:
"If you have no one to belong to, could you become my principal wife?
She replied, "A woman already has a husband; why should it not be possible?"
He immediately took her back on the carriage and installed her as his principal wife.
Utpalavarṇā managed the household, bringing harmony to all members of the family; husband and wife held each other in high esteem for eight years.
At that time, the elder said to his wife:
"I have a loan outstanding in the town of Ujjayanī which I have not yet collected for eight years now; when calculated for interest and growth, it has reached the sum of one hundred million."
"Now I wish to go collect a debt, which will cause us to part for a short while.

His wife said, "The customs in that town are such that women are licentious; if you go there, you might lose your manly integrity. As for wealth and property, they are but dung and soil—what is there to be reckoned with?"
He replied, "Though I am short-sighted and ignorant, I have not reached such a state of confusion.
The wife spoke again:
"If you must certainly depart, I wish to hear a single vow.
He replied, "Very well!"
He then said, "If I give rise to this thought, it shall perish along with my mindfulness, even as I return through the gate.
Thereupon, he went elsewhere to that town; as there were many places where debts were to be collected, he remained there for years.
Having been away from home for a long time, his longing for his wife grew ever deeper, and he thought to himself:
"How can I avoid violating my former vow while yet fulfilling my present desire?"
He further thought to himself:
"If I were to engage in sexual misconduct, I would betray my original vow;
however, taking another wife does not constitute a violation of that commitment."

Thereupon, he made inquiries and encountered a woman of elegant and exquisite countenance, whose gaze was never fickle; feeling a profound sense of respect and affection for her, he went to propose marriage.
Because the father recognized his talent, wisdom, and great wealth, he joyfully granted it to him.
Once the debts had been fully settled, he was about to return to his native country; he first established himself in a separate residence before finally departing.
He went out in the morning and returned in the evening, which was different from how it had been before; Utpalavarṇā found this strange and secretly questioned his attendants.
The attendants replied, "There is a young woman outside, and for this reason he acts in this manner."
When her husband returned in the evening, Utpalavarṇā asked him:
"My lord, you have a new wife; why do you conceal her and not let me see her? He replied:
"I feared you might resent me, and for that reason I remained outside.
The wife said, "I have no jealousy;
the divine spirits bear witness to this. You may call me back at once to assist you in managing the household."
He immediately returned it, and it was indeed his daughter.
When mother and child met, they did not recognize one another; later, while washing her head, he observed her features closely and began to suspect she was his daughter.
He then questioned her regarding her native village, her parents, and her clan. The girl answered him in full detail, and only then did he know her for certain.
The mother, filled with alarm and lamentation, said:
"In the past, I shared a husband with my mother; now, I share a son-in-law with my daughter. Life and death have become so bewildering that we have reached this state!
If one does not sever craving and desire to leave the household life and study the Way, how can such perverse delusion ever come to rest?"
She then left him and went to the gate of the Jetavana. Exhausted by hunger and thirst, she sat down beneath a tree.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an immeasurable multitude as he preached the Dharma. Seeing many people coming and going in and out, Utpalavarṇā thought it must be a festival where food and drink would be available, so she entered the monastery.
Seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, preaching the Dharma for the assembly, they heard the teaching and attained understanding, whereby their hunger and thirst were extinguished.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One surveyed the entire gathering to see who was ready to be delivered;

seeing that only Utpalavarṇā was ready to attain the fruit of the Path, he immediately preached for her the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. At once, while sitting there, she became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Having attained the fruit, she stood before the Buddha with her palms joined in single-minded devotion.
When the Buddha had finished preaching the Dharma, the assembly dispersed; Padmāvatī then prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Within the Buddha’s Dharma, I pray that I may attain renunciation.”
The Buddha granted her request and told the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī:
"You may now ordain this girl as a follower of the Way.
Following these instructions, she was immediately ordained, received the precepts, and through diligent and energetic practice, she eventually attained arhatship.
Having attained arhatship, she sported in the various dhyānas and liberations; her countenance radiated such brilliance that it was twice as superior as it had been before.
When the time came, she took her bowl and entered the city to beg for food. A certain brāhmaṇa, seeing her, felt a sense of attachment and thought to himself:
"This bhikṣuṇī cannot be won over now; I must find her dwelling place and devise a skillful means to pursue her."

After Utpalavarṇā had finished her almsround, she returned to the Andhavana grove and entered her dwelling; the brahmin followed after her and observed her, thereby discovering her place of residence.
Later, when the time arrived, she went out again to beg for alms; that brahmin then slipped inside and hid beneath her bed.
On this day, the bhikṣuṇīs spent the entire night preaching the Dharma, and upon returning to their quarters, they were so utterly exhausted that they lay down and fell into a deep sleep.
Thereupon, the brahmin emerged from beneath the bed and engaged in unchaste conduct; the bhikṣuṇī immediately became aware of it and leaped up into the air.
At that moment, the brahmin, still upon the bed, was born directly into hell while alive.
Utpalavarṇā, having traveled through the air from there to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated with her head at his feet and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked:
"At that time, what were your thoughts?"
He replied, “It is like being scorched by burning iron.
The Buddha said:
"It is thus without offense.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If one stays alone overnight, would there be an offense?"
The Buddha said,
"One who has attained the Way commits no offense.
At that time, there was a band of thieves who gathered together and deliberated, saying:
"We should divide our goods at some location where we can exchange them for fine food and obtain beautiful garments.

They all said, "This Anāthapiṇḍika Garden is the residence of bhikṣuṇīs; there must be beautiful garments and there will surely be many offerings of superior quality. If we go there to divide our goods, we will certainly obtain what we desire."
At that time, the leader of those bandits, who had faith and delight in the Buddha-dharma, was displeased upon hearing this and immediately thought to himself:
"These people will surely harass and disturb the bhikṣuṇīs; I shall secretly dispatch one person to go ahead and inform them."
He then sent her away, saying to the bhikṣuṇī:
"In the evening, wicked men will surely come; I fear they will certainly trouble you, so please take your leave."
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they immediately entered the city of Śrāvastī.

A great minister of that city had previously donated a residence to the community of bhikṣus, but no monks were residing there; the bhikṣuṇīs arrived in the evening and went there to stay for the night.
At that time, the bandits entered the Andhavana grove at night but saw nothing at all; the leader of the bandits thought with joy:
"That the bhikṣuṇīs have escaped this peril—how delightful!"
She then took her finest upper garment, filled it with the most excellent food and drink, both raw and cooked, and hung it upon a tree branch, thinking:
"If there be any bhikṣuṇī who has attained the Way and supernormal powers, may she take this food and clothing."
Thereupon, in the time it takes a strong man to flex and extend his arm, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā went from Śrāvastī to the tree in the Andhavana grove and took it.
On the following day at mealtime, he prepared the food he had obtained as an offering for the elder Upasena and Baddhālī.

When the time arrived, they both went; he served them various kinds of food, and once they had finished eating, he provided water for washing. He then took a small seat and sat before the assembly, requesting that they preach the sublime Dharma.
Having finished preaching the Dharma to Upasena, he rose from his seat and departed.
Vāḍananda remained behind and said to Utpalavarṇā, "Sister!..."
"From where did you obtain this fine food?
Pāṭalī related the matter in detail. Upananda said:
"Show me your robe. He showed it to him immediately.
Upon seeing it, Upananda conceived a greedy attachment and demanded it at once.
Utpalavarṇā said: "This cannot be obtained! Why is that?"
"Women have little merit and should possess only five robes.
Bāṇaṃdanta said, "It is like a person who gives elephants and horses as alms, yet does not provide them with saddles or bridles."
"You are just like this; why do you provide various kinds of delicacies as offerings, yet begrudge this single garment and refuse to give it?
Having thus sought it with countless skillful means, he was finally compelled to yield and gave it to him.
When Ba-nan-da returned to his residence with the robes he had obtained, the bhikṣus saw him and said to him, "You are a person of great merit; you have obtained these fine robes. He replied:
"I have no merit; it was only through forceful persuasion that I obtained this bhikṣuṇī.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they censured him in various ways:
"How could you use forceful persuasion to seize the robe of a bhikṣuṇī?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, distressed by the clamor and commotion caused by the frequent coming and going of the fourfold assembly, addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now wish to enter a quiet chamber for three months; I do not permit anyone to come to my presence, with the exception of one bhikṣu who brings me food."
"You all should likewise establish a regulation together.
Following these instructions, they immediately established it:
"From now on, it is not permitted to go to the Buddha's presence at will; this applies to all except for a single monk who is delivering food. One who violates this incurs a *pāyattika* offense."
At that time, the Elder Upasena had not heard of the monastic regulations; later, upon arriving in Śrāvastī, he asked another bhikṣu, "In which room is the Buddha staying?"

The bhikṣu pointed the way, and they immediately arrived before the room; he knocked on the door with his hand, and the Buddha opened it himself. He stepped forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha asked Upasena:
"Your assembly is pure and your deportment is complete.
How do you instruct and transform them so that they have become like this?"
He replied: "If anyone seeks to go forth from me, I instruct them to practice the twelve dhūtas:

you should, for as long as life lasts, dwell in the forest (āraṇyaka), beg for food (piṇḍapātika), eat at a single sitting (aikāsanika), eat one kind of food (khalupaśvāsika), accept food in a single portion (pātra-pūraka), beg for alms in regular order (sāvadāna-piṇḍapātika), dwell among cemeteries (śmāśānika), wear rag-robes (pāṃśukūlika), possess only the three robes (traicīvarika), sit wherever a seat is spread (yathāsaṃstarika), sit under a tree (vṛkṣamūlika), and sit in the open air (ābhyavakāśika)."
“World-Honored One!
If there is a person who can practice this Dharma for as long as their life lasts, they may enter my assembly, and I shall act as their teacher.
The Buddha praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! You may truly be called one who skillfully trains his assembly.
He asked again:
"Do you know whether this community of monks has established a regulation? He replied,
"I do not know."
Why is this? I have heard from the Buddha:
"That which the Buddha has not yet prescribed, one must not arbitrarily prescribe."
"It has been established; you should observe it.
The Buddha related the aforementioned matter to him in full, and he replied:
"I cannot comply with the Sangha's regulation; I shall confess the *pāyattika* offense."
The Buddha said,
"Excellent! It is as you have spoken."
At that time, the resident bhikṣus stood before the dwelling and waited for Upasena to come out, saying to him:
"You have violated the monastic regulations; you ought to perform the *pāyattika* confession."
He asked, "What *pāyattika* offense have I committed?
The monks then related the preceding events in full.
He replied:
"I do not repent according to the regulations of the Saṃgha. Why is this?"
I have personally heard from the Buddha:
"If the Buddha has not prescribed a rule, the Sangha may not prescribe one;
once the Buddha has prescribed a rule, the Sangha may not contravene it."
Thereupon the Buddha came out himself and said to the bhikṣus:
"From now on, if there is an araṇyaka bhikṣu such as Upasena, you are permitted to bring him to my presence."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they thought to themselves:
"We too should practice these dhūtas so that we may go directly to the Buddha's presence.
Thereupon, each of them began to practice them.
At that time, the lodgings provided by the lay devotees for offerings were no longer being accepted by anyone. They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"I now permit the fourfold assembly to see me at their own convenience."
At that time, when the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī heard this instruction from the Buddha, she went with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs toward the place where the Buddha was.
On the way, they encountered Upasena; among Upasena’s assembly, there was a bhikṣu whose robes were coarse and tattered, and [Mahāprajāpatī] asked him: “Elder!...”
"Why are you wearing this?
He replied, "I have no other clothes."
The bhikṣuṇī then pointed to her own robe and said, "Can you wear this? He replied:
"I can. He asked again, "The robe you are wearing— can you give it to me?"
He replied, "I can," and immediately exchanged it.
She proceeded to where the Buddha was, prostrated herself at his feet with her head, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha asked Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
"For what reason are you wearing these tattered and worn-out robes?"
He answered with the aforementioned matters.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him and sent him back to his residence.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned that bhikṣu:
“Did you indeed exchange a coarse and inferior garment for a fine garment with a bhikṣuṇī?
She replied, “It is true.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
“You foolish person!
"One should not have excessive desire!
Because of this, the bhikṣus reported the matter concerning Upananda to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Upananda:
"Is it truly so? He replied, "It is truly so."
"World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
There were some bhikṣus who had bhikṣuṇīs among their relatives who were well-known and able to obtain clothing;
yet these bhikṣus wore coarse and tattered robes. The bhikṣuṇīs asked them:
"Why are you wearing these coarse garments?
He replied, "There is no place from which they could have been obtained."
He said, "Why do you not come and take it from me? He replied:
"The Buddha has established a rule:
'It is not permitted to receive robes from bhikṣuṇīs. The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"Only those who are close can know what may be taken and what may be given.
We pray that you report this to the Buddha!
The bhikṣus then reported this to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having praised in various ways fewness of desires and contentment, and having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.'"

At that time, the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs of Śrāvastī received a gift of robes together and proceeded to divide them among themselves; sometimes a robe suitable for a bhikṣu was obtained by a bhikṣuṇī, and sometimes a robe suitable for a bhikṣuṇī was obtained by a bhikṣu.
The bhikṣuṇīs said to the bhikṣus:
"Please exchange robes with us. They replied:
“The Buddha does not permit me to take the robe of a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative.
The bhikṣuṇīs said, “When one exchanges robe for robe, how can you say that you ‘take’ it?”
He then went and informed the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having praised fewness of desires and contentment in various ways, and having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding "not a relative": one who has no kinship with her parents extending back through seven generations.
Regarding trade: it is permissible if it is mutually beneficial and each party acts according to what is appropriate for them.
To take a robe from a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī* constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one takes clothing from a relative who has violated the precepts or holds wrong views, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a *śrāmaṇera* takes clothing from a *bhikṣuṇī*, a *śikṣamāṇā*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one gives as an act of spontaneous generosity without seeking anything in return, and takes only after knowing that the other person has a surplus, one does not commit an offense.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, Vāpananda, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl, went to the dwelling of the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā. She rose and sat down with such lack of care that she did not realize her body was exposed; seeing this, Vāpananda emitted semen.
The bhikṣuṇī, knowing this, said:
"Venerable sir, give me this robe to wash.
He then took it off and gave it to her.
Having obtained the robes, they immediately placed them inside their own bodies because they were impure.
Furthermore, the bhikṣus also gave robes to the bhikṣuṇīs, instructing them to wash, dye, and beat them.
At that time, because of these many affairs, the bhikṣuṇīs neglected their recitation, meditation, and the practice of the Path.
When the laypeople saw this, they rebuked them in various ways, saying:
"The bhikṣuṇīs constantly take washing, dyeing, and beating clothes as their occupation; what difference is there between them and householders?"
Then the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated herself at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha asked Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī,
"For what reason do all these bhikṣuṇīs have their hands and feet stained with dye?
She answered him fully, explaining the matter as it had occurred.
After the Buddha had taught the sublime Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs, they each returned to their respective dwellings.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked them:
"Is it true that you have caused bhikṣuṇīs to wash, dye, or beat your robes?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The bhikṣus, on account of this, reported the matter concerning Upananda to the Buddha.
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī to wash, dye, or beat his used robes, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
There were some elderly and infirm bhikṣus who were unable to wash, dye, or beat their own robes.
There were certain bhikṣuṇīs who were relatives and capable of washing, dyeing, and beating [cloth]; they all came to him, seeking to have these tasks done for him.
The bhikṣus said:
"The Buddha has not permitted us to have bhikṣuṇīs wash, dye, or beat our robes."
The bhikṣuṇīs said: "Only a close relative can know what is permissible and what is not; we pray that you will inform the Buddha of this!
The bhikṣus then reported this to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having praised fewness of desires and contentment, and having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash an old robe, or dye it, or beat it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.'"
"Old clothing" refers to that which has stains on its body.
If one has it washed, it may be washed but not dyed or beaten.
If he orders it dyed, it is dyed but not washed and not beaten;
if he orders it beaten, it is beaten but not washed and not dyed;
if he orders it washed and dyed, it is washed and dyed but not beaten.
If one instructs [a layperson] to wash and beat [the robe], but they only wash and beat it without dyeing it;
or if one instructs them to dye and beat it, but they only dye and beat it without washing it;
or if one instructs them to wash, dye, and beat it, but they only wash, dye, and beat it—[in all these cases], it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one orders [a robe] to be washed, but it is not washed and is dyed;
or if one orders it to be washed, but it is not washed and is beaten;
or if one orders it to be washed, but it is not washed and is both dyed and beaten—in all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If he is told to dye, he dyes it without first washing or beating it, or he washes and beats it;
if he is told to beat, he beats it without first washing or dyeing it, or he washes and dyes it;
if he is told to wash and dye, he beats it without first washing and dyeing it.
If one orders [a non-relative] to wash and beat [the robe], yet they do not wash and beat it but dye it;
or if one orders them to dye and beat it, yet they do not dye and beat it but wash it—it is the same in these cases.
If one orders a non-relative to wash, dye, and beat it, yet a relative washes, dyes, and beats it; [it is likewise].
If one causes a person who is not a relative to wash, dye, or beat [the robes], yet both a relative and a non-relative wash, dye, and beat them together;
or if one causes both a relative and a non-relative to wash, dye, and beat them together, yet only the relative washes, dyes, and beats them;
or if one causes both a relative and a non-relative to wash, dye, and beat them together, yet only the non-relative washes, dyes, and beats them.

If she causes relatives and non-relatives to wash, dye, or beat [the robes] together, and they both—relatives and non-relatives—wash, dye, or beat them together, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense in all such cases.
If a robe is not yet ready for washing, dyeing, or beating, and one causes a person who is not a relative to wash, dye, or beat it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one causes a relative to wash, dye, or beat it, but a person who is not a relative actually performs the washing, dyeing, or beating, there is no offense.
The rest is as explained in the section on "Taking Garments. The five matters are concluded.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
In that city, there was an elder named Good-Garment (*Suvāsa*) who had faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma and constantly went to listen to and receive its teachings.
At that time, the elder put on his finest robes and, accompanied by his retinue, went out from the city to pay his respects to the World-Honored One and the bhikṣus.
After the Buddha had taught him the Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him, the elder prostrated, took his leave, and was returning home when he encountered Bhaṇḍana.
Bhadanta further preached the Dharma for him, and as they were about to part, he said:
"Venerable One! Please accept my humble vegetarian meal tomorrow."
He replied, “I am not lacking in food; my suffering is that I have no clothes.
Could you give me even one garment from your body?”
The householder said, "I shall give it, but I must deliberate upon it once I have returned home; I cannot grant it to you immediately. Upananda said:
"I have heard that the householder delights in giving; why then is he so stingy toward me alone?
He further said:

"I preach the Dharma which can bring about liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress. For the sake of delivering you all, I have abandoned my own affairs."
"Why do you now begrudge this single garment?
Thereupon, the elder immediately took it off and gave it to him.
Having gone to the city gate, the gatekeeper asked:
"You previously went out with heavy robes, yet now you return with light ones;
did you give them to a woman, or were they plundered by bandits? He replied:
"I did not give it to the woman, nor was I robbed by a bandit;
I was merely forced to give it by the śramaṇa son of the Śākyas!
The gatekeeper said:
"Do not speak such words! I have heard that the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have few desires and are content; even when someone offers them a gift, they are unwilling to accept it.
How is it that you now forcibly beg for people's belongings?"
He answered as above.
Those who did not have faith in or delight in the Buddha-dharma, upon hearing this, cried out:
"It was only right that he be seized! If you continue to associate with him, it will become even worse than this!"
"The śramaṇa son of the Śākyas constantly praises giving and censures taking what is not given;
yet now he forcibly seizes another's clothing—how does this differ from robbery?
When the elder returned home, the questions and answers within his household were all as described above.
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they rebuked him in various ways and led him to the Buddha’s presence to report the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One."
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu begs for robes from a householder or a householder’s wife, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika.'"
At that time, some monks were wearing coarse and tattered robes. When their relatives saw them, they said to them, "Why are you wearing these ruined garments? Why do you not take some from us?"
He replied, "The Buddha does not permit us to beg for robes from householders or housewives.
You may give them to the Saṃgha; we shall take them from the Saṃgha."
The relatives said, "We specifically wish to give it to the bhikṣu;
we do not wish to give it to the Saṃgha so that others might receive it."
The bhikṣus said:
"If the Buddha would allow us to beg for robes from kinsmen among laymen and laywomen, we too would not wear such tattered and wretched garments."
The relatives said, “Only those who are kin know what may be given and what may be taken; we pray that you will inform the Buddha of this!
The bhikṣus then reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
“From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu asks for a robe from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika.’”

At that time, a large number of bhikṣus were traveling with a caravan of merchants; they lost their way and encountered bandits who plundered them, leaving them naked and bare-skinned as they returned toward Śrāvastī.
The practitioner asked, "Who are you? He replied:
"I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas.
He asked again,
"Where are your robes and bowl?"
He replied, "I was robbed by bandits. He proceeded to the Jetavana,
where the exchange of questions and answers with the bhikṣus was likewise the same.
He asked again:
"If you are a bhikṣu, how did you receive the precepts, perform the poṣadha, and conduct the pravāraṇa? He replied:
"Having thus received the precepts, performed the *poṣadha*,
and observed the *pravāraṇā*," the monks, having ultimately not been given the robes, went to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha rebuked them, saying:
"Why do you appear before the Buddha naked?
Can you not obtain tree leaves or grass to cover your bodies?
He then addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forth, for one who goes naked before the Buddha, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"The Buddha does not permit us to beg for robes from laymen or laywomen who are not our relatives."
"Our relatives live very far from here; how can we obtain robes?
The Buddha said, "Have you already gone to where the elder bhikṣus are?"
He replied, “I have arrived.
He asked again:
"Why did you not give him the robe? He replied,
"The bhikṣus were just now questioning me together."
"How should one receive the precepts, perform the *poṣadha*, and conduct the *pravāraṇā*?
Although he answered in accordance with the Dharma, he was still not granted [permission].
From afar, the Buddha rebuked the resident bhikṣus:
"Why is it that you see a monk who is naked and yet do not show him compassion?
Having praised fewness of desires and contentment, praised the precepts, and praised the observance of the precepts for the sake of the monk who had lost his robe, he addressed the monks:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu requests a robe from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative, except under specific circumstances, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
The specific circumstances are:
the robes have been taken away, lost, burned, washed away by water, or destroyed; these are called the specific circumstances."
If one’s robes have been taken away, or even until they are ruined, and there still remains another robe, or if there is a robe located elsewhere, in all such cases one must not beg for more.
It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
The sixth section on the *duṣkṛta* offenses for *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs* is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, a large number of bhikṣus were traveling from the village of Pāṭaliputra toward the place where the Buddha was staying; they encountered bandits and lost their robes, whereupon they spoke to one another as follows:

"Although the Buddha has permitted us to seek robes from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative due to five specific causes and conditions, I do not yet know from whom I should now seek one."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"These bhikṣus have lost their robes and do not know from whom to beg for them.
We should seek them on their behalf; if there are elders [who can provide them], we shall take them ourselves."
Having reflected thus, he spoke these words to the monk who had lost his robe.
The monk who had lost his robe said: "Excellent!"
Thereupon, the group of six bhikṣus went throughout the city and said to the laymen and laywomen:
"There were certain bhikṣus coming from the town of Pāṭali who wished to visit the World-Honored One; they encountered bandits and lost their robes."
"You all may each contribute by reducing your own portions and give it to him.
Having heard this, the laymen and laywomen each reduced their own shares, obtaining a great quantity of clothing so that everyone was fully provided for.
The bhikṣus who had lost their robes said, "We have enough; there is no need to beg further.
The group of six bhikṣus replied:
"You have the cause and condition for begging for robes, whereas we do not;
please allow us to beg on your behalf so that we may obtain some.
The bhikṣus who had lost their robes said:
“As you wish, Venerable Sir.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went about begging once more and obtained a great quantity of robes.
Then, the lay devotees gathered and discussed it together, saying:
"There are not yet many bhikṣus who have lost their robes; among the men and women, great and small, in our city, we have already offered our portions in charity, and it should more than suffice."
"Why do you seek it again?
Are you not desiring to accumulate, sell, or trade it, rather than practicing the holy life?
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?
They replied: "It is true."
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, having had his robes taken away, lost, burned, washed away, or destroyed, should beg for robes from a householder or housewife who is not a relative.'"
If a householder or a householder’s wife wishes to give many robes, this bhikṣu should accept two robes;
if he accepts more than this, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. [The seventh section is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Upananda frequently visited a certain householder’s home to preach the Dharma for them, attending to their illnesses and legal affairs.
One morning, a bhikṣu dressed in his robes and carrying his bowl entered the city to beg for food; he happened upon this household and overheard the husband and wife discussing:
"Upananda has been kind to us; we should use the price of such a robe to have one made and give it to him."
When that bhikṣu returned from his almsround, he said to Baddhananda,
"You are possessed of great merit! Baddhananda replied:
"What merit do you possess?
He replied, "Just now,
while begging for alms, I went to the house of a certain lay devotee and heard the husband and wife discussing together:"
"Upananda has been kind to me; I shall have robes made for him using this amount of money for cloth.
Go now to him, and you will certainly succeed without doubt."

On the following morning at mealtime, Baddhālī put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to that house. The householder came out to greet him, and Baddhālī said, "Did you have this robe-fund made into a robe for my sake?"
He replied, "So be it! Then, Bhadanta said:

"You know for yourself that I do not wear coarse clothing; if you make fine garments, I shall wear them myself and will always keep you in mind. In times of illness or legal affairs, I shall attend to your needs.
However, if they are not of good quality, I shall give them to my disciples or store them away in my chest. To merely produce such items would be a waste, as there would be no merit from their use."
At that time, the householder said to those around him, "This man is insatiable;
he is difficult to support and difficult to satisfy.
Although I have resolved to give him more, even fivefold or sixfold what I originally intended does not yet please him."
"Though he was formerly very kind, now he has become stingy!
Thus, they did not give it to him.
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they rebuked him in various ways, led him to the Buddha’s presence, and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upāli (Bhadanta):
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, when a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative has made a plan, saying:
"We shall procure the price for such a robe and have it made into a robe to give to a certain bhikṣu,"'"
This bhikṣu, having not previously been invited to do so at his own discretion, went to the householder or the householder’s wife and asked:
"Will you have a robe made for me using such an amount of money for robe-cloth?"
He replied, "So it is! and then said:
"Excellent, householder, housewife! You may make such a robe for me, for the sake of its beauty.
This constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Previously not having invited [the monks] at their own discretion" means:
previously not asking the bhikṣus what kind of robe they required.
"Of superior quality" means:
If one seeks to have it made exceptionally fine, surpassing what was previously promised,
or if one requests fine clothing from relatives, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
The *śikṣamāṇā*, *śrāmaṇera*, and *śrāmaṇerī* [commit] *duṣkṛta*; the eighth [offense] is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a family with whom Upananda regularly went in and out; the husband and wife there discussed together:
"I shall each provide for Upananda by having robes made from this amount of robe-fund and giving them to him.
When the bhikṣus who were begging for alms heard this, they informed him again.
Upananda then went to the layman and the laywoman's wife and asked them:
"I have heard that you have each made robes for me using such an amount of cloth-fund as this.
Is it truly so? They replied:
"So be it! said Upananda. "We may join them together to make a single robe, ensuring it is of excellent quality."
"If it is of excellent quality, I shall wear it myself and will always keep you in mind;
if it is not of good quality, I shall place it in a vessel, for to merely discard this object would yield no merit from its use."
Then the householder and his wife spoke with great anger:
"This man is insatiable; he is difficult to support and difficult to satisfy.
Although we sought to have him share in the making of a single garment, he was not content even with five or six times what we had intended to give."
"A person such as this is unworthy of existing!
Thus, he was no longer permitted to come and go.
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they censured him in various ways, led him to the Buddha's presence, and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you did so?
He replied: "It is true."
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative has consulted together, saying:

"Before being invited to choose his own gifts, that bhikṣu went to the layman and the laywoman and asked them:

He replied, “It is so! and then said:
"Excellent, householder and housewife!
You may join together to make one robe for me, so that it may be beautiful.

For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. The nine matters are concluded.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the king’s minister said to his attendants:

The messenger received the command and went to where Upananda was, saying:
