Part One: The Rules on Expiation (Naiḥsargika-pāyattika). The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, a great number of lay devotees (gṛhapati) collectively invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha. Among them were those who split firewood, those who drew water, those who swept and sprinkled the ground, those who spread out sitting mats, those who scattered flowers, those who prepared high seats, and those who provided the food.

At that time, in the early morning, Baddhālitta put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went first to the house where he had been invited; arriving at the place where the people were, he praised whatever they were doing and further said to them:
"What you are doing now is joyful, excellent, and good."
The people said: "We are truly joyful and shall perform various offerings!
We will ensure that the food and drink are of every kind of sweetness and excellence, and we shall also give clothing as alms to the assembly of monks."
Bhadanta said: "The multitude has already given many robes and articles to the Saṃgha;
if you were to give more as well, it would merely result in a surplus that becomes useless."
Why do you pointlessly discard this useful merit and not give it to me?
If you were to give it to me, I would wear it myself, constantly keep it in mind, and attend to my needs during illness or legal affairs.
Having heard this, the people gathered together for consultation, and among them some said:
"If the Sangha does not require it, we may give it to them, so that we may obtain the merit of giving and using it."
Others said, "This was originally intended as a gift for the Sangha; how can it now be diverted to a single person?
Since many spoke in favor of giving it away, they eventually bestowed it upon him.
At that time, when Upāli (Baddhalita) returned to the monastery carrying a heavy load of robes, the bhikṣus exclaimed, "You are a person of great merit;
how is it that upon going out for but a moment, you have obtained such robes?"
Bhadanta said, "What is obtained through clever eloquence is not merit.
He then explained in detail the circumstances by which he had acquired the robe.
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they censured him in various ways:
"You foolish man! How can you divert property intended for the Saṃgha and take it for yourself?"

When the householder had prepared the meal offerings, he sent a messenger to inform the Buddha. Thereupon, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus preceding and following him, went to the house and sat upon the prepared seat.
The lay devotees served the food with their own hands and, having finished the meal, provided water for washing, yet they made no offerings.
Those who previously did not wish to give to Upananda secretly consulted one another, saying,
"Today our food was prepared without anything lacking."
"We have no reason to take the property intended for the Sangha and give it to a single person alone; having omitted this *dakṣiṇā*, how can we not feel shame and remorse!
The bhikṣus asked, "What were you whispering about in private?"
He answered with the facts as they were.
The bhikṣus reprimanded Upananda in various ways:
"You foolish man!..."
"How can one divert property intended for the Sangha and take it for oneself?
At that time, the World-Honored One, having taught the sublime Dharma to the lay devotees, rose from his seat and departed.
The elder bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu diverts property intended for the Saṃgha into his own possession, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.'"
There were certain bhikṣus who, not knowing that this was property belonging to the Saṃgha, diverted it for their own personal use;
later, having realized this, they felt shame and remorse, and reported the matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having praised fewness of desires and contentment, and having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is impossible that one who, not knowing that an item was given to the Saṃgha, diverted it for personal use, would thereby commit an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika)."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a donor intends to give property to the Saṃgha, diverts it for his own personal use, he commits a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense."
"Knows" means: either knowing by oneself or hearing from another.
"Wishing to give property to the Saṃgha" means:
If a person has resolved their mind and says,
"I shall take this object and give it to that community of monks," yet turns around and gives the object intended for the Sangha to another person, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
To divert [the property] to other monks, the community of bhikṣuṇīs, the dual community (ubhayato-saṃgha), the community of the four quarters, or to a stūpa, constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
It is likewise if one diverts property intended for the community of bhikṣuṇīs, the dual community, or the community of the four quarters.

If one diverts property intended for a stūpa to oneself, or to the community of bhikṣus, the community of bhikṣuṇīs, the dual communities, the saṃgha of the four quarters, other individuals, or another stūpa, it is all a duṣkṛta offense.
If one intends to divert property intended for another person, it is likewise.
Even if one diverts a single mouthful of food intended for this animal to give it to that animal, it is an *dukkaṭa* offense.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one has informed the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha grants it; [there is no offense].
If a donor personally diverts property intended for the Sangha and gives it to oneself, one does not commit an offense. [The fourteenth rule is concluded.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, Pilindavatsa was residing on Mount Lakuṇḍaka; he flew into the air and smeared and sprinkled his dwelling with plaster.
At that time, King Bimbisāra went to that mountain. When Pilindavatsa saw the king approaching, he suddenly returned to the ground and said:
"Welcome, Great King!"
"You may sit here. Once the king was seated, he asked:
"Why did you do this yourself? Is there no gardener?"
He replied, "There is none.
The king then spoke to a minister:
"You may give this [man] to the bhikṣu as a gardener. Piṅgala said,
"The Buddha does not permit me to keep a gardener."
The king said, "You may inform the Buddha.
After the king had departed, [the messenger] immediately informed the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having praised fewness of desires and contentment, and having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit the bhikṣus to keep gardeners."
The minister whom the king had commanded did not believe in or delight in the Buddha-dharma, so he ultimately did not give [the man] to him; Pindola likewise did not seek him out.
Later, when Pindola entered the city for alms with his robes on and his bowl in hand, the king and his ministers saw him from afar atop the palace and thought to themselves:
"I previously promised that gardener to that bhikṣu; I do not know whether he has obtained him or not."
He immediately questioned the minister he had previously commanded, and the minister replied,
"I have not yet given it.
The king asked again:
“How many days has it been since I commanded you to come?
The minister replied,
“It has already been five hundred days.”
The king said,
"Give them to him according to this number of days.
Following these instructions, the ministers immediately provided five hundred households, assigning one person from each household to him.
At that time, five hundred households took turns each day, sending one person from each to clean the rooms and attend to whatever tasks were required.
Then, on the day of the festival, the villagers—both men and women—adorned themselves, their clothing resplendent and beautiful, as they went out to enjoy the festivities.
There was a poor woman who was walking along, weeping loudly.
At that time, Pilindavatsa entered the village to beg for food; seeing the woman weeping, he asked her mother, "For what reason is your daughter weeping like this?"
He replied, "Today all these people are dressed in their finest attire, going out for recreation.
My family is poor and cannot compare with them; that is why I weep."
At that time, Pilindavatsa saw the cow eating grass and said to his mother, "Bring me some grass.
She immediately brought it and gave it to him.
Pilindavatsa then tied the grass together, and it transformed into two golden flower garlands, which he gave to the girl's mother, saying:
“There are two kinds of supreme gold in the world:
Jāmbūnada gold and that produced by supernatural power.
You may take this and give it to the girl to wear.”
Having received it, she was filled with supreme joy and wore it as she went in and out; there was no one who did not envy her.
At that time, a certain man, seeing this, gave rise to resentment and jealousy, and immediately addressed King Bimbisāra, saying:

"A certain family in a certain village has obtained a fine hidden treasure; the flower garland worn by their daughter is peerless in the world, such as has never before existed even within Your Majesty’s inner palace."
The king immediately called out to him, saying, "You have found a hidden treasure; you may show it to me. He replied:
“I truly did not obtain it.
The king asked again,
“Where did your daughter obtain the garment she is wearing?”
He replied, “This was created by Piliṅga through the transformation of woven grass.
Upon hearing these words, the king became extremely angry and astonished.
"How could transformed grass become a golden garland?
He then commanded his officials to arrest and imprison her.
Later, when Pilinga returned to that village, he saw the woman from before weeping bitterly and asked her:
"Why are you now weeping so bitterly? He replied,
"My family members are in prison."
He asked, "For what kind of offense? He replied:
“May the Venerable One grant me this golden flower garland. He said:
“Do not weep!”
"I shall cause you to find your way out.
Piṅgala then went first to the place of the prison warden; when the warden saw him, he greeted him, saying:
"Venerable One!"
"For what reason have you come here, bending yourself so? He replied,
"The gardener has been imprisoned, and that is why I have come."
"Would you now release him for me? He replied,
"This man has discovered a fine treasure, yet he did not show it to the King."
"If you show it to the king, you will be able to leave.
Pilingiya said, "I made this by tying together grass; it is not a hidden treasure."
The man said, "To bind grass and have it become gold— that is impossible.
Piṅgala then transformed his seat so that it all became a golden couch, and he spoke, saying:
"What seat do you see yourself sitting upon now?
They all saw themselves sitting upon golden couches and were struck with great terror; they descended from the couches, prostrated themselves, and said:
"We pray that you will grant us your forgiveness and quickly release us!"
"If the King hears that I have sat upon a golden couch, he will surely punish me severely.
Pilinga said, "Release the park keeper, and then I shall untie you."
He replied, "I did not see it. He asked:
"By whom? He replied, "By the king."
Pilinga then extinguished the fire and flew to where the king was, remaining suspended in mid-air.
At that time, the king was atop a high tower; seeing him, he prostrated and asked:
"Venerable Sir!"
"For what reason have you come?
He replied, "The park keeper has been imprisoned; that is why I have come."
"I pray that you release him!
The king said, "That man has obtained a fine hidden treasure; only if he shows it to me shall he be released!"
Piliṅga said, "I made this by tying together grass; it is not a hidden treasure.
The king said:
"It is impossible for grass tied together to become gold.
At that moment, Pilindavatsa struck a pillar of the king’s palace with his staff, and it immediately transformed into a golden pavilion.
He asked, "What materials were used to build this high tower of yours, O King?
Upon seeing him, the king was filled with joy and immediately issued an edict to release him.

Piliṅga thus displayed his supernormal powers in this manner four times. When the people heard of and witnessed these miraculous transformations, they conceived a heart of faith and joy toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha; they offered the monks food before and after their meals, *tambula*, non-timely drinks, various requisites for bathing, ointments for the body and feet, and oil for lamps.

At that time, the community of monks received a great quantity of fresh and processed butter, oil, honey, and rock sugar; they were unable to consume it all, so it was piled up on the ground, flowing and spreading everywhere, staining their robes, beds, mats, and bedding.
When the laypeople saw this, they asked,
"Whose property is this? Someone replied:
"This is what the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have accumulated.
The householders said, "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas,
claim to practice moderation in eating, yet they hoard such things as these and consume them to their heart's content."
These people, seeking liberation and freedom from birth, old age, and death, now seek only such delicious flavors.
They lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they censured them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I do not permit the storage of ghee, honey, or rock honey received for the evening meal; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense!"
At that time, many bhikṣus were ill and were unable to obtain attendants (kappiyakāraka) to receive [food] day by day;
they had neither money nor a place to purchase it.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having praised having few desires and knowing contentment, and having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit sick bhikṣus to receive ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar for consumption, even for up to six nights."
At that time, the bhikṣus exceeded the six-night limit; the elder bhikṣus rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu is ill, he may take four kinds of medicinal electuaries (caturvidha-lehyabhaisajya):'"
"Ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar may be accepted for one time up to seven days.
If [the limit] is exceeded, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If one receives them on the first day, receives them again on the second day, and continues receiving them until the seventh day, yet keeps them until the appearance of the dawn on the eighth day, in all such cases it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
One should announce that it is to be relinquished to the Sangha; the Sangha shall then relinquish it to a layperson or a *śrāmaṇera*.
If it is used for lighting lamps or for anointing the feet, only the monk who relinquished the medicine may use it; no other bhikṣu whatsoever is permitted to consume it.
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. Fifteen cases concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a band of eight-month thieves who constantly lay in wait to capture people, killing them to offer as sacrifices to the gods; consequently, all the people and the bhikṣus were filled with terror.
As the day for the sacrifice drew near and they had yet obtained nothing, the bandits deliberated together, saying:
"There must be bhikṣus in this āraṇya; it will be easy to capture them."
They immediately went to a certain place.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they each fled.
Finding nothing, the bandits consulted together again, saying:
"When we arrive at another place, we must not be negligent, lest we miss the day of the sacrifice.
At that time, there was one among the assembly who had renounced the path, and he said to the others:
"I have heard the Buddha's teaching: it is not permitted for a bhikṣu to be separated from his robe even for a single night."
"Let us simply guard it together; by dawn, he will surely return.
The crowd said, "If he does not return, we shall kill you."
"If you have no regrets, we shall remain. He replied, "Excellent!"
Thereupon the bandits stopped.
At that time, the bhikṣus, fearing they would incur the offense of staying overnight separated from their robes, all returned during the latter part of the night.
The bandits asked:
"Do you think I have already departed?
He replied, "I know you are here;
it was because the Buddha did not permit me to stay overnight apart from my robes that I returned!"
The bandits then killed him, taking his blood when they needed blood and cutting off his flesh when they needed flesh.
Those who did not die thought to themselves:
"If the World-Honored One had permitted us to deposit each of our robes with laypeople within the boundary before the eight months were complete, we would not have encountered this calamity."

Having reported this to the Buddha, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus on this matter. After praising fewness of desires and contentment, praising the precepts, and praising the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From now on, it is permitted for bhikṣus dwelling in forest hermitages (*āraṇyaka*) who have not yet completed the three-month rainy season retreat to entrust each of their robes to the householders within the boundary (*sīmā*) during the eighth month; they may stay apart from them overnight without incurring an offense."
There were some bhikṣus living near a village who also deposited each of their robes with laypeople within the boundary and stayed overnight apart from them.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I do not permit those living near a village to stay overnight apart from their robes."
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who stayed overnight apart from his robes in an araṇya where there was no fear.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I do not permit staying overnight apart from one's robes even in an araṇya where there is no fear."
"Only after there is cause for suspicion or fear shall you be permitted [to do so].
At that time, the bhikṣus entrusted their robes to other families and did not go to look after them at all; after many days, they became damp and foul, being gnawed by insects and rotting away.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"You should go and look after the drying.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus went there repeatedly, which the lay devotees found distasteful and tiresome.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to inspect it once every ten days.

At that time, there were bhikṣus who had business for the Saṃgha, business for the stūpa, business for their upādhyāyas or ācāryas, or other matters requiring them to go outside the boundary; yet, for the sake of their robes, they did not dare to go out.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"If there is an essential matter that requires one to go outside the boundary, I allow you to be separated from your robes for one night.
When the bhikṣus had stayed outside the boundary for one night but their business was not yet finished, they returned and reported it again to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"I allow you to stay for six nights.
Once the permission for six nights was granted, some bhikṣus went about wearing coarse and tattered robes even after the six nights had passed.
The elder bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?
They replied: [Yes].
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage) has entered the three-month rains retreat and the eight months have not yet expired.'"
If there is danger in a location, it is permitted to entrust each robe individually to a layperson within the boundary;
if one must go outside the boundary for a valid reason, one may remain separated from these robes for up to six nights.
"If it exceeds [this period], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"The three-month *varṣā* (rainy season retreat)" refers to the earlier *varṣā*.
"One whose eight months are not yet complete" refers to one who is in the latter half of the rainy season retreat (*paścima-varṣā*).
"Each individual robe" refers to:
Whether it be the *saṃghāṭī* or the *uttarāsaṅga*, one may entrust whichever single robe is most important;
however, one must not entrust the *antarvāsaka*, because it is worn next to the body and cannot be worn alone during prostrations, entering the Saṃgha, or begging for alms.
Furthermore, one must not entrust two robes.
There are circumstances under which one may stay outside the boundary for up to six nights:

if there is business concerning a stūpa, or matters involving one’s preceptor (upādhyāya), teacher (ācārya), or other affairs, one may leave each of one’s robes at the house of a layperson and remain outside the boundary for a maximum of six nights.
If one stays for one night, two nights, or even up to five nights, and does not return once the business is finished, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This concludes the sixteen cases concerning *śrāmaṇeras* and *duṣkṛta* offenses.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal on the following day.
On that very day, there occurred a terrifying rain; in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, the rain filled a single alms bowl.
The earth receives this water as if a single drop of oil had fallen upon a heap of hot sand; were it otherwise, it would form a vast great ocean.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Just as the rain falls now within the Jetavana, so too does it fall throughout Jambudvīpa."
"You all may come forth and bathe therein; this is the final rain of universal equality.
The bhikṣus then came out and bathed naked in the rain.
At that time, Viśākhā sent a maidservant to inform the Buddha,
"The meal is prepared.
When the maidservant arrived at the Jetavana, she saw the bhikṣus all bathing naked and thought to herself:
"This is a non-Buddhist ascetic, not a bhikṣu," he reported back in this manner.
Viśākhā then thought to herself:
"This must be a bhikṣu bathing in the open air; this foolish slave girl did not know it and thought he was a heretic.
She then sent another message, saying:
"Go to the gate of the Jetavana and make this proclamation:"
"The meal is prepared; may the Noble One know the time.
The maidservant then went back to the gate of the Jeta Grove, intending to announce it as she had been instructed;
however, at that time the bhikṣus had finished bathing and returned to their quarters, and not seeing a single person there, she thought again:
"The various non-Buddhist practitioners who were present have now vanished;
we see them no longer. He then returned home and reported this again.
Viśākhā then thought to herself:
"It must be that the bhikṣu has finished bathing and is resting.
He sent a messenger again with these words:
"You may enter the gate and announce it in the courtyard."
He immediately followed these instructions, entered the gate of the Jeta Grove, and announced it within the courtyard.
Hearing the sound of the announcement, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Viśākhā has informed me that the time has arrived; all of you put on your robes, take up your bowls, and together accept her invitation."
The bhikṣus, having received the command, all assembled in the Hall of Universal Gathering.
The maidservant then stepped forward and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"The meal is prepared; may the Holy One know the time."
The Buddha said, “You may go on ahead; I shall follow shortly.

Thereupon, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, the World-Honored One, together with the bhikṣus, vanished from the Hall of Universal Assembly and reappeared upon the seat prepared by Viśākhā, his robes remaining dry.
When Viśākhā saw that the Buddha and the Saṃgha were suddenly seated there with their robes unwet, she thought to herself:
"I have gained a great benefit, for I have made offerings to such noble masters and noble disciples; though the heavens pour down rain in torrents, their robes remain unwet."
Filled with joy and exultation, he personally served various kinds of fine food with his own hands.
When the meal was finished, he offered water for washing, joined his palms in reverence, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the World-Honored One will grant me my wish!"
The Buddha told Viśākhā:
"In this world, the Buddha is forever free from all desires.
Viśākhā spoke again, saying:
“May the Buddha grant me a pure wish that can be fulfilled.
The Buddha said, “Excellent!”
Viśākhā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This morning I sent a maidservant to inform you that the meal was prepared. She saw that all the bhikṣus were bathing naked; she then returned and told me that everyone in the Jeta Grove were non-Buddhist outsiders, and that there were no bhikṣus.”
"Blessed One!
Why would a bhikṣu bathe naked in the presence of his upādhyāya and ācārya?
We pray that the Buddha will permit the bhikṣus to keep rain-bathing robes; I shall provide rain-bathing robes for all the bhikṣus of Śrāvastī for as long as I live."
He further said:
"Recently, on a minor errand, I went to the Āciravatī River and saw several bhikṣuṇīs bathing there, naked."
When the people of the time saw this, they all mocked him with derisive words, saying:
"Even when women wear clothes, they are not yet considered beautiful; how much less so for one who has left the household life, who goes about with his body naked."

"I pray that the Buddha will also permit the bhikṣuṇīs to possess robes for bathing in water; I, too, shall provide robes for bathing in water for all the bhikṣuṇīs of Śrāvastī for as long as I live."
He further said:
"The Buddha taught that there are three kinds of illnesses:
one kind is that which results in death whether medicine is obtained or not;..."
There are two types who recover whether they obtain medicine or not;
there are three types who recover if they obtain medicine but die if they do not.
I pray that you will permit the bhikṣus to take various medicines, and I shall provide all the necessary medicines for the bhikṣus of Śrāvastī throughout my life.
He further said:
"The Buddha spoke of three kinds of illness:
one is that which can be cured by obtaining food appropriate to the illness, yet one dies because such food is not obtained;..."
Two types [of beings] can survive with food appropriate to their illness, but cannot survive without it;
three types can survive with food appropriate to their illness, but will die without it.

"I pray that you will permit the bhikṣus to eat food according to their specific ailments; I, too, shall provide for my entire life the requisite food for the bhikṣus of Śrāvastī according to their ailments.
He further said, "If the attendants of the sick go out to beg for alms, they will neglect their duties."
"I pray that you will permit the bhikṣus to accept food from those who care for the sick; I myself shall provide food for those who care for the sick in Śrāvastī for as long as I live.
He further said, "When visiting bhikṣus arrive, they are utterly exhausted from their journey; having just arrived, they do not know where to beg for food."
"I pray that you will permit the bhikṣus to accept food from me for visiting bhikṣus, so that they may rest from their exhaustion and learn the places where alms are sought;
I shall also provide food throughout my life for visiting bhikṣus in Śrāvastī."
He further said:

"If a bhikṣu traveling on a long journey enters a village for alms and becomes separated from his companions, he may find himself on a remote path where he might encounter bandits in the eighth month or lose his way."
"I pray that you will allow me to provide travel provisions for traveling bhikṣus; I shall also provide food throughout my life for traveling bhikṣus in Śrāvastī.
He further said, "I have heard that the World-Honored One has permitted the bhikṣus of the Aṇāpinḍada country to eat gruel."
"I pray that you will allow the bhikṣus to accept my rice gruel; I shall provide rice gruel for all the bhikṣus in Śrāvastī for as long as I live.
He further addressed the Buddha, saying, "I pray that the World-Honored One will accept from me, for as long as I live, clothing, food, and medicinal decoctions."
The Buddha asked Viśākhā,
"What benefit do you see that you seek these nine wishes? She replied:

"In this country, bhikṣus from various regions will surely come to inquire after the World-Honored One's health. If they say that a certain bhikṣu named so-and-so has passed away there, having attained the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat, I shall ask them:
'Did that bhikṣu ever come here?'"
He replied, "I have. I then thought to myself:
"That bhikṣu must have previously received from me at least one kind of offering; he has thus conceived joy and increased his roots of goodness.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One said to Viśākhā, "I grant you eight wishes, but one wish cannot be granted."
Then Viśākhā took a small seat and sat before the Buddha. The Buddha spoke these verses of sympathetic joy for her:
“Joyfully bestowing food and drink upon the Buddha and his noble disciples, one establishes merit that destroys stinginess and greed;
receiving the fruit of this reward, one shall always experience delight.”
"Born in heaven with long life, returning here free from the dust of defilement, the great fruit of practicing the Dharma is to dwell forever in the bliss of the pure heavens.

At that time, the World-Honored One further expounded various sublime Dharmas for them, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them. He then returned to the Jeta Grove, assembled the bhikṣus, and after praising fewness of desires and contentment, praising the precepts, and praising the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I authorize the bhikṣus to receive rain-bath robes; the bhikṣuṇīs to receive water-bath robes; and [I authorize] the receipt of medicine according to illness, food according to illness, food for those tending the sick, food for visiting bhikṣus, food for bhikṣus traveling on distant journeys, and congee."
At that time, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:

"The Buddha has permitted us to keep a rain-bathing robe. Thereupon, they constantly begged for and kept them; yet they did not maintain them properly, did not give them to others, and did not perform the ritual of pure donation (śuddhaka-dāna), but instead carried heavy loads and traveled while wearing them.
The bhikṣus saw this and asked,
"Have you not heard that the Buddha has prohibited the keeping of extra robes? They replied:
"Although the Buddha has established a rule, he permits the keeping of a rain-bath robe.
The bhikṣus asked again:
"Do you always keep rain-bath robes that you do not formally receive, nor give to others, nor perform the ritual transfer of purity (pariśuddhi) for?"
He replied, “It is so!
The elder bhikṣus rebuked him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so? They replied: [Yes, it is true.]
“It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu, when one month of spring remains, should seek a rain-bathing robe, he should wear it for the remaining half-month.’”
"If one seeks it less than one month [before the end of the season] but wears it for more than half a month, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the "rain-bathing robe":
it is used during the rainy-season bathing period and is also used during the summer bathing period.
If there remains one month of spring and someone has previously promised to give a rain-bath robe, a knowledgeable bhikṣu should go to that person and say:
"Now is the time to sew and dye the rain-bath robe."
"If you obtain one, it is well;
if you do not obtain one, you should speak again, saying:
'I have already finished sewing and dyeing all my robes for use during the rainy season.'"
"If you obtain it, that is well;
if you do not obtain it, you should speak to him again, saying:
'You previously promised to give a rain-bath robe to a certain bhikṣu; now is precisely the time.'"
If he obtains it, that is well;
if he does not obtain it, that bhikṣu should seek elsewhere and keep it until the middle of the eighth month, maintaining it for one hundred and thirty-five days.

If one exceeds this [measure], and does not make it into another robe, nor accepts it as one's own possession, nor gives it to another, nor performs a formal act of purification (*pariṣkāra-dāna*), it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *śrāmaṇera*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The seventeenth [section] is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus arrived at a village of merchants.
The merchants said, "Venerable sirs, stay here for the rains retreat; when we return from our journey, we shall offer you the requisites for the retreat."
The group of six bhikṣus said:
"If you wish for us to stay, you may simply give [the robes] to us.
We shall make the robes during the rainy season retreat; once the retreat is over, we will wear them and go to pay our respects to the Buddha."
The merchants deliberated together:
"We shall first offer the requisites for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat); the bhikṣus will then remain here.
Thus, the members of our household, both great and small, may hear the words of the Dharma, receive the eightfold precepts, and purify their body, speech, and mind."
He then gathered the items and gave them to him, after which he departed.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus received the offerings for the *varṣā* retreat; once the merchants had left, they went elsewhere.
At that time, the merchants returned home after gaining profit and said to their families:

"Although I previously gave provisions for the rainy-season retreat to the bhikṣus, now that we have returned safely with our profits, I shall provide further offerings; you all may set your minds at ease and listen to the Dharma."
The family members replied,
“The bhikṣus departed immediately after they had set out.
The merchants then invited the bhikṣus to a location nearby.
The bhikṣus replied, "You may make offerings to those you previously invited; we cannot accept your offerings.
At that time, the merchants became indignant and said:
"I originally accepted alms from this donor to remain here for the *varṣā* retreat; to receive goods and then depart—how is this any different from stealing?
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
“Is it true that you did so?
They replied: “It is true.”
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, it is not permitted to accept offerings for the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) during the course of the retreat; anyone who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
At that time, King Prasenajit had rebels on his border and dispatched Yaśoda and Pūraṇa to go and suppress them.
The two of them deliberated together:
"If we go now, we may even lose our lives; we should pool our resources to make offerings to the bhikṣus.
They immediately took their wealth and went to where the bhikṣu was, saying:
"I am now going to suppress the rebels and fear that I may not return; I offer these items as a gift for my dwelling, and pray that you will accept them.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The World-Honored One has not permitted us to receive gifts for our dwelling during the period of the rains retreat."
Not knowing what to do, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Ānanda:
"How many days remain until the end of the *pravāraṇā*?"
He replied, “Ten days remain.
After the Buddha had praised fewness of desires and contentment in various ways, and having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I allow the bhikṣus to observe the earlier or later retreats and, ten days before the *pravāraṇā*, to accept robes offered in times of urgency.

Once the Buddha had permitted the acceptance of robes offered in times of urgency, the bhikṣus began to store them constantly; they did not maintain them properly, did not give them away to others, did not perform the ritual of pure donation (*śuddhaka-dāna*), and instead carried heavy loads of robes about from place to place.
The elder bhikṣus saw this and asked,
"Have you not heard that the Buddha has prohibited the keeping of extra robes? They replied:
"Although the Buddha has established a rule, he permits the acceptance of *ātyayika-cīvara* (emergency robes).
The bhikṣus asked again:
"Do you always keep emergency robes without maintaining them [properly], without giving them away, and without performing the ritual of *viśuddha-dāna*?"
He replied, "It is so!
The elder bhikṣus censured him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: [Yes].
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From now on, it is not permitted to habitually keep emergency robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*) that have not been formally received, nor to fail to bestow them upon others or perform the ritual of pure donation (*viśuddhi-dāna*);

they may be kept until the time for [regular] robes arrives. Once it was permitted to keep them until the time for robes arrived, some bhikṣus still kept them beyond that period. The elder bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so? They replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, during the preceding or subsequent period of the rainy season retreat, when ten days remain before the *pravāraṇā*, receives an urgent gift of robes;
if he needs them, he may accept them until the time for [distributing] the robes.'"
"If [the robe] exceeds [the limit], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding "an urgent gift of robes":
this refers to gifts given during times of urgency, such as when there is a military expedition or when a woman is about to give birth, and so forth.
Once the time has passed, one no longer gives.
"The time for robes" refers to the period when the kaṭhina robe is being received.
Once the *kaṭhina* robe has been relinquished, it is called the "non-robe season.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Section eighteen ends.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Upananda asked a merchant for an almsbowl at an improper time, saying:
"I have need of a bowl now; you may give it to me."
He replied: "Venerable sir, wait a moment!
There is currently a gathering of merchants; if I do not join them, I shall be fined five hundred gold coins."
Bhadanta said: "I have heard that you were diligent in providing for those practicing the Path; why is it that you now abandon meritorious deeds to prioritize worldly affairs?"
Having heard this, the merchant thought to himself,
"Even if I am to be punished, I must first offer my gift.
He then purchased a bowl for him and went to deliver it, but consequently failed to arrive by the appointed time.
When the crowd saw this, they all said,
"He should be punished!
The merchant said:
"I did not act out of personal malice to contravene the consensus of the multitude.
A śramaṇa begged me for my bowl; unable to part with it, I simply failed to deliver it.
Those who did not have faith in or delight in the Buddha-dharma all said:
"He has acted as a śramaṇa while openly violating the communal regulations; he ought to be severely punished!
They then proceeded to punish him.
Once the merchant had been punished, he spoke with indignation:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know the proper timing; they refused to wait even a moment and caused me to be punished.
The people reviled and censured them in various ways:
"These śramaṇas always preach knowing the proper time, having few desires, and being content; yet now they act otherwise!"
"Now, at an improper time, you have forcibly begged from others.
You lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have violated the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upāli (Baddhananda):
"Is it true that you did this?
He replied: "It is true."
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he asked the bhikṣus:
"What do you think? Is a bowl that has no patches still a bowl? He replied, "It is."
He asked again:
"Is this bowl one with a patch, or even up to five patches? He replied:
"Yes! he said, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"A bowl that has no repairs, one repair, and so on up to four repairs is [an acceptable] bowl."
Five mends do not constitute a [new] bowl.
For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus: from now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, when his bowl has fewer than five mends, seeks a new bowl for the sake of its beauty, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"This bowl should be relinquished within the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha should take the lowest-quality bowl among the assembly and give it to him, saying:
'You shall accept this bowl until it breaks; such is the proper rule.'"
"There are three kinds of bowls:
iron bowls, sūma bowls, and earthenware bowls.
Furthermore, there are another three kinds:"
There are three grades: superior, middling, and inferior. The superior grade consists of receiving three *pātra* of cooked rice, excluding soups and vegetables;
the inferior grade consists of receiving one *pātra* of cooked rice, excluding soups and vegetables.
"Medium" refers to that which is between the superior and the inferior.
"To seek what is good" means to seek firmness and to seek victory.
If one already possesses an alms bowl with no patches, up to and including one with four patches,
yet further begs for another bowl with no patches, up to and including one with four patches, and obtains it, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense in all such cases.

If one already possesses an alms bowl with no patches, up to and including one with four patches, and further begs for a bowl with five patches, receiving it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense in all such cases.
Regarding what must be relinquished within the Saṃgha:
the newly acquired bowl should be relinquished to the community of monks; it must not be relinquished to only one, two, or three individuals.
Regarding the forfeiture of the bowl: one should go before the Saṃgha and declare:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, Bhikṣu [Name], having a bowl that has not yet reached five mends, have requested a new bowl and thereby committed an offense of forfeiture; I now forfeit it to the Saṃgha."
The motion is thus made.
The Saṃgha should perform a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to appoint a monk who knows the Dharma to carry it out within the assembly.
One monk shall proclaim:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, whose bowl has not yet reached five mends, has requested a new bowl and now relinquishes it to the Sangha.
The Sangha now appoints the bhikṣu, so-and-so, as the distributor of bowls."
"If it is the time for the Sangha and the Sangha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus:
'Venerable Sangha, please listen!'"
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, whose alms bowl has not yet reached five mends, has requested a new bowl; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha now appoints the bhikṣu, so-and-so, as the distributor of bowls.
"Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has finished appointing the monk so-and-so as the bowl-distributor."
"Since the Saṃgha is patient and remains silent,
this matter is thus upheld.
This bhikṣu should then announce that the bhikṣus each take their bowls and depart.
Then, taking the bowl he has relinquished, he goes before the senior monk (*sthavira*) and asks:
"Do you need this bowl?

If the senior monk says he needs it, he should take the senior monk's bowl and examine it; if it is missing, or if it is too large, or too small, or cracked and damaged, or crooked and tilted, he should not give [his bowl] to him.
If these five conditions are absent, one should give it.
Having given it, one takes the bowl of the presiding elder (sthavira) and proceeds; from the second elder down to the person who has newly received full ordination, it is done in the same manner.
The Saṃgha should take the last bowl and give it to the bhikṣu who relinquished his bowl;
if no one takes any of the bowls during their distribution, they should be returned to him.
The Saṃgha should instruct him, saying:

"This is your bowl; you must cherish and protect it well. Do not set it on the ground; do not use it to remove refuse; do not use it to store leftover food overnight; do not use it to warm water; do not use it to hold incense; do not use it to hold medicine. Protect it in this manner;
if it should break, you are permitted to ask for another."
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. [Section 19 ends.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Upananda obtained many alms bowls; after using them for five or six days, he would set them aside. Thus, old bowls were found everywhere.
When the householders saw them, they asked, "Who has accumulated these?"
Someone said, "It is Upananda. The elders said:
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, always say they have few desires and know contentment, yet now they are insatiable, gathering and accumulating things like bowl-sellers.
They lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!”
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they rebuked him in various ways and brought him to the Buddha’s presence to report the matter to him.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upāli (Bhadanta):
“Is it true that you did so?”
He replied, "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!"
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu keeps an extra alms-bowl beyond one night, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.'"
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who alone obtained two alms-bowls. He thought to himself:
"The Buddha does not permit me to keep an extra bowl for even one night.
He immediately gave one bowl to another bhikṣu; after giving it away, his bowl broke, and he wandered about without a bowl.
The bhikṣus asked, "Previously you had two bowls; why do you no longer have them now?
He answered with the aforementioned circumstances, and the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked that bhikṣu:
"After how many days did the bowl you gave to another break? He replied:
“Ten days. After the Buddha had praised having few desires and being content, praised the precepts, and praised the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu keeps an extra bowl for up to ten days, and exceeds that period, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
If he obtains two bowls, he should ask his preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya):
'Which of these two bowls is superior?'"

If the preceptor (upādhyāya) or the instructor (ācārya) is not skilled at discerning [the quality of the robes], they should each wear them for five days; then, knowing which is superior, they should keep it for themselves and give the inferior one to another.
The novice commits a *duṣkṛta*; the twentieth [offense] is concluded.
The Buddha was staying at the town of Aṭṭhapiṇḍika.

At that time, the bhikṣus were making *kauśeya* bedding for themselves; they made it themselves and had others make it, they carried the cocoons themselves and had others carry them, and they boiled them themselves and had others boil them.
When the laypeople saw this, they said:
"We boil cocoons; these bhikṣus do the same.
What difference is there between the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, and us?"
"These people constantly preach loving-kindness and patience toward sentient beings, yet now they personally boil cocoons themselves.
They lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
There was one bhikṣu who, having spun wild silk cotton, requested other bhikṣus to make bedding for him.
Having insufficient cotton, he went to the cotton merchant's house and said, "The cotton for my bedding is short; please give me a little more as a gift. The man replied:
“There is no finished cotton cloth yet.
The bhikṣu spoke again:
“You may make it for me.”
That person immediately began boiling the cocoons before the bhikṣu; as the pupae moved, they made a sound.
The bhikṣu instructed him, saying, "Press them down into the hot water!"
That person immediately rebuked him, saying:
"You constantly preach the dharma of non-killing, yet now you teach people to kill.
You have no conduct of a śramaṇa; you destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!"
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they censured them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding out of koseya silk, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika.'"
"Kauśeya" refers to silk produced by silkworms.
"Bedding" (śayanāsana) refers to:
A bedding mat that remains intact even after being folded three times from its initial completion is called a "bedding" (*śayanāsana*).
It should be relinquished to the Sangha and must not be relinquished to any other individual.
The Sangha may spread it upon the ground, or upon a rope bed or a couch.
Except for the monk who has set aside the mat, all other members of the Saṃgha may sit or lie down in order of seniority.
To resolve to make one, or to employ the means toward making one, constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense;
once it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Even if one does not make it oneself nor cause another to make it, but accepts it when offered by another, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
For a *śrāmaṇera*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The twenty-first [offense] is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in the city of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, many Vṛji youths used pure black woolen blankets, which were lustrous and lovely, as their clothing and bedding;
the bhikṣus of the Vṛjis also imitated them in doing so.

At that time, some householders entered the room and saw them; they were struck with great fear, thinking these were members of the Vṛji nobility gathered for recreation, and they asked the passers-by: "Whose noble attire is this?"
He replied, "This is not for a person of noble status; it is intended only for the Bhikṣus of the Vṛji.
Thereupon, the lay devotees criticized and rebuked him, saying:

“O monks, just as kings, ministers, or noblemen dress themselves when riding in chariots or on horseback, I have heard that you monks wear robes made of cut patches while seeking the path to the unconditioned;
yet now, acting in such a manner, you lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!”
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they censured him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked that bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding out of pure black sheep’s wool, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.'"
"Pure black" refers to that which is naturally black or dyed black.
It should be relinquished to the Saṃgha; the Saṃgha may spread it upon rope beds or wooden beds, but it must not be spread upon the ground.
The remainder is as explained in the section on *kauśeya* bedding; [this concludes the twenty-second].
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the city of Kauśāmbī.
Then, the Bhikṣus of the Vṛji clan were making bedding from black sheep’s wool, adding a small amount of white and inferior-colored wool, and then said:
"It has already been purified.
When the elder bhikṣus saw this, they asked,
"Have you not heard that the Buddha has prohibited making bedding out of pure black sheep’s wool?"
He replied, "I have heard it!
However, I have already put on white and lower-grade woolen garments; they are no longer purely black."
The bhikṣus said, "It is entirely black with only a slight admixture; what is there to distinguish it?
They censured him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked that bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I allow the bhikṣus to make bedding using two parts of pure black wool from rams, a third part white, and a fourth part inferior."
For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding, he must use two parts of pure black wool from a ram, one-third part white, and one-fourth part inferior;
if he exceeds these proportions in making it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
If a bhikṣu makes a bedding (śayanāsana) measuring forty *pātra*, he should use twenty *pātra* of pure black wool, ten *pātra* of white, and ten *pātra* of inferior quality;
if it exceeds [the required amount] by one *pātra* of black wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The remainder is as explained in the section on bedding made of pure black wool; [this concludes] twenty-three.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the city of Kauśāmbī.
Then, the bhikṣus of the Vṛji clan had this thought:
"The Buddha has permitted us to use two parts of pure black wool for sheep, a third part white, and a fourth part of inferior quality to make bedding.
Thereupon, they begged for these three types of wool in great quantities to make it themselves or have others make it.
In the place where he resided, there was nowhere that it did not exist.
When various lay devotees came and saw this, they asked:
"Whose property is this?"
He replied, "The Bhikṣus of the Vajjīs.
The laypeople criticized and rebuked him, as described in the section on the extra alms-bowl.
The elder bhikṣus heard various reproaches and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked those bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or seat-cover, he must keep it for six years.'"
"If, within six years, whether one has discarded it or not, one makes a new bedding, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu kept a rag-heap bedding which he found useful. He wished to go from Śrāvastī to the town of Sāketa, but as the bedding was too heavy to carry, he did not know what to do and reported this matter to the bhikṣus.
When the bhikṣus arrived at the place where the Buddha was, they informed him of this matter.
On account of this, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"This bhikṣu wishes to go to the village of Sāketā, but his bedding and requisites are heavy; seeing that they are of great utility, he is unable to part with them."
Furthermore, if they cannot carry it away,
the Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement) to exchange it for something lighter.
That bhikṣu should then request this from the Saṃgha, saying:
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], have personally kept bedding and utensils that I find to be of good quality.
Now, wishing to travel to such-and-such a place, I am unable to take them with me because they are too heavy."
"I pray that the Saṃgha will exchange [this] with me for something lighter from the Saṃgha!
Thus he should request a second and a third time.
A single bhikṣu within the Saṃgha should then announce:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has personally kept bedding and requisites that he finds useful.
Now, wishing to travel to such-and-such a place, he is unable to take them with him because they are heavy; [he requests permission to leave them behind]."
I request the Saṃgha to exchange this for something lighter; may the Saṃgha now grant the exchange.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I shall state it thus.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has personally kept bedding and requisites that he finds to be of good quality; however, wishing to travel to such-and-such a place, he is unable to carry them away because they are heavy.
He requests from the Saṃgha an exchange for lighter ones, and the Saṃgha now grants this exchange."
"Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has finished exchanging the light bedding of the Sangha with that of the bhikṣu so-and-so."
"The Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent;
this matter is thus upheld.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding, he should keep it for six years;

if he discards it or does not discard it before the six years are complete and then makes another new bedding—except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha—he commits a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"Six years" means that the count of days has reached six full years.
The remainder is as explained in the section on bedding made of pure black wool; this concludes the twenty-fourth [section].
The Buddha was staying in the city of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the Vṛji people were making monastic rugs (*niṣīdana*) out of pure black sheep’s wool, and the Bhikṣus of the Vṛji clan also begged for it to make them.

The laypeople grew weary of being solicited for alms; on a later day, they went to the monks' quarters to visit and saw that the bhikṣus were keeping many sitting mats made of pure black sheep’s wool. They then reviled them, as described in the section concerning pure black bedding.
The elder bhikṣus heard of this and reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked those bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For ten reasons, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu makes a new niṣīdana out of pure black sheep’s wool, he must use a piece from an old niṣīdana measuring one Sugata-span to destroy its fine color.'"
"If it is not destroyed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
One Sugata-span (*sugata-vidatthi*) is two feet square.
Regarding the "spoiler of fine color":
it may be placed over a new item at will.
The rest is as explained in the section on the woolen bedding of pure black; this concludes the twenty-fifth [rule].
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, several bhikṣus were traveling along the road carrying loads of wool on their backs. Seeing them, the people on the road all reviled and scolded them, saying:
"We have families to support, yet we carry loads of wool; how can you monks do the same?"
The bhikṣus are likewise so.
Merely wearing dyed, cut-and-sewn robes and shaving their heads to beg for alms—how are they different from me?
They lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!

There was a bhikṣu living in the mountains who was accustomed to carrying loads of wool. Being utterly exhausted from the journey, he fell prostrate upon the courtyard floor of the saṃghārāma upon his arrival.
When the other bhikṣus saw him, they thought he was possessed by a ghost and immediately sprinkled urine over him.
He said, "Venerable sir!
Why have you sprinkled me?"
He replied, "I feared he was possessed by a ghost; that is why I sprinkled [water] on his ears!
The other said:
"I am not possessed by a ghost; it is simply because I am weary from the road and faint with heat due to the heavy burden of wool on my back!
The bhikṣus said, "The Buddha has ordained that bhikṣus possess only three robes and an alms bowl, just as a flying bird carries its feathers with it."
"Do you not hear [me], yet you still carry this!
Having rebuked him in various ways, he reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned that bhikṣu:
“Is it truly so? He replied, “It is truly so.”
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten reasons, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”
“If a bhikṣu carries wool on a journey, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
At that time, there was a householder who had built a cell for the Saṃgha and thought to himself:
“If a bhikṣu comes to this cell, I shall provide for him and also bestow robes upon him.”
A certain bhikṣu came and stayed in his room, whereupon he offered him some wool. The bhikṣu would not accept it, so the householder said:
"I have gathered this wool specifically for the sake of bhikṣus; it was not for my own self."
The bhikṣu replied, "The Buddha has not permitted me to carry wool myself; how could I accept it?

Furthermore, there was another bhikṣu who required wool to make bedding, but as he did not know how to make it himself, he wished to ask another bhikṣu to do so. However, he did not dare to accept [the offer], and for this reason he reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked that bhikṣu:
"How far from here is the person you wish to borrow? He replied:
"Go three yojanas from here.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, having praised fewness of desires and contentment, and having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:"
“If a bhikṣu obtains wool and needs to carry it to a certain destination,
he may carry it himself for up to three yojanas.
If he exceeds this distance, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.”
If a bhikṣu obtains wool and needs to carry it to a destination, he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) carry it;

if there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, he is permitted to carry it himself, but he must not carry it on his shoulders, wear it on his head, or bear it on his back. One who violates this incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a śrāmaṇera, it is a duṣkṛta.
There is no offense if it is within three yojanas.
If one carries it by passing it from hand to hand, or if someone else carries it on one's behalf;
if one carries it for three *yojanas* and returns, or carries five or six *pātra*s;
or if one uses it to make a waist-belt, a hat-strap, and so forth—these twenty-six cases are concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus had the bhikṣuṇīs wash, dye, and card the wool of rams for them. Out of a desire to provide offerings, the bhikṣuṇīs did not dare to refuse;

consequently, they became burdened with many tasks and duties, which interfered with and caused them to neglect their recitation, meditation, and the practice of the Path. When the lay devotees saw and heard of this, they criticized and reviled them.
The bhikṣuṇī Prajāpatī, together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, went to where the Buddha was, as described above in the section concerning the washing of old robes.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī to wash, dye, or card sheep’s wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.'"
At that time, there were bhikṣus who had bhikṣuṇīs among their relatives; this was also as explained above regarding the washing of old robes.

They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having praised fewness of desires and contentment, having praised the precepts, and having praised the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu should have a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or card wool from a ram, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
The remainder is as explained above regarding the washing of old robes; this concludes the twenty-seventh [section].
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Upananda engaged in various kinds of trade and was able to profit others, yet no one was able to profit him.
A certain non-Buddhist practitioner obtained an unfinished garment and took it to another non-Buddhist household,
saying, "Please sew this for me.
The people there replied:
"My household has many affairs and I cannot do this.
The śramaṇa sons of the Śākya are leisurely and have no business, yet they receive many offerings of robes; you may go there to borrow them or trade for them.
However, those śramaṇas often manage to force great merchants to give them [goods]; when you go, you must be cautious."
Thereupon, the non-Buddhist took it to the monastery and inquired, saying,
"Who among you can sew this robe for me?
Everyone replied that they could not.
He further said to Upananda, "I have heard, Venerable Sir, that you possess many ready-made robes; may I trade one robe with you? He replied:
“You non-Buddhists, your minds are not firm or upright; you are fickle and changeable. Now that you have obtained [this], you immediately say that the price is unequal;
if you had said nothing later, it would have been granted to you.”
He replied, "Others may do so, but I shall never regret it. Thereupon,
Upāli-bhadanta dyed coarse cotton with a turbid dye, beat it while wet to make it dense and thick, and gave it to him.
Having received the robe, he returned to the assembly of non-Buddhists.
The non-Buddhists asked him,
"Did you succeed in obtaining the robe?"
He replied, “I have already made the exchange.
[The other said,] “Take it and let me see it.”
He immediately showed it to them; when the non-Buddhists saw it, they all said, "Alas!
To exchange a garment of great value for this tattered robe is not even a fivefold or sixfold difference."
"You may take it back; we shall set aside our business for a moment to sew it for you.
He then took it back and said to Baddhananda, "O son of the Śākyas!"
"How can you deceive me with such tattered robes?
Return them to me; I will not spread your wickedness! Baddhananda replied:
"I knew that the minds of the non-Buddhists were not firm or upright, being subject to change, regret, and instability; therefore, I did not wish to associate with them.
Since you say you do not regret [your decision], I have followed along with you."
"Why do you only now speak these words?
He then refused to give it to him, whereupon the man wept bitterly.
The lay devotees asked:
"Why are you weeping? she asked.
She answered him fully with the facts of the matter.
The laypeople then criticized and rebuked her, saying:
“Laypeople who engage in buying and selling may still feel regret within seven days;
why then can you, O śramaṇas, not do so for even a moment?
Your appearance and dress differ from those of ordinary people, yet your commercial dealings exceed theirs.”
Thus his evil reputation spread far and wide. When the elder bhikṣus heard of it, they censured him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is truly so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"For the sake of ten benefits, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of trade and commerce to seek profit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.'"
"By means of what has been done, one exchanges it for what is being done;
by means of what has been done, one exchanges it for what has not yet been done; by means of what has been done, one exchanges it for both what is being done and what has not yet been done."
Exchanging the unperformed for the unperformed;
exchanging the unperformed for the performed;
exchanging the unperformed for both the performed and the unperformed.
If one exchanges what has been made for what has not been made, or what has been made for what is yet to be made;
if one exchanges what has been made for what has not been made;
or if one exchanges what has been made for what has not been made—all these constitute *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses.
If a bhikṣu wishes to engage in trade, he should employ a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) and say to them:
"For my sake, exchange this item for that item.
Furthermore, he should form a mental intention:
"One should think: 'It would be better for him to obtain my profit than for me to obtain his profit.
If one engages in trade, it should be with the five classes of monastics;
if one trades with a layperson, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. [The twenty-eighth section is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, Nanda and Upananda used gold, silver, gold coins, and various types of currency to purchase goods, and they also sold goods to receive payment.
Then, a band of robbers arrived at Rājagṛha seeking wealthy households; seeing the two bhikṣus extensively buying and selling goods with gold, silver, and money, they deliberated together, saying:

They tortured him until he was on the verge of death and then seized his robes and bowl before departing.

World-Honored One.”

Having rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:

That bhikṣu should discard this object in a pit, in fire, in flowing water, or in the wilderness; he must not record its location.

Part Five of the First Division: The Nine and Eleven Dharmas of Defeat (Pārājika). The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a Dharma-preacher bhikṣu named Śāraṇa, who was intelligent and possessed great eloquence; none among the fourfold assembly, nor among the non-Buddhists, śramaṇas, or brahmins, could equal him.

He would take what is wrong for right and what is right for wrong; he would claim to know what he did not know and claim not to know what he did know. Constantly employing his skillful rhetoric, he would best the speech of others.
When the bhikṣus saw this, there was none who did not express their admiration and submission, asking:
"In your debate with others, you took what is wrong to be right.
Do you yourself believe it to be right, or do you know it is wrong?"
He replied:
"I truly knew it was wrong; out of shame at having fallen into defeat, I spoke falsely!
The elder bhikṣus rebuked him in various ways:
“The Buddha always praises abstaining from false speech and also teaches others not to speak falsely.
Why do you now utter such a lie for the sake of victory and defeat?”
They reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Śāraṇa:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied: “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu speaks falsely, it is a pāyattika.'"
At that time, the bhikṣus saw a bhikṣuṇī and said she was a bhikṣu;
they saw a bhikṣu and said he was a bhikṣuṇī;
or they saw a man and said he was a woman.
Sometimes they see a woman and call her a man;
sometimes they see a non-Buddhist and call him a son of the Śākyas;
or they see a son of the Śākyas and call him a non-Buddhist.
Thus, seeing various differences in views and speech, they felt shame and remorse,
thinking, "Have we perhaps committed a *pāyattika* offense?
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"It is impossible for a bhikṣu to commit a pāyattika offense by speaking according to what he has conceived in his mind."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu intentionally utters a falsehood, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "intentionally uttering a falsehood":
As it was explained regarding the offense of falsely claiming superhuman attainments, the same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. This concludes the first matter.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, various bhikṣus were diligently studying together with their preceptors (upādhyāya) and teachers (ācārya), as well as those who shared the same preceptors and teachers; from the first watch of the night until the last, they never slept.
The group of six bhikṣus thought to themselves:
“Now these bhikṣus instruct one another day and night without ceasing; before long they will surpass us, see through our faults, and seek out our failings.”
"We shall join together to revile and vex him so that he abandons his work.
They then went to him and said, "You are of low and base lineage! You are but a common craftsman!"
"You have committed many great evils; you have no acts of benevolence or goodness!
When the other bhikṣus heard this, they became distressed and abandoned their studies.
The group of six bhikṣus then said to others:
"I have already ruined their recitation, meditation, and practice of the Path.
The elder bhikṣus rebuked him in various ways:
"How can you destroy these bhikṣus and cause them to abandon their studies?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a city named Takṣaśilā.
At that time, in that city, a certain brāhmaṇa possessed a prize bull that was swift and possessed great strength."
There was another householder who also had a single ox, no different from the other's.
The two men then compared the strength of their two oxen, wagering fifty gold coins that whoever's ox was inferior would lose.

The Brahmin’s ox immediately gained the victory; thereupon, the householder was ashamed at having lost his money and obtained another ox twice as superior as the first, whereupon he doubled the wager for another round of the match.
The Brahmin then said to the ox:
"That householder has obtained another ox whose strength is extraordinary; he wishes to double the wager against you.
Are you able to do it?"
He replied, "I can!
They immediately gathered in one place to test the strength of the two oxen.
At that time, fearing that his ox would not prevail, the brahmin reviled and urged it on:
"Crooked-horn! Pull hard! Poor-neck! Pull harder!"
"Why is your gait not steady now?
Upon hearing these words, the ox lost much of its strength and was no longer a match for that other ox.
Having paid double the amount of goods, the Brahmin asked the ox:
"You previously said you were capable; why are you not so now?
He replied, "I was indeed capable, but upon hearing this disparagement, my strength has completely vanished."
"You may further sever your gambling addiction by making it double its former intensity, requiring you to pull a hundred carts up a steep slope;
