while you are exerting your strength, you should be enticed with sweet words, saying: 'Guanjiao!'"
"Your gait is steady and upright, your physical form is beautiful, and you can easily pull a hundred carts up a steep slope.
Thereupon they wagered once more, and he indeed emerged victorious.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, spoke in verse:
"One should speak words that are pleasing; One should not utter speech that is disagreeable.
Even animals are gladdened by hearing them, As they pull heavy loads up steep inclines."
"Therefore, having no enemies, one obtains double the joy.
How much more so among human beings, where praise and blame cause neither increase nor decrease? "O Bhikṣus!"
Even animals, upon hearing disparaging words, lose their strength; how much more so for humans!
Now, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu disparages another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika."
"Regarding 'reviling':
it refers to calling someone of a lowly artisan caste.
In such cases, although one speaks the truth, one intends to disparage them."
If he hears and understands it, there is a *pāyattika* offense for every word;
if he does not hear or understand it, there is a *dukkaṭa*. If he says:
"If you say, 'You are low-born,' and the other person says it is not so;
yet you insist that it is true, for every such statement, there is a *pāyattika* offense."
If a bhikṣu reviles a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣuṇī reviles a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
if she reviles a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī disparages any of the five groups [of practitioners], it is a duṣkṛta offense.
There is no offense in the following cases:
when speaking for the sake of their benefit, when speaking as instruction or admonition, or when speaking with their consent; these two matters being concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus applied themselves diligently to study and inquiry, as described in the section on "Reproach.
Fearing that they might surpass them, the group of six bhikṣus then incited discord among them.
Arriving at the midst of the bhikṣus, he spoke to them, saying:
"I have been close friends with you, yet he says that you are of low and base birth, a mere craftsman and a commoner, who has committed great evils and lacks any virtuous or benevolent conduct."
"When I hear their words, they are no different from what I have said myself.
When he reached those other bhikṣus, it was likewise so.
Upon hearing this from one another, their minds all became distracted; they abandoned their studies and training, grew resentful toward each other, and ceased speaking together.
A certain bhikṣu asked the bhikṣus:
"For what reason do you not speak with me? The bhikṣus replied:
Someone said, "You are saying that I am evil! He replied, "Who said so?"
He replied, "The group of six bhikṣus. The other said:
The group of six bhikṣus also said, "You are spreading reports of my faults.
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked the group of six bhikṣus in various ways:
"How can you engage in divisive speech and cause dissension!"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied: “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"You foolish person! How can you, while sharing in the same Dharma, engage in divisive speech and incite strife?"
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, there was a lion named Supuṣpadanta and a tiger named Supratiṣṭhitakhura, who were close friends."
There was a wild fox who constantly followed them in search of food, yet the lion and the tiger would not speak with him.
Later, the wild fox thought to himself:
"Now these two beasts hold each other in great affection; I shall sow discord between them so that they will each seek their own food. What remains will surely be abundant, and I shall obtain it."
He then went to the tiger’s side and spoke this verse:
“O Śarabha, you are fierce and powerful; Your birthplace and your physical strength are wondrous.
Yet your sharp fangs proclaim your cruelty; Hearing this, my heart finds no joy.”
"Then he went before Siṃha and spoke another verse:
'O Virtuous Tusk, you are valiant and fierce; Your birthplace, your appearance, and your strength are sublime.
Virtuous Claw speaks ill of you; Hearing this, my heart is not pleased.'"
Upon hearing the verse, the two beasts were each displeased with one another. Good-Tusk (Sudanta), being wise, immediately thought to himself:
"Good-Claw (Supāda) will not speak to me; this must surely be the result of the wild fox's instigation and discord."
Later, he obtained a single calf and gave it to the tiger, but the tiger refused to eat it.
Thereupon, Śunaḥśepa questioned him with a verse:
"You have set aside yours to give this to me; for what reason do you not eat?"
Those who were once close and affectionate, now find no fault in one another yet no longer take pleasure in each other’s company.
Could it be that you have believed the words of a fox to sow discord between us?
If you continue to harbor feelings of resentment, it will surely result in a lasting bond of enmity.
"Inferring from this, there is no other cause; it must be the slander of a wild fox.
This lowly creature has alienated my beloved; I shall now kill and cast her away!
Thus he spoke to the bhikṣus:
"Even animals consider strife and discord to be wrong, how much more so for human beings!
I now establish this precept for the bhikṣus: from this day forward, this precept shall be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, through double-tongued speech, causes strife and discord among bhikṣus, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remainder is as explained in the section on disparagement; the three matters are concluded.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, Upananda frequently entered and left the house of a certain lay devotee, preaching the Dharma for him, settling his legal disputes, and relieving him of various sufferings from illness.
Later, that family’s fortunes declined and their members perished almost entirely, until only the wife and her mother-in-law remained.
At that time, Baddhananda, out of a sense of intimacy and affection, would preach the Dharma for the mother-in-law when the wife was away, and stop when the wife arrived;
likewise, he would preach the Dharma for the wife when the mother-in-law was away, and stop when she arrived.
Each conceived a suspicious thought, believing that he surely intended to engage in impure conduct;
they then spoke of it among themselves until the news reached far and near.
Those who did not have faith in or delight in the Buddha-dharma began to revile him, saying:
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, practice what is not the Dharma; they are more dissolute than worldly libertines!
They lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you did this?
He replied: "It is true."
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu expounds the Dharma to a woman, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
At that time, there was a bhikṣu of great majesty and virtue who, when the time arrived, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.

He came upon a certain house, where a woman came out, prepared a seat for him, and served him delicious food. When he had finished eating, she sat before him on a small stool and said, "Virtuous One!"
"Preach the Dharma for me.
The bhikṣu observed her and knew that in a mere moment the "wind of the blade" would arise, causing her to die and fall into hell;
yet, if he were to preach the Dharma for her, she would immediately transcend the dust and leave behind defilement while still seated upon her mat.
Although he saw and knew this, he thought to himself:
"The Buddha has prescribed that it is not permitted to preach the Dharma to women; even unto death, I must not violate this."
She replied, "Sisters, be at ease; you must not say anything.
Having spoken, she departed.
Not long after he had departed, the woman indeed died from a sudden wind-illness.
The bhikṣu took pity on her and returned to the monastery to tell the others.
The bhikṣus then led him to the Buddha's presence and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked that bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha then asked the bhikṣu again:
"If you were to preach the Dharma for him, how many words would it take for him to understand?
He replied, "Five or six words."
Thereupon, the Buddha, having praised fewness of desires and contentment, and having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I allow the bhikṣus to preach the Dharma to women for up to five or six sentences."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu teaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences, it is a pāyattika."
At that time, some bhikṣus entered the homes of others, and when a woman requested them to preach the Dharma, the bhikṣus spoke five or six sentences and then remained silent.
The women said, "We do not yet understand; we pray that you will explain it further. The bhikṣus said:
"Sisters! The Buddha does not permit us to preach the Dharma to women for more than five or six words. The women said:
"You may explain it to other bhikṣus; through this, I shall attain understanding.
The bhikṣus said, "The Buddha has not yet permitted us to preach the Dharma to women on account of a bhikṣu."
Having reported this to the Buddha, the Buddha convened the community of bhikṣus on account of this matter and addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit a bhikṣu to preach the Dharma to a woman."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who entered the house of a high minister; as he had no fellow bhikṣu with him, several women requested that he preach the Dharma to them.
He replied, "The Buddha has not permitted me to preach the Dharma to women for more than five or six sentences."
The women then called their children forward to stand before him and said,
"Venerable Sir,
please preach the Dharma for this child; through this, we shall attain understanding."
He replied, "The Buddha has not yet permitted me to preach the Dharma to women on account of a young boy.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, who, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I allow you to preach the Dharma to women in the presence of a man who understands.
At that time, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Although the Buddha has allowed us to preach the Dharma to women in the presence of a man who understands, such a man who understands is difficult to encounter."
He still did not explain it.
When this was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus on this matter and addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, I permit a man who can distinguish between wholesome and unwholesome speech to teach the Dharma to a woman.”
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences, except when there is a man present who understands good and bad speech, it is a pāyattika."
At that time, there was an upāsaka who took a daughter from a family that did not honor the Dharma as his wife. He said to the bhikṣus:
"Virtuous ones!
Please preach the Dharma for my wife so that she may come to have faith and joy in the Triple Gem."
"For the sake of receiving the three refuges, the five precepts, and the eightfold precepts;
for the sake of explaining the ten wholesome paths and the ten unwholesome paths.
Yet, none of the bhikṣus spoke for him.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit you to grant women the three refuges, the five precepts, and the eightfold precepts, and to explain to them the ten wholesome paths and the ten unwholesome paths."
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
Regarding the "five words":
Form is impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
The six statements are:
the eye is non-self; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are non-self.
If a bhikṣu, having finished speaking five or six words to a woman, says:
"Sister, the Dharma is correctly limited to this much."
He rose from his seat and departed.
On another occasion, he returned and sat down again to explain that there was no offense.
If he had finished speaking five or six words when another woman arrived, he would then speak for the sake of the latter woman.
In such circumstances involving these causes and conditions, if one speaks to an immeasurable number of women, there is no offense.
If one is reciting a sutra oneself and a woman comes to listen;
or if a woman asks about the meaning and one must ensure she understands—even if it exceeds five or six words—there is no offense. This concludes the four matters.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus possessed power, while the other virtuous bhikṣus lacked power;

the group of six bhikṣus constantly obstructed the five kinds of *karmavācanā*: the *tajjanīya-karman* (act of censure), the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence), the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), and the *adārṣa-vihāra-karman* (act of subordination).
If a bhikṣu has been subjected to the five kinds of *karmavācanā*, and the Saṃgha wishes to revoke them, they must not be obstructed or refused.

Later, when the group of six bhikṣus lacked influence while the virtuous bhikṣus possessed it, and there was a matter for the Saṃgha to perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*), the time arrived for the group of six bhikṣus to make robes. The bhikṣus said:
"We shall now summon the group of six bhikṣus to perform the monastic business together.
If they do not come and relinquish their robes, we shall entrust them [to others] ourselves, so that we may carry out the proceedings in accordance with the Dharma."
He immediately assembled the Sangha and sent a messenger to tell the group of six bhikṣus:
"You should come; the Sangha is now gathered.
The group of six bhikṣus replied:
"We have a matter to entrust; we now send this person to deliver our instructions.
Having thus entrusted a bhikṣu, he should come before the assembly. If the Saṃgha ought to perform the five kinds of formal acts (karmas) for him, they should perform those five kinds of formal acts;
if they ought to revoke the five kinds of formal acts for him, they should revoke those five kinds of formal acts.
Once the *karmavācanā* was completed, the bhikṣu who had been entrusted with the matter returned to where the group of six bhikṣus were.
The group of six asked him,
"What did the Saṃgha do?"
He replied, "The formal acts (karmas) that we desire, the Saṃgha does not perform at all;
those that we do not desire, the Saṃgha performs instead."
The group of six bhikṣus then went to where those bhikṣus undergoing formal disciplinary action were and said to them, "Do not be distressed; we shall provide you with assistance."
"I did not entrust you to you because I was unaware that you were performing the *karmavācanā*; it was merely for the sake of instruction!
Had I known, I would have set aside my affairs and gone there myself.
For what reason should I allow him to complete this *karmavācanā*?"
They went again to the bhikṣu who had been released from the *karmavācanā* and said to him:
"We have not released you from the *karmavācanā*, nor do we accept your confession!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked the group of six bhikṣus.
"How can it be that after the Saṃgha has finished settling a legal matter according to the Dharma, they initiate it again?
Having approached the Buddha, they informed him of this matter.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
“Is it truly so? He replied, “It is truly so.”
"World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"
“If a bhikṣu, after the Saṃgha has finished settling a matter, raises it again, it is a pāyattika.
At that time, some bhikṣus did not know that the Saṃgha had finished settling the matter and raised it again;
later, when they realized this, they felt shame and remorse, and some went on to expiate their offenses and repent.
The elder bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"It is impossible that one who does not know that the Saṃgha has finished its deliberation on a case should, upon returning, reopen the matter and thereby commit a pāyattika offense."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that the Saṃgha has finished a formal legal proceeding, should reopen it, he commits a pāyattika offense.
Furthermore, there were certain bhikṣus who had conducted formal proceedings in an improper manner, and they thought to themselves:
"If the Buddha would permit us to initiate a legal action again even after we have settled a matter contrary to the Dharma, that would be well.
They reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now, it is permitted that the Saṃgha’s legal decision on a matter may be reopened.
From this day forward, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, knowing that the Saṃgha has completed a legal decision on a matter, reopens it, he commits a pāyattika.'"
If one initiates a matter when the Saṃgha has settled the case according to the Dharma, it is a pāyattika;
if one initiates a matter when the Saṃgha has not performed the formal act (karmavācanā) to settle it, it is a dukkaṭa;
if one initiates a private matter, it is a dukkaṭa.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. These five matters are concluded.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī; together with a saṃgha of five hundred bhikṣus, he went to the town of Aṭṭhapiṇḍaka.
At that time, the householder thought to himself:
"The Buddha has come here after a long interval and will soon depart again.
We should draw near to the bhikṣus to learn how to recite the sūtras and verses, and inquire about what we do not understand."
"After the World-Honored One has departed, we shall have someone to rely upon.
He then went to where the bhikṣus were and spoke these words:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Please teach us how to recite the sūtras and verses. The bhikṣus said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to teach laypeople to recite the scriptures."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to instruct laypeople in the recitation of the sūtras.

At that time, there were monks who had left home from various countries; when they recited the verses of the sūtras, their pronunciation and phrasing were incorrect, and the lay devotees (gṛhapati) then criticized and reproached them, saying:
"How is it that a bhikṣu, attending closely day and night, does not understand the speech of men, women, eunuchs, or those with dual sexual organs, nor the rules regarding the quantity of speech?"
When the bhikṣus heard this, they were each filled with shame and reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked them:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha then rebuked the householders from afar: "You foolish people!
How can you criticize those from other lands for reciting the sūtras with incorrect sounds and phrases?"
He addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu instructs a person who has not received full ordination to recite the sūtras, it is a pāyattika.’”
Later, there were other laypeople who sought to receive instruction in the recitation of the sūtras. The bhikṣus said to them:
"People like you find fault with our pronunciation and phrasing; do not receive [instruction] from us!"
"You have come here again now, only to exhaust yourself in vain! He replied,
"Virtuous One!..."
"I do not disparage the Buddha-dharma, nor do I seek other fields of merit.
How can it be that because this person has faults, you would not teach me?
Furthermore, there were other śrāmaṇeras who also wished to receive the sūtras, and the bhikṣus said:
“You must receive full ordination; then we shall instruct you.
The śrāmaṇeras said, “We have left the household life so that we may recite the sūtras and verses; why must we receive full ordination before we can be instructed?”
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"From now on, I permit you to instruct those who have not yet received full ordination in the recitation of sūtras, provided that you do not recite alongside them."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu teaches a sūtra to a person who has not yet received full ordination and recites it together with them, it is a pāyattika."
"Reciting together" means reciting at the same time; or,
before the sound of the instruction has ceased, the other has already recited it.
If one recites while the other has not yet finished, it constitutes a *pāyattika* for every sentence.
One should first instruct them, saying:
"Wait until I have finished speaking, and then recite."
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. The six matters are concluded.
The Buddha was staying at the village of Aṭṭhapiṇḍika.

Because the Buddha was about to depart, those householders all came to where the bhikṣus were; they sat in meditation together with the bhikṣus in the same hall, or practiced walking meditation together, remaining awake throughout both the first and last watches of the night without sleeping at all.
At that time, the bhikṣus would spend an entire night preaching the Dharma once every five days; being utterly exhausted, they would lie down to sleep.
One bhikṣu, not applying himself with focused mindfulness, fell into a deep sleep; his robe slipped off his body, leaving his form exposed.
When the lay devotee saw this, he covered them again with his robe; this happened three times, whereupon he spoke with anger and reproach:
"These people constantly hear various censures regarding desire, yet now they expose their bodies and arouse themselves."
"If this is so, and you do not delight in the Path, why do you not return to lay life?
Upon hearing this, that bhikṣu felt shame;
when the elder bhikṣus heard it, they too were deeply abashed, and they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked that bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked that bhikṣu in various ways:
"I have always praised sleeping with an undisturbed mind, for it is free from the five evils.
Why do you now fail to maintain mindfulness?

If a bhikṣu behaves improperly while walking, sitting in meditation, standing, or lying down, people will see it and be displeased; they will not give rise to faith, and those who already have faith will regress. Thus, he does not act as a great light for the world."
He addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu stays overnight with a person who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.’”
Later, when various laypeople wished to approach the bhikṣus to practice dhyāna and cultivate the Path, the bhikṣus drove them out and would not allow it.
The laypeople said,
"Venerable Sirs!..."
Do not drive us away; we seek no other field of merit, but take refuge solely in you, Great Virtue.
How can it be that because one person has committed a transgression, you cast us all aside and neglect us?

Some influential laypeople then burst into the rooms; unable to stop them, the bhikṣus had to go outside and sleep in the open, where they were tormented by mosquitoes, gadflies, wind, rain, and dust.
At that time, the Buddha traveled from the town of Aṭṭhapiṇḍika to the Gośīrṣa Garden in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
Rāhula went separately to the Vargīya monastery, swept and sprinkled one room, spread out the bedding, and having finished fetching water, closed the door and went to where the Buddha was.
After he had departed, the monk who was distributing bedding gave it to another person, and that monk immediately entered the room to stay there.
After Rāhula had listened to the Dharma during the first watch of the night, he returned to the room he had been assigned.
That bhikṣu heard this and asked, "Who is it? They replied:
"It is Rāhula! the bhikṣu said, "Why have you come?"
He replied, "This is my room. The other bhikṣu said:
"The bhikṣu who distributes bedding has given this to me.
Rāhula said, "I previously swept the area and prepared the bedding; I have gone for a moment to the Buddha's presence to listen to and receive his teachings."
"How can you wish to refuse to return it to me?
That bhikṣu said, "Even though you have taken care of it, as a senior elder (*sthavira*), I ought to receive this dwelling."
Rāhula said, "May I dwell with you? He replied:
"No! He then sought to enter and sit, or to stand and dwell before the eaves, but was denied in all these cases as well.
Thereupon, Rāhula thought to himself:
"I shall go to the other rooms and do the same; only upon the latrine can I find rest!
He then went into the latrine.
At that time, there was a black snake in the latrine, which the Buddha saw with his divine eye (divyacakṣus) and thought to himself:
"If I do not go, Rāhula will be killed by a snake in a mere moment.
He then went before the latrine, snapped his fingers and cleared his throat, and Rāhula likewise made a sound in response.
The Buddha asked, "Who are you? He replied:
"It is Rāhula! He asked again, "Why are you here?"
He answered with the facts as they were.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One took Rāhula back to his own quarters. When the night had passed, he assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked that bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you did not admit Rāhula?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"You foolish man! How can a wild fox drive away a lion?"
At that time, because of this, the bhikṣus again informed the Buddha that the aforementioned laypeople had entered their rooms and were sleeping in the open air.
After the Buddha had praised in various ways having few desires and knowing contentment, praised the precepts, and praised the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to stay together with those who have not yet received full ordination for two nights."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu stays overnight with a person who has not received full ordination for more than two nights, it is a pāyattika."
"To stay overnight together" means to stay overnight in the same room;
that is, there is a roof above and four walls.
If there is a covering above but no single wall or two walls, it is a *pāyattika*;
if there are not three walls, there is no offense.
If there are four walls, whether the upper covering is half-finished, less than half-finished, or more than half-finished, it is in all cases a *pāyattika*.
If it is covered only slightly, there is no offense.

In these various cases, if one stays for more than two nights and, during the latter part of the night, places one's side against the bed or turns over, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense in all instances.
There is no offense in the following cases:
when they share a roof but there is a partition between them;
or when one is ill and unable to rise or move about.
If there are various obstacles;
or if one practices constant sitting without lying down;
or if that person lies down, the bhikṣu remains seated.
He sat while the bhikṣu lay down.
The same applies to the bhikṣuṇī; thus the seven matters are concluded.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī.
At that time, there was a famine and it was difficult to obtain food through begging. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Each of you should go to stay in retreat according to your acquaintances.

There were some bhikṣus who stayed in retreat on the banks of the Pārāvatī River; for various reasons, as described in the section concerning those who falsely claimed to have attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*), up until the point where the Buddha questioned them:
“You have praised one another; was this true or false?
They replied, “Some was true, and some was false.”
The Buddha said:
"One who speaks falsely incurs a *pārājika* offense.
He then rebuked those bhikṣus who were actually guilty in various ways, saying:
“How is it that you have declared to those who have not yet received full ordination that you have attained superhuman states?
Having rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu, toward one who has not yet received full ordination, speaks of having attained a superhuman state, saying:
'I know thus; I see thus.'"
"If it is true, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), as explained above:
if one speaks to a person who has not yet received full ordination, claiming for oneself that one has attained a superhuman state, for every such statement, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one speaks to a person who has received the full ordination (upasampadā) without being asked, for every word spoken, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense in the following cases:
speaking at the time of entering *nirvāṇa*;
or when a person who has received full ordination asks a question, and one speaks after the eight matters have been concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, various bhikṣus committed saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses: some intentionally emitted semen, some touched the bodies of women, some spoke coarse and wicked words to women, and some praised their own bodies for the sake of receiving offerings from women;
some requested *parivāsa* (probation) from the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha granted them *parivāsa*; some performed *mānatva*, some performed *mūlāpakarṣa*, and some were cleared of their offenses.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus mocked them all within the Saṃgha, causing the other bhikṣus to feel even greater shame.
Furthermore, there was another bhikṣu who committed the offense of intentional emission of semen; the Saṃgha granted him the penance of *parivāsa*.

At that time, a donor invited the Sangha for the midday meal and specially prepared fine seats for those bhikṣus. The group of six bhikṣus arrived at the donor's house beforehand and sat upon the fine seats.
The layperson said, "Do not sit in these places!"
"I shall offer alms to the bhikṣus and take my seat at the head of the assembly.
The group of six bhikṣus said,
"That bhikṣu should not sit here!"
The householder said,
"Whether it should be given or not, I know that myself!
The group of six bhikṣus said:
"Previously you should have sat here, but now you should sit in the lowest seat.
The householder asked again, "Why is this so?"
He replied, "That bhikṣu has committed an offense.
The householder asked again:
"What offense have you committed?
He replied, "I have intentionally emitted semen."
The householder then rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas constantly preach the removal of thoughts of desire, the extinction of the fever of desire, and the severing of the perceptions of desire;
yet now they act in such a way as to defile the path."
"You have no conduct of a śramaṇa; you destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked the group of six bhikṣus in various ways:
"How can you speak of another's grave offense to one who has not yet received full ordination?"
They reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu speaks of another's grave offense (sthūlātyaya) to one who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.'"
There were certain bhikṣus who, not knowing that it was a grave offense, spoke of it to persons who had not yet received full ordination; later, upon realizing this, they became doubtful:
"Have I perhaps committed a pāyattika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:

"If a bhikṣu does not know that another has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), and yet speaks of it to one who has not received full ordination, and thereby commits a pāyattika offense—such a thing is impossible."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing of another's grave offense, speaks of it to one who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika."
At that time, the World-Honored One commanded the Saṃgha to perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of appointing Śāriputra to go among the followers of Devadatta and proclaim:
"If there are those who accept the five points of Devadatta, they do not see the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha."
The bhikṣus had this thought:
"If one speaks of another's grave offense to a person who has not yet received full ordination, is it necessary to perform a formal ritual (karmavācanā), or is it not?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If the Saṃgha has not performed the formal act (karmavācanā), one must not disclose another’s grave offense to a person who has not received full ordination."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, speaks of it to one who has not received full ordination, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika."
"Regarding a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*):
it refers either to a *pārājika* or a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
A person who has been subjected to a formal act (*karmavācanā*) by the Saṃgha must follow the instructions of the Saṃgha; if instructed to speak to person A, yet speaks to person B;"
If one teaches regarding this offense while speaking of another offense, it is all a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu speaks of a bhikṣuṇī’s grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣuṇī speaks of a bhikṣu’s or a bhikṣuṇī’s grave offense, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī speaks of a grave offense (sthūlātyaya) of a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a person who has not yet received full ordination hears that a certain bhikṣu has committed a grave offense and questions the bhikṣu [about it].
The bhikṣu asked in return: "What have you heard? He replied:
"I have heard it thus and so! and then he says:
"I have also heard it thus!"
The section on the nine non-offenses is concluded.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

Then the World-Honored One praised the Vinaya in various ways; he praised the recitation of the Vinaya, the upholding of the Vinaya, and Upāli. He spoke of the five merits of a bhikṣu who maintains the Vinaya:
First, personally and firmly guarding the category of precepts;
second, being able to sever the doubts of those who possess a sense of shame and remorse;
third, abiding oneself within the True Dharma.
Fourth, fearlessness in speaking within the Saṃgha;
fifth, subduing enemies.
At that time, the bhikṣus had this thought:
"The Buddha has spoken thus for our sake; how could we not diligently practice the recitation and inquiry of the Vinaya?
Thereupon, they applied themselves to its study with arduous effort, never flagging by day or night.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus thought to themselves:

"Now these bhikṣus are diligently receiving, reciting, and inquiring about the Vinaya day and night; they will surely become very intelligent and understand the characteristics of all offenses. Once they see our faults, it will ultimately be to our detriment."
"I shall now join together in disparaging the Vinaya and those who study the Vinaya, so that they will abandon their practice and no longer recite or study it.
He then went to where the bhikṣus were and asked them,
"What are you reciting and studying?"
He replied, "The Vinaya. The group of six bhikṣus said:
"What is the use of reciting and practicing the miscellaneous minor precepts?
Why not recite and practice the sūtras on the various meanings such as the five aggregates and the six sense bases?
As for reciting the Vinaya, it does not exceed four matters, thirteen matters, and two indeterminate rules."
"What is the use of extensive knowledge?
To have much knowledge and much vision only increases a person's doubts. The bhikṣus said:
"You are so knowledgeable yet so full of doubt; I say the same of you!
Thus, they no longer recited or practiced.
The group of six bhikṣus said to one another:
“Those bhikṣus no longer recite or study the Vinaya; we are at ease and have attained great peace and happiness!
When the other bhikṣus heard this, they asked, “What are you saying?”
He answered exactly as it was.
Then the elder bhikṣus reprimanded him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so? He replied, "It is truly so."
"World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu speaks thus: 'What is the use of these minor rules?
When these rules are recited, they cause people distress!'"
"To disparage the precepts in this manner constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding "the precepts":
these refer to the *Prātimokṣa*, the Sūtra of Precepts recited during the fortnightly *poṣadha*.

If a bhikṣu gives rise to the thought with the intention of causing others to distance themselves from the Vinaya—neither reciting nor reading it—and disparages the precepts, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu gives rise to the thought:
"I shall disparage [the precepts] so that the Prātimokṣa may not endure for long," and he then disparages the training rules, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If one instructs others to distance themselves from the various sūtras spoken by the Buddha and disparages them, it is a pāyattika;
if one disparages them with the intent to cause the Dharma not to endure for long, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If a bhikṣu reviles the precepts of a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika;
if he reviles the precepts of a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣuṇī disparages the precepts of a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
if she disparages the precepts of a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī disparages the precepts of the five classes of followers, it is all a duṣkṛta offense.
If the five classes of followers disparage the precepts of upāsakas or upāsikās, it is all a duṣkṛta offense.

If one fears that a newly ordained person might give rise to doubts, abandon their practice, or fall away from the resolve for enlightenment, it is not yet permissible to instruct them in the recitation of the precepts; this concludes the section on the ten matters regarding non-offenses.
The Buddha, together with five hundred bhikṣus, traveled from the kingdom of Kośala toward the town of Aṭṭhapiṇḍika.
At that time, hearing that the Buddha was about to arrive, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"These lay devotees have no faith or delight in the Buddha-dharma, and they lack a great lecture hall; where will the Buddha and his great assembly dwell?"
They immediately gathered to deliberate and began cutting down the grass and trees themselves to manage the site.
At that time, the lay devotees (gṛhapati) criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"We, the white-robed laity, cut down grass and trees; for what reason do those who have left the home life act in this manner?"
"These [monks] constantly preach loving-kindness and patience, and protect and care for sentient beings; yet now they cut them down and harm them without principle.
They lack the conduct of śramaṇas and destroy the Dharma of śramaṇas!"
When the Buddha had arrived, he went to the new lecture hall, took his seat, and asked the bhikṣus,
"Who built this hall? They replied:
“We ourselves have made them.
He asked again,
“Who cut down these trees and grasses?”
They replied, "It was indeed us.
The Buddha rebuked them in various ways, saying:
"You foolish person, you should not do this!
To conceive the notion of a living being within grass and wood—
to do such a thing causes others to harbor ill will!"
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu kills living plants or grasses, it is a pāyattika offense.’”
At that time, the bhikṣus sent park-keepers or śrāmaṇeras to cut down grasses and trees.
The elder bhikṣus asked them,
"Has the Buddha not prohibited the killing of living plants and trees?"
They replied, "We have had others do it for us; thus we do not violate the Buddha's regulations. The elder bhikṣus said:
"What difference is there between committing suicide and causing another to kill?
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned the bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so for you? They replied, "It is truly so."
"World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu kills living plants or grasses himself, or causes another to kill them, it is a pāyattika.
At that time, some bhikṣus were building a new dwelling. Several lay devotees (gṛhapati) went to inspect their residence and said to the bhikṣus, "Excellent, Venerable Sirs!"
"All these materials for this dwelling have been donated by us; please complete it quickly so that we may obtain the merit of providing such requisites.
The bhikṣus replied, "The Buddha has not permitted us to cut down grass or trees ourselves, nor to have others do so."
"How can this be accomplished?

Thereupon, the bhikṣus had no dwellings to live in; the weeds in the courtyards reached their waists, and they were also lacking tooth-sticks. Not knowing what to do, they reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"There are four kinds of seeds:
root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, and fruit-seeds."
All grasses and trees grow from four kinds of seeds. If a bhikṣu requires any of these, he says to a *kappiya-kāraka*:
"You know this! If the latter does not understand, he speaks again:
"Look at this! If he does not understand, one speaks again, saying: "I need this!"
If they do not understand, he should speak again, saying:
"Give this to me! From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu cuts down a 'village of spirits' himself, or causes another to do so by saying,
'Cut this down!',
it is a pāyattika."
If it is living grass and one perceives it as such, or has doubt regarding it, it is a *pāyattika*;
if it is dry grass and one perceives it as living grass, or has doubt regarding it, it is a *dukkaṭa*;
if it is dry grass and one perceives it as such, there is no offense.
If one chops with a knife or an axe, for every chop, it is a *pāyattika*.
It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, to kill living plants or trees without a valid reason is a *duṣkṛta*.
If it has been burned by fire, split, or cut, one knows that it will certainly not grow; thus the eleven matters regarding non-offenses are concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus repeatedly committed offenses:

They were improper in both ascending and descending from their beds; they ate repeatedly; they ate separately from the community; and they entered the village at improper times without informing a virtuous bhikṣu.
When the other bhikṣus saw this, they said to them:
"Do not repeatedly commit these various offenses; you should recognize your own faults and repent before others."
"Do not fail the faithful offerings and suffer for a long night!
The group of six bhikṣus said,
"What offense have we committed?"
The bhikṣus said, "You have committed such and such an offense.
The group of six bhikṣus did not answer whether they had committed it or not, but instead spoke of other matters.
The bhikṣus said: "We did not ask you;
why do you not answer whether there is an offense or no offense, yet speak of this matter?
The group of six bhikṣus replied:
"I know that you did not ask about this matter; I have spoken of it myself!
The bhikṣus rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so for you? They replied, "It is truly so."
"World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu does not answer in accordance with the truth, but instead utters evasive speech, it is a pāyattika.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus continued to commit their previous offenses; although the other bhikṣus again instructed them as before, the group of six remained silent and did not respond.
The bhikṣus asked, "The Buddha has established a precept that does not permit failing to answer in accordance with the truth; why do you remain silent?
The group of six bhikṣus replied:
“The Buddha has prescribed that one must not answer evasively; if I now remain silent, what offense would there be?
The bhikṣus said, “What difference is there between speaking evasively and remaining silent?”
Having rebuked them in various ways, he reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"What difference is there between speaking irrelevantly and not speaking at all?
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu intentionally does not answer when questioned, it is a pāyattika.
If he does not answer when questioned, for every question, it is a pāyattika."
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one answers by mistakenly taking another’s words as one’s own, or fails to answer because of prior resentment and a refusal to speak together, there is no offense. Section Twelve concludes.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra spoke these words:
“The bhikṣu Dabba follows desire, hatred, delusion, and fear!”
When the bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked him, saying,
"Why do you falsely accuse those appointed by the Saṃgha of acting out of desire, hatred, delusion, or fear?
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣu Maitrībala:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, in the presence of others, falsely slanders a person appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.'"
Thereupon, Maitrībala was no longer able to slander him in the presence of others; he then went alone and slandered the bhikṣu Dharmadatta, acting out of desire, hatred, delusion, and fear.
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked him, saying:
"The Buddha has already established a prior prohibition; why do you still falsely accuse those appointed by the Saṃgha?
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Maitrāyaṇīputra:
"Is it true that you did this?
He replied: "It is true."
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"What difference is there between speaking before others and speaking to oneself?
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, this precept should be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu falsely accuses a person appointed by the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.

If one falsely accuses a person appointed by the Saṃgha through a *jñapti-karman*, a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, or a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, then for every word spoken out of desire, hatred, delusion, or fear, it is a pāyattika;
if one makes such a false accusation against someone who was appointed by the Saṃgha but not through a formal *karman*, or against anyone else, it is a duṣkṛta for every word spoken.
It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If, being truly driven by desire, hatred, delusion, or fear, one says:
"I shall speak; you should listen.
The thirteenth [offense] is concluded without transgression.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī.
There was a monastery site that was low-lying and damp. A certain bhikṣu received a room in such a location; he took his bedding out and spread it on the open ground to air-dry.
When it was time for alms, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. After he had left, a heavy rain fell and the waters rose, flooding and sweeping away the bedding.
Upon returning from his meal, he did not see it and immediately began searching urgently; he found either a large bed, or a small bed, or a *kuśeya* (a type of mat), or blankets and pillows.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they asked,
"From where did you obtain these bedding materials and other items?
He answered with the aforementioned account.
The elder bhikṣus rebuked him, saying:
"What you have done is contrary to the Dharma!
A person who serves as a provider of bedding for the Saṃgha is difficult to find."
Once it was spread out, there was no one to take it up and fold it away.
Why did you not lift it when leaving, causing it to be washed away?
If it is lost forever, this room will be left empty!
Having rebuked him, he informed the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked that bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways as described above, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu spreads bedding belonging to the Saṃgha in an open space and does not remove it when departing, it is a pāyattika offense.’”

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus had a park-keeper and a śrāmaṇera spread out the monastic bedding on an open space; when they departed, they did not instruct them to put it away, so it was pecked and nibbled by birds and rotted and torn by mud and rain.
The elder bhikṣus saw this and said to him:
"Have you not heard that the Buddha has established a rule prohibiting the spreading of monastic bedding in the open air and failing to put it away when departing?"
He replied, "I had someone spread it; it does not contravene the Buddha's regulations. The bhikṣus said:
"What is the difference between spreading [the seat] oneself and having someone else do it?
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so? He replied, "It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu, having spread out bedding belonging to the Saṃgha on an open space himself, or having had someone else spread it out,
departs without putting it away himself or instructing another to put it away, it is a pāyattika."

There were certain bhikṣus who spread out the Sangha’s bedding on an open space. Later, the group of six bhikṣus came and either sat or lay down upon that bedding, and when they departed, they did not put it away.
The former bhikṣu said that the group of six bhikṣus should be censured, while the group of six bhikṣus said that the former bhikṣu should be censured.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"A preceding bhikṣu should entrust [his bowl] to a succeeding bhikṣu, and the succeeding bhikṣu should lift it up."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows: "If a bhikṣu,
having personally spread bedding belonging to the Saṃgha upon an open space, or having had someone else spread it,

or if it has been spread by another, sits or lies down upon it, and when departing does not himself remove it, nor instruct another to remove it, nor entrust its removal to someone else, it is a pāyattika."

There were some bhikṣus who, seeing that the bedding of the Saṃgha was soiled and filthy, placed it upon ashes, dust, or cow dung to dry it in the open; they remained within the boundary and did not dare to leave it unattended.
They reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"If the rain has ceased and the harvest can be gathered, you are permitted to leave."
There were some bhikṣus who were drying the bedding and requisites of the Saṃgha and did not dare to go outside the boundary.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If it is certain that it will not rain upon returning, you are permitted to go outside the boundary.
Furthermore, there were some bhikṣus who were sunning the monastic bedding; they sat in meditation at the edge, or fell into deep sleep and spoke in their dreams.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I do not permit you to sit in meditation or sleep soundly while leaving your bedding out in the sun; anyone who violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
Furthermore, there were monks who spread out the bedding and requisites belonging to the Saṃgha but did not immediately fold them away; they were damaged by being left in the sun.
The monks reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If one does not collect and put them away at the proper time, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Furthermore, there were some bhikṣus who saw monastic bedding spread out in the open air; yet, because they had neither spread it themselves nor caused others to spread it, and neither sat upon it nor lay down upon it themselves, they did not collect and put it away.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If one sees bedding belonging to the Saṃgha spread out in the open air and does not put it away, it is a pāyattika offense."
There were some laypeople who came into the monastery and asked for the monks' bedding, wishing to spread it out on the open ground.
The bhikṣus would not give it to them, whereupon the laypeople spoke of it with great derision and resentment.
They reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"I allow you to give it!"
Having given it, he wished to depart early and instructed them to go quickly; the layperson became angry again.
This was reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should not instruct them to depart immediately; rather, one should wait for the time of their departure before taking it up.
If one does not take it up, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, there were laypeople who invited the Saṃgha and borrowed bedding from the monks to spread out in their homes.
When the bhikṣus sat down and departed without putting it away,
the Buddha said:
"It should be put away."
"If one does not pick it up, it is a pāyattika.

If various bhikṣus go to a bhikṣuṇī monastery and leave the bedding of the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha spread out in the open air, and if they do not pick it up because they consider it not to be the bedding of the saṃgha, it is likewise a pāyattika.
Furthermore, there were some bhikṣus who carried their own beds and mats; the laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas are like performers or like illusionists!"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I do not permit carrying [the bowl] oneself; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."

Furthermore, during a great assembly, the monks spread out bedding on the open ground. Whenever the bhikṣus sat down or rose up, they would immediately fold it away; consequently, the bedding quickly fell into disrepair. They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "If it does not rain, you are permitted to lift [the bedding] only after all affairs have been concluded.

Once the Buddha had granted permission for such entrustment, the bhikṣus who later sat or lay down on the bedding would then entrust it to their upādhyāyas, ācāryas, fellow upādhyāyas and ācāryas, other virtuous elders, and sick bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should not entrust one's affairs to the upādhyāya, the ācārya, fellow upādhyāyas or ācāryas, or other virtuous elders, nor to a sick bhikṣu. To violate this rule constitutes a duṣkṛta offense."
The bhikṣus entrusted [their bedding] to one bhikṣu, but that single bhikṣu was alone and exhausted by the task. They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“According to the number of bedding items: if there are few, entrust them to a few bhikṣus;”
"If there are many, entrust them to many bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus did not know what constituted being entrusted with a commission and what did not; they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"To cause him to know the entrustment is called 'entrusting the responsibility'.
If one does not lift it oneself, does not instruct another to lift it, and does not entrust someone else to lift it, yet one foot crosses outside the boundary, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if both feet cross, it is a *pāyattika*.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. The fourteenth [offense] is concluded.
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī.

There was a dwelling place that was low-lying and damp. At that time, seventeen groups of bhikṣus were observing the rains retreat in a single room; when they departed, they did not put away the monastic bedding, and it all became rotten and ruined.
Later, the group of six bhikṣus arrived and said to the resident bhikṣus,
"Open a room for us and show us where the bedding is.
The resident bhikṣus then opened the room where the group of seventeen bhikṣus had been in retreat and gave it to them.
Having entered, he felt the bedding with his hand and found it decayed and turned to dust.
He asked the resident bhikṣu, "Who previously lived here? He replied:
“The group of seventeen bhikṣus.
Thereupon, the group of six bhikṣus rebuked the group of seventeen bhikṣus in various ways and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned the group of seventeen bhikṣus:
“Is it truly so? He replied, “It is truly so.”
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu, within a monastic dwelling, spreads bedding belonging to the Saṃgha himself, or causes another to spread it;

or if it has been spread by another, and he sits or lies upon it, yet when departing does not lift it up himself, nor instruct another to lift it, nor entrust it to someone else to be lifted, it is a pāyattika."
The rest is as explained in the section on spreading bedding in the open air, up to the fifteenth [rule].
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of seventeen bhikṣus had newly constructed a dwelling, and the group of six bhikṣus arrived later and said to the resident bhikṣus:
"Open the rooms for me in order!
An elder bhikṣu asked,
"Which one do you prefer?"
He replied, "I would like the new house being built by the group of seventeen bhikṣus.
He was then assigned to them.
The group of six bhikṣus went immediately to that place and said to them, "You must leave; we shall dwell within!
The group of seventeen bhikṣus replied:
"This room is fortunately large; you may stay here together with us.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus thought to themselves:

"These bhikṣus possess a sense of shame and remorse, and they study the Dharma and Vinaya. Since they do not sleep or lie down during the first or last watches of the night, they will surely see our transgressions; it is not appropriate for us to dwell together with them."
He then said to them, "We do not wish to dwell together; you may seek another room.
The group of seventeen bhikṣus replied:
"If you do not wish to dwell together with us, the Elder may stay in the front room while we stay in the rear rooms.
The group of six bhikṣus said,
"That too is not permitted!"
They further sought permission to stay under the eaves or to dwell in the open air within the courtyard, but were refused in all cases.
Since they were not permitted to stay and yet refused to leave, they were forcibly dragged out, whereupon the seventeen groups of bhikṣus cried out loudly.
The bhikṣus came out and asked,
"For what reason did you cry out so loudly? He replied:
“The group of six bhikṣus forcibly dragged me out!
The bhikṣus rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
“How could you forcibly drag someone out?”
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu forcibly drags another bhikṣu out of a monastic dwelling, it is a pāyattika.'"
Since the group of six bhikṣus could not pull him out themselves, they instead ordered a park keeper and a śrāmaṇera to pull him out.
When the other bhikṣus saw this, they asked,
"Has the Buddha not prohibited pulling a bhikṣu out of a monastic dwelling?"
He replied, "I did not pull it myself. The bhikṣus said:
"What difference is there between doing it oneself and having another do it?
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so? He replied, "It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:”
“If a bhikṣu drags another bhikṣu out from within a monastic dwelling—whether he drags him himself or causes another to drag him—it is a pāyattika.
There was a sick bhikṣu in a room who wished to go out into the courtyard but was unable to move;
he said to the other bhikṣus, “Excellent, venerable sirs!”
"Pull me out of the room.
The bhikṣus said, "The Buddha does not permit us to pull a bhikṣu out of a room."
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who, while bathing in the bathhouse, fell to the ground from heat exhaustion.
The other bhikṣus did not dare to pull him out; he died of suffocation, and they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"It is impossible that one would commit a pāyattika offense by having a sick person led out of their room when such a person requires to be led out."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, personally drags a bhikṣu out of a monastery dwelling, or causes another to drag him out, saying: 'Get out! Begone!'"
"Do not stay here! [If you do so, it is] a pāyattika.
If [the monk] is in the rear house and is dragged to the front house;
If one drags [an object] from inside a room to outside the door;
or from outside the door to the courtyard;
or from the courtyard to outside the gate—these all constitute a *pāyattika* offense.
If one drags out their robes and bowl, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one brings someone whom they dislike to live in the same room with them, intending to cause them to leave;
whether they leave or not, it is in all cases a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu drags a bhikṣuṇī out, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī drags a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī out, it is a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī drags a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī out, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī leads out the five classes of persons [from the assembly], it is a duṣkṛta offense.

However, if one leads out a person who lacks a sense of shame and remorse, or if one leads a disciple out for the purpose of subduing them, in these cases there is no offense. (The sixteenth section is concluded.)
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kośala together with a great community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the bhikṣus were distributing bedding and seats; some obtained rooms within buildings, while others obtained places under trees.

When it was time, the group of six bhikṣus put on their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the village to beg for food. After eating, they gathered at a crossroads with various householders, non-Buddhists, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, discussing matters of state, warfare, profit and loss, and other such various worldly affairs.
Those people all reproached them, saying:
"We, being householders, discuss worldly matters here for the sake of our domestic affairs;
yet these śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas also discuss worldly matters here—what difference is there between them and us?"
Returning at dusk, he conversed further with the park-keeper and the group of śrāmaṇeras at his dwelling;
it was not until nightfall that he finally sought out a room.
Arriving at one of the rooms, he asked the bhikṣus who had resided there previously,
"How many years of seniority do you have? They replied:
"I am [so-and-so] years old.
The group of six bhikṣus said, "You should go out; it is the senior monks who should remain!"
The bhikṣus said: "Elder! For what reason have you come in the dark?"
He replied, "I followed after the Buddha. The bhikṣus said:
"I have followed after the Buddha as well.
If I were to seek another room, I would again cause distress to the bhikṣus, just as the Elder has now caused me distress."
The group of six bhikṣus then spread out bedding and stayed there;
during the first and last watches of the night, they recited sūtras and hymns in loud voices and engaged in mutual debate;
during the middle watch, they snored and slept, obstructing the other bhikṣus from sitting in meditation and practicing the Path.
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked the group of six bhikṣus in various ways:
"By causing such harassment to the bhikṣus, you do not cherish the Buddha-Dharma!"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is true,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, after other bhikṣus have already finished spreading out bedding and mats, comes later and spreads out [bedding] again, it is a pāyattika.'"
There were some bhikṣus who, having finished spreading their bedding, went out for a short while.
Later, the group of six bhikṣus had a layperson spread bedding over it again.
When the other bhikṣus saw this, they asked:
“Have you not heard the Buddha’s regulation that once another has finished spreading bedding, one must not spread more upon it?
He replied, “I had a layperson do it; thus, I did not violate this regulation.”
The bhikṣus said, "What is the difference between spreading it oneself and having someone else do so?
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so? They replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, after other bhikṣus have already finished spreading out bedding, later comes and spreads it himself or causes another to spread it, it is a pāyattika.'"
There were some bhikṣus who, having already spread their bedding and finished, went out for a short while;
later-arriving bhikṣus, unaware of this, spread their own bedding over it.
When the bhikṣus who had first spread the bedding returned, the bhikṣus who had spread the latter bedding became suspicious.
"I shall not commit a *pāyattika* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If it is not the case that a monk commits a *pāyattika* offense by laying out bedding after another has already laid it out without knowing of it, such a thing is impossible.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a monk, knowing that another has already laid out bedding, comes later and either lays it out himself or causes another to lay it out, it is a *pāyattika*.'"

At that time, a great assembly of many bhikṣus gathered; although the dwellings were large, the number of rooms was few. Consequently, the bhikṣus who arrived later had no place to stay. Those bhikṣus who had already spread out their bedding called them in to stay with them, but the newcomers feared they would commit an offense of falling (pāyattika) and did not dare enter.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"It is impossible for one who does not cause offense or harassment to commit an offense of falling (pāyattika)."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another has already spread out bedding and seats, later comes and forcibly spreads his own, or causes another to spread it, with the thought:
'If he does not like it, he shall leave of his own accord.'"
"A *pāyattika*. It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Section seventeen concludes.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a multi-storied building at a certain residence, where a bhikṣu was dwelling on the upper floor. He had spread out a bed with pointed legs; he constantly maintained mindfulness as he sat, lay down, or moved up and down, never acting with haste or violence.
At that time, a visiting bhikṣu arrived; because he was the senior elder, [the resident bhikṣu] passed the bed to him.
This bhikṣu’s body was large and heavy, and without focusing his mind, he threw himself onto the bed. The legs of the bed gave way, striking the head of the [resident] bhikṣu below.
His head was split open and he cried out loudly. The bhikṣu from the upper story immediately descended to apologize, but the bhikṣu below rebuked him, saying:
“O resident bhikṣus, previously I never heard the sound of anyone sitting or rising.
How is it that as soon as you arrived, such a thing occurred?
Have you not heard the World-Honored One praise the practice of mindfulness?”
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they came to question him, and he answered with the aforementioned matters.
The bhikṣus censured him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked that bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, on an upper story of a multi-storied monastery building, sits or lies down forcefully upon a rope bed or wooden bed with pointed legs, it is a pāyattika.'"
When staying in a gabled house, one should place beds with pointed legs on the lower level, and those without pointed legs on the upper level;
if there are no beds without pointed legs, one should support them with large objects;
if there are no such supports, one should lash them crosswise.
If there is no obstacle, one should cover it and place it on the ground;
if one does not do so, but sits or lies down—even on a bed with a single pointed leg—it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one covers a loft with planks or wooden slats and knows for certain that they will not fall off, there is no offense. Section eighteen concludes.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.

At that time, the bhikṣu Chanda frequently entered and left various households; he even observed their earnestness and found it difficult to go against their wishes, all as previously described in the account of building a private dwelling for oneself when there is a patron.
Chanda then sought out a site for a dwelling; finding a good location, he erected a high foundation and constructed four walls by piling up thin bricks, covering them with an extremely heavy roof.
Because the roof was so heavy, the walls collapsed all at once, burying and killing the Brahmins' barley crop. They then rebuked him in anger, saying:
"Do these śramaṇas wish to live for an eon, or do they intend to provide for their descendants?"
"One or two layers of roofing would have sufficed for a lifetime; why was it made so excessively thick that it has collapsed like this?
He further said, "These fellows do not deprive their parents of anything, so they may indulge themselves in committing such evil deeds as these."
"He lacks the conduct of a śramaṇa and has destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard these various reproaches, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned Channa:
“Is it truly so? He replied, “It is truly so.”
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”

"If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling, starting from the level ground and piling up [the walls] while leaving space for windows and doors, he must ensure it is extremely solid with two or three layers of roofing;
if he exceeds this, it is a pāyattika."
If it reaches the fourth layer, whether covered with grass, tiles, or wooden planks, each individual blade of grass, tile, or plank constitutes a *pāyattika* offense;
during the preparatory stages, as well as while burning or cutting them, they all constitute *duṣkṛta* offenses;
once the covering is finished, it is a *pāyattika*.
The novice commits a *duṣkṛta* offense; the nineteenth [case] is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, Chanda was constructing a large dwelling and used water containing living beings to moisten the mud and grass, and he also had others do so.
Udāyin used water containing living beings for drinking, eating, and bathing.
When the lay devotees saw Chanda using water with living beings to sprinkle on mud and grass,
they asked Udāyin for a drink and gave him the water containing living beings.
The layperson said,
"There are insects in this water. He replied:
"Drink only water; do not drink [water containing] insects!
The laypeople said, "Venerable Sir!..."
"Since you have drunk the water, how can you not have drunk the insects?
He then did not reply at all.
The lay devotees criticized and rebuked him, saying:

"These śramaṇas constantly preach that they compassionately protect and mindfully care for sentient beings; yet now, by using water containing insects for mud-plastering, food, and bathing, they show no heart of pity!"
"You lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned Chanda and Udāyin:
"Is it truly so for you? They replied, "It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living beings, takes it to pour on mud, or uses it for food, drink, or other purposes, it is a pāyattika.
Water with living beings refers to that which is caught by a water-strainer or seen with the naked eye.
Whether pouring water on mud or giving food and drink, for every insect [killed], it is a *pāyattika*.
If there are insects, and one perceives them as such, or has doubt that there are insects, it is all a *pāyattika*;
if there are no insects, yet one perceives them as such, or has doubt that there are insects, it is all a *duṣkṛta*.
