Regarding water containing insects, there are internal and external applications.
Internal application refers to things such as food and drink.
External uses include:
pouring on plaster, bathing, and washing clothes, among others.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one looks closely and does not see [the insect], or if it is not caught by the strainer, there is no offense. The twentieth case concludes.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not instruct the bhikṣuṇīs nor did they preach the Dharma to them; consequently, [the nuns] remained empty-handed and gained nothing.
Yet, the bhikṣus instead reviled and scolded them:
"Because of you all, the Buddha’s True Dharma shall be diminished by five hundred years!
You cause all people to show no respect for śramaṇas, to treat bhikṣus with contempt, and to withhold offerings!"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated herself at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha asked Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"Has there been any elder bhikṣu who has instructed the bhikṣuṇīs, preached the Dharma to them, and thereby attained anything? She replied:
“No, World-Honored One!
Because the bhikṣus do not provide instruction and do not preach the Dharma, the bhikṣuṇīs are empty and have nothing to gain.”
On the contrary, they reviled them, saying:
"Because of you, the Buddha’s True Dharma has been diminished by five hundred years, and people no longer show respect or make offerings to śramaṇas!"
Thereupon, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs in various ways; having instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them, he sent them back to their respective dwellings.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the monks:
"O you elders, did you truly fail to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs and fail to preach the Dharma to them, and instead scold and revile them?"
He replied, "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!"
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should not revile others in such a manner; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense.
From now on, the bhikṣus should instruct the bhikṣuṇīs and should preach the Dharma to them."
Thereupon, the bhikṣus instructed the bhikṣuṇīs and preached the Dharma to them, and they immediately attained realization.
Later, the group of six bhikṣus also went to the dwelling place of the bhikṣuṇīs and said, "Sisters, assemble;
we shall instruct you and preach the Dharma."
The bhikṣuṇīs immediately gathered in one place, and the group of six bhikṣus proceeded to address them with coarse and vulgar speech regarding sexual desire.
Among those bhikṣuṇīs, there were some who had attained the various dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and right attainments (samāpatti), and they all refused to listen or accept [the words].
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs all praised them, saying, "These bhikṣus are truly capable of providing instruction; there is none who surpasses them!
Thereupon, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, went to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha asked Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Do the bhikṣus instruct the bhikṣuṇīs and preach the Dharma to them? She replied:
"There were certain bhikṣus who instructed the bhikṣuṇīs and taught them the Dharma, whereby they gained much benefit.

Then the group of six bhikṣus arrived and had the bhikṣuṇīs assemble, saying they would instruct them; instead, they spoke coarse and vulgar words regarding sexual desire. The group of six bhikṣuṇīs praised this, saying it was excellent and that nothing could surpass it."
After the Buddha had taught the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs, he sent them back to their respective dwellings.
On account of this matter, he assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is truly so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a monk instructs bhikṣuṇīs without having been appointed by the Saṃgha to do so, it is a pāyattika offense."

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went outside the boundary enclosure and, having appointed themselves as instructors of the bhikṣuṇīs, went to the dwelling place of the bhikṣuṇīs and said to them:
"The Saṃgha has now appointed us to come and instruct you!"

The bhikṣuṇīs gathered in one place as before, but the group of six bhikṣus again addressed them with coarse and wicked speech. Eventually, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī went to the Buddha’s dwelling and requested that they be sent back to their own quarters, as described above.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly go outside the boundary of the monastery grounds and, among yourselves, designate someone to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu is endowed with ten qualities, the Saṃgha should appoint him to instruct and admonish the bhikṣuṇīs."
What are the ten? First, accomplishment in ethical discipline, accomplishment in dignified deportment, and constant dread of even minor transgressions;

second, extensive learning, being able to discern with precision that which the Buddha taught as good in the beginning, middle, and end, possessing excellent meaning and excellent phrasing, complete and pure, the characteristic of the holy life (brahmacarya).
Third, he is well able to recite and explain the two divisions of the Vinaya;
fourth, he is skilled in discourse, articulating principles with clarity;
fifth, he has left the household life from a noble family, and his faculties are exceptionally distinguished.
Sixth, within the Buddha-dharma, one has never been defiled;
seventh, one’s deportment is calm and composed, the body is free from leaning or crookedness, and one wears the Dharma robes clean, pure, and properly arranged;
eighth, one is revered and honored by the community of bhikṣuṇīs.
Ninth, being able to preach the Dharma in accordance [with the listeners], instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them;
tenth, having reached twenty years of age, or more than twenty.
There are five qualities for which one should not be appointed, or if already appointed, one should be dismissed:
First, they completely forget and lose the sūtras and precepts they have recited;
second, their sense faculties are incomplete;
third, they have many desires.
Fourth, manifesting an evil appearance;
fifth, instructing bhikṣuṇīs to associate with evil persons.
Now, for the sake of the bhikṣus, I shall establish a precept. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, not being appointed by the Saṃgha, instructs a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika offense. "Not appointed" means:
not having been appointed by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
Regarding "instructing": it refers to preaching the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*).
If one instructs bhikṣuṇīs without having been appointed to do so, for every word spoken, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
To instruct a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī [in this manner] constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
This concludes the twenty-first section on śrāmaṇeras’ duṣkṛta offenses.
*Pañcavargika-vinaya*, Fascicle Six.
The Five-Part Vinaya, Volume Seven. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Song Dynasty,
together with Zhu Daosheng and others.
The Twenty-second Matter of the First Division, Part Five. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus were instructing the bhikṣuṇīs in succession, saying to them:
"Tomorrow it is the turn of Bhikṣu Panthaka to instruct you; you should go to him to hear and receive his teaching of the Dharma!"
Having spoken these words, he returned to his dwelling and said to Panthaka,
"Tomorrow you should instruct the bhikṣuṇīs! On the following day at mealtime,
the Elder Panthaka put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.

After the meal, he returned home, swept the interior and exterior, took pure water, prepared hand and foot towels, spread a seat on the open ground, took up a rope bed for himself, and sat in meditation at its side.
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went to where Bhadra was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat down before him.
Thereupon, Bhadra asked the bhikṣuṇīs, "Have you ever heard the Eight Rules of Respect?"
He replied, “I have heard it.
He spoke again:
"Sisters, listen further:
first, every half-month, the community of bhikṣuṇīs should request from the community of bhikṣus a person to provide instruction;
second, during the period of the rainy season retreat (varṣā), the community of bhikṣuṇīs must rely upon the community of bhikṣus."

Third, when the *pravāraṇā* (self-examination) is held, a bhikṣuṇī must perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) to dispatch three bhikṣuṇīs to the assembly of bhikṣus to request [the disclosure of] offenses seen, heard, or suspected;
fourth, after a śikṣamāṇā has completed two years of training in the six rules, she must seek to receive full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) before both assemblies;

fifth, a bhikṣuṇī must not revile a bhikṣu, nor must she speak ill of a bhikṣu in the homes of laypeople, whether regarding his violation of the precepts, his violation of proper decorum, his wrong views, or his wrong livelihood.
Sixth, a bhikṣuṇī may not raise charges against a bhikṣu, whereas a bhikṣu may reprimand a bhikṣuṇī.

Seventh, when a bhikṣuṇī commits a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), she must seek the practice of *mānatva* for half a month within both assemblies of monks; having completed the *mānatva*, she must then undergo *ābhuhaṇa* (rehabilitation) before a community of twenty bhikṣus and twenty bhikṣuṇīs to clear her of the offense.
Eighth, even if a bhikṣuṇī has been fully ordained for a hundred years, she must nevertheless pay homage to a newly ordained bhikṣu.
Having spoken these eight rules of respect, he then spoke in verse:
“Desiring a virtuous mind, do not be negligent; One should diligently study the noble Dharma.
If one possesses wisdom and a single-minded heart, Then one shall no longer have sorrow or affliction.”
Having spoken this verse, he closed his eyes and sat upright.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs whispered to one another, saying:
"This bhikṣu knows only this single verse; how can he possibly instruct and admonish us?"
Having heard this, Paṇḍaka thought to himself,
"These bhikṣuṇīs treat me with contempt. Thereupon, he leaped into the air,
manifested a single body and then multiplied it into infinite bodies, before merging them back together into one.
They passed through stone walls as if they were open space; they walked upon water as if it were solid ground, and entered the earth as if it were water;
sometimes they manifested only half their bodies, and sometimes they manifested their entire bodies;
sometimes smoke issued from the upper part of their bodies while fire blazed from the lower part.
Sometimes the upper part of his body blazes with fire while the lower part emits smoke;
sometimes the upper part of his body pours out water while the lower part emits fire;
or sometimes the upper part of his body emits fire while the lower part pours out water.
Sometimes he sat or lay in mid-air like a bird in flight;
sometimes he reached out his hand to touch the sun and moon, or stood upright with his body reaching as far as the Brahma-vaśavartin heaven.
Having manifested these supernatural transformations, he returned to his original seat and spoke verses as before.
When the bhikṣuṇīs saw this miraculous manifestation, their hearts were filled with great joy, and they said:
"Virtuous One! We pray that you will further instruct us through your supernormal powers!"
Thereupon, Panthaka leaped up in the east and sank down in the west, leaped up in the west and sank down in the east, and did likewise in the other directions;
having performed such various miraculous transformations, he returned to his seat and recited the aforementioned verses until sunset, after which he departed.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs arrived at the city gate in the evening; as the gate was already closed, they knocked on the door seeking entry, and the gatekeeper asked, "Who are you?"
He replied, "It is a bhikṣuṇī. The gatekeeper asked:
“Where did you come from at night? They replied,
“Venerable Panta instructed us, and for that reason we returned late.”
The gatekeeper said, "You may return to your original place; even if the King himself were to come, I would not dare open it!
Since the bhikṣuṇīs could not enter, some stayed beneath the gate, some by the edge of the moat, and others under trees, where they were tormented at night by mosquitoes, gadflies, wind, and dust.

The next day, when the gates opened, she was the very first to enter. At that time, the lay devotees asked one another, "These bhikṣuṇīs have entered before the break of dawn; from where have they come?"
Some people said, "This is precisely what happens when one seeks out a man and returns with him!
Those who did not have faith in or delight in the Buddha-dharma rebuked them in various ways, saying:
"We are laypeople who do not practice the holy life, yet you, bhikṣuṇī, are just like us!
You have shaved your head in vain and put on these dyed robes!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked Paṇḍaka.
“How did you instruct the bhikṣuṇīs until sunset?
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Paṇḍaka:
"Is it truly so? He replied, "It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu, having been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, remains until sunset, it is a pāyattika. "Appointed by the Saṃgha" means:
appointed by means of a formal motion and two proclamations (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
If the Bhikṣu-saṃgha has already appointed [an instructor], he should say to the Bhikṣuṇīs:
"Sisters! If it is not a time of difficulty, you should provide instruction and admonition."
"In times of difficulty, one may not provide instruction.
If one goes to the nuns' residence to provide instruction, one should say:
"Lay out the seats; I shall go."

"If you are unable to go there, you should, at your place of residence, sweep and sprinkle as before; you should take a senior bhikṣu as a companion, and only go alone after you have ascertained that no one else is present."
Having explained the Eight Rules of Respect, if it is early in the day, it is also well to further explain other teachings;
one should weigh the time of day—early or late—to ensure that they arrive at their residence before the day ends.
If the teaching of the Dharma is finished, those who should depart may do so;
however, if there is a place of danger, a bhikṣu should escort the bhikṣuṇī to her destination.
If a bhikṣu instructs a bhikṣuṇī until sunset, for every word spoken, it is a pāyattika.
For a śrāmaṇera, it is a duṣkṛta. The twenty-second [offense] is concluded.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus took turns in instructing the bhikṣuṇīs, and the bhikṣuṇīs all attained the various dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and right absorptions (samāpattis).
However, the group of six bhikṣus went to instruct them without being appointed by the Saṃgha, speaking only coarse, evil, and unwholesome words.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs remained silent and did not consent; however, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs praised them, saying, "Excellent!
There is nothing superior to this!
Thereupon, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, went to where the Buddha was and reported this matter to him.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?
They replied: "It is true."
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu enters the dwelling place of bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika.'"

At that time, some bhikṣus had business arising from various causes—whether matters concerning a stūpa, the Saṃgha, or private affairs—for which they needed to enter the dwelling place of the bhikṣuṇīs. Feeling ashamed and not daring to do so, they did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"If it is not for the purpose of providing instruction, entry is not permitted.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, not having been appointed by the Saṃgha, enters the dwelling place of bhikṣuṇīs for the purpose of instructing them, it is a pāyattika.
There were some bhikṣus who, although appointed by the Saṃgha, still felt ashamed and did not dare to enter;
because the bhikṣuṇīs lacked instruction, they went empty-handed with nothing gained.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"The bhikṣu appointed by the Saṃgha is permitted to enter."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, not having been appointed by the Saṃgha, enters the dwelling place of bhikṣuṇīs for the purpose of instructing them, it is a pāyattika."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrā was ill; she sent a messenger to inform Śāriputra:
"I pray that the Venerable One will come and preach the Dharma to me for the last time!"
Śāriputra said, “The Buddha has not permitted one to enter the dwelling place of the bhikṣuṇīs for the purpose of exhortation without having been appointed by the Saṃgha.
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I permit the Saṃgha to preach the Dharma for a sick bhikṣuṇī even without being formally appointed.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, not having been appointed by the Saṃgha, enters the dwelling place of bhikṣuṇīs for the purpose of instructing them;
except when there is a valid reason, it is a pāyattika.
A 'valid reason' is as follows:"
"A bhikṣuṇī who is ill—this is what constitutes a 'circumstantial cause' (nidāna).
If one enters the dwelling place of the bhikṣuṇīs for the purpose of instructing them without having been appointed by the Saṃgha, for every step taken inside, it is a pāyattika;
if one foot has entered the door, it is a duṣkṛta.
The *śrāmaṇera* [offense], the twenty-third *duṣkṛta*, is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the elder bhikṣus were successively instructing the bhikṣuṇīs. Some of the bhikṣuṇīs made individual invitations for offerings, using alms-bag carriers, waist-straps, lamp oil, food, clothing, and medicinal decoctions as gifts.
When the group of six bhikṣus saw this, they said to the other bhikṣus,
"We should be appointed as instructors.
The bhikṣus replied:
“As the Buddha has taught, you do not possess the ten qualities for accomplishment; why then do you seek to be appointed?
The group of six bhikṣus then spoke these words:
“The bhikṣus instruct the bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of gain and offerings.”
The bhikṣus rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One."
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows: 'If a bhikṣu speaks thus:'"
"If a bhikṣu, for the sake of gain from offerings, instructs a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
If he says that for the sake of gain from offerings he instructs a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta."

If one says that a bhikṣu practices the twelve dhūtas, sits in meditation, recites the sūtras, and performs various meritorious deeds—all for the sake of offerings and profit—each such statement constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; this concludes the twenty-four *duṣkṛta* offenses concerning śrāmaṇeras.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, some bhikṣus sat in private, secluded places with bhikṣuṇīs; they subsequently gave rise to defiled attachments and no longer delighted in the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Some returned to secular life, while others became followers of external paths.
When the laypeople saw this, they all reviled them, saying:
"These śramaṇas sitting alone in a secluded place with a bhikṣuṇī are exactly like laymen facing courtesans!"
"Having consumed the faithful offerings of the people, yet performing such an act, you possess no conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked that bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this time forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place alone with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.'"
The same applies to sitting alone in a secluded place with a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī.
For a śrāmaṇera, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If many bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs sit together;
If various difficulties arise, one must sit with another in a secluded place; in all such cases, there is no offense. [The twenty-fifth section ends.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who resided in a forest hermitage and did not, from the beginning, associate with any monastics or laypeople.
In the morning, that bhikṣu dressed himself, took up his bowl, and entered the village for alms; on the way, he encountered two bhikṣuṇīs.
One bhikṣuṇī said to the other, "I now wish to become acquainted with this bhikṣu; would you be willing to do so as well?"
He replied, “Very well!
When the bhikṣu arrived, he paid him homage; however, the bhikṣu remained silent and did not speak with him.
The two bhikṣuṇīs again deliberated together, saying:
"Now this bhikṣu does not wish to become acquainted with us while on the road; we should go together to his dwelling place to pay our respects and inquire after his well-being."
The next morning, the two bhikṣuṇīs went early to where the bhikṣu was staying and paid their respects with inquiries after his well-being;
yet, whether he prostrated once or twice, he did not speak with them, only addressing them when they had prostrated for the third time:
"O venerable ones!"
After the two bhikṣuṇīs had finished their prostrations, they departed.
Later, when that bhikṣu entered the village again to beg for food, the two bhikṣuṇīs saw him in the street; they paid him homage, exchanged greetings, and conversed with him.
The two bhikṣuṇīs then offered a piece of cloth and dyed thread to the bhikṣu; the bhikṣu accepted them and said, "Venerable sir, you are utterly exhausted;
please go to my dwelling to rest for a while, and then go forth for alms."
She then went to rest.
Having rested and being about to go out for alms, the bhikṣuṇī spoke again:
"There is vegetable sauce here; once you have obtained food, you may return here to eat it."
The bhikṣus again accepted their words, received food, and brought it back; this happened more than once. Sometimes a bhikṣu would return from his almsround early and wait for the bhikṣuṇī;
sometimes a bhikṣuṇī would return early and wait for the bhikṣu, eventually going to other households to praise one another.
Later, that bhikṣu obtained a fine robe and gave rise to a mind of flattery and deceit, thinking:
"I shall now give this robe to that bhikṣuṇī; she will certainly not accept it, and thus I shall fortunately receive the full benefit of her generous gift."
Having formed this thought, he first praised that bhikṣuṇī in front of the bhikṣus, saying:
"The bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has left the household life from a noble family; her faith is firm and upright, and she is of few desires and easily contented."
The bhikṣus said, "One who has left the household life ought indeed to act thus!
Having praised him, they took the robe and gave it to that bhikṣuṇī, and she immediately accepted it.
Frustrated that her original plan had failed, she harbored resentment in her heart and returned to tell the bhikṣus:
"A certain bhikṣuṇī has shallow faith and is full of desire, never satisfied!"
The bhikṣus said: "A moment ago you spoke of so-and-so as one who has few desires and is content;
why do you now speak of him in this way?"
He answered with all the details as above.
The bhikṣus rebuked him in various ways:

"How could you, without relinquishing the object in your mind, falsely pretend to give it to others, knowing that they would not accept it, thereby vainly hoping to evoke a sense of gratitude in them?"
He reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked that bhikṣu:
“Is it true that you did so?”
He replied, “It is truly so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"Have you not heard me praise the giving of things to others, through which one subsequently attains great merit?
Why is it that you now do not give from your heart, but instead feign giving?"
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept shall be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika. At that time, there were bhikṣus who had robes and bedding belonging to their relatives, all of which were coarse and worn out; they could not even obtain medicine for their illnesses."
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"If the World-Honored One would allow us to accept clothing and requisites from our relatives who are bhikṣuṇīs, we would not suffer such hardship.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to give clothing and requisites to their related bhikṣuṇīs.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika.

At that time, the two communities of monks in Śrāvastī obtained some finished robes and divided them among themselves; however, some bhikṣus received robes suitable for bhikṣuṇīs, and some bhikṣuṇīs received robes suitable for bhikṣus. They wished to exchange them with one another, yet they did not dare to do so.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to exchange robes with bhikṣuṇīs."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange for trade, it is a pāyattika."
If one gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative but has broken the precepts or holds wrong views, it is a duṣkṛta;
if one gives a robe to a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī who is not a relative, it is a duṣkṛta.
For a śrāmaṇera, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

However, if it is for the purpose of managing affairs, for the purpose of skillfully expounding the sūtras and Dharma, or for the purpose of having him recite many sūtras and precepts or providing him with robes, there is no offense. [The twenty-sixth section concludes.]
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī with few acquaintances who obtained some unfinished cloth; not knowing how to make it herself, she said to the other bhikṣuṇīs, "I do not know how to make robes; I pray that you will make one for me."
The bhikṣuṇīs said: "Sisters! We have many duties and cannot do it."
"You may go among the community of bhikṣus and ask; those who have a heart of compassion will surely complete it for you.

He then went among the community of bhikṣus and said, "I have few acquaintances and have obtained this unfinished robe, but I do not know how to finish it myself. I pray that you will complete it for me."
The bhikṣus answered as before.
They then went to the Venerable Udāyin and informed him as before. Udāyin said:
"I can certainly do it!
Do not come to urge me so frequently; act according to my wishes, and I shall do it for you. He replied:
"As you wish, Venerable Sir.
Thereupon Udāyin took the cloth and began to cut and sew it, but after some time he had not finished it. That bhikṣuṇī came and asked, "Venerable Sir!..."
"Is the robe finished?
Udāyin replied, "We already have an agreement; why do you come to urge us now?"
He replied, “I have come to inquire after you; I did not dare to urge you.
He then returned to his own dwelling.
Later, Udāyin used threads of various colors to embroider the image of a man and woman in union upon the central panel.
When the image was completed, he called for the bhikṣuṇī to return; she came immediately to take it, and Udāyin said to her:
"Do not yet unfold it to look at it, nor show it to anyone."
When the bhikṣuṇī Pāṭhikaputrī was on her way to the Buddha’s dwelling, she spread it out at the crossroads;
yet once she had received the robe and departed, she did not spread it out to inspect it, nor did she show it to anyone.

When the bhikṣuṇī Prajāpatī arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, she was wearing [the garment] at the head of a major thoroughfare. When passersby saw her, there were none who did not clap their hands and laugh aloud, saying to one another:
"This bhikṣuṇī is truly capable of such clever embroidery; she has fashioned the image she desired and worn it upon her own robe."
That bhikṣuṇī was deeply ashamed and immediately returned to her residence.
The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī folded this robe, took it to the Buddha’s dwelling, spread it out, and said to the Buddha:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will look upon what has been done!”
After the Buddha had taught various dharmas to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, he sent her back to her residence;
he then assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Udāyin:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"You foolish man! How can you do such a thing as to defile and insult another's robe?"
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.'"
There were some bhikṣus who had bhikṣuṇīs among their relatives whose robes were worn out. Having obtained pieces of cloth through begging, they did not know how to make them.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"If the World-Honored One would allow us to make robes for our relative bhikṣuṇīs, we would not have this hardship."
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to make robes for their own relatives who are bhikṣuṇīs."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika.
When a bhikṣu takes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a duṣkṛta.
When cutting and when dyeing, it is all a *pāyattika* offense;
when sewing, for every stitch it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The remainder is as explained in the section on "Giving Robes. [The twenty-seventh section ends.]
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, various bhikṣus were traveling through the human settlements in the kingdom of Magadha together with various bhikṣuṇīs—sometimes one bhikṣu with one bhikṣuṇī, and so on up to many pairs. Whether crossing deep waters or ascending steep slopes, they saw one another’s forms and gave rise to defiled and attached thoughts. No longer taking pleasure in practicing the holy life (brahmacarya), they eventually returned to secular life or became followers of external paths.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled them, saying:
"These śramaṇas are like people traveling with their wives or courtesans!
They reviled them in various ways, as described above in the section concerning sitting in private, secluded places.
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they rebuked him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked them:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu travels along a road together with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.'"
There were some bhikṣus traveling along a road with a large group of companions who saw bhikṣuṇīs also traveling on that same path and thought to themselves:
"We might not be committing a pāyattika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
“It is impossible that one could commit a pāyattika offense without having previously made a mutual agreement.”
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu travels along a road with a bhikṣuṇī by prior appointment, it is a pāyattika.
There were some bhikṣus who, having made a prior appointment to travel a road with a bhikṣuṇī, subsequently did not dare to go, or else the two avoided one another.
Because they had previously made an appointment and thus harbored doubts, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one has previously made an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to travel together on a road, it is not possible that one would commit a pāyattika offense by either not going or by avoiding each other."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, having made a prior appointment with a bhikṣuṇī, travels along a road together from one village to another, it is a pāyattika."
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who, while on a dangerous road, saw a bhikṣu and called out to him, saying:
"Venerable Sir, come quickly!
Let us travel together along this path!"
That bhikṣu then went to her and said:
"Sister! The Buddha has established a precept forbidding one from traveling along a road together with a bhikṣuṇī."
The bhikṣuṇī said, “This path is perilous and difficult, and I am a woman of weak strength; only by relying on the Venerable One can I pass through.
He answered her as before, and the bhikṣu then departed.
Later, the bhikṣuṇī was stripped of her clothes by bandits; standing naked, she cried out loudly:
"The bandits are stripping me!
The bandits are stripping me!"
That bhikṣu heard it from afar; he went to his dwelling place and spoke of it to the bhikṣus there.
The bhikṣus then led him to the presence of the Buddha and reported this matter to him.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to travel together with bhikṣuṇīs on a road when there is a dangerous place or a place where they have cause for apprehension."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, having made a prior appointment with a bhikṣuṇī, travels together with her along a road from one village to another, except when there is a valid reason, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the "circumstances":
if one has many companions or is in a place where there is suspicion or fear, these are called the circumstances.
If a bhikṣu agrees in advance to travel together with a bhikṣuṇī on a road through a place where no villages are situated for half a yojana, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one makes a prior appointment with a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī to travel together on a road, it is likewise.
For a śrāmaṇera, this constitutes a duṣkṛta offense. The twenty-eighth [offense] is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, various bhikṣus in the kingdom of Magadha were traveling by boat together with various bhikṣuṇīs; sometimes one bhikṣu was on the same boat as one bhikṣuṇī, and so on up to many. When they were boarding or disembarking from the boats, they saw each other’s bodies, and laypeople criticized and reviled them.
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, [the report] reached the Buddha, who then addressed the bhikṣus as was previously explained in the section on traveling together on a road:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu makes a prior appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to travel together by boat, it is a pāyattika.'"
There was a bhikṣuṇī on the bank of the Ajiravatī River, waiting for a boat to cross.
Later, a bhikṣu arrived, and the bhikṣuṇī said to him:
"Venerable Sir!"
"This place is perilous; let us cross together.
The bhikṣu replied, "The Buddha has prohibited us from traveling in the same boat with bhikṣuṇīs."
The boatman spoke again:
"Just board the boat together, each at one end.
The bhikṣu would not agree.
The bhikṣuṇī said, "If you cannot do so, Venerable Sir, please cross first.
The bhikṣu then crossed ahead; before the boat had reached the shore, the bhikṣuṇī was stripped naked, her flesh bared.
When the boatman saw this, he rebuked them, saying:
"You have all left the household life together, yet you cannot protect one another; how much less can you do so for others!
You lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!"
That bhikṣu returned to the monastery and told the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus took him to the Buddha and reported this matter to him.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned that bhikṣu:
“Is it truly so? He replied, “It is truly so.”
"World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways: "You foolish man!"
"How could you abandon a bhikṣuṇī, allowing bandits to strip her naked?
Having rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, having made a prior appointment with a bhikṣuṇī, travels together by boat—whether upstream or downstream—with the exception of crossing directly across, it is a pāyattika."
The remainder is as explained in the section on "Traveling Together on the Road," ending at twenty-nine.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, Nanda and Bhadra ate food praised by bhikṣuṇīs; when the bhikṣus saw this, they rebuked them in various ways.
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were traveling through the countryside and arrived at the city of Rājagṛha.
A certain householder, hearing that the two had come, went out to meet them, prostrated himself with his head at their feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
For him, they preached the sublime Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him.
The lay devotee immediately invited the visiting bhikṣus for a meal the following day; they accepted by remaining silent.
The lay devotee then returned home, prepared various kinds of food and drink, and spread out fine seating mats.
When the time came, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana donned their robes, took up their bowls, and went to her house.
As Śāriputra was about to enter first, the bhikṣuṇī Sthūlanandā was already there in the house; hearing the sound of their voices, she immediately stopped and did not go in.
Seeing that various kinds of food and drink had been prepared and fine seats were laid out, that bhikṣuṇī asked:
"Is this to invite the king?
Or is it for a wedding?"
He replied, "We do not invite the King here, nor is it for a marriage; we merely wish to make offerings to the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana!"
The bhikṣuṇī said, "Why do you not invite the Great Dragon, but instead offer sustenance to this bhikṣu of meager virtue?
The householder asked:
"Who are the great dragons? He replied,
"The group of six bhikṣus!"
He further said:

"If you wish to invite a clansman who has left the household life—a bhikṣu practicing the dhūta austerities, the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path, and one who has attained the stages from stream-enterer to arhat—then you should do so.
However, if you wish to seek a fine husband, fine sons, rebirth in heaven, liberation, or wealth and honor in this present life, you should make offerings to the group of six bhikṣus."
Having praised him in this way, they remained silent.
Only then did Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana enter; the bhikṣuṇī approached them and asked after their welfare, saying, "Excellent, Venerable Sirs!"
"You may sit here.
He then spoke again to the householder, saying, "Excellent, householder!"
"You have now gained great benefit and merit by inviting such a 'Great Dragon' bhikṣu.
The householder then rebuked him, saying, "Just now you called him one of 'small virtue,' yet now you call him a 'Great Dragon. Practicing such inconsistency, how can you be so shameless?"
"From this day forward, do not enter my house!
I shall no longer provide offerings for you!
Thereupon, the householder personally served the food with his own hands; when the meal was finished, he offered water for rinsing and took a small seat to sit before the two bhikṣus.
Having preached the sublime Dharma, they rose from their seats and departed, returning to where the Buddha was.
Seeing them from afar, the Buddha spoke to them, saying:
"Welcome, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana!"
“From where does the guest bhikṣu eat? He replied,
“World-Honored One!”
"Just now I went to the house of a lay devotee, where there was a bhikṣuṇī whom some called Little Virtue and others called Great Dragon.
The Buddha asked, "What did she say?"
He answered the Buddha with the facts as they were.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly eat food that was offered because of the praise of a bhikṣuṇī?"
He replied, “It is truly so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu eats food that has been praised by a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.'"
There were certain bhikṣuṇīs who praised a bhikṣu’s meal in a secluded place; later, when they learned of it, they felt shame and remorse, thinking:
"Have I perhaps committed a pāyattika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"It is impossible that one would commit a pāyattika offense by eating food when one does not know that it was obtained through the commendation of a bhikṣuṇī."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that he has received food through the praise of a bhikṣuṇī, eats it, it is a pāyattika.
At that time, a certain family invited five hundred bhikṣus for a meal; the bhikṣuṇīs whom that family had previously supported spoke as follows:
"Serve food to the bhikṣus; do not let the proper time pass!
When the bhikṣus heard this, they felt ashamed and did not dare to eat again, returning to report the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having not first offered praise, says these words at the time of eating:
'Give good food to the bhikṣus; let the bhikṣus eat this food.'"
"It is impossible for one to commit a *pāyattika* offense [in this case].
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, knowing that he has received food due to the cause of a bhikṣuṇī’s praise, eats it—except when the donor had previously resolved to give it—it is a *pāyattika*.'"
Regarding "praising": it refers to praising one who has attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussadhamma*).
If a *śikṣamāṇā*, *śrāmaṇera*, or *śrāmaṇerī* eats food obtained through the pretext of such praise by a *bhikṣu*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The section on the *śrāmaṇera* and the thirty *duṣkṛta* offenses is concluded.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
There was then a high minister who constantly made offerings to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
A certain poor man saw this and thought to himself:
"This great minister has attained a most excellent benefit, being able to provide such offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha; if I possessed wealth, I too would act in this same way."
He further thought to himself:
"I have nothing at present; I must work for hire in order to provide offerings.
He immediately took up employment, eating only one meal a day and setting aside a portion of that meal for the purpose.
The host asked, "Why have you set aside a portion of food? He replied:
"I shall leave this for now and take it all later.
After some time had passed, knowing that he had obtained what was sufficient, he said to the host:
"You may use the full amount as wages to prepare various kinds of food and utensils for me."
The host asked, "You are currently poor;
how is it that you have used all your earnings to suddenly prepare such a variety of food and drink? He replied:
"I have seen the ministers of Rājagṛha constantly inviting the Buddha and the Saṃgha to provide them with various kinds of offerings.
I made this vow: 'I, too, shall act in this same way.
For this reason, I am working as a laborer in order to fulfill this intention."
"Now, calculating the cost, it will suffice for a single offering; this is why I have prepared the utensils for the meal all at once.
Upon hearing this, the host gave rise to a sense of rare wonder, thinking:
"If even such a poor person, toiling his body as a hired laborer, uses whatever small wealth he has obtained for making an offering, how much more so should I, who possess great riches?"

At the very moment he resolved his mind [on awakening], food and drink were already prepared; yet, being unable to do it himself, he immediately hired laborers at double the rate to prepare all manner of delicacies as they pleased.
At that time, the laborers took their provisions and went to where the Buddha was, preparing food and drink of the most exquisite flavors in the world.
Because his intention was so profound, spirits came to assist him; in the blink of an eye, everything was spontaneously prepared.
It happened that it was a festival day with an abundance of offerings, and many people vied with one another to invite the monks to their homes for a meal.
The bhikṣus said to one another, "Today this poor man has exerted himself to the utmost to prepare a feast; we should each take a small portion for his sake."
Although they admonished one another, the food consumed was extremely small, yet because there were so many invitations, they eventually became fully satiated.
At that time, the poor man had finished preparing the meal and announced that it was time.
Thereupon, all the bhikṣus gathered and took their seats, while the Buddha remained in his dwelling.
At that time, the poor man personally served the food with his own hands; filled with joy, he set down the meal, yet although the bhikṣus accepted it, what they received was very little.
The poor man thought to himself:
"Are these bhikṣus showing compassion for my poverty because they fear there will not be enough food?
Or is it because the food is poor and unfit to eat?"
He immediately questioned them,
and among the bhikṣus, those with little sense of shame replied:
"Fearing that you might have little food, we ate beforehand at various other households."
The poor man spoke resentfully:
"How is it that you first accepted my invitation, yet ate at another's house?
I originally exerted all my efforts, intending to provide for you until the end!"
"Now, Venerable Ones, although you cannot eat it, I pray that you will take it as you please; do not let any remain.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus then forced themselves to eat, yet they still did not finish even half of what was offered.
When the community of monks had finished eating, the poor man again thought to himself:
"Since I forcefully urged the monks to eat, will I not incur an offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, poor man! That you,
seeing others perform meritorious deeds, were able to hire your labor out of a desire to emulate them."
Although you have received a human body, the causes and conditions for birth in heaven are already fully complete.

From the moment you first resolved to make offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha, you have obtained immeasurable merit with every act; even if the assembly of monks did not eat a single grain of rice, there would be no aspect of your merit that was not fully realized.
"You shall now further receive retribution in this present life.
Upon hearing this, the poor man was filled with joy and leaped for gladness.
The Buddha further preached various sublime Dharmas to him; immediately upon that seat, he distanced himself from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Having seen the Dharma, he took the three refuges, undertook the five precepts, rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, circumambulated him to the right, and withdrew.

At that time, there were five hundred merchants coming from the country of Ujjayinī; their journey was remote and desolate, and they had been without food for three days. They sent a messenger on horseback ahead to seek out cooked food, addressing people everywhere:
"We are five hundred merchants coming from the country of Ujjayinī; we have been without food for three days, and therefore I have been sent ahead to seek various cooked foods."
"If there is anyone who has cooked [food], do not calculate its price!
The people of the city said, "There is none here;
however, a certain poor man has prepared a feast at a monastery, and he has a great deal left over."
"Go and seek it; you will surely obtain it, have no doubt.
Thereupon, the messenger immediately galloped off and reported the situation in full.
The poor man replied:
"I am now providing this food not for the sake of wealth or profit;
you should simply come quickly, without haggling over the price.
When the messenger heard this, he was delighted that it exceeded his expectations and returned to report the news.
In a short while, they all arrived together and said, "Give us food quickly; we shall reward you handsomely!
His answer was also as it had been before.
Even after serving the food and they were fully satiated, he asked the others:
"What business does this man have that he is able to provide such various arrangements?"
Someone reported the matter in full; upon hearing it, the merchants were all the more struck by its rarity, and they immediately gathered a hundred thousand taels of gold to repay his gift.
Furthermore, he asked again:
"Is such-and-such a person in this city now? He replied:
"He has already died.
He asked again,
"Does he have any descendants?"
He replied, "The donor from earlier is indeed his son.
When the merchants heard this, they spoke to the poor man as before:
"Your father was our teacher," they said, and they gave him another hundred thousand pieces of gold to reaffirm their old friendship.

When the ministers of Rājagṛha and the landlord from whom he had rented the house heard of and saw this, they were filled with even greater joy; each of them sent another hundred thousand pieces of gold to establish new bonds of goodwill.
On that very day, King Bimbisāra appointed him again as a high minister.
Within a single day, he became resplendent with wealth and honor; the people of the land called him the "Sudden-Rise Householder" (Aṭṭhaka-seṭṭhi).
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked them:
"Is it true that you accepted an invitation from someone, yet first ate food provided by another?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"You foolish man! How could you have already accepted an invitation from someone, yet first eat another's food?"
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu eats repeatedly, it is a pāyattika.’”
At that time, eighty bhikṣus, including Piṅgalavatsa, all suffered from serious illnesses and were unable to eat their fill at once; they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I now permit sick bhikṣus to eat repeatedly."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats repeatedly, except for a specific cause, it is a pāyattika.
The 'specific cause' is:"
"When one is ill, this is called a cause and condition.
At that time, the World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to accept the kaṭhina robe, whereby they would not incur offenses regarding five matters.
The bhikṣus then had this thought:
"Is it not an offense to eat more than once while this robe is being made?
And is it also not an offense once the robe is finished?
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"There is no offense during the period for robes; there is an offense once the period for robes has passed.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu eats repeatedly, except on account of a specific cause, it is a pāyattika.
A 'specific cause' refers to:
the time of illness, the time of [receiving] robes; these are called specific causes."
There were some laypeople who knew that bhikṣus were not permitted to eat more than once a day, and they thought:
"I shall employ a skillful means to provide robes for the bhikṣus;
when the bhikṣus come to receive them, I shall also provide them with offerings."
They immediately prepared robes and invited the bhikṣus. The bhikṣus said, "We do not accept food;
please give us only the robes. The laypeople said:
“Venerable Sir!
If you accept my food, I shall then give you this robe.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
“World-Honored One, if you would permit me to eat frequently for the sake of receiving robes, I shall not lack for clothing.
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to eat repeatedly when robes are being offered.
From this day forth, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu eats repeatedly, except for a specific cause, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
"Regarding 'circumstances':
the time of illness, the time for robes, and the time for the distribution of robes—these are called circumstances.

At that time, Ānanda went to the house of a householder. The householder had prepared various foods and drinks; however, Ānanda forgot his previous invitation and accepted this food. As he was about to eat, he remembered and said to the host:
"You may go back and take your meal; I have already accepted an invitation and cannot eat again.
The householder spoke with resentment:
"How is it that after having accepted my food, you suddenly regret it midway?"
Thereupon Ānanda hurried back and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If such circumstances arise, one should first give with the mind, forming this thought:
'My allotted portion, I give to such-and-such a bhikṣu.'"
"Only after this may you eat.
If one eats without intending to give to others, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, there may be cases where an invitation is received first, but the meal is prepared later; [in such cases, one should not eat until the food is ready].
There were cases where a later invitation was received, yet food had already been prepared for an earlier one.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"At that time, one should say:
'Eat according to what was previously prepared.
Regarding 'eating repeatedly' (paryāśana): having first accepted an invitation from one person, to then eat at another location is called eating repeatedly."
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If it is food assigned by the Saṃgha, or food from a separate room, or if a layperson has come to receive the eight precepts and provide an offering, or if it is regular food, there is no offense. [The thirty-first rule concludes.]
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, Devadatta, seeking to secure support, exhorted various householders to invite four, five, or ten monks from each family.
The elder bhikṣus rebuked the bhikṣu who had accepted the invitation, saying:
"How can you, for the sake of assisting Devadatta, accept a separate meal offered by a group?
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you accepted a separate invitation for a communal meal from Devadatta? They replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu accepts an individual invitation for a communal meal, it is a pāyattika.'"
A sick bhikṣu was dragging himself along while begging for alms, and his affliction grew even more severe.
The lay devotees said to him, "Do not drag yourself along while begging; you may come and take food from us!"
He replied, "The World-Honored One has established a precept that does not permit us to accept separate invitations for communal meals. However,
if it is for the purpose of making offerings to the Sangha, we may then receive our own shares."
The laypeople said, "Our families are poor and cannot provide extensively; we can only manage to prepare what we have the strength for to offer to the sick.
Venerable Sir!"
"If you need it, you may come and take it.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"From now on, I permit sick bhikṣus to accept special invitations for communal meals.
Regarding the time for robes and the time for the distribution of robes, it is as explained in the section on frequent eating.
"From this day forward, this precept should be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for a communal meal apart from [the usual] invitations, except when there is a valid reason, it is a pāyattika.
Valid reasons are:
when one is ill, when it is the season for robes, or when robes are being offered; these are called valid reasons."

There were some bhikṣus who wished to make robes, but because they had to go out for alms, the robes were not completed immediately, which hindered and interrupted their practice of the Path. They thought to themselves:
"If, when making robes, the Buddha would allow us to accept invitations to communal meals, the robes could be finished quickly and our practice of the Path would not be interrupted."
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit the bhikṣus, when making robes, to accept special invitations for communal meals."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for a communal meal apart from the specific circumstances, it is a pāyattika offense.
The specific circumstances are:"
"Illness, [the time for] robes, the time for the distribution of robes, and the time for making robes—these are called the causes and conditions.
There were some bhikṣus traveling with companions who, upon reaching a village, said to their companions:
"We shall enter the village to beg for food; you may wait for us a short while."
He replied, "There is no need for you to beg for alms; I shall provide them to you. The bhikṣu said:
“The World-Honored One has not permitted us to accept separate invitations for communal meals.
Thereupon, they entered the village to beg for alms, and their companions abandoned them and departed.
After the bhikṣus had finished begging, they could no longer catch up with their companions; they were stripped naked by bandits. The bhikṣus then thought to themselves:
“World-Honored One, had you permitted me to accept special invitations for meals while traveling on the road, I would not have encountered this calamity.

There were also bhikṣus who traveled by boat with other passengers; when it was time for them to beg for food, the boatmen abandoned them and departed, causing them to suffer hardships just as described above.
They all reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"From now on, I permit the bhikṣus to accept invitations for communal meals while traveling on foot or while traveling by boat."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for a communal meal apart from [the usual] invitations, except when there is a valid reason, it is a pāyattika.
A 'valid reason' is:"
"The times of illness, the time for robes, the time for the distribution of robes, the time for making robes, traveling on a road, and traveling by boat—these are called 'circumstantial causes.

It is the constant rule of the Buddhas that there are two great assemblies each year at the end of the spring and summer months; monks from all directions come to pay their respects, and because they are so numerous, invitations for meals are very infrequent and alms-food is difficult to obtain."
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"If the World-Honored One would allow us to accept separate invitations for meals during the Great Assembly, we would not suffer such hardship."
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
“I now permit the bhikṣus, during the time of a great assembly, to accept separate invitations for communal meals.”
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for a communal meal apart from a formal group, except when there is a valid reason, it is a pāyattika. A valid reason is:
[as previously specified]."

The time of illness, the time of [receiving] robes, the time of giving robes, the time of making robes, the time of traveling on a road, the time of traveling by boat, and the time of a great assembly—these are called the causes and conditions.

At that time, King Bimbisāra’s younger brother, named Kāla, followed a certain spiritual path. Every year, he would invite ninety-six kinds of śramaṇas to hold a great assembly. However, having heard that the śramaṇas of the Śākya clan did not accept special invitations for communal meals, he was unable to extend his hospitality widely to the entire community of monks. Because he lacked the śramaṇas of the Buddha’s Way, he became sorrowful and unhappy, thinking to himself:
"How can I bring the śramaṇas of the Śākya clan here?"
"We must first entrust ourselves entirely to the King; only then can our purpose be fulfilled.
They then reported this to the King.
On account of these matters, the King immediately went out to visit the Buddha and related his younger brother's aspirations in detail.
After the king had departed, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus on this matter and addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now permit the bhikṣus to accept invitations for communal meals when there is a gathering of śramaṇas. From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for a communal meal from a private donor, except when there is a valid reason, it is a pāyattika offense.’”
The "causes and conditions" are:

the time of illness, the time for robes, the time for receiving robes, the time for making robes, the time of traveling on a road, the time of traveling by boat, the time of a great assembly, and the time of a gathering of śramaṇas; these are called causes and conditions.
Regarding "inviting a group for a separate meal":
if one invites four or more persons from among the community, this is called inviting a group for a separate meal.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If, having initially accepted an individual invitation for a communal meal, they go there and divide [the food], saying they have accepted separate invitations, the group is no longer formed; thus, they do not commit the offense of the thirty-two [rules]. End of section.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a famine in various regions, making it difficult to obtain almsfood. Consequently, all the bhikṣus gathered in Rājagṛha.
People from the four distant directions said, "In the past, we saw the bhikṣus every morning and evening; why is it that they have now ceased to appear and we no longer see them?"
Some said, "Alms are difficult to obtain here; they have all gone to Rājagṛha, which is why we do not see them. The others said:
"We would rather build small huts and provide one monk with a night's lodging and a meal each day.
If there is no one to receive the food, we shall gather it together and wait for those who arrive later."
They did exactly as they were told.

At that time, there was a family that constantly prepared fine food; the group of six bhikṣus would always stay at their house while traveling through the countryside, so that the other bhikṣus could no longer obtain any.
The other bhikṣus said to the layperson, "For the sake of the Saṃgha, you have prepared food for one night's stay."
"How can I be prevented from having even a moment's peace?
The householder replied,
"I originally built this dwelling for the Saṃgha, yet the group of six bhikṣus occupies it and refuses to leave, preventing me from seeing the rest of the monks again."
"This is their fault, not my own error.
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked the group of six bhikṣus in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so? They replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this time forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, at a place where a single meal is offered, eats more than one meal, it is a pāyattika.'"
At that time, Śāriputra suffered from a wind-disorder (vāta-roga). Having gone to a place where food was provided and partaken of a single meal, he wished to travel elsewhere.
The bhikṣus said to him, "Venerable sir, you are afflicted by illness; there is no need for you to travel further."
"We shall provide for one another with our portions of food. They replied,
"The World-Honored One does not permit staying at a single lodging place or consuming more than a single meal."
When various lay devotees heard that Śāriputra was ill, they also collectively requested him to remain, but his reply was as it had been before.
Thereupon, Śāriputra departed while still suffering from his ailment. The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"If the World-Honored One would allow a sick bhikṣu to stay at a single meal site beyond the limit of one meal, then this suffering would not exist."
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
“I now permit sick bhikṣus to eat more than one meal at a single eating place.”
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, when not ill, at a place where a single meal is offered, eats beyond one meal, it is a pāyattika."

At a place where a single meal is being offered, if many bhikṣus arrive at the same time in the evening, whether a donor offers non-time-appropriate drinks or oil for anointing the feet, they are permitted to receive them in order.
Tomorrow, one should receive food according to one's turn;
if there is none, then after having finished this single meal, one should depart.
If the donor requests one to stay, staying is permitted.
If you have departed and there is a matter requiring your return, you should inform the host; if the host permits you to stay, you may remain, but if he does not permit it, you should depart.
If other bhikṣus arrive later, they should receive one meal; if there is any remainder, it should be given to the bhikṣu whom the host has retained.
If a bhikṣu arrives and there are many places where food is provided, the bhikṣus should divide themselves among them and stay separately.
If one stays at a house of relatives for more than one meal, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If there are various obstacles preventing her from going, she does not commit an offense. Section thirty-three concludes.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a woman who wished to return to her husband’s home and had prepared various kinds of cakes as provisions for the journey.
A bhikṣu, wandering for alms in regular succession, went to her house, and the woman asked him:
"What do you require? He replied,
"I require food!"
He asked again,
"Are you able to eat khādanīya? He replied:
"Yes! he replied, immediately taking a bowl and filling it with various kinds of cakes to give him.
Having received them, that bhikṣu said to the other bhikṣus:
"There is much fine food at such-and-such a house; you should go there to beg for it.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they all went there to beg, and all the cooked food that was offered was completely exhausted.
At that time, her husband’s family sent someone to urge her [to come], and she replied, "My provisions have not yet been prepared!
She then prepared various kinds of food; this happened up to three times, and whenever a bhikṣu came to beg, she gave him everything she had.

Her husband’s family pressed her three times for a reply, but she answered each time as before. They then became greatly incensed and, suspecting she had other intentions, sent a messenger with this message:
"We have already sought another bride; we will no longer take you, blind girl!"
Thereupon, the girl’s family all spoke with resentment, saying,
"It is because of these śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas that our daughter has been made a widow!
They further reviled her in various ways, their mouths overflowing with foul words.
A neighbor said, "He slighted your daughter; what does that have to do with the śramaṇa?
She then answered him fully.
Those who did not believe in or delight in the Buddha-dharma all said:
"It is truly fortunate that by showing respect to the śramaṇas, such a thing as this has occurred;
if one were to associate with them even more closely, it would surely be even worse than this."
At that time, there was another caravan leader who said to the merchants:
"Prepare your provisions; such-and-such a day is most auspicious, and we shall set out together."
They immediately prepared various kinds of food and drink.
There was a bhikṣu who went on his alms round in due order and arrived at the house of a merchant.
The merchant asked him, "What do you require?"
He replied, “I need food! He asked:
"Can you eat cakes and flour? He replied, "I can!"
He immediately took his bowl, filled it to the brim, and gave it to him.
Having received it, the bhikṣu said to the other bhikṣus, "The house of so-and-so has much delicious food and drink; you may go there to beg."
The bhikṣus all went there and obtained [provisions] until their food supplies were completely exhausted.
The merchant leader said, "The auspicious day has now arrived; we should set out together!"
The merchants said, "Our provisions have not yet been prepared!
The leader of the merchants said:
"I previously issued a proclamation to prepare provisions.
For what reason do you say now that they are not yet prepared? He replied:
"A śramaṇa has come to beg, and I have given him everything until it was exhausted.
The caravan leader said, "Today is an auspicious day; we cannot but set out."
"I shall go on first; you may follow later.
Thereupon he set out, and upon his return, he arrived safely and gained great profit.
A certain other merchant followed later but encountered bandits; having lost all his goods, he wept and said:
"The śramaṇa son of the Śākyas has met with such dire misfortune!
The bandit asked, "I am the one who robbed you of your property; why do you resent others?"
He answered them by relating the matter in full.
Upon hearing this, the bandits spoke to him again:
"Since you have drawn near to these śramaṇas, you ought to beat them to death and seize their property!"
"If there are others who associate with them, they too shall be treated in this same manner!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: [Yes].
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this time forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson who freely offers him much food and drink, whether cakes or parched grain, he may accept two or three bowls if he so desires.'"
"To receive more than this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

There were some sick bhikṣus who entered a village to beg for food; a certain householder offered them as much as they desired, but when it exceeded two or three bowls, they did not dare to accept any more.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I now permit a sick bhikṣu to accept more than two or three bowls."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson who freely offers much food and drink, whether cakes or parched grain flour;
if he requires it, he may accept two or three bowls."
"If one who is not ill receives more than this, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
There were some bhikṣus who went to a house where they had been invited to eat; having finished their meal, they further requested food from the host and took it away.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If you eat at the house where you have been invited, you must not ask for any food to take away;
however, if you do not eat at the house where you were invited, I allow you to take it away."
There were certain bhikṣus who, having received two or three bowls and taken them away, did not share them with the other bhikṣus for a meal.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"You should eat together with the bhikṣus.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson and they offer him food and drink at his own will—whether it be cakes or parched grain;'"
If one does not eat at that person's house, one should accept two or three bowls and go outside to eat together with other bhikṣus.
If one is not ill and accepts more than this, or does not eat together with other bhikṣus, it is a pāyattika offense.
Regarding "giving food at one's own discretion":
whenever someone comes to beg, one should give immediately.
If a bhikṣu receives [food] in his first bowl, he should, upon returning, tell the other bhikṣus:
"I have already received one bowl from such-and-such a family; two bowls remain. If you require them, go and take them.
If he has received the second bowl, he should say:
"I have already received two bowls from such-and-such a family; one bowl remains. If you require it, go and take it."
If one receives a third bowl, one should say:
"I have already received three bowls of food from such-and-such a family; do not go there again to take more!
If one does not speak thus, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. The thirty-fourth [offense] is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was famine in various places and it was difficult to obtain alms; consequently, all the bhikṣus returned to Rājagṛha.
The lay devotees of Rājagṛha asked the bhikṣus, "How many people are in the Saṃgha?"
"How much food is there?
He replied, "There are so many monks, and there is this much food."
At that time, the householders deliberated together, saying:
"We should prepare food for the bhikṣus according to our respective capacities.
Thereupon, some individuals prepared food for one bhikṣu, while others prepared food for as many as ten bhikṣus.
Suppose there are two people, or even up to ten, who together prepare a meal for one bhikṣu, or even for ten bhikṣus.
Having prepared the food and utensils, the lay leaders further think to themselves:
"Although we have prepared this food according to our means, whether it is for one person or ten, it will certainly not be sufficient for all."
"Now we shall collect goods to provide food for everyone; if it should prove insufficient, I myself will make up the deficiency.
He then immediately began to collect them.

Among those present were some who were poor; though their hearts felt no stinginess, they lacked fine rice. Consequently, they contributed whatever they possessed—beans, wheat, and the like—to fulfill this collection.

That householder master then assigned the tasks accordingly; however, the food and drink were coarse and poor, so that the elderly and sick bhikṣus would not eat it at all, instead taking it to give to beggars or to non-Buddhists, and going themselves to the homes of their acquaintances to eat.
When the laypeople learned of this, they criticized and reviled him, saying:
"We have diminished our own portions for body and mouth, as well as those of our wives and children, to plant them as a field of merit.
Why does this bhikṣu disregard this food of ours and give it to beggars and various non-Buddhists, seeking instead to obtain fine flavors?"
