"These people originally sought liberation to escape old age, sickness, and death; how is it that they now instead seek beauty?
They lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!"
At that time, it was the turn of the host of Baddhālī to supervise the meal distribution. After Baddhālī had finished eating among the assembly, he went again to his house and requested fine food.
The man asked him, "Venerable Sir!..."
“Did you not eat among the assembly? He replied, “I did eat among the assembly;
however, fearing that the donor might lose the merit of giving special offerings, I have come back again.”
That person then rebuked him, saying:
"In this present age of famine and scarcity, when all people's resources are exhausted, we have prepared this communal meal together.
Why do you slight it and seek something more exquisite?"
When the bhikṣus heard this, they censured him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu eats again after having finished his meal, it is a pāyattika.’”

At that time, eighty bhikṣus, including Piṇḍola-bhāradvāja and others, fell ill. The other bhikṣus requested food on their behalf, but they could not finish eating it all and discarded the remainder in front of their rooms.
When the laypeople saw this, they asked,
"What kind of food is this? He replied:
"This is the leftover food of a sick bhikṣu. The laypeople said,
"Why did you not take less?"
He replied, "There are some sick bhikṣus who eat much and others who eat little; this is why we were unable to take only a small amount.
The householder spoke again:
"In this world of famine, by giving even a single grain one can be reborn in heaven!
Why then do you discard it without practicing charity?
Or again, someone might say:
"These śramaṇas would rather cast it upon the ground than give it to others!
Since we have already offered it to the Saṃgha, they consider it a great transgression if even a single grain falls to the ground."
"How can a bhikṣu fail to cherish such an object?
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Ānanda:
"Is there anyone who can eat this food?

He replied, "The bhikṣu who attends to the sick has been invited to receive this food; however, his own portion was not sufficient for him to eat, and though he wishes to consume these leftovers, he does not dare."
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
“I now permit the bhikṣus to eat the leftover food of a sick bhikṣu.
At that time, after the community of monks in Rājagṛha had finished their meal, there was a bhikṣu who obtained food outside and brought it back.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they informed the Buddha about this.
The Buddha said:
"You may give this food to the sick bhikṣu."
He immediately gave it to them.
The sick bhikṣus said, "This food will increase our illness; we have no need for it."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow the bhikṣus to consume food by performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover-food) procedure in the presence of a sick bhikṣu.
At that time, the Saṃgha in Rājagṛha had finished eating and departed, yet another bhikṣu obtained food elsewhere and brought it back.
When the sick bhikṣu had recovered, he did not know what to do and reported this again to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"He should eat by performing the *kṛtapiṇḍaka* (leftover-food) rite in the presence of a bhikṣu whose meal has not yet concluded."
If there is no one who has not yet eaten, it should be performed in the presence of a bhikṣu who has not yet eaten;
if there is no such bhikṣu among the assembly, one should seek for one nearby;

if none is found nearby, one should quickly confer full ordination upon the śrāmaṇera who is to receive it, and thereafter perform the *khalupaścādbhakti* (leftover-food) rite in the presence of that person before eating.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"From now on, this precept should be proclaimed as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, having finished his meal, eats food without performing the ritual for leftover food (kṛtapiṇḍapāta), it is a pāyattika.'"
There was a bhikṣu who, early in the morning, invited various bhikṣus to partake of a light meal, providing them with drinks, *khādaniya* (solid food), and *bhojaniya* (soft food).
The bhikṣus, believing they had already finished their meal, did not dare to eat more. They reported this matter to the Buddha.

The Buddha said: "This is not called 'having eaten enough. There are five kinds of eating that are called 'having eaten enough': [1] having finished the meal; [2] having formally accepted the food; [3] having ceased further eating; [4] having declared that one has had enough; and [5] having risen from one's seat."
Rice, solid rice, cakes, parched grain, fish, and meat—
within each of these five types of food, there are five factors that constitute "sufficient food" (*paryāpta-bhakta*):
first, the presence of food;...
Second, bestowing; third, receiving and consuming;
fourth, no longer receiving further benefit.
Fifth, when the body has moved from its original place,
if one obtains further timely food, such as rice or cakes, and eats them without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover-food) ritual, there is a *pāyattika* offense for every mouthful.
The bhikṣus did not know how to perform the ritual for leftover food (vighasa-kalpa) and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Place the food in a bowl, hold it up with your hands, bare your right shoulder, place your right knee on the ground, and speak these words:"
"Venerable sir, attend to me with one-pointed mind!
I, [Name], have finished eating; please perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite for me.
That bhikṣu then takes the bowl and asks:
"Is this food for me? He replied, "Yes!"
He then eats a small portion and returns the remainder.
If he does not eat at all, he simply takes it and returns it, saying:
"This is my leavings; I give them to you."
"This is also called 'leftover food' (*ucchista*). It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*. The thirty-fifth rule concludes.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there were two bhikṣus who were close friends; one was intelligent, while the other was dull-witted.
This dull-witted one repeatedly committed transgressions.
Those who were clever and intelligent constantly spoke of his transgressions, instructing him to repent for his errors.
Those who were dull-witted, however, became increasingly resentful in their hearts and thought to themselves:
"I, too, shall now watch for his faults and offenses!"
He watched him but could find no fault; then, once the other had finished eating, he invited him to eat more, claiming that the food had not been set aside as leftover (avasiṭṭha).
Because of their close friendship, the bhikṣu felt no suspicion at all and immediately ate it for him.
After he had eaten, [the monk] said:
"The food you have eaten is not 'leftover food' (vighasa); you have committed an offense and should repent!
Do not fail to cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya), lest you suffer for a long night!"
Then that bhikṣu rebuked him, saying:
"It was because I wished to benefit you that I instructed and rebuked you!
Why do you harbor resentment over this and entrap me in an offense?"
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked that bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:

‘If a bhikṣu, without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of leftover food), forcibly urges another bhikṣu who has already finished eating to eat, desiring to cause that other to commit an offense, it is a *pāyattika*.’”
There was a bhikṣu who had already finished his meal, but the other bhikṣus did not know this and called him again to eat. That bhikṣu said,
"I have already finished eating."
The bhikṣus then became doubtful, thinking:
"Could it be that we have not actually committed a pāyattika offense?
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"If one calls for food when one does not know that another has finished eating, and thereby commits a pāyattika offense, such a thing is impossible."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has finished eating, forcibly urges him to eat without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual for leftover food) with the intent to cause him to commit an offense, it is a *pāyattika*."
If one encourages a bhikṣu who has already finished eating to eat food for which the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover-food) rite has not been performed,
then for every mouthful he eats, it is a *pāyattika*.
It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
The thirty-six rules concerning *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, and *śrāmaṇerīs* regarding *duṣkṛta* offenses are concluded.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

Then, as the World-Honored One had not yet prescribed that bhikṣus should receive food before eating, the bhikṣus each ate at the homes of their acquaintances without having formally received the food.
The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"We do not like seeing these evil people wearing robes of cut and dyed cloth, yet eating food that has not been formally offered.
To eat food that has not been offered is theft!"
At that time, Mahākāśyapa was wearing rag-robes and gathering discarded food from various places in the streets and alleys to eat.
When the laypeople saw this, they reviled him, saying:
"This śramaṇa is exactly like a dog; he eats whatever food he happens to find—impure and loathsome!"
"How can we cause them to enter our homes?
When the elder bhikṣus had heard these two matters, they reported them to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and first questioned the bhikṣus:
"Do you truly eat food without having received it?
They replied, "It is indeed so."
"World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he further said to Kāśyapa:
"Although you have few desires, you are detested by others; you should not eat food that has been discarded."
"If one eats it, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish this precept for the bhikṣus; from this time forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu places food in his mouth that has not been received [by hand], it is a pāyattika.

At that time, when the bhikṣus were having people prepare food for them, they did not dare to taste it; because the food was sometimes too salty and sometimes too bland, the cooks became resentful and refused to prepare it anymore.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I now permit you to prepare food for people to taste, provided that they do not swallow it."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, without having received food, places it in his mouth, except for tasting food, it is a pāyattika."
At that time, the bhikṣus did not accept the tooth-sticks or water, and so they did not dare to chew them or rinse their mouths;
consequently, their breath was foul and their vision grew dim. When they spoke with others, people caught the odor and asked, "Venerable Sir!..."
"Why does your mouth smell?
The bhikṣus were deeply ashamed and begged for willow twigs and water.
The people said:
"You are lazy yourself; who would begrudge you a tooth-stick and water?
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"Now it is permitted not to receive tooth-sticks or water.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu places food in his mouth without having received it, except for tasting food, tooth-sticks, or water, it is a pāyattika.'"
At that time, Śāriputra suffered from a wind disorder (vāta-roga).
Maudgalyāyana went to visit him and asked, "When you were living at home, did you ever have this illness? He replied:
"Yes. "By what treatment was it cured? He replied:
"Eat lotus roots!
Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana went to Lake Anavatapta, took some lotus roots, and gave them to him.
Śāriputra asked:
"Where did you obtain this? He replied,
"From Lake Anavatapta."
He asked again,
"From whom did you receive it? He replied:
"I [received it] from a dragon," he said,
and thus did not dare to eat it.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should accept food from a dragon.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa was begging for alms at a poor household, and Śakra Devānām Indra thought to himself:
"Now the Venerable Kāśyapa is begging from a poor family; I shall now employ a skillful means to cause him to accept my food."
Then, during Kāśyapa’s almsround, [the Buddha] manifested as a poor weaver weaving at a loom;
he further manifested as a woman providing the warp for him. When Kāśyapa came to beg from them, they took his bowl, filled it with food and drink of a hundred flavors, and gave it to him.
Having received it, Kāśyapa thought to himself, "This man is poor; from where did he obtain this?
He immediately entered meditative concentration and observed, realizing that it was Śakra, the Lord of Devas. He then spoke to him, saying:
"Kauśika! Do not do this again!
Thereupon, he did not dare to eat.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I now permit the bhikṣus to receive food from devas. At that time,
the World-Honored One traveled along a remote path and arrived at the village of the Vālmīka spirits at dusk.
At that time, the spirit, seeing the Buddha, was filled with joy and invited the Buddha and the Sangha to receive a meal the following day. The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
The spirit then prepared various kinds of food and drink throughout the entire night; at dawn, he spread out seats and invited the Buddha and the Sangha.
The Buddha commanded the bhikṣus to accept the invitation together, and they all took their seats.
The spirits and deities served the food with their own hands, but the bhikṣus did not dare to accept it; they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to receive food from ghosts.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the Śāla grove.
At that time, there was a monkey that came down from a tree, took the Buddha’s bowl, and attempted to carry it away. The bhikṣus seized it and would not let him go.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Allow the monkey to take the bowl."
He immediately took his bowl and climbed a tree, gathering a bowl full of honey to offer to the Buddha.
When the Buddha saw that there were insects in it, he would not accept it. The monkey looked closely and, seeing the insects, immediately picked them out;
he then offered it to the Buddha again, and the Buddha accepted it for him. Thereupon, the monkey leaped for joy and retreated, walking backward as he withdrew.
The Buddha took this honey and gave it to the bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus did not dare to eat it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to eat food given by a monkey."
At that time, a horse merchant invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
After water had been served, someone said:
"The horse stable has caught fire!"
Because he did not extend the food to him, he said to the bhikṣu,
"Take the food yourself!
Having said this, he departed.
The bhikṣus were doubtful and did not dare to eat.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible), I allow the bhikṣus to eat by means of the donor’s words, taking them as an acceptance of the food."
Furthermore, there were laypeople who threw food from a distance to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not accept food thrown from a distance."
There were some elderly and sick bhikṣus whose vision was failing; when receiving food, they would touch the hands of those who had purified them, and washing their hands repeatedly was troublesome.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should receive grass or leaves and spread them out, pressing the edge with the hand so that the food adheres to them; this also counts as 'receiving' [the food]."
The bhikṣus then spread out the grass and leaves extensively.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not spread them extensively; they should be spread only as far as one's hands can reach."

There were some laypeople who treated the bhikṣus with contempt and disdain; unwilling to hand the food to them directly, they placed it on the ground before the bhikṣus and told them to take it for themselves.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If a donor is contemptuous and unwilling to hand over the food, it is permitted to take it using those words as the formal acceptance of the food.
There are four ways of receiving [alms]:..."

"One receives with the body what is given by the body; one receives with objects what is given by objects; one receives with the hand what is given by the hand; one receives by being instructed to take it.
There was salt water, and because the bhikṣu had not received it [through the proper formalities], he did not dare to drink it.
They reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If it is not salted but is naturally salty, you are permitted to drink it without having formally received it."
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. [The thirty-seventh rule concludes.
The Fifth Part of the Vinaya, Fascicle Seven.
The Mahīśāsaka Vinaya in Five Parts, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Jibin during the Song Dynasty,
together with Zhu Daosheng and others.
The First Section on the Pārājika Rules. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

At that time, the monks had not yet been prohibited from eating at improper times. Consequently, the monks went out for alms during the deep of night; some fell into ditches or trenches, some came into contact with women, some were robbed by bandits, and some were harmed by insects or wild beasts.
Because they ate without regard for the proper timing, their cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya) was neglected.
At that time, Kāḷodāyin, wearing variegated robes, his face black and his eyes blood-red, was begging for alms in the darkness.
A pregnant woman saw him in a flash of lightning and, greatly startled, cried out: "A piśāca!"
"Pisaca! Kāḷodāyin replied, "I am a śramaṇa begging for alms; I am not a pisaca."
He then reviled him harshly, saying:
"Why do you not slit your own belly with a knife instead of begging for food in the darkness of the night!
Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are satisfied with a single meal; why is it that you now eat without distinction between day and night?"
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they censured him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Kālodāyin:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had taken emetic medicine; as it was not yet time for his meal, his stomach felt empty and distressed.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"Anoint your body with ghee.
When it still did not improve, the Buddha said:
"Anoint the body with parched grain flour.
When it was still not cured, the Buddha said:
"Anoint the body with parched grain flour mixed with ghee."
When he was still not cured, the Buddha said:
"Bathe with warm water.
When he was still not cured, the Buddha said:
"Give him warm broth to drink.
Still, he was not cured. The Buddha said:
"Place a basin filled with melted fat and have him sit within it."
By means of these [preparations], one may remain until dawn; under no circumstances is it permitted to eat at an improper time (*vikāla*).
"Improper time" refers to the period from after midday until the appearance of the morning light; this is called the improper time.
If a bhikṣu, when it is not the proper time, perceives it as not the proper time, or has doubt that it is not the proper time;
or when it is not the proper time, perceives it as the proper time—in all these cases, it is a pāyattika.
When it is the proper time, if he perceives it as not the proper time, or has doubt that it is not the proper time, it is a dukkaṭa.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. The thirty-eighth [offense] is concluded.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the World-Honored One had not yet prohibited bhikṣus from consuming food kept overnight.
There was a shrine of a deity that served as a place of recreation, where crowds vied with one another to bring fine foods to view the spectacle;
sometimes it would remain for two or three nights, with an abundance of delicacies.

The bhikṣus received such a quantity of food that they could not finish it all; it accumulated in their rooms until there was no spot where it was not present, attracting insects and rats that gnawed through and destroyed the walls of the dwellings.
The laypeople saw this and asked,
"Who has piled up this food? Someone said:
“Shramanas, disciples of the Śākya!
they all cried out in derision,
“These shaven-headed fellows know only how to greedily accept things, without a thought for the waste and expense!”
"There is no conduct of a śramaṇa; you have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
Furthermore, there was another forest-dwelling bhikṣu who lived in a forest hermitage and thought to himself:
"Begging for food day after day hinders and obstructs the practice of the Way."
He then begged for various kinds of food, either eating them as they were or drying them in the sun.
At that time, some bhikṣus saw him while traveling and said to him,
"Did the World-Honored One not say that clothing is merely for covering the body and food is merely for sustaining the life?"
"Why have you accumulated so much food and drink, leaving them scattered about to dry?
That bhikṣu replied, "This place is far from a village;
begging for alms every day would hinder and obstruct my practice of the Way. Therefore, I beg for all at once in order to rest from such toil."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked that bhikṣu:
“Is it true that you did so?”
He replied: "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!"
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept shall be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu eats leftover food that has been stored overnight, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding "leftover food from the previous night":
food that has already been accepted and kept overnight is called "leftover food from the previous night.
If one eats this food, for every mouthful, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense. This concludes the thirty-ninth [rule].
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

At that time, this country was suffering from famine, and it was difficult to obtain alms. Twenty-eight generals of the ghost-spirits came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"In this world of famine, we pray that the Buddha will travel among the people.
We shall transform the masses and cause them to give rise to wholesome minds.
The World-Honored One silently granted his consent.

At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām-Indra, and Brahmā Sahāmpati, the Lord of the Sahā World, also came to the Buddha, prostrated themselves at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. They addressed the Buddha as before, and the Buddha likewise silently granted his consent.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, together with a great community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, as well as five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, five hundred upāsakas, and five hundred upāsikās, traveled through the kingdom of Magadha from the city of Rājagṛha.
Furthermore, there were a thousand male and female non-Buddhists and five hundred beggars who all followed behind the Buddha, seeking alms from his leftovers.

Wherever the World-Honored One went, there was no one who did not exhaust their resources to make offerings; yet those who brought offerings from afar could not even set them down, for the food and drink were so abundant that they far exceeded what was needed.
The bhikṣus each gave the remains of their own food to male and female followers of external paths and to beggars.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, receive everything they obtain; yet they do not finish eating it themselves, but give it to those with false views!"
"It is better to be like one who milks a cow, knowing how to keep the calf!
Or again, some said:
"If even the śramaṇa Śākyaputrīyas provide offerings to non-Buddhists, why should we not serve them?"
Thereupon, the World-Honored One proceeded to the town of Anāpinḍada.

At that time, there was a great brāhmaṇa named Śramaṇa who, with five hundred wagons heavily laden with food and drink, followed the Buddha for more than five months, seeking an opportunity to provide offerings, yet in the end he was unable to do so.
His family sent word after him, saying:
"The time for farming is about to pass; you should return to attend to your work.
At that time, the brahmin went to where Ānanda was and said to him:
"I have five hundred chariots laden with various foods and drinks, which I wish to offer to the Buddha and the Sangha;
yet, though I have followed the Buddha for more than five months, I have not yet been able to make this offering."

As my family’s letter urges me on, I cannot remain here any longer; I wish to spread my eating utensils along the path so that the Buddha and the Sangha may tread upon them as they pass, thereby fulfilling my long-held aspiration.
Ānanda replied, "I shall inform the World-Honored One," and he immediately informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "You may take the brahmin to see the family providing the offerings; if there is anything lacking, instruct them to prepare it.
Having received these instructions, Ānanda took the brahmin to see the family providing the offerings, where he saw that there was no porridge, nor oil, honey, or fried cakes.
He then prepared seven kinds of gruel and two kinds of cakes, and in the early morning, he informed the Buddha that the cakes and gruel were ready.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Help him serve them."
Ānanda accepted the instruction and assisted in distributing the rice gruel and cakes.
At that time, there was a female non-Buddhist ascetic (tīrthika) carrying a small girl in her arms; because she had a child, Ānanda gave her two extra cakes.
The various non-Buddhists said, "This bhikṣu is lustfully attached to this woman; that is why he gave her two cakes in particular.
Others further said:
"It was simply because she was holding her child; it does not mean she showed partiality!
As they argued back and forth in such a tumultuous manner, the seating area fell into disorder.
Seeing this, Ānanda felt uneasy in his heart and went to where the Buddha was, reporting the preceding matter to him.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Ānanda:
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu gives food to an outsider, whether male or female, it is a pāyattika.'"
Furthermore, there were certain bhikṣus who gave food to naked ascetics; one of them entered Rājagṛha carrying a bundle of cakes wrapped up, and people asked him, "Where have you come from?"
He replied, “I have come from among the shaven-headed householders.
He asked again:
"What is inside this package? He replied,
"It is honey-glazed cakes."
He asked again,
"From whom did you receive it? He replied:
"The laypeople regard the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, as fields of merit, and the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, in turn regard us as fields of merit; it was from them that we received this.
Thereupon, people criticized and reviled them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know moderation; they greedily accept gifts without satiety!"

"We have already diminished and divided our own resources—both from our bodies and from our households—to provide for our offerings; yet you now take these and give them to this person of false views and evil character!
If he were truly worthy of offerings, we ourselves would offer them; why rely on a śramaṇa?"
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they censured them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"What difference is there between having robes and not having robes?
Having rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu gives food to a naked outsider, whether male or female, it is a pāyattika.'"
Some non-Buddhist practitioners came to beg during their mealtime; the bhikṣus did not dare to give them anything, whereupon the outsiders became angry and reviled them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, teach others to practice giving, yet they themselves are miserly!"
"What path could there be?
Furthermore, when laypeople heard that he had inspired such faith and reverence, they also mocked and rebuked him, saying:
"How can a śramaṇa constantly beg from others, yet not give to others?"
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who did not dare to give even when relatives of non-Buddhist outsiders came to beg.
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to give food to those of other paths, provided they do not give it with their own hands.
From this day forward, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu gives food with his own hand to a naked ascetic of another path, whether male or female, it is a pāyattika.'"
If non-Buddhists come to beg, one should set aside a single morsel from one’s own portion in a separate place and let them take it themselves;
one should not give them food belonging to the Saṃgha.
If there are beggars—whether begging for food for dogs or birds—one should measure one's own portion of food and take a share accordingly before giving from it;
one must not take more than one's own allotted portion to give as alms.
For a śrāmaṇera, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one’s parents are followers of non-Buddhist paths, there is no offense if one gives with one's own hand. [The forty rules are concluded.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, several laypeople came to the monastery and asked the bhikṣus,
"How many people are there in the Saṃgha? The bhikṣus replied:
"How many monks are there?
The laypeople replied, "We shall invite the entire assembly of monks tomorrow; we hope you will deign to attend our modest meal."
The group of six bhikṣus said:
"If you provide us with milk, curd, butter, oil, fish, and meat, we shall accept your invitation."
The people replied, "We must borrow or purchase them to prepare for it.

Having said this, they each returned to their own homes; some failed to borrow what they needed, while others could not find what they sought to buy. The next day, when the provisions were ready, they cried out that the time had arrived.
The community of monks, having put on their robes and taken up their bowls, went to his house, sat down in their assigned seats,
and water was served followed by food. The group of six bhikṣus said, "Why is there no milk, curd, butter, oil, fish, or meat?"
He replied, "I could not obtain a loan, nor was I able to purchase anything. Thereupon,
the group of six bhikṣus overturned their bowls and departed.
The laypeople all said this:
"These men did not receive fine food and turned their bowls upside down and left! Are they kings?"
"Are you a high minister?
One who has left the household life does so to seek liberation, begging for food only to satisfy one's needs;
why then do you now, on the contrary, indulge in delicious flavors?"
"They lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
“Is it truly so? He replied, “It is truly so.”
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson to seek milk, curd, butter, oil, fish, or meat, it is a pāyattika.
Subsequently, when the bhikṣus obtained various fine foods, they did not dare to eat them;
or having eaten them, they confessed their transgression and repented.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"It is impossible that one who does not seek out fine food, but eats what is obtained spontaneously, would commit a pāyattika offense."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu goes to the homes of laypeople and requests such fine foods as milk, curd, butter, oil, fish, or meat."
"If one eats it, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
There were some sick bhikṣus whom a physician instructed to eat rich food.
The bhikṣus said, "The Buddha does not permit us to request such things; how can we obtain it?"
He thought to himself:
"If the Buddha permits me to seek this food, my illness will surely be cured.
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I now permit sick bhikṣus to seek choice foods.
From this day forward, this precept should be stated as follows:"
“If there are such fine foods in a household—
namely milk, curd, butter, oil, fish, or meat— and if a bhikṣu,
being without illness, seeks them for his own sake and eats them, it is a pāyattika.”
If one seeks [food] for a sick bhikṣu from the home of a relative or from the home of an acquaintance, there is no offense.
For a śrāmaṇera, this constitutes a duṣkṛta; the forty-first rule is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, Bāṇa-datta (Bhadrananda) regularly received offerings from a certain brāhmaṇa. On a later occasion, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to the brāhmaṇa’s house; however, the brāhmaṇa was not there, so he sat down alone with the brāhmaṇa’s wife and conversed with her.
At that time, a brahmin, having conceived lustful thoughts, turned back midway; seeing Upananda conversing with his wife, he thought to himself:
"This bhikṣu is preaching the Dharma now; it is not the time for practicing desire."
He then went back outside; his lustful mind grew even more intense, and after a short while he entered again, finding that Upananda had still not departed.
Again, as before, he suppressed his desire and went out, only to enter once more after a brief moment, saying to his wife:
"Quickly give the bhikṣu food and send him on his way; do not let him neglect his practice of the Path!"
The wife, understanding his intention and wishing not to cause her husband to deviate from the Way in pursuit of desire, replied:
"Let the bhikṣu eat slowly; what urgent matter is there?"
When he had spoken thus three times, Upananda still refused to leave. The brahmin then said to him:
"We laypeople have many affairs; at times when we are alone, it is appropriate for us to approach our wives."
"You do not know the proper time; you sit here refusing to leave. Who would think that you people are practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*)?
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upāli (Bhadanta):
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu sits with a woman in a house where food is being served, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Eating" refers to men and women mutually consuming one another through passion.
"Sitting" refers to:
If one knows that it will hinder the task and yet sits down intentionally,
it is likewise for a bhikṣuṇī.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If many people are sitting together, if there is a partition or screen between them, or if a husband and wife are observing the eight precepts on a given day, they do not commit an offense. [The forty-second case concludes.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, Upananda was regularly receiving offerings from a certain brahmin. Later, when he arrived at the brahmin’s house, the brahmin was not present, so he sat in a secluded place with his wife.
The brahmin returned and said to his wife:

"I have no doubt that you sat with the bhikṣu in a secluded place; however, had others seen it, they would surely have said that you committed an evil act, thereby bringing disgrace upon the śramaṇas and dishonor to my family!"
He spoke again to Bāḷhaka:
"I truly do not doubt you, Venerable One; yet it is not right for you, so guard yourself against this ill repute!
His wife, relying on the power of her own beautiful appearance, the power of having many children, and the power of her skill in acquiring wealth, then rebuked her husband, saying:
"I am sitting with the bhikṣus; do not trouble them!
You need not speak such excessive words now!
The brahmin then became greatly incensed and rebuked Upananda, saying:
“We laypeople do not even sit alone in private with the wives of others;
yet you śramaṇas have done this instead? You lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!”
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they censured him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upananda:
