"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this time forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu takes the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.'"

There were bhikṣus traveling on the road, or transporting goods, or fumigating their alms bowls, who inadvertently killed various insects; they all felt shame and remorse, and some went on to repent for their transgressions and purify themselves of the offense.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"It is impossible that one who kills a living being by mistake should incur a pāyattika offense."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "an animal":
Excluding dragons, it refers to other animals.
Therefore, "taking life" means that one first has the intention to kill and then severs their life-force.
If one takes the life of an animal, for each instance regardless of the number, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is likewise.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This concludes the fifty-first [offense].
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of seventeen bhikṣus went to the dwelling place of the group of six bhikṣus. The group of six bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"These bhikṣus possess a sense of shame and dread of blame; they have few desires and are content."
"He has now come here; he will surely perceive our faults.
We should employ skillful means to cause him to give rise to doubt and regret;
once doubt and regret have arisen, he will certainly return to his teacher."
Having reflected thus, he said:
"Have you all properly received full ordination?
Is there a boundary field for the reception of the precepts?"
Is the *karmavācanā* performed according to the Dharma?
Have you not committed any *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, or *dukkaṭa* offenses?
"Do you well guard your body and speech?
Have your Upādhyāya and Ācārya previously well received the full ordination, and do they also well guard their body and speech? He replied:
"We ourselves do not know, nor do we know how our preceptors and ācāryas are;
we now ask the Venerable One—please tell us!"
"When I received full ordination, were my preceptor (upādhyāya) and preceptor-instructor (ācārya) entirely in accordance with the Dharma?
He replied, "If I speak the truth, you will not believe it; you may ask those whom you yourself trust."
Then the group of seventeen bhikṣus went to their teacher and asked about these matters. The teacher replied, "Your conduct in every matter is in accordance with the Dharma;
when I received the precepts in the past, it was also like this."
"Who has caused you all to harbor such doubt and regret?
They replied, "The group of six bhikṣus."
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they censured them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu causes another bhikṣu to give rise to doubt or regret, it is a pāyattika.'"
There were certain bhikṣus who, having committed an offense, felt doubt and regret, and asked other bhikṣus:
"Having committed such and such an act, what kind of offense have we incurred?"
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The Buddha has established a precept that forbids causing another bhikṣu to give rise to doubt or regret.
They then replied:
“I do not know. He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one does not wish to cause another person to give rise to doubt or regret, yet speaks of the offense they have committed—there is no such case where this constitutes a *pāyattika*.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu intentionally causes a bhikṣu to give rise to doubt or regret, thinking, "I shall cause this bhikṣu to suffer distress for even a short time," it is a *pāyattika*.'"
"Regarding doubt and regret:
there is doubt concerning one's birthplace, doubt concerning the reception of the precepts, doubt concerning the violation of the precepts, and doubt concerning robes.
If one causes a bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī to feel doubt and regret, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
If a bhikṣuṇī causes a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī to feel doubt or regret, it is a pāyattika;
if she causes a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī to feel doubt or regret, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī causes the five groups [of monastics] to feel doubt or regret, it is all a duṣkṛta offense. [The fifty-second rule is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus possessed great influence; they obstructed the Saṃgha’s formal acts (karmans) and the lifting of such acts, and when the Saṃgha would not comply, they would depart.
They then went to the place of the bhikṣu who had been subject to the act of banishment and said to him: "Do not be distressed!"
"I have already assisted you in obstructing the *saṃgha-karman*.
When the Saṃgha did not follow me, I rose and departed; thus, the *karman* was not valid.
He then went to the bhikṣu who had performed the dissolution of the *karman* and said to him:
"Do not say, 'The Saṃgha has dissolved my *karmavācanā*!
When the Saṃgha was dissolving the *karmavācanā*, I already opposed it.
Since the Saṃgha did not follow me, I rose and departed; thus, the dissolution of the *karmavācanā* is invalid."
"You may now seek further absolution from the Saṃgha yourself!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they censured them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
“Is it truly so? He replied, “It is truly so.”
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu rises and leaves while the Saṃgha is engaged in formal business, it is a pāyattika.
At that time, there were matters on which the bhikṣus wished to depart, yet they did not dare to do so.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to rise and depart after having conveyed their consent regarding the matter at hand."
One who conveys the consent (*chanda*) should say to one person:
"Venerable sir, attend closely!
The Saṃgha is now conducting its business; I, the bhikṣu so-and-so, convey my consent regarding this matter of the Saṃgha that accords with the Dharma."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, when the Saṃgha is conducting formal business, rises and departs without having given his consent (chanda), it is a pāyattika."
"Monastic legal proceedings" refers to the *jñapti-karman*,
the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
If one leaves the area where a karman is being performed under a roof, each time one goes out, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If it is a formal act (kamma) performed in the open air, one commits a pāyattika offense by departing and going beyond the distance of one fathom from the face of the Saṃgha.
If it is a person possessing supernormal powers (ṛddhi), one commits a pāyattika offense by departing and rising four finger-breadths above the ground.
If one leaves while the Saṃgha has not yet performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to settle a matter, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if one leaves after a private chamber has settled a matter, it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.
It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
If the Saṃgha has not performed a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to settle a matter, nor has it settled the matter in a private room, a śrāmaṇera may remain within that assembly;
if he rises and departs, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. The same applies to a śikṣamāṇā and a śrāmaṇerī.
If the Saṃgha performs an illegal *karmavācanā*, one who rises and departs without having granted their consent (*chanda*) does not commit an offense; this concludes the fifty-third [rule].
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of seventeen bhikṣus went to the dwelling place of the group of six bhikṣus and tickled one another.
There was a bhikṣu who, while being tickled by the community, died from suffocation because he could not restrain his laughter.
The group of seventeen bhikṣus wept for him in grief.
The elder bhikṣus asked:
"Why do you weep? He replied, "A bhikṣu died while playing and laughing; for this reason, I weep."
He asked again,
"By what means did you come to this? He replied:
"We tickled one another until we could not help but laugh, and consequently, we fainted.
The bhikṣus reprimanded them in various ways and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of seventeen bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so? They replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu tickles another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.'"
If a bhikṣu tickles a śrāmaṇera, or even an animal, it is a duṣkṛta.
It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. [The fifty-fourth rule is concluded.]
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a group of seventeen bhikṣus went to the river Ajiravatī to fetch water; they proceeded to bathe there, swimming, playing, splashing, and dousing one another.
At that time, King Prasenajit, together with Queen Mallikā, ascended the tower and saw them from afar.
He said to the queen, "Behold your field of merit!
The queen replied to the king:
"This was before the Buddha had yet established the precepts; these young renunciants have simply not yet understood the Dharma!
O King, do not see this and give rise to a lack of faith and respect toward other bhikṣus, for you would suffer for a long night!"
After the group of seventeen bhikṣus had finished their various performances, they stood upon the water and put on their robes.
The lady said to the king,
"Your Majesty, please observe the field of merit I serve!"
Having put on his robes, he took water from a jar and threw it into the air, then flew after it, passing over the palace roof like a king of geese.
The lady spoke again to the king:
"Behold further the field of merit to whom I serve."
The King was greatly delighted, and his faith and reverence increased all the more.
Thereupon, the Queen said to the brahmin Nalinda:
"Go to the Buddha's presence and report this to him."
He immediately accepted the instruction and went; the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him, before sending him back.
On account of this matter, he assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of seventeen bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu plays in the water, it is a pāyattika.'"
If one plays in water, or even splashes one another with water contained in a vessel, it is all a *pāyattika*.
If one plays by clapping snow or fiddling with dew on the tips of grass, it is all a *dukkaṭa*.
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta.
If it was not done in jest, none of these constitute an offense. [Fifty-five cases concluded.]
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the World-Honored One had not yet prohibited bhikṣus from sleeping in the same room as women—
whether it be one bhikṣu with one woman, or many bhikṣus with few women.

Sometimes there were few bhikṣus and many women staying together in the same room; they gave rise to defiled and attached thoughts, leading some to return to secular life or become followers of external paths.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled them, saying:
"These śramaṇas stay in the same rooms as women; how are they any different from white-robed householders?"
"You lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
At that time, there was a young woman whose husband had passed away, and she thought to herself:
"Where now shall I seek another worthy partner?"

Again, he thought: "I cannot now go from door to door and house to house; I shall instead construct a guesthouse where those both living at home and those who have left the home life may stay as they please, so that I may select [a candidate] from among them."
He did exactly as instructed;
he made an announcement along the roads that those who needed lodging might stay.
At that time, Anuruddha arrived at that village in the evening and asked for a place to stay. Someone said to him:
"There is [a place] at such-and-such a house.
He went there immediately to seek lodging.
Ānanda had previously possessed a handsome appearance; after he attained the Way, his countenance became twice as radiant as usual.
When the widow saw him, she thought to herself:
"I have now found a fine husband! She then pointed out the location, saying: [The place where...]
“You may stay overnight here!
Āniruddha then went forward into the room and sat down cross-legged.
Not long after he had sat, other merchants arrived seeking lodging, and the widow replied:
"Although I am a frequent guest here, I have now given [the lodging] to the bhikṣu; it is no longer at my disposal.
The merchant then repeated the host's words and requested lodging from Anuruddha.
Aniruddha said to the widow,
"If it is by my leave, you may stay for the entire night.
The merchant then went forward.
The widow thought again:
"I must invite the bhikṣu back inside; if I do not, there will be no end to his future visits.
She immediately prepared a fine bed within, lit a lamp, and spoke to Aniruddha, saying:
"You may enter. Anuruddha then entered, sat down cross-legged, and fixed his mindfulness before him.
After everyone had fallen asleep, the widow spoke to him:
"Venerable sir!
Do you know the reason why I have invited you? He replied:
"Sister! Your intention is rightly set upon merit. The widow said:
“I certainly did not do this!
She then related the matter in full detail, and Anuruddha said, “Sister!
"We ought not to commit such evil deeds;
even the Dharma established by the World-Honored One does not permit them. The widow said:
"I am of noble birth, in the prime of my youth, fully accomplished in ritual propriety, and possessed of abundant wealth and treasures;
I wish to serve as an attendant to the Venerable One, and pray that you will graciously accept me."
Aniruddha answered her as he had before, and the widow thought again:
"A man is deluded only by physical form; I shall stand before him with my body exposed."
She immediately removed her clothes and stood before him, smiling and conversing.
Aniruddha then closed his eyes and sat upright, practicing the meditation on the skeleton (aṭṭhikasaññā).
The widow thought to herself again:
"Although I have done this, he has still not been subdued.
Thinking thus, he wished to go up onto the bed to sit together with her.
Thereupon, Anuruddha leaped up into the air; the widow was then greatly ashamed, felt deep remorse, quickly put on her clothes again, joined her palms in repentance, and said:
“Venerable Sir!
I was truly foolish; I dare not give rise to such a thought again from this day forth!
I pray that you will show me compassion and forgive me, and accept my confession of transgression!”
Anuruddha said, “I accept your confession!
Thereupon, he preached various sublime dharmas—good in the beginning, middle, and end; excellent in meaning and phrasing; perfectly pure, the very nature of the holy life (brahmacarya).
Upon hearing this, the widow was distanced from dust and free from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Aniruddha then went to the Buddha’s presence as he had envisioned and reported the matter concerning the former bhikṣu in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so? They replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu sleeps in the same room as a woman, it is a pāyattika.'"
If a woman, including one who has just given birth or one who possesses both sexual organs, stays overnight in the same room [with a monk], it is a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases.
Regarding "room," it is as explained in the section on staying overnight with those who have not yet received full ordination.
If one sleeps in the same room as a non-human female, a female animal, or a eunuch, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is *duṣkṛta*.
If they share the same roof but have separate partitions;
or if it is a large assembly where the Dharma is being taught;
or if the mother, sister, younger sister, or close relative is ill and is accompanied by a man of discernment who does not lie down—none of these constitute an offense. (End of section fifty-six.)
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.

At that time, the World-Honored One had not yet prohibited bhikṣus from drinking alcohol. There were some bhikṣus who, in taverns or at the houses of laypeople, drank wine until they were greatly intoxicated; some fell into pits or ditches, some crashed into walls or objects, and some broke their robes and bowls or injured their bodies.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and rebuked them, saying:

"Among us laypeople, there are still those who do not drink alcohol; yet these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, who have abandoned worldly burdens to seek the Way, are all intoxicated beyond measure, surpassing even the common folk, while wearing in vain these dyed and cut garments!"
"You lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
At that time, the World-Honored One traveled from the kingdom of Kauśāmbī to the village of Bhadrayāṇī.
There, at the dwelling place of a certain matted-hair brahmin, there was a venomous dragon that constantly rained down great hailstones, destroying the crops in the fields.
The local residents constantly thought to themselves:
"Among the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, who possesses such majestic power as to be able to subdue this dragon?

When they heard that the Buddha had arrived in this town together with twelve hundred and fifty disciples, everyone was filled with joy; they all went out to welcome him, prostrating their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In this village there is always a wicked venomous dragon that destroys the crops.
I have constantly prayed for someone of great majestic power to come and subdue it!”
At that time, Śākata was fanning the Buddha from behind.
The Buddha turned his head and asked him, "Did you hear what these householders were saying? He replied:
"Listen! The second and third exchanges were likewise.
Then, Śākyaṭa thought to himself:
“The World-Honored One has asked three times and has already commanded me to subdue this evil dragon.
He immediately went forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed for the dragon’s abode, thinking to himself:
“I shall now subdue this dragon so that its form is not destroyed, yet its body becomes as minute as a mote of dust.”
He immediately entered the chamber and sat down to one side. The dragon’s body emitted smoke, and Saṃghāta’s body also emitted smoke;
the dragon’s entire body burst into flames, and Saṃghāta’s entire body also burst into flames;
the dragon’s fire produced five colors, and Saṃghāta’s fire also produced five colors.
Thereupon, he transformed his dragon body into the likeness of a log, placed it inside his alms bowl, and carrying it to the Buddha's location, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This evil and venomous dragon has now been subdued; where should it be placed?"
The Buddha said,
"Place it in the midst of the world-system.
Śākyamuni received these instructions and, in the time it takes for a person to bend and extend their arm, he placed it in the midst of the world-system and returned in an instant.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, having departed from the town of Bhaddavatiya, intended to return to Kauśāmbī. At that time,
the lay devotees of Bhaddavatiya, hearing that Sāketa had subdued the evil dragon, were all greatly rejoiced and asked the bhikṣus, "Who is this Sāketa?"
At that time, Śākyaṭa was behind the Buddha. The bhikṣus said, "The one behind the Buddha is he!
The lay devotees immediately stepped forward, prostrated at his feet, and addressed him, saying:
"Please accept our invitation!
[The Buddha] accepted it by remaining silent.
The lay devotees said:
"Venerable sir!
What kind of food do you require? He replied:
"I was a layman when I enjoyed the habit of drinking wine and eating meat.
The householder, being pleased, immediately prepared them for him.

Śāketa went to his home, ate the meat and drank the wine until he was thoroughly satiated; then, returning to Kauśāmbī, he fell asleep intoxicated outside the monastery, vomiting and spitting, with his robes and bowl strewn about.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw from afar with his divine eye and said to Ānanda, "Come with me to look outside the monastery.

Having received these instructions, he followed the Buddha outside and saw him. The Buddha and Ānanda carried him back and placed him by the well; the Buddha drew water himself and had Ānanda wash him. He then laid him upon a rope bed, with his head toward the Buddha. After a short while, he turned over and extended his feet toward the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Did Śāketa previously revere the Buddha?
They replied: [He did.]
"Reverence! He asked again,
"Are you able to maintain reverence now?"
He replied, “I cannot! He asked again:
"Should one drink this wine, and thereby lose one's original nature?
He replied, "One should not!"
He asked again:
"Sagata was previously able to subdue the evil dragon; can he now subdue the frog? He replied:
"No! The bhikṣus again reported the previous matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
Having reprimanded the bhikṣus in various ways for those causes and conditions, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu drinks intoxicants, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
At that time, after the Buddha had established the precept, Śākya dared not drink again;

however, due to his prior habituation, he felt as if his breath were cut off and he was on the verge of death, and his food and drink did not digest. Not knowing what to do, he reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Let him smell the wine vessel!
He smelled the wine vessel and was not mistaken; the Buddha said:
"Place wine within cakes, or within soups and congees, so that they may eat it.
When they ate it without [the intended] error, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to give wine to them."
When Śākyaṭa had recovered, he informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Since you have recovered, you should gradually cease [the consumption].
Even if you no longer feel aversion upon smelling a wine vessel, you must not smell it again."
There is wine that possesses the color of wine, the taste of wine, and the fragrance of wine;
there is wine that possesses the color of wine and the fragrance of wine, but lacks the taste of wine;
and there is wine that possesses the color of wine and the taste of wine, but lacks the fragrance of wine.
If there is alcohol, or that which is not alcohol but possesses the color, fragrance, and taste of alcohol, and drinking it causes intoxication—if one drinks such things, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If there is that which is not alcohol but possesses the color, fragrance, and taste of alcohol, yet drinking it does not cause intoxication—one may drink it in a secluded place if one so desires.

If there is that which is not alcohol and lacks the color, fragrance, and taste of alcohol, yet drinking it causes intoxication—if one drinks it, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense. If there is that which is not alcohol and lacks the color, fragrance, and taste of alcohol, and drinking it does not cause intoxication—one is permitted to drink it.
If a bhikṣu drinks alcohol, for every swallow he commits a pāyattika offense.
It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense. This concludes the fifty-seventh rule.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus showed no respect for their preceptors (upādhyāya) or teachers (ācārya), nor did they respect the precepts;
other bhikṣus likewise followed their example.
When the elder bhikṣus saw this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six and the other bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu shows disrespect toward his teacher, it is a pāyattika.’”
If a bhikṣu treats his three teachers or the precepts with contempt, it is a pāyattika for each instance;
if he treats other bhikṣus with contempt, it is a duṣkṛta.

This applies even down to cases where the teacher orders him to sweep the ground and he does not sweep, or instructs him to sweep in one direction and he sweeps in the opposite direction—in all such cases, it is a duṣkṛta.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense. [The fifty-eighth rule is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kośala together with a great saṃgha of five hundred bhikṣus, traveling toward the town of Aṭṭhapiṇḍika.

At that time, when those bhikṣus heard that the Buddha was coming, and there were no halls or dwellings available, they built one themselves by cutting grass and digging the earth. The Buddha then rebuked them in various ways, as was previously described in the account of the construction of the lecture hall.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu digs the earth and takes soil himself, it is a pāyattika.’”
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus employed gardeners and śrāmaṇeras to dig the earth and take soil.
When the other bhikṣus saw this, they said:
"The Buddha has prescribed that one must not dig the earth; why do you now commit such an evil deed?"
He replied, "I have had someone dig it! The bhikṣus said:
"Is there any difference between having someone dig and digging for oneself?
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: [It is true.]
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu digs the earth himself, or causes another to dig it, it is a pāyattika.

There were some laypeople who sent materials for a bhikṣu-saṃgha to build a dwelling. After a long time they came to inspect it and, seeing that the dwelling was not yet finished, they asked the bhikṣu building the dwelling:”
"Why do you not quickly bring this merit to completion for me?
He replied, "The Buddha does not permit us to dig the earth ourselves or to have others dig it; how then can it be completed?"
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you require soil, you should say to a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle such things):"
"Know this; see this. I need this; give me this.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu digs the earth himself,
or causes another to dig it, saying: 'Dig here!'"
"A *pāyattika*. It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, to dig the earth when there is no business to do is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one takes dry earth, there is no offense; [the fifty-ninth rule is concluded].
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus quarreled with other bhikṣus; having finished quarreling, they stood outside the door listening to their words.
Having heard this, he said to the bhikṣus,
"Why do you speak such words? He asked them:
"From whom did you hear it? He replied,
"I was listening from outside the door."
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they censured them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did such a thing?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu, in a secluded place, silently eavesdrops on what other bhikṣus are saying, it is a pāyattika.’”
At that time, some bhikṣus were disputing the principles with other bhikṣus, debating right and wrong.
Another bhikṣu listened from behind a wall and gave rise to doubt, thinking:
"I wonder if I have not committed a pāyattika offense?"
Some among them confessed their offenses and repented.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is impossible that a bhikṣu who listens silently to a dispute while discerning right from wrong should incur a pāyattika offense.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, having already engaged in a dispute, listens silently and thinks thus:'"
"If one says, 'I shall remember and uphold what the bhikṣus have said,' it is a pāyattika.
To listen silently to the speech of bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, or śrāmaṇerīs is a duṣkṛta."
If a bhikṣuṇī listens to the words of a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
if she listens to the words of a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a *śikṣamāṇā*, *śrāmaṇera*, or *śrāmaṇerī* listens in silence to the conversation of the five classes of monastics, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. This concludes the sixty [rules].
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the parents of the seventeen groups of youths were filled with affection for them; the mother spoke thus:
"My sons are unaccustomed to hardship and their natures are delicate; what craft can I teach them so that they may attain lasting peace and happiness?"
The father said,
"He should be taught arithmetic, writing, and painting!
The mother said:
"If he were taught calligraphy or painting, I fear it would damage his eyes;
if he were taught arithmetic, I fear his fingers would ache;
if he were taught accounting, I fear it would afflict his mind."
They further deliberated together:
"We should cause him to go forth among the sons of the Śākyas, so that he may attain the unconditioned in this life and enjoy eternal bliss in future lives.
When those seventeen youths wished to go forth, they spoke to one another:
"I must wait for Upāli to arrive so that we may take our leave together.
At that time, Upāli returned from his journey and went to where the youths were. The youths said:
"Do you know? We wish to go forth in the Dharma of the Tathāgata and are waiting for your leave.
When Upāli heard this, he also wished to go with them and returned to inform his parents.
The parents immediately granted permission and thought to themselves:
"Whom shall we appoint as his teacher?
They then thought again:
“Piliṅgavatsa rescued their leader from among the bandits and brought him back; now he shall be their disciple.
Thereupon, each of them took his son and went to Piliṅgavatsa, saying, “Venerable Sir!”
"Venerable Sir, you have shown great kindness toward this child; I now offer him to you, and pray that you will accept him as your disciple!
Piṅgalavatsa immediately ordained him and conferred upon him full ordination.
After he had received the precepts, he was unable to go alone at night to the latrine or the place for washing his hands, so [the teacher] always accompanied him.
Once, seeing his teacher in the darkness and not recognizing him, he thought it was a ghost and cried out in a loud voice, saying: "Piśāca!"
“Piśāca! The teacher said,
“Do not be afraid!”
"I am a human being, not a ghost!
Or, when he sought food at night, the Master said:
"The Sangha has food; it shall be given to you at dawn."
He asked again,
"If the Sangha has no food, where should they obtain it?
The Master said:
"If there are no monks, we must beg for food.
Having heard these words, she cried out loudly,
"When the bhikṣus return from begging for food, we shall already be dead!"
The Buddha heard this during the night and asked Ānanda,
"Whose crying voice is that?
Ānanda reported the matter to the Buddha in full detail.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus at dawn and asked Piṅgala-bhadra:
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"You should not confer full ordination upon those who are less than twenty years of age;
being under twenty, they are largely incapable of fulfilling their duties and will consequently lead to the breaking of the precepts."
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu confers full ordination upon a person who is less than twenty years of age, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
At that time, the youth Kāśyapa had received full ordination before he was twenty years old; later, he became doubtful and did not know what to do, so he reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Has the youth Kāśyapa attained anything?
They replied: [He has.]
"He has attained the stage of Srotāpanna!

The Buddha said, "This person is indeed the first to receive full ordination; however, it cannot be called receiving the precepts through the formal rite of the white fourfold motion (jñapti-caturtha-karman) in accordance with the Dharma."
Now, it is permitted to count the years spent in the womb to complete twenty;
if they are still not sufficient, it is further permitted to use intercalary months to complete them;
if they are still not sufficient, it is further permitted to use the years of one's time as a śramaṇa to complete them.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a person is less than twenty years of age, confers full ordination upon them, it is a pāyattika offense."
"This person does not obtain the precepts; the bhikṣus may also censure him, for such is the nature of this dharma!
If one is under twenty years of age, yet perceives oneself as being under twenty, or doubts whether one is under twenty, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one is actually full twenty years of age, yet perceives oneself as being under twenty, or doubts whether one is full twenty, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.

If one knows that [the candidate] is less than twenty years of age, yet conceives the thought of conferring full ordination upon them and undertakes the preparatory rites, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense throughout the process up until the fourth *karmavācanā* has not yet been completed.
When the fourth *karmavācanā* was concluded, the preceptor committed a *pāyattika*;
the remaining teachers and monks committed *dukkaṭas*. [The sixty-first rule is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kośala with a great community of five hundred bhikṣus, proceeding toward the city of Kapilavastu.
When the Śākyas heard that the Buddha was coming from that country, they established a regulation together:
"If anyone does not go out to welcome the Buddha, they shall be fined five hundred pieces of gold!

Thereupon, each of them, accompanied by their elders and juniors, went out to welcome the World-Honored One; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and stood to one side. The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them. They collectively invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to observe the summer retreat for the four months of the rainy season, and the World-Honored One granted his consent by remaining silent.
Each person provided offerings according to their means: some families prepared them for one day up to ten days;
others, two families together, prepared them for one day; and so on, up to ten families.

Some provided only the morning meal, or only the afternoon meal, or only *tambala* (refreshments), or only gruel; some provided bathing facilities, or drinks after midday; others offered oil for anointing the body and feet, or oil for lamps.
At that time, Śreṇika Bimbisāra was absent, and there was no one yet to receive his offering.
He asked those around him, "In the end, who received my gift? They replied:
"There has been no recipient yet!
He asked again,
"What offerings have the Buddha and the Sangha not yet accepted?"
He replied, "I have only not yet received the medicine!
He then invited the Buddha and the Sangha to receive summer retreat medicine, either delivering it himself or sending someone else to deliver it.
He went again to where the group of six bhikṣus were and said,
"Venerable sirs!
If you require medicine, please come and take as much as you wish."
The group of six bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Now the King has invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for the four months of the rains retreat to provide medicine, whether by sending someone to deliver it or even delivering it himself;
yet he has us go and fetch it ourselves. Observing this mind of his, we see that he holds us in contempt!"
"We shall wait until the time when his five kinsmen assemble and demand from him the most difficult-to-obtain medicine; he will certainly be unable to provide it, and thus we shall cause him shame!
They further thought:
"This king possesses such merit that perhaps there is no medicine he does not have; first we must search for something that others do not possess, and only then ask him for it."
He immediately went in search of them, but was missing only one kind. Thereupon, he waited for a time when the King’s five types of kinsmen were assembled and requested it from him.
The King then ordered his men to search throughout the kingdom, yet they were unable to find it anywhere.
The King said to the group of six bhikṣus,
"I have sought it in various places, but it is absolutely impossible to obtain.
The group of six bhikṣus then spoke to the King, saying:
"The King himself requested that I provide medicine for four months to the Buddha and the Sangha, yet now he cannot grant me even a single kind!
The King said, "Venerable Sir!..."
It is not that I do not wish to give it to you, nor is it that I have no object to offer; however, though I have searched everywhere for this medicine, it is absolutely impossible to find!
Furthermore, the four months [of summer retreat] have already passed; why do you trouble me so?
The group of six bhikṣus then humiliated the king before the assembly, saying:
"Previously you invited us to take whatever medicine we required, yet now you are unable to provide even this one kind."
When the other bhikṣus heard this, they asked the group of six bhikṣus, "What did you say?
The group of six bhikṣus answered truthfully. The bhikṣus rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so? They replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for the four-month *pravāraṇā*, and if he accepts beyond that limit, it is a *pāyattika* offense.'"
At that time, some bhikṣus were afflicted by an autumn illness. When Śreṇika’s son, Mānava, entered their rooms and saw them, he asked:
"Venerable sirs, what is your ailment?"
He replied, "I have fallen ill with an autumn disease!
He then immediately invited the bhikṣus, saying:
"You may take medicine from me!
The bhikṣus said, "The King previously invited us for four months, and that period has now expired; the Buddha does not permit us to accept medicine beyond this time."
The king then invited them for another month.
The bhikṣus said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept further invitations."
Not knowing what to do, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to accept an invitation for an additional month. From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for the four-month *pravāraṇā*,
and accepts beyond that period— except in the case of a renewed invitation—
it is a *pāyattika* offense. Furthermore, when some lay devotees came to visit the monastic quarters and saw that the bhikṣus were suffering from autumnal ailments, they asked:
"What medicine do you require?
I shall send it to you. The bhikṣus said:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept medicine sent by our own relatives.
Not knowing what to do, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to accept invitations for food provided by others. From this time forward, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for the four-month period of the *pravāraṇā*;
and if he accepts beyond that limit—excepting repeated invitations or invitations where food is provided by others—he commits a *pāyattika* offense.'"
At that time, Śreṇika Bimbisāra had this thought:
"Because of these medicinal substances, the group of six bhikṣus has humiliated me before the assembly!
I should now gather as many medicinal substances as possible."
He then gathered a great quantity of it.
Having gathered it, he had this thought:
"If I were to use this medicine of mine for the rest of my life, I would not be able to exhaust it."
"I shall now invite the bhikṣus to accept medicine for as long as I live!
He immediately went and made a long-term invitation to the bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept long-term invitations."
Not knowing what to do, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to accept long-term invitations."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for the four-month *pravāraṇā*,
and if he accepts beyond that period— excepting a renewed invitation, a personal invitation, or a permanent invitation— it is a *pāyattika* offense."
If someone offers medicine to the Saṃgha, the bhikṣu who assists with communal affairs should ask:
"Should this medicine be kept within the village, or placed inside the monastery?"
If one says, "Leave it in the village," one should say [to the donor] when the time comes:
"I require such-and-such medicine; prepare it for me and ensure there is no deficiency! If one says:
"Place it within the monastery."
It should be placed in a central room so that it may be easily obtained; the Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
One bhikṣu should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
I now propose that the monastic medicine be placed in such-and-such a room.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen.
This is the formal announcement.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
We shall now place the monks' medicine in such-and-such a room.
Those elders who consent, remain silent;..."
If you do not approve, please speak.
The Sangha has finished using the designated room to store medicine for the Sangha.
The Sangha approves, as indicated by its silence.
"Maintain this matter in this way.
The bhikṣus did not know who should be appointed to guard the monastic medicines. They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one announcement) to appoint one bhikṣu as the keeper of medicines."
A certain bhikṣu shall announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today the Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu so-and-so to serve as the guardian of medicines for the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus as a formal motion:
'Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!'"
Now, such-and-such a bhikṣu is appointed to serve as the monk who guards the medicine for the Saṃgha.
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has already appointed the bhikṣu [Name] as the keeper of medicines;
the Sangha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.
At that time, the bhikṣus appointed an ignorant bhikṣu who was incapable of guarding the medicine. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not appoint an ignorant bhikṣu. If one possesses five qualities, he should be appointed as the guardian of the Saṃgha’s medicine."
"What are the five?
Not following after desire, hatred, delusion, or fear; and knowing what is medicine and what is not.
That bhikṣu who guards the Saṃgha's medicines should store harītakī, āmalaka, vibhītaka, pippalī, dried ginger, granulated sugar, and rock honey in new vessels.
If a vessel is not leaking, it should be filled with ghee, oil, or honey; it should be held with its mouth tied shut using leather, and the name of the medicine should be inscribed upon it.
If a sick bhikṣu requires it, one should joyfully give it to him.
If a patient knows for themselves that they require this medicine, they should take it themselves;
if they do not know, they should ask a physician;
if there is no physician, they should ask their Upādhyāya or Ācārya.
"If I have such-and-such an illness, what medicine should I take?
If the preceptor or the ācārya does not know, one should take the medicine and consume it two or three times; if it does not cure the ailment, one should again take other medicine and consume it.
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. This concludes the sixty-second [offense].
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus repeatedly violated the precepts. The other bhikṣus admonished them, saying:
"You all repeatedly violate the precepts; you should recognize your own faults and repent according to the Dharma!"
"Do not, by this conduct, betray the faithful offerings of others and suffer for a long night!
The group of six bhikṣus replied,
"We do not study this precept!"
"I shall first question those who uphold the Dharma and the Vinaya, whose wisdom surpasses yours.
The bhikṣus rebuked him in various ways and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so? They replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"You foolish person! You should not commit such evil karma!

These bhikṣus, wishing not to perform the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, or various formal acts (*karmas*) together with you, have admonished you in accordance with the Dharma out of compassion for you."
How can you say: "I will not train in these precepts!
I shall first question those who uphold the Dharma and the Vinaya, whose wisdom surpasses yours!"?
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu repeatedly commits offenses, and the bhikṣus admonish him in accordance with the Dharma, yet he speaks thus:'"
"If I do not train in this precept!
I shall ask other bhikṣus who uphold the Dharma and uphold the Vinaya!
constitutes a pāyattika offense.
"A bhikṣu who wishes to seek understanding should question those who uphold the Dharma and uphold the Vinaya; such is the proper way for this Dharma!
Those who uphold the Dharma are those who recite and preserve the teachings spoken by the Buddha.
One who upholds the Vinaya has five duties: first,
to recite from the four *pārājika* rules up to the two *aniyata* rules.
Second, reciting the four matters up to the thirty matters;
third, extensively reciting the two hundred and fifty precepts;
fourth, extensively reciting the precepts of the two divisions.
Fifth, one should extensively recite all the Vinayas.
If a bhikṣu does not recite the Prātimokṣa, during the non-retreat season he should rely on the first four types of those who uphold the Vinaya;
however, during the retreat season, he must rely on one who extensively recites all the Vinayas. If he does not so rely, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. [The sixty-third rule concludes.
The Fifth Part of the Vinaya, Volume Eight.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśa during the Song Dynasty,
together with Zhu Daosheng and others.
The Sixty-fourth Matter of the First Division. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus repeatedly violated the precepts. The other bhikṣus admonished them, saying, "Do not suffer for a long night," as described above in full.
The group of six bhikṣus asked,
"Where did the Buddha establish this rule?
The bhikṣus replied:
"Do you not know? He replied, "I do not know!"
The bhikṣus said: "We shall now tell you the place where the rule was established.
Then, at the time of the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha), they spoke to him:
"The Buddha has established this rule herein.
The group of six bhikṣus said:
"We have only now learned that this rule was spoken in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* during the fortnightly *poṣadha*."
The bhikṣus rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, at the time of the recitation of the precepts, should speak these words:'"
"I have only now learned that this Dharma was recited in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* during the half-monthly *poṣadha*.

If the other bhikṣus know that this bhikṣu has already sat through the recitation of the precepts two or three times, he cannot escape on the grounds of ignorance. He must be dealt with according to the law for the offense he has committed;
furthermore, his ignorance should be rebuked:
"This was an unwholesome act!
When the precepts were being recited, you did not listen with a single-minded focus, nor did you take them to heart.
This constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu, having conferred full ordination upon another bhikṣu, fails to instruct him by explaining the precepts in detail;
and if, whether sitting in the recitation of the Prātimokṣa two or three times, he says such words—whether knowing [the rule] or not—he commits a pāyattika offense.
The case for the bhikṣuṇīs is also thus; this concludes the sixty-fourth [section].
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

Then, various bhikṣus frequently entered the palace of King Prasenajit, where they saw many beautiful women and gave rise to minds of defiled attachment. They no longer took pleasure in practicing the holy life (brahmacarya), and some even returned to secular life or became followers of external paths.
When the ministers saw this, they said:
"Why does the King not keep his palace women strictly concealed, but instead allows various people of different surnames to see them?
At that time, Ānanda, who was constantly receiving the King's offerings, dressed himself in the morning, took up his bowl, and entered the inner palace.

At that time, the King was still sleeping with Queen Mallikā and had not yet risen. When the Queen saw Ānanda approaching, she hurriedly pulled on her robes and descended from her bed; however, the garment she wore was so fine and slippery that it slipped off without her realizing it, leaving her crouching on the ground in shame.
The king then reproached him, saying:
"I am burdened by the affairs of state; I sleep during the dark of night and cannot rise early.
How is it that you, O Bhikṣu, have come directly here at dawn?"
Ānanda, filled with shame, immediately returned to the Buddha’s presence and reported in detail to the Buddha everything regarding the bhikṣus entering the palace as well as his own conduct.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked them:
“Is it true that you did so?”
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha further recounted the story of Ānanda, reprimanding him in various ways, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are ten faults in entering the inner palace of a king:
first, if the king is intoxicated when he approaches other palace women, he will forget it once he has sobered up."
First, if she suddenly becomes pregnant, people will certainly suspect the bhikṣu.
Second, when the palace women see the bhikṣu, they may laugh or joke; because they suspect he has feelings for them, they will harbor ill will.
Third, if the king has secret plans and outsiders learn of them, they will immediately suspect that the bhikṣu transmitted the information.
Fourth, if precious objects are lost within the royal palace, people will immediately suspect that they were taken by a bhikṣu.
Fifth, if a minister’s position is seized, outsiders will certainly say:
"It is because of this bhikṣu!"
Sixth, if anyone encounters misfortune or incurs punishment, outsiders will certainly suspect it was caused by the actions of the bhikṣu.
Seventh, if someone who has not yet deserved an official post is granted one by the king,
they will likewise suspect it is due to the power of the bhikṣu.
Eighth, if the king is fond of going out on excursions and sightseeing, resulting in great labor and expense, he will likewise suspect and resent the bhikṣus for causing such things.

Ninth, within the palace there are many beautiful women, rare treasures, and ornate garments; when a bhikṣu sees these, he will surely give rise to defiled attachment, break the precepts, and return to secular life.
"Tenth, if among the princes there should be one who commits rebellion, people will surely suspect that he was instigated by this bhikṣu.
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu enters a royal palace and crosses the threshold of the gate, it is a pāyattika.
After the Buddha had established this precept, the bhikṣus did not dare to cross the threshold of the city gates when seeking alms; not knowing what to do, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I now permit you to enter the palace, provided that you do not cross the threshold of the inner harem!
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu enters the royal palace and crosses the threshold of the inner harem gate, it is a pāyattika.
At that time, King Prasenajit went out annually with his various palace women to travel through the borders of the kingdom, where there were pavilions and pleasure palaces in every location.
There were some bhikṣus who, having arrived at a village in the evening, sought a place to stay.
The laypeople said, "The King is not currently in this palace; you may enter it to stay for the night."
"The King has faith in and delights in the Buddha-dharma; upon hearing it, he will surely rejoice!
The bhikṣus did not dare, and consequently had no place to stay overnight.
They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"Now, it is permitted for bhikṣus to enter the empty palaces of kings. From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

'If a bhikṣu enters a king's palace when the treasures have not yet been brought out or the treasures have not yet been stored away, and he crosses the threshold of the inner palace gate, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Treasures" refers to all things held in high esteem, including various forms of female beauty; these are all called treasures.
"Those who have not yet emerged" refers to:
"The woman was in the palace and had not yet come out.
"Had not yet been hidden" means that while the woman was in this palace, she had not yet been made to conceal herself.
At that time, if one crosses the threshold of the inner palace gate with both feet, it is a *pāyattika*;
for every step taken further inside, it is a *pāyattika* per step;
if one crosses with only one foot, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one enters the house of another minister or a householder and crosses the threshold of the inner door, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing).
For a *śrāmaṇera*, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.
If one is invited by the king to enter, there is no offense. [The sixty-fifth rule concludes.]
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the two kingdoms of Kośala and Magadha were plundering one another, and the roads between the two countries were cut off.
When the bhikṣus of Rājagṛha had finished their summer retreat, they thought to themselves:
"We must now travel together with these bandits in order to reach the place where we may pay our respects to the World-Honored One."
"If those guards, acting as accomplices to the bandits, should capture me, King Prasenajit—who has faith in and delights in the Buddha-dharma—will certainly not punish me.
He then went with the bandits to the border of that kingdom; as expected, he was captured and brought before the commander of the guard, who said to him, "This is a thief!"
The general asked,
"And as for those wearing the kashaya— what kind of people are they? He replied:
"He is also a thief!
The bhikṣu then said of himself:
"I am not a thief; I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas!"

"Having completed the rains retreat in Rājagṛha, one ought to inquire after the World-Honored One’s health; however, because the road is difficult and perilous, I have traveled with you as a companion!
The patrol commander said, "You are not a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas!"
"He must have come in these robes to act as a spy!
He was then sent to the King's presence; the bhikṣu spoke as before, and the King released him.
Among the surrounding ministers, there were those who did not believe he was a śramaṇa, and they said:
"This thief is merely wearing the robes of a bhikṣu; since the King has faith in and delights in the Buddha-dharma, let him release him!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: [Yes].
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From this time forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu travels as a companion with thieves, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
There were some bhikṣus who traveled on a road together with bandits; not knowing they were bandits, they felt shame and remorse upon realizing it, thinking they had committed a *pāyattika* offense.
Some left the path to avoid them, while others remained behind.
The bandit then asked,
"Why have you done this? He replied:
"The Buddha has established a rule that we are not permitted to travel as companions with you.
Upon hearing these words, the bandits became greatly incensed; they beat the bhikṣus and stripped them of their robes until their flesh was bare.
The bhikṣus returned and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"If one does not know that they are robbers, it is impossible for one to commit a pāyattika offense by traveling together with them."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that they are robbers, travels together with them as companions, it is a pāyattika.
There were some bhikṣus traveling on a road who encountered robbers; they immediately felt ashamed and remorseful, thinking they had committed a pāyattika offense.
They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"It is impossible for one to commit a pāyattika offense by traveling together with thieves on a road without having previously made an appointment to do so."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu agrees to travel as a companion with a thief, it is a pāyattika.
There were some bhikṣus who agreed to travel with thieves along a nearby road; some did not go, while others took a different path, and all of them became doubtful.
"We fear we may have committed a *pāyattika* offense.
They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of monks and addressed the bhikṣus:

"Even if one has made an appointment with a thief to travel along a nearby road, if one ultimately does not go or goes by a different route, it is impossible that one would commit a *pāyattika* offense."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a thief to travel together along a road from one village to another village, it is a pāyattika."
If one makes an appointment to travel with an evil bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If various dangers arise and they travel together by prior agreement, there is no offense. [The rule concerning the sixty-sixth case is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, various bhikṣus traveled along a road with women—either one bhikṣu with one woman, or even many.

Or, two bhikṣus, or even many, may travel together with one woman, or even many, across water; as they see each other’s forms, they give rise to minds of defiled attachment, and some may even return to secular life or become followers of external paths.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled them, saying:
"These śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas travel the same road as women; what difference is there between them and those who travel with their wives?
Who would think that such people practice the holy life (brahmacarya)!"
"You lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
At that time, there was a householder who frequently beat his wife; having beaten her, he went out. The wife thought to herself:
"My husband beats me often; he might secretly kill me. I must now avoid him!"
Thereupon he departed;
having gone outside the village, he saw a bhikṣu and approached him, asking:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Where are you going? He replied,
"I wish to go to such-and-such a place."
Thereupon, the woman followed after him.
Her husband thought to himself:
"I have just beaten my wife; she might even kill herself!"
He immediately returned home, but searching for her, he could not find her.
He asked his neighbors, saying,
"Have you seen my wife?"
They all replied,
"We have not seen him!
Then they left the village and saw a female non-Buddhist ascetic, whom they asked:
“Have you seen such-and-such a woman? He replied,
“I saw her being taken away by the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya.”
That man immediately pursued him in haste; having caught up with him, he said to the bhikṣu, "Why have you run off with my wife?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I have committed no evil deed; it was only that your wife and I were traveling along the same road!
The wife spoke again to her husband, saying:
"Do not harbor ill will toward this bhikṣu; my traveling together with him was no different from being with a kinsman!"
Hearing his wife’s words, he thought to himself:
"She has deceived me in this way; there must surely have been some evil deed!
He then beat the bhikṣu until he was on the verge of death before letting him go. That bhikṣu then thought to himself:
"I am now utterly exhausted and unable to proceed on the road; I shall enter the fire-light samādhi to rest myself, so that my body may gain strength before I advance."
Having thought this, he gathered his robes and bowl, entered the fire-light samādhi, and smoke issued from his body.
When the woman saw this, she said to her husband,
"You did not believe my words!"
"Observe the body of that bhikṣu as it emits [light]!
In a moment, the entire body of that bhikṣu became brilliantly radiant.
The wife spoke again, saying:
"Do not disbelieve my words!
Observe further how that bhikṣu’s body is.
That bhikṣu, by the power of this samādhi, immediately went to where the Buddha was and reported all the preceding matters in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so? They replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu travels along a road together with a woman, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
There were some bhikṣus traveling together who, midway along the road, saw several women also traveling that same path; they felt doubt and regret, thinking:
"Have we perhaps committed a pāyattika offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu travels along a road with a woman without having made an appointment to do so, it is impossible for him to have committed a pāyattika offense."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a woman to travel together along a road, it is a pāyattika.

There were some bhikṣus who, having made an appointment with a woman to travel together along a road, subsequently did not dare to go, or took a different route, yet still gave rise to doubt and regret.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:

“If a bhikṣu has previously made an appointment with a woman to travel together on a road, yet ultimately does not go, or goes by another route, it is impossible for him to commit a pāyattika offense.”
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a woman to travel together along a road from one village to another, it is a pāyattika."
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. [Thus ends the sixty-seventh rule.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kośala, traveling among the people with a great saṃgha of bhikṣus numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty.
Some of the bhikṣus stayed in houses, some under trees, and some in the open air.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, together with the group of seventeen bhikṣus, gathered a great quantity of firewood and grass, lit a fire in the open air, and sat by its side to warm themselves.

At that time, a snake emerged from a hole in a tree. When the bhikṣus saw it, they threw objects at it; the snake immediately retreated back inside, but coming out again when it became hot, the bhikṣus threw at it once more.
It retreated back inside again, but after a short while it came out once more. One bhikṣu threw at it, and the snake bit him, and he died instantly.
The bhikṣus surrounded him and wept. The elder bhikṣus asked, "For what reason are you weeping? They replied:
"This bhikṣu has passed away after being bitten by a snake," he said,
recounting the aforementioned events in detail.
The elder bhikṣus rebuked him in various ways:
"How is it that you saw the snake emerge again and again, yet still did not avoid it, resulting in its biting you to death?
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this incident, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
“Is it truly so for you? They replied, “It is truly so.”
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu kindles a fire, it is a pāyattika.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus had park-keepers and śrāmaṇeras kindle fires.
When the elder bhikṣus saw this, they rebuked them, saying:
“Have you not heard that the Buddha has prohibited the lighting of fires?
He replied, “I had the garden keeper and a śrāmaṇera light them; it was not an offense!”
The bhikṣus asked,
"What is the difference between lighting it oneself and having someone else light it?
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?
They replied: "It is true."
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu lights a fire himself, or causes another to light one, it is a pāyattika.
There were some sick bhikṣus who consulted a physician, and the physician said:"
"One should take such medicine, kindle a fire,
and bathe. The sick bhikṣu said,
"The Buddha does not permit me to kindle a fire myself, nor to have someone else kindle it."
"I pray that you will further instruct me on how to take other medicines!
The physician said,
"Virtuous One!..."
"You should indeed take this medicine, light the fire, and bathe.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"If the Buddha would allow us to light the fire ourselves or have someone else light it, our illness will then be cured."
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I now permit a sick bhikṣu to kindle a fire, or to have someone else kindle it for him."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, being not ill, personally kindles a fire or causes another to kindle one, it is a pāyattika."
There were some bhikṣus who needed to cook soups and congees, yet they did not dare to light a fire.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to cook soups and congees, but they must not roast meat.
From this day forward, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, being without illness, kindles a fire for the purpose of roasting, it is a pāyattika.'"
The bhikṣus wished to fumigate their bowls and kindled fires;
furthermore, they lit lamps and candles to ward off predatory beasts, but not knowing what to do, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
“I now permit the bhikṣus that, under such circumstances, they may kindle a fire by themselves or have someone else kindle it.”
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, being without illness, lights a fire for the purpose of warming himself, or causes another to light one, it is a pāyattika."
If one kindles a fire for roasting meat such that the flames reach a height of four finger-widths, it is a pāyattika.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. [The sixty-eighth rule concludes.]
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, some bhikṣus went to the home of an acquaintance and saw precious ornaments used for adorning the body. They picked them up to examine them and then returned them to their original place.
Later, they were stolen by someone; when the owner came back to search for them, he did not know where they were.
Someone said, "I saw a bhikṣu seize it!
and immediately went to ask the bhikṣu:
“I have lost such and such a treasure; did you see it, Bhikṣu?
He replied, “I picked it up earlier and returned it to its original place.”
The owner said, "When the bhikṣu took it, I no longer saw it; please return it to me!
The bhikṣu replied:
"I truly did not take it!
But the owner did not believe him and proceeded to spread a false reputation against the bhikṣu.
At that time, there was a non-Buddhist ascetic who had placed five hundred gold coins in a bag; having gone to the water's edge to drink, he forgot them and did not take them with him.
A certain bhikṣu who came along later saw this and thought,
"Whose property is this?
He then looked around in all four directions and, seeing the person before him, had this thought:
"He must have consented; I shall take it back and return it to him.
He immediately took it and departed.
Before the man had gone far, he remembered the gold bag and hurried back.
The bhikṣu asked,
"For what reason have you returned?
That person then spoke with anger:
"O inauspicious one! Why do you question me? the bhikṣu said.
"Even if I am inauspicious, you should speak to me and return my meaning! He said:
"I forgot one bag by the water's edge; that is why I have returned to search for it!"
The bhikṣu then produced it and showed it to him,
saying, "Is this your bag? When the man saw the bag, he spoke again with anger:
“O ill-omened creature!
Why do you seize my bag?
Wait a moment while I count the contents within!”
The bhikṣu replied,
"I have not untied this bag at all, nor have I looked inside it.
If you wish to take it, why would I show it to you?"
"I feared you might have lost it, so I have brought it back to you!
The man spoke again:
"In my bag there were one thousand gold coins; now five hundred are missing. You must return them to me!"
The bhikṣu answered him as he had before, but the man forcibly dragged the bhikṣu to the place where the judicial authorities were.

At that time, the judicial authorities did not have faith in or delight in the Buddha-dharma; they adjudicated the case unjustly, immediately bound him in reverse, beat the donkey-cry drum, and intended to execute him at a crossroads.
At that time, King Prasenajit, seeing from afar atop his high tower, asked those around him,
"Is that he? They replied:
"This is a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas.
The king then issued a command:
"Bring him back to the hall of justice; I shall come out myself!"
He immediately went out and asked that man,
"Why are you tormenting this bhikṣu?
The man reported to the king as he had done before.
The king questioned the bhikṣu again, who answered the king as he had before.
The king asked that man:
"Is this truly your bag?"
He replied, “Yes!
The king then placed five hundred gold coins into the bag, but the bag would not hold them.
The king spoke again, saying, "You said there were a thousand pieces of gold in your bag; why do you not accept them now?
That person then confessed, saying:
"In reality there were five hundred; it was because of my anger that I falsely accused the bhikṣu!
The king then asked the judicial officers:
"If a person should deceive the king to his face, what punishment should be meted out?"
The judges said, "This man deserves death, and his property shall be confiscated by the state.
The king then applied this law: he seized the man's wealth, bound him hand and foot, beat the donkey-drum, and executed him at a crossroads.
Someone said to him:
"You have slandered the śramaṇa son of the Śākyas; you ought to receive this retribution!
If you slander them again, it shall be even more severe than this!"
Or again, some said:
"A śramaṇa son of the Śākyas once took my treasure; I fear this may now be true!
Then the bhikṣu addressed the king, saying:
"Grant this man his life; do not cause the Buddha-dharma to incur an ill reputation.
The king immediately released him and rebuked the judge, saying:
"If there should ever again be such a judgment, I shall deal with you as I have just dealt with you!"
Those who did not have faith in or delight in the Buddha-dharma criticized him in various ways, saying:
"We, who are mere laypeople, still feel shame at grasping precious objects; why then do the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, act in such a manner?"
"He lacks the conduct of a śramaṇa and has destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked him in various ways and reported the matter in its entirety, from beginning to end, to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: [Yes].
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From this time forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu takes hold of precious objects or things equivalent to precious objects, it is a pāyattika.'"
