At that time, Visākhā Mātṛ, adorned with the most exquisite jeweled ornaments, was sporting in a grove with her kinsmen. As the grove was near the Jetavana, she observed that the people were still not yet satiated with their joy and merriment, and she thought to herself:
"It is not fitting for me now to indulge in such negligence; it would be well to take this opportunity to pay my respects to the World-Honored One."
She then took the maidservant to the Jetavana Monastery; upon reaching the gate, she thought again:
"It is not appropriate for me to appear before the World-Honored One while wearing these ornaments."
She then removed her precious robe and placed it by the side of the moat.

At that time, Śāriputra saw her from afar while walking in meditation. Viśākhā approached, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. The Buddha preached the Dharma to her in various ways, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening her. After a short while she withdrew, and as she kept what she had heard in mind, she forgot the precious robe she had left behind and returned for it.
After the city gates had closed, he remembered it and thought to himself:
"If I were to tell others that I have lost this treasure, it might cause harm to the Buddha-Dharma!
He remained silent until dawn.
Then Śāriputra informed the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"Go and fetch it! Having received these instructions, he immediately went to fetch it.
He said to Śāriputra, "Tomorrow at dawn, I shall personally escort him back!
Having received these instructions, he immediately sent him; Vimalakīrti’s mother praised him, saying:
“Excellent! I have such a great teacher and fellow practitioners of the holy life!
If other outsiders had obtained this object, for what reason would they have returned it to me?
I abandoned it last night; I should now conclude the matter!”
He immediately took it and offered it to the Sangha of the four quarters, saying to Śāriputra,
"You may use this to construct a *caitya* hall for the Sangha.
Śāriputra did not dare to accept it.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "Accept them!

Furthermore, there were various lay devotees who would enter the monastery once every five days to pay their respects; they would sometimes take off their signet rings or remove their jeweled earrings, only to forget them when they departed.
The bhikṣus saw them but did not dare to take them; however, when other people saw them, they took and carried them away.
When the lay devotees returned to the monastery to search for them, they asked the bhikṣus:
"I lost such and such jewels; did you, bhikṣus, see them?"
He replied, "I saw it, but I did not dare to take it. The laypeople said:
"The Venerable One has seen it; why does he not take it?
He may return it to me; what need has one who has left the household life for such an object? He replied:
"I truly did not take it!
But he still did not believe him and proceeded to spread an evil reputation against the bhikṣu.
Furthermore, there were other bhikṣus traveling together as companions who stayed overnight at one place; among the companions was one who had left something behind.
The bhikṣu saw it but did not dare to take it; someone else took it instead.
His companions asked the bhikṣu, "I have lost such and such an object; did you see it, Venerable Sir?"
He replied, "I saw it, but I did not dare to take it.
His companions said:
“Venerable sir, seeing this, why do you not take it?
You may return it to me; what need has one who has left the household life for such things? He replied:
"I truly did not take it!
But he did not believe him and proceeded to spread a false reputation against the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:

"If the Blessed One would permit us, within the monastery grounds and our lodgings, either to take treasure ourselves or to have someone else take it, then the householder would not lose his treasure, nor would we incur an ill reputation."
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I now permit the bhikṣus, within the monastery or at their lodgings, to take up precious objects themselves or to have others take them up for them."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, whether it be a jewel or an object equivalent to a jewel, takes it himself or causes another to take it, except within a monastery or a dwelling place, it is a pāyattika."
"If one takes precious objects or things equivalent to precious objects within a monastic dwelling or at a lodging place, and a master later comes to claim them, they should be returned.
This matter should be handled in this way! Regarding "precious objects": [the text continues].
"Items such as pearls, mani-jewels, lapis lazuli, jade, gold, and silver;
'such precious things' refers to all other objects."
"Within the monastery grounds" means:
the dwelling place of the Saṃgha and land belonging to the Saṃgha.
"A lodging place" means:
When staying overnight at another's house outside the monastery, or when traveling with companions and lodging in the wilderness,
if a monk sees an item inside the monastery, he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) take it;
if there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, he should take it up himself.
If someone comes seeking [an item], one should assemble the Sangha and inquire about the characteristics of the lost object; only then should it be returned.
If the item has already been taken up for storage and one wishes to travel elsewhere, one should entrust it to another person.
If a bhikṣu goes to another's house and sees something belonging to them, he should have a *kappiyakāraka* (a pure person) pick it up;
if there is no *kappiyakāraka*, he should pick it up himself.
If someone is present, he should immediately entrust it to that person before departing.
If no one is present, one should call out to the owner to come forth and entrust the item to them before departing.
When a bhikṣu travels along a road with companions, if he sees an object, he should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) take it;
if there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, he should take it himself and return it [to its owner].
Upon returning, one should assemble the people and first ask:
"Did you lose anything? If they say:
"Lost! One should ask: "What object?"
If it is as they say, then return it to them.
If he travels by a different route from his companions and they do not meet, he should entrust it to a lay follower (upāsaka) who has faith when reaching a village to return it.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. The sixty-ninth [offense] is concluded.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣus bathed twice or thrice daily and used a great deal of soap powder (*snāyaka*). When the lay devotees saw this, they criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣus bathe so frequently and use such amounts of soap powder that they are just like kings or high ministers!"

Having originally left the household life with the desire to seek liberation, he does not recite the sutras or practice contemplations such as that of the foulness of the body; instead, he spends his days and nights adorning his physical form!
He lacks the conduct of a śramaṇa and violates the dharma of a śramaṇa!
At that time, there was an interpreter of omens who said to King Bimbisāra:
"Soon a malefic star shall appear; Your Majesty ought to bathe in a certain spring in order to ward off this calamity."
"If it is not so, we may lose our kingdom or face peril to our lives!
The king then commanded his attendants to manage that spring.
They immediately received the order and went there; seeing bhikṣus filling the pool and bathing therein, they returned and informed the king.
The king said, "Wait until the bhikṣu has finished bathing!
Thus he sent messengers three times each day and night; with one departing and another returning, there was never a moment's interval.
The brahmin spoke again to the king, saying, "This star is about to rise; if you bathe after it has risen, there will be no benefit.
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately prepared his carriage and went out to the spring, where he bathed in the downstream current.
The ministers censured them with these words:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know the proper timing!
They are neither diligent nor mindful of contemplating the impurities of the body."
"Your sole intent is to adorn yourself and bathe your body!
You lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and destroy the Dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: [Yes].
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I establish this precept for the bhikṣus: from this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu bathes within the half-month, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
There were some sick bhikṣus to whom a physician said that they would only recover by bathing. The bhikṣus said:
“The Buddha does not permit us to bathe frequently; please consider another remedy!”
The physician said, "There is only bathing; there is no other method.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"If the Buddha permits us to bathe frequently when ill, my illness will surely be cured.

Furthermore, there were other bhikṣus who performed various kinds of labor; their bodies were covered in mud and soil, and their robes were stained and filthy. Because of this, they became increasingly exhausted and thought:
"If the Buddha permits us to bathe frequently while working, our extreme fatigue will certainly be relieved and our robes will remain clean."
Furthermore, there were other bhikṣus who, while traveling on the road, became utterly exhausted; they wished to bathe but did not dare, thinking:
"If the Buddha would permit us to bathe frequently while traveling, our extreme exhaustion might be relieved."
Furthermore, there were some bhikṣus whose robes were soiled by wind, rain, dust, and mud. They thought to themselves:
"If the Buddha would permit us to bathe frequently when we are soiled by wind, rain, dust, and mud, we would not be defiled by such dust and mire."
With one month and a half remaining of spring and the first month of summer, the bhikṣus were oppressed by the heat and broke out in sweat. They thought to themselves:
"If the Buddha would permit us to bathe frequently during the hot season, we could be free from this affliction."
Each reported this to the Buddha. On account of these matters, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
“I now permit the bhikṣus to bathe frequently when they are ill, when working, when traveling on a journey, during wind and rain, or during the heat; there is no offense.”
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu bathes within a half-month, except for a specific cause, it is a pāyattika.
A 'specific cause' is:"
"When one is ill, when working, when traveling on a road, during wind and rain, or during the heat—these are called the causal conditions.
Regarding "when one is ill":
this refers to needing to bathe due to illness.
"During work" refers to attending to various affairs, even down to sweeping the floors of one's quarters.
"While traveling on the road" refers to:
One yojana, two yojanas, or even traveling half a yojana.
As for "during wind and rain":
it refers to being defiled by the mud and mire caused by wind and rain.
"During the heat" means:
being oppressed by heat and perspiring.
It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
If one bathes a teacher or a sick person, and their bodies are already wet, there is no offense due to the bathing. [End of the seventy rules.]
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of seventeen bhikṣus was building a new dwelling. The group of six bhikṣus wished to reside within it and drove the group of seventeen out;
when the group of seventeen refused to leave, they beat them, whereupon they cried out loudly.
The elder bhikṣus asked,
"Why are you crying out so loudly? He replied:
"The group of six bhikṣus struck me!
The elder bhikṣus rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so for you? They replied, "It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu strikes another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
There was a bhikṣu who choked on his food and asked another bhikṣu to massage his back; the bhikṣus did not dare to do so, and he died.
They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu strikes another bhikṣu with a mind of anger, it is impossible for him to incur a pāyattika offense."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger, strikes another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
If he strikes a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, any other person, or an animal, it is a duṣkṛta."
If a bhikṣuṇī strikes a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
if she strikes a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, any other person, or an animal, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī strikes any of the five groups of renunciants, other persons, or animals, it is a duṣkṛta offense. This concludes the seventy-first [offense].
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went again to the quarters of the group of seventeen bhikṣus seeking lodging. When they refused to leave, the group of six made a gesture with their hands as if to strike them, whereupon the group of seventeen cried out loudly.
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they went out and asked,
"For what reason did you cry out so loudly? He replied:
"The group of six bhikṣus wishes to strike me!
The elder bhikṣus reprimanded them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so for you? They replied, "It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu makes a threatening gesture with his hand toward another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
There were some bhikṣus who, while preaching the Dharma, used hand gestures or pointed out locations;
they then became doubtful and remorseful, thinking: "Have I not perhaps committed a pāyattika?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu, without a mind of anger, merely gestures with his hand toward another bhikṣu and commits a pāyattika offense, such a thing is impossible."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger, makes a threatening gesture with his hand toward another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
If he makes the threatening gesture and the hand reaches [the other], it is a pāyattika."
If one makes a gesture with the hand but does not reach [the target], it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
The remainder is as explained above in the section on striking a bhikṣu; this concludes the seventy-second [rule].
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the group of seventeen bhikṣus accepted the dwelling they had built; because the group of six bhikṣus were of higher seniority, they entered next and took up residence therein, whereupon the former moved to dwell in rooms to the left and right.
The group of six bhikṣus deliberated thus:
"The group of seventeen bhikṣus are modest, conscientious, and fearful; they dwell in close proximity to us and will surely observe our transgressions!"
"We shall employ skillful means to cause him to depart!
They then went to him and said, "This was originally an empty room; it is full of many terrifying things."
"Do not dwell therein! The group of seventeen bhikṣus said, "We have firmly closed the doors; what is there to fear?"
That night, in the darkness, the group of six bhikṣus created various terrifying apparitions; at dawn, they asked the group of seventeen bhikṣus:
"Did you sleep peacefully last night?"
They replied, “We heard the signs of fear, so we closed our doors and reflected, yet we were not afraid at all!
The group of six bhikṣus then deliberated together, saying:
"We cannot terrify him with this; we shall wait for him to go outside and then enter beneath his bed.
Having thus stolen inside, during the darkness of night, they would either pull at his clothes, or pull at his feet, or lift the bed and move it to another place.
Thereupon, the group of seventeen bhikṣus cried out in great alarm. The elder bhikṣus came and asked, "Why are you crying out so loudly?
They replied:
"There should be no thieves here; I do not know who pulled at my clothes,
who pulled at my feet,
or who lifted my bed and moved it to another place?"
The elder bhikṣus then took a light and shone it upon them, seeing the group of six bhikṣus crouching beneath their beds. They asked, "Why are you here?"
He replied, "I wish to terrify the group of seventeen bhikṣus!
The elder bhikṣus reprimanded him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so? They replied:
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this time forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu terrifies another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.'"
A visiting bhikṣu asked an established bhikṣu, "What should one be wary of in this room?
Some did not dare to speak; others spoke but subsequently gave rise to doubt, fearing they had committed a pāyattika offense.
They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu intentionally terrifies another bhikṣu and commits a pāyattika offense, such a thing is impossible."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu intentionally terrifies another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
The remainder is as explained in the section on striking a bhikṣu. [The seventy-third rule is concluded.]
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣu Dharmma had this thought:
"Pūrṇa (Bhadanta) previously seized my robe; because of this, the Buddha rebuked me and established a precept for the bhikṣus."
"I shall now declare within the Saṃgha that he has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Having thought this, he immediately went to where the senior bhikṣu was and said to him: "Bhadanta, Bhadanta, Bhadanta!
Bhaddāli, Bhaddāli, Bhaddāli! Bhaddāli has touched a woman’s body, used coarse and wicked speech, and praised his own bodily offerings."
The bhikṣus asked, "How do you know this? He replied:
"I was traveling together with him and saw him doing this.
The elder bhikṣus rebuked him, saying:
"Why did you conceal it when you were not angry?"
“Did you confess your anger?
After he had been rebuked, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned Dharma:
“Is it truly so? He replied, “It is truly so.”
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu conceals a grave offense (sthūlātyaya) of another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
There were some bhikṣus who did not know that the offense committed by another was a grave one; later, when they came to know it, they became doubtful and regretful, thinking:
"Have I perhaps committed a pāyattika?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"If one does not know that a bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), it is impossible for one to commit a pāyattika offense."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), conceals it for more than one night, he commits a pāyattika."
If, from dawn until the appearance of the morning light, one commits this at each successive hour, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
once the morning light has appeared, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a *śrāmaṇera*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one wishes to speak but there is no one present, or if one conceals [the offense] for fear that a dispute might arise, there is no violation. [The seventy-fourth case ends.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Upananda thought to himself:
"The bhikṣu Dharmma agreed to travel with me and gave me his robe; since he was unwilling to go, I took the robe back.
Because of this, the World-Honored One rebuked me and established a precept for the bhikṣus."
"Later, he will again bring forth my offenses; I shall now falsely accuse him with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Having formed this thought, he spoke to the elder bhikṣus, saying:
"I have indeed touched the body of a woman, spoken coarse and wicked words, and praised myself for receiving offerings; the bhikṣu Dharmadatta has done the same."
The bhikṣus asked, "How do you know this? He replied:
"I saw him together with her!
The bhikṣus rebuked him, saying,
"How can you defame a bhikṣu with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu, with groundless charges of a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, slanders another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.’”
To slander a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, to slander a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī constitutes a pāyattika offense;
to slander a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī to slander the five classes of practitioners constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense; this concludes the seventy-fifth rule.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Upananda thought to himself:
"The bhikṣu Dharmma agreed to travel with me, and even went so far as to exonerate me of my offenses, as described above."
"I have slandered him with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, yet it could not harm him.
Now I shall deal with him on another matter!
He then went to his location and said to him:
"You are my disciple! I am your teacher!
You have first offended me, and I too have offended you."
"Now let us reconcile and no longer harbor mutual resentment; you may go together with me as before to the various households to eat many fine foods.
He immediately reconciled and followed along.
Bhadanta would suddenly take them to places where there was no food; when someone came to invite them, he would signal with a wink of the eye, hand gestures, or other signs to make them leave.
He would calculate that they would not reach the monastery in time for the midday meal, and so he would send them away, saying:
"There is no food here today; you may return to the monastery!"
After he had departed, he went to the house where he had been invited and ate a great deal of fine food.
When Dharmadatta returned to the monastery, it was already past midday. After his meal, Upāli (Baddhananda) returned and asked Dharmadatta, "Did you get any food?"
He replied, “I am not equal to it!
Then he again feigned consolation, saying:
"Although you have missed one meal today, tomorrow I shall cause you to obtain something most delicious!
The next day, where he went was again as described above.
This continued for three days, after which he said to Dharma:
"I have brought you to all places where fine food is obtained, yet you have found none.
I fear it is because you are rebuked by your ancestors or provoked by the devas, or perhaps it is the result of your own karmic offenses; do not harbor resentment toward me!"
"You must return quickly so that you may reach the monastery by midday!
Dharmaya hurried back, but he did not arrive until after noon; having been emaciated by hunger for many days, he was unable to rise again.
After his meal, Upananda returned to his residence and asked again: "Did you eat? He replied:
"It is too late!
he then said, "You have deceived your teacher; you ought to be punished accordingly!"
"If you do this again in the future, I shall make it even more severe than this!
At that, Dharmā finally realized his teacher was deceiving him;
he cried out in anger, saying, "How can a bhikṣu practice such fraud, causing me to go three days without food until I was on the verge of death?"
The elder bhikṣus asked,
"For what reason did you cry out so loudly? He replied:
“Bhadananda has tormented me for three days, causing me to go without food!
The elder bhikṣus reprimanded him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upāli (Bhadanta):
"Is it true that you did this? He replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
"Come together to various households; I will give you much delicious food and drink. "
"If one does not give [the food] but instead dismisses them and sends them back, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
There were some bhikṣus who, having gone together with other bhikṣus to various households, were unable to obtain food; they felt shame and remorse, and thought to themselves:
"Have we perhaps committed a *pāyattika* offense?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu does not eat because he does not wish to trouble others, it is impossible for him to commit a pāyattika offense."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
'Come together to various households; we will give you much delicious food and drink.'"
"If, out of vexation, one does not give [the food] but instead sends the person back, it is a *pāyattika*.

There were some bhikṣus who took a bhikṣu attending to the sick to various households to request food on behalf of the sick bhikṣu; fearing that the patient might miss the midday meal, they sent him back in haste.
Having already sent him away, he felt shame and remorse, thinking:
"Could it be that I have committed a *pāyattika* offense?
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"If a bhikṣu, not for the sake of eating alone, dismisses another bhikṣu, it is impossible that he commits a pāyattika offense."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
'Come together to various households; I will give you much delicious food and drink!'"
Having arrived, he did not give [anything] and spoke thus: "Go away!
It is not pleasant for me to sit or speak with you; it is pleasant for me to sit alone and speak alone!"
"If one intends to cause another to be annoyed, it is a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu acts in this way to annoy a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, or even an animal, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣuṇī causes such annoyance to a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
if she causes annoyance to a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, or even to an animal, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī causes such vexation to the five groups [of monastics], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. The sixty-seventh rule is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, a large number of bhikṣus were traveling together with companions when they entered the kingdom of Kośala; they encountered bandits who plundered them, leaving their robes and bowls completely exhausted, until they arrived at a military outpost.
The commander of the patrol asked,
"Venerable sir, where did you encounter the bandits?"
He replied, "In such-and-such a place," and immediately consulted with the patrolmen:
"If the king hears that a bhikṣu encountered bandits within our territory, he will surely punish us.
He then said to the bhikṣu,
"Venerable One!..."
"Wait a moment; I shall pursue and capture this thief.
He then went out in pursuit and, after a short while, caught up with him. He immediately surrounded him on all sides and searched for his belongings, obtaining them all.
The dyed robes and the white robes were each placed in one spot, and the patrolmen deliberated,
saying, "To whom should these be returned first? Someone said:
"You should first return them to the bhikṣus; the King has faith in and delights in the Buddha-dharma, so those who hear of this will surely rejoice!
He then said to the bhikṣus, "Each of you may take your robes!"
The bhikṣus became doubtful about the robes; some said, "This is my robe," while others said, "This is not my robe. Consequently, they did not dare to take them.
The patrolmen asked, "Why do you not take them?"
He replied, "I did not recognize my own clothes; that is why I did not take them.
The patrolmen said:
"Next, let the one who takes the consciousness take it!
Thereupon, the non-Buddhist took the bhikṣu’s fine robe, while the bhikṣu subsequently obtained the non-Buddhist’s coarse one.
The patrolmen, knowing that the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, all wear fine robes, yet seeing that they had now instead received the coarse garments of the non-Buddhists, said:
"What extraordinary qualities do you śramaṇas possess?
You do not even know the characteristics of your robes; how then can you claim to know the minds of others?
If you truly knew the characteristics of robes, for what reason would the non-Buddhists be able to obtain such fine garments from you?"
The bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was and reported this matter to him.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned them further:
"Is it true that you did not recognize the characteristics of the robe?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he shall mark it with three colors.'"
"Whether it be blue, black, or madder-brown.
If one does not make a mark with these three colors, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one does not make a mark, or if one wears [the robe], for every instance of wearing it, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one does not put it on, for each night [of non-compliance], there is a *pāyattika*.
It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one obtains a new robe that already has a mark made upon it, and does not [re-mark] it, there is no offense. This concludes the seventy-seventh [rule].
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the robes, bowls, and various requisites of the seventeen groups of bhikṣus were scattered in various places and could not be gathered up; the six groups of bhikṣus then took them and hid them away.
Having realized his loss, he asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Such and such items of mine were here and there; who took them away?"
He replied, "Since there have been many people here just now, would you not take it with you?
He then asked:
"Where have those people who came earlier gone?
He replied, "To the east, west, south, or north; I know not where they have gone."
Then the group of seventeen bhikṣus pursued them from all four directions, catching up with those who had come, and said to them:
"We have lost our robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle cases; you must return them to us!"
The people said, "Venerable sir!
We have come for the sake of the Dharma; we have not come to commit theft!"
Having received these words, they returned in shame.
The group of six bhikṣus asked them,
"Did you actually see the person who came by just now?"
He replied, "I saw it. [The other asked,] "Did you obtain the robe?"
He replied, "I may not.
Thereupon, the group of six bhikṣus took out their robes and bowls and showed them to him.
"Is this your robe and bowl? He replied, "It is!"
When the various bhikṣus saw this, they rebuked them in many ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu hides another bhikṣu’s robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, or any such individual articles of daily use, or causes another to hide them, it is a pāyattika.’”

Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who did not put away their robes, bowls, or personal belongings; the other bhikṣus did not dare to put them away for them, and consequently they were lost. Because of this, they became suspected and acquired a bad reputation.
They thought to themselves: "If the Buddha would allow us to put away others' clothing and requisites, then those items would not be lost, and we would not suffer such ill repute."
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one has a robe taken up for another person without the intention of hiding it, there is no basis for claiming that one has committed a pāyattika offense."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, for the sake of amusement, hides a bhikṣu’s robe, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, or any such individual article of daily life, or causes another to hide it, it is a pāyattika."
If one conceals the belongings of a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, or even the property of an animal, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī conceals the belongings of a bhikṣu or another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika offense;
if she conceals the belongings of any other person, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī conceals the property of the five groups [of monastics], it is a duṣkṛta offense. The seventy-eighth [offense] concludes here.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus possessed power, while the other virtuous bhikṣus lacked power.

The group of six bhikṣus obstructed the formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) of the virtuous bhikṣus; the Buddha’s various reprimands regarding this were all as previously described in the section on legal adjudication according to the Dharma.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu, when the Saṃgha is deciding a matter, has already formally given his consent (*chanda*) in accordance with the Dharma, yet later censures it, it is a pāyattika.’”
"Regarding 'reproaching later':
it means saying, 'I did not originally give my consent (chanda) in this manner.
If the Saṃgha has not performed the formal act (karmavācanā) to settle the matter, yet one reproaches them later, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. The seventy-ninth [offense] is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus each required a single robe, which the Saṃgha had already granted them. Later,
they obtained three robes ready for use and discussed among themselves, saying,
"To whom should these robes now be given?"
Some said, "One should first offer it to the World-Honored One. Others said:
"He should first be given to Mahākāśyapa;
Mahākāśyapa is constantly praised by the World-Honored One and is also a senior elder.
The group of six bhikṣus said:
"He should first give it to Kokālika.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus, "Did Kāśyapa ask for many robes or few?"
He replied, "I do not seek it; I take it only after it has been given.
Because of this, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"This robe is a robe of non-desire; it is not for those possessed by desire.
One who cannot discipline their mind is unfit for this *kāṣāya*.
But one who has already abandoned greed and is always single-minded in the precepts [is fit]."
"One who has thus disciplined the mind is worthy of these robes.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"These robes should be given to Kāśyapa."
He then gave it to him.
Thereupon, the group of six bhikṣus said:
"Now these bhikṣus are showing favoritism toward their acquaintances by diverting the property of the Saṃgha to give it away!"
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they censured them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied: "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!"
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows: ‘If a bhikṣu speaks thus:’”
"If a bhikṣu, out of favoritism toward those he knows, diverts monastic property to give it to them,
it is a pāyattika. It is the same for a bhikṣuṇī.
The *śikṣamāṇā*, *śrāmaṇera*, and *śrāmaṇerī* [commit] *duṣkṛta* offenses; the eighty [rules] are concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣu Dharma had this thought:
“Bhadananda first seized my robe; the Buddha rebuked me and established a precept for the bhikṣus;
I stated that he had committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, yet he in turn slandered me with a groundless charge of saṃghāvaśeṣa;
furthermore, he cut off my food for three days!”
"How shall I repay this enmity? He further thought:
"He gave me a pure gift of robes and did not return them; that alone is sufficient to repay his insult!"
He then did not return.
Later, when Upāli (Baddhalita) went to him to ask for his robe, Dharmā said, "The teacher previously gave it as a gift; why does he now ask for it back?"
Bhadanta said, "I made this a pure gift (śuddha-dāna), not an act of almsgiving (dāna)!
Still, he did not return it.
Bhadrananda then forcibly seized it, whereupon the man cried out loudly.
Hearing this, the elder bhikṣus all came out and asked,
"Why are you crying out so loudly?"
He replied, "Bhadanta,
Bhadanta Upananda forcibly took my robe away!
The elder bhikṣus then rebuked Bhadanta Upananda.
"How can you give a pure gift to an untrustworthy person and then take it back?
He further rebuked Dharma:
"When people gave a pure gift to you, why did you not return it?"
They reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upananda: "You foolish man!
“Did you truly give pure gifts to people who are untrustworthy?
He replied, “It is indeed so.”
"World-Honored One!
he said, and then asked Dharma again: "You foolish man!
"He has truly given this as a pure gift to you; are you unwilling to return it?
He replied, "It is indeed so."
"World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should not give a pure gift to five kinds of people:"
First, they do not know one another;
second, they have not yet become intimately acquainted;
third, they have not yet become familiar with one another.
Fourth, those who are not friends but share the same teacher;
fifth, those who are of an improper class.
Only when these five conditions are absent may one give pure gifts to them.
"Furthermore, there are two things for which one should not perform a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*): first, being unable to praise others;
second, being unable to establish a good reputation for others."
"Furthermore, there are two things for which one should not perform the ritual of purification through gifting (*viśuddha-dāna*):
first, being unable to receive heavy valuables from others as a gift of purification and protect them as if they were one's own;
second, being unable to purify and give away one's own heavy valuables, yet feeling no resentment when another uses them."
"Furthermore, there are two things for which one should not perform a pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*):
first, not knowing whether that person is still alive;
second, not knowing whether that person is on the path [to liberation]."
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The Buddha has permitted us to perform the ritual of pure giving.
Thereupon, they performed the ritual of pure giving for their parents, brothers, and sisters.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not perform the ritual of pure giving (śuddhika-dāna) to laypeople; one should perform it for the five groups of monastics.
There were some bhikṣus staying alone in their rooms who possessed extra robes (atireka-cīvara) but did not know how to perform the ritual of pure giving. They reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should perform a 'distant indication' for pure giving (*pariśuddha-dāna*).

If one needs to exchange anything among the three robes, one should bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, kneel on the right knee, take hold of the robe, and speak these words with the mind:"
"I now relinquish this [name] robe of mine, consisting of so many strips.
A second and third time, he speaks thus.
Thereafter, he receives the extra robe according to the same procedure, expressing it with words born of his mind:
"I accept this [number] of strips of this robe-cloth of mine.
The second and third times should be spoken in the same manner.

Having accepted it in this way, the robe-cloth that was relinquished should be used for a pure gift (*śuddhadāna*); furthermore, one should again perform the ritual as before, speaking with the words arising from the mind:
"I give this extra robe as a pure gift to [Name]; I shall take it from him for use.
If one does not need to undergo the formal act of acceptance (*parivāsa*), the extra robe should be purified by giving it away in this manner.
Regarding the method for the exclusive pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*), when the eleventh day arrives, one should again follow the previous procedure, generating the thought and speaking the words:
"I take back this long robe from [Name]."
Thereafter, one should again receive and maintain it according to the previous method, or perform a purification offering (*viśuddhi-dāna*).
If performing a purification offering in the presence of another person, one should perform a successive purification offering (*paramparā-viśuddhi-dāna*) according to the previous method:
holding the extra robe, one should speak these words: "I offer this extra robe as a purification offering to you, Venerable Sir."
That bhikṣu should ask: "Venerable sir!
This robe has been made a formal gift (netthāra) to me; to whom shall I give it?"
He replied, "Give it as you wish from among the five aggregates.
That bhikṣu should then say to him:
"I now give this to [Name]; Venerable One, if you require it, please take and use it, and cherish it well!
The monk who has received it as a purified gift (viśuddhi-dāna) later speaks of this matter to the monk whose name was mentioned;
however, the monk whose name was mentioned, fearing he would incur the offense of possessing extra robes (atireka-cīvara), does not dare to accept it.
Not knowing what to do, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"One should not speak to a bhikṣu by his name."
I now establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu gives a pure gift of clothing to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, and then takes it back, it is a pāyattika."
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
If one gives a robe to another and then demands it back, and the other takes it back, there is no offense. [Case 81 concluded.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

At that time, Upananda was constantly receiving offerings from a certain family. Later, when that family invited the Saṃgha, Upananda put on his robes and took up his bowl in the early morning, entered the city, and went from house to house engaging in conversation.

When the time for the meal arrived, the bhikṣus put on their robes, took up their bowls, and went to his house. After they had been seated for some time, they said to the host, "The time for the midday meal is passing; why do you not serve the food?"
He replied, "I have invited the Saṃgha for the sake of Upananda; we must wait for him to arrive.
At that time, Upananda arrived only at midday, and among the bhikṣus, some had eaten, some had eaten little, and some had not eaten at all.
Because of this, the host reproached Baddhālī, saying:
"What urgent business do these śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas have?

Having previously accepted my invitation, they passed by various households and only arrived at midday, causing the bhikṣus to be unable to eat the food I had prepared for them, and making all the food and drink I prepared go to waste!"
The bhikṣus rebuked Baddhananda in various ways, saying:
"You do not benefit the Buddha-dharma; instead, you cause such suffering and distress to the Saṃgha!"
They reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied: “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu, having accepted an invitation, goes to another household before the meal, it is a pāyattika.’”
Later, the host of Upananda himself carried cooked food to the monastery to provide for the Saṃgha and Upananda.
Upananda ate first; having finished, he departed and went to another house.
The messenger gathered the Saṃgha again, intending to serve the special food; however, because Upāli was absent, they did not serve it for a long time.
The bhikṣus said to him, "The time for the meal is nearly past; why do you not serve it?"
He replied, "I was originally going to descend for the sake of Upananda; as soon as he arrived, I would have descended.
However, Upananda did not come at all, and so he was unable to descend.
The various criticisms and reproaches directed at Pūraṇa Kāśyapa were also voiced by the bhikṣus.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned Pūraṇa Kāśyapa:
"Is it truly so? He replied, "It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu, having accepted an invitation, goes to another household before or after the meal, it is a pāyattika.
There were some bhikṣus who had business for the Saṃgha, business for the stūpa, or private business requiring them to enter other households; yet they did not dare to go.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I allow the bhikṣus to inform other bhikṣus before they may depart."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, having accepted an invitation, goes from house to house before or after a meal without informing another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika."
There were some bhikṣus who harbored mutual resentment and did not speak with one another;
others were practicing meditation or were fast asleep, so they did not know to whom they should report.
Upon leaving their rooms and seeing the other bhikṣus, they would run after them, shouting from afar to announce [the matter].
When the laypeople saw this, they reviled them, saying:
"The bhikṣus run like deer, run like rabbits, and screech like bald owls!
They lack the conduct of śramaṇas and destroy the dharma of śramaṇas!"
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they censured them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus, "Is it true that you did such a thing?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should not announce from afar!
From this day forward, this precept should be stated as follows:"
“If a bhikṣu, having accepted an invitation, goes to another household before or after a meal without informing a nearby bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
The bhikṣus thought: “Should we also inform [a fellow bhikṣu] during the time for robes?”
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Except during the time for [distributing] robes."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, having accepted an invitation, goes from house to house before or after a meal without informing another bhikṣu who is nearby, except when there is a valid reason, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding "circumstances":
the time for robes is called a circumstance.
If one goes to the eastern house after having announced [the invitation] at the western house, it is not considered a formal announcement.
If one enters various households without having announced one's arrival, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for the first foot to cross the threshold;
it is a *pāyattika* offense for both feet to cross the threshold.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one has announced [one's visit] to one household and, because of that, goes to another household, there is no offense;
likewise, if there is no bhikṣu to whom one may announce it, there is also no offense. (The eighty-second case concludes.)
The Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kośala together with one thousand two hundred and fifty great bhikṣus.
Some of the bhikṣus obtained lodging in rooms, some obtained shelter under trees, and others stayed in the open air.

At that time, in the early morning, the group of six bhikṣus put on their robes and took up their bowls, and in the streets and alleys they engaged in worldly conversation with laypeople until sunset.
Travelers who saw them rebuked them, saying:
"This is no place for the discourse of those who have left the household life; why do you not dwell in an araṇya and maintain restraint over your sense faculties?"
Some said, "These people do not delight in the Buddha-dharma nor do they respect the precepts; having found a place for idle chatter, they have simply forgotten that evening has fallen!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so? They replied:
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this time forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
There were some bhikṣus who had business requiring them to enter a village at an improper time, yet they did not dare to do so.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I now authorize entering a village at an improper time for those with a specific reason.
From this day forward, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time without approaching a virtuous bhikṣu to inform him, except when there is a specific reason, it is a pāyattika.'"
As for the "causal conditions":
in times of difficulty, these are called causal conditions.
For a śrāmaṇera, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If one travels along a road passing through a village, or must go there at dusk to stay overnight, or if the eight difficulties arise, none of these constitute an offense. [The eighty-third case concludes.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, not far from the city, there was a sacred tree to which the multitude paid homage; they would do so for seven days during the festival season, after which they would discard the four kinds of *tūla* cotton used as bedding and depart.
Later, the bhikṣus collected them to use as cords for rope beds and wooden beds, or to make pillows and mattresses.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These items are foul and filthy, breeding many insects; how can the bhikṣus sit or lie upon them?"
"They lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned the bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so? They replied, "It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu makes a sitting or lying mat stuffed with *tūla* [cotton down], it is a *pāyattika* offense. Regarding *tūla*:
it refers to the flowers of the willow, the white poplar, the *phali*, and the *śāmba*.
If one resolves upon it and employs the means with the intent to store [it], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
once it is completed, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is not destroyed, or if one sits [upon it], for every act of sitting, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one lies down, for every instance of lying down, it is a *pāyattika*.
If another gives [something] and one accepts it, it is a *pāyattika*.
One must first discard [the object], and only then may one perform the confession of the offense.
If it were not so, the offense would be even more grave.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. The eighty-fourth [rule] is concluded.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus were using high beds; when the elderly or infirm bhikṣus were getting on or off these beds, they would fall to the ground, injuring themselves or exposing their bodies.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reproached them, saying, "These śramaṇas are like kings or nobles; they are extravagant and lack frugality.
At that time, King Prasenajit gave his own bed and couch to Upananda.
Having received it, Baddhanta spread it out inside his room.
It was the constant practice of the World-Honored One to inspect the various rooms once every five days.
Baddhanta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Look at me sleeping on my bed!
The Buddha rebuked him, saying: "You foolish man!"
How can you remain settled in the den of birth and death without the intent to seek liberation?
You must not keep high beds or spread out rugs of brocade and embroidery; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
He then assembled the community of bhikṣus on account of this matter and addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu makes a rope bed or a wooden bed for himself, the legs should be no higher than eight fingers of the Sugata, excluding the part that enters the frame.’”
"If it exceeds [the prescribed height], it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Whether one makes a bed oneself or causes another to make it, if it is too high, it must be cut down, and the offense must be confessed.
If one receives a gift of a high bed, at the time of receiving it, one should form this thought:
"If this bed is not in accordance with the Dharma, I shall cut it further.
If one accepts [the bed] without forming this thought, it is an *pāyattika*;
furthermore, one should first cut it and then perform the confession (*deśanā*).
The same applies to bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta. [Section 85 concludes.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣus made needle cases from bone, ivory, and horn; they sought these materials everywhere, even picking them up from among refuse heaps to fashion them.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled them, saying:
"These śramaṇas are like dogs, like birds, or like craftsmen working with ivory and horn; they are impure and loathsome!"
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who went to slaughterhouses and, seeing animals about to be killed, requested them in advance.
The butchers all reviled and scolded them, saying:
"Look at these śramaṇas; they only wish for many killings, and they rejoice as soon as they see one being slaughtered!"
"Day and night he constantly preached compassion and protected sentient beings with mindfulness;
yet now he has no heart of benevolence or pity!

At that time, there was a worker in ivory and horn who had faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma. He regularly provided for the bhikṣus, either making items himself from ivory and horn or commissioning others to do so by seeking out ivory and horn for them, until he was brought to ruin because of this.
No one else was permitted to perform any further labor.
The family members said to one another,
"If he remains a slave to this śramaṇa forever, we shall each have to divide our own livelihoods!"
A neighbor said to him,
"Because you place your faith and respect in the śramaṇas, you shall soon fall into poverty!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: [Yes].
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu makes a needle case from bone, ivory, or horn, it is a pāyattika.'"
If a bhikṣu conceives the intention and employs the means with the desire to do so, it is a duṣkṛta;
once it is completed, it is a pāyattika.
He must also first destroy what has been done and then perform repentance.
If one makes a nasal irrigation tube, there is no offense.
The rest is as explained in the section on beds; this concludes the eighty-sixth [rule].
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, some bhikṣus sat on monastic beds and mattresses without having spread out sitting cloths, soiling them with grease and grime.
Furthermore, another bhikṣu passed stool, thinking it was merely wind escaping; upon realizing what had happened, he washed it and hung it out to dry in front of his cell.
The World-Honored One asked Ānanda,
"Whose mat is this?
He then answered him in full detail.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: [Yes].
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should not sit upon a monastic bed or mat without having spread out a sitting cloth; one who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
Now, I permit the bhikṣus to keep sitting cloths for the sake of protecting their bodies, their robes, and the monastic beds and mats."
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The Buddha has already permitted us to make sitting mats.
Thereupon, they made them wide and large, which hung down to the ground and became soiled with mud.
When the laypeople saw this, they asked the bhikṣus,
"What kind of garment is this that hangs down to the ground? They replied:
"This is our sitting mat," he said,
and then rebuked him, saying,
"Venerable sir!..."
"Why do you not act in accordance with your station?
Although you have left the household life, how could you not cherish your wealth?
The sons of Śākya always preach few desires and contentment, yet now you act in such a manner!"
"They lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned the bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so for you? They replied, "It is truly so."
"World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"
“If a bhikṣu makes a sitting mat (niṣīdana), he should make it according to the prescribed measure:
two Sugata-spans in length and one and a half spans in width;
if it exceeds these, it is a pāyattika.”

The Venerable Udāyin was large in stature, while his sitting mat was small and insufficient to accommodate his knees; as the Buddha was inspecting the rooms, Udāyin pulled at the mat as if he were tanning leather.
The Buddha asked,
"For what reason have you done this? He replied:
“World-Honored One!
My body is large, but this seat is small; I am pulling and stretching it in order to make it wider and longer.
The Buddha rebuked him, saying:
“You foolish man, you still do not cease from your jesting!
Now listen: I shall further increase your punishment by one more hand of dismemberment.
He then assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
“From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu makes a niṣīdana, he should make it according to the prescribed measure:
two Sugata-spans in length and one and a half spans in width;’”
"If it is continuous, it shall measure one span.
If it exceeds this, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding "continuous, measuring one span":
Cut it into three parts and continue with the long head;
as for the remaining one part, apply it to the four corners, or do not apply it at all.
With the exception of bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇerīs, the rest is as explained regarding the bed [in rule 87]. Thus ends eighty-seven.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a monk named Pilāṭa developed a carbuncle on his body; pus and blood flowed profusely.
When his robes touched the wound, they would tear and cause excruciating pain when removed.
The Buddha went to his room and saw him, asking that bhikṣu:
"Is your illness slightly abated? Can you endure the suffering? He replied:
"The illness does not subside; the suffering is unbearable!
When clothing touches the ulcer, it stings; when removed, it peels away and causes pain.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I now authorize the bhikṣus, for the sake of protecting their bodies, their robes, and the monastic sitting mats, to keep a wound-covering cloth made of fine and smooth material."
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The Buddha has permitted us to make wound-covering robes.
Thereupon they made them excessively large, wrapping them all around their heads and feet so that they trailed on the ground, becoming stained with mud.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled him in various ways, as described in the *Nisītha*.
When the elder bhikṣus heard of it, they censured him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so? They replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I establish this precept for the bhikṣus. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu makes a garment to cover sores, it should be made according to these measurements:
four Sugata-spans in length and two spans in width.'"
"If it exceeds [the prescribed period], it is a pāyattika offense.
A wound-covering cloth is to be worn during the time one has a disease or a wound;
once the wound has healed, it should be given away as a pure gift (śuddha-dāna).
The remainder is as explained in the section on sitting mats; the eighty-eighth [case] concludes here.

While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the Buddha permitted the Mother of Viśākhā to offer *varṣāśāṭikā* (rain-bathing robes) to the Saṃgha. The bhikṣus then made them excessively large, which led the lay devotees (*gṛhapati*) to criticize and rebuke them. Eventually, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, all as described above.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu makes a rain-bath robe, he should make it according to the prescribed measurement.'"
"It shall be five spans of the Sugata’s hand in length and two and a half spans in width.
If it exceeds these measurements, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The remainder is as explained in the section on the *vraṇapaṭṭa* (wound-covering cloth); this concludes the eighty-ninth [rule].
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus made robes for the Sugata according to the prescribed measurements; however, some exceeded them.
Laypeople criticized and rebuked them, and the matter was eventually reported by the bhikṣus to the Buddha, as described above.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this day forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu makes a robe of the Sugata’s standard measurement, and it exceeds that, it is a pāyattika offense.’”
Regarding the measurement of a Sugata-cīvara:
it is nine Sugata-spans in length and six spans in width; this is called the measurement of a Sugata-cīvara.
Nanda was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha; not knowing how he should make his robes, he informed the Buddha of this matter.
The Buddha said, "I permit Nanda’s robes to be two finger-widths shorter than the Buddha’s robes."
Furthermore, there were some bhikṣus who were short of stature and did not know how to make their robes; they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to make robes according to the length of your own bodies."
The remainder is as explained in the section on the rain-bathing robe; thus ends the ninety rules.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
Then Nanda and Upananda held this consultation together:
“The Blessed One has already prescribed that diverting goods intended for the Saṃgha into one’s own possession constitutes an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
We shall now divert these and give them to you.”
They then each spoke of various donors, and they obtained them from one another.
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Nanda and Upananda:
"Is it true that you did so?
They replied: "It is true."
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. From this time forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, knowing that a donor intends to give property to the Saṃgha, diverts it to another person, he commits a pāyattika.'"
The remainder is as explained in the section concerning the diversion of property intended for the Saṃgha into one’s own possession.
[End of Section 91. *Mahīśāsaka Vinaya*, Scroll Nine; *Mahīśāsaka Vinaya*, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Song Dynasty, together with Zhu Daosheng and others.
Section One, Part Six: The Dharma of Confession. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the female lay follower (upāsikā) Vaṅgīśvarī was devoted to the Buddha’s Dharma and constantly made offerings to śramaṇas; she was dignified and refined among people.

Later, out of faith, she left the household life. Possessing few desires and being content, she received many offerings; once, as she was returning from alms-gathering with her food, she saw a bhikṣu and asked him, “For what purpose are you walking about like this?”
He replied, "I am begging for alms.
He asked again:
"Can you accept this food from me? He replied, "I can."
He then gave it to him.
Entering another house to beg for food, that bhikṣu said to the other bhikṣus:
"The bhikṣuṇī Vāgīramātā can obtain food and drink; you may take it from her!"
When the bhikṣus heard this, they immediately went there; as soon as the bhikṣuṇī received food, she gave it back to them, thinking:
"I shall take what I receive last and eat it when I return home!"
Having obtained and taken it out, she again encountered a bhikṣu who questioned her as before; she gave it to him as well and returned with an empty bowl.
After the meal, the bhikṣus gathered to discuss the matter, saying:
"That bhikṣuṇī was fortunate enough to obtain much food and drink; why should we trouble ourselves to seek alms elsewhere?"
"We shall simply follow after her every day!
Thereupon, early the next morning, they entered the village and followed her.
Whenever that bhikṣuṇī obtained food, she would give it to them, returning with an empty bowl.

On the morning of the third day, while she was going on her almsround, a householder traveling in a horse-drawn carriage happened upon her; as the bhikṣuṇī sought to avoid him, she immediately fell to the ground.
At that time, King Prasenajit had issued a decree:
"Whoever within my realm treats the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, with contempt shall be severely punished.
The elder was immediately seized with great terror; he alighted from his carriage, helped him up, and apologized, saying:
“I have not offended you; why do you treat me so abruptly?
He replied, “Indeed, I see no offense, but it is because I am hungry and exhausted!”
He asked again,
"Did you not obtain alms? He replied:
"I gave all the food I received to the bhikṣus, and that is why this misfortune has come upon me!
He further said,
"I pray that you will accept my food!"
He consented by remaining silent.
He immediately gave it away and returned it to the bhikṣu.
When the elder had dismounted from his carriage, the crowd was already large, and they all reviled him, saying:
"Although this bhikṣuṇī gives without weariness, the recipient should know their own measure!
This class of people always speaks of having few desires and being content, yet now they greedily take, merely to distress their fellow practitioners!"
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did such a thing?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”

After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus: "I now establish the *pāṭidesanīya* dharma for the bhikṣus. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu receives food from a bhikṣuṇī.'"
That bhikṣu should confess his transgression to the other bhikṣus, saying:
"I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I now confess my transgression before the Venerable Ones!
This is called the method of confession.
There were some bhikṣus whose relatives, who were bhikṣuṇīs, were able to obtain food and drink; seeing that the bhikṣus were struggling with the difficulty of begging for alms, they said to them:
"Do not distress yourselves; take from me!"
The bhikṣus said, "The Buddha does not permit us to receive food from bhikṣuṇīs. The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"Only those close to us know who should give and who should receive.
We pray that you will inform the Buddha of this!
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
“From now on, I permit the bhikṣus to receive food from bhikṣuṇīs who are their relatives.
From this time forth, this *pāṭidesanīya* rule should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu receives food from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, that bhikṣu should confess his transgression before the other bhikṣus, saying:
'I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I now confess my transgression before the Venerable Ones!'"
"This is called the method for repenting transgressions.
Furthermore, there were certain sick bhikṣus who went out begging for food while still ill; their illnesses would then invariably worsen. Other bhikṣuṇīs said to them:
"Do not exhaust yourself with hardship; receive food from us!"
The sick bhikṣu said,
"The Buddha does not permit me to receive food from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative.
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I now permit a sick bhikṣu to receive food from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative."
From now on, this *pāṭidesanīya* rule should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, being free from illness, accepts food from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative."
That bhikṣu should confess his transgression to the other bhikṣus, saying:
"I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I now confess my transgression before the Venerable Ones!
This is called the method of confession.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs, whether in the monasteries, in their own residences, or in various households, prepared for the bhikṣus the morning meal, the afternoon meal, *taṃpala*, and congee;
they also provided them with baths and offered various oils and ghee.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I now permit you to accept food offerings from bhikṣuṇīs, but you must not accept it in the streets or alleys!"
From now on, this *pāṭidesanīya* rule should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, being free from illness, receives food with his own hands from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative while in a street or alleyway."
That bhikṣu should confess his transgression to the other bhikṣus, saying:
"I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I now confess my transgression before the venerable ones!
This is called the procedure for confession.
If a bhikṣu is outside a village while a bhikṣuṇī is inside the village receiving food;
or if a bhikṣu is inside a village while a bhikṣuṇī is outside the village receiving food;
or if a bhikṣu is in the air while a bhikṣuṇī is on the ground receiving food; [in these cases, it constitutes an offense].
If a bhikṣu is on the ground and a bhikṣuṇī is in the air receiving food, it is all a duṣkṛta offense.
For a śrāmaṇera, it is a duṣkṛta offense. [The first case concludes.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

At that time, a householder invited the Saṃgha of both divisions for a meal. The group of six bhikṣus sat facing the group of six bhikṣuṇīs and instructed their respective servers to give each other extra portions, so that the other virtuous bhikṣus could no longer obtain food.
He said to the host,
"Since you have invited the monks today, why do you not provide more food?
The host replied:
"Now this bhikṣu has disturbed my mind; I do not know who should benefit from it and who should not.
Thereupon, the host rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"These [monks] encouraging one another to eat are just like taking a wife along when receiving an invitation from others!
They lack the conduct of śramaṇas and destroy the Dharma of the śramaṇas!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so? They replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had reproached him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish for the bhikṣus the *pāṭidesanīya* rules. From this day forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu has been invited to a meal at a layperson’s house, and a bhikṣuṇī there says:
"Give rice to this bhikṣu; give soup to this bhikṣu. "
The bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister, step back for a moment and wait until the bhikṣus have finished their meal!"
If, among the bhikṣus, not even a single bhikṣu says to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister! Step back a moment and wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating!"...
Those bhikṣus should confess their transgression to the other bhikṣus, saying:
"I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I now confess my transgression before the Venerable Ones!"
"This is called the method for repenting transgressions.
At that time, five hundred bhikṣus were eating at the house of an elder. A bhikṣuṇī whom they regularly supported arrived, and the bhikṣus spoke with one voice, saying:
"Step back a moment!"
“Wait a moment!
That bhikṣuṇī was deeply ashamed and immediately departed.
When the host saw this, he questioned the bhikṣus:
"What offense has this bhikṣuṇī committed that you all drive her away with one voice? Or again, some said:
"These śramaṇas fear that the bhikṣuṇīs will take their share of food; for this reason they act thus!"
"Having gone forth together, they are jealous of one another and do not get along; how much less so with others!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:

“If, at the time of eating, a bhikṣuṇī does not instruct a bhikṣu to take more food out of desire, hatred, delusion, or fear, yet remains silent, it is impossible for him to commit a pāyattika offense.”
From now on, this *pāṭidesanīya* rule should be recited as follows:
"If a monk has been invited to a meal at a layperson's house, and a nun instructs the person serving the food, saying:
'Give rice to this monk; give soup to this monk.'"
