The bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister! Step back for a moment and wait until the bhikṣus have finished eating."
If not even a single person among the assembly speaks, that bhikṣu should confess his transgression before the bhikṣus, saying:
"I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I now confess my transgression before the Venerable Ones!"
"This is called the method for repentance.
If a bhikṣuṇī instructs a bhikṣu to eat, the foremost elder (sthavira) should speak;
if he does not heed the elder's words, the second elder should speak next, and so on down the line until the newly ordained monk.
If a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī instructs a bhikṣu to serve him food, and the bhikṣu does not say,
"Step back for a moment," it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to eat more food, and the latter eats it in an unequal manner, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
For a śrāmaṇera, it is also a duṣkṛta offense. Thus ends the second rule.
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.

At that time, the householder Ghoṣila had faith in and delighted in the Buddha’s Dharma; having seen the Dharma and attained its fruit, he constantly made offerings to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
At a later time, when his wealth was completely exhausted, his kinsmen and relatives brought food to him.
Yet the bhikṣus still came to his house and departed with their alms bowls full, so that the members of his household could no longer endure the suffering of hunger.
When the neighbors saw this, they all reproached him, saying:
"Though the donor may never grow weary of giving, the recipient ought to know contentment!
How can you encroach upon and deplete another's household until their wealth is exhausted?"
"We gave them a portion of our food, yet they still seized it from us!
They lack any heart of compassion and seek only their own gratification!
They possess no conduct of a śramaṇa and destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!"
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!"
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"I now authorize the bhikṣus to perform a formal *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for the householder Ghoṣila, declaring him a 'family under training' (*śaikṣa-kula*), up to and including prohibiting even a single bhikṣu from entering his home."
A single bhikṣu should announce:
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This householder Ghoṣila has had various kinds of food taken by the bhikṣus when they went to his home; they returned with their bowls full, leaving nothing behind, and have thereby caused the wealth and goods of his household to be completely exhausted.”
Now we perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) regarding a householder’s family, even to the extent of not permitting a single bhikṣu to enter their residence again.
If the Saṃgha is ready and the Saṃgha consents,
this is the motion (*jñapti*).
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This householder Ghoṣila has had various kinds of food taken from his home by monks who fill their bowls and return with them, leaving nothing behind, until his household wealth has been completely exhausted.”
Now we perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for a householder’s family, up to and including the prohibition against a single bhikṣu entering their residence again.
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
The Saṃgha has completed the *kula-karma* for Ghoṣila as a *śikṣāpada-gṛhīta-kula*.
Since the Saṃgha is silent, it consents.
This matter is thus upheld.
At that time, the bhikṣus performed the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the formal act of declaring a family to be under training) for other families in various places.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I do not permit the performance of the *śikṣādattaka-karman* for other families in various places!"
If the wife is a noble one (āryā) and the husband is an ordinary person (pṛthagjana),
or if the wife is an ordinary person and the husband is a noble one, in neither case should the *kula-śikṣāpada-karman* be performed for them.
"If both husband and wife are noble ones (*ārya*) and free from the mind of stinginess and greed, only when their wealth is completely exhausted shall you perform the *śaikṣaka-karman* for them.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not dare to go to the house of Ghoṣila again; everyone in that household, young and old alike, could not help but long to see him.
Then Ghoṣila went to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus:
"I have taken refuge in the Triple Gem and shall no longer seek other fields of merit.
I pray that the Venerable Ones will come and go to my home!"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to go!
Although the bhikṣus went, they did not eat.
The elder said,
"I have taken refuge in the Triple Gem and shall no longer seek any other fields of merit.
I pray that you will accept my food!"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to receive one-third of the contents from their bowls.
Once the Buddha had permitted them to receive one-third, the bhikṣus went to beg from every house until the household wealth was completely exhausted, becoming even more destitute than before.
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they censured them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish for the bhikṣus the *pāratideśanīya* dharma. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘There are families who are under the status of a *śaikṣa-kula* (a family under training), and the Saṃgha has performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) regarding them as such.’”
If a bhikṣu accepts food from such a family of practitioners, that bhikṣu should confess his transgression before the other bhikṣus, saying:
"I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I now confess my transgression before the Venerable Ones!"
"This is called the method for repentance.

While Ghoṣila’s wealth was not yet exhausted, he established a separate station for interest to provide for the sick monks among the Saṃgha, and likewise established a station for medicine in the same manner.
The sick bhikṣus later felt ashamed and did not dare to accept [the offerings], whereupon the elder said:
"I originally provided these goods and established this medicine shelf for the sake of the sick bhikṣus within the Saṃgha."
"If we do not accept it, we shall certainly not take it back with us!
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"Since they requested a gift before their wealth was exhausted, we now permit the bhikṣus to accept it as they see fit.
From this day forward, this precept should be stated as follows:
'There are families of noble lineage (śaikṣa-kula) for whom the Saṃgha has performed the formal act of declaring them a family under training.'"

If a bhikṣu, being free from illness, has not previously received an invitation, yet accepts food at a family that is under a formal restriction, that bhikṣu should confess his transgression before the other bhikṣus, saying:
"I have fallen into a blameworthy practice; I now confess my transgression before the Venerable Ones!"
"This is called the method for repentance.
Furthermore, there was another bhikṣu who, though not ill, took food from a family under formal disciplinary action (karmavācanā).
Having received it, he felt doubt in his mind:
"I shall therefore not commit a *pāṭidesanīya* offense.
He took it back and gave it to another bhikṣu.
After the other bhikṣu had finished eating, he asked:
"Why do you not eat? He replied, "I am free from illness,
yet having received this food from a family under formal disciplinary action (karmavācanā), I fear committing a *pratideśanīya* offense."
That bhikṣu said, "Regarding what you have doubted, I have now committed it!
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"If one takes food from a family under formal disciplinary action (karmavācanā) but does not eat it oneself,
yet gives it to another, there is no offense in either case."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"There are families who have been subjected by the Saṃgha to the formal act (kamma) of being 'families under training' (sekkhasīla).
If a bhikkhu, being free from illness, has not previously received an invitation, yet accepts food with his own hand from such a family..."
That bhikṣu should confess his transgression to the other bhikṣus, saying:
"I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I now confess my transgression before the Venerable Ones!
This is called the method of confession.

If the wealth and property of a family of noble disciples (śaikṣa-kula) have been exhausted, and the Saṃgha possesses gardens or fields, these should be granted to them so they may be made aware of it, allowing them to exceed their usual limits while the remainder is used for the Saṃgha’s own support.
If there are no gardens or fields, when the Saṃgha receives extraordinary offerings, they should have those families of noble disciples perform services so that they may obtain the leftovers.
If even this is not possible, once they have received alms-food, they should go to those families to eat and give the remains to them.
If one cannot do so, they should be brought to a monastic dwelling (saṃghārāma), provided with a room and bedding, given food in due order, and provided with non-timely drinks;
if there are robes that can be divided, these should also be shared with them.
The female householders of that family, as well as the bhikṣuṇīs, should also manage matters in this same manner.
For a śrāmaṇera, it is a duṣkṛta. The three rules are concluded.
The Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in the city of Kapilavastu.
At that time, there were certain bhikṣus dwelling in forest hermitages. When some laypeople sent them food, they were robbed by bandits; the bhikṣus then complained and rebuked them, saying:
"Why did you not inform us?"
"If I had known this, I would have carried a staff for my own protection and might not have come!
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so for you? They replied, "It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now establish for the bhikṣus the *pāṭidesanīya* dharma. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”

"If a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage) experiences doubt or fear, and without first scouting the area, accepts food within the monastery grounds, that bhikṣu should confess his transgression before the other bhikṣus:
'I have fallen into a blameworthy practice; I now confess my transgression before the Venerable Ones!'"
"This is called the method for repentance.

At that time, five hundred slaves of the Śākyas rebelled and took up residence in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*). The women of the Śākya clan wished to go there to pay their respects and to give alms to the Saṃgha.
Having heard this, the slaves consulted together and said,
"We shall ambush and seize them on the road!
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they went and spoke to the Śākya women.
"There is a thief here who wishes to plunder you; do not come forward!
The women then stopped.
The slaves spoke again:
"The reason the women of the Śākya clan have not come must surely be that the bhikṣus went there beforehand and spoke to them!
He immediately questioned the bhikṣus; the bhikṣus did not speak falsely, but answered with the truth.
The slave then beat the bhikṣus, seizing all their robes and bowls, only releasing them when they were on the verge of death.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"You should not say that there is a thief; you should simply tell the messenger not to come."
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know that outsiders were about to arrive, and they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"You should always look out from afar; if you see someone coming, run to inform them."
If there is food intended for him, he should quickly send it back.
From now on, this *pāṭidesanīya* rule should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣu dwelling in an *araṇya* (forest hermitage) where there is suspicion or fear, should personally receive food within a monastery without having first scouted the area, and does not go outside to receive it."
That bhikṣu should confess his transgression before the other bhikṣus, saying:
"I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I now confess my transgression before the Venerable Ones!
This is called the method of confession.
Someone arrived suddenly with food that had already entered the monastery.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Listen: by accepting [the food] from one person, you yourself set aside one portion, while the remainder is shared with the assembly;
then, using your own portion, trade it for food with one person from among the assembly."
Command them to depart quickly. If they cannot depart, one should hide the person carrying the food so that the bandits do not see them;
if they cannot be hidden, one should give them a *kāṣāya* robe to wear and send them away;
if even that is not possible, one should temporarily shave their head, dress them in the Dharma robes, and have them depart.
For a śrāmaṇera, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If food is given while a military force is passing through, or if a thief personally brings food to offer, one does not commit an offense. This concludes the section on the four offenses involving confession.
7. The Rules of Training (Śaikṣa-dharmas). Vinaya of the Five Divisions, First Division, Part Seven: The Rules of Training. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

At that time, the bhikṣus wore their lower robes (antarvāsaka) either too high, or too low, or unevenly, or like the leaves of a tala tree, or like an elephant’s trunk, or like a round myrobalan fruit, or with fine pleats.
A lay follower saw them and rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas wear their lower robes in such a way that they resemble those of women or even performers; they consider this to be beautiful, yet it lacks the dignity of the Dharma."
"They do not even know how to put on their robes, let alone the principles [of the Dharma]!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned them:
"Is it truly so for you? They replied, "It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now establish for the bhikṣus a training rule (śikṣāpada). From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”

"One should train oneself: 'The lower robe shall not be worn too high, nor too low, nor uneven; it shall not resemble the leaf of a tala tree, nor an elephant's trunk, nor a round *nāḍī* fruit; it shall not have fine pleats.'"
"Upper garment": reaching at least half the shank. "Lower garment":
[reaching below the navel].
"From the ankles downward,
'unevenly attached' means that the four corners are not aligned."
"Like a tāla leaf" means it is high in the front and low in the back.
"Like an elephant's trunk" means:
"Let one corner hang down like a round *nāḍika* fruit":
gather the upper part to make it round, using it to cover the front of the abdomen.
Regarding "fine pleats":
one makes fine pleats around the waist.
If one wears it in this manner without understanding [the rule] or asking [for clarification], it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one understands [the prohibition] but wears it without careful consideration, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if one understands [the prohibition], yet disregards the precept and disregards the person [who taught it], and wears it, it is a *pāyattika*.
It is the same for bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta.
There is no offense if one is ill or during times of mud and rain.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣus put on their robes; some were too high, some too low, and some were uneven.
Laypeople criticized and rebuked them, leading up to the formulation of the rules of training for the bhikṣus, all as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'One should train oneself not to wear the robe unevenly—neither too high nor too low.
The meaning of 'high,' 'low,' and 'uneven' is as explained above."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, various bhikṣus entered the houses of laypeople without properly covering their bodies, or they sat in such houses;
or they entered the houses of laypeople with their robes tucked up over their right shoulders, or they sat in such houses.
Or they enter the homes of laypeople with their robes tucked back over the left shoulder, or sit in such lay dwellings;
or they enter the homes of laypeople with their robes tucked back over both shoulders, or sit in such lay dwellings;

or they enter the homes of laypeople shaking their bodies, shaking their heads, shaking their shoulders, clasping hands, hiding themselves, resting their hands on their hips, propping their cheeks, or dangling their arms, or they sit in such lay dwellings.
Some enter the houses of laypeople with their gaze cast upward, or looking left and right; some sit in such houses after entering them in this manner.
Some enter the houses of laypeople walking on tiptoe, or sit in such houses after entering them in this manner.
Some enter the houses of laypeople walking on their heels, or sit in such houses after entering them in this manner.
Or entering the house of a layperson with their head covered, or sitting in such a house;
or entering the house of a layperson laughing and joking, or sitting in such a house;
or entering the house of a layperson with a loud voice, or sitting in such a house.
Or they entered the houses of laypeople without decorum, or sat down in those houses of laypeople.
When the householders saw this, they criticized and rebuked them as before.
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they censured them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked them:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: [Yes].
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish for the bhikṣus the dharmas to be trained in. From this time forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'One should train oneself to enter the houses of laypeople with the body well-covered; ...
[and so on] ... one should train oneself to sit in the houses of laypeople with composed decorum.'"
The Buddha was traveling through the country of Varga with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus. He arrived at Mount Śūmāra and stayed in the Forest of Dread.
At that time, Prince Bodhi had newly constructed a lecture hall on this mountain, but no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas had yet entered and sat within it.
When the prince heard that the Buddha had arrived at this mountain and was staying in the Bhairava Forest, he addressed the young brahmin Sājāya:
"In my name, inquire after the World-Honored One:
'Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you light and well in your daily life?'"
"I have newly established a lecture hall on this mountain, yet no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas have entered it to sit within.
I only pray that the World-Honored One and the assembly of monks will first accept this hall and receive a modest offering therein, so that I may enjoy peace and security for a long night."
"If the Buddha has a teaching, I shall receive it with earnest attention!
Having said this to the Buddha, return quickly to report it to me.
The māṇava received these instructions.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and fully conveyed the Prince’s intention; the Buddha accepted it by remaining silent.
Then, knowing that the Buddha had granted permission, Sāḍha returned and informed the Prince.

The Crown Prince prepared many kinds of delicious food throughout the night; the next day, he personally delivered it to that lecture hall, where both the interior and exterior of his residence were spread with cloths of various colors.
When the time arrived, he addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I pray that you will deign to exercise your majestic power!
The Buddha, surrounded before and behind by five hundred bhikṣus, went to that lecture hall and stood at the foot of the steps.
The Prince bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will ascend this humble hall, so that I may obtain peace and happiness throughout the long night."
The Buddha still did not ascend; this was repeated three times.
When the request was made for the last time, the Buddha looked toward Ānanda.
Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s sacred intention, spoke to the prince, saying:
"Collect these multicolored robes; the Buddha will not tread upon them out of compassion for future generations!
The Prince immediately ordered the robes to be gathered and spoke again as he had before.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One ascended with the assembly of monks and took his seat. The Prince personally served the food with his own hands; however, the bhikṣus received it by pinching the bowls with one or two fingers, and as the food was placed inside, they immediately lost their grip on the bowls. The food and drink spilled and overflowed, defiling the crystal ground.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled them, saying,
"These bhikṣus are just like pampered children, or like those who engage in deceitful games.
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they reprimanded them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: [Yes].
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish for the bhikṣus the rules of training (śaikṣa-dharma). From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'One should train oneself to receive food with a single-minded focus.'"
"Receiving food with a single-minded focus" means:
holding the bowl with the left hand with single-minded focus, while supporting its rim with the right hand.
This occurred when the Buddha was in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣus received food until their bowls overflowed, and they discarded the soup and rice.
The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣus greedily receive food without satiety, like starving people!"
Furthermore, there were some bhikṣus who, at the homes of laypeople, would eat rice until it was all gone without waiting for the soup;
and when they received the soup, they would again eat it all up without waiting for the rice.
The laypeople criticized them, saying, "These bhikṣus are as greedy for food as dogs!

Furthermore, some bhikṣus took food from various places within their alms bowls; others scooped out the center of the bowl to eat; others curved their fingers to gather up the food from the bowl; and others ate by sniffing at the food.
When the laypeople saw this, they all reviled and censured them.
When the elder bhikṣus heard of it, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so? They replied, "It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now establish for the bhikṣus a training rule (śikṣāpada). From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”

"One should train oneself: not to receive food with an overflowing bowl; to eat both the soup and the rice together; not to pick at the food here and there within the bowl; not to scoop out the center of the bowl to eat; not to hold the bowl with bent fingers while eating; and not to eat by sniffing the food."
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, some bhikṣus looked here and there while eating, and the laypeople criticized them, saying:
"These bhikṣus are like dogs or birds; they eat their own food while simultaneously watching the food of others!"
"They do not even know the proper method for eating, much less other profound principles!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned them:
"Is it truly so for you? They replied, "It is truly so."
"World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should not eat while looking around to the left and right."
At that time, the bhikṣus did not dare to look around; they closed their eyes while eating and could not see when the soup and rice were being served.
The group of six bhikṣus took the edible food and, opening their eyes, asked, "Who has taken my food?"
He replied: "Did you yourselves not see it?
Yet you instead question others!"
After the other bhikṣus had rebuked them in various ways, they informed the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish for the bhikṣus a training rule (śaikṣadharma). From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'One should train oneself to eat while looking attentively at the alms bowl.'"
"Regarding 'gazing intently at the bowl':
it means fixing one's gaze upon the bowl while it is being filled with food.
This occurred when the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha."
At that time, the bhikṣus discarded their food and drink, and the laypeople criticized them, saying,
"These bhikṣus eat like small children! Furthermore,
when five hundred bhikṣus were eating at the house of a certain layperson, some among the white-robed householders said:
"Bhikṣus do not discard any rice while eating.
When someone said they did discard it, the two men subsequently made a wager on the matter.
On that day, the bhikṣus happened not to discard any rice, but later they saw them discarding rice while eating in another place, whereupon they were criticized and rebuked as described above.
When the bhikṣus heard of this, they censured them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked them:
"Is it true that you did such a thing?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish for the bhikṣus a training rule (śikṣāpada). From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'One should train oneself not to discard food.'"
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, some bhikṣus used their eating hands to grasp clean food vessels, which became defiled by grease and filth; other bhikṣus loathed this.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and rebuked them, saying,
"How can you hold a vessel for pure food with hands that have been used for eating?
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they censured [the offenders] in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: "It is true."
“It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"When eating, one should not hold the vessel for pure food with the right hand.
Later, when laypeople were serving rice, the bhikṣus received it with their left hands; the laypeople did not give it to them and said, "You have not informed the bhikṣus."
Having reported this to the Buddha, the Buddha convened the community of bhikṣus on this matter and addressed the bhikṣus:
“One should wash one’s hands thoroughly before grasping a vessel for rice.
I now establish for the bhikṣus a rule of training (*śaikṣadharma*). From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"One should train not to take hold of a vessel for pure food with hands that have been used for eating.
"Hands used for eating" refers to hands soiled by food or made greasy by fat.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, some bhikṣus made a slurping sound while eating, and other bhikṣus made a chewing sound.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣus eat like dogs licking water.
Furthermore, there was a brāhmaṇa who invited the bhikṣus for gruel; as the bhikṣus slurped the gruel, one bhikṣu said:
"Now these bhikṣus are eating like when one is shivering with cold!"
Having spoken these words, doubt and regret arose in his mind:
"I have now reviled the Saṃgha.
Not knowing what to do, he reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked that bhikṣu:
"With what intention did you speak these words? He replied:
"If there is a mind of resentment or a mind of playfulness," the Buddha said,
"if one rebukes with a mind of resentment, there is no offense."
"To mock with a playful mind constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish for the bhikṣus the rules of training (*śaikṣadharma*). From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"One should train oneself not to slurp while eating, nor to make noise while chewing.
This was when the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, some bhikṣus were licking their food; when the laypeople saw this, they criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣus are just like oxen eating!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned the bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so for you? They replied, "It is truly so."
"World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish for the bhikṣus a training rule (śikṣāpada). From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"One should train oneself not to lick the food while eating.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, various bhikṣus had their hands full of food, and as they ate, some of it fell and dropped onto the ground.
Furthermore, there were some bhikṣus who ate with their mouths wide open;
others waited with their mouths wide open before the rice had even reached them, whereupon flies entered their mouths, and they spat out much of the food after finishing their meal;
still others ate while wrinkling their noses.
When the laypeople saw this, they all reviled and censured them. When the elder bhikṣus heard of it, they reprimanded them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked them:
"Is it true that you did such a thing?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish for the bhikṣus a training rule (*śaikṣadharma*). From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'One should train oneself not to eat with a hand that is not full.'"
"One should train oneself: 'One shall not eat with the mouth wide open.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not wait with the mouth wide open until the rice arrives.
One should train oneself: 'One shall not eat while wrinkling the nose.'"

"One should train oneself not to disparage or criticize the food.

The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, some bhikṣus stood while urinating and defecating. When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled them, saying:

'One should train oneself not to stand while defecating or urinating.'"
At that time, some bhikṣus were ill and unable to squat on the ground; they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I allow the bhikṣus, when they are ill, to stand while defecating or urinating."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"One should train oneself not to stand while defecating or urinating, except in cases of illness.
This was when the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

"One should train oneself not to defecate or urinate in water.

if he is a person with his head covered, a person with his robe tucked over one shoulder, a person with his robe tucked over both shoulders, a person holding a parasol to shield his body, a person riding a vehicle, or a person leaning on a staff—preaching the Dharma to such individuals is in all cases as previously described.

The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus took portions of food from a family that had invited them for the sake of the group of seventeen bhikṣus; the group of six bhikṣus detained the group of seventeen bhikṣus so that they would not return early.
As the sun was approaching midday, the group of seventeen bhikṣus climbed a tree to look for him.

Part Two, Section One: The Pārājika Dharmas for Bhikṣuṇīs. First, the Pārājika Dharmas for Bhikṣuṇīs. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, you have already established a precept for the bhikṣus:

'If a bhikṣu, while training together with other bhikṣus in the same code of discipline, should engage in sexual conduct despite his weakness in morality and without having relinquished it—even with an animal—this bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in community.'"
"As for this precept, how should I uphold it?
Should it be upheld by a single division of the Saṃgha, or by two divisions of the Saṃgha?
The Buddha said:
"It shall be maintained by the two assemblies of monks.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣuṇī, while training together with other bhikṣuṇīs in the rules of the Dharma, has become lax in her observance of the precepts yet does not relinquish them, and intentionally engages in sexual intercourse—even with an animal—this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion.'"
At that time, the Elder Upāli again asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, you have already established a precept for the bhikṣus:
'If a bhikṣu, whether in a village or in an open space, takes what is not given with a thieving mind, he shall not co-reside [with the Sangha]. "
"How should I uphold it? The Buddha said,
"It should be upheld by the two divisions of the Saṃgha."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, whether in a village or in an open space, takes what is not given with a thieving mind—
whether a king or a high official should seize her, bind her, kill her, or banish her, saying:"
"You thief! You fool!"— if [the monk] says this,
that bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in community with the others.
At that time, Upāli again asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, you have already established a precept for the bhikṣus:
‘If a bhikṣu, whether it be a human or one resembling a human, should take his own life, he shall not dwell in communion.’”
"How should I uphold it? The Buddha said,
"It should be upheld by the two divisions of the Saṃgha."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, whether toward a human being or one who resembles a human being, kills them herself, or gives them a knife or poison to kill them, or instructs another to kill them, or instructs another to kill themselves, or praises death and extols death, saying: 'Alas!'"
"What is the use of living a life of evil?
Death is better than life.
Thinking thus, he kills according to that thought.
"By such various causes and conditions, because of that death, that bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense and shall not live in community.
At that time, Upāli again asked the Buddha:

'If a bhikṣuṇī, without knowing or seeing the superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), the noble benefit and fulfillment, should claim for herself: "I know thus; I see thus. "

"I said I knew what I did not know, and I said I saw what I did not see; it was a false and deceptive lie."
"Except in the case of overweening pride, this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in communion.
