The bhikṣuṇī said,
“If a person fixes their mind upon an improper object of desire, even their spirit will wither away just like this!
Thereupon, Śrībhadra, after having made various physical contacts with this bhikṣuṇī, departed.
When the bhikṣuṇīs returned from their meal and saw her from afar as they entered the gate, they all suspected that she had committed unchaste acts with Sthūlanandā and asked,
"Have you already broken your pure conduct?"
She replied, “I have not violated the holy life; I have merely touched the body of a man!
The novice nun also said the same.
"So be it! the bhikṣuṇīs rebuked her in various ways, saying:
"The Buddha has in many ways censured physical contact with the bodies of men, while in many ways he has praised not touching the bodies of men!"
"How can you now commit such an evil deed?
Having rebuked her thus, she went to the Buddha's presence and reported the matter to him.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and questioned Thullanandā:
“Is it truly so? He replied, “It is truly so.”
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had thus rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“For ten reasons, I now establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, her mind transformed by the intensity of lust, accepts various kinds of touching from a man—
from below the hairline to above the knees and behind the elbows."
"This bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in communion.
Regarding "bhikṣuṇī": one who has received full ordination through the formal procedure of a jñapti-caturtha-karman.
The section beginning with "When lust has overwhelmed and transformed the mind" is as explained in the *Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa* precept concerning contact with a woman's body.

At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs allowed men to take their hands, take hold of their robes, made appointments with them, traveled alone with them, stayed alone with them, conversed alone with them, sat on the same seat alone with them, and maintained physical proximity to men. Because of this defiled mind of desire, they no longer delighted in the Path; some returned to secular life, while others became followers of external paths.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, wearing newly dyed robes, rubbed and polished her body, and painted and adorned her eyebrows and eyes, went to a place where many people gathered.
Several men seized her hand and grasped her robe, saying:
"Your hands are soft and lovely! Your robe is fine and smooth!"
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and asked the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Did you truly commit the eight aforementioned acts?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣuṇī, her mind transformed by lustful desire, accepts a man’s grasping of her hand, his grasping of her robe, an appointment to meet together, walking alone with him, staying alone with him, speaking alone with him, sitting alone on one seat with him, or physical intimacy with a man.'"
"One who possesses these eight factors commits a *pārājika* offense and shall not live in communion with the community.
"Grasping the hand" refers to [grasping] from the elbow downward.
"Seizing the robe" refers to the garment worn on the body.
"Making a mutual appointment" refers to:
When the appointed time arrives, one goes to a certain place to engage in sexual acts or to touch the body; having arrived there,
one travels alone with a man— that is,
traveling along a single path together with a male.
"Living alone together" means living in one place with a man alone.
"Speaking alone together" means:
"Speaking alone with a man in one place;
sitting alone on one seat with him" means:
sitting alone on one bed with a man.
Regarding "physically drawing near to a man":
when sitting on the same seat, she turns her body toward the man.
If she commits the offense of taking his hand, up to and including turning her body toward the man, each instance constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
If one commits seven offenses and, although having already performed repentance for them, subsequently commits one offense such that the total reaches eight, it likewise constitutes a *pārājika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, the bhikṣu Chanda repeatedly committed offenses:
he ascended and descended from his bed improperly, ate frequently, ate apart from the community, and entered a village at improper times without informing the virtuous bhikṣus;
consequently, the Saṃgha of bhikṣus performed the *ajñapti-karman* (formal act) of "not seeing the offense" against him.
Her elder sister, the bhikṣuṇī named Ucchā, came and went with her, conversing with her and providing her with food and clothing.
When the other bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they said to her, "Sister!..."
This bhikṣu has been subjected by the harmonious Saṃgha of bhikṣus to the formal act (karman) of "not seeing one's offense.
The bhikṣus have already ceased to dwell with him, ceased to perform affairs with him, and ceased to converse with him.
"How is it that you now come and go with him and converse with him, providing him with food and clothing? Ucca said,
"This is my younger brother!"
"If I do not look after them, who then shall?
The elder bhikṣuṇīs reprimanded her in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and questioned Ucchā:
“Is it truly so? He replied, “It is truly so.”
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked her in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
“A bhikṣuṇī who is on friendly terms with Ucchā should be sent to a secluded place to admonish her:”
"‘Do not comply with the Saṃgha’s formal act (karmavācanā) against the bhikṣu who does not acknowledge his offense!
If she accepts this, it is well;
if she does not accept it, a number of bhikṣuṇīs should go and admonish her. If she accepts it, it is well."
"If she still does not accept [the admonition], the community of bhikṣuṇīs should go again to admonish her.
The bhikṣus received this instruction; the bhikṣuṇīs then sent one bhikṣuṇī to admonish her, and even when the entire community of bhikṣuṇīs went to admonish her, she would not accept it.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions. After he had reproached Uccā in various ways from afar, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From this time forth, this precept should be recited as follows:"

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that the Saṃgha has lawfully performed the *adarśana-āpatti-karman* against a bhikṣu—whereby the bhikṣus do not dwell with him, do not work with him, and do not speak with him—should nevertheless associate with him."
The bhikṣuṇīs said to that bhikṣuṇī: "Sister!

This bhikṣu has been subjected by the Saṃgha of bhikṣus to the *karma* of not seeing one's offense; the bhikṣus do not dwell with him, do not work with him, and do not converse with him. Do not follow him!"
"If, despite being admonished in this manner, he persists and does not relinquish it,
he should be admonished a second and a third time.
If, after the second and third admonitions, he relinquishes this matter, it is well."
"If she does not relinquish [the position], this bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in communion.
The rest is all as explained in the section on Devadatta’s schism of the Saṃgha.
Non-offenses are also as explained there.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs Śuklā and Bhadrā were always together in their daily conduct. Later, when Bhadrā passed away, Śuklā wept for her in grief.
The bhikṣuṇīs said to her: "Do not speak thus!
All conditioned phenomena are entirely subject to decay and extinction."
As the Buddha has taught, there is separation from those one loves, and nothing endures forever.
It is impossible for conditioned phenomena not to decay or disperse!
Sūṣoma said: "I shall no longer weep for him! Why is this? Because..."
"When he was born, he did not cultivate the holy life!
The bhikṣuṇīs asked, "How do you know this?"
She replied, "He was traveling with me, and I personally witnessed him engaging in sexual intercourse with a man.
The bhikṣuṇīs rebuked her, saying:
"How can you conceal your transgressions while alive and only reveal them at death?
The elder bhikṣuṇīs reprimanded her in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and asked Sūṣoma:
"Is it true that you did so?
He replied: "It is true."
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From this time forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī sees another bhikṣuṇī commit a pārājika offense and conceals it.'"
At a later time, if that bhikṣuṇī remains, dies, travels far away, is expelled, leaves the religious life, or undergoes a change of gender, she says:
"I previously saw with my own eyes her committing a pārājika offense."
"This bhikṣuṇī commits a pārājika offense and shall not live in community with the others.
Regarding concealment:
from dawn until the first watch of the night, at every interval she incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
From the first watch of the night until the appearance of the dawn light, at every interval it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
when the dawn light appears, it is a *pārājika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one wishes to speak but there is no bhikṣuṇī present to receive it;
or if one has entered the meditative absorption of great equanimity (mahopekṣā-samādhi); or if any of the eight difficulties (aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ) arise—in all these cases, there is no offense.
The eight difficulties are:
First, illness;
second, kings; third, bandits.
4. Water; 5. Fire; 6. Robes and alms-bowl;
7. Life; 8. The Eight Grave Rules for the Holy Life are concluded. 2.
The Nuns' Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas, Part Two of the Second Division of the Five-Part Vinaya. Regarding the Nuns' Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas: At that time, the Elder Upāli questioned the Buddha:
“The Blessed One has already laid down a rule for the bhikṣus:
‘If a bhikṣu acts as a go-between, even for a single instance of sexual union, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.’”
"How should I uphold it? The Buddha said,
"It should be upheld by the two divisions of the Saṃgha."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī acts as a go-between, whether for the purpose of illicit intercourse, taking the man's intent to the woman or taking the woman's intent to the man, even to the extent of a single act of sexual union."
"This nun has committed her first *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; she should confess it.
The Elder Upāli asked again: "The World-Honored One has already established the precepts for the bhikṣus: [that they must not sit on a high seat when a layperson is seated on a low seat, etc.]"

"If a bhikṣu, being himself unrighteous and out of malice and anger, should defame a bhikṣu who is free from a pārājika offense with groundless charges of a pārājika offense, it constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
"How should I uphold it? The Buddha said,
"It should be upheld by the two divisions of the Saṃgha."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, being herself unrighteous and out of malice and anger, slanders a bhikṣuṇī who is free from a pārājika offense with groundless charges of a pārājika offense, desiring to destroy her holy life."
If, at a later time, whether questioned or not, that bhikṣuṇī says:
"This matter of mine was groundless; I slandered out of a state of malice," then that bhikṣuṇī has committed an initial saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which is to be confessed.
The Elder Upāli again asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, you have already established a precept for the bhikṣus:
‘If a bhikṣu, being himself unrighteous and out of malice and anger, takes a portion or something resembling a portion from a different category, it constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.’”
"How should I uphold it? The Buddha said:
"It should be upheld by the two divisions of the Saṃgha."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, being herself unrighteous and out of malice and anger, takes a fragment or something resembling a fragment from a different category and accuses a bhikṣuṇī who is not guilty of a pārājika offense of having committed a pārājika offense, desiring to destroy her holy life."
At a later time, whether questioned or not, that bhikṣuṇī says:
"In this matter, I took a fragment or something resembling a fragment from a different category; out of anger, I slandered that bhikṣuṇī."
"Upon the first offense, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and may be expiated.
At that time, the Śākyas made this mutual agreement:
"We shall not intermarry with those of commoner status; should anyone violate this, they shall be severely punished!"

At that time, a woman of the Śākya clan, Kṛṣṇā Licchavī, had lost her husband. Her husband’s younger brother wished to take her as his wife, but she would not consent. When he made this request three times, she vowed not to grant it.
He then thought to himself: "This woman must surely have an illicit attachment to another; I shall kill her!"
She then made an excuse, saying she was holding a memorial service for her brother, and said to him, "I am holding a service for your husband; come and offer incense!
When he had gone there, she made him drunk with wine, engaged in impure acts with him, and then scratched his flesh with her fingernails. She then reported the matter to the authorities, saying:
"The Licchavi woman Kālī is my wife, yet she is now having an illicit affair with another man!
The official immediately dispatched men to arrest her.
When the woman awoke from her intoxication, she saw that her body was wounded and bruised in many places, and she thought to herself:
"This man must surely be put to death!
Thinking thus, he fled to Śrāvastī and went to the bhikṣuṇīs to leave the household life and study the Path.
As the officials could not capture him, they learned that he had gone to Śrāvastī and sent a formal letter to King Prasenajit, saying:
"In my country, women who commit crimes deserve death; if they defect to your country, you should send them back to me!
Likewise, if your country has criminals who defect to mine, I shall also send them back."
At that time, King Prasenajit immediately asked his attendants,
"Has such a woman entered my kingdom? They replied:
“There are! The bhikṣuṇīs have already been ordained into the path.
Your Majesty previously issued a decree:”
"If there were anyone within my realm who committed an offense against a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, they would be subject to severe punishment.
Now that they have already left the household life, no one dares to insult or humiliate them."
The King then sent a reply in writing, saying:
"It is true that this woman came into my kingdom; she has now entered the religious life, and her offense cannot be pursued.
If there is any other matter, I shall respectfully follow your instructions!"
The Śākyas then reviled and scolded them, saying:
"If one commits such a transgression, they can no longer be disciplined; they will throw our country into chaos!
Among these bhikṣuṇīs, there is no longer any distinction between those who can be saved and those who cannot; what kind of path is this?"
"They lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and questioned the bhikṣuṇīs:
“Is it truly so for you? They replied, “It is truly so.”
"World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked her in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus: "I now establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly ordains a woman who has committed an offense as a bhikṣuṇī, that bhikṣuṇī commits an initial saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which must be confessed.'"
Furthermore, there were female thieves, female pickpockets, and women condemned to death, to whom the householders said:
"If you can leave the household life, we shall spare your lives!"
She then sought to go forth and immediately addressed the bhikṣuṇīs,
saying, "I pray that you will grant me ordination! The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to ordain those such as yourselves.
They reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If the master permits it, I allow bhikṣuṇīs to ordain them."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman with an offense has not been permitted by her guardian, should ordain her, that bhikṣuṇī commits an initial saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which is to be confessed."
Furthermore, there were women who had committed offenses and were unable to go forth in the Buddha-dharma, so they entered among the non-Buddhist sects.
Later, when the lay devotees saw them, some said:
"These are our women who committed offenses; we shall seize their non-Buddhist robes!"
Some said, "The fact that he is an outsider who has left the household life is already a sufficient punishment;
he may well depart! They then released him.
These women later approached the bhikṣuṇīs and spoke thus:
"Sisters! It was not that we lacked reverence and faith in the Buddha’s Dharma that we went forth among the outsiders."
"Sisters, we were unwilling to be ordained, but being driven by necessity, we entered the fold of the non-Buddhists!
We were afraid of this, yet now you have granted us permission to leave the household life; we pray that you will compassionately ordain us!"
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there are women with offenses who have already left the household life, I now permit their ordination!"
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī knows that a woman with a transgression has not been permitted by her guardian to go forth into the religious life—excepting those who have previously gone forth."
"This bhikṣuṇī has committed her first saṃghāvaśeṣa offense; she must confess it.
Regarding "one who has committed an offense":
whether she has committed adultery or theft, this is called having committed an offense.
The Master: One who is the source of both killing and giving life is called a master.

If a bhikṣuṇī conceives the intention to ordain this woman, and proceeds through the preparatory means up to the assembly of the Saṃgha, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense for all stages until the three *karmavācanās* are completed.
When the third *karmavācanā* is completed, the preceptor commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
the rest of the *bhikṣuṇī* saṃgha all commit a *sthūlātyaya*.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Ucchā repeatedly committed offenses:

Because she was improper in both ascending and descending from her bed, ate repeatedly, ate apart from the community, and entered other households at improper times, the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha performed an act of *tajjaniya-kamma* (censure) against her for not recognizing her offense.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, knowing that Ucchā’s mind was not yet subdued and that she did not show respect or obedience toward the Saṃgha, did not follow the assembly but instead, together with her own followers, performed the act of releasing her from the suspension outside the boundary.
Once that bhikṣuṇī had been released from her suspension, she became even more arrogant and showed no respect for the Saṃgha.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they rebuked her in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and asked Stūlanandā:
"Is it true that you did so? She replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now, for the sake of the bhikṣuṇīs, I shall establish this precept. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that the Saṃgha has lawfully expelled another bhikṣuṇī who is not yet tamed in mind and does not comply with the Saṃgha, should herself, together with her followers, effect the revocation of that expulsion outside the boundary, this bhikṣuṇī commits an initial saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which is to be confessed.'"
Regarding the intent to carry out a formal act of suspension (*pravāsanīya*) and the preparatory efforts, up until the third *karmavācanā* has not yet been completed,
all constitute a *duṣkṛta*. Once the three *karmavācanās* are completed, the presiding monk (*karmācārya*) commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*,
while the rest of the monks commit a *sthūlātyaya*.

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs were traveling alone on a road. When laypeople saw them, they mocked them with coarse and lewd words of sexual desire; some seized and fondled them, while others sought to engage in impure acts with them.
Furthermore, there were many bhikṣuṇīs traveling in the company of merchants. When Steyanandā saw a certain man, a defiled attachment arose in her mind, and she gradually fell behind the group.
The bhikṣuṇīs said to her:
"Why do you not travel quickly to catch up with your companions?
This place is fearsome; do not be plundered by wicked people!"
He replied, "Did you see the person who came later? The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"I see him! said Thullanandā. "I see this man, and my heart is deeply attached to him!"
The bhikṣuṇīs rebuked her, saying:
"How could you, while on the road, become lustfully attached to a man?
Furthermore, there were many other bhikṣuṇīs who crossed a river to collect cow dung; having already crossed, the water rose and they were unable to return, whereupon they were plundered by bandits.
Furthermore, there were certain bhikṣuṇīs who slept alone and consequently lost their robes and bowls, or violated their celibacy.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw or heard of this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and asked the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Is it true that you did so? They replied: [Yes, it is true.]
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣuṇī travels alone, stays overnight alone, crosses a body of water alone, or walks behind a man alone on a road with lustful attachment, that bhikṣuṇī has committed an initial saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and must confess it.'"
At that time, there were some bhikṣuṇīs traveling on the road who, being beset by doubt and fear, fled toward a village to seek refuge in the homes of their relatives.
Furthermore, there were other bhikṣuṇīs who were utterly exhausted from the journey, as well as those who were old or sick and unable to keep pace with the others;
some encountered shallow water, while others encountered bridges or boats, yet they did not dare cross alone.
There was a lodging where she feared men and did not dare to stay overnight alone in another place.
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know what to do and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of these matters, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"In cases where there is a specific cause and condition, I permit you to go alone according to your own will.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"

"If a bhikṣuṇī travels alone, sleeps alone, crosses water alone, or walks behind a man alone on the road with a mind of attachment, except when there is a valid reason, this bhikṣuṇī commits an initial *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which is to be confessed."
As for "circumstances":

when fleeing in fear; when one is so exhausted by old age or illness that one cannot keep pace with companions; at a place where the water is narrow and shallow, or where there is a bridge or boat; or in a place where one fears men—these are called circumstances.
If he travels alone where there are no villages, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for half a *yojana*;
if there are villages, from one village to another, it is likewise a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
If one is behind [the nuns] and sees the bhikṣuṇī from afar but does not hear her voice;
or if one hears her voice but does not see her form—in both cases, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one neither sees nor hears her, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If one crosses water alone, and the water is ten cubits wide and half a thigh deep, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is less than that, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
When staying overnight, one should ensure that their hands can reach one another.
If they do not reach [the destination], it is a *sthūlātyaya* during the first watch and the middle watch of the night;
when the dawn light appears, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

At that time, a certain householder offered his residence as a gift to the community of bhikṣus. The community of bhikṣus then exchanged it with the community of bhikṣuṇīs for the Anāthapiṇḍika Grove.

Later, Queen Mallikā offered the royal garden to the community of bhikṣuṇīs. The community of bhikṣuṇīs demolished the houses at the previously exchanged site and rebuilt them within the royal garden; consequently, the former location became an empty space.
At that time, the householder’s son Dānavent made this thought:
"In the past, my father gave this dwelling to the Saṅgha, and the Saṅgha traded it for the nuns.
Now that the nuns no longer reside there, I may take it back and cultivate crops upon it."
She then took possession of it.
The bhikṣuṇīs said to her,
"Do not take the property of the Saṃgha!"
She replied, "Although my father gave it to the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha did not use it; therefore, it should rightfully revert to me! The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"We will not relinquish this land; do not go to the authorities and speak against us, lest we be made to pay even more!
Since he was unwilling to return it, they immediately went to the authorities and spoke of the matter, whereupon he was forced to pay a great amount.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled them, saying:
"How can these bhikṣuṇīs go to the authorities to speak against others, causing them to lose their great wealth?
If these women will even speak out against those who provide them with offerings, how much more so would they do so toward others!"
"You lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they reprimanded her in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and questioned the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Is it truly so for you? They replied, "It is truly so."
"World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī goes to an official and speaks against someone, this bhikṣuṇī commits an initial *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which is to be confessed.
If a bhikṣuṇī is mistreated by others, she should inform her parents;
if she has no parents, she should inform her kinsmen."
If there are no relatives, one should inform the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
If bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs who possess the power to do so fail to provide protection, it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
When speaking, one should say:
"He has slighted me. Please reprimand and admonish him for my sake!"
One should not speak thus.
If one goes to an official to bring charges against another person, for each round-trip, it constitutes one *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is an *dukkaṭa*.
At that time, there was a merchant whose wife had died, and he thought to himself:
"Where shall I now seek a beautiful wife?
At that moment, the bhikṣuṇī Caṇḍā Sumana had a disciple named Sumā who was exceptionally beautiful; seeing her, the merchant conceived a mind of lustful attachment and thought:
"By using food as an inducement, we may perhaps obtain the fruit.
He then said to them, "If you require ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, *pūyāśana*, or *khādya*, you may take all of these from me."
That bhikṣuṇī then went to fetch it.
Once they had become familiar with one another, she asked the bhikṣuṇī:
"Do you know my intention in giving you food?"
He replied, "You have given me food for the sake of seeking merit.
The other said:
"It is not for this reason!
I have lost my wife, and seeing your pure cultivation, I am deeply attracted to you; can you restrain yourself? He replied:
"I cannot! The man spoke again:
"If you will become my wife, I shall provide you with rare treasures, most exquisite clothing, and food and drink according to the season, ensuring that you never lack for anything."
She answered as she had before.
When the other merchants saw this, they assisted in pressuring her, saying:
"If you do not wish to become another's wife, for what reason did you accept his food and drink?"
"If you truly cannot do so, we shall take away your robes and bowl!
Or again, some said:
"Send him away quickly; let no one hear of this!"
"If the King were to find out, he would surely punish us severely!
When the laypeople heard this, they criticized and rebuked them, saying,
"How can a bhikṣuṇī accept food and drink from a man who is attached to her?"
"These women have no conduct befitting śramaṇīs; they destroy the dharma of the śramaṇīs!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they reprimanded them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and asked the bhikṣuṇī Sumā:
"Is it true that you did so? She replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now I shall establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī accepts food or drink from a man who harbors lustful intentions toward her, that bhikṣuṇī commits an initial saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which is to be confessed.'"
There were certain men who invited bhikṣuṇīs for meals before or after [the midday meal], and in doing so, they gave rise to defiled and attached thoughts.
The bhikṣuṇīs, knowing this, did not dare accept the invitations and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, being free from a mind of attachment, accepts food or drink from a man who has a mind of attachment, and thereby commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense—that is impossible."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, with a mind of attachment, accepts food or drink from a man who has a mind of attachment, that bhikṣuṇī commits an initial saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which is to be confessed."
Furthermore, there was another bhikṣuṇī who, with a mind of attachment, accepted food and drink from a man with a mind of attachment. Having accepted it, she felt doubt:
"I fear I have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense!"
She then took it back and gave it to the other bhikṣuṇīs.
The other bhikṣuṇīs asked, "Why did you not eat this delicious food?
She answered them fully with the facts of the matter, and the other bhikṣuṇīs said:
"What you fear, I too should fear!
[The monk] reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, with a mind of attachment, receives food from the hand of a man who has a mind of attachment;
if she does not eat it herself but gives it to another to eat, in all such cases there is no offense."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, with a mind of attachment, receives food with her own hand from a man who has a mind of attachment and eats it, that bhikṣuṇī commits an initial saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which is to be confessed."
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
At that time, those merchants thought again:
"I previously attempted to entice that bhikṣuṇī with food; was it because our association had been too brief that we did not succeed?"
"Now I shall further entice him with food; perhaps his long-held resolve will change!
He then went to the man's location and said, "What I previously did was a mere jest, which led to my being insolent. I pray that you accept my repentance!"
"From now on, as before, receive food from me.
That bhikṣuṇī said: "Stop, stop!"
"Man! Previously you troubled me, causing the Buddha to reprimand you with severity and leading him to establish precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs.
Why should you seek further humiliation today?"
Her preceptor said to that bhikṣuṇī, "Previously you were able to obtain much fine food and drink; why can you no longer do so now? She replied:
"That person previously offended me, and because of that, the Buddha established a precept; therefore, I dare not take it again!
The Upādhyāya spoke again:
"You need only refrain from giving rise to defiled attachment; what hardship is there in taking food?"
"If another person develops defiled attachment, how does that concern you?
That bhikṣuṇī reproached her preceptor, saying:
"The Buddha has in various ways censured intimacy with men and praised staying far away from them."
"How can you instruct me to accept food from a man with a mind of lustful attachment?
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked that teacher, saying:
"How can you instruct your disciple to receive food from a man with a mind of lustful attachment?"
Having rebuked her in various ways, he reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and asked Caṇḍa Sumanā:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī instructs another bhikṣuṇī to speak these words:’”
"You need only refrain from giving rise to defiled attachment; what harm is there in accepting food and drink from a man with whom you have such attachment?
This nun has committed her first *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which is to be confessed.
"If one gives this instruction, for every utterance there is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. Upāli asked again:"
“The Blessed One has already laid down a precept for the bhikṣus:
‘If a bhikṣu makes diligent efforts to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, it constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.’”
"How should I uphold it? The Buddha said,
"It shall be upheld by the two divisions of the Saṃgha."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī exerts herself with skillful means to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṅgha, the other bhikṣuṇīs should say to that bhikṣuṇī:

'Do not exert yourself with skillful means to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṅgha. You should instead be in harmony with the Saṅgha; for when the Saṅgha is in harmony, it is joyful and free from strife, being of one mind and one training, like water and milk mixed together, so that you may together propagate the Teacher’s instruction and live in peace and happiness.'"
If, after being admonished in this manner, she persists and does not relinquish [her position], she should be admonished a second and a third time.
If, after the second and third admonitions, she relinquishes this matter, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī, having been admonished three times, commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and must undergo confession.
Upāli asked again: "The World-Honored One has already established a precept for the bhikṣus:
'If a bhikṣu assists in the schism of a harmonious Saṃgha, it constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.'"
"How should I uphold it? The Buddha said,
"It should be upheld by the two divisions of the Saṃgha."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī assists in the schism of a harmonious Saṃgha—whether it be one, two, or many—and says to the other bhikṣuṇīs:
'What these bhikṣuṇīs say is said with knowledge, not said without knowledge;'"
"They preach the Dharma and do not preach what is not Dharma;
they preach the Vinaya and do not preach what is not Vinaya—all of which is what our hearts accept and delight in.
The bhikṣuṇīs said to these bhikṣuṇīs:
"Do not speak these words: 'What this bhikṣuṇī has said was said knowingly, not unknowingly;
she spoke the Dharma, not what is not Dharma.'"
"To speak of what is in accordance with the Vinaya and not speak of what is contrary to the Vinaya is precisely what our minds accept and delight in. Why is this?
Because these bhikṣuṇīs do not speak with knowledge, they do not speak the Dharma, and they do not speak the Vinaya.
Do not take pleasure in assisting those who would break the harmony of the Saṃgha; you should instead take pleasure in assisting those who bring about its harmony.

Because the Saṃgha is in harmony, it dwells in joy and without contention, being of one mind and one training, like water and milk mixed together, collectively upholding the Teacher’s instruction and practicing in peace and happiness.
"If she is thus admonished and yet persists in her refusal to relinquish [the matter], she should be admonished a second and a third time.
If, after the second and third admonitions, she relinquishes the matter, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī, having been admonished three times, commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which is to be confessed."
Upāli asked again: “The World-honored One has already laid down a precept for the bhikṣus:
‘If a bhikṣu is of evil character and difficult to speak with, and while training together with the bhikṣus in the Sūtra of the Precepts, repeatedly commits offenses up to the saṃghāvaśeṣa.’”
"How should I uphold it? The Buddha said,
"It shall be upheld by the two divisions of the Saṃgha."
From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī is of an evil nature and difficult to speak with, and having studied the *Śīla-vinaya* (Precepts Sūtra) together with the other bhikṣuṇīs, repeatedly commits offenses."
When the bhikṣuṇīs admonished her for her transgression in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, she replied:
"Ayyās, do not speak to me of what is good or what is evil!"
"I shall not address you with either pleasant or unpleasant words.
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke to her again, saying:
"Do not act so as to make yourself unaddressable!"
"You should speak words in accordance with the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs, and the bhikṣuṇīs should likewise speak words in accordance with the Dharma to you.
In this way, through mutual instruction and mutual purification of offenses, you shall constitute the Saṃgha of the Tathāgata."
"If she is thus admonished and persists in not relinquishing [the matter], she should be admonished a second and third time.
If, after the second and third admonitions, she relinquishes this matter, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī, having been admonished three times, commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and must confess her transgression."
Upāli asked again: "The World-Honored One has already laid down a precept for the bhikṣus:
'If a bhikṣu, residing in dependence upon a village, commits evil conduct and defiles a family, up to and including a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.'"
"How should I uphold it? The Buddha said,
"It should be upheld by the two divisions of the Saṃgha."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī resides in dependence upon a village and engages in evil conduct that defiles the families there—
if her evil conduct is seen, heard, and known by all;..."
She has corrupted their families, as is known through both seeing and hearing.
The bhikṣuṇīs say to this bhikṣuṇī:
"You have engaged in evil conduct and corrupted their families."
I have seen, heard, and known that you have engaged in evil conduct;
I have also seen, heard, and known that you have defiled families.
You must depart; you should not remain here!
That bhikṣuṇī said: "The venerable ladies act according to desire, hatred, delusion, and fear. Why is that?"
"There are bhikṣuṇīs who have committed such identical offenses, yet some are expelled while others are not.
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke to her again, saying: "Do not speak these words:"
“Venerable sisters, following their own desire, hatred, delusion, or fear, there are bhikṣuṇīs who have committed such identical offenses, yet some are expelled while others are not.
You have engaged in evil conduct and defiled the families of others.”
We have seen, heard, and known that you engage in evil conduct;
we have also seen, heard, and known that you defile families. You must abandon these words spoken out of attachment, aversion, delusion, or fear.
Depart from here; you should not remain among us.
If, after being admonished in this manner, she persists and does not relinquish [her position], she should be admonished a second and a third time.
If, after the second and third admonitions, she relinquishes this matter, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī, having been admonished three times, commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and must confess her transgression.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs Śuklā and Bhadrā engaged in misconduct together; they acquired an evil reputation and concealed their offenses from one another, thereby causing distress to the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣuṇīs said to them:
"You have committed evil deeds and have acquired an evil reputation. Separate yourselves;
abandon these acts of misconduct that cause distress to the Saṃgha! By doing so, you will increase and expand within the Buddha-dharma and attain a dwelling in peace and happiness!"
The two bhikṣuṇīs said:
"We have committed no evil deeds, nor do we have an evil reputation, nor have we caused distress to the Saṃgha.
There are two other bhikṣuṇīs here who together commit evil deeds, have an evil reputation, and cause distress to the Saṃgha."
The bhikṣuṇīs said: "Do not speak such words!
For what reason?
"In this community, there are no other two bhikṣuṇīs who commit evil acts to harass the Saṃgha except for you two.

You should distance yourselves from one another and abandon these evil deeds that provoke and disturb the Saṃgha; thus you shall increase and expand within the Buddha-dharma and attain dwelling in peace and happiness!"
When they had thus admonished them, the two bhikṣuṇīs stubbornly persisted and would not relinquish their position. The bhikṣuṇīs reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and questioned those two bhikṣuṇīs:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"A single bhikṣuṇī who is on friendly terms with those two bhikṣuṇīs should be sent to a secluded place to admonish them."
If she accepts it, that is well;
if she does not accept it, a large number of bhikṣuṇīs should go to admonish her; if she accepts it, that is well;
if she does not accept it, the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs should go to admonish her.
The bhikṣus received the instruction and immediately commanded the bhikṣuṇīs to go and admonish them; however, after three attempts, they all refused to comply.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs reprimanded them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, because of this matter, assembled the two divisions of the Saṃgha. After he had rebuked those two bhikṣuṇīs from afar in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If two bhikṣuṇīs together commit evil deeds, acquire an evil reputation, conceal each other's offenses, and cause vexation to the Saṃgha...'"
The bhikṣuṇīs said to them:
"You two bhikṣuṇīs have committed evil deeds and have acquired an evil reputation; you conceal each other's offenses and cause distress to the Saṃgha."
"You should distance yourselves from one another, abandon these evil deeds that cause provocation to the Saṃgha, and increase within the Buddha-dharma so that you may dwell in peace and happiness!
Those two bhikṣuṇīs replied,
"We have committed no evil acts, we have no evil reputation, we do not conceal our faults from one another, nor do we provoke the Saṃgha."
"In this community there are two other bhikṣuṇīs who together commit evil deeds and cause distress to the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke to them again, saying:
"Do not speak such words!"
Why is this? Because within this community there are no other two bhikṣuṇīs who commit evil acts to harass the Saṃgha, except for yourselves.

You should distance yourselves from one another, abandon these evil deeds and the acts of harassing the Saṃgha, so that you may increase and expand within the Buddha-dharma and dwell in peace and happiness!
If, despite being admonished in this manner, she persists and does not relinquish [the matter], she should be admonished a second and a third time.
If, after the second and third admonitions, she relinquishes the matter, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī, having been admonished three times, commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and must undergo confession.
"Mutually concealing offenses" refers to:
whether it be a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *sthūlātyaya*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, a *duṣkṛta*, or failing to guard one's speech.
Regarding "disturbing the Saṃgha":
whether it be during the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, or various *karmavācanas*, all are as explained in the section on Devadatta’s schism of the Saṃgha.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs Śuklā and Bhadrā engaged in misconduct and acquired an evil reputation; yet, as described above, they caused the Buddha’s Dharma to flourish and spread, and they themselves dwelt in peace and happiness.
The two bhikṣuṇīs said:
"We have committed no evil deeds, nor have we caused any disturbance to the Saṃgha.
It is because the Saṃgha sees us as weak and treats us with contempt that they speak such words!"
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke again: "Do not say such things!
For what reason?"
The Sangha does not see your weakness, nor do they treat you with contempt.

You yourselves have committed evil deeds and provoked the Sangha; you should distance yourselves from one another, abandon these evil acts and the provocation of the Sangha, so that you may flourish within the Buddha-dharma and dwell in peace and happiness!
When she was thus admonished, she persisted and would not relinquish her position.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs rebuked her, leading up to the present time when the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs is established, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If two bhikṣuṇīs engage in misconduct together, acquire an evil reputation, and conceal each other's offenses, thereby causing distress to the Saṃgha.'"
The bhikṣuṇīs said to them:
"You two bhikṣuṇīs must not together engage in evil conduct, incur an evil reputation, conceal each other's offenses, and cause distress to the Saṃgha."

"You should distance yourselves from one another, abandon these acts of wrongdoing that cause offense to the Saṃgha, and increase within the Buddha-dharma so that you may dwell in peace and happiness!
The two bhikṣuṇīs replied, "We have committed no evil deeds,
we have no evil reputation, we have not concealed our offenses from one another, nor have we caused offense to the Saṃgha."
"The monks saw that we were weak and, because they treated us with contempt,
spoke such words! The bhikṣuṇīs replied again,
"Do not speak such words!"
Why is this? The Saṃgha does not see your weakness and treats you with contempt!

You should distance yourselves from one another and abandon these acts of wrongdoing that disturb the Saṃgha; thus you shall increase within the Buddha-dharma and attain dwelling in peace and happiness!
If, after being admonished in this manner, she persists and does not relinquish it, she should be admonished a second and a third time.
If, after the second and third admonitions, she relinquishes the matter, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī, having been admonished three times, commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and must confess her transgression.
The rest is as stated above.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, Chanda’s mother was named Sumana; because she was of an evil disposition, people at the time came to call her Caṇḍa-Sumana.

She was fond of quarreling with others, and when the Saṃgha adjudicated the matter, she immediately claimed that the Saṃgha acted out of favoritism, hatred, delusion, and fear. The bhikṣuṇīs said to her:
"Do not be fond of quarreling with others, and do not speak these words:
'The Saṃgha acts out of favoritism, hatred, delusion, and fear!'"
Why is this? Because the Saṃgha does not follow after craving, aversion, delusion, or fear.
Abandon these words, and you shall increase and expand within the Buddha-dharma, attaining a dwelling in peace and happiness!
When she was thus admonished, she persisted and would not relinquish her position; consequently, the rules for bhikṣuṇīs were now established as previously described.
From this time forward, this precept should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī is fond of quarreling with others, and the Saṃgha has adjudicated the matter, yet she says that the Saṃgha acts out of favoritism, hatred, delusion, or fear, and the bhikṣuṇīs say to her:"
"Do not take pleasure in quarreling with others, and do not speak such words as:
'The Saṃgha follows favoritism, anger, delusion, and fear. Why is this?..."

"The Saṃgha does not follow after craving, aversion, delusion, or fear; you should abandon these words, so that you may increase and expand within the Buddha’s Dharma and dwell in peace and happiness!
If, despite being thus admonished, they persist and do not relinquish [their position], they should be admonished a second and a third time.
If, upon the second and third admonitions, she relinquishes this matter, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī, having been admonished three times, commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and must confess her transgression.
The rest is as stated above.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Caṇḍasumana was fond of quarreling with others; when the Saṃgha adjudicated the matter against her, she spoke with anger:
"I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṃgha, and I renounce the precepts to become a follower of an external path."
"Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas also train in the precepts and possess a sense of shame; I shall practice the pure holy life among them!
The bhikṣuṇīs said to her: "Do not take pleasure in quarreling with others; do not speak such words."
"I shall abandon the Buddha, and even there I shall practice the holy life!
Why is this? Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas lack the training in precepts and lack shame and remorse; how could you possibly practice the holy life among them?
"Abandon this evil view; by doing so, you will increase and broaden your practice within the Buddha-dharma and attain a dwelling in peace and happiness!
Although she was thus admonished, she stubbornly persisted and would not relinquish it. Consequently, as previously described, the Buddha has now established a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī is fond of quarreling with others, and the Saṃgha has settled the matter, she then says:
"I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṃgha, and I renounce the precepts to become a follower of a non-Buddhist path."'"
"Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas also train in the precepts and possess a sense of shame; I shall practice the pure holy life among them!
When the bhikṣuṇīs said to her, "Do not take pleasure in quarreling with others; do not speak such words:"
“I renounce the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha! Why is this?

“If a bhikṣuṇī uses double-tongued speech to cause dissension among bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika.

“If a bhikṣuṇī preaches the Dharma to a man and exceeds five or six words, except when there is a woman present who understands the distinction between what is well-spoken and what is ill-spoken, it is a pāyattika.”
“If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that the Saṃgha has already settled a matter in accordance with the Dharma, should reopen it, she commits a pāyattika offense.
“If a bhikṣuṇī teaches a woman who has not yet received full ordination the sūtras and recites them together with her, she commits a pāyattika offense.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī sleeps in the same room as a woman who has not yet received full ordination for more than two nights, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī speaks to a woman who has not yet received full ordination about having attained superhuman states (uttarimanussa-dhamma), saying:
'I know thus; I see thus.'"
If it is true, it is a *pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing of a bhikṣuṇī’s grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), should speak of it to a woman who has not yet received full ordination, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha, it is a *pāyattika*."
"If a bhikṣuṇī speaks thus: 'What is the use of these minor precepts?
When these precepts are recited, they cause people distress!'"
"To disparage the precepts in such a manner constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
The ten items are concluded. "If a bhikṣuṇī cuts down a 'village of spirits' herself, or causes another to cut it down, saying: 'Cut this!'"
“An *pāyattika*. “If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally does not answer when questioned, it is an *pāyattika*.
“If a bhikṣuṇī falsely slanders a person appointed by the Saṃgha, it is an *pāyattika*.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, on an open space, spreads bedding belonging to the Saṃgha herself, or causes another to spread it;
or if it has been spread by another, she sits or lies down upon it."
"When departing, if a bhikṣuṇī does not herself put away [the bedding], nor instruct another to put it away, nor entrust someone else with putting it away, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, within a monastic dwelling, spreads out a communal bed or bedding herself, or causes another to spread it;

or if it has been spread by another, and she sits upon it or lies down on it, then when departing, if she does not herself put it away, nor instruct another to put it away, nor entrust someone else with putting it away, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure, personally drags a bhikṣuṇī out of a monastery cell, or causes another to drag her out, saying these words: ‘Get out! Begone!’”
"Do not stay here! [If she does so, it is] a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another has already spread bedding, later comes and forcibly spreads it herself or causes someone else to spread it, thinking:..."
"If you do not wish to remain, you shall depart of your own accord.
This constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, while on an upper story of a multi-storied monastery building, sits or lies down with force upon a rope bed or wooden bed with pointed legs, it is a *pāyattika* offense."
“If a bhikṣuṇī knows that water contains living organisms, yet takes it to pour on mud, or uses it for food, drink, or other purposes, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī eats repeatedly, except when there is a valid reason, it is a pāyattika.”
"Regarding the 'causes and conditions':
the time of illness, the time for robes, and the time for the distribution of robes—these are called causes and conditions.
[The twentieth rule concludes. "If a bhikṣuṇī accepts an invitation for a communal meal from individuals, except when there is a cause and condition, it is a pāyattika offense."
The "causes and conditions" are:

the time of illness, the time for robes, the time for receiving robes, the time for making robes, the time of traveling on a road, the time of traveling by boat, and the time of a great assembly; these are called causes and conditions.
“If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, at a place where a single meal is being offered, should eat more than one meal, it is a pāyattika.

“If a bhikṣuṇī goes to the home of a layperson and they freely offer her much food and drink—whether parched grain or flour—if she does not eat there, she may accept two or three bowls; having left, she must eat it together with other bhikṣuṇīs.”
"If, being free from illness, she accepts food beyond this limit and does not share it with other bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished her meal, eats food without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (leftover-food) rite, it is a pāyattika."

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has finished her meal, forcibly urges her to eat without performing the ritual for leftover food (kṛtapiṇḍapāta), desiring to cause the other to commit an offense, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī places food into her mouth without having received it [from another], except for tasting food, tooth-sticks, and water, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika.”
“If a bhikṣuṇī eats food that has been kept overnight, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī sits in a secluded place with a man inside a house where food is being prepared, it is a pāyattika.”
“If a bhikṣuṇī observes an army on the march, it is a pāyattika.
[The thirtieth rule is concluded. “If a bhikṣuṇī has a reason to go into an army and stays there for two or three nights;
if she exceeds that, it is a pāyattika.”
“If a bhikṣuṇī, having a reason, stays in an army for two or three nights and observes the arraying of troops or their engaging in battle, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī speaks thus: ‘As I understand the Buddha’s teaching, the things that obstruct the path do not actually obstruct the path,’ [it is a pāyattika].”
The bhikṣuṇīs said to that bhikṣuṇī: "Do not speak such words!
Do not slander the Buddha; do not falsely accuse the Buddha!"
"The Buddha has taught that these dharmas which obstruct the Path truly do obstruct the Path.
You must abandon this evil, false view!
If, after being admonished in this way, he persists and does not abandon it, he should be admonished a second and a third time.
"If, after a second and third admonition, she abandons this matter, it is well;
if she does not abandon it, it is a *pāyattika*.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has not repented according to the Dharma and has not abandoned her evil and heterodox views, speaks with her, sits with her, sleeps with her, or engages in communal affairs with her, it is a *pāyattika*."
“If a śrāmaṇerikā should speak these words:
‘As I understand what the Buddha has taught, if one experiences the five desires,
they cannot obstruct the Path,’ the bhikṣuṇīs should say to that śrāmaṇerikā:”
"Do not speak such words!
Do not slander the Buddha; do not misrepresent the Buddha!
The Buddha has said that the five desires obstruct the Path, and they truly can obstruct the Path."
"You, śrāmaṇerī, must abandon this evil, heterodox view!
If she is thus instructed yet persists in not abandoning it, she should be instructed a second and a third time.
If, after the second and third instructions, she abandons this matter, it is well.
If she does not relinquish them, the bhikṣuṇīs should say to this śrāmaṇerī: "Leave!
From now on, do not say that the Buddha is your teacher, and do not walk behind the bhikṣuṇīs!"
"Whereas other śrāmaṇerikās are permitted to stay together with the bhikṣuṇīs for two nights, you have no such privilege.
Fool, get out! Begone! Do not stay here!"
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a śrāmaṇerī has been lawfully expelled, keeps her, employs her, lives with her, or converses with her, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally causes another bhikṣuṇī to feel doubt or regret, thinking:
'I shall cause this bhikṣuṇī to be troubled, even if only for a short time,' [it is a pāyattika]."
“An *pāyattika*. “If a bhikṣuṇī, when the Saṃgha is conducting its business, rises and leaves without having given her consent (*chanda*), it is an *pāyattika*.
“If a bhikṣuṇī tickles another bhikṣuṇī, it is an *pāyattika*.”
“If a bhikṣuṇī plays in the water, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī sleeps in the same room as a man, it is a pāyattika.”
[The forty rules are concluded. "If a bhikṣuṇī drinks alcohol, it is a pāyattika. If a bhikṣuṇī treats her teacher with disrespect, it is a pāyattika."
"If a bhikṣuṇī digs the earth herself,
or causes another to dig it, saying: 'Dig here!'"
“[This constitutes] a *pāyattika*.
“If a bhikṣuṇī, after having engaged in a dispute, listens in silence with the thought:
‘I shall remember and retain what these bhikṣuṇīs say.’”
“An offense of expiation (pāyattika).
“If a bhikṣuṇī accepts an invitation for the four-month *pravāraṇā*;
if she accepts beyond this limit—except for a renewed invitation, a personally delivered invitation, or a long-term invitation—it is an offense of expiation.”
"If a bhikṣuṇī repeatedly commits offenses and the other bhikṣuṇīs admonish her in accordance with the Dharma, she says:
'I will not train in this precept!'"
"You should ask other bhikṣuṇīs who uphold the Dharma and uphold the Vinaya!
This is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, at the time of the recitation of the precepts, speaks these words:"
"I have only now learned that this Dharma was recited in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* during the half-monthly *poṣadha*.

If the other bhikṣuṇīs know that this bhikṣuṇī has already sat through the recitation of the precepts two or three times, she cannot escape by claiming ignorance. She shall be dealt with according to the law for the offense she has committed;
furthermore, her ignorance must be rebuked:
"What you have done is unwholesome!
When the precepts were being recited, you did not listen with a single-minded focus, nor did you take them to heart.
This constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
“If a bhikṣuṇī makes an appointment with a thief to travel together along a road, from one village to another village, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī makes an appointment with a man to travel together along a road, from one village to another village, it is a pāyattika.”
“If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, lights a fire for the purpose of warming herself, or causes another to light one, it is a pāyattika.
[Fifty rules concluded. “If a bhikṣuṇī takes up a jewel or anything equivalent to a jewel, or causes another to take it up—except within a monastery or a lodging—it is a pāyattika.”
"If one takes treasure or items such as treasure within a monastic dwelling or at a lodging site, and a claimant later appears to seek them, they must be returned.
This matter should be handled in this way!
"If a bhikṣuṇī bathes within a half-month, except for a special cause, it is a pāyattika."
"Circumstances" refers to:
times of illness, times of work, times of traveling on a road, times of wind and rain, and times of heat; these are called circumstances.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger, strikes another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger, makes a threatening gesture with her hand toward another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally terrifies another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.”
“If a bhikṣuṇī, with groundless charges of a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, slanders another bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*.
“If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī:
‘Come together to various households; I will give you much delicious food and drink!’”
Having arrived, he would not give [anything] and spoke these words: "Go away!
It is not pleasant for me to sit or speak with you; it is pleasant for me to sit alone and speak alone!"
If, with the intent to cause annoyance, [she acts thus], it is a *pāyattika*.
"If a bhikṣuṇī acquires a new robe, she should mark it with one of three colors:
blue, black, or madder-brown."
"If one does not make a mark with three colors, it is a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣuṇī, for the sake of amusement, hides another bhikṣuṇī’s robe, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, or any such individual article of daily life, or causes someone else to hide it, it is a *pāyattika*."
“If a bhikṣuṇī, when the Saṃgha is conducting its business, has already given her consent (chanda) in accordance with the Dharma, yet later revokes it, she commits a pāyattika.
[The sixty rules are concluded. “If a bhikṣuṇī speaks thus:
‘The bhikṣuṇīs give away property belonging to the Saṃgha to those they are acquainted with,’ [she commits a pāyattika].”
“An *pāyattika*. If a bhikṣuṇī, having given a pure gift of clothing to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, forcibly takes it back, it is an *pāyattika*.”

"If a bhikṣuṇī, having accepted an invitation, goes from house to house before or after a meal without approaching another bhikṣuṇī to inform her, except when there is a valid reason, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the "circumstance":
the time for robes is called the circumstance.
"If a bhikṣuṇī uses cotton wool to stuff a sitting or lying mat, it is a pāyattika offense."
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes for herself a rope bed or a wooden bed, the legs should be eight fingers high according to the measure of the Sugata, excluding the portion inserted into the mortise holes;
if they exceed this, it is a pāyattika."
“If a bhikṣuṇī makes a needle case from bone, ivory, or horn, it is a pāyattika.
“If a bhikṣuṇī makes a robe according to the measurement of the Sugata’s robe, and it exceeds that measurement, it is a pāyattika.”
Regarding the measurement of a Sugata’s robe:
it is nine Sugata-spans in length and six spans in width; this is called the measurement of a Sugata’s robe.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a donor intends to give property to the Saṃgha, diverts it to another person, it is a pāyattika."

68. At that time, among the bhikṣuṇīs, some consumed raw or cooked garlic before midday, at midday, or after midday; whether eating it alone or mixed with other food, their dwellings became foul-smelling.
When various laypeople came to look and smelled the odor of garlic, they criticized and reviled it, saying,
"This is just like a food-preparation area in a householder's home!
Furthermore, when some bhikṣuṇīs went to a householder’s home, the householder, upon smelling the odor of their eating garlic, spoke to them, saying:
"The elder sister has gone far away, yet her mouth reeks of garlic!
the bhikṣuṇīs felt ashamed.
Furthermore, there was a garlic seller who invited the bhikṣuṇīs to take some garlic; because of this, he fell into poverty and his food and drink were no longer sustained.
The family members said:
"If you cannot give us food, release her so that she may go!
You yourself shall remain for the rest of your life as a slave to the bhikṣuṇīs!"
When the neighbor heard this, he rebuked her, saying, "Your family has no food of its own; why do you concern yourself with the bhikṣuṇīs?
She answered him by relating the matter in full.
There were those who lacked faith and did not delight in the Buddha-dharma, who said:
"It is because you have associated with bhikṣuṇīs that you have come to such suffering;
if you associate with them again, it will surely be even more severe than this!"
"These women have left the household life seeking liberation, yet now they are greedily attached to fine flavors!
They lack the conduct of śramaṇīs and violate the dharma of śramaṇīs!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard these various reproaches, [the Buddha] then established the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī eats garlic, it is a pāyattika.
If she eats raw garlic, for every swallow it is a pāyattika."
To eat raw garlic is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one eats it when ill, or if one is forced to eat it by another’s compulsion, there is no offense.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs slapped their female organs with their hands; this gave rise to lustful thoughts, and consequently, some returned to secular life or became followers of external paths.

Stūlanandā also slapped her female organ with her hand, causing it to swell so greatly that she could no longer walk. Her disciple went to the family where they were regularly supported and said, "The teacher is ill;
please fetch some food for her!"
She immediately gave it to her.
The women of the household soon came to inquire after her, saying,
"Auntie, what ailment or suffering do you have?"
He replied, “I am ill. He asked again:
"What kind of illness is this?
We are both women; why do you not speak?
She then answered him by relating the matter in full detail.
Thereupon, the women reproached them, saying:
"These men constantly disparage sensual desire, the perception of desire, the fever of desire, and the thoughts of desire, yet now they commit such an act!"
"Why do you not abandon the path and enjoy the five desires?
You lack the conduct of a śramaṇī and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇī!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked her in various ways. This led to the formulation of the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī slaps her female organ with her hand, it is a pāyattika.
If she slaps it with her hand, for every slap, it is a pāyattika."
If impurity is emitted, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. [Section seventy ends.

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs used animal glue to fashion male organs; inserting them into the female organ, they gave rise to lustful thoughts, and consequently some returned to secular life or became followers of external paths.
Furthermore, there was another bhikṣuṇī who had made a device and fastened it to her foot, inserting it into her female organ.

At that time, a śrāmaṇerikā was frying oil when a fire broke out and burned the house; the bhikṣuṇī, overcome with panic and fear, forgot to remove it and went outside with it still attached to her foot.
The firemen saw it and asked, "Auntie!
What is that at your feet?"
She answered truthfully, whereupon he immediately rebuked her. Consequently, he now establishes this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as was previously explained:
"From now on, this precept shall be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī inserts the male organ into the female organ, it is a pāyattika.'"
If one emits semen, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs inserted one finger, up to five fingers, into the female organ to wash; they injured the flesh until blood flowed, thereby causing illness.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they censured her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs were established, as described above:
"From now on, this precept should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī washes her female organ with water, it is a pāyattika.'"
Since the Buddha did not permit washing, [the robes] became foul-smelling and impure, and worms bred within them during the heat.
The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, went to the place where the Buddha was and said to him:
“World-Honored One!”
"We women's bodies are foul-smelling and impure; we rely entirely upon washing with water. We pray that you will grant us permission!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit the bhikṣuṇīs to perform purification with water."
After the Buddha had granted his permission, it was again as before: the bhikṣuṇīs saw [the conduct] and rebuked them in various ways, even reporting the matter to the bhikṣus, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī washes her female organ with water, she should use two fingers up to the first joint;
if she exceeds this, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
However, if there is a sore within the organ, or if an insect has entered, or if grass or stone has entered, it is not an offense to insert a finger past one joint.

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs shaved the hair from two places—the armpits and the private parts—and as a result, lustful desires arose within them; consequently, some returned to secular life and others became followers of external paths.

At that time, Thullanandā had also shaved the hair of her private parts. When a daughter was being married in the house of a patron, the girl wished to see her; the patron sent a messenger to summon her, and the bhikṣuṇī went immediately.
At that time, the family was preparing a bath for their daughter, and the girl said,
"Let the bhikṣuṇīs bathe first!
They immediately called them to bathe, and they replied:
"I do not need to bathe! she said.

But the women forcibly stripped her of her clothes and made her bathe; upon seeing that she had shaved the hair in her private parts, they immediately asked, "Sister, for what reason have you shaved this?"
He then asked them in return, "Why have you shaved it?
The women replied:
"I am for the sake of being a man!
The bhikṣuṇī said: "I am also like this!"
The women then reviled them, saying:
"These men constantly disparage sensual desire, yet now they perform such acts and do not cultivate the holy life!
Why do they not return to secular life and indulge themselves in the five desires?"
"They have no conduct of a śramaṇa and they destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they censured them in various ways. This leads to the formulation of the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī shaves the hair from her armpits or private parts, it is a pāyattika.
If she shaves them, for every stroke of the razor, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
However, if there is a need to shave for the sake of treating a sore, or if a person forcibly seizes them and shaves them, in all such cases there is no offense.

At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs stood together and conversed with bhikṣus in private, secluded places; they gave rise to minds of defiled attachment, and consequently some returned to secular life or became followers of external paths.
When the laypeople saw this, they said:
"These bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs are standing together and conversing in a secluded place; they must certainly be discussing matters of sexual desire!"
"You lack the conduct of a śramaṇī and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇī!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw and heard this, they censured her in various ways. This leads on until the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
“From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī stands together with or speaks together with a bhikṣu in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika.’”
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
If there are many bhikṣuṇīs and only one bhikṣu,
or if it is during a time of the eight difficulties, there is no offense.

At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs were standing together and conversing with laypeople and followers of other paths in secluded places, which led to their bodies being touched, coarse and lewd words regarding sexual desire being spoken, or even being forcibly compelled to engage in sexual acts.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they censured her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs was established, as described above:
"From now on, this precept should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī stands together or converses with a layperson or a follower of another sect in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remainder is as stated above.

At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs stood together and conversed with a bhikṣu in a secluded place; they gave rise to defiled and attached thoughts... [omitted] ...down to the point where the Buddha now formulates the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, which is also as stated above.
“From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī stands together with or speaks together with a bhikṣu in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika.’”
The remainder is as stated above.

At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs stood together and conversed with laypeople and followers of other paths in exposed places, causing their bodies to be touched. This leads on until the Buddha now establishes the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, also as stated above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī stands together with or speaks together with a layperson or a follower of another sect in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remainder is as stated above.
At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs stood alone with a bhikṣu in a street or alleyway, whispering together and sending their companion bhikṣuṇīs far away; the laypeople then reviled them.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs was established, as described above:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī stands alone with a bhikṣu in a street or alleyway, whispering together, and sends away her companion bhikṣuṇī so that she is far removed, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remainder is as stated above.

At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs stood alone in the streets and alleys with laypeople and followers of other paths, whispering together and sending their companion bhikṣuṇīs far away. When the householders saw this, they reviled and censured them. Consequently, the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:

'If a bhikṣuṇī stands alone in a street or alleyway with a layperson or a follower of another sect, whispering together and sending away her companion bhikṣuṇī to keep her at a distance, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remainder is as stated above.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs bathed naked; when the laypeople saw them, they surrounded them and mocked them with derisive laughter.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they rebuked them in various ways, leading up to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, which is also as stated above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī bathes naked, it is a pāyattika. For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a dukkaṭa.'"
If one prevents a person from coming, or bathes in a secluded place, or is shielded by a tree or clothing, there is no offense.
At that time, the eighty bhikṣuṇīs went out to bathe without their bathing robes; they did not know what to wear while bathing.
