When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they censured her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs was established, as described above:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī goes out without her bathing robe, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If the garment is dyed, washed, or beaten; or if it is consumed by fire, carried away by water, or otherwise ruined, there is no offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Caṇḍasumana’s disciple alone obtained five new robes.
She said to her preceptor, “Please wear these for me first, so that I may obtain merit!”
Once the preceptor had put them on, he did not give them back; the disciple, however, continued to wear coarse and tattered clothes.
When the bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they asked, "You alone have received five new robes; for what reason do you not wear them?"
She replied, "I previously used it to make offerings to my preceptor, and the preceptor did not return it.
The bhikṣuṇīs then rebuked Caṇḍasumana:
“How is it that a disciple, having obtained a new robe, first offers it as an act of worship and does not keep it for herself?
The elder bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha, and he proceeded to establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī receives a new robe and first offers it [to another], yet does not subsequently return it, she commits a pāyattika offense.'"
If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a new robe and offers it to another bhikṣuṇī, that bhikṣuṇī should wear it for one day;
if she wishes her to wear it again, she should do so, following the donor’s intention as to how long or short the duration shall be.
If one exceeds this limit, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who obstructed the Sangha from distributing robes; the other bhikṣuṇīs waited for her, which interfered with their sitting meditation and practice of the Path.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs rebuked her, saying:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī obstruct the Sangha from distributing robes?
They rebuked her in various ways, leading up to the present time when they established the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī obstructs the distribution of robes by the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.'"
If one is unable to go because of illness, or if one does not hear [the instruction], there is no offense.

At that time, there was a junior bhikṣuṇī who had obtained an unfinished robe; having few acquaintances and not knowing how to sew it herself, she took it to the bhikṣuṇī Sthūlanandā and requested that she make it for her.
She replied,
"I have many affairs and cannot do it for you!
She then took it to another bhikṣuṇī, and that bhikṣuṇī made it for her.
Thullanandā asked, "Who made this for you?
Bring it here so we may see if it is in accordance with the Dharma."
He immediately showed it to him.
[The other] then said:
"This robe is not in accordance with the Dharma; you should quickly tear it apart!"
"I shall make it for you once more.
He immediately tore it apart and took it away, refusing to make it;
that bhikṣuṇī was unable to complete it and went about wearing coarse, tattered robes, while the pieces of the ruined cloth were hung out to dry on the roof.
At that time, a fire broke out; being consumed by the flames, [a portion of the roof] was blown by the wind and fell onto the house of a layperson, spreading the fire to several other households.
When the layperson saw that the fire had originated from the nunnery, he spoke with anger and reproach:
"We have provided for these bhikṣuṇīs, yet they have instead become our enemies!"
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads on to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as was explained above.
“From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī herself tears a bhikṣuṇī’s robe, or causes another to tear it, and does not return it by sewing it back together, it is a pāyattika.’”
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣuṇī who dismantled a bhikṣuṇī’s robe; it could not be finished in one day, but only after four or five days. She reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the two divisions of the Saṃgha and addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now permit the bhikṣuṇīs to complete their robes in four or five days.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:”
“If a bhikṣuṇī dismantles a bhikṣuṇī’s robe, or causes another to dismantle it, and more than four or five days pass without it being completed, it is a pāyattika.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣuṇī who dismantled a bhikṣuṇī’s robe but became ill and was unable to complete it; she reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit the bhikṣuṇīs that once they have dismantled another’s robe, if they become ill, it shall not be considered completed."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having had a bhikṣuṇī’s robe dismantled, fails to complete it within four or five days while not being ill, it is a pāyattika."
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs went to various families wearing coarse and tattered robes, having separated themselves from their five robes.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they censured her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs were established, as described above:
"From now on, this precept should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī goes about separated from her five robes, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Regarding 'being separated from the five robes':
from one house to another, even as far as exiting the door of one's residence, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*."
If [the robe] is being washed, dyed, beaten, or sewn, there is no offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs gave bhikṣuṇī robes to laypeople and women of external paths.
He then proceeded to wear them. When other laypeople saw him, they prostrated toward him, but he said:
"I am a layperson! I am a non-Buddhist!"
The laypeople then criticized and reviled them, saying:
"How can bhikṣuṇīs give bhikṣuṇī robes to laypeople and women of external paths?
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they censured them in various ways. Consequently, the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī gives a bhikṣuṇī’s robe to a layperson or a female follower of another path, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Regarding the robes of a bhikṣuṇī:
they have leaf-patterns, borders, and patches.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
If there is a robe belonging to that nun, and she exchanges it for [the robe in question], or if she uses it to repay a debt, in all such cases there is no offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Cchama was about to come to Śrāvastī; when the bhikṣuṇī Caṇḍasumana heard that she intended to arrive, she went to her host’s house and said:
“Let us prepare some offerings for the bhikṣuṇī Kṣamā when she arrives!
She replied, “I have also heard that she will come; I wish to exhaust my own resources to prepare fine food and drink, as well as to offer robes.”
That bhikṣuṇī then said: "Why do you not give this robe as an offering to the Saṃgha?
Within the Saṃgha there are those who are rightly directed and rightly practicing; there is nothing they do not encompass."
"What is the use of giving to a single bhikṣuṇī?
Having heard this, the host immediately redirected the offering to the Saṃgha.
When Bhikṣuṇī Kṣema arrived, he prepared many delicious foods and drinks for her, serving them with his own hands. When she had finished eating, he spoke to her in secret:
"This is precisely the time for the distribution of robes, yet the bhikṣuṇī Caṇḍasumana has thwarted this matter of ours!
The bhikṣuṇīs asked, "What are you saying?"
She answered with the facts as they were.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs rebuked her in various ways:
"How can you intercept gifts intended for an individual and give them to the Saṃgha?"
Having rebuked her in various ways, he then established a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs up to the present time, as described above:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī intercepts an object given for an individual and gives it to the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.'"
"One who gives to others" refers to one who distributes items separately within the Saṃgha; this is called "giving to others.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī to do so constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Khemā arrived at Śrāvastī, and the bhikṣuṇī Caṇḍasumana said to her:
"I shall entrust myself to the host so that they may look after you!"
Kṣema said, "There is no need for you to give me instructions! Caṇḍasumana spoke again:
"You have accepted my entrustment; having now obtained gain and offerings, you shall further bring them across through merit!
Thereupon, Kṣema remained silent and gave his consent, whereupon he immediately led him to various households.

The bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā had a large following and practiced the samādhi of loving-kindness; everyone revered her, and they no longer made offerings to the bhikṣuṇī Caṇḍasumana. Consequently, Caṇḍasumana gave rise to a heart of jealousy and said:
"I instructed various families so that she might receive many offerings, yet she instead speaks ill of me, causing me to no longer obtain food!"
The bhikṣuṇīs reproached her in various ways, saying,
"How can a bhikṣuṇī cherish and guard a family's interests?
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they also reproached her in various ways, leading up to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, out of favoritism, shows partiality toward a family, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding 'showing partiality toward a family':"
Desiring that other families make offerings to oneself and not to others;
for a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, this constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
*Pañcavargika-vinaya*, fascicle twelve.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya), Fascicle Thirteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Jibin during the Song Dynasty,
together with Zhu Daosheng and others.

The Second Division, Part Four, Case Number Eighty-nine: At that time, certain bhikṣuṇīs did not observe the rainy season retreat and wandered through the countryside. They encountered bandits during the eighth month, or met with various calamities such as floods and fires.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they rebuked them in various ways, saying:
"How can these bhikṣuṇīs not observe the summer rains retreat?
This led to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī does not observe the rains retreat, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding 'the rains retreat':"
Regarding the preceding and subsequent retreats (*pūrvavārṣika* and *paścimavārṣika*): if there is no compelling reason, to wait for the subsequent retreat constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the eight difficulties arise, there is no offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs were observing the rainy season retreat in a place where there was no community of bhikṣus. Consequently, they had various doubts:
whether one should be ordained or not, whether one should be granted the precepts or not, and whether making robes was in accordance with the Dharma or not.
Regarding the precepts, she had various doubts such as these, yet she did not know whom to ask.
Furthermore, she was treated with contempt by wicked people and non-Buddhists.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they reprimanded her in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and asked the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Is it true that you did so? They replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways, saying:
“Did I not previously state that the bhikṣuṇīs should observe the rains retreat in dependence upon the community of bhikṣus according to the Eight Rules of Respect?
Having rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I shall now establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣuṇī does not observe the rains retreat in dependence upon the community of bhikṣus, it is a pāyattika offense.
Even if she observes the retreat in dependence upon the community of bhikṣus, if there is no instruction or admonition, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If, during the rainy season retreat, the community of bhikṣus moves away, dies, or renounces the path;
or if they are constrained by forceful means; [the same applies].
If one is ill, there is no offense in any case.
At that time, although the bhikṣuṇīs were in retreat, they traveled about during it and encountered dangers such as bandits and fires.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they rebuked them in various ways. Consequently, the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
“From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī travels during the rainy season retreat, it is a pāyattika. As for ‘travels’:”
If one goes from one village to another, or if there is no village within half a yojana, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If the eight difficulties arise, there is no offense.

At that time, after the bhikṣuṇīs had completed their rainy-season retreat, they did not request [the monks] from the saṃgha of bhikṣus to address their offenses regarding what was seen, heard, or suspected; as there was no one to instruct them, they were ignorant and lacked knowledge, unable to train in the precepts.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs reprimanded them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the two communities of monks and asked the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha reproached her in various ways, saying:

"Did I not previously state that after a bhikṣuṇī has completed the rainy season retreat, she should request from the assembly of bhikṣus the removal of offenses regarding what was seen, heard, or suspected?"
Having rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the rainy season retreat, does not request the saṃgha of bhikṣus to address her regarding charges of what has been seen, heard, or suspected, it is a pāyattika.'"
"There is no offense if the Saṃgha is not assembled, or during times of the eight calamities.
At that time, various householders invited the bhikṣuṇī Cārumatī to observe the rains retreat in Śrāvastī, saying:
"If you accept our invitation, we shall provide for you with all necessary supplies at the appropriate times!"
He then accepted their invitation and remained there permanently, no longer traveling elsewhere.
Those householders criticized and reproached him, saying:
“We should attend to other matters; these bhikṣuṇīs do not know how to exercise judgment, nor do they know when to depart!
They always speak of having few desires and being content, yet now they show no satiety!”
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads on until the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as was explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, having accepted an invitation for the rains retreat, does not depart after staying for one night, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
There is no offense if one is ill, if there is fear, if the invitation was not for a fixed period, or if one does not go because the residence is not a place where invitations are accepted.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs were traveling through dangerous areas within the kingdom; lacking protection, they were robbed by wicked people.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they rebuked them in various ways. Consequently, [the Buddha] now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as was explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī travels alone in a place within the country that is dangerous and where there is no one to rely upon, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Even though many bhikṣuṇīs travel together, if there is no lay companion, it is called 'traveling alone.
To go from one village to another, or if there is no village, to travel half a yojana, constitutes a pāyattika offense."
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If there is an urgent danger and she flees, in all such cases there is no offense.

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs left the borders of the country and traveled through a place of terror where there was no protection; they were stripped of their belongings by evil people. This led to the formulation of the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs up to the present, as explained above.
“From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī travels alone through a border region or a place of fear without anyone to rely upon, it is a pāyattika.’”
The rest is as stated above.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs, having completed their rains retreat in the vihāra at the residence of Viśākhā, departed for other places while leaving the monastery empty, without having made any formal entrustment of the premises.
Later, when a fire broke out, someone saw it and said to the mother of Viśākhā:
"The bhikṣuṇī vihāra you have built has been consumed by fire!"
She then sent her male and female servants to go and rescue them, so that they were not completely consumed by the fire.
Later, when the bhikṣuṇīs returned, Viśākhā’s mother asked them: "Aunties!..."
“Have you not lost anything?
He replied, “I have lost such and such items!”
She then proceeded to recount at length the items she had lost, whereupon Visākhā rebuked her, saying:
"How can you dwell in my monastery during the rainy season retreat and depart without entrusting your belongings to someone?"
This caused the fire to burn, and furthermore, she spoke at excessive length regarding the lost items!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they censured her in various ways. This leads to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the rainy-season retreat, departs without entrusting the vihāra to someone else, it is a pāyattika.'"
If she does not entrust [the robe] and steps out with one foot through the door, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if she steps out with both feet, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If other bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs come and reside there;
or if there is no one to whom the dwelling may be entrusted, there is no offense.
At that time, after the bhikṣuṇīs had completed their rains retreat at the residence of the Mother of Viśākhā, they departed without returning the residence to its owner.
Later, when a fire broke out, someone saw it and said to the mother of Viśākhā:
"The bhikṣuṇī vihāra you have built has been consumed by fire!"
Visākhā said: "Let it burn itself out!
Previously, when the bhikṣuṇīs went out without entrusting [the vihāra] to someone, they caused this fire to break out."
"After returning, she again passed by and spoke at length about the lost items, bringing an ill reputation upon me!
Later, when that bhikṣuṇī returned once more, Viśākhā asked her: "Āryā!..."
"When you departed, did you leave anything behind in the vihāra? He replied, "No!"
He then rebuked him, saying:
"Why did you go away without returning my vihāra, allowing it to be completely consumed by fire?
Had you told me, I would have protected it myself so that this would not have happened!"
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads to the formulation of the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the rainy season retreat, departs without returning the vihāra to its owner, it is a pāyattika.'"
The rest is as stated above.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs visited the royal palaces and painted halls, and also toured various places of amusement;
they went to a lotus pond where many people had gathered to look on, and the bhikṣuṇīs spoke to the men there, saying:
“Step aside a little; do not come too close to me!
The men said, “You ill-omened person!”
"One who has shaved their head and wears the cut-and-sewn robes should not come here;
that you have come here is because you seek a man!
Why do you make me avoid you?"
She then seized him and dragged him away, uttering coarse and lewd words of sexual desire.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways; consequently, as previously described, the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī engages in various kinds of sightseeing, it is a pāyattika.
To form the intention and to employ the preparatory means constitutes a duṣkṛta.'"
If one sets out on the journey, for every step taken, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one does not go for the purpose of watching a performance, there is no offense in any case.

At that time, during the fortnightly *poṣadha*, the bhikṣuṇīs did not come before the community of bhikṣus to request an instructor. Because they had no one to instruct them, they remained ignorant and deluded, unable to train in the precepts.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and asked the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked the bhikṣuṇīs in various ways:
"Did I not previously teach you the Eight Rules of Respect, instructing you to request a teacher of exhortation every half-month?"
Having rebuked her, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī does not request a teacher of instruction from within the Saṃgha once every half-month, it is a pāyattika.’”
If a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī does not seek instruction or confess their transgression, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
There is no offense if they do not obtain [instruction] despite requesting it, or if they are ill.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Cīrā passed away. The bhikṣuṇīs erected a bone stūpa for her within the bhikṣu saṃghārāma. Her kinsfolk circumambulated it three times each day, weeping and saying:
"O you who bestowed the Dharma upon us!"
"Those who gave me robes, food, bedding, seats, and medicine—
how can they suddenly abandon me and pass away forever?
Thus the bhikṣus became weary and distressed, and their practice of meditation and the Path was hindered and abandoned.
At that time, Upāli came into the monastery and asked the resident bhikṣus,
"What is this sound? They answered him in full detail regarding the matter, and Upāli immediately sent someone to demolish it.
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they deliberated together, saying:
"We must all take up staves and strike that bhikṣu; if we do not go with him, we shall no longer dwell together!"

Having deliberated thus, they all took up their staves and went to the monastery; upon seeing the bhikṣus, they surrounded them with the intent to strike, but desisted when they realized they were not the intended targets.
Moving forward, they encountered Upāli on a narrow path; they blocked him from both front and rear and raised their staves, intending to strike him.
Upāli immediately used his supernormal power to fly to where the Buddha was and reported the matter to him.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the two divisions of the Saṃgha and asked the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One."
The Buddha rebuked the bhikṣuṇīs in various ways, saying:
"What you have done is contrary to the Dharma!
How can a bhikṣuṇī strike a bhikṣu?"
Having rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī enters the dwelling place of bhikṣus, it is a pāyattika.'"
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who, while traveling on a road, saw an empty monastery and wished to enter to pay their respects, yet they did not dare to go in;
they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, because of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit bhikṣuṇīs to enter empty monasteries!
From this day forward, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī enters a dwelling where bhikṣus reside, it is a pāyattika.'"
There were certain bhikṣuṇīs who, having business within the saṃghārāma, felt they ought to enter but did not dare to do so.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
“Now it is permitted for a bhikṣuṇī who has business requiring her to enter a saṃghārāma to inform a bhikṣu; only after the bhikṣu has granted permission may she enter!
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī enters a dwelling where bhikṣus reside without informing a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.’”
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who had business requiring them to enter the saṃghārāma; however, as some of the bhikṣus were either practicing meditation or sleeping, they were unable to inform them.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit the bhikṣuṇīs to enter within the precincts; upon seeing a bhikṣu, they shall announce themselves."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī enters a residence where bhikṣus dwell and sees a bhikṣu, and does not inform him, it is a pāyattika."

There were some bhikṣuṇīs who, when faced with urgent danger and wishing to enter a saṃghārāma to seek refuge, did not dare to enter; consequently, they were either plundered by bandits or harmed by wild beasts.
They reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit bhikṣuṇīs to enter the monasteries at their own discretion when there is an urgent difficulty."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī enters a residence where bhikṣus dwell and sees a bhikṣu, she must announce her presence; except in cases of urgent distress, it is a pāyattika."
If no bhikṣu is seen, one must not enter without having made an announcement; one must go and announce it once a bhikṣu is seen.
That bhikṣu should deliberate: if it is a time when entry is permitted, he should allow entry;
if it is not a time for entry, he should not allow entry.
If one sees [a nun] and does not announce it, or enters without being permitted, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs who had not yet reached twelve years of seniority kept followers; they were unable to instruct them, nor could they provide for their needs, and the disciples remained ignorant and uninformed, unable to train in the precepts.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they censured her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs were established, as described above:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī who has not reached twelve years of seniority keeps a retinue, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
"One who has not yet reached twelve years of age" means one whose period of receiving the precepts has not yet completed twelve years.
"One who keeps dependents" means:
If one acts as an upādhyāya for another and,
having resolved to maintain a following of disciples, reaches the point where the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has not yet been completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Once the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is completed, it is an *upādhyāya-pāyattika*.
For other nuns, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

At that time, although some bhikṣuṇīs were twelve years of standing, they were deaf, blind, mute, or afflicted with various other ailments; being ignorant, they took on disciples whom they were unable to instruct or care for, and these disciples remained foolish, dark, and ignorant, unable to train in the precepts.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and asked the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked her in various ways, saying:

"How can a bhikṣuṇī who is blind, deaf, mute, or afflicted by various other ailments keep a disciple? She is unable to instruct or admonish her, nor can she provide for her needs, leaving the disciple ignorant and uninformed, unable to train in the precepts."
Having rebuked her, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now authorize the bhikṣuṇīs to maintain a following through a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
That bhikṣuṇī should go before the community of bhikṣuṇīs, remove her leather sandals, bare her right shoulder, kneel on her right knee with palms joined, and make this declaration:"
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have already completed twelve years [of seniority] and wish to maintain a group of disciples;
I now request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for maintaining a group of disciples."
"Excellent! May the Saṃgha perform for me the *karmavācanā* for maintaining a retinue.
Thus he requested three times.
The bhikṣuṇīs should deliberate and examine whether this bhikṣuṇī is capable of maintaining a group of disciples.
If she is not capable, they should not perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for her to maintain a group;
if she is capable, they should perform it for her.
A single bhikṣuṇī—whether she be a senior elder or one equal to a senior elder—who is knowledgeable in the Dharma and the Vinaya, shall announce:
"Listen, noble ladies of the Saṃgha!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, has already completed twelve years [of seniority] and wishes to take so-and-so as a follower;
she has requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (karmavācanā) for taking followers, and the Saṃgha now grants her the formal act for taking followers.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience.
This is the motion.
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!"
This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has already reached twelve years of standing and wishes to take so-and-so as her disciple;
she has requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (karmavācanā) for taking a disciple, and the Saṃgha now grants her this formal act for taking a disciple.
"Whichever of you, venerable sisters, approves, remain silent;
if you do not approve, speak.
The Sangha has completed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the nun so-and-so to maintain a group of disciples."
The Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent;
this matter is thus upheld.
"Now, for the sake of the bhikṣuṇīs, I shall establish a precept. From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī who has reached twelve years of age has not been granted the *karmavācanā* for maintaining a following by the Saṃgha,
yet she maintains a following, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The remainder is as stated above.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon married girls who were less than twelve years of age; these women were ignorant and lacked understanding, being incapable of training in the precepts.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they censured her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs were established, as described above:
"From now on, this precept shall be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon a married girl who is less than twelve years of age, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
"One who has not yet reached twelve years of age":
although she has already been married, she has not yet reached twelve years of age.
"Married" means:
The case of the man has already been explained;
the remainder is as described above regarding the taking of attendants.

At that time, although the girls were twelve years old and had been married, they were deaf, mute, or afflicted with various diseases. The bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon them, yet these women were foolish and ignorant, unable to train in the precepts.

When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they censured her in various ways, even saying: "We now authorize the bhikṣuṇīs to perform the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to confer full ordination upon a married girl who has reached twelve years of age."
That person who wishes to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) should go before the community of bhikṣuṇīs and declare:
"May the noble community of nuns listen!
I, so-and-so, having been married, am now twelve years of age; I seek full ordination with preceptor so-and-so, and I now request the community for the conferral of full ordination."
"Excellent!
May the Saṃgha grant me the full ordination out of compassion!
Having thus requested three times, the bhikṣuṇīs should deliberate whether they may grant it or not.
A formal act (*karmavācanā*) for a single bhikṣuṇī should be performed as previously described.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"

"If a bhikṣuṇī, when a girl who has been married for twelve years, grants her the full ordination (upasampadā) without the Saṃgha having performed the formal ritual (karmavācanā), it is a pāyattika offense."
The rest is as explained in the section on maintaining a retinue.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs conferred the training precepts upon girls who were not yet eighteen years of age; these girls were ignorant and lacked understanding, and were thus incapable of undertaking the training precepts.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they censured her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs were established, as described above:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī confers the training precepts upon a girl who is not yet eighteen years of age, it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the "virgin": one who has not yet had intercourse with a man.

If she initiates the intention and the preparatory acts, up until the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion followed by one proclamation) is not yet completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
When the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) is completed, it is a *pāyattika*; for the rest of the assembly, it is all a *duṣkṛta*.

At that time, although the bhikṣuṇīs had granted the training precepts (*śikṣamāṇā*) to girls who were eighteen years old, those girls were deaf, mute, or afflicted with various other ailments. Therefore, I now authorize the bhikṣuṇīs to grant the two-year training precepts to girls who are eighteen years old by means of the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
A person who wishes to receive the training precepts should go before the community of bhikṣuṇīs and declare:
"May the noble community of nuns listen!
I, [Name], with [Name] as my preceptor, now request from the community the two-year period of training."
"Excellent!
Ayyā Saṅgha, out of compassion for me, please grant me the two-year training in the precepts.
Having thus requested three times, the bhikṣuṇīs should carefully deliberate whether they may grant it or not.
A single bhikṣuṇī should perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) as previously described.
She should inform the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī, although the girl is eighteen years of age, confers the training precepts upon her without the Saṃgha having performed the formal ritual (karmavācanā), it is a pāyattika.
The remainder is as stated above.
At that time, the wife of the householder who was the patron of the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā requested to go forth.
Thullanandā said, "First give me a robe, and I shall ordain you."
The hostess then rebuked him, saying: "I am the mistress!
Why did you first seek my robe and only afterwards allow me to be ordained?"
"Instead of wishing to deliver me from birth, old age, sickness, and death, they have instead sought to profit from my robes!
These women possess no conduct of a śramaṇī and destroy the dharma of a śramaṇī!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked them in various ways. This led to the formulation of the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī says to a laywoman: "First give me a robe, and I shall ordain you. "
"A *pāyattika*. If a bhikṣuṇī speaks thus to a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If that person is in debt, and she ordains them only after the debt has been repaid, there is no offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā said to the bhikṣuṇīs,
"Perform for me the formal act of authorization to maintain a group of disciples. The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"As the Buddha has taught, one should be granted the *karmavācanā* for maintaining a retinue;
since you do not possess these qualities, the *karmavācanā* for maintaining a retinue cannot be granted to you."
That bhikṣuṇī then said: "The bhikṣuṇīs follow favoritism, hatred, delusion, and fear!
They perform the service for those they fear, but do not perform it for those they do not fear."
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads up to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as explained above.
“From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī is told by other bhikṣuṇīs: “As the Buddha has taught, you should undergo the formal act (karmavācanā) of being authorized to maintain a following,”’”
"You do not have such a thing!
Thus, if one rebukes the bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs did not go to listen when the exhortation was given, nor did they go to listen during the formal ritual (karmavācanā); consequently, they remained ignorant and uninformed, unable to train in the precepts.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs reprimanded her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs is established, as was explained above:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, at the time of instruction or during a formal ritual (karmavācanā), does not go to listen, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Instruction" refers to the teaching of the eight points of respect and other such dharmas.
"Karma" (formal ecclesiastical act) refers to:
The *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
At that time, there were one hundred and ten bhikṣuṇīs; although there were śikṣamāṇās who had completed two years of training, [the community] did not grant them full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Later, she fell gravely ill, suffering from various ailments such as deafness, blindness, and muteness, which barred her from receiving the precepts.
When the nun Khemā’s disciple had completed two years of training in the precepts, Khemā likewise did not grant her full ordination, saying:
"Continue to train in these precepts for now."
Later, she contracted leprosy and did not know what to do.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs reprimanded her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precepts were established for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, when a śikṣamāṇā has completed two years of training and there are no obstacles, does not grant her full ordination (upasaṃpadā), but says:
"You must first train in these precepts. "
"...a *pāyattika* offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs ordained courtesans who would not accept instruction or admonition.
They were like oxen with deep necks that cannot pull a cart; when yoked to a cart, they only wish to bolt out from under the shafts.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs rebuked her in various ways, and so on, until now the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs is established as previously described:
"From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī ordains a prostitute, it is a pāyattika.'"
If she has generated the aspiration [to ordain], but the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) is not yet completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Once the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is completed, the preceptor (*upādhyāyī*) commits a *pāyattika* offense;
the rest of the assembly of nuns commit *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If she loathes the female body and seeks to transcend it, there is no offense.

At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon śikṣamāṇās who had not yet completed two years of training; those [śikṣamāṇās] were foolish, ignorant, and lacked understanding, and thus were unable to train in the precepts.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they censured her in various ways. This leads to the formulation of a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon a śikṣamāṇā who has not completed two years of training, it is a pāyattika.'"
The rest is as explained in the section on maintaining a retinue.

At that time, although the śikṣamāṇās had completed two years of training, the bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon them despite their having various ailments such as deafness, blindness, or muteness.

When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they rebuked her in various ways; consequently, the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs as previously described, concerning women who have been married for twelve full years.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī grants full ordination to a śikṣamāṇā who has completed two years of training, without the Saṃgha having performed the formal ritual (karmavācanā), it is a pāyattika.'"
The rest is as explained in the section on maintaining a retinue.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon śikṣamāṇās who had completed two years of training but were not actually practicing the precepts; these women were ignorant and lacked understanding, being unable to train in the precepts.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs reprimanded her in various ways, even as far as saying: "Now, for the sake of the bhikṣuṇīs, we shall establish this precept, just as was explained above:
'From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
If a bhikṣuṇī grants full ordination to a śikṣamāṇā who has completed two years of training but has not yet trained in the precepts, it is a pāyattika.'"
The rest is as explained in the section on maintaining a retinue.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon a pregnant woman. When she entered a village to beg for food, some laypeople saw her and mocked her, saying:
"This bhikṣuṇī carries a heavy burden; you should give her food quickly!"
Some said: "Let us first examine his belly! Others said:
"These did not practice the holy life!
Or some said: "These practiced the holy life, but that was during their time before they had gone forth."
He then rebuked the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"Why did you not wait until after the birth was complete before ordaining her?
By this, you have brought disgrace upon the holy life!"
"The bhikṣuṇīs do not know who may be ordained and who may not; they lack the conduct of śramaṇas and destroy the Dharma of the śramaṇas!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they censured them in various ways. Thereupon, as previously described, [the Buddha] now formulated a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon a pregnant woman, it is a pāyattika.
The formulation of the intention, up to the completion of the fourth *jñapti-karman*, is all as explained above."
If one wishes to confer the full ordination (upasampadā), one should first examine [the candidate] for signs of lactation; if there are no signs of pregnancy, there is no offense.
If it is only after the ordination has been completed that she is known to be pregnant, there is likewise no offense.

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon women who had recently given birth; with one hand holding their alms bowls and the other cradling their infants, they went out to beg for food.
When the laypeople saw this, they mocked him, saying,
"Quickly give food to two people!
The laypeople then reviled, disparaged, and rebuked him.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs reprimanded her in various ways, up until the point where the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as was explained above:
"From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon a woman who has recently given birth, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remainder is as explained above regarding the keeping of attendants.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon their disciples year after year; because the number of disciples was so great, they were unable to instruct and admonish each one individually. Consequently, the disciples remained ignorant and deluded, unable to train in the precepts.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they censured her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs was established, as described above:
"From now on, this precept should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon a disciple every year, it is a pāyattika.'"
"A bhikṣuṇī may, after an interval of one year, confer full ordination upon one disciple.
The rest is as explained in the section on maintaining a retinue.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon their disciples within the community of bhikṣuṇīs, and only after one night had passed did they proceed to the community of bhikṣus to receive the ordination."

If a person receiving the precepts contracts an illness that constitutes a barrier to ordination during the single night [of the probationary period], the community of bhikṣus shall no longer confer the precepts upon them.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured them in various ways; consequently, as previously described, the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon a disciple while staying overnight apart from her, it is a pāyattika.'"
From the initial resolution of the mind until the appearance of the dawn light, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
When the dawn light appears, for the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation);
for the rest of the community of teachers, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If the Saṃgha is not assembled in harmony, or if one of the eight difficulties arises, there is no offense.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs who had newly received the precepts did not rely upon or attend to their upādhyāyikās; because there was no one to instruct and admonish them, they were ignorant and knew nothing, and were thus unable to train in the precepts.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they rebuked her in various ways. This leads up to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as explained above:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī who has newly received full ordination does not rely upon and attend to her preceptor (upādhyāyī) for six years, or causes another to rely upon one [instead], it is a pāyattika.'"
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If the *upādhyāyī* does not require [the disciple] to rely upon her, there is no offense.

(120) At that time, after the bhikṣuṇīs had conferred full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon their disciples, they did not take them under their care, did not instruct them, and did not teach them to recite; thus the disciples remained ignorant and uninformed, unable to train in the precepts.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they censured her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the Buddha established a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs as previously described:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī keeps a female disciple but does not herself take care of her during the first six years, nor instructs another to take care of her, it is a pāyattika.'"
"If a disciple does not accept the instruction, there is no offense.

At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon their disciples but did not take them away from their original homes. Men who were previously acquainted with them saw them and, giving rise to defiled and attached thoughts, began to mock them and engage in coarse, lewd, and sexual speech.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they censured her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs was established, as described above:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī keeps a disciple but does not take her along herself, nor causes someone else to take her away from her original location by a distance of five or six yojanas, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Her own place" refers to either her birthplace or her place of marriage.
If the disciple does not comply, there is no offense.
At that time, because the bhikṣuṇīs who were fellow students did not tend to one another when ill, some did not recover at the proper time, while others even passed away.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they rebuked them in various ways, leading up to the present occasion where the precepts are now being established for the bhikṣuṇīs, as was explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, when a fellow student is ill, does not nurse her herself nor instruct another to nurse her, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Co-students" refers to those with the same preceptor (upādhyāya) or preceptor-instructor (ācārya), as well as those who are constant companions.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī [to do so], it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If their places of residence differ, there is no offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs ordained women who were under the authority of others, and the laypeople criticized and reviled them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs have no distinction between those who may be ordained and those who may not!"
Some householders said: "One should seize his robes and bowl and hand them over to the authorities. Others said:
"King Prasenajit has issued a decree:
'If anyone treats a bhikṣuṇī with contempt or insults her, they shall be punished with a heavy penalty.
You must release her immediately and ensure that no one hears of this!"
They all said, "These women have no conduct befitting śramaṇīs; they destroy the dharma of the śramaṇīs!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked them in various ways. This leads up to the formulation of the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
“From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī ordains a woman who belongs to another, it is a pāyattika.
‘Belongs to another’ means:”
Whether it be an official subordinate or another person,
from the initial resolution of mind up until the completion of the fourth *jñapti-caturtha* motion, it is also as explained above.
If the owner consents, there is no offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs ordained women who were chronically ill, unable to train in the precepts, ignorant, and lacking understanding.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they rebuked them in various ways. This leads up to the present, when the Buddha established the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī ordains a woman who has a chronic illness, it is a pāyattika.
A 'chronic illness' refers to:"
If one has long suffered from chills and fever that recur at regular intervals,
the procedure from the initial resolution of mind up to the completion of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is as described above.
If this illness occurs after the precepts have been received, there is no offense.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs ordained women who were under the authority of their husbands. Laypeople criticized and reviled them, either wishing to seize their robes or wishing to dismiss them. Consequently, up until now, the precepts have been established for the bhikṣuṇīs, all as explained in the section concerning women belonging to others.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī ordains a woman who belongs to a husband, it is a pāyattika.
The formulation of the intention and the conclusion of the formal motion (jñapti-caturtha-karman) are also to be recited as above."

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs ordained women who were in debt; consequently, the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, all of which is as explained above in the section concerning the ordination of women belonging to others.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī ordains a woman who is in debt, it is a pāyattika.
The formulation of the intention, up to the completion of the fourth formal motion (jñapti-caturtha-karman), is also as explained above."
If one says,
"Once you have completed your ordination, you may then repay the debt," and thus ordains this person, there is no offense.

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs stood together and conversed with men in dark places; they gave rise to defiled and attached minds, no longer delighting in the cultivation of the holy life (brahmacarya), which led some to return to secular life or become followers of external paths.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads to the formulation of a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as previously explained:
"From now on, this precept shall be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī stands together with or converses with a man in a dark place, it is a pāyattika.'"
If one speaks in a dark place, for every utterance there is a *pāyattika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if it is a place of suspicion or fear, or if the lamp suddenly goes out.
At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs would sit upon the couches in the homes of acquaintances they frequented.
The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"We do not rejoice at seeing these inauspicious objects!"
They did not know whether it was permissible to sit or not, and there was no established rule regarding this!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured them in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precepts were formulated for the bhikṣuṇīs, as explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī sits upon another's bed without first informing the owner, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.'"
If the host instructs one to sit, there is no offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs gave food with their own hands to laypeople and male followers of other paths.
They thought to themselves:
"This bhikṣuṇī must have given me food with a mind of lustful attachment!
Thinking thus, he teased her and spoke coarse, evil words of sexual desire.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they censured him in various ways; consequently, the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, with her own hand, gives food to a layperson or a male follower of another sect, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one does not give with one's own hand, or gives with one's own hand to a relative, in all such cases there is no offense.
130. At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs spoke of the faults of the bhikṣus to the laypeople, saying:
"Those bhikṣus have broken their precepts, broken their dignified conduct, and broken their right views!"
When the bhikṣus heard this, they became angry and ceased to provide instruction and admonition.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and asked the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Is it true that you did so?
They replied: [It is true.]
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways, saying:
“Did I not previously teach you the Eight Rules of Respect?
Having rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs. From this day forth, this precept should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣuṇī speaks of the faults of a bhikṣu to a layperson, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta."
If a layperson hears [the teaching] first and asks about it, one should counter-question them, saying: "How did you hear it? If they say:
"I have heard it thus and so!
If the bhikṣuṇīs hear this and respond accordingly with the truth, they do not commit an offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Caṇḍasumana, having quarreled with someone, beat herself, struck herself, and cried out loudly in weeping.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. [The Buddha then continued: "I shall now establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as was explained above:
'From this day forward, this precept shall be recited as follows:
If a bhikṣuṇī, having quarreled with another, strikes herself and weeps, it is a pāyattika.'"
If she strikes herself or beats herself, in each and every instance it is a *pāyattika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs, pointing at Caṇḍaśūmānā from afar, spoke of her quarrelsome behavior; she then thought they were insulting her and cried out loudly:
"The bhikṣuṇīs have reviled me!
The bhikṣuṇīs immediately went to her and asked,
"In what way did we revile you?"
"Do you not know which path it was?
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked her in various ways, saying:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī, without clearly understanding another's words, falsely claim that she has been insulted?"
Thus, up until now, the precept has been established for the bhikṣuṇīs as previously explained.
From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, without having clearly understood another's words, falsely becomes angry with them, it is a pāyattika."
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs were quarreling with one another, each making a solemn oath: "If this is so, may I fall into hell."
"Just as Devadatta and Kokālika have received their retribution, so shall I!
If I were not like this, you would receive such retribution!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they censured her in various ways. This leads to the formulation of the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī makes a solemn oath, and by means of that oath falsely accuses another, it is a pāyattika.
For each such oath she utters, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs threw excrement and urine outside the fences and walls, defiling both humans and non-humans.

At that time, there was a brahmin minister who wore his crown, having purified himself through fasting and ritual cleansing. Having bathed at dawn and put on garments scented with incense, he intended to go to a celestial shrine to petition for the restoration of his office. Wrapping his head as he traveled, he feared encountering those with shaven heads or those wearing cut-and-sewn robes;
thus, upon reaching the wall outside the bhikṣuṇī’s quarters, he happened to encounter someone throwing excrement, which drenched his head and flowed over his entire body.
He spoke in great anger: "I feared seeing such inauspicious people, yet now I am drenched by this thrown filth! This must surely be an inauspicious omen for my life!"
"However, I must go to King Prasenajit and say, 'You have killed a shaven-headed slave girl!
Thereupon he turned back and encountered a brahmin physiognomist.
The brahmin asked, "Why is it so?
He answered him in full detail regarding the matter.
The physiognomist said:
"This is a great omen of good fortune!
You shall now obtain one thousand gold coins and regain your original official position!"
Still not ceasing his anger, he took this body defiled by excrement and went straight to the king’s presence.
The king asked:
"Why are you like this?"
He then answered with the full details of the matter.
The king clapped his hands and laughed loudly; he immediately issued an edict granting him one thousand gold coins and restoring his former official rank.
Thereupon, the king’s various ministers began to mock and reproach him, saying:
"To throw excrement to defile others—how could this be the intention of one seeking the Way to save and benefit sentient beings!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked her in various ways. This led to the formulation of the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs as previously described.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī throws feces or urine over a fence or wall, or causes another to throw them, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs threw refuse and leftover food outside the fences and walls, thereby defiling humans and non-humans.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled her, saying:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī throw refuse over a wall to soil people?
These women have no sense of propriety!"
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads on until the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as was explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī throws refuse or leftover food over a fence or wall, or causes another to throw it, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

At that time, the ground in front of the Rājārāma Vihāra was exceedingly level and even, growing soft and fine grass; many people constantly played and frolicked there, disturbing the bhikṣuṇīs as they sat in meditation and practiced the Path.
The bhikṣuṇīs, feeling weary and disgusted, then collectively defecated and urinated therein, making it foul and impure to drive away the crowd.
When the people later returned as usual to play and sport, they soiled their hands, feet, clothing, and utensils; they then spoke with great indignation:
"Who has here wantonly discharged excrement and urine?"
Some said, "This is a bhikṣuṇī! and they all reviled her, saying:
"How can these women who have left the household life to seek the path with such purity defile such a fine place and cut off the joy of others?
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked her in various ways. This led to the formulation of the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī voids excrement or urine upon living grass, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.'"
If it is a case of urgent illness, there is no offense.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs again threw refuse and leftover food onto the ground in front of the royal garden vihāra in order to drive away the crowds; consequently, the laypeople criticized and disparaged them.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the Buddha established this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above:
"From now on, this precept shall be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī throws away sweepings or leftover food onto living grass, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If she throws it into a pit or an unclean place, there is no offense.

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs stayed overnight in families where food was being prepared; hearing the sounds of the husband and wife during their union, they conceived lustful thoughts, no longer took pleasure in the Path, and subsequently returned to secular life or became followers of external paths.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. [The Buddha then continued: "I shall now establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as previously explained.
From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī stays overnight at a household where food is being prepared, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Regarding 'those who eat':
it refers to men and women who eat by way of sexual intercourse.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense."
If one is ill and must stay overnight, or if various difficulties arise,
there is no offense in any of these cases. At that time, the bhikṣus asked the bhikṣuṇīs,
"Where is the house of so-and-so located?"
“Where does this road lead?

The bhikṣuṇīs, treating them with contempt, did not answer. The bhikṣus became resentful and disdainful, and ceased to provide instruction. Consequently, they remained ignorant and deluded, unable to train in the precepts.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. [The Buddha then] established a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs up to the present point, as was explained above:
"From now on, this precept should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, when questioned by a bhikṣu, does not answer, it is a pāyattika.'"
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus addressed the bhikṣuṇīs with coarse and wicked speech. Although the bhikṣuṇīs replied, they felt ashamed and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit the bhikṣuṇīs to answer when a bhikṣu questions them in accordance with the Dharma."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when questioned by a bhikṣu in accordance with the Dharma, does not answer, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta."
If one previously harbored mutual resentment, did not speak with the other, did not respond, and did not commit an offense—this constitutes the one hundred and fortieth [rule].
At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs traveled by carriage to visit laypeople. The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs are like the wives of kings or women of noble families; they travel back and forth by carriage, lacking any sense of decorum or discipline!"
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they censured her in various ways. This leads to the formulation of the precept for bhikṣuṇīs as explained above:
"From now on, this precept shall be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī travels by riding in a vehicle, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Vehicles" refers to carriages, elephants, horses, and even wooden clogs; all such items are termed "vehicles.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī to do so constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
If one is old, or ill, or coerced by force, or traveling on a journey—even down to having a disease in a toe—there is no offense.
*The Ten-Section Vinaya*, Volume 13; *The Five-Part Vinaya*, Volume 14; Mūlasarvāstivāda.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśa during the Song Dynasty, together with Zhu Daosheng and others.
Part Two, Section Four. At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs went to visit laypeople while wearing leather sandals and carrying parasols.
The laypeople criticized and reviled them, saying, "These bhikṣuṇīs come and go like courtesans!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they censured them in various ways. Consequently, the Buddha now establishes the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī walks about wearing leather sandals and carrying a parasol, it is a pāyattika.
As for the 'parasol':"
"Even down to a grass canopy.
Regarding leather sandals:
even down to a single layer.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense. There is no offense in the cases mentioned above.

At that time, there were a husband and wife who both went forth into the religious life. When the husband, as a bhikṣu, returned from begging for alms, he went to the dwelling place of his wife, who was a bhikṣuṇī, to eat.
His wife, a bhikṣuṇī, stood before him holding a water pitcher, fanning him with a fan and offering him water, while repeatedly asking whether it was warm or cold.
Her husband, the bhikṣu, kept his head bowed as he ate; he did not look at her nor speak with her.
When that bhikṣu was formerly a layman, there was a woman with whom he had an illicit affair who also left the household life and resided there; when she came out and saw him, the bhikṣu smiled.
The bhikṣuṇī who was his wife, driven by a heart of jealousy, struck the bhikṣu on the head with a water jar until it broke.
The other bhikṣuṇīs rebuked her, saying:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī take up a water jar and a fan, stand before a bhikṣu, and provide him with water and a fan?"
She then struck his head until it was broken!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs were established, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, holding a water vessel and a fan, stands before a bhikṣu to give him water or to fan him, it is a pāyattika.'"
If one wishes to provide water, once it has been given, one should move far away and must not remain standing in front.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, this constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs were reciting medical treatises and prescriptions for treating illnesses, whereupon the laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These women study nothing but medical arts; they have no intention of seeking the Path!"
"Why do you not use this to recite the Buddhist scriptures?
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked her in various ways; consequently, the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī recites medical prescriptions for treating diseases, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.'"
There is no offense if one recites it for the sake of one's own illness, out of compassion, or because one is compelled by force.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs taught others to recite medical treatises and prescriptions for curing diseases, which led the laypeople to criticize and reproach them.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads up to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs as previously described:
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī instructs another to recite medical scriptures or prescriptions for treating diseases, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remainder is as stated above.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs treated people’s illnesses by compounding, boiling, and pounding various medicines, never resting from the first watch of the night until the last.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These people are like physicians or the disciples of physicians!
Why do they not seek the Way to cure the disease of birth and death, instead engaging in these worldly affairs?"
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads on to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as was explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī treats others for illness as her means of livelihood, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
If it is out of compassion, or if one is coerced by force, or if it is not for the sake of gain, there is no offense.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs taught people how to treat illnesses. When various laypeople came and said, "Preach the Dharma for us! they replied:
“Treating heat is thus; treating cold is thus; treating wind is thus; treating various illnesses is thus.
The laypeople said, “We have come for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of treating illness!”
He further reviled them, saying:
"These people study nothing but medical arts; they do not know the Dharma!
If that were not so, why did you not instruct me in the Dharma?"
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. Thereupon, up to the point where he now establishes the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, it is as explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī teaches others the treatment of diseases as a means of livelihood, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
The rest is as stated above.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs worked for the families of their acquaintances, and the laypeople criticized and reproached them, saying:
"These women have abandoned the work of their own families to work for other households!"
"You have no conduct of a śramaṇa; you destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked her in various ways. This leads up to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, for the sake of food or drink, performs labor for a lay household, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If it is out of compassion, or if one is coerced by force, there is no offense.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs lay on the same bedding as laywomen and women of other sects; their bodies touched one another, giving rise to lustful thoughts. They took no pleasure in the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and consequently returned to secular life or became followers of other sects.
Later, those women followed their acquaintances and said:
"The body of such-and-such a bhikṣuṇī has such-and-such beauty!
When laypeople later saw the bhikṣuṇīs, they would point at them and mock them, saying: [as before].
"Those with beautiful bodies are this bhikṣuṇī! They are that bhikṣuṇī!
Because of this, the bhikṣuṇīs felt ashamed.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads up to the present time when the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs is established, as previously described:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī lies down on the same bedding with a laywoman or a woman of a non-Buddhist sect, it is a pāyattika.'"
"If they share the same bed and covers, there must be a partition between their inner garments.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs lay down with bhikṣus, *śikṣamāṇās*, and *śrāmaṇerīs* using the same clothing; therefore, I now establish this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as was explained above."
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī lies down on the same bedding with a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remainder is as stated above.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs slept with laywomen and women of other sects, covering one another so that they saw each other’s bodies; consequently, lustful thoughts arose. This leads up to the formulation of the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs, which is also as stated above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī sleeps with a laywoman or a woman of another sect, covering one another, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remainder is as stated above.
If there was already a covering, or if one covers again over what is already covered, there is no offense.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs slept with other bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇerīs, and they saw each other’s bodies; this led up to the present formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, which is also as stated above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī sleeps with another bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, or a śrāmaṇerī, covering one another, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remainder is as stated above.

At that time, one hundred and fifty bhikṣuṇīs smeared their bodies with perfumes and also had others do so; they gave rise to lustful thoughts, took no pleasure in practicing the holy life (brahmacarya), and consequently returned to secular life or became followers of external paths.
When the laypeople smelled the fragrance, they reviled them, saying:
"These people smear their bodies with incense just like courtesans!
They lack the conduct of śramaṇas and destroy the dharma of śramaṇas!"
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads on until the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as was explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī applies perfume to her body, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding 'perfume':"
Root incense, stem incense, leaf incense, flower incense, insect incense, and resin incense.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If it is for the purpose of treating a disease, or if one is forced by another to apply it, there is no offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs used *tse-ku* (a fragrant substance) to rub their bodies so that they would become lustrous.
The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These people rub their bodies with oily ointments to make them look glossy and lustrous, just like lustful women!
They have no conduct befitting a śramaṇa; they destroy the Dharma of the śramaṇas!"
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads on until the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as was explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī uses *tse-k'u* (a type of exfoliating powder) to rub her body, it is a pāyattika.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrakapilā had little moisture in her body; being parched and cracked, she consulted a physician."
The physician said,
"You should use *ze-ku* (millet) to rub your body! He replied:
“The Buddha does not permit me to rub my body with dried mud; I pray that you will consider another treatment!
The physician said, “There is no other treatment!”
The bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"If the World-Honored One would permit me to rub my body with *ze-ku* when ill, I shall no longer suffer from this affliction.
