She reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit bhikṣuṇīs, when they are ill, to rub their bodies with *takkola*.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, rubs her body with *takka* (a medicinal paste), it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta."

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs kept flower garlands or wore them; they developed a mind of defiled attachment, took no pleasure in practicing the holy life (brahmacarya), and consequently returned to secular life or became followers of external paths.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they rebuked her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs was established, as previously described:
"From now on, this precept should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī keeps flower garlands or wears them, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Even to the extent of binding grass or leaves upon the head for the sake of ornament, all such acts are termed 'wearing flower garlands.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, this constitutes a duṣkṛta offense."
If one is coerced by forceful means, there is no offense.

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs, wearing precious necklaces and ornaments, gave rise to thoughts of lustful desire and no longer took pleasure in practicing the holy life (brahmacarya); consequently, they returned to secular life or became followers of external paths.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they censured her in various ways. This leads to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as previously described:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī wears jeweled necklaces or ornaments, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
This applies even to making necklaces out of wood; it is the same for all such cases.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense. There is no offense in the cases mentioned above.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs wore garments that were too tight, making their bodies appear slender and well-proportioned; this gave rise to lustful thoughts. Consequently, the Buddha established a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī wears clothing that exposes the body, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.'"
There was no offense as described above.

At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs kept all kinds of ornaments for adorning the body, which gave rise to thoughts of lustful desire; consequently, up to the present, the Buddha has established the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs, as explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī keeps various kinds of ornaments for adorning the body, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.'"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs wore their hair long. Consequently, the Buddha now formulated a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as previously explained.
"From this day forward, this precept shall be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī wears her hair long, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
If a bhikṣuṇī allows her hair to grow long, it is a pāyattika offense.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, to keep their hair or to allow it to grow long without shaving it is a duṣkṛta offense.
One should shave once every half-month;
if more than this time elapses, it is called "long hair.
If there is no one to shave them, or if one is compelled by force and unable to shave, in all such cases there is no offense.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs wore the ornaments used by women in white robes and gave rise to thoughts of lustful desire.
At that time, the host of the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā had recently taken a wife; the wife gave her ornaments to her so that she might wear them.
Having put it on, she covered her head and slept on the bed.
When her husband returned from outside and wished to approach his wife, he uncovered her head and only then realized what was there; he rebuked her, saying:
"If I had not uncovered your head before engaging in sexual intercourse, would I not have incurred a grave offense?"
"How can a bhikṣuṇī do such a thing? She has no conduct of a śramaṇa!
She destroys the dharma of a śramaṇa!"
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways; consequently, the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī wears ornaments for adorning the body, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a dukkaṭa.'"
There was no offense as described above.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs were making ornaments for others, and the laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These women are like courtesans making ornaments!"
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways; consequently, the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī makes ornaments for another person, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a dukkaṭa.'"
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs were spinning thread, and the laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These women rely on others for their food and clothing, yet they do not think of practicing the Path to repay the faithful offerings made to them; why are they spinning thread?"
"There is no conduct of a śramaṇa!
You have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked her in various ways. This leads to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī spins thread, it is a pāyattika. For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a dukkaṭa.'"
If one makes a waist-cord, a meditation belt, a shoulder-sling, or needle-cases for sewing, there is no offense.
(160) At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs stayed at the homes of laypeople they were acquainted with, spreading out bedding and mats. The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"How can you leave your own home to stay in the homes of others?"
"We do not rejoice at seeing this inauspicious object!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked her in various ways. This leads to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, without having asked the permission of a layperson, should suddenly spread out bedding or furniture in their house and dwell there, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If she stays at the home of a relative, there is no offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs spread out the master’s bedding and seating in the homes of laypeople, or they had others spread them out.
When departing, she neither lifted it herself nor instructed others to lift it.
The laypeople criticized and rebuked her, saying:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī spread out mats for people to sit or lie upon, and then depart without lifting them up?"
"We shall always serve as their slaves!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked her in various ways. This leads to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as explained above.
“From this day forward, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī goes to the home of a layperson and spreads out bedding or seating for the host, or causes another to spread it out.’”
"If, when departing, one does not lift [the object] oneself nor instruct another to lift it, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*."
If one has been instructed to report [the offense], there is no violation.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs cooked raw food themselves, and the laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"How can bhikṣuṇīs cook raw food themselves?"
"Since you have already cooked food for yourself, why do you go to others to beg for it?
You lack the conduct of a śramaṇī and violate the dharma of a śramaṇī!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked her in various ways. This leads to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs as explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī cooks raw food for herself to make a meal, it is a pāyattika offense.
There is no offense if it is for the sake of illness."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā came to Śrāvastī, and the bhikṣuṇī Caṇḍasumana lent her a vihāra for her to reside in.

Kṣemā had attained the *maitrīcitta-samādhi*, possessed great majestic power, and was surrounded by a circle of accomplished followers; thus, Caṇḍa’s disciples all held her in high esteem and desired to follow her.
Cāṇḍā discovered this and spoke with angry reproach:
"I lent you the vihāra for you to dwell in, yet you have instead enticed away my disciples!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways.
“How could she borrow another’s vihāra and later become angry and slander her?
Thus, up until the point where he establishes the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, it is as explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, having first been permitted to stay, later becomes angry and slanders [the host], it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.'"
If there is a factual basis and she acts out of anger or resentment, there is no offense.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrakāpilā developed an abscess on her thigh; without informing the Saṃgha, she summoned a male physician to lance it, drain the pus, wash it, and apply medicinal ointments.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they rebuked her, saying:
"Since you have already detached from desire, it may be so for you!
But would one who has not yet detached from desire not commit a grave offense?"
Thus, up until now, the precept has been established for the bhikṣuṇīs as previously explained.
"From this day forward, this precept shall be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, without having informed the Saṃgha, should cause a man to treat her illness, it is a pāyattika.'"

If one wishes to treat a man's illness, one should strike the *ghanṭī* to assemble the Sangha; once they have gathered before the patient, he should then wrap his body in robes, leaving only that part exposed which requires treatment.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If she causes a woman to repair it, there is no offense.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs would open the city gates at night and depart without telling those behind them to close them; when thieves came in the night, they plundered the robes and bowls of the bhikṣuṇīs.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs reproached her in various ways, and so forth, until now the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs is established as previously described:
"From this day forward, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī opens the main gate at night and goes out without informing the other bhikṣuṇīs to close it, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
There is no offense if there is no place of fear.
At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs went to the homes of laypeople at an improper time.
There was a very wealthy family, which bandits constantly sought to plunder but had not yet found an opportunity; they therefore questioned passersby:
"Who enters and leaves this house?"
Someone said: "The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā is on good terms with this family; they frequently visit one another.
The thief then went and said to Thullanandā:
“Sister! So-and-so is calling for you.
She followed these words and went there at dusk; the host opened the door for her, whereupon the thief burst inside and plundered all their possessions.
The host rebuked him in anger, saying:
"If this bhikṣuṇī had not come at an improper time, I would not have opened the door, and I would not have met with this calamity!
To seek merit through offerings and instead bring about disaster—how is this any different from nurturing an enemy?"
The elder bhikṣuṇīs reprimanded her in various ways, up until the point where, as previously stated, the Buddha now formulated a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs:
"From this day forward, this precept shall be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī enters the home of a layperson at an improper time, it is a pāyattika.'"
Furthermore, there were certain bhikṣuṇīs who did not dare go when called by laypeople; they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of the two divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit bhikṣuṇīs to go when summoned by laypeople."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī enters the house of a layperson at an improper time without being invited, it is a pāyattika."
"Improper time" refers to the period from after midday until the appearance of the dawn light.
If a layperson calls, one should carefully examine whether that messenger is a person who can be trusted.
Furthermore, you should interrogate them thoroughly to ascertain whether their account is true or false;
if doubts still remain, upon reaching the gate, you should first ask the household:
"Did you ultimately summon him or not?"
Only then should one enter.
Furthermore, one must deliberate: is this not a time when it is dangerous?
If one goes to the house of a layperson at an improper time, stepping one foot across the threshold constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If both feet have stepped out [the boundary], it is a *pāyattika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, there was a householder who invited the community of bhikṣuṇīs for a meal.

Before the meal, several bhikṣuṇīs put on their robes, took up their bowls, and went to a certain household, where they asked the person preparing the food for a drink, or for the scorched crust from the pot, or for some rice.
The food-preparer thought to himself:
"I have now prepared this food specifically for these people; what difference does it make whether it is given before or after?"
He then gave it all to them, and they consumed the food and drink entirely.

When the host arrived at the appointed time, he struck the *ghanṭā* to assemble the Saṃgha and ordered that the meal be served. The cook reported the matter in full, whereupon the lay devotee rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs are like small children; they cannot endure even a little!"
"Eating greedily like this, what path can there be?
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked her in various ways. This leads to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī accepts an invitation, and the host has not yet announced that she may eat at will,
if she eats, it is a pāyattika.'"
If one eats food before the formal invitation to eat has been proclaimed, for every mouthful, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
(170) At that time, after the bhikṣuṇīs had performed the formal act of expulsion according to the Dharma, the expelled bhikṣuṇī refused to leave.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs reprimanded her in various ways, saying:
"What difference is there between one who has undergone the formal act of expulsion and one who has not?"
Thus, up until now, the training rule has been established for the bhikṣuṇīs as previously explained.
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having been subjected to the formal act of expulsion (pravāsanīya-karman), does not depart, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the formal act of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*):
it is performed by means of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one is ill, if the eight difficulties have arisen, or if an illegal *karmavācanā* (formal act) is being performed, there is no offense in any of these cases.

At that time, when the bhikṣuṇīs were assembling for a formal gathering according to the Dharma, some bhikṣuṇīs did not go immediately; the other bhikṣuṇīs waited for them, which hindered the practice of the Path.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs reprimanded her in various ways, and so on, until now the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs is established as previously stated:
"From this day forward, this precept shall be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī does not immediately go when the Saṃgha has assembled in accordance with the Dharma, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
There is no offense if one is ill, if one does not hear [the announcement], or if the eight calamities arise.

At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs went to watch singing, dancing, and performances; they gave rise to defiled attachments and no longer delighted in the Path, eventually leading some to return to secular life or become followers of external paths.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled them, saying:
"These people watching songs, dances, and performances are just like lustful women!
They lack the conduct of śramaṇas and destroy the dharma of śramaṇas!"
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads on to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī watches performances of singing, dancing, or instrumental music, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.'"
There is no offense, as explained above regarding the observation of the royal palace and the observation of paintings.
At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs went to the borderlands; the people of those borderlands seized them to make them female slaves, or plundered their robes and bowls, or violated their pure conduct.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads up to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above:
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī goes to a border region, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Border regions" refers to places where there are no bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs.
For śikṣamāṇās and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If she flies through the air, there is no offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs ordained a person with both sexual organs (ubhayavyañjana). The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"How can the bhikṣuṇīs ordain a person with both sexual organs?"
"There is no one who can be saved, nor anyone who cannot be saved!
There is no conduct of a śramaṇa; you have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked her in various ways. This leads to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī ordains a person with both sexual organs, it is a pāyattika.
If she has doubts, she should first examine them.'"
From the initial resolution of the mind until the three *karmavācanās* are not yet completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Once they are completed, for the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), it is a *pāyattika*;
for the other *bhikṣuṇīs*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs ordained women whose two vaginal canals were joined into one.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs rebuked them in various ways, leading up to the present formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī ordains a woman whose two channels have merged into one channel, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
"If, after the ordination is completed, such an illness occurs, there is no offense.
The rest is as stated above.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs ordained women who were constantly menstruating; while they were going on almsround, blood flowed and stained their feet.
When the laypeople saw this, they looked upon them with contempt and reviled them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of who is fit for ordination and who is not; they ordain such as these, defiling people's beds and mats!"
"They lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked them in various ways. This leads up to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī ordains a woman who is constantly menstruating, it is a pāyattika.
The rest is as stated above."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs did not pay homage to the bhikṣus; they neither welcomed nor saw them off, nor did they invite them to sit.
The bhikṣus became resentful and ceased to provide instruction and admonition. Consequently, the bhikṣuṇīs remained ignorant and uninformed, unable to train in the precepts.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this and rebuked them in various ways, reporting the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and asked the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked her in various ways, saying:
"Did I not previously state that according to the Eight Rules of Respect, one ought to pay homage to bhikṣus?
From this day forward, this precept shall be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī sees a bhikṣu and does not rise, does not pay homage, and does not invite him to sit, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta."
If one is ill;
or if there is prior resentment or enmity such that one does not speak with the other, there is no offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs had this thought:
"The Buddha did not permit us to shave the hair of our private parts; we shall now burn it off with fire!
They immediately set fire to it.

At that time, a brahmin who had lost his sheep went searching for it; arriving at the nuns' alleyway, he smelled the scent of burning hair and concluded that the nuns had stolen and slaughtered his sheep. He then went to the king and reported the matter to him.
The king immediately summoned the bhikṣuṇī and asked her: "Auntie!
Did you kill the Brahmin’s sheep?"
He replied, "I do not kill. He was asked:
"If you had not killed it, how could there be the smell of burning wool?
He answered truthfully.
Upon hearing this, the king laughed loudly and immediately released him to go. When the ministers heard of this, they reviled and censured him, saying:
"How is it that a bhikṣuṇī does not mindfully practice the Path, but instead burns the hair in her private parts?
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked her in various ways. This led to the formulation of a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī burns the hair of the private parts, it is a pāyattika.
The remainder is as explained in the section concerning shaving the hair of the private parts."
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs went to the homes of laypeople without wearing their saṃkakṣikās (undershirts). The wind blew up their upper robes, exposing their bodies.
When the laypeople saw this, they mocked them and spoke coarse and vulgar words together, which caused them great shame.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads to the formulation of a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs as previously explained:
"From now on, this precept shall be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī enters the home of a layperson without wearing a saṃkakṣikā, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If there is no washing, dyeing, beating, or sewing, there is no offense in any case.

(180) At that time, various bhikṣuṇīs sat face-to-face with laypeople (*avadātavasana*), leaning their bodies close together while preaching the Dharma as if whispering in private. Consequently, they gave rise to defiled and attached thoughts, which led some to return to secular life or become followers of external paths (*tīrthika*). The laypeople then criticized and reviled them.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs was established, as described above:
"From now on, this precept shall be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī sits facing a layperson with their bodies close together and preaches the Dharma to them, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs danced and sang for themselves, and the laypeople criticized and reviled them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs dance and sing for themselves like courtesans!"
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads on until the Buddha now formulates a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as was explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī herself sings or dances, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.'"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs obstructed the acceptance of the kaṭhina robe. Because the bhikṣuṇīs waited for a long time without it arriving, it hindered and interrupted their practice of the Path.
The elder bhikṣuṇīs reproached them in various ways, leading up to the present formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī obstructs the acceptance of the kaṭhina robe, it is a pāyattika offense.
There is no offense if she is ill or if she has not heard [the announcement]."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs obstructed the relinquishing of the kaṭhina robe, leading up to the present formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs as previously described:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī obstructs the relinquishing of the kaṭhina robe, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remainder is as stated above. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Khemā was clever and possessed of ready eloquence; she would pose difficult questions to the bhikṣus.

The bhikṣus were unable to answer them and felt great shame. Thereafter, whenever they saw the bhikṣuṇīs, they would immediately take a side road to avoid them. Consequently, there was no one left to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; they became ignorant and dull-witted, unable to study the precepts.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads down to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as explained above:
"From now on, this precept shall be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī interrogates a bhikṣu with difficult questions, it is a pāyattika.'"

There were some bhikṣuṇīs who, being possessed of doubt, did not dare to pose questions or challenge [the teachings]. Because of this, they remained ignorant and lacked understanding, unable to train in the precepts.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit the bhikṣuṇīs to first inform the bhikṣus; those who wish to ask may then do so."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, without having informed a bhikṣu, should arbitrarily inquire about the meaning [of the Dharma], it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta."
At that time, Upananda frequently went to and fro at the residence of the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā.
Later, putting on his robes and taking his bowl, he went to her place; as she rose and sat down with careless ease, they saw one another's bodies.
Bhadrananda then discharged his impurity; Stūlanandā took his undergarment to wash it, but inserted her own impurity into her own body, whereby she subsequently became pregnant.
When the bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they asked,
"Are you not practicing the holy life? She replied:
"It is not that I have failed to practice the holy life!
It is because I placed my own male impurity within my own body that I have become pregnant!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked her in various ways. This leads on to the formulation of the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī inserts her own impurity from a man into her own body, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs performed the fire-worship rituals of non-Buddhists, kindling fires and reciting their mantras.
The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These people cannot even purify their own views; how could they possess the Way?
They lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!"
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. Consequently, for the sake of the bhikṣuṇīs, the precept was now established, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī performs the practice of non-Buddhist fire-worship by kindling a fire, it is a pāyattika.
If she does so out of wrong view, it is a sthūlātyaya.'"
If one performs various such acts of the non-Buddhists, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense for all.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs were bathing in a place where people were present; when the crowd saw them, they watched and mocked them.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they rebuked her in various ways. This leads up to the formulation of a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī bathes in a place where there are people present, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs recited the incantations and arts of non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
The laypeople criticized and reviled them, saying:
"These women recite non-Buddhist mantras and lack the aspiration for the Path!
Thus it was, leading up to the present time when the precepts were established for the bhikṣuṇīs, all as explained in the recitation of the medical prescriptions for curing diseases.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī recites non-Buddhist incantations or teaches others to recite them, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
At that time, the community of bhikṣuṇīs conferred full ordination upon themselves; they were foolish, ignorant, and incapable of training in the precepts.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads down to the point where the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as was explained above:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon a candidate before a single assembly, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
If he has resolved his mind [to leave], but the formal procedure (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) has not yet been completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Once it is completed, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) commits a *pāyattika* offense;
the rest of the monastic community commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

190. At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs themselves performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of taking on disciples, themselves performed the formal act of the two-year training in the precepts, and themselves conferred the two-year training in the precepts; yet they were unable to instruct their disciples, being foolish, ignorant, and incapable of learning the precepts.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways.
This leads up to the present time, when the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs is established as previously described:
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī performs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of herself becoming a mentor for a following, it is an offense of expiation (*pāyattika*).
"If a bhikṣuṇī performs the formal act of herself undertaking the two-year training in the precepts, it is an offense of expiation."
"If a bhikṣuṇī herself grants the two-year training in the precepts, it is a pāyattika.
The remainder is as stated above.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs performed the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for the completion of the two-year training in the precepts, but only after one night had passed did they grant them full ordination (upasampadā). Because difficulties arose in the interim, they were consequently unable to receive full ordination.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs were established, as previously described:
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:

'If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the formal procedure (karmavācanā) for the two-year training in the precepts, confers full ordination (upasampadā) after a night has passed, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
If he resolves [to do so] and it reaches until the appearance of the dawn light, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Once the dawn light has appeared, for the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), it is a *pāyattika*;
for the rest of the community of teachers, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There is no offense if one is ill, if difficulties arise, or if the Saṃgha does not assemble.

At that time, after the bhikṣuṇīs had completed the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) for the two-year training in the precepts, they waited until the night had passed before conferring the training; meanwhile, difficulties arose, and consequently, the training could not be received.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads down to the formulation of the precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as previously explained:
"From now on, this precept shall be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the formal ritual (karmavācanā) for two years of training, confers the training upon that person only after a night has passed, it is a pāyattika.'"
If one has formed the intention [to commit the offense] but the dawn has not yet appeared, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Once the dawn has appeared, for the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), it is a *pāyattika*;
for the rest of the community of teachers, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
There was no offense as previously explained.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs were weaving their own robes, and the white-robed laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"How can these bhikṣuṇīs not be mindful of practicing the Path?"
She wove it with her own hands, just like other weavers!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they censured her in various ways. [The Buddha then established a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.]
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī weaves a robe for herself to wear, it is a pāyattika.
If she weaves and casts the shuttle, for every casting, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
However, if one weaves a waist-cord or a meditation belt, there is no offense.

At that time, King Prasenajit’s attendants and various bhikṣuṇīs were traveling and sightseeing in a dangerous area when they were stripped of their belongings by bandits; some had their brahmacarya violated, while others were taken captive.
The other bhikṣuṇīs reported this to the king, who said, "I am no longer my own master; what can I do with these bhikṣuṇīs?
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked him in various ways, saying:
"Why do you wander through places of terror? ...
[the passage] up to "now for the sake of the bhikṣuṇīs, I shall establish this precept," is as previously stated.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī travels through a region that is dangerous and fearful, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta."
If she was already traveling on the road and a danger subsequently arose, there was no offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs made images of themselves, and they also had others make them.
At that time, Stūlanandā also had an image made for herself. Upon seeing her own likeness, a mind of defiled attachment arose within her, and she thought:
"My physical appearance is such as this; why should I disparage it by practicing the holy life?"
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they censured her in various ways; consequently, the Buddha now establishes a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as was explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī makes an image of herself, or causes another to make one for her, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Making an image of oneself" means:
either painting one, or making one out of wood, or out of clay.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one secretly prepares [ornaments] and shows them to her, there is no offense.
At that time, because the bhikṣuṇīs adorned women, those women gave rise to a lack of joy in the path and subsequently returned to secular life or became followers of external paths.
The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"How can these bhikṣuṇīs adorn women as if they were their mothers?
What difference is there between this and adorning oneself?"
They did not contemplate the practice of the Path, but instead engaged in improper adornments; they lacked the conduct of a śramaṇī and violated the dharma of a śramaṇī!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked them in various ways, leading up to the present time when the precepts were established for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
“From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī adorns a woman, it is a pāyattika. ‘Adorns’ means:”
If one combs their hair, or even inserts a single flower, or puts on a single bracelet, each such act constitutes a *pāyattika*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs were bathing in the water and went against the current; being touched by the water, they conceived thoughts of lustful desire, which ultimately led them to return to secular life or become followers of external paths.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways. This leads to the formulation of a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as explained above:
"From now on, this precept shall be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī swims against the current in water, it is a pāyattika.'"
If one goes against the current, for every step there is a *pāyattika*;
if semen is emitted, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If there is no lustful mind, there is no offense.

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs lay on their backs beneath a leaky roof; as water dripped into their bodies, they conceived lustful thoughts, which ultimately led them to return to secular life or become followers of external paths.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured her in various ways, even up to the point where the Buddha now establishes this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as was explained above:
"From this day forward, this precept shall be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī lies on her back at a place where water flows downstream, it is a pāyattika.'"
The rest is as stated above.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs wrapped their waists with ropes, desiring them to appear slender and beautiful, thereby giving rise to thoughts of lustful desire.
The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying: [text continues]
"These women treat their waists so as to make them slender like those of courtesans!
They have no mind for the Way, but only engage in perverse acts!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked them in various ways. This led to the formulation of the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī trims her waist to make it slender, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.'"

At that time, two hundred bhikṣuṇīs adorned their bodies in various ways to make them beautiful, thereby giving rise to lustful thoughts... [omitted] ...down to the point where the Buddha now establishes this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī applies various treatments to her body, it is a pāyattika.
The remainder is as explained above."

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs dressed in the manner of courtesans; this gave rise to a lack of aspiration for the Path, leading them eventually to return to secular life. Consequently, the Buddha established a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as previously described.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī dresses in the manner of a courtesan, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.'"

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs dressed in the manner of laywomen, which gave rise to a lack of joy in the Path. Consequently, up until now, the precepts have been established for the bhikṣuṇīs as previously described.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī dresses in the manner of a laywoman, it is a pāyattika.
The remainder is as stated above."

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs, out of lustful desire, gazed at their own bodies and gave rise to thoughts of craving. Consequently, up until now, the precepts have been established for the bhikṣuṇīs, as explained above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, examines her own body, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.'"

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs looked into mirrors and gave rise to a mind of dissatisfaction with the Path. Consequently, the Buddha now formulated a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, as previously described.
"From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī looks into a mirror, it is a pāyattika.
If she looks into water, it is a duṣkṛta."
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If there is a sore on the face, looking into it does not constitute an offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs engaged in various forms of divination for themselves and also sought divinations from others.
The laypeople criticized them, saying, "Since these women do not abandon their wrong views, how can they possibly attain the Path?
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they rebuked them in various ways. This led to the formulation of the precepts for the bhikṣuṇīs, as described above.
"From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī divines for herself or seeks divination from another, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.'"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs discussed among themselves in private:
"Will we who have left the household life attain ultimate liberation?
Or will we not attain ultimate liberation?"
"Should she renounce the religious life or not?
If she were to renounce it, would she find a good husband?
And how many sons would she have?"
"What is the nature of physiognomy and fortune-telling?
Because of such discussions, worldly sentiments arose; they no longer took pleasure in the Way, and consequently, some returned to secular life or became followers of external paths.
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they rebuked her in various ways, saying:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī engage in worldly discourse and thereby forget the aspiration for the Path?"
Thus, up until now, the precept has been formulated for the bhikṣuṇīs as previously described:
"From this day forward, this precept should be stated as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī engages in worldly discourse, it is a pāyattika.'"
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. [Section 207 ends.

**The Fifth Division of the Second Book of the Pañcavargika Vinaya: The Method for Confession of Faults in the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya.** At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs were fond of consuming ghee (*sarpi*) and frequently begged for it from others.
The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"Ghee makes people look radiant and is something consumed by the world;
why do these bhikṣuṇīs not seek the flavor of the Dharma?"
To be greedily attached to and crave beauty, seeking a fine complexion—how is this different from being with a courtesan?
You have no conduct of a śramaṇa!
You destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, they censured them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Saṃgha of both divisions and asked the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish for the bhikṣuṇīs a *pāṭidesanīya* rule. From this day forth, this precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī eats ghee, she must confess her transgression before the bhikṣuṇīs.'"
"I have fallen into a blameworthy state; I now repent before the Venerable Sisters!
This is called the method of repentance.
At that time, when the bhikṣuṇīs were eating in the midst of the Saṃgha, at a meal invited by a household, or while begging for alms, they obtained ghee but did not dare to eat it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit bhikṣuṇīs to consume ghee even if they have not requested it."
From now on, this precept should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī begs for ghee to eat,
that bhikṣuṇī should confess her transgression before the other bhikṣuṇīs."
"I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I now repent before the venerable nuns!
This is called the rite of repentance.
There were certain sick bhikṣuṇīs who required ghee, yet they did not dare to ask for it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the Sangha of both divisions and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I now permit sick bhikṣuṇīs to beg for ghee as food."
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, being without illness, begs for ghee for her own sake and eats it,
that bhikṣuṇī should confess her transgression before the other bhikṣuṇīs:"
"I have fallen into a blameworthy dharma; I now repent before the venerable nuns!
This is called the dharma of repentance.
For a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
When a bhikṣuṇī begs for oil, honey, rock sugar, milk, curd, fish, or meat, it is all as explained above.
6. The Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya: Rules of Training for the Community. The Second Part, Section Six: The Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya: Rules of Training for the Community. At that time, Upāli asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, you have already established the rules of training for the bhikṣus:
‘One should train oneself not to wear the lower robe too high.’”
"...up to: 'One should not climb a tree taller than a person, except for a great cause;
this is how one should train. How should I uphold this?
The Buddha said:
"It should be maintained by the two assemblies of monks.
From now on, this precept should be recited as follows:
'One should train oneself not to wear the lower robe too high.'"
"One should not wear the lower robe tucked down.
"One should not wear the lower robe unevenly.
"One should not wear the lower robe like a palm leaf."
"It is not as good as wearing the lower robe like an elephant's trunk.
"It is not as good as wearing the lower robe like a round myrobalan fruit.
"One should not wear the lower robe with fine pleats."
“Do not wear the robe too high.
Do not wear the robe too low.
Do not wear the robe unevenly.”
“Covering the body well, one enters the house of a layperson.
“Covering the body well, one sits in the house of a layperson.
“One does not lift the robe over the right shoulder, entering the house of a layperson.”
"One should not sit in the house of a layperson with one’s robe draped over the right shoulder.
One should not enter the house of a layperson with one’s robe draped over the left shoulder."
"One should not sit in the house of a layperson with one’s robe folded back and placed over the left shoulder.
One should not enter the house of a layperson with the robe folded back and placed over both shoulders on the left and right."
"One should not sit in the house of a layperson with one’s robe draped over both shoulders by folding it up from the left and right.
One should not enter the house of a layperson shaking the body.
One should not sit in the house of a layperson shaking the body."
"One should not shake the head when entering the house of a layperson.
One should not shake the head while sitting in the house of a layperson.
One should not shake the shoulders when entering the house of a layperson."
"One should not shake one's shoulders when entering the house of a layperson to sit.
One should not join one's hands when entering the house of a layperson.
One should not join one's hands when sitting in the house of a layperson."
"One should not enter the house of a layperson while concealing one's body.
One should not sit in the house of a layperson while concealing one's body.
One should not enter the house of a layperson with hands placed on the hips."
"One should not sit in the house of a layperson with hands on the hips.
"One should not enter the house of a layperson resting the chin on the hand.
"One should not sit in the house of a layperson resting the chin on the hand."
"One should not swing one's arms while entering the house of a layperson.
One should not swing one's arms while sitting in the house of a layperson.
One should not look upward while entering the house of a layperson."
"One should not look upward while sitting in the house of a layperson.
One should not look left or right while entering the house of a layperson.
One should not look left or right while sitting in the house of a layperson."
"One should not enter the house of a layperson while squatting.
One should not sit in the house of a layperson while squatting.
One should not enter the house of a layperson while standing on tiptoe."
"One should not walk on tiptoe; one should sit in the house of a layperson [with feet flat].
One should not enter the house of a layperson with the head covered;
one should sit in the house of a layperson with the head uncovered."
"One should not enter the house of a layperson while laughing or joking.
One should not sit in the house of a layperson while laughing or joking.
One should not enter the house of a layperson with a loud voice."
"Do not speak in a loud voice while sitting in the house of a layperson.
Enter the house of a layperson with composed dignity.
Sit in the house of a layperson with composed dignity."
"Receive food with a focused mind.
Do not receive food so that it overflows the bowl.
Eat both the soup and the rice together."
"One should not take food from various places within the bowl.
One should not scoop out the center of the bowl to eat.
One should not bend the fingers to gather food from the bowl."
“Do not eat food by smelling it.
‘Eat while gazing intently at the bowl.
‘Do not discard rice or food.”
"One should not hold a vessel for pure drink with a hand soiled by food.
One should not slurp while eating.
One should not make chewing noises while eating."
"Do not lick the food while eating.
"Do not eat with a handful of food.
"Do not open your mouth wide to eat."
"Do not wait with the mouth wide open before the rice has arrived.
Do not eat with the nose wrinkled.
Do not speak while food is held in the mouth."
"One should not eat with puffed-out cheeks.
One should not bite off half a morsel.
One should not reach out one's arm to take food."
"Do not eat by shaking the hand.
"Do not eat by sticking out the tongue.
"Do not eat by swallowing with the mouth full."
"Do not grasp the rice and throw it into the mouth from a distance.
Do not sprinkle rice or water from the bowl onto the interior of a layperson's house.
Do not cover the soup with rice in hopes of obtaining more."
"Do not disparage the food.
"Do not ask for more food for yourself.
"Do not look at the bowl of a fellow monk with a disparaging mind."
"One shall not stand while defecating or urinating, except when ill.
One shall not defecate or urinate in pure water, except when ill.
One shall not defecate or urinate upon living grass or vegetables, except when ill."
"One should not preach the Dharma to a person wearing wooden clogs, except in the case of illness.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person wearing leather sandals, except in the case of illness."
"One should not preach the Dharma to a person who has exposed their chest, except in the case of illness.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person who is seated while one is standing, except in the case of illness."
"If a person is seated on a high seat and a bhikṣuṇī is below, she should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
If a person is lying down and a bhikṣuṇī is sitting, she should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness."
"If a man is in front and a bhikṣuṇī is behind, she should not preach the Dharma to him, except in the case of illness.
"If a man is on the path and a bhikṣuṇī is off the path, she should not preach the Dharma to him, except in the case of illness."
"One should not preach the Dharma to a person with their head covered, except in the case of illness.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person who has tucked up their robe, except in the case of illness.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person who has tucked up their robe on both the left and right sides, except in the case of illness."
"One should not preach the Dharma to one who is holding a parasol to cover the body, except in the case of illness.
One should not preach the Dharma to one who is riding a mount, except in the case of illness.
One should not preach the Dharma to one who is leaning on a staff, except in the case of illness."
"One should not preach the Dharma to one who is holding a blade.
One should not preach the Dharma to one who is holding a bow and arrow.
One should train oneself: 'Unless there is a great cause, one must not climb a tree that exceeds the height of a person.'"
"Great causes and conditions" refers to the various perils of wild beasts; these are called great causes and conditions.

The Third Division, Part One: The Method for Receiving the Precepts. Regarding the initial method for receiving the precepts at the beginning of the Third Division: The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha and addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a king named Urumā; he had four sons born of concubines:
the first was named Cakṣu, the second Akṣa, the third Hastin, and the fourth Nīla."
They were intelligent and far-sighted, and both possessed majestic virtue.
The first lady had a son named Changsheng (Long Life), who was stubborn, frivolous, and ugly, and was despised by all people.
The lady thought to herself:
"Although my son is grown, his talent does not equal that of others;
yet those four sons all possess majesty and virtue. The destiny of the kingdom must surely fall upon such as these."
"What plan should be devised to secure my son's foundation?
He further thought: 'The King sees me with trust and affection, more so than the other consorts!'"
"It is precisely right that one should first seek through emotion and subsequently establish through principle!
Thinking thus, she immediately adorned herself and, when the king entered, she showed him double the reverence and respect.
When the king wished to approach her, she immediately wept; the king asked for the reason, and the lady replied:
"My humble wish has not been fulfilled; with this, all is ended!"
The King said,
"If your wish is indeed reasonable, I swear I shall not go against it!
He then addressed the King, saying:
"The four sons of the King all possess majesty and virtue; although my son is the eldest, his talent does not equal theirs, and he will surely be usurped if he inherits this great enterprise!
If the King banishes these four sons, my mind shall find peace!"
The king said, "My four sons are filial and fraternal; they have committed no offense against the state.
How could I now cast them out?"
The lady spoke again:
"My heart is weary, for I truly bear the burdens of both the household and the state!
Your Majesty’s four sons all possess majesty and virtue, and the people each cherish their attachment to them."
"Once they compete, they will surely destroy one another; why must the fortune of a great state necessarily belong to the descendants of the King?
The King said: "Stop, stop!"
"Do not speak of this again!
He then summoned his four sons and commanded them to leave the country.
The four sons obeyed his orders and immediately prepared their departure.
At that time, the mother of the four sons and their sisters all requested to go together;
furthermore, many of the Mallas, artisans, brahmins, elders, householders, and all the people desired to follow them, and the king granted them all permission.

Thereupon, the four sons bowed in farewell and departed. Crossing the Gaṅgā River, they reached the north of the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*), where the land was level and vast, pure and serene in every direction, and abounded in various fruits and diverse species of birds and beasts.
The four sons saw this and called out to the brahmins, elders, and householders to stop, whereupon they deliberated together, saying:
"Among all the places we have passed through, none is superior to this!"
"Is it suitable for us to dwell here?
They all agreed without dissent.
Thereupon they halted their journey and began constructing a city.
Within a few years, those who returned were as numerous as in a marketplace; the population gradually flourished until it became a great kingdom.
Several years after his departure, the father king missed his sons and asked his ministers, "Where are my four sons now?"

He replied: "To the north of the Snowy Mountains, near the Śākya forest, a city has been built and established; its population is flourishing, the land is fertile and the fields abundant, and there is no lack of food or clothing."
Upon hearing this, the king sighed three times, saying: "My son is capable!
He sighed thus three times.
From this point on, they were consequently known as the Śākya clan.
Nīla had a son named Gaṇḍuṣa. Gaṇḍuṣa’s son was named Gauthula.
The son of Gautama was named Niṣṭhāna. Niṣṭhāna had four sons:
the first was named Śuddhodana, the second Śuklodana, the third Droṇodana, and the fourth Amṛtodana.
King Śuddhodana had two sons:
the first was named Bodhisattva and the second was named Nanda.
King Śuklodana had two sons:
The first was named Ānanda; the second was named Devadatta.
King Droṇodana had two sons:
the first was named Mahānāman; the second was named Aniruddha.
Amṛtodana had two sons:
the first was named Vappa and the second was named Bhadrika.
The Bodhisattva had a son named Rāhula.
"The Bodhisattva had little inclination for the life of a renunciant; his father the King, fearing he would study the Way, constantly entertained him with the five desires.

When he reached the age of fourteen, the King prepared a grand carriage for an excursion. As they passed through the eastern city gate, he encountered an old man with white hair and a hunched back, leaning on a staff and walking with feeble steps."
He asked the charioteer,
"Who is this? The charioteer replied:
"An old man! he asked again,
"What is meant by 'old'?"

He replied: "When one’s years are advanced and the faculties have matured, the form changes and the complexion fades; sitting and rising are extremely difficult, and little of life remains—therefore, this is called old age."
The Bodhisattva asked,
"Am I to be exempt from this? He replied:
"Not yet! he said, and immediately turned his carriage back toward the palace. He thought to himself that he had not yet transcended the law of old age, and he was filled with sorrow and distress.
The King asked the charioteer:
"Was the Prince pleased with his excursion?
He replied, "He was not pleased!"
He asked again,
"For what reason? He replied:
"I encountered an old man; for this reason, I am not joyful.
Fearing that the physiognomist’s words might prove true and that [the prince] would leave the household life before long, the king further increased the five sensual pleasures to entertain him.

After a long time, the Bodhisattva again commanded his charioteer to prepare the carriage for a tour. As they went out through the southern city gate, he encountered a sick man whose body was emaciated and who was leaning against the gate gasping for breath.
He asked the charioteer, "Who is this person?"
He replied, “It is a sick man!
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'sickness'? He replied:
"The four great elements increase or diminish; one is unable to digest food and drink; the breath becomes weak and faint; and life hangs by a thread—therefore it is called sickness."
He asked again, "Will I be spared? He replied:

"Not yet! he said, and immediately turned his carriage back toward the palace. He thought to himself that he had not yet escaped old age and sickness, which increased his sorrow and anxiety even further.
The King again questioned his charioteer:
"Does the Prince find pleasure in this excursion?
He replied, "I find it even more unpleasant than before."
He asked again,
"For what reason? He replied:
"Because I have encountered a sick person, I am not joyful.
Fearing that the Prince would renounce the world before long, the King further increased the five sensual pleasures, providing him with entertainment day and night.

After a long time, the Bodhisattva again commanded his charioteer to prepare the carriage for an excursion. He went out through the western city gate and encountered a dead man; the corpse was being carried in front, while the men and women of the household followed behind, wailing in grief.
He asked the charioteer,
"Who is this? The charioteer replied:
"He is dead! He asked again, "What is meant by 'dead'?"

He replied: "When the vital breath ceases and the spirit departs, there is nothing further to be known; cast away in the empty wilderness, one is forever separated from kin—therefore, it is called death."
He asked again, "Will I be spared? He replied:

"Not yet! the Bodhisattva thought to himself. "I have not yet escaped the laws of old age, sickness, and death; this only increases my sorrow and anxiety. He immediately turned his chariot around to return. On the way, he encountered a man who had shaved off his hair and beard, wore dharma robes, and carried an alms bowl, walking while keeping his eyes fixed upon the ground.
He asked the charioteer,
"Who is this person? His clothing is of a different era."
He replied, “I am a renunciant. He asked again:
"What is meant by 'leaving home'?
He replied, "To discipline oneself well, to be endowed with all dignified deportment, to constantly practice patience, and to have compassion for sentient beings— this is called leaving home."
Having heard this, the Bodhisattva exclaimed three times, "Excellent! This alone is truly refreshing!
He then descended from his carriage and, with reverence, inquired:
"Why is it that your appearance and attire differ so radically from those of the world?
The answer was as before.
The Bodhisattva repeated his question three times:
"How excellent! This indeed is a joy! Having said this, he mounted his carriage and headed toward the palace.
A certain woman saw the Bodhisattva from afar; a heart of lustful desire arose within her, and she immediately spoke a verse:
"A mother has joy in having such a son, and his father likewise rejoices greatly;
a woman has joy in having such a husband—this joy exceeds even that of Nirvana."
Upon hearing the sound of Nirvana being proclaimed, the Bodhisattva leaped for joy and thought to himself:
"When shall I attain this unsurpassed Nirvana?
He returned to his palace and reflected, yet he had not yet transcended the laws of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
The king asked the charioteer,
"Did the prince enjoy his excursion today? He replied:
"When first departing, you were displeased; upon returning, you were very joyful!
He asked again, "For what reason?"
He replied: “I encountered a dead person on my way out, which is why I was not joyful;
I saw a bhikṣu upon my return, which is why I am delighted.”
The king thought again:
"The physiognomist’s words are true; he will certainly leave the household life!
He then increased the five sensory pleasures, providing entertainment day and night.
After the Bodhisattva had been entertained by the courtesans, he fell into a brief sleep, while the assembly of courtesans all became drowsy and slumbered.

The Bodhisattva soon awoke and observed that the attendants were lying with one another as pillows; some had their bodies exposed like wooden mannequins, with runny noses, tears in their eyes, and saliva flowing from their mouths. Lutes, harps, zithers, and flutes lay scattered across the floor.
Furthermore, he saw the palace as being like a cemetery.
Having seen this, the Bodhisattva exclaimed three times, "Alas!
Alas! He ran to look at the palace where his father, the king, resided; the state of that palace had likewise undergone such a transformation.
Again he exclaimed, "Alas! What calamity!
and felt a profound sense of weary detachment.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva commanded the slave Chandaka:
"Rise and saddle the horse; do not let anyone hear! Chandaka replied:
"Night is not a time for travel; one should not go out on inspection. Furthermore, there are no enemies pressing upon the inner palace.
I do not understand for what reason you have ordered the horses to be saddled at night."
The Prince replied:
"Are you unaware that there is a great enemy?
Old age, sickness, and death are enemies—the greatest of all!"
"Quickly saddle the horse; do not delay!
He immediately saddled the white horse, led it into the central courtyard, and said, "The horse has arrived here!"

The Bodhisattva then went to where the horse was; as he was about to mount it, the horse neighed with great sorrow. Fearing that obstacles might arise, the devas immediately dispersed the sound of the horse's neighing so that no one could hear it.
The Bodhisattva mounted his horse and headed toward the gate; the gate opened of its own accord.

He proceeded toward the city gate, which likewise opened by itself. Having exited the city, he headed for the Anupiya Grove, not far from the city. There, he dismounted, removed his precious robes, and said to Chanda:
"You may lead the horse and take these precious robes back to the palace. On your way, convey my prostrations to my parents and say to them:"
"Now I am departing to study the Way; I shall return before long, so please do not grieve for me!
Chanda knelt down weeping and said:

"The physiognomist formerly prophesied that the Prince would become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, possessing the seven treasures and a thousand sons, ruling over the four continents and governing the world through the True Dharma without the use of weapons, naturally bringing about a time of Great Peace."
"Why do you now abandon this royal throne, cast off your precious robes, and undergo suffering in the mountains and wilds?
The Bodhisattva asked in return:
"What did the physiognomist predict at that time?"
He replied: "If I do not delight in the world, I shall leave the home life to study the Way and shall surely attain the path of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Having heard these words, why do you now grieve?
Return home at once and inform your parents:
'Even if my bones wither and rot, until I have exhausted the source of birth, old age, sickness, and death, I shall never return!'"
Thereupon, Chanda wept bitterly as he went forward to prostrate himself; he circumambulated him three times to the right, led the horse, and took the precious robe back to the palace.

The Bodhisattva continued on his way and saw a hunter wearing a *kāṣāya* robe; he went to that place and traded his own garment, worth hundreds of thousands, for it, so that he might wear it and depart.
The Bodhisattva again proceeded toward the *sumana* tree. Beneath the tree was a barber; he requested that the man shave his hair, and the barber did so immediately.
In the time it takes to bend and extend one’s arm, Śakra Devānām Indra arrived before the Bodhisattva, received the hair upon his robe, and carried it back to his celestial palace.
Having shaved his head, he thought to himself:
"I have now truly gone forth; naturally, I am endowed with the precepts.
Thereupon, he traveled by stages until he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha.
King Bimbisāra had five wishes from his youth:
first, that when his father the king passed away, he would succeed to the throne;
second, that while he was reigning as king, he might encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Third, they vow to see the Buddha with their own eyes, drawing near to him and making offerings;
fourth, they vow to give rise to a joyful mind and hear the True Dharma;
fifth, they vow that upon hearing the Dharma, they shall immediately attain faith and understanding.

When the Bodhisattva entered the city to beg for alms, his deportment was dignified and composed; he walked while keeping his eyes fixed upon the ground. At that time, as he did not yet possess an alms bowl, he carried lotus leaves along the road, yet the leaves remained attached to their roots.
At that time, the king and his ministers, from atop a high tower, saw the Bodhisattva from afar and marveled at his extraordinary and elegant appearance. Turning to address his ministers, he said:
"I have never before seen or heard of anyone like this; he must surely be a divine sage!"
They all replied: "In the past we heard that to the north of the Snowy Mountains, in the city of Kapilavastu, there is a king named Śuddhodana who has fathered a son named Bodhisattva.

A physiognomist examined him and prophesied: 'If he remains at home, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin Rāja), sovereign over the four continents, with the seven treasures arriving of their own accord—namely, the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the minister-treasure, and the military commander-treasure.'"
The king had a thousand sons, brave and powerful; he governed the world according to the Dharma, so that weapons were never used and peace prevailed naturally.
If he did not delight in the world, he would leave the household life to study the Way, and upon attaining enlightenment, he would be titled Buddha and deliver sentient beings from birth and death.
"Having heard this, he has gone forth as a monk; this person must surely be him!
When the king heard these words, he was filled with great joy and said:
"Of my five former vows, one has already been fulfilled. There remain four other vows, which I shall surely attain now!"
He immediately commanded two men:
"Go and observe where the Bodhisattva is resting;
I shall go there myself."

Having received these instructions, they hurried away; seeing that the Bodhisattva had finished his almsround and was returning to Mount Varanasi, he sat cross-legged facing the kingdom of Pāpīyas. One person remained there to watch him, while the other returned to report.

The king immediately prepared his carriage and went out to visit the Bodhisattva at his lodging at the foot of the mountain; the king then proceeded on foot up the mountain until he reached the Bodhisattva’s dwelling.
The Bodhisattva said, "Welcome, Great King!"
"Are you not exhausted?
The king then bowed his head at the Bodhisattva’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Bodhisattva, saying,
"In what land were you born in your previous life?"
"What is your clan and where did you renounce the world? The Bodhisattva replied:
"I was born north of the Snowy Mountains in the city of Kapilavastu in the country of the Śākyas; my father’s name is Śuddhodana and my clan is Gautama."
The king, wishing to test the Bodhisattva, said to him:
"Bhikṣu, you are of noble lineage and high birth; for generations you have been a scion of royalty. Your holy virtue is innate, and you ought to rule over the four seas."

"The four seas look up with earnest expectation; none fail to gaze upward in reverence. If you would deign to lower your will, we shall likewise serve as tributary vassals, facing north to attend upon you.
The Bodhisattva replied, "In rank, there is nothing more honorable than that of a Wheel-Turning King, yet I have already renounced even that; how much more so the four seas!"
"This is why I have left the household life to seek the Way, desiring to deliver all beings from the great suffering of birth and death!
Why do you not request that I first deliver you once my Way is perfected, instead of making such trivial demands as these?"
The King said: "Excellent! These words are most pleasing!
On the day you attain the Way, I pray that you will deliver me and the people of this land first!"
The Bodhisattva consented to this, and the king was greatly delighted; he prostrated at his feet and withdrew.

After the king had departed, the Bodhisattva proceeded toward the Bodhi tree. Not far from the tree, he saw a man named Svastika mowing grass; he asked him for a small amount of grass, which he carried to the foot of the tree, spread it out, and sat down cross-legged. With body erect and mind upright, he focused his mindfulness before him. He immediately eliminated the five hindrances and, free from desires and unwholesome states, attained even the fourth dhyāna, dwelling in its mastery and penetrating the practice of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
With this purified mind, he clearly illuminated the three knowledges (*vidyā*), namely:

The clear knowledge of past lives, the clear knowledge of others' minds, and the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows are as described in the *Sūtra on the Auspicious Response and Original Arising*.
Thereupon he arose and proceeded to the village of Uruvilvā.

Having first attained the Way of the Buddha, he sat beneath the trees of the forest and, during the first watch of the night, contemplated the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order:
"Because this exists, that comes to be;
because this ceases, that ceases."

That is to say: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth;

and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair. If ignorance ceases, then volitional formations cease; if volitional formations cease, then consciousness ceases; if consciousness ceases, then name-and-form ceases; if name-and-form ceases, then the six sense bases cease; if the six sense bases cease, then contact ceases; if contact ceases, then feeling ceases; if feeling ceases, then craving ceases; if craving ceases, then clinging ceases; if clinging ceases, then existence ceases; if existence ceases, then birth ceases; and if birth ceases, then aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair all cease.
Having seen this meaning, he spoke these verses:
"All phenomena have arising as their condition; The Brahmin first practiced dhyāna.
Once he understood this law of conditions, He was able to eliminate all doubt."

"There are two extremes in the world that one should not associate with:"
First, there are those who are greedily attached to sensual desires and claim that desire is without fault;

Abandoning these two extremes, one attains the Middle Way, whereby vision, knowledge, wisdom, and awakening arise, leading toward Nirvana.
What is called the Middle Way?
It refers to the Eightfold Path:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; this is the Middle Way.
Furthermore, there are the Four Noble Truths:
the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
What is meant by the Noble Truth of Suffering?

Namely: the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair, the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
To state it briefly: the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
What is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering?
It is the craving for existence, together with the co-arising afflictions, which find delight and attachment in various places; this is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering.
What is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?
It is the complete severance of craving without remainder, its total extinction, and nirvana; this is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
What is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering?
What is called the Eightfold Noble Path is the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

It has caused even those of noble lineage to disregard worldly glory.
We should go together to the Great Śramaṇa’s abode and purely cultivate the Brahma-faring!"
The four men were filled with joy, and with their hearts yearning for the Way, they went to where Yaśas was and asked him:
"Is the holy life you practice complete and most excellent?"
He replied, "This path is immeasurable; it is the most supreme!
He then led the four men to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

The Buddha taught them various sublime dharmas, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them; all of them, while still seated, became free from dust and defilement, attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, perceived the Dharma, and realized the fruit.
Having seen the Dharma and attained the fruit, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that you will grant me ordination and the full precepts!”
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, bhikṣu! From that point until the bowl appeared in his hand, it was as described above.
Not long after receiving the precepts, he practiced with diligence and without slackening, and attained arhatship.
At that time, there were eleven arhats in the world.

As for the fifty people with whom Yaśas had previously associated, having heard that Yaśas was practicing the holy life under Gautama, they deliberated together on going forth from home and eventually attaining arhatship, all as described above.
At that time, there were sixty-one arhats in the world.
The physiognomist Āḷāra knew that when the Bodhisattva attained buddhahood, he would turn the wheel of Dharma in the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī;
he further thought: "After my life has passed, among my disciples, the brahmin Nāla shall succeed me."
"All my offerings shall belong to him; he will surely become attached to them and no longer remember the Buddha’s intention to appear in the world.
I would now rather establish a residence for him by the Deer Park and instruct him to recollect three times each day:
'The Buddha shall appear in the world!'"
