‘When he appears in the world, you should cultivate the holy life under him!
Having thought this, he immediately built a residence for him and instructed him as he had intended.
Before long, Āyu passed away. Nāla subsequently obtained offerings; his attachment became so deep that he no longer remembered at all that a Buddha was to appear in the world.
At that time, the Naga King Elapatra had this thought:
"In the past, Kāśyapa Buddha prophesied to me:

'In the future, after hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of years have passed, Śākyamuni Buddha will appear in the world; that Buddha shall prophesy the time when you shall be liberated from your naga body.'"
"The time has now arrived; we must go to see the Buddha.

For the sake of seeing the Buddha, on the six days of the fast, that nāga placed silver grain in a golden bowl and golden grain in a silver bowl within the Ganges River. He also adorned two maidens and spoke this verse:
"Who is the supreme among kings?"
How can that which is defiled and that which is undefiled both become stainless?
What is called ignorance?
And by what stream is one swept away?
"What must one attain to be called wise?
How is it that the outflows cease, and why is this called liberation?
After the Dragon King had spoken this verse, he thought to himself:
"If there were anyone capable of explaining this verse, they would be a Buddha!
If you have heard it from a Buddha, please show me where that Buddha resides!
At present, among all other śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, Māras, Brahmās, and the entire world, I do not see anyone capable of explaining this verse."
Having reflected thus, he proclaimed:
"If there is anyone capable of explaining this verse, I shall give them a golden bowl and a silver bowl filled with gold and silver grain, as well as these two daughters."

At that time, many other śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, elders, and householders vied with one another to explain the meaning of this verse for the dragon; though the dragon king spoke it for them, none were able to understand it.
At that time, the brahmin Nāla was honored and respected by the people of the kingdom of Magadha, all of whom said:
"This brahmin possesses great knowledge and insight; he will surely be able to explain it!"
They then went together to invite him.
The Māṇava thought to himself:
"I am honored by the entire kingdom; if I say I cannot do it, I shall be abandoned by all these people."
"Although I do not yet understand it, I shall employ skillful means to preserve this reputation!
He then said to the crowd, "All of you, come with me to where the nāga is; I shall explain it!"
Thereupon, the multitude, together with the Māṇava, respectfully surrounded him and went to where the nāga was; they spoke to the nāga, saying:
"You may recite your verse, and we shall expound upon it!"
The dragon then spoke a verse, and the Māṇava said:
"This is very easy to understand!
I shall come after seven days to explain it."
He then recited that verse and first questioned other śramaṇas, brahmins, and the six teachers such as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa;
none were able to explain it, and they all responded with deceptive anger and abuse, saying:
"This is meaningless!"
He intended to conceal his own lack of understanding.
The Māṇava thought again:
"My teacher told me long ago that the Buddha would appear in the world, and that I should practice the holy life under him."
"Now the śramaṇa Gautama is at the Deer Park; he must surely be able to explain this, so I shall go and ask him.
He further thought: "Even these six teachers, who are advanced in years and possessed of extensive learning, cannot explain it!"
"How much more so for the śramaṇa Gautama, who is himself young and has only recently left the household life—how could he possibly understand this!
He further thought:
"Light and darkness exist naturally; they cannot be measured against one another by priority or posteriority."
"Though Gautama is young, he must not be underestimated!
Having thought this, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side; there he recited the verses of the Dragon King to question the Buddha.
The Buddha then spoke for them:
“The sixth king is supreme; One who is defiled is equal to the defilement itself.
If one is undefiled, there is no stain; One who is defiled is called a fool.”
"The fool is swept away by the currents; he who can extinguish them is wise.
Having abandoned the currents so as not to flow again—this is called liberation.
When the Māṇava heard these verses, he knew deeply that this was the Buddha; he recited, practiced, and took them up, and on the seventh day he went to the place where the dragon was.
At that time, eighty-four thousand people were on both banks of the Ganges River, wishing to hear the Māṇava explain the meaning of the verses.
The Māṇava spoke again to the nāga, saying:
"Recite your previous verse."
The Dragon King then spoke, and the Māṇava immediately recited the verses spoken by the Buddha and explained them for him.
Upon hearing the verses, the Dragon King leaped for joy and thought to himself:
"The Buddha has appeared in the world!"
I have now already attained the vision of the Buddha! Why is this?
Because I do not see any other śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, brahmā, or anyone else in the entire world who is able to explain this meaning.
Having reflected thus, he asked the māṇava: "Tell me truly!
From whom did you hear the verse you have spoken?"
"I do not now see any other śramaṇas, brahmins, or anyone in the entire world who is able to speak this verse,
except for the Buddha, or from having heard it from the Buddha!"
He replied, "I tell you truly:
the Buddha has appeared in the world, and it is from him that I have heard this!
The Dragon King, filled with joy, asked:
"Where is the Buddha now? I wish to see him!
The Māṇava knelt down, extended his right hand to indicate the direction where the Buddha was, and said:
"The Buddha is now there!
The Dragon King was even more filled with joy and three times proclaimed:
"Namo to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha!"
He then said to the māṇava,
"You may escort me to where the Buddha is, so that I may inquire after the World-Honored One's well-being. He replied:

"So be it! The Dragon King immediately restored his own body; his form became vast and great, his eyes like large bowls, his breath like thunder, and fire issued from his mouth. He surged upward through the water, and eighty-four thousand people all followed after him.
Having reached the shore, he next transformed himself into a Wheel-Turning Sage King and went ashore to visit the Buddha;
seeing from afar that the World-Honored One’s countenance was extraordinary and sublime, like a mountain of gold, the Dragon King rejoiced and his reverence increased immeasurably.
The Buddha saw the Dragon King and addressed him by name, saying: "Welcome, Dragon King Elāpattra!
Upon hearing this, the Dragon King felt even greater joy and reverence.
"The World-Honored One knows my name; the Sugata recognizes my name!

Having spoken thus, he prostrated at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and recited the original verse once more to question the Buddha. The Buddha then spoke for him the verse that the Māṇava had received.
Having heard this, the Dragon King was first filled with great joy, and then he wept with sorrow.
The Buddha asked the Dragon King,
"For what reason do you alternate between joy and sorrow in such a brief moment?"
He replied: "World-Honored One!
I recall that in the past, under Kāśyapa Buddha, I purely cultivated the brahma-faring."
At a later time, he took a stalk of purple flowers, went to where the Buddha was, and asked:
"World-Honored One!
If a bhikṣu kills this grass, what kind of offense does he incur?"
The Buddha replied to me, saying, "By reason of this cause and condition, some may fall into the most painful hells!
Upon hearing these words, I did not believe them nor did I respect them; I then intentionally pricked a leaf of an eranda tree, thinking thus:
"Let us see what karmic fruit there is!
he exclaimed, yet he did not abandon this view nor did he repent his transgression.
After his life ended, he was now born among the long-lived nāgas; because of this karma, I am called the Nāga Elāpattra.
Having received this body, I again went to the Buddha's dwelling and asked:
"When shall I be able to escape from this nāga body?
The Buddha answered me, saying:

"In the future, after more than hundreds of thousands of billions of years have passed, there will appear in the world a Buddha named Śākyamuni; that Buddha shall grant you the prediction of your attainment of liberation!"
"Now that I have beheld the World-Honored One, I have conceived a sense of rare wonder and realized for the first time that the words of all Buddhas are not false; this is why I smile with joy.
Furthermore, I recall how I formerly disobeyed the Buddha’s teachings, and now I am again unable to receive the Buddha’s clear precepts; this is why I weep in sorrow."
Again, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that you will prophesy when I shall be able to escape this nāga body!
The Buddha said:

"In the future, after more than hundreds of thousands of billions of years have passed, Maitreya Buddha will appear in the world; at that time, you shall be liberated from your dragon body, leave the household life to receive the precepts, extensively cultivate the pure conduct (brahmacarya), and attain the exhaustion of the source of suffering!"
The Buddha then accepted the three refuges from the dragon, making him an upāsaka;
he further preached various sublime dharmas to eighty-four thousand people, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them— namely, the discourse on giving, and so forth,
up to the discourse on the bliss of the essential departure [from suffering].
Once they were all filled with joy, he further expounded for them the Dharma that all Buddhas constantly teach: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
At that very seat, eighty-four thousand people distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; they saw the Dharma and realized the fruit.
Having seen the Dharma and attained the fruit, he received the three refuges and subsequently the five precepts.
Thereupon, the Dragon King said to the young brahmin:
"Why do you now require this dragon girl?"
"Nāgas are prone to anger; they may even harm one another with poisonous fire!
Whatever gold, silver, or precious objects you require, I shall give them all to you. He replied:
"Stop, stop! Dragon King!
I have no need for the dragon girl, nor do I have need for gold or silver!"
"Because I heard the Buddha's final verse, I have attained freedom from the desires of the desire realm.
After the Buddha had finished preaching the Dharma, he said to the Dragon King,
"You may now return to your dwelling!"
The Dragon King accepted the instruction, prostrated, and withdrew.
After the Dragon King had departed, the Māṇava approached, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I pray that you will grant me the going forth and the full ordination!
The Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣu!"
"Even until the alms bowl was in his hand, it was as described above.
Not long after he had gone forth, through diligent practice without slackening, he attained arhatship.
At that time, there were sixty-two arhats in the world."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One departed from the Deer Park and traveled by stages until he reached the Śāla Grove, where he sat beneath a tree.
Not far from the grove was a pleasure garden, where at that time thirty companions, each accompanied by his wife, were sporting within it.

One man, being without a wife, hired a courtesan and dressed her in fine garments; they went together to this garden, intending to indulge their passions to the full. However, while they were about to enjoy themselves, that courtesan suddenly fled from him in her fine clothes. They set out together to pursue and search for her until they reached the Śāla grove, where they saw from afar the World-Honored One, his appearance preeminent like a mountain of gold. Having seen him, they conceived a sense of rare wonder and all approached the Buddha’s presence. Prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, they withdrew to sit to one side and asked the Buddha: “Great Śramaṇa!...”
"Did you see a woman coming?
The Buddha said,
"Do you wish to seek for yourself, or do you wish to seek for another?"
He replied, "I would rather seek it for myself than for a woman!
The Buddha said:
"Sit down for a moment!
I shall preach the Dharma for you.
They all followed the instruction, prostrated once more, and sat down.
The Buddha expounded various sublime dharmas for them, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them, up to the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
All thirty persons were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; they saw the Dharma and realized the fruit.
Having seen the Dharma and attained the fruit, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that you grant me ordination and the full precepts!
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, bhikṣu! ... [the account] up until his attainment of arhatship is as described above.
At that time, there were ninety-two arhats in the world.

At that time, there were also sixty people traveling through the Śāla grove on their way to a wedding; seeing from afar that the World-Honored One’s appearance was exceptionally sublime, like a mountain of gold, they all approached the Buddha’s presence and prostrated themselves at his feet.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they all attained arhatship as described above.
At that time, there were one hundred and fifty-two arhats in the world.
*Pañcavargīya-vinaya*, Fascicle 15.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya), Volume Sixteen.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhayaśas of Jibin during the Song Dynasty,
together with Zhu Daosheng and others.
In the first section of the third part, concerning the method for receiving the precepts, it says: "Thereupon the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
'Each of you should travel through the world in separate groups; there are many who are virtuous and capable of receiving instruction and admonition.'"
"I shall now go alone to the abode of Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa to convert him.
The bhikṣus received these instructions and departed to their respective groups, while the World-Honored One proceeded to Kāśyapa's dwelling.
Kāśyapa served a venomous dragon, which was kept in a separate quiet chamber; no one dared to enter it except for Kāśyapa himself.
When evening fell, the Buddha went to that place and requested to stay overnight, seeking lodging within the dragon’s chamber.
He replied, "I do not love it at all; there is a venomous dragon within that I fear might harm you!
The Buddha said:
"There is no suffering; the dragon will not harm me!
He replied, "If you have no fear, enter and stay as you please!"
The Buddha then took the grass and entered the room, where he spread out a seat and sat down, thinking:
"I shall gradually transform the dragon's body so that its form becomes like a bundle of straw, which I will place inside my alms bowl to subdue it."
Just as he had sat for a short while, the dragon became greatly enraged and smoke issued from its entire body; the Buddha likewise emitted smoke.
The dragon set its whole body ablaze, and the Buddha likewise emitted fire from his entire body. Both fires blazed intensely, and the dragon’s chamber was filled with a brilliant glare.
Then Kāśyapa and his disciples came and circled the dragon’s chamber, lamenting with sorrow: "What a pity!
The Great Śramaṇa did not heed our words and has been harmed by the dragon!"
At dawn the next day, the Buddha took the bowl containing the dragon and went out, saying to Kāśyapa:
"This bowl contained a venomous dragon feared by all people; now it has been subdued!"
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"Though this great śramaṇa possesses such supernatural power, it is not equal to the truth of my own Way!
Thereupon, by his supernormal power, the World-Honored One—like a strong man extending or contracting his arm—placed the dragon in the midst of the world-systems and returned to Kāśyapa’s location.
Kāśyapa asked the Buddha,
"Upon what does the dragon rest?
The Buddha replied:
"Place it in the midst of the world-system.
Kāśyapa thought again:
"This Great Śramaṇa is exceedingly miraculous; in a mere moment, he has taken the dragon and placed it in the midst of the world-system!"
"Even so, it is not as good as my having already attained the path of Arhatship!
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha, "I pray that the Great Śramaṇa will stay here; I myself shall provide for his needs!"
The Buddha said,
"If you can come personally every day to invite me, I shall accept your invitation! He replied:
"Excellent! Not far from Kāśyapa, there was a lush grove where the Buddha stayed. During the night, the Four Heavenly Kings descended to attend upon him and also wished to listen to the Dharma.
The radiance of the Four Heavenly Kings was like four masses of fire; when Kāśyapa rose at night, he saw what resembled four great masses of fire beside the Buddha, not knowing what they were.
The next day, he invited the Buddha and said, "The meal is prepared; we pray that you will deign to partake.
He asked again:
"Last night, there were four masses of light here; they resembled fire but were not fire. What were they?
The Buddha said, "Last night the Four Heavenly Kings descended to make offerings and listen to the Dharma; those were their lights!"
Kāśyapa thought again:
"This great śramaṇa possesses such immense majestic power that he has caused the Four Heavenly Kings to come in person to make offerings!
Nevertheless, even so, it is not equal to my own attainment of the path of arhatship!"
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa, "You go on ahead; I shall follow shortly!

Just as Kāśyapa departed, the Buddha, in the time it takes to bend and extend one's arm, reached the Jambū tree in Jambudvīpa, took its fruit, and returned. Before Kāśyapa had even arrived, the Buddha was already seated there.
Kāśyapa arrived later and, seeing the Buddha, asked him:
"I did not return by any other path, nor was there any place I passed through where I saw the Great Śramaṇa."
"What path has the Great Śramaṇa come by?
The Buddha said, "Just after you had departed, I went to the Jambū tree, gathered its fruit, and returned; it is fragrant, delicious, and fit for eating."
"I now give this to you; you may try eating it!
Kāśyapa thought again:
"The Great Śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers, yet he is not my equal, for I have already attained the path of Arhatship!"
After the Buddha had finished his meal, he returned to that forest grove.
During the night, Śakra Devānām Indra descended in person to attend upon him and also desired to listen to the Dharma.
Śakra’s radiance illuminated the entire grove, surpassing even that of the Four Great Kings; when Kāśyapa saw it at night, he likewise did not know what kind of light it was.
The next day, he came again to invite the Buddha, reporting that the meal was prepared and inquiring about the meaning of the light.
The Buddha said:
"Last night, Śakra Devānām Indra made offerings and listened to the Dharma; that was his light!"
Kāśyapa thought again:
"This great śramaṇa is indeed powerful, for he has caused Śakra himself to come and make offerings;
yet, he is not my equal, who has already attained the path of an arhat!"
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa, "You go on ahead; I shall follow shortly.
As soon as Kāśyapa had departed, the Buddha went to the Harītakī grove at the edge of Jambudvīpa, gathered some of its fruit, and returned; he was already seated before Kāśyapa had arrived.
Kāśyapa arrived later and questioned him as before;
the Buddha said, "After you had just departed, I went to the harītakī grove on the edge of Jambudvīpa, gathered some of its fruits, and returned."
"It is fragrant, delicious, and fit for eating; I now give it to you, so please try some!
Kāśyapa again thought as before.
After the Buddha had finished eating, he returned to that grove.
At night, Brahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, descended in person to serve as his attendant and to listen to the Dharma.
Brahmā’s radiance was twice that of Śakra; when Kāśyapa saw it at night, he likewise did not know what kind of light it was.
The next day, he came again to invite the Buddha, reporting that the meal was prepared and inquiring about the meaning of the light.
The Buddha said, "Last night, the Brahma King descended to make offerings and listen to the Dharma; that was his light!"
Kāśyapa thought again:
"This great śramaṇa is indeed powerful, for he has caused even the Brahmā King to come in person to make offerings;
yet, he is not my equal, for I have already attained the path of arhatship!"
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa, "You go on ahead; I shall follow shortly.
As soon as Kāśyapa had departed, the Buddha went to the Āmalaka grove at the edge of Jambudvīpa, gathered some of its fruit, and returned; the rest is as described above.
"After the Buddha had finished eating, he returned to that forest grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One required water for washing; the Nairañjanā River naturally curved its course, flowing past the Buddha so that he might use it."
The next day, Kāśyapa came again to invite the Buddha, reporting that the meal was prepared. Seeing that the river had changed its course, he immediately asked, "Who has diverted this flow?
The Buddha said:
"I needed water yesterday, and the water came winding toward me of its own accord!
Kāśyapa thought again:
"This great śramaṇa is indeed possessed of supernatural power; when he directs his mind toward water, the water flows in a winding course for him."
"Yet it is not equal to my having already attained the path of Arhatship!
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa, "You go on ahead; I shall follow shortly."
As soon as Kāśyapa had departed, the Buddha went to Godānīya and took the milk from the cows there; the rest is as described above.
"After the Buddha had finished eating, he returned to that forest grove."
At that time, a maidservant of the brahmin Sona died, and her clothes were discarded in the cemetery. The Buddha took them and returned with them, thinking, "Where shall I wash these?
Just as this thought arose, Śakra Devānām Indra descended and pointed to the ground with his finger; water gushed forth, forming a pond, and he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"You may wash it here!
The mountain deity of Abhiṣāka sent a large stone basin and also addressed the Buddha, saying:
"You may use this to wash it!"
He further thought:
"Upon what shall I lean while washing these robes?
Not far from the pond was a *kaho* tree; its deity bent a branch so that the Buddha could grasp it.
When the Buddha had finished washing his robes, he hung them out to dry in mid-air.
The next day, Kāśyapa came again to invite the Buddha and informed him that the meal was prepared; seeing the matter of the washed robes, he questioned the Buddha about it all.
The Buddha answered him in full detail, but Kāśyapa’s thoughts remained as they were before.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa, “You go on ahead; I shall follow after you.”
As soon as Kāśyapa had departed, the Buddha went to Uttarakuru and took naturally grown non-glutinous rice; the rest is as described above.
"After the Buddha had finished eating, he returned to that forest grove."
At that time, on the following day of the festival, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"If I do not invite the Buddha now, and the multitude should see him, they will surely abandon me and vie with one another to serve him!"
He then desisted and did not invite him.
The Buddha, knowing this from afar, went again to Uttarakuru to fetch food and ate it.
When that day had passed, Kāśyapa came again to invite the Buddha, saying that the meal was prepared, and asked once more:
"The Buddha did not come yesterday; where did he eat?
The Buddha said, "Yesterday, during the festival, you thought to yourself:"
"If the Buddha were to come, everyone would see him together, and they would surely abandon me to venerate and serve him in competition.
For this reason, I went to Uttarakuru to fetch food and eat it."
Kāśyapa thought again:
"This great śramaṇa is indeed miraculous; he even knows the thoughts of others.
Yet, he is not as I am, who have already attained the path of an arhat!"
Thereupon, the Buddha went with Kāśyapa to his home; after they had finished eating, they returned to that forest.
At that time, Kāśyapa’s five hundred disciples were all splitting firewood together, but their axes would not lift. They reported this matter to their teacher, who said:
"I suspect this is the doing of the Great Śramaṇa; go and ask him!"
He immediately asked the Buddha about this, and the Buddha asked:
"Do you wish for it to be lifted? He replied:
"I wish to lift it!
The Buddha said, "You may go; the axe shall lift itself!"
Once it had been raised, it refused to come down again.
He reported this to his teacher, who instructed him to ask the Buddha. The Buddha asked:
"Do you wish for it to come down?"
He replied, “Yes. The Buddha said:
"You may go; the axe shall fall of its own accord!
Once it had fallen, the axe stuck fast to the firewood and could not be lifted.
He reported this again to his teacher, who instructed him to ask the Buddha. The Buddha asked:
"Would you like me to lift it? He replied, "Yes."
The Buddha said, "You may go;
you shall be able to lift and use them yourselves!
Thereupon, they were all able to use them.
He wished to light a fire again, but the fire refused to ignite.
He reported this to his teacher once more, and the teacher instructed him to ask the Buddha. The Buddha asked:
"Do you wish for it to ignite?"
He replied, “Yes. The Buddha said:
"You may go; the fire will naturally burn itself out!
The fire then indeed burned itself out.
Once it had gone out, however, it refused to be extinguished.
He reported this again to his teacher, who instructed him to ask the Buddha.
The Buddha asked, "Do you wish for it to cease? He replied:
"Very well," the Buddha said,
"you may go; the fire shall extinguish itself!"
The fire then extinguished itself.
When he further wished to pour water to extinguish the embers, the water remained inside the jar and refused to come out at all.
He reported this again to his teacher, who instructed him to ask the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Do you wish to leave? He replied, "Yes."
The Buddha said, "You may go;
the water shall come forth of its own accord!
And the water immediately came forth.
Having come out, he again refused to stop.
He reported this to his teacher once more, who instructed him to ask the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Do you wish for him to stop?"
He replied, “Yes. The Buddha said:
"You may go; the water shall cease of its own accord!
The water immediately ceased.
At that time, black clouds rained heavily for seven days, so that the forest where the Buddha resided and the house of Kāśyapa were submerged in a vast expanse of water.
Fearing that the Buddha might be swept away by the water, Kāśyapa came aboard a boat to look for him; he then saw the World-Honored One walking up and down upon the surface of the Nairañjanā River.
Kāśyapa thought again:
"This Great Śramaṇa is indeed possessed of spiritual power; though the waters have risen in a great flood, he has not been submerged, but is instead walking upon them."
"Yet it is not as good as my having already attained the path of Arhatship!
Thereupon, the World-Honored One ascended into the void and addressed Kāśyapa, saying:
"You are not an Arhat!"
"Why do you falsely claim to have attained the Way?
Kāśyapa replied, "It is indeed so."
"It is so, World-Honored One!
It is truly so,
World-Honored One!"
He spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that I may go forth under the Great Śramaṇa and receive full ordination!
The Buddha said:
"Have you informed your disciples yet? He replied, "Not yet."
The Buddha said,
"You may inform them first.
Kāśyapa accepted this instruction and immediately returned to tell his disciples:
"Do you know? I wish to practice the pure life of brahmacarya under the Great Śramaṇa.
It would be well for you to follow me; do not take pleasure in following your own whims!"
The five hundred disciples spoke with one voice:
“We have seen the Buddha subdue the dragon and have already conceived faith; we were merely waiting for our teacher!
We pray that we may all follow him!”
Thereupon, the teacher and his disciples went together to where the Buddha was and said to him:
“We, the teacher and his disciples, all wish to leave the household life and receive full ordination!
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, bhikṣu! Receive full ordination;
within my well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya, you shall be able to exhaust all suffering and purely cultivate the holy life!"
Kāśyapa and his five hundred disciples’ hair and beards fell away of their own accord; the saṃghāṭī robes were donned upon their bodies, and the alms bowls appeared in their hands.
Once they had received the precepts, they cast their former garments and fire-worshipping implements into the Nairañjanā River. This was the full ordination of Kāśyapa and his five hundred disciples.
“Kāśyapa had two younger brothers: the elder was named Nadī-Kāśyapa and the younger was named Gayā-Kāśyapa.
The elder brother had three hundred disciples, and the younger had two hundred disciples; they lived one yojana downstream from their elder brother.
Seeing the implements for fire-worship being carried down by the current, they feared that their brother had been harmed by evil persons or swept away by the great waters.”

The two younger brothers immediately led five hundred disciples upstream; seeing that their elder brother and his disciples had all become śramaṇas, they asked in wonder, "For what reason have you come to this?"
He replied, "This path is supreme; among the methods for transcendence, there is none superior to it!
The two younger brothers and their five hundred disciples all deliberated together, saying:
"Our elder brother is foremost in wisdom, yet now he delights in this; this path must surely be supreme!
We shall all go together with him and leave the household life.
They immediately went together to the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and said to him:
"May you grant us permission to leave the household life and receive full ordination!
The Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣus!"
...and so on, until the bowl was in his hand, as described above.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Where can I find abundant food, drink, and bedding, so that I may instruct these one thousand bhikṣus who were formerly brahmins?"
"On that Mount Gayā, there is an abundance of food, drink, and bedding!
Having thought this, he took a thousand bhikṣus and went to that place, instructing them with three matters: first, instruction through supernormal powers;
[the other two being instruction through mind-reading and instruction through teaching].
Second is instruction through teaching the Dharma;
third is instruction through formal admonition.
What is meant by instruction through supernormal power?
As explained in the section on supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
What is meant by "teaching and instructing through the Dharma"?
It is said:
"Monks! You should contemplate this; you should not contemplate that.
You should bring this to mind; you should not bring that to mind."
"One should cultivate this, one should abandon this, and one should practice in reliance upon this!
What is meant by "instruction" and "admonition"?
It is said:
“Monks! Everything is ablaze! In what way is everything ablaze?
The eye is ablaze; forms are ablaze. Eye-consciousness, eye-contact, and the feeling born with eye-contact as its condition are also ablaze. By what are they ablaze?
The fire of desire blazes; the fires of hatred and delusion blaze.
This applies even to mental phenomena and their objects.
When a noble disciple hears such a teaching, they give rise to disenchantment and detachment, and thereby attain liberation!
"Knowledge and liberation have arisen; what was to be done has been accomplished; the holy life has been established; there will be no further existence!
When this Dharma was spoken, the taints of a thousand bhikṣus were exhausted, and their minds attained liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"In the past, I made a vow with King Bimbisāra that once I had attained the Way, I would deliver him. Now it is time to go to him!
He then set out for Rājagṛha, gradually traveling there surrounded by a thousand bhikṣus before and behind him.

When King Bimbisāra heard that the Buddha had attained enlightenment and had converted the three brothers, including Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, along with their thousand disciples, and was now coming to this town, he immediately issued an edict to the forty-two thousand villages within his realm, commanding each village to produce two eminent men to go together and welcome the Buddha.
Eighty-four thousand people rode on elephants, horses, and chariots, escorting him from front and rear.
At that time, it was the end of spring and the heat was already at its peak; everyone thought to themselves, "May we obtain even a little shade!"
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra, knowing his thought, immediately manifested a cloud-canopy, and a cool breeze began to stir gently.

He himself transformed into a Brahmā deity, wearing yellow robes and holding a seven-jeweled staff and a seven-jeweled-handled whisk; hovering one cubit above the ground, he led the way before the Buddha.
At that time, a man from Magadha wished to stand before the Buddha; Śakra drove him away, and everyone there looked upon him with disdain, speaking these verses:
"His form resembles that of Brahmā, He holds a staff and treads through the void;
With gentle words he speaks— Whose servant is he?"
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, replied in verse:
"Released from all bonds, Supreme Tamer of Men, Arhat, Well-Gone One— I am his attendant."
Then King Bimbisāra thought to himself:
"I shall offer this very place where the Buddha is staying as a gift to the Buddha and establish a vihāra there."
The Buddha, knowing their thoughts, stayed that evening at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the great assembly all harbored a doubt:
"We do not know whether it is the Buddha or Upaga Kāśyapa who is the disciple."
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts of the assembly, addressed Uruvilvā Kāśyapa with these verses:
“Uruvilvā, what have you seen, That you have abandoned the practice of fire-worship?”
"I now ask you personally; you should answer according to the truth.
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa replied in verse:
"Constantly craving delicious flavors, my mind runs wild among sounds and sights."
"I perceived these impurities, and therefore I abandoned the practice of fire-worship.
At that time, although the great assembly heard the Buddha and Kāśyapa each recite a verse, they had not yet realized their underlying meaning and still harbored doubts.
The Buddha, knowing the minds of the assembly, again questioned them with a verse:
"The five flavors are sweet to the mouth, And sounds and forms delight the heart.
You see these as defilements; By what means can you attain freedom from them?"
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa replied again in verse:
"I have seen the path of rest, wherein there is no attachment to anything;
it is neither different nor capable of being differentiated—it is here that I renounce the sacrificial fire."
At that time, although the great assembly heard the verse again, they still harbored doubts.
The Buddha, knowing their thoughts, addressed Kāśyapa:
"Rise and fan the Buddha!"
He immediately accepted the instruction and rose to fan him.
He then said to Kāśyapa,
"Display your supernatural transformations!"
He then further manifested various supernatural transformations:
he divided his body into ten billion forms and then merged them back into one;
he passed through stone walls as if they were open space and entered the earth as if it were water; and he walked upon water as if it were solid ground.
Sitting or reclining in mid-air like a bird in flight;
his entire body blazing brightly with smoke rising like clouds;
touching the sun and moon with his hand and standing level with the Brahma Heaven, he moves with sovereign ease and without obstruction.
Some emitted water from their upper bodies while fire blazed from their lower bodies;
others emitted fire from their upper bodies while water issued from their lower bodies.
Thereafter, they descended and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The World-Honored One is my teacher; I am the World-Honored One's disciple!
Having spoken thus three times, he addressed the great assembly, saying:
"All that I know, down to these supernatural transformations, is entirely due to the grace of the Great Teacher!"
Thereupon, the great assembly first realized that Kāśyapa was a disciple of the Buddha, and they felt immeasurable joy and reverence toward him in the presence of the Buddha.
It is the constant law of all Buddhas not to preach the Dharma until people’s minds have been transformed.

Knowing that the great assembly was already filled with joy and reverence, the Buddha preached various sublime dharmas to instruct, benefit, and gladden them, as well as the teachings constantly expounded by the Buddhas:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
King Bimbisāra and eighty-four thousand people, while still seated, became free from dust and defilement and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Having seen the Dharma and realized the fruit, they received the three refuges and the five precepts.
Thereupon, King Bimbisāra prostrated himself and invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for the midday meal on the following day. The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.

Rejoicing, the king returned to his palace and ordered various kinds of exquisite food to be prepared. At dawn, he arranged seats in the Bamboo Grove and went out in person to announce: "The meal is ready!"
The Buddha and the great assembly sat down in order. The king personally served them with his own hands, full of joy and without weariness.
When the meal was finished, he offered water for washing and stood to one side, saying to the Buddha:
"I now offer this Bamboo Grove to the World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:
"You may give it to the Sangha; its merit will be even greater!
The King spoke again to the Buddha:
"May you graciously accept it!
The Buddha said, "Simply offer it to the Sangha; I am within the Sangha!"
The King then followed these instructions and bestowed [the gift] upon the Saṃgha of the four directions;
thereafter, he took a small seat and sat before the Buddha.
For him, the Buddha recited verses of sympathetic joy and auspicious benediction, just as he had recited for Pileiyuan (Vairaṇyā).
Having finished speaking, he further expounded various sublime dharmas for him and sent him back to his residence.
The king rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew.

"At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha. There was a town named Nālada where there lived an old brahmin named Sāriputta, who had two hundred and fifty disciples studying under him."
Among his disciples were two preeminent followers: the first named Upatiṣya and the second named Kolita.

At that time, Ājñātakauṇḍinya entered the city for alms, wearing his robes and carrying his bowl; his countenance was serene and joyful, his faculties were tranquil and composed, his garments were neatly arranged, and he walked while keeping his eyes fixed upon the ground.

At that time, Upatiṣya was out on a stroll when he saw Aṭṭhaka from afar; his majestic deportment was so composed and orderly that Upatiṣya marveled at such an unprecedented sight. Waiting until he had arrived, he asked:
"What kind of doctrine do you follow, that your clothing is so unconventional?"
"Is there a teacher whom we may follow and from whom we may hear [the Dharma]?
Aṅgīrasa replied, "The śramaṇa Gautama is our great teacher; he is the one we revere, and it is from him that we have received instruction."
Upatiṣya said: "What kind of Dharma does your Great Teacher teach? Aśvajit replied:
"I am but a youth, and my studies have only recently begun; how could I possibly proclaim the Master’s vast and profound meaning?
Now, for your sake, I shall briefly explain its essentials.
This is what my Master has taught:"
"Phenomena arise from conditions and also cease from conditions;
all phenomena are empty and without a master.
Having heard this, Upatiṣya attained realization and understanding in his heart, and he gained the pure Dharma-eye. He then returned to his dwelling and recounted the Dharma he had heard to Kolita.
Upon hearing this, Kolita was likewise freed from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; he then asked:
"Where does the Tathāgata currently reside as he travels and transforms beings?"
He replied, "He is currently at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove. Kolita said:
"The Tathāgata is our teacher; let us go together to pay him homage and inquire after his well-being!
Upatiṣya said, "When my teacher was on the verge of death, he entrusted these two hundred and fifty disciples to me for their accomplishment."
"How can we depart alone without informing you?
The two men then went to their disciples and said, "We wish to follow the śramaṇa Gautama to practice the pure life of brahmacarya; each of you may do as you please."
At that time, all two hundred and fifty disciples were delighted to follow them, and the two men led their disciples together to the Bamboo Grove.
Seeing them from afar, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Those two who are coming—one named Upatiṣya and the other named Kolita—are approaching."
"These two individuals shall, among my disciples, be the foremost, possessing immeasurable wisdom and being the first in supernormal powers.
After a short while they arrived, and the Buddha taught them the Dharma in gradual stages:
the discourse on giving, ethical discipline, and rebirth in heaven;
They reviled sensual desire as impure and praised renunciation.
Then and there, on their very seats, their outflows were exhausted and their minds were liberated.
They all came forward and said to the Buddha, "We wish to go forth from the household life to purely cultivate the holy life!"
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, bhikṣu! Practice the holy life within my Dharma, and you shall reach the end of the source of suffering!"
"This is what is called 'leaving the household life and receiving full ordination.

At that time, as the World-Honored One was traveling through Rājagṛha, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa and his brothers along with their thousand disciples, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana along with their two hundred and fifty disciples, all left the household life to study the Path;
the various noble clansmen, elders, and lay devotees of Rājagṛha likewise all left the household life. A great assembly gathered around him in that kingdom, and he preached the Dharma for them.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the World-Honored One had not yet instructed the bhikṣus to have preceptors (upādhyāya) and teachers (ācārya).
Because they lacked preceptors and teachers, their deportment lacked proper measure; they wore their upper and lower robes entirely contrary to the Dharma.
They do not distinguish between pure and impure matters;
they do not maintain mindfulness before them, nor do they properly guard their sense faculties.
They enter villages to beg for food and accept impure alms.
One takes food with one's own hand and does not receive it from another;
when someone offers food, one takes it by scooping it from their hand;
one holds the rim of the bowl with the fingers and does not lift the bowl to receive the food.
When eating, they spoke loudly and in a disorderly manner.
Those who did not have faith in or delight in the Buddha-dharma criticized them, saying:
"These śramaṇas are even worse than the non-Buddhists; they possess no dignified deportment, even to the point of speaking loudly and in a disorderly manner!"
"You lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
Those places you did not pass through all obtained wholesome benefit.
Furthermore, there was another sick bhikṣu who had no one to attend to him; because of this, he passed away.
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they censured them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha rebuked them in various ways, saying:
"How is it that you allow your minds to be distracted, such that your conduct—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—is entirely contrary to the Dharma?
Having rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one wears the upper and lower robes improperly, or even speaks loudly and disruptively during mealtime, all such acts constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
From this day forward, for the sake of ten benefits, I authorize the monks to have a preceptor (*upādhyāya*)."

When the preceptor naturally gives rise to a heart of affection for the disciple as if for a son, and the disciple naturally gives rise to a heart of reverence for the preceptor as if for a father, and they diligently exhort one another while maintaining mutual respect and esteem, they will be able to cause the Buddha-dharma to increase and expand so that it may endure for a long time.
The procedure for requesting the Upādhyāya:
One should bare the right shoulder, remove one's leather sandals, kneel with the right knee on the ground, cup the Upādhyāya’s feet with both hands, and speak as follows:

“I, [Name], now request the Venerable One to be my Upādhyāya; may the Venerable One act as my Upādhyāya. I delight in having the Venerable One as my Upādhyāya upon whom to rely; it is because the Venerable One is my Upādhyāya that I shall receive full ordination.”
Thus he requested three times.
The preceptor should reply: "So be it!"
"I instruct you now: do not be negligent!
The disciple should thus respectfully serve the upādhyāya.
If one enters a village without informing the upādhyāya, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one wishes to travel together with other bhikṣus, one should likewise inform the upādhyāya.
If one departs without informing him or without his permission, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
The same applies if other bhikṣus call upon one to travel with them.
If one wishes to take from another bhikṣu items such as robes, alms bowls, or leather sandals, one must likewise announce one's intention;
if one does not announce it, or if one announces it but takes the items without being granted permission, in all such cases it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
If one wishes to give robes or alms bowls to another bhikṣu, it is also the same.
If another bhikṣu wishes to carry one’s robes and alms bowl or to fetch them for one, one should also inform him;
if one does not inform him, or if one informs him but he does not grant permission and one nevertheless acts, in all such cases it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If other bhikṣus request that one carry their robes and bowl or take them for them, it is also the same.
For whatever task is to be done, even down to shaving the head—whether one is shaving oneself or shaving for another—one must always announce it.
Except for the acts of defecation and urination and the use of the tooth-stick,
if the Upādhyāya commits a grave offense, the disciple should diligently apply skillful means to cause it to be swiftly eliminated;
if he fails to apply such means, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If the Saṃgha ought to grant the teacher (upādhyāya) the probationary period (parivāsa), or the penance of mānatva, or the restoration to the original status (mūlāpakarṣa), or the rehabilitation (āvarhaṇa), the disciple should diligently employ skillful means to request that the Saṃgha quickly grant him the probationary period up to the rehabilitation;
if he does not act diligently, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

On the day the preceptor is to be cleared of the offense, the disciple should sweep and sprinkle the area, prepare seats, arrange the *śalākā* voting sticks, assemble the Saṃgha, and seek out a monk to perform the *karmavācanā*;
if he does not do so, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If the Saṃgha intends to perform a *karma* of censure, a *karma* of expulsion, a *karma* of dependence, a *karma* of formal accusation, or a *karma* of subordination against the preceptor, the disciple should diligently entreat the Saṃgha not to do so;
if he does not so entreat the Saṃgha, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the Saṃgha must perform these various *karmans*, the disciple should request that they not violate the Dharma;
if he does not so request, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the preceptor is ill, the disciple should attend to him on his left and right.
If the preceptor has property, one should inform him and take it to exchange for food appropriate to his illness or medicine appropriate to his illness;
if the preceptor has no property, one should use what one possesses oneself to exchange for them;
if one likewise possesses nothing, one should seek it on his behalf.
Furthermore, one should preach the Dharma to the sick preceptor morning and evening; as long as the preceptor’s illness has not been cured, one must not travel.
If one does not do so, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a disciple commits a grave offense, the preceptor should likewise attend to them until their illness has been cured.
At that time, the bhikṣus conferred the precepts with a single utterance, saying:
"Take refuge in the Buddha!"
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who conferred the precepts with two utterances, saying:
"Take refuge in the Buddha; take refuge in the Dharma!
There was also a bhikṣu who conferred the precepts with three utterances, saying:
“Take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha!
Having reported this to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
“One should not confer the precepts with only one word, two words, or three words!”
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who conferred the precepts upon someone by saying, “Come, bhikṣu! (Ehi-bhikṣu). The elder bhikṣus rebuked him, saying:
“How can you confer the precepts by saying ‘Come, bhikṣu! just as the Buddha did?”
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not confer the precepts upon a 'Come, bhikṣu' (ehi-bhikṣu) by that [method]!
At that time, the bhikṣus had this thought:
"But since the Buddha bestows the precepts upon the bhikṣus, may we also receive them?
If we may, how should they be bestowed?
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Now I permit you to confer the precepts upon the bhikṣus; they should be conferred by means of a formal motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
One who wishes to confer the precepts shall bare the right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, pay homage to the Saṃgha, place his right knee on the ground, and make this formal motion:
'May the virtuous Saṃgha listen!'"
I, [Name], having received the full ordination from the preceptor [Name], now request the Saṃgha to grant me the full ordination.
May the Saṃgha deliver me out of compassion!
Thus he makes this request three times.

Among the assembly, there should be one monk who knows the Dharma—whether he be a senior elder (sthavira) or one equal to a senior elder—who makes a formal announcement (*jñapti*) to the Saṃgha, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
This person, [Name], wishes to receive full ordination, with [Name] serving as preceptor.
The Sangha now grants full ordination to [Name], with [Name] as preceptor.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus as a formal motion. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This person, [Name], wishes to receive full ordination, with [Name] as preceptor.
The Saṃgha now grants full ordination to [Name], with [Name] as preceptor.
"Whichever elders approve, remain silent;
if you do not approve, speak.
A second and third time, it was done in this same manner.
"The Sangha has already consented that so-and-so receive full ordination with so-and-so as preceptor;
the Sangha consents, because it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld."
At that time, some bhikṣus—ranging from groups of four up to nine—conferred full ordination upon individuals ranging from one to many.
The elder bhikṣus rebuked them and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I permit a group of ten to confer full ordination.

Thereupon, the bhikṣus used non-humans, laypeople, those subject to *pravāsanīya* (banishment), those subject to *utkṣepanīya* (suspension), those who have made a self-accusation, those with differing views, the insane, those with distracted minds, those with diseased minds, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs to complete the group of ten and conferred full ordination.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Ten bhikṣus who are in accordance with the Dharma should confer the full ordination.
Yet the bhikṣus conferred the full ordination upon those who were sleeping, intoxicated, insane, distracted in mind, mentally deranged by illness, or holding heterodox views.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not confer the full ordination upon those who are asleep, nor even upon those who hold divergent views!
One should confer the full ordination upon a person who is in accordance with the Dharma by means of ten bhikṣus who are themselves in accordance with the Dharma."
The bhikṣus took as their upādhyāyas those who were asleep, intoxicated, insane, mentally deranged, or whose minds were impaired by illness.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not take such persons as one's upādhyāya!"
The bhikṣus again appointed two people, and even up to ten people, as preceptors (upādhyāya).
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should appoint only one person as a preceptor; one should not appoint two, nor even ten!"
There were some people who wished to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), but they were unable to assemble ten bhikṣus who were in accordance with the Dharma. They thought to themselves:
"If the Buddha would allow us to receive full ordination during the time of the *poṣadha*, the time of the *pravāraṇā*, or when the Saṃgha assembles on its own, there would be no such hardship!"
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow that full ordination be received during the time of the *poṣadha*, during the time of the *pravāraṇā*, or when the Saṃgha assembles of its own accord."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were in discord with their preceptors and teachers, and they consequently raised objections against those receiving the full ordination.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"If the person receiving the ordination has no grounds for objection, one should not raise such objections against them."
"If one raises an objection for the sake of creating difficulty, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who, on account of minor or superficial matters, forcibly raised objections against those receiving the precepts; some said they resembled the blind, others said they resembled the lame; seeing their shortness or smallness, they said they were not yet twenty years of age, or they said their parents had apparently not given permission for them to leave the household life.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not raise an objection against a person receiving the precepts on account of some minor, superficial matter;
if one raises such an objection, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The bhikṣus continued to raise objections, and they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If it accords with the wishes of the upādhyāya and the ācārya, you should grant them the full ordination."
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus within a boundary who conferred the precepts as a separate assembly.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"They should go outside the boundary and, by means of a formal motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), establish a small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*) to confer the precepts."
First, one bhikṣu should proclaim the boundary markers of the four directions.
Another bhikṣu should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

As the boundary markers have been proclaimed by the bhikṣu so-and-so, the Saṃgha now establishes this as a *sīmā*-maṇḍala for communal residence, communal *poṣadha*, and communal receipt of offerings.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen.
The motion is thus made. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

As the boundary markers have been proclaimed by the bhikṣu so-and-so, the Saṃgha now establishes this as a *sīmā*-maṇḍala for the purpose of communal residence, communal *poṣadha*, and communal receipt of offerings."
"Whichever elders approve, let them remain silent;
if they do not approve, let them speak.

The Saṃgha has already established the boundary marks proclaimed by the bhikṣu so-and-so to form a *kṣetraghaṭita* (boundary-marked) *sīmā*, and has completed the common dwelling, the common *poṣadha*, and the common receiving of offerings."
"Because the Saṃgha has consented by remaining silent,
this matter is thus upheld.
After the bhikṣus had demarcated the boundary of the *sīmā*, they departed without formally relinquishing it.
They informed the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"One should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) to relinquish the boundary and then depart. A bhikṣu made the motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
At this place of boundary-determination, the Saṃgha now relinquishes this boundary.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen."
[The motion] is thus announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
At this site of boundary-determination, the Saṃgha now relinquishes this boundary."
"Whichever elders approve, let them remain silent;
if you do not approve, speak.
The Sangha has finished relinquishing this boundary."
"Because the Saṃgha remains silent,
this matter is thus upheld.
At that time, the bhikṣus led the person about to receive the precepts to the place of ordination and addressed the Elder, saying:
"I shall perform the *karmavācanā*. He replied,
"I do not recite the *karmavācanā*."
This applies even down to the junior monks; they may not confer the precepts [for others].
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"All must recite the *karmavācanā*. If one who has been ordained for ten years or more does not recite it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."

The bhikṣus took the two individuals seeking ordination to the place of ordination, intending to confer the precepts upon them; however, as the two quarreled over who should go first, they were unable to confer the precepts.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The one who arrives first at the place of ordination should be granted the precepts first."
If both arrive at the same time, the one who is older in years should be granted ordination first;
if they are of the same age, the one whose preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is senior should be granted it first;
if the preceptors are also the same, they should undergo the *karmavācanā* simultaneously, and the one whose name is called first shall receive it first.
"The same applies to three people.
Upāli asked the Buddha:
"May other matters also be settled by a *karmavācanā* with three people?"
The Buddha said, "Yes. He asked again:
"Is it permissible to perform a *karmavācanā* with four people?
The Buddha said,
"In no case may one perform a *karmavācanā* with four people!"

When the bhikṣus were about to lead those seeking ordination to the place of ordination to confer the precepts upon them, they encountered bandits who robbed them, nearly killing them before they returned.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"If the World-Honored One would permit us to establish an ordination platform within the monastery grounds, we would not have encountered this calamity."
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"I now permit you to establish a boundary for the precept-receiving site within a monastic dwelling by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. First, you should relinquish the boundary of the monastic dwelling through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*."
A monk who knows the Dharma makes the proclamation:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This community of monks dwelling together, performing the uposatha together, and receiving offerings together, has previously established this boundary; it is now being dissolved."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus:
'Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!'"
In this dwelling place, the Saṃgha has lived together, performed the Poṣadha together, and received offerings together; the previously established boundary is now being dissolved.
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has completed the dissolution of the previously established boundary;
the Sangha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.
Once the boundary of the *saṃghārāma* has been dissolved, one should then establish the *sīmā* for the *karmavastu*.
A single bhikṣu should announce the four boundaries of the *śīlā-maṇḍala*, and another bhikṣu should perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* as described above.
Having completed the binding of the *kṣetramaṇḍala*, one should further bind the boundary of the monastic quarters (*saṃghārāma-sīman*).
One bhikṣu should proclaim the characteristics of the four boundaries, and another bhikṣu should proclaim the exclusion of the interior land.
Then, another bhikṣu should make the formal motion (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu [Name] has proclaimed the boundary markers of the four directions and excluded the interior land. Now the Saṃgha shall establish a Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā) for communal residence, communal Poṣadha, and communal receipt of offerings."
"If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience.
This is the motion. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

This bhikṣu, [Name], has proclaimed the boundary marks of the four directions and excluded the interior land; now the Saṃgha establishes this as a Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā) for communal residence, communal Poṣadha, and communal receipt of offerings.
"Whichever elders consent, let them remain silent;
if you do not consent, speak.

The Sangha has already established for the bhikṣu so-and-so the boundary marks of the four directions and the exclusion of the interior land, creating a great boundary for the Sangha, for communal residence, communal *poṣadha*, and communal receipt of offerings."
The Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.
At that time, there was a certain Mānava of a non-Buddhist sect who wished to go forth in the True Dharma and receive full ordination; he went to where Śāriputra was and said:
“Please allow me to go forth and receive full ordination.
Śāriputra did not grant it; thus he went in turn to all five hundred bhikṣus, but none of them granted it, so he returned home weeping.
The Buddha perceived this with his divine eye and asked Śāriputra,
"For what reason has this young brahmin returned weeping?
Śāriputra answered him in full detail regarding the matter.
He asked again,
"Has this man ever uttered a single word of kindness toward the bhikṣus? He replied:
"Yes," he replied.
He was asked again,
"What virtuous words did you say?"
He replied, "I was previously begging for alms when this person praised me, saying:
'This śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, is virtuous and worthy; one should give him food.'"
The Buddha said, "This kindness should be repaid; you may ordain him!
Śāriputra, having received these instructions, immediately conferred the full precepts upon him.
Furthermore, there was another non-Buddhist wanderer, a māṇava, who, being of little merit, was unable to obtain alms through begging. He thought to himself:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, find it easy to obtain alms; when they are ill or emaciated, people are happy to give them medicine."
"I would rather go to him now to leave the household life and receive full ordination!
Having thought this, he went to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus:
"Grant me the going-forth and bestow upon me full ordination."
The bhikṣus then conferred full ordination upon him.
Because of his meager merit, he encountered a period when the sequential invitations for meals had been interrupted.
The bhikṣus said to him, "You should put on your robes, take up your bowl, and go begging for food!"
He replied: "Venerable Sir!
It was out of fear of begging for alms that I went forth into homelessness within the Buddha-dharma."
"Now, how can you instruct me to beg for alms?
The elder bhikṣus rebuked him, saying,
"How can you ordain someone who is incapable of begging for alms?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not ordain such a person; to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
When ordaining a person, one should first ask: "
"What kind of renunciation have you undertaken?
If they say it is for the sake of food and drink, they should not be ordained;
if they say it is to seek the wholesome Dharma, out of weariness with birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, they should be ordained.
When bestowing the full ordination, one should first explain the four reliances:
"Can you rely for the rest of your life upon these four things: rag-robes, alms-food, sitting under a tree, and discarded medicine?"
"If one says they are able, one should confer it upon them;
if one says they are not able, one should not confer it.
There was a great elder, a brahmin, who grew weary of and distressed by the world, and he thought to himself:
"The śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, practice the True Dharma and extensively cultivate the holy life; by going forth among them, one may reach the end of suffering.
Having thought this, he went immediately to the monastery and sought to go forth and receive full ordination.
The bhikṣus said:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught the four reliances; if you can rely upon these for as long as life lasts, we shall grant you the going forth and bestow the full ordination."
The brahmin asked, "What are the four reliances?
The bhikṣus then explained them to him.
The brahmins said, "These four reliances are despised by the world; we cannot rely upon them!
They spoke again:
"If, Venerable Sir, you had first conferred the full ordination upon me and only then spoken thus, I would have been compelled to act accordingly!
Having said this, he returned home.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"If the Buddha would allow us to confer full ordination upon him first, and only thereafter explain the four reliances to him, this person would not fall away from the Buddha-dharma."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow that after one has received full ordination (*upasampadā*), one should then explain the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*).

At that time, the bhikṣus who had received full ordination returned ahead, while those newly ordained followed behind; they encountered a former female courtesan with whom they had had illicit relations.
The courtesan asked,
"Did you enter the path because you were unable to make a living? He replied:

“I am weary of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction; desiring to bring an end to the source of suffering, I shall practice the True Dharma with equanimity herein and extensively cultivate the holy life.”
She spoke again: "If it is as you say that there will be no time for our union, you may now engage with me in our final act of desire!
They then engaged in it together, returning only at the close of day.
The bhikṣus asked,
"For what reason did you stay behind?
He answered truthfully, whereupon the bhikṣus expelled him, saying:
"Get out! Get lost! If one performs such an act within the Dharma of the bhikṣus, they are no śramaṇa and no son of the Śākya!
Upon hearing this, that bhikṣu fainted and fell to the ground, saying these words:
"If they had told me when I was receiving the precepts, even at the cost of my life, how could I have ever transgressed this!
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Once the full ordination has been completed, one should immediately explain to them the twelve dharmas, the four pārajika dharmas, the four similes, and the four reliances."

At that time, as the Buddha had not yet permitted the bhikṣus to have ācāryas, when their upādhyāyas passed away, they lacked both upādhyāyas and ācāryas. Consequently, they put on their upper and lower robes improperly, and even during mealtime they spoke in a distracted manner, as described above.
The elder bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, for the sake of ten benefits, I allow the bhikṣus to have ācāryas."

The ācārya naturally gives rise to the thought of regarding the disciple as a son, and the disciple naturally gives rise to the thought of regarding the ācārya as a father; all matters are as explained in the section concerning the upādhyāya.
Since the Buddha had permitted the existence of ācāryas, [the monks] did not know how many kinds of ācāryas there were, and they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"There are five kinds of ācāryas:"

The preceptor for going forth (pravrajyā-ācārya), the preceptor for instruction (śikṣā-ācārya), the preceptor for ritual acts (karmācārya), the preceptor for receiving the scriptures (adhyayana-ācārya), and the preceptor for dependence (niśraya-ācārya).

The bhikṣus did not know who was the preceptor for going forth (*pravrajyā-ācārya*) up to the preceptor for dependence (*niśraya-ācārya*). They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When one is first ordained and receives the śrāmaṇera precepts, that person is called the preceptor for going forth;
when one receives the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*), the one who teaches the rules of decorum (*īryāpatha*) is called the preceptor for instruction (*anuśāsaka-ācārya*)."
When performing the *karmavācanā* at the time of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), one is called the *karmācārya*;
when receiving the transmission of the scriptures, even for as little as a single day’s recitation, one is called the *śrutoddeśācārya*;
and even if one merely relies on him for a single night’s stay, he is called the *niśrayācārya*.

Since the Buddha had permitted the existence of a preceptor (*ācārya*) for dependence, [monks] then took as their dependents: bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, those with deranged minds, those with distracted minds, those with diseased minds, those who have been suspended (*utkṣiptaka*), those who have been expelled (*pravāsanīya*), those living in a different location, those living in seclusion (*pārivāsika*), those performing *mānatva*, those performing the restoration of the original status (*yadbhūyaskāraka*), those subject to the rite of deliverance from guilt (*āvarhaṇīya*), those who have made a confession, those subject to the majority decision (*yadbhūyas-kalpa*), and those subject to various formal acts (*karman*).
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I do not permit reliance upon the aforementioned persons;
I permit reliance only upon bhikṣus who act in accordance with the Dharma."
In this regard, there are cases where the request for dependence is valid and cases where it is not;
there are cases where the granting of dependence is valid and cases where it is not;
and there are cases where the undertaking of dependence is valid and cases where it is not.
Regarding the failure to properly request dependence (*niśraya*):

if a bhikṣu requests dependence from a bhikṣuṇī, or from a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, or even from various persons performing formal acts (*karmakāraka*), this is called a failure to properly request dependence.
If one requests dependence from a bhikṣu who acts in accordance with the Dharma, yet does not speak these words:
"I, [name], now seek your venerable self as my dependence; may your venerable self act as my dependence, and I shall dwell in dependence upon your venerable self."
"Venerable sir, please instruct me; I shall receive the Venerable's instruction.
This also does not constitute a formal request for dependence (*niśraya*).
That which constitutes a formal request for dependence is as follows:
When a bhikṣu who acts in accordance with the Dharma makes the request as described above, this is called the successful completion of the request for dependence (*niśraya*).
As for when the granting of dependence is not accomplished:

if a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, or even any person performing formal ritual acts (*karmakāraka*) grants dependence to a bhikṣu, this is called the non-accomplishment of the granting of dependence.
If, after a bhikṣu has requested according to the Dharma, that person does not say to him,
"Do not be negligent," this also does not constitute granting dependence.
This is called "non-establishment and non-reliance.
Regarding "establishment and reliance":
when a bhikṣu has requested according to the Dharma and in accordance with the Dharma, he says:
"Do not be negligent!
This is called "granting dependence. One who does not accomplish the reception of dependence is as follows:

If a bhikṣu receives dependence from a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, or even from those who perform formal acts (karmakāraka), in all such cases it is not called receiving dependence.
If, toward a bhikṣu who acts in accordance with the Dharma, one does not speak as above, saying:
"I, [name], now seek your reliance, up to: 'I shall receive your instruction and admonition.'"
Nor does one successfully receive the formal reliance upon a preceptor;
this is called "failing to receive reliance.
As for successfully receiving reliance:
To a bhikṣu who acts in accordance with the Dharma, one should speak as follows:
"I, [name], now seek your reliance; I shall receive your instructions and admonitions."
This is called "establishing the basis for receiving dependence.

At that time, some bhikṣus would receive dependence across a partition; or they did so without respect, with their heads covered, their shoulders covered, wearing leather sandals, or while sitting or lying down.
The elder bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“One should bare the right shoulder, remove one’s leather sandals, kneel with the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and speak the aforementioned words before him:
‘I, [name], now seek your venerable one as my preceptor; I shall receive your venerable instructions.’”
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus did not respect their preceptors (upādhyāya) or teachers (ācārya), nor did they respect the precepts; other bhikṣus also followed their example.
The elder bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned the group of six bhikṣus and the other bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha rebuked them in various ways: "You are foolish!
How can you fail to respect your teacher and fail to respect the precepts?"
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, if any bhikṣu does not respect his preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya), or does not respect the precepts, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
Some bhikṣus still remained disrespectful; they reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"You should enact the rite of not speaking with them.
The bhikṣus then performed the rite of not speaking with them for as long as they lived, and furthermore, they would not look upon one another, or even drive them out from their dwellings.
They also applied the practice of not speaking with foolish bhikṣus and innocent bhikṣus;
furthermore, they applied the practice of not speaking with them without having first declared their offenses.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not, for the rest of one's life, practice the rite of not speaking together with those who show disrespect toward their preceptors (upādhyāya) or instructors (ācārya);
nor should one practice the rite of not speaking together with those who are foolish or those who are innocent;
nor should one practice the rite of not speaking together without having first declared their offense."
There are five ways of not speaking with others: first,
saying the words, "Do not speak with me!"
Second, "Do not inform me of anything you have done! Third, "Do not enter my room!
Fourth, "Do not take hold of my robes and bowl, nor assist me in performing various tasks!"
Fifth: "Do not come to see me!
The bhikṣus then enacted the practice of not speaking with one another over a minor matter.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"One should not employ the practice of not speaking with another for a minor matter. However, if a disciple accomplishes five conditions, the teacher should employ the practice of not speaking with him:
being without shame toward the teacher, without remorse, lacking respect, lacking affection, and failing to make offerings—these are the five conditions."
"If these five conditions are absent, one should not perform the act of not speaking with [the disciple].

There were some bhikṣus who, having performed the act of not speaking with their disciples, subsequently resumed speaking and living together with them; consequently, the disciples became even more arrogant.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not perform the act of not speaking together with someone and then later return to speak with them again.
I did not intend for the act of not speaking together to cause that person to lose their formal reliance (niśraya)."
"To subdue and bring rest toward Nirvāṇa, one performs the rite of not speaking with another; if one speaks with them again, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who performed the rite of not speaking with their disciples, yet other bhikṣus would suddenly speak with them, whereby the disciples became twice as arrogant toward their teachers.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not impose the practice of not speaking with others upon a disciple and then speak with them.
Since the Buddha did not permit others to engage in conversation with him, [the monks] consequently returned to lay life or became followers of external paths because of this matter.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If you wish to instruct another to repent before their teacher, you are permitted to speak with them.
At that time, there was a teacher who practiced the 'not speaking' method with his disciple, and the disciple refused to repent.
