They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not fail to repent one's transgression!
One should perform repentance in this manner: [insert repentance formula here]."
Baring his right shoulder, placing his right knee on the ground, and cupping the teacher’s feet with both hands, he humbled himself deeply and said:
"I am small; I am deluded!"
"From now on, I dare not do so again!
At that time, there was a teacher who would not accept his disciple's confession of transgression.
This matter was reported to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there is still shame, remorse, respect, and affectionate veneration, one should not refuse to accept an apology;
when an apology is accepted, the offense is then extinguished.
At that time, there were also various teachers who did not know whether their disciples had violated the precepts or not.
They did not know how to repent for their transgressions, nor did they repent;
when they saw their disciples violate the precepts, they did not instruct or rebuke them.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“The teacher should know whether the disciple has transgressed the precepts or not;
whether they have repented or not. Upon seeing a transgression of the precepts, he should instruct and reprimand them.”
"If one does not know [this] and does not admonish [the offender], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

At that time, the resident bhikṣus did not pay homage to the visiting bhikṣus, the visiting bhikṣus did not pay homage to the resident bhikṣus, and the resident bhikṣus did not pay homage to one another.
A certain bhikṣu arrived at a monastery and did not pay homage to the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus asked him,
"From where have you come?"
He replied, "I have come from such-and-such a place. The bhikṣus said:
"You should know that the bhikṣus residing at your place are all as arrogant as this; we ought not to dwell together with them.
Having reported this to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"You should pay obeisance to them all!"
"If one does not prostrate, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who prostrated through a wall or partition, or prostrated from afar, or while lying down, saying with their mouths:
"I pay homage (*vandāmi*)."
Some simply raised their hands, while others merely lowered their heads slightly.
The elder bhikṣus rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not perform such a salutation!"
"You should pay homage with single-minded reverence: remove your leather sandals, bare your right shoulder, kneel with both knees on the ground, and prostrate at their feet.
A certain bhikṣu, as he was bowing to each of the bhikṣus one by one, lost his companions.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Simply pay homage to your teacher; pay general homage to the others and then depart.

At that time, the bhikṣu Upasena, who had been ordained for two years, took a disciple who had been ordained for one year to the place where the Buddha was. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and sat down to one side.
Later, when the disciple next paid homage to the Buddha, his robe-bag fell onto the Buddha’s knees.
The Buddha asked Upasena: “Whose disciple is this?”
He replied, "They are my disciples!
The Buddha asked:
“How old are you? He replied,
“I am two years old!”
He asked again, "How old is your disciple? and the answer was, "One year!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"What you have done is contrary to the Dharma!
How can you, not having yourself yet abandoned milk, proceed to give it to others?
Having rebuked him thus, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should not confer the full ordination upon others for one year, nor even up to nine years;
only after ten years and in accordance with the Dharma may one confer it.
If one has not yet completed ten years, or if one confers the full ordination in a manner contrary to the Dharma, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense."
"One who is nine years old should still remain in dependence upon another.
*Pañcavargīya-vinaya*, Fascicle 16; *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya*, Fascicle 17.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Song Dynasty, together with Zhu Daosheng and others.
Part Three: The Initial Method for Receiving Precepts, Part Two. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a naked ascetic (nirgrantha) who was extremely intelligent; the people of Magadha called him a "knower" and a "seer.
He came to the monastery and said, "Among the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, who dares to debate with me?"
At that time, the bhikṣus were sporting in various meditative absorptions; they neither engaged in discussion nor spoke with one another.
Śāriputra thought to himself: "They have made such a statement;
if no one engages them in discussion, they will surely bring disgrace upon the Buddha’s Dharma."
"I should now engage him in debate.
He further thought:

"This Nirgrantha is revered and honored by the people of the kingdom of Magadha; if I ask him a question on a single point of doctrine and he cannot explain it, he will surely lose his reputation and will not turn toward the Great Dharma."
"I shall now grant him seven days for debate.
Having thought this, he said to him:
"I shall engage in debate with you for seven days."
At that time, the elders, householders, śramaṇas, and brahmins of Rājagṛha all deliberated together, saying:
"The śramaṇa Śāriputra, son of the Śākyas, is the second teacher; he has agreed to debate with the first teacher, the Nirgrantha, for seven days. We should go together to listen."
When the appointed time arrived, from the first day through the sixth, he discussed various other matters and caused them all to be rendered speechless.
On the seventh day, Śāriputra stated that desire arises from conceptualization, while the Nirgrantha son asserted that desire arises from sensory opposition.
Then Śāriputra spoke these verses:
“The root of all worldly desires Arises entirely from conceptual thought.
Abiding in the root of worldly desire, One possesses a mind of defiled attachment.”
The Nirgrantha then challenged him with a verse:
“If desire arises from thought And there is attachment therein,
Then a bhikṣu’s evil reflections Have already caused him to lose the holy life.”
Śāriputra replied again in verse:
"If desire does not arise from conceptual thought, but arises from sensory opposition,
then when your teacher beholds various forms, why would he not experience desire?"

When the Nirgrantha had heard this verse, he was unable to offer a rebuttal; instead, a wholesome mind arose within him, and he desired to leave the household life to study the Path under the Buddha’s Dharma.
At that time, Upananda was present in that assembly, possessing a handsome and tall appearance, whereas Śāriputra was short and small in stature.
He thought to himself:
"If this short and small bhikṣu possesses such wisdom and talent, how much more so must one who is dignified and imposing!
He then went to where Upananda was and said to him:
"Grant me the going forth and the full ordination.
Vāṇada immediately ordained him.
After Śāriputra had finished his discourse, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha asked,
"For what reason did you debate with the Nirgranthas for seven days?
He answered in full detail regarding the matter.
The Buddha praised him, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!"
"You have shown great compassion and brought great benefit.

However, when those Nirgrantha bhikṣus questioned Upāli regarding the Sūtras and Vinaya, he was unable to answer them at all. Consequently, they came to despise the Buddha’s Dharma, claiming that the bhikṣus knew nothing, and they returned once more to the non-Buddhist path.
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked him, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu of ten years' standing not know the Dharma, yet fail to resolve his disciple's doubts, thereby causing him to return once more to the state of an outsider?"
They reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied: "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!"
After the Buddha had rebuked him as above, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one does not know the Dharma for oneself, yet causes another to go forth and receive full ordination, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
"If a bhikṣu accomplishes ten qualities, he may confer the full ordination upon others:
he accomplishes the precepts, accomplishes dignified conduct, and stands in awe of even minor transgressions;
he is learned and is able to uphold the Dharma taught by the Buddha."
He is well-versed in reciting the two divisions of the Vinaya and can analyze their meanings;
he is able to instruct his disciples in the training in higher virtue, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom;
he is able to dispel the doubts of his disciples and is also able to cause others to have their doubts dispelled.
He can cure the illnesses of his disciples, and he can also cause others to cure their illnesses;
if a disciple gives rise to evil and heterodox views, he can instruct them to abandon them, and he can also cause others to instruct them to abandon them;
if a disciple’s attachment to a country arises, he can turn their mind away from it, and he can also cause others to turn them away from it.
If one has completed ten years, or more than ten years,
and furthermore accomplishes ten qualities, one should confer the full ordination upon others:
knowing the grave offenses and knowing the minor offenses;
He knows what constitutes a grave offense and what does not;
he knows what constitutes an offense with remainder and what constitutes an offense without remainder;
he knows what constitutes an offense subject to formal ritual (kamma) and what does not.
One should know the causes and conditions of offenses;
one must have completed ten years of seniority, or more than ten years.
Furthermore, one who has accomplished five qualities should confer the full ordination upon others:

He is able to instruct his disciples in the training of higher virtue, the training of higher mind, and the training of higher wisdom; his conduct is earnest and precise, and his mindfulness is ever-present.
Furthermore, he accomplishes five qualities:
three as mentioned above, plus intelligence and eloquence.
Furthermore, they accomplish five dharmas:
accomplishment in ethical discipline, accomplishment in meditative concentration, accomplishment in wisdom, accomplishment in liberation, and accomplishment in the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Furthermore, one accomplishes five qualities:
abiding in the precepts oneself and teaching others to abide in the precepts;
abiding in meditative concentration oneself and teaching others to abide in meditative concentration;
Abiding oneself in wisdom, one teaches others to abide in wisdom;
abiding oneself in liberation, one teaches others to abide in liberation;
abiding oneself in the knowledge and vision of liberation, one teaches others to abide in the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Furthermore, he accomplishes five qualities:

he accomplishes the aggregate of precepts of one beyond training, the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training, the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training, the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training.
Furthermore, one accomplishes five qualities:
being able to instruct disciples in higher ethical discipline and the higher holy life;
and knowing what constitutes an offense and what does not.
One who knows whether an offense has been confessed or not yet confessed,
and who is ten years of age or more than ten years of age, should bestow the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others.
The same applies to admitting *śrāmaṇeras* and acting as a *niśraya* (preceptor) for others.
A certain renunciant from a non-Buddhist sect came to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus,
"Virtuous ones!
Grant me the going forth and confer the full ordination upon me."
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"You should first perform for him the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* of a four-month probationary period (*parivāsa*) to test him. If he meets with the approval of the bhikṣus, you may then perform the *karman* for his renunciation and the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*)."

He should instruct the non-Buddhist to remove his leather sandals, bare his right shoulder, prostrate at the feet of each member of the Saṃgha one by one, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and say:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
I, [Name], formerly a follower of external paths, now seek to go forth within this Dharma and Vinaya, and I beg the Saṃgha for a period of four months of separate residence (parivāsa).
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the rite of separate residence; if it accords with the intention of the bhikṣus, they may thereafter grant me the going forth and the full ordination!
Thus he requests three times.
A bhikṣu who knows the Dharma should then announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This person, so-and-so, was formerly a non-Buddhist; he wishes to go forth and receive full ordination within this Dharma and Vinaya, and now requests from the Sangha the practice of the four-month *parivāsa* (probation).
The Saṃgha now grants the four-month period of separate residence; if it is in accordance with the Saṃgha’s intention, he shall be granted ordination and receive the full precepts.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen.
The motion is as follows: "Venerable Sangha, listen!

This person, so-and-so, was formerly a non-Buddhist; he wishes to go forth and receive full ordination within this Dharma and Vinaya, and now requests from the Sangha the practice of the four-month *parivāsa* (probation).”
The Saṃgha now intends to grant the four-month period of separate residence; if it is to the satisfaction of the Saṃgha, he shall be granted the going-forth and the full ordination.
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has already granted the four-month *parivāsa* (probation) for separation to the outsider [named] So-and-so;
the Sangha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.
That which is contrary to the Sangha’s intention:
if one enters a village too early and returns only at dusk;
or if one frequently visits the homes of widows, prostitutes, or elderly maidens, frequently converses with them, and employs various means to seek sexual desire.
If, upon hearing disparagement of the non-Buddhist teachers one formerly served, one harbors anger and resentment;
if, upon hearing praise of the Triple Gem, one feels neither joy nor delight;

if one takes no pleasure in the dignified deportment of bhikṣus, takes no pleasure in reciting and studying the Buddha’s sūtras, and takes no pleasure in receiving instructions and admonitions—this is called being discordant with the intent of the Saṃgha.
"If there is no such obstacle, it is called 'concordance,' and one should grant him the full ordination (upasampadā) upon leaving the household life.
At that time, the bhikṣus ordained a debtor and granted him the full ordination; having received the full ordination, he entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms.
A creditor saw him and said, "You owe me a debt; who has permitted you to go forth? Another said:
"One should seize his robes and bowl, take him by force, and hand him over to the authorities! Others said:
"He has already entered the City of Fearlessness; you should release him and let him go."
"Why is this? King Bimbisāra has issued a decree: 'If there is anyone within the kingdom who insults or humiliates a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, they shall be punished with a heavy penalty.
Thereupon, the creditor rebuked him, saying:
"These śramaṇas have no such thing as those who can be saved and those who cannot be saved.
How can they save debtors?
They lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!"
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they censured them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should not ordain a person who is in debt and grant them full admission to the order.
At the time of ordination and the granting of full admission, one must first ask: [Is this person free from debt?]"
"Do you owe a debt? If he says, "I do not."
"One should respond, 'I accept; I am to be delivered';
or if one says, 'I am defeated.'"
"One should neither ordain nor receive [them].
Whether one ordains or receives them, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
It is the same if one does not inquire."
"The case of Duanu was also like this.

At that time, there was a young boy whose parents sent him to a teacher to learn writing and various arts. That teacher, however, made him perform other labor as well and frequently beat him with a staff; consequently, the boy abandoned his teacher and returned home.
His parents immediately sent him back to his teacher’s place, whereupon he thought to himself:
"My teacher has already tormented me, and now my parents show no concern or pity for me.
Where can I find deliverance from this suffering?"
"I must only go forth and receive full ordination.
Having thought this, he immediately went to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus:
"Grant me the going forth and the full ordination."
The bhikṣus then ordained him.
Once his teacher had lost him, he questioned his parents, who said, "We sent him back immediately; why has he not returned?"

Thereupon, the parents and the teacher went out in the four directions to search for him. Upon reaching the monastery, they questioned the bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus all said they had not seen him; only the teacher remained silent. Having failed to find him, they returned home.
Later, when this boy entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms, his teacher saw him and rebuked him, saying:
"The Śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas always say that one should not speak falsely; how is it that you ordained me as a man and yet said you did not see me?"
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they censured him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should not ordain another who is a slave, as was explained above."
"From now on, if you ordain others, you should go from room to room to pay respects to the monks, announcing your own name so that all the monks may know it.

At that time, Piṅgala-vatsa conferred the full precepts upon a group of seventeen boys from Śrāvastī who were less than twenty years of age; they could not endure hunger and cried out while seeking food, as described in the section concerning the origin of the precepts.
When conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*), one should ask:
"Are you twenty years of age?
At that time, the bhikṣus ordained forest-dwelling bandits and conferred full ordination upon them. Later, when they entered the city of Rājagṛha for alms, the lay devotees saw them and said:
"This man previously killed such-and-such relatives of mine and plundered my wealth and property.
Another said, "We should seize him and hand him over to the authorities!"
He continued until he addressed the bhikṣus, stating that they should not ordain them, as previously explained.
Furthermore, there were other bandits who, weary of committing evil deeds, sought to leave the household life and receive full ordination.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to take him to a place where people do not recognize him, and there grant him the going-forth and the full ordination."
At that time, there was a man who was a source of trouble to the village.
He said to the king, "I pray that Your Majesty will command him not to commit evil again!
The king replied:
"Bring him here; I shall kill him for you!
Upon hearing this, the man immediately fled in rebellion, and though they searched everywhere, they could not find him.
He reported this again to the king, who then issued a decree stating that anyone who captured him was permitted to execute him on the spot.
Hearing this again, that person thought:
"By what means can I now preserve my life?
Only by following the path of the śramaṇa sons of the Śākya can I be saved!"
He then went to the monastery to seek ordination, and the bhikṣus immediately conferred it upon him.
Later, when he entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food, people saw him and sought to seize and kill him; some even said:
"Since he has already left the household life, he is as good as dead; there is no need to kill him again. Or others might say:
"This person has already entered the City of Fearlessness."
...and so on, until he addressed the bhikṣus, saying that they should not ordain [such persons], as explained above.
At that time, there were two śrāmaṇeras under Baddhananda, one named Khaṇḍa and the other named Māgadha, who engaged in mutual sexual misconduct.
The elder bhikṣus heard of this and reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you keep two śrāmaṇeras?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should not keep two śrāmaṇeras; to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, there was a family that had been harmed by non-human beings, and only the father and son remained.
The father thought to himself:
"My household is ruined; I fear the calamity will not yet have ended. Furthermore, we are now hungry and destitute—where can I find relief from these misfortunes?"
He further thought to himself:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, receive many offerings and have access to medicines for illness; I should now take my son to leave the household life and receive full ordination."
Having reflected thus, he went to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus,
"Grant me the going forth and the full ordination.
The bhikṣus then granted him the going forth and the full ordination.
Entering the city to beg for alms, he carried his child with one hand while holding his bowl with the other.
When the laypeople saw this, they reviled him, saying,
"This śramaṇa son of the Śākyas does not cultivate the holy life."
Some said, "This was indeed his son from before he left the household life!
But why did the bhikṣus not wait until he had grown up before ordaining him?"
He then had this man carry the child while begging for alms.
Who would not say that this violated the holy life (*brahmacarya*)?
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they reported it to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not ordain young children!

At that time, the people of Magadha were afflicted by seven kinds of severe illnesses: malignant sores covering the entire body, carbuncles, leprosy, hemiplegia, demonic possession, erysipelas, and the oozing of fat. To treat these various diseases, there was only Jīvaka;
no one else was capable. King Bimbisāra issued a decree, commanding Jīvaka, saying:
"You shall attend to the illnesses of those within my palace, as well as those of the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, but you must not treat anyone else!

Consequently, all those who were ill sought to leave the household life and receive full ordination; the bhikṣus all granted them the going forth and full ordination. In doing so, they had to seek medicinal herbs, compound them, boil them, and grind them, resulting in many tasks and duties that obstructed and caused them to abandon their practice of the Path.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled them, saying:
"These śramaṇas are like physicians or medical disciples, constantly compounding decoctions and medicines to treat those suffering from grave illnesses."
"There is no longer anyone who can be saved or cannot be saved.
There is no conduct of a śramaṇa; the dharma of a śramaṇa has been destroyed!
Furthermore, there was another elder who suddenly contracted seven kinds of grave illnesses and went to speak with Jīvaka:
"Have it treated for me. He replied,
"Have you not heard the King's decree?"
The householder spoke again:
"Treat me secretly, and I shall hire you with one hundred thousand gold coins.
He answered as before.

The elder further added two hundred, three hundred, four hundred, five hundred, and even a thousand gold coins; eventually, he offered all the family’s wealth and even his wife and children as slaves.
The answer was as before.
That householder then thought again:
"Since this has not borne fruit, I must simply go forth and receive full ordination."
She then went to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus,
"Please grant me the going forth and the full ordination.
The bhikṣus immediately granted her the going forth and the full ordination.

Jīvaka treated him for seven days until he was completely recovered; thereafter, Jīvaka was no longer permitted to treat the people of the royal palace, as some among them had already died of the illness.
Once the elder had recovered, he immediately returned to secular life.
Jīvaka saw him and asked,
"Since you have already left the household life, why have you abandoned the path? He replied:
"Originally I had no intention of leaving the household life; it was only because you refused to treat my illness that I temporarily became a monk.
Now that the illness has been cured, I am therefore returning to secular life."
Thereupon, Jīvaka went to where the Buddha was and reported the matter to him in full:
"If the King were to learn of this, my punishment would not be small!
I pray that the Buddha instruct the bhikṣus that they should not ordain those who are seriously ill!"
The Buddha taught Jīvaka various sublime dharmas and sent him back to his residence.
The Buddha then asked the bhikṣus:
"Did you truly ordain those who were seriously ill?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should not ordain those who are seriously ill!
This was also as explained above.

At that time, some bhikṣus ordained persons who were subjects of the government. Later, when they entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms, the laypeople recognized them and criticized them, saying:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ordain persons who are subjects of the government?"
"These people are neither those who can be saved nor those who cannot be saved.
They lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!

Furthermore, King Ajātaśatru had a valiant general whose strength equaled that of a thousand men; the people of the time called him the "Thousand-Man Strongman. Loathing the sufferings of the world, he thought to himself:
"The śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, practice the True Dharma; I shall go to them to leave the household life in order to bring an end to the source of suffering.
He then went to the monastery to seek ordination, and the bhikṣus immediately ordained him.
Later, when the king wished to dispatch his army, he could not find this man and immediately questioned those under his command.
His subordinates reported to the king:
"We do not know where he is."
The king then issued an order, saying:
"If you do not arrive when the army assembles, you shall be punished according to military law!
When the day for the assembly arrived, he questioned them again.
"Has that person arrived yet?
He replied, "He has not yet arrived!"
The king said, "The infantry lacks such a man, just as the elephant corps lacks its foremost elephant.
Once his armor was removed, he learned that the śramaṇa son of the Śākyas had ordained him for the homeless life; the king then spoke in anger:
"In this way, before long, these śramaṇas shall surely convert all my troops!
The king immediately established a strict decree:

"If there is anyone who again converts an official, his preceptor’s ribs shall be broken, his ācārya’s tongue shall be cut out, and he, along with the other monks, shall receive eight lashes of the leather whip *revatā* and be driven out of the kingdom."
When the elder bhikṣus heard these various reproaches, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did this?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should not ordain those who belong to government officials!
This was also as explained above.
At that time, the bhikṣus resided permanently in Rājagṛha. The laypeople criticized them, saying:

"Even the followers of other paths know to move their dwellings according to the seasons; yet these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, delight in remaining in one place, never moving throughout the four seasons—how are they any different from worldly people?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You may announce to the bhikṣus that the Tathāgata is now about to travel toward the south; those who wish to follow him may go as they please."
Ānanda received the instruction and proclaimed this intent everywhere.
Among the bhikṣus, there were those who had been ordained for one year up to nine years—those who were intelligent, conscientious, and desirous of training in the precepts—who thought to themselves:
"If my upādhyāya or ācārya departs, I shall follow him; if he does not depart, I shall remain."

"Why is this? If I were to rely upon this request of mine, he would likely make further requests in turn; thus, there would be much business and many affairs, which would obstruct and cause the abandonment of the practice of the Way.
Once the Buddha had set out on his journey, those who followed him were very few.
The Buddha was traveling through the southern regions with a small number of bhikṣus, gradually making his way back toward Rājagṛha.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Ānanda:
"Why is it that so few bhikṣus have accompanied me on my journey south?"

Ānanda answered with the details of the matter. After the Buddha had praised in various ways having few desires and being content, and having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“One who accomplishes five qualities attains freedom from dependence:
accomplishment in morality, accomplishment in concentration, accomplishment in wisdom, accomplishment in liberation, and accomplishment in the knowledge and vision of liberation.”
All is as explained in the section on the bestowal of the precepts upon those who have received them.

At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Śākya; various bhikṣus ordained individuals whose parents had not given their permission, and the lay devotees criticized and rebuked them as described above.
Later, in the early morning, the Blessed One dressed himself, took his bowl, and went to King Śuddhodana’s palace.
At that time, Rāhula’s mother was with Rāhula on a high tower; seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, she said to him:
"Do you see that śramaṇa?"
He replied, “I saw them! He spoke again, saying:
"He is your father; you may go and seek the remainder of your father's wealth.

Once the Buddha had entered the palace, he sat upon the open ground in the central courtyard. Rāhula ran down to approach the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood within the Buddha’s shadow, saying:
"This shadow is most pleasant!"
"I pray that the Buddha will grant me my father's remaining wealth!
The Buddha said to him,
"Do you truly wish to have it?"
He replied, "I wish to obtain it!
The Buddha then led him back to his residence and addressed Śāriputra:
"You may ordain him. Śāriputra addressed the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, you previously established the rule that one may not keep two śrāmaṇeras. Since I already have Cunda, I am no longer permitted to ordain this one."
The Buddha said:
"Now, I permit those like you who are able to provide instruction and admonition to maintain two śrāmaṇeras.
You should ordain them in this manner:"
First, bestow the Three Refuges of the upāsaka, instructing them as follows:
"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha of bhikṣus."
Thus it was said three times.
He further instructed him, saying:
"I, [Name], having taken refuge in the Buddha, having taken refuge in the Dharma, and having taken refuge in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus..."
He should also say this three times:
"I am a lay follower (upāsaka) of the Buddha, the Blessed One.
He should then further instruct him, saying:

"I, [Name], for as long as life lasts, shall refrain from killing; for as long as life lasts, shall refrain from stealing; for as long as life lasts, shall refrain from sexual misconduct; for as long as life lasts, shall refrain from false speech; and for as long as life lasts, shall refrain from drinking intoxicants."
Furthermore, one should instruct them, saying:
"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha of Bhikṣus.
This should be recited three times.
"I now go forth as a śrāmaṇera under the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, with [Name] as my upādhyāya."
One should immediately say:
"To refrain from taking life for as long as one lives is a śrāmaṇera precept;
to refrain from stealing for as long as one lives is a śrāmaṇera precept."
To refrain from sexual misconduct for as long as life lasts is a śrāmaṇera precept;
to refrain from false speech for as long as life lasts is a śrāmaṇera precept;
to refrain from drinking intoxicants for as long as life lasts is a śrāmaṇera precept.
To refrain from singing, dancing, performing, or attending performances for the rest of one’s life is a śrāmaṇera precept;
to refrain from wearing flower garlands, scents, or unguents on the body for the rest of one’s life is a śrāmaṇera precept;
to refrain from sitting or lying on high or large beds for the rest of one’s life is a śrāmaṇera precept.
"To refrain from accepting gold, silver, or money for as long as life lasts is a śrāmaṇera precept;
to refrain from eating at improper times for as long as life lasts is a śrāmaṇera precept.
These constitute the ten śrāmaṇera precepts.
At that time, King Śuddhodana, hearing that the Buddha had already ordained Rāhula, was deeply distressed. He went to the place where the Buddha was and said to him:
"When you first left the home life in the past, there was still Nanda; even so, he could not cause me such distress as I feel now."
Nanda has already left the household life once more; my remaining affections were placed solely upon this son.
Now that he too has become a renunciant, the great concerns of both family and state are forever severed. Unable yet to forget my feelings, how can I bear it myself?
The King, further reflecting upon his own experience, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The love for one's offspring penetrates even to the very marrow of one's bones.
How can the bhikṣus entice and steal away people's children to ordain them as followers of the Way?"
“I pray that from now on the Buddha will command all bhikṣus: ‘If one’s parents do not permit it, one shall not go forth into the religious life.
After the Buddha had taught the King various sublime dharmas, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him, the King took his leave and returned to his palace.
Thereupon, he assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned them:
"Your parents did not give their permission; have you truly conferred the full ordination upon them?
They replied, "Indeed we have."
“World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, no one shall be ordained without the permission of their parents!”
The rest is as previously related.
At that time, there was a wealthy householder in Rājagṛha who had faith and joy in the Buddha’s Dharma; he constantly provided meals for bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.
Later, he was killed by a non-human spirit, leaving behind only two young children. Consequently, they fell into great poverty and were constantly gathering leftover food.
Because the two boys had previously seen many bhikṣus, as soon as they saw a bhikṣu from afar, they ran toward him, seized his robes and bowl, and sat upon the bhikṣu’s knees.
The bhikṣus, fearing they would soil their robes and bowls, immediately avoided and moved far away.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reproached them, saying:
"This family was formerly wealthy, and there was not a day that the śramaṇas did not visit."
Now that you see me destitute and alone, you immediately abandon and avoid me; you do not recognize the kindness of my nurturing, regarding only food as your kin.
You lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they censured them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?"
He replied, “It is truly so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he asked Ānanda,
"How old are those two children?
Are they already able to drive away the crows from the food?"
He replied, "I am able!
The elder is eight years old, and the younger is seven."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit you to ordain even small children, up to those who are able to drive away crows.
Once the bhikṣus had ordained the two small children, they constantly instructed them only to drive away the crows from the food, but did not give them proper meals.
The laypeople saw this and said:
"These śramaṇas always praise the giving of equal food;
yet now, having ordained these two small boys, they merely have them drive away crows and do not give them proper food."
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Just as the portion of food obtained by the senior monk, one should likewise give a portion of it to the śrāmaṇera."
"The crow-scarecrow boy should also be granted an equal share.

At that time, there was a mānava who had killed his mother; reflecting on the gravity of his crime, he was constantly filled with remorse and fear, not knowing how to extinguish this sin. He thought to himself:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, practice the True Dharma equally and purely cultivate the Brahma-faring. If I were to go forth among them, my sin would likely be somewhat lightened."
He then went to the monastic quarters and said to the bhikṣus,
“Grant me the going forth and the full ordination. The bhikṣus asked:
“Māṇava! You are a follower of an external path and do not have faith in the Buddha’s Dharma; why do you now wish to go forth within it?
He then answered truthfully.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

“One who has harmed his father or mother shall no longer be born within my Dharma; he should not be granted ordination or the full precepts (upasaṃpadā). If he has already received the full precepts, he should be expelled.”

At that time, there was a forest-dwelling bandit who had killed a bhikṣu living in the forest. From that point on, his mind was constantly tormented by heat, as if he were roasting his own body over hot embers; day and night he suffered in pain without a moment’s respite. He thought to himself:
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, practice the True Dharma and purely cultivate the holy life. If I were to go forth among them, I might be able to escape this burning affliction.”
Having thought this, he went immediately to the monastery to seek ordination.
The bhikṣus said to him, "You are a forest bandit;
you constantly sought to kill people and plunder their wealth, lacking any heart of compassion."
"Why do you now wish to go forth in the Dharma and Vinaya of the Buddha?
He then answered truthfully.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"That bhikṣu is an arhat; this person shall not be born again within my Dharma. He should not be granted the going forth or the full ordination; if he has already received the full ordination, he should be expelled."
At that time, Devadatta, with an evil mind, caused blood to flow from the Buddha’s body. The bhikṣus did not know how they should treat him and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

“One who, with an evil mind, causes blood to flow from the Buddha’s body is no longer born within my Dharma. He should not be granted ordination or the full precepts; if he has already received the full precepts, he should be expelled.”
“The same applies to one who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha, such as Devadatta;

they should not be granted ordination. At that time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kośala with a great community of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. Gradually journeying on, he arrived at the banks of the Kālī River and stayed beneath a śāla grove.
A certain bhikṣu rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This Śāla grove is the place where the brahmacarya of many bhikṣuṇīs was violated.”
The Buddha asked,
"How do you know this? He replied:
"I was here at that time!
He asked again,
"Did you violate the brahmacarya of a bhikṣuṇī?"
He replied, “It is so!
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:

"One who has committed sexual misconduct with a bhikṣuṇī shall not be born again within my Dharma; he should not be granted the going forth or the full ordination, and if he has already received the full ordination, he should be expelled."
At that time, there was a son of an asura who, weary of birth, old age, sickness, and death, thought to himself:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, practice the True Dharma and purely cultivate the holy life."
"I shall go forth under him to exhaust the source of all suffering.

Having thought this, he transformed himself into human form and went to the monastery to seek ordination. The bhikṣus immediately conferred the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon him. He ate the portion of one person, and even the portions of up to seven people, yet he was still not satisfied;
he further ate the leftover food of the Saṃgha, but it was still insufficient.
At that time, there were two lay devotees in the city of Rājagṛha who, on the same day, each invited five hundred monks.
All the bhikṣus went together to one house, while only the bhikṣu Vairāṭīputra went alone to another location; in a short while, he finished eating the portions for five hundred people.
The laypeople criticized them, saying,
"How can these bhikṣus ordain non-humans?
Once those bhikṣus realized they had been discovered by humans, they suddenly returned to their original state.
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"In my Dharma, non-humans do not arise; one should not grant them the going-forth or the full ordination. If they have already received the full ordination, they should be expelled."
"When receiving full ordination, one should ask:
'Are you not a non-human being?

At that time, the Dragon King Svayambhu, weary of birth, old age, sickness, and death, thought of leaving the household life. He transformed himself into a young brahmin student (*māṇava*), and so forth, until the bhikṣus ordained him and conferred full ordination upon him, just as described above.
The dragon’s dharma is such that it cannot transform its body at two times: when engaging in sexual desire and when sleeping.
Later, while in deep sleep, his body filled an entire hall and the sound of his breathing was like the roar of thunder, disturbing the bhikṣus as they sat in meditation; they all went out to look.
Upon hearing the sound of human voices, he immediately awoke and resumed his form as a bhikṣu, sitting cross-legged;
they called for him to open the door, and he opened it at once. The bhikṣus asked, "Who are you?"
He replied, “I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas.
He spoke again:
"Do not speak falsely!
The transformed bhikṣu then answered truthfully.
The bhikṣus, not knowing what to do, reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Animals do not take birth within my Dharma; they should not be granted the going-forth or the full ordination. If they have already received the full ordination, they should be expelled."
"From now on, when receiving the precepts, those who do not know one another should observe each other for seven days.

At that time, the bhikṣus ordained eunuchs and conferred upon them full ordination; they then called upon the śrāmaṇeras and gardeners to engage in unchaste conduct with them, and when they went outside and encountered others, they did likewise.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled them, saying:
"The Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ordain eunuchs; they must surely engage in impure acts together.
There are those among these people who should not be ordained and those who cannot be ordained!"
...up to: "If one has already received full ordination (upasampadā), they should be expelled; this is also as explained above.
When receiving full ordination, one should first ask: 'Are you a man?'"
The same applies to those with both sexual organs.
At that time, there was a family that had been harmed by non-human beings, and only the head of the household remained. He thought to himself:
"I am now destitute and starving; what means should I employ to save my life?"

"Those śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, obtain much clothing, food, medicine for illness, and medical supplies; I shall now shave my own head, don the kāṣāya robe, and remain at home, constantly going to the monastery to eat according to the order of the seats."
Having thought this, he immediately shaved his own head and became a bhikṣu. He went to where the bhikṣus resided to seek alms.
All the bhikṣus accepted his prostrations, and he likewise prostrated to them.
The bhikṣus asked:
"For what reason do you pay homage to others and receive their homage?
How many years of seniority do you have?"
"When did you receive the precepts?
Who were your Upādhyāya and Ācārya? He replied:
"I have shaved my head and donned the dharma robes myself; I have no preceptor and no date for receiving the precepts.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"If one shaves their own head and claims to be a bhikṣu, they are not born into my Dharma; they should not be granted the going forth or the full ordination. If they have already received the full ordination, they should be expelled."
At that time, a monk named Nigaṇṭha, who had been a disciple of Bānaṇḍa and had previously left the religious life, later returned to seek ordination again.
The monks did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"One who abandons internal dharmas and follows external paths does not take birth within my Dharma; they should not be granted ordination or the full precepts (upasampadā). If they have already received the full precepts, they should be expelled."
At that time, Sundarananda Vatsiputra did not relinquish his precepts and committed sexual misconduct; he later confessed his transgression himself.
The bhikṣus, not knowing what to do, reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"If one confesses of their own accord that they have committed an offense bordering on a pārājika, they shall not take root within my Dharma; they should not be granted full ordination, and if they have already received full ordination, they should be expelled."
"When receiving the precepts, one should ask:
'Have you previously left the household life to purely cultivate the Brahma-faring?

At that time, the bhikṣus lived without receiving formal dependence (niśraya) and lacked anyone to instruct them; being foolish, ignorant, and lacking knowledge, they were unable to train in the precepts."
The elder bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should accept dependence (niśraya). If one stays for even a single night without accepting dependence, one is not permitted to drink water within the monastery grounds."
"If one drinks it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Since the Buddha would not permit him to remain without receiving formal dependence (*niśraya*), the bhikṣu did not dare to stay within the monastery grounds any longer.
At that time, another bhikṣu, seeking a place to dwell, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha asked,
"From where have you come? He replied:
"From such-and-such a place.
He asked again,
"Who are the first, second, and third elders of that residence?"
He replied, "I do not know. He asked again:
“Who is the elder residing on the left and right of him?
He replied: “I do not know him either.”
He asked again,
"For what reason do you not recognize it? He replied:
"I avoided my dwelling place and did not enter among that assembly; for this reason, I did not recognize him.
He asked again:
"For what reason did you avoid your dwelling place?"

He replied, "The Buddha does not permit one who has not received formal dependence (niśraya) to do so; if one has not received dependence, he is not even permitted to drink water within the monastery grounds. For this reason, I avoid it."
The Buddha rebuked that bhikṣu in various ways:
"What you have done is contrary to the Dharma!
You should not avoid your dwelling place for the sake of receiving formal dependence!"
Having rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one receives dependence (niśraya) for the sake of avoiding staying at a residence, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

Furthermore, there were some bhikṣus traveling on the road who, upon seeing a monastery (saṃghārāma), entered to receive dependence. They encountered bhikṣus engaged in meditation or met with mutual anger, and thus were unable to receive it; because of this, they lost their companions.
Having received formal dependence (*niśraya*), he immediately departed.
The bhikṣus asked him, "For what reason did you depart immediately after receiving formal dependence? He replied:

“The Blessed One does not permit one to avoid a residence by seeking formal dependence (niśraya). Now that I see the community residing here, I dare not bypass them without having received dependence; furthermore, I must keep pace with my companions, and for these reasons, I am departing.”
Those who had lost their companions encountered bandits on the road.
The elder bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I allow one to stay for a single night without receiving formal dependence (niśraya)."
"Although he stayed for one night, there were still various difficulties.
He reported this again to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit staying without receiving formal dependence (niśraya) for up to six nights."
Furthermore, there were monks who stayed for more than six nights without receiving formal reliance (*niśraya*). They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I do not permit staying for more than six nights!"
"To do so is an *dukkaṭa* offense.
At that time, the bhikṣus were indiscriminately acting as preceptors for others and were indiscriminately relying on others as their preceptors.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“None of you should act in this way!
You should rely upon an elder bhikṣu who is in accordance with the Dharma and is well-able to provide instruction and admonition.

If a person receiving reliance intends to move to another location, they must first ask their upādhyāya and ācārya; only after knowing that there is someone there upon whom they can rely should they go.”
There were some disciples who took their leave of their preceptors (upādhyāya) and instructors (ācārya) at the very moment they were about to depart.
The Buddha said:
"I do not permit taking leave at the last moment; one must first inform the teacher two or three days in advance."
The preceptor should deliberate upon the destination; he may permit the departure only if there is someone available to rely upon.
Upon arriving at that residence, he should first pay homage to the stūpa, then pay homage to the senior monks (upādhyāya), request a dwelling, and thereafter seek formal reliance (niśraya).
The bhikṣu acting as the preceptor for dependence should ask: "Who are your upādhyāya and ācārya?
Where did you previously reside?"
"What sutra do you recite?
If the answer is in accordance with the Dharma, one should grant them formal reliance (*niśraya*);
if it is not in accordance with the Dharma, one should say to them:
"If you do not know me and I do not know you, you may go to where you know [your teacher] and seek dependence there.
If one has doubts, one should say:
"Wait a moment."

The person receiving dependence should stay for a short while, up to six nights, observing [the preceptor]. If he is satisfied, one should grant the dependence; if he is not satisfied, one should speak as stated above.
Furthermore, there was a sick bhikṣu who sought formal reliance (niśraya). That bhikṣu thought to himself:
"The Buddha has taught that a bhikṣu should look after his disciples in such and such a manner."
"Now this man is ill; I cannot look after him," he said, and thus refused to grant him formal reliance (*niśraya*).
The sick bhikṣu did not know what to do and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "From now on, it is permitted not to receive formal dependence (*niśraya*) during times of illness; one shall receive it only after the illness has been cured.
Furthermore, there was a monk who was nursing a patient and sought formal dependence from him, whereupon that monk said to him:
“A Buddhist bhikṣu should regard his upādhyāya and ācārya in such and such a manner.
Since you are currently attending to the sick, we cannot grant you formal reliance (niśraya).”
The attending bhikṣu, being unable to find a preceptor (niśraya), felt shame and abandoned the patient to go seek one.
Consequently, the patient was left without a caregiver; his condition either worsened or he passed away.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I allow a monk who is tending to the sick not to receive formal dependence (*niśraya*) until the patient has recovered; only then shall he receive it.

Furthermore, there were monks who sought formal dependence at places where they had attained the fruits of the path by practicing as they pleased, but the resident monks did not grant it, and consequently, those monks lost their attainment of the fruits of the path.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If it is a place where one practices the Path according to one's inclinations and attains the fruits of the Path, and there is no one to serve as one's formal preceptor (niśraya), you are permitted to mentally rely upon the senior monks (sthavira) or those equal to seniors within that community, dwelling with them while honoring them as if they were teachers."

At that time, the preceptors (*ācārya*) of the bhikṣus had either passed away, ceased their monastic practice, traveled far away, become followers of external paths, or gone outside the boundary; [the bhikṣus] did not know whether they had lost their formal reliance (*niśraya*).
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There are eight ways in which one loses their *niśraya* (preceptor):
if the preceptor travels far away, if he leaves the monastic life, if he dies, or if he becomes a follower of a non-Buddhist path;..."
If he sees his former preceptor,
or if the teacher upon whom he relies says:
"Go once more to such-and-such a person to receive formal reliance (niśraya)."
If the teacher upon whom one relies goes beyond the boundary and stays overnight;
or if [the student] has completed five years and possesses intelligence and eloquence by the time the dawn appears—
these are the eight cases in which the reliance is lost.
At that time, the bhikṣus divided the offerings for the rainy season retreat equally with the śrāmaṇeras, whereupon the śrāmaṇeras failed to show respect toward the Saṃgha.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One portion should be divided and given to three śrāmaṇeras."
The śrāmaṇera still did not show respect, so they reported this again to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "He should be punished!
When the bhikṣus punished the śrāmaṇera without first consulting his preceptor, the preceptor was displeased.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should speak to his preceptor.
The preceptor then provided unlawful assistance to the śrāmaṇera, and they reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
“The teacher should not unrighteously assist a śrāmaṇera.
Furthermore, there was another śrāmaṇera whom the Saṃgha punished by cutting off his food.
Later, when the host invited the Saṃgha for a meal, the bhikṣus went and sat down in order, but the host did not serve the food.
The bhikṣus said, "The time for the meal has already arrived; why do you not descend to eat? He replied:
"Let the Saṃgha assemble!
The bhikṣus replied,
"The Saṃgha has assembled!"
The host said, "The śrāmaṇera for whom I intended to provide offerings has not yet arrived. The bhikṣus said:
“He cannot come! He asked, “Why not?”
He replied,
"The Sangha has imposed a penalty of withholding food. The host said:
"The remaining punishments are not few; how can you bear to cut off his food?
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "One should not cut off his food."

"He should be punished by being made to sweep the ground, remove filth, carry stones, repair the walking path (caṅkrama), and construct stairways; he should be punished with various tasks such as these.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose male organ disappeared and whose female organ appeared.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"One should receive the precepts by means of this very [ceremony], request a teacher by means of this very [ceremony], and go to the dwelling place of the bhikṣuṇīs according to one's age to abide by the dharma of the bhikṣuṇīs."
If one has previously committed an offense shared with bhikṣuṇīs, one should repent before the bhikṣuṇīs;
if one has previously committed an unshared offense, there is no further repentance.
The same applies when a bhikṣuṇī’s sexual organs undergo a transformation.
There was a śikṣamāṇā whose sexual organs changed; not knowing what to do, she reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"She should be ordained immediately with these very [organs]. If she has reached twenty years of age, she shall receive full ordination (upasampadā) from a community of ten bhikṣus."
"If one has not yet reached twenty years of age, they are a śrāmaṇera.
It is the same for a śrāmaṇerī.
A certain śrāmaṇera underwent a change of gender and did not know what to do; he reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"One should be ordained immediately with this very [precept]. If she has reached the required age, she should be granted the two-year precept; she shall receive the two-year precept within the community of bhikṣuṇīs.
If she has not yet reached the required age, she should not be granted the two-year precept, and remains a śrāmaṇerī."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, being consumed by the fire of desire and unable to endure it, cut off his own genitals.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha rebuked him, saying: "You foolish man!
"One should not cut where it should not be cut, yet one does not cut where it should be cut!
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one cuts the head or half [of the garment], it is a duṣkṛta offense."
If both are cut off, it is a sthūlātyaya;
if one testicle is removed, it is a sthūlātyaya;
if both testicles are removed, he should be expelled from the community.
"If one has been bitten by a wild beast, or harmed by an enemy, or has undergone self-mutilation, or is no longer capable of male function, such persons should all be expelled.
At that time, the bhikṣus ordained those whose hands and feet had been severed and conferred full ordination upon them. When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled them, saying:
"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas have no standard for whom may be ordained and whom may not!"
"There is no conduct of a śramaṇa!
You have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should not ordain such persons!
Even if one were to ordain them, it would merely be called 'receiving the full precepts' [in name only];"
If one acts as a preceptor for such a person, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

From this day forward, those who have had their hands cut off, their feet cut off, both hands and feet cut off, their ears cut off, their noses cut off, both ears and noses cut off, their fingers cut off, the head of their male organ cut off, whose eyes have been gouged out, who have been whipped until their auspicious marks were ruined, who have encountered legal punishment, who are hunchbacked or lame, who have lost their voices, who have goiters internally or externally, whose bodies are curved inward, whose bodies are curved outward, whose bodies are curved both inward and outward, who have squinting eyes, whose one arm is excessively long, whose one arm is excessively short, who are left-handed, who are mute, deaf, blind, suffering from consumption, insane, extremely old, lacking dignified deportment, extremely ugly, or who bring disgrace upon the Saṃgha—none of those belonging to such categories may be ordained.
"If one has already crossed over [the threshold], they are said to have received full ordination (*upasampadā*), as explained above.
The monks ordained those who stammered; the Buddha said:
"One should not ordain those who stammer and grant them full ordination."
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who conferred the full ordination (upasampadā) upon others without first having them receive the śrāmaṇera precepts;
there were bhikṣus who conferred the full ordination without having requested a preceptor (upādhyāya);
and there were bhikṣus who conferred the full ordination without the candidates having formally requested it.
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who conferred full ordination upon naked persons;
there were also bhikṣus who conferred full ordination upon those who did not possess robes and bowls.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"None of these should be done!
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who borrowed another's robes and bowl to receive full ordination; once he had received full ordination, the other bhikṣus said to him:
"Put on your robes and take up your bowl; let us go together for alms.
He replied, "I have no robes or bowl."
The bhikṣus asked:
"Has the Buddha not prohibited one who lacks robes and bowl from receiving full ordination?
They replied:
"The Buddha has prescribed:
'I shall accept another's robe and bowl on loan.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha."
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:

"I allow that those who wish to receive the precepts be led outside the ordination platform (*sīmāmaṇḍala*) to a place where they can see but cannot hear the words spoken; meanwhile, ten members of the assembly should be invited onto the ordination platform."
The Upādhyāya should say to the Karmavācanā-officiant: "Venerable One!
Now perform the karmavācanā."
Furthermore, one should say to the preceptor:
"Venerable Sir!
I now receive the *karmavācanā*."
The *karmavācanā* master should address the Saṃgha in this way:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
So-and-so seeks to receive full ordination from So-and-so; So-and-so shall serve as the preceptor."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall announce this.
Then the preceptor should rise from his seat, go before the upādhyāya, and ask him:
"Have you already delivered this person?
If he says they have not been delivered, one should say: "Deliver them first.
If he says they have been delivered, one should ask:
"Have you already appointed a preceptor?
If he says he has not, one should tell him to first appoint one;
if he says he has already appointed one, one should ask the disciple:
"Are your robes and bowl complete?
If he says they are not complete, one should tell him to first provide himself with robes and a bowl;
if he says they are already complete, one should ask:
"Is this your own, or did you borrow it from someone?
If he says he borrowed it from someone, one should tell him that he must have his owner relinquish it;
if he says it is his own, one should then go to comfort the person who wishes to receive the precepts and say:
"Do not be afraid; in a moment, I shall take you and place you in a high and secure location!
"If one does not previously know another, one should not confer full ordination upon them when obscured by clouds and mist."
When a teacher causes [a student] to put on the robes, he should look closely and in accordance with the Dharma to see whether there is any serious illness;
he should further ask:
"Of your three robes, which one is the saṃghāṭī?"
"What is the uttarāsaṅga? What is the antaravāsaka?
If he does not know, one should say:
"This is the saṃghāṭī, this is the uttarāsaṅga, and this is the antarvāsaka.
He should then be given the three robes and the bowl.
Furthermore, he should be told:
"Listen, [Name]! Now is the time for truthful speech. I shall now question you; if it is true, speak truly; if it is not true, speak untruly.
People have such illnesses as these:"
"Leprosy, white leprosy, carbuncles, consumption, insanity, hemorrhoids, abscesses, and scrofula—
do you have any of these? If he says he has none, one should ask again:
"Have you not incurred debts to others?
Are you not a government official?
Are you not a slave?"
Are you a man? Are you a human being?
Have you reached the age of twenty?
Are your robes and bowl complete?
Have you received the precepts from your preceptor? What is your name?
"What is the master’s name?

At that time, the bhikṣus performed the *poṣadha* in the open air and were distressed by mosquitoes, gadflies, wind, rain, and dust.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Permission is granted to construct a *poṣadha* hall.
However, that *poṣadha* hall had no floor covering, and it soiled the feet of the bhikṣus; they washed them repeatedly and fell ill.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should smear the ground with mud, cleaning and preparing it well;
furthermore, it is permitted to spread ten kinds of garments as well as soft grasses such as *babhru*.
Since the Buddha has permitted the spreading of garments, [the monks] then spread brocade upon the ground."
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled them, saying,
"These śramaṇas are just like the king’s ministers!
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not walk upon a brocade rug!
At that time, the bhikṣus scattered flowers over the bhikṣu on the high seat, and the laypeople criticized and reviled them, saying:
"They are just like kings and great ministers!"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"One should not do so! Furthermore,
there were some laypeople who, for the sake of making offerings to the Dharma, wished to scatter flowers upon the bhikṣus seated on high thrones.
The bhikṣus did not permit it, whereupon he spoke with anger and reproach, saying:
"These bhikṣus are unworthy of receiving offerings!
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The laypeople may scatter flowers as they please; however, if they fall upon the head or the robes of a bhikṣu, he should brush them away, though there is no fault if they fall upon a high seat.
At that time, the laypeople, having heard the Dharma, were filled with joy and wished to make offerings.
The bhikṣus feared they would fall into the state of being hired laborers and did not dare accept [the offerings] many times.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to receive them as an offering for the Dharma."
At that time, the bhikṣus stopped preaching after a short while, whereupon the devas and spirits, thinking the discourse was finished, departed.
After a brief moment they preached again, and those beings returned once more; this happened not just once, until they spoke with resentment, saying:
"These bhikṣus preach without restraint, like children at play!"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“One should set a time limit for preaching the Dharma; when the preaching of the Dharma is finished, one should recite a benediction.
At that time, Kapphiṇa was staying on Mount Isigili and had this thought:
"Should I now go to the assembly of the Sangha for the *poṣadha*?
Then he thought again: "I am always pure; why must I go?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing his thoughts, vanished from Rājagṛha and reappeared before him. He took a seat and said to him:
"Do not harbor such a thought as this:
'I am always pure; why should I go to the poṣadha again?'"
"If you do not go, and if you do not respect the *poṣadha*, who then shall respect it?

Having thus instructed them, the World-Honored One immediately vanished from that place and appeared in Rājagṛha. On this matter, he assembled the community of bhikṣus and recounted Kapphiṇa’s thoughts as well as his own instructions, declaring to the bhikṣus:
"I now authorize the bhikṣus to perform the *poṣadha* in harmony. If one does not attend, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
A single learned Dharma-preacher monk—whether he be a senior elder or one equal to a senior elder—should speak as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
Today is the fifteenth day for the *poṣadha* recitation of the precepts; let the Sangha perform the *poṣadha* recitation with a unified mind."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience.
This is the motion. "Venerable sirs!
Now, for the Poṣadha ceremony, the Prātimokṣa is being recited; all should listen together and reflect upon it well.
If you have any offenses, you should disclose them; those who are without offense should remain silent.
By remaining silent, you should know that I and the venerable ones are pure;
as with noble silence, so it is for me and the venerable ones.

If a bhikṣu, within such an assembly, remains silent even after being exhorted three times, yet remembers having committed an offense and does not disclose it, he incurs the offense of intentional lying.
Therefore, regarding the offense of false speech, the Buddha has declared it a dharma that obstructs the Path;
one who reveals it shall attain peace and happiness. In this context, "Prātimokṣa" means:
because these precepts protect the sense faculties, increase wholesome dharmas, and serve as the foremost gateway to all wholesome dharmas, they are called Prātimokṣa.
Furthermore, when these rules of training are enumerated and their names and phrases are analyzed, they are collectively called the *Prātimokṣa*.
The bhikṣus did not know how many kinds of *poṣadha* there should be, so they informed the Buddha about this. The Buddha said:
"There are five kinds of *poṣadha*:"
1. Mental recollection and verbal declaration;
2. Declaring purity before others;
3. Expansive and abbreviated recitation of the precepts.
"Fourth, the *pravāraṇā* poṣadha;
fifth, the harmonious (*saṃgha-sāmagrī*) poṣadha.
The bhikṣus did not know how many kinds of recitation of the precepts (*śīla-vinaya*) should be performed, and they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"There are five ways of reciting the *Poṣadha*:
first, having recited the *Śikṣāpada-anuśaṃsā*, one says, 'The rest is as the Saṃgha has regularly heard.'"
2. Having recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa and the four *pārājika* rules, one says, "The remainder is as is regularly heard from the Saṃgha.
3. Having recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa up to the thirteen [saṃghāvaśeṣa] rules, one says, "The remainder is as is regularly heard from the Saṃgha.
4. Having recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa up to the two *aniyata* rules, one says, "The remainder is as is regularly heard from the Saṃgha."
5. "The detailed exposition.
The bhikṣus did not know how many kinds of upholders of the Vinaya there were, so they informed the Buddha about this.
The Buddha said:
“There are five kinds of upholders of the Vinaya,” as previously stated.
“There are five kinds of merit for a bhikṣu who upholds the Vinaya.”
It is as previously stated.
A bhikṣu who upholds the Vinaya has seven kinds of suitability:
first, being well-versed in all dharmas;
2. Being able to discern what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma;
3. Skillfully discerning the Vinaya;
4. Skillfully upholding the Teacher’s instructions.
Fifth, when arriving in other places, one’s speech is fearless;
sixth, one abides in the Vinaya oneself;
seventh, one knows the common and uncommon precepts.
Furthermore, there are seven appropriatenesses:
first, abiding in the precepts oneself, perfecting one's deportment, and being cautious and fearful of even minor transgressions;
second, being extensively learned and able to uphold the teachings spoken by the Buddha.
Third, reciting the precepts of the two divisions;
fourth, knowing what constitutes an offense;
fifth, knowing what does not constitute an offense.
Sixth, knowing how to repent;
seventh, knowing when not to repent.
Furthermore, there are seven appropriatenesses:
Three are as above;
fourth, not following after craving;
fifth, not following after anger.
Sixth, not following delusion;
seventh, not following fear.
At that time, the bhikṣus within the boundary performed the *poṣadha* separately as a distinct assembly, which was contrary to the Dharma.
Furthermore, there is a harmonious *poṣadha* that is not in accordance with the Dharma;
there is a *poṣadha* in accordance with the Dharma performed by a separate assembly;
and there is a *poṣadha* in accordance with the Dharma performed by a harmonious assembly.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The first three *poṣadha* ceremonies were faulty; the *karmavācanā* was not accomplished, and they committed a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The last *poṣadha* ceremony was faultless; the *karmavācanā* was accomplished, and there was no offense."
At that time, King Bimbisāra established a five-year intercalary cycle, which all the non-Buddhists, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas followed and adopted; however, the bhikṣus alone were unwilling to use it.
The ministers and the people all reviled them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, who dwell within the king's realm, do not employ the king’s intercalary month.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should comply with the laws of the king.
The bhikṣus did not know how to comply with the laws of the king, so they reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Let us hold the *poṣadha* ceremony one night less frequently.
The bhikṣus then began to regularly hold the *poṣadha* ceremony one night less frequently. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not regularly hold the *poṣadha* ceremony one night less frequently!"
"Listen to three [days] and omit one; thus, over five years, there will be an excess of one month, in order to conform to the royal intercalary month.

At that time, when the bhikṣus went to various places for the uposatha on the day of the precept recitation, they encountered wild fires, floods, or August bandits; they faced dangers to their holy life (*brahmacarya*), dangers to their robes and bowls, and dangers to their lives.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"On the day of the *poṣadha*, one should not go elsewhere to perform the *poṣadha*; those who go commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.

It is permitted that at the place where you reside, if there is level ground, or soft grass, or a large tree, or a large flat rock, you should perform a formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to designate it as a *poṣadha* site."
A bhikṣu announced: “Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
We now demarcate this place as a site for the poṣadha.”
"If it is the time for the Sangha and the Sangha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus:
'Venerable Sangha, please listen!'"
Now this place is designated as the site for the *poṣadha*.
Which elders consent? Those who consent remain silent;
those who do not consent speak.
The Sangha has completed the formal act of designating the place for the Poṣadha;
because the Sangha consents by remaining silent,
this matter is thus upheld.
The bhikṣus performed the poṣadha ceremony in the open air and were distressed by wind, rain, mosquitoes, and gadflies.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"I allow you to designate a central room that is convenient for coming and going, and to formally establish it as a poṣadha hall through the aforementioned *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*."

The bhikṣus again wished to perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to designate many rooms as places for the *poṣadha* ceremony. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to do so.
The bhikṣus then again disputed over the priority [of the designation], and they reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted to perform the *poṣadha* in many rooms where the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) has not been heard.
There were some lay devotees who came into the monastic quarters and said to the bhikṣus:
"If you perform the *poṣadha* in the rooms we have built for you, we shall provide morning and evening meals, *tarpaṇa*, foot ointment, body ointment, and oil for lighting lamps."
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"If the World-Honored One would permit us to perform the *kaṭhina* ceremony in many rooms as places for the *poṣadha*, we would not lose this offering."
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to perform the *karmavācanā* for many rooms and hold the *poṣadha* in succession therein.
Because the rooms were small and could not accommodate everyone, they reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen from under the eaves at the front or back, or sit in the courtyard.
When the bhikṣus heard the sound but could not understand the words, they feared that the poṣadha would not be accomplished.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one is present during the *poṣadha*, one is said to have performed the *poṣadha*.
However, when the monks were to perform the *poṣadha*, they were unwilling to assemble at the appointed time, thereby neglecting their seated meditation and the practice of the Path.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should announce that the time has come by striking a ghaṇṭā, beating a drum, or blowing a conch.
The bhikṣus then fashioned drums of gold and silver and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should use copper, iron, tile, or wood, and place a leather crown upon the head.
