Not knowing who should strike it, they reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"A śrāmaṇera or a park-keeper should be made to strike it."
He struck it many times, and because of this, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "It should be struck three times.

After the striking was finished, he hung it in the central courtyard. When outsiders came and struck it repeatedly, the bhikṣus thought it was the time for monastic business and all went out, neglecting their practice of the Path.
Sometimes it rained so heavily that they made no sound.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"You should move them to a secluded spot beneath the eaves."
A visiting śrāmaṇera was next to strike [the drum], but not knowing the proper place, he missed the appointed time.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The resident monks should strike it; you are permitted to keep a communal drum, a private drum, a drum for the Saṃgha of the four directions, and one reserve drum."
The bhikṣus again fashioned conchs out of gold and silver and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should blow a sea conch, or one made from horn.
A śrāmaṇera or a park-keeper may blow it; even the provision of a single conch for reserve is as previously explained."
The bhikṣus did not know with what kind of wood to make the ghaṇṭā (wooden clapper), so they informed the Buddha about this. The Buddha said:
"With the exception of lacquer trees and poisonous trees, you are permitted to make it from any other wood that produces a clear sound."
"If there is no śrāmaṇera, a bhikṣu may also strike [the gong].
The rest is as above.
The bhikṣus did not know who should announce that "the time has arrived" three times; they reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Let the śrāmaṇeras and the gardeners hear it.
Since the monks' residence was large and they could not all hear it, they informed the Buddha of this matter.
The Buddha said, "One should ascend to a high place and proclaim it."
The bhikṣus did not know whether [the assembly] had gathered or had not yet gathered; they reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The bhikṣus sitting nearby should speak to one another so that they may know."
Later, some visiting bhikṣus arrived and did not know [the number]; they reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should count them.
The bhikṣus counted them again but forgot once more; they reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should distribute the voting sticks (*śalākā*) and collect them to count.
When one person distributed them and collected them himself, they became disordered.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One person should be specifically appointed to collect them.
The bhikṣus then made tally-sticks out of gold and silver and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"They should be made of copper, iron, ivory, horn, bone, bamboo, or wood, excluding trees that are poisonous or lacquered."
Some bhikṣus made them too short and some made them too long. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If they are short, they should be lengthened by five finger-breadths;
if they are long, they should be shortened by one cubit (one extended hand)."
The bhikṣus made [the robes] either coarse or fine, and they reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Coarse [robes] shall not exceed the thickness of a small finger, and fine [robes] shall not be less than that of a *māṣa*."
"It should be lacquered, placed in a tube, and suspended in the *poṣadha* hall.

The bhikṣus did not know who should distribute the voting sticks (*śalākā*), so they informed the Buddha about this. The Buddha said, "A bhikṣu of the lowest seat (*avarabhūmikabhikṣu*) should be made to distribute them."
A junior bhikṣu did not know how to proceed, so he informed the Buddha about this. The Buddha said, "One who knows should take [the voting sticks].
Another bhikṣu then threw the voting sticks to the Saṃgha; he informed the Buddha about this, and the Buddha said:
"One should hand it over with the hands.
Having received it, they did not count it; having counted it, they did not announce it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Having collected them, you should count them; having counted them, you should announce them. The announcement should be made as follows:"
"There are so many bhikṣus, so many śrāmaṇeras, and in total, so many people who have left the household life.
At that time, there was a layperson (avadātavasana) listening to the poṣadha; later, when the bhikṣus committed an offense, the layperson exposed it.
They reported this to the Buddha, who said:
"One should not allow laypeople to listen, and the same applies to śrāmaṇeras.
Although the bhikṣus sent the śrāmaṇeras to a place where they could not be seen, they were still able to hear.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"You should place them in a place where they cannot see or hear.
Yet there were some śrāmaṇeras who, knowing that it was time for the poṣadha, entered beneath the beds in advance and were still able to hear the precepts being recited.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should look under the bed and illuminate it thoroughly with fire.
When the fire illuminated the room, it caused smoke to fill the house or burned the floor coverings. They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should make oil lamps and lamp bases; these may be kept both by the Sangha and as private property.
The bhikṣus then made them out of gold and silver. They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"One should use copper, iron, clay, or wood."

There were some laypeople who, having completed the construction of a new house, invited the bhikṣus to first perform the *poṣadha* ceremony and preach the Dharma within it, so that they might enter the residence to make offerings.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I permit you to receive [the invitation].

Furthermore, there were households of laypeople who were being harassed by non-human spirits; they invited the bhikṣus to perform the *poṣadha* ceremony and preach the Dharma within their homes, thereby providing offerings for their peace and well-being.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to accept it!"
There was a householder who was walking with sugarcane, and the bhikṣus did not dare to accept it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to accept it!"
Some laypeople asked the bhikṣus,
"What day is it today?
The bhikṣus did not know, and they consequently spoke with derision and reproach:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not even know the days of the month, let alone the profound principles.
Having reported this to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"If you wish to go to the home of a layperson, you should first ask your teacher about the date."
"If the teacher does not know, you should ask another person.

At that time, on the day of the *poṣadha*, several lay devotees (*gṛhapati*) brought timely food, timely drinks, seven-day medicines, and lifetime medicines to the monastery to make offerings; they wished to listen to the Dharma and receive the eightfold precepts.
The bhikṣus paid them no attention at all, so [the visitors] became angry and took their belongings back home.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The senior bhikṣu should instruct the junior bhikṣus to sweep the ground, fetch water, and have a lay attendant (karmadāna) prepare vessels to hold the items they have brought."
The bhikṣus did not give any food at all to the guests; the guests then criticized and reviled them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, always praise the practice of giving, yet they only receive the gifts of others without giving anything to others."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"One should give food to the guest. Once it was given,
he placed it directly into the guest's hand without providing a vessel, whereupon the guest again criticized and rebuked him, saying:
"The bhikṣus have treated me like a child.
When this was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"One should provide them with vessels for their food."
When the meal is finished, the senior monk or those equal to the senior monk shall preach the Dharma and offer a prayer of blessing.
After the guests have departed, if there are four or more monks, they should perform the *poṣadha* in full detail.
If there are two or three people, they should face one another and speak these words of purification:
"Today is the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the fortnight for the Saṃgha’s poṣadha.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], am pure; Venerable One, please bear this in mind!"
Thus he should say this three times.
If one person is present, they should wait a short while; if someone else arrives, they may perform the *poṣadha* together.
If no one else arrives, one should bare the right shoulder, kneel on the right knee with palms joined, and recite these words aloud while reflecting in the mind:
"Today is the fourteenth or fifteenth day; the community of monks performs the *poṣadha*. I now accept the *poṣadha* in my mind.
Thus he says three times.
He then addresses the bhikṣus:
"This is the *poṣadha* rule; from now on, you should observe it thus for as long as life lasts. Otherwise, there is an *āpatti* of *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, some lay followers entered the monastery and asked the bhikṣus, "How many people are in the Saṃgha?"
He replied, "There are so many monks. The other said:
"We invite the Saṃgha for tomorrow's meal.
When the bhikṣus from the surrounding areas heard this, they all went there the following day; however, the seating was insufficient and the food and drink were also scant.
The bhikṣus said, "You have invited the Saṃgha; why do you not give us food? They replied:
"Yesterday I asked the monks and provided food according to their number;
yet you did not previously accept my invitation but instead demanded it by force. To eat without being invited is worse than the practices of the non-Buddhists."
"These people have no conduct worthy of a śramaṇa; they destroy the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should not go unless invited; to go [uninvited] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who had business that required them to attend a gathering, yet when the day came for them to go to the house where they were invited, they felt ashamed and did not dare to go.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"If it is not for the sake of food, you are permitted to go. At that time,
there was a layperson who invited the Sangha for a meal, and some visiting bhikṣus arrived.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"You should say to the host: "
"May a visiting bhikṣu be permitted to enter?
If he is permitted to enter, that is well;
if not permitted, one should further say:
"Give us our share of the food; we shall eat it together with you on equal terms.
If they obtain it, that is well;
if not, each should receive their portion in a bowl and go outside to eat together. If they obtain it there, that is well.
"If you still cannot obtain any, and there is food within the monastery, you should take it and give it to them.

At that time, due to a famine, alms were difficult to obtain; monks from other places all abandoned their residences and gathered in Rājagṛha. Consequently, the monastic quarters were entirely empty and left without anyone to guard them;
the buildings and bedding were either burned by fire, soaked by water, or damaged by insects.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"In all the residences in the vicinity of Rājagṛha, one should first perform the formal act of two announcements (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to relinquish the boundaries as previously described. Thereafter, one should perform the formal act of two announcements to collectively establish a single great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) as previously described, so that the bhikṣus need not relinquish their original residences and yet may receive their share of offerings."
Later, when that other place had once again become prosperous and pleasant, they longed to see the bhikṣu and sent a messenger to say:
"We pray that you will travel among us; we shall provide you with food and clothing."
At that time, King Bimbisāra also wished for the bhikṣus to travel about to teach and transform others, and he said to them:
"I pray that you will travel; if there should be any lack or deficiency, I shall order the local authorities to provide whatever is required."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"First, perform the two-fold proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) as previously described to relinquish the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) of Rājagṛha; thereafter, each may, according to his own wish, proclaim the boundary markers anew and re-establish a small boundary (kṣudra-sīmā)."
There were forest-dwelling (*āraṇyaka*) bhikṣus who did not know how far their own territory (*sīmā*) should extend. They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"The natural boundary (*prakṛtisīmā*) extends two *krośas* from one's person."
"If one establishes a boundary, it may be according to its distance, whether far or near.
At that time, the bhikṣus established a boundless boundary. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one establishes a boundless boundary, the establishment of the boundary is not valid; whoever does so commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!"

The bhikṣus again established boundaries of twelve yojanas or ten yojanas; when it was time for the recitation of the precepts, they had to travel for four or five days to reach them, during which they might encounter wild fires, violent floods, or bandits who plundered them, thereby facing hardships regarding the holy life, hardships regarding robes and bowls, and even threats to their lives.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one establishes a boundary of twelve yojanas or ten yojanas, the establishment of the boundary is not valid; those who do so commit a *duṣkṛta* offense."
"Now, I permit [the boundary] to extend at most three yojanas.
At that time, the bhikṣus established boundaries without proclaiming the characteristics of the four directions. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If the characteristics of the boundary are not proclaimed, the establishment of the boundary is not valid; one who violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense!"
At that time, the bhikṣus established the boundaries (sīmā) using sentient beings or smoke and fire as their markers; they either joined two boundaries together or allowed two boundaries to overlap.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"In all such cases, the establishment of the boundary is invalid. One who violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
There were two monasteries where the bhikṣus wished to perform the *poṣadha* together, receive offerings together, and establish a boundary together.
They informed the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to each perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to dissolve their original boundaries, and then assemble together to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to establish a common boundary."
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who wished to dwell together, perform the poṣadha together, yet receive offerings separately and establish boundaries separately.
They informed the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to dissolve the original boundary first, and only then assemble to establish a new one."
Furthermore, there were certain bhikṣus who wished to dwell together and receive offerings together, yet perform the poṣadha and establish boundaries separately.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This should not be done; one who violates this commits a sthūlātyaya offense."

Furthermore, there was another residence where the bhikṣus wished to establish separate dwellings, separate poṣadha ceremonies, and separate boundaries for receiving offerings. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“I allow you to first dissolve the original boundary, and then each establish a new one.”

Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who wished to establish separate residences, perform separate poṣadha ceremonies, yet receive offerings together within a single boundary. They informed the Buddha of this matter.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to establish such a boundary."
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"No rivers, no lakes or ponds, and no oceans may be demarcated as a boundary.
If one travels upon the water, the area reached by the water sprinkled by a strong person among the assembly shall constitute the natural boundary."
The Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove.
Ājñātakauṇḍinya was on Mount Lenguoluo; on the day of the poṣadha, he would invariably manifest as a green rainbow, sitting cross-legged within it, and come to where the Buddha was.
Many people came to look at him; for this reason, he subsequently had to go out on foot.
His rag-robe was heavy, and he was utterly exhausted by the journey. The bhikṣus thought to themselves:

"If the World-Honored One would allow the bhikṣus to establish an 'unclothing-boundary' (a-kāṣāyī-sīmā) within a village or the precincts of a village, it would not cause the Elder to be so exhausted."
They reported this to the Buddha.
After the Buddha had praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"I now authorize the bhikṣus to establish, within a village or its precincts, a 'boundary for not losing robes' (*acīvarāpattika-sīmā*) by means of a formal motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*)."
A single bhikṣu should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Within this boundary, whether it be the village or the village precinct, where there is common residence, common *poṣadha*, and common receipt of offerings, we now establish this as a 'non-loss-of-clothing' boundary (*akālacīvara-sīmā*)."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus:
'Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!'"

In this place of boundary demarcation, whether it be within a village or the village boundary, where there is communal residence, communal *poṣadha*, and communal receipt of offerings, we now demarcate this as an *acīvarāpatti* (non-forfeiture of robes) boundary.
"Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has finished establishing the 'boundary for not losing one's robe'."
"Because the Saṃgha remains silent,
this matter is thus upheld. At that time,
the bhikṣus first established the *acīvarāsaṃsarga-sīmā* (the boundary for not losing one's robes) and subsequently established the *mahāsīmā* (the great boundary).
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should first establish the great boundary (mahā-sīmā), and afterwards, based upon it, establish the 'not losing one's robe' boundary (a-cīvara-apahāra-sīmā).
Thereupon, the bhikṣus established the robe boundary at all times and went about wearing coarse and tattered robes.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do so! You should resolve it by means of a formal motion and a second proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman)."
A bhikṣu announced: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
In this delimited area—whether it be within a village or the village boundary—a *acīvarāpavādana-sīmā* (robe-keeping zone) was previously established; the Saṃgha now dissolves it."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"
At this place of boundary-binding, the Sangha now releases it.
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has completed the dissolution of the previously established "not losing one's robe" boundary;
since the Sangha consents by remaining silent,
this matter is thus upheld.
At that time, the bhikṣus first dissolved the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) and afterwards dissolved the clothing boundary (cīvara-sīmā).
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should first dissolve the clothing boundary and afterwards dissolve the great boundary."
At that time, the bhikṣus lost their robes in order to protect the summer retreat, and they lost the summer retreat in order to protect their robes.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"I allow you to return and re-establish the robe-boundary."
At that time, there was a certain residence where, on the day of the *poṣadha*, a disciple took leave of his preceptor (*upādhyāya*), intending to travel to a certain place.
The preceptor did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"The preceptor should deliberate:
if there are doubts or fears regarding the road, and the preceptor permits [the disciple] to go, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
If he does not grant permission and the disciple nevertheless insists on leaving, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense for slighting his teacher.
Furthermore, even if there are no fears or terrors along the road, it may be that alms-food is difficult to obtain in that region;
or if the traveling companions are ignorant, do not recite the precepts, do not know the *poṣadha*, and do not know the *poṣadha-karman*.

If in that region there are no persons who uphold the Dharma, uphold the Vinaya, or understand the discipline; or if in that region people are fond of mutual strife and contention; or if in that region there is a schism in the Saṃgha; or if in that region one falls ill and lacks appropriate food, medicinal decoctions, bedding, or a caregiver; or if in that region clothing and food are difficult to obtain—then permission to depart is granted [in these cases], yet it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If none of these circumstances exist, permission to depart is granted without fault.

At a certain residence, on the fifteenth day, the bhikṣus gathered for the poṣadha ceremony to recite the Prātimokṣa. They requested the foremost elder to recite the precepts, but the elder said, "I have forgotten them."
From the second watch until dawn, if [the recitation] is not chanted, the *poṣadha* cannot be performed.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to appoint one bhikṣu to go to another assembly to chant the precepts—whether briefly or in full—and return by the end of the day."
"If you do not obtain [it], you should not remain in this place; to remain here constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus committed an offense but did not confess it during the *poṣadha*.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do so; one who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Again, there were bhikṣus who confessed their transgressions to those who had committed offenses. They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not do so!
There was a certain residence where, on the day of the *poṣadha*, the entire Saṃgha committed an offense.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"I allow that one bhikṣu be appointed through a formal motion and second proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) to go to another assembly to repent and become pure, while the rest of the people here repent before that bhikṣu."
If it can be obtained, that is well;
if it cannot be obtained, all [monks] should assemble in the Poṣadha hall, and one monk should announce the second *karmavācanā* as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
The Saṃgha now all possesses this offense and is unable to repent;
let us set it aside for now and repent of it later.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent.
"I declare it thus. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha now all possesses this offense, which shall later be confessed."
"Whichever elders consent, let them remain silent;
if you do not consent, please speak.
The Sangha has finished dealing with this offense."
“Since the Saṃgha remains silent,
it is thus held that this matter is settled.
Then the Poṣadha ceremony was performed.
"One should not fail to perform the *poṣadha*!
A certain sick bhikṣu committed an offense and said to another bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!..."
"I have committed an offense. He replied,
"I too have committed an offense."
He was unable to repent before he passed away.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"If the World-Honored One would allow a bhikṣu who has committed an offense to repent, this bhikṣu would not have had to die without having repented."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to confess your transgressions before a bhikṣu who has not committed the same offense; however, you must not confess before one who has committed the same offense.
There was a certain residence where the entire Saṃgha had all committed the same offense and did not know what to do. They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should also deal with the offense as prescribed above.
There was a sick bhikṣu who committed an offense and spoke to another bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!
I have committed this offense. He said:
"I too have committed this offense.
Without being able to repent for it, he passed away.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
“If the World-Honored One would allow one to confess before a bhikṣu who has committed the same offense, this bhikṣu would not have to die without having confessed.
Having reported this to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
“From now on, it is permitted for those who have committed the same offense as well as those who have not to both confess before one another.”
At a certain residence, while the bhikṣus had gathered for the uposatha and the recitation of the precepts, one bhikṣu said to the bhikṣu presiding over the recitation:
"Wait! I recall having committed an offense; I wish to confess it."
The bhikṣus rebuked him, saying:
"How can you create such an obstacle at the time of reciting the precepts?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If, while the precepts are being recited, one remembers having committed an offense, one may speak to the person sitting beside them, whether by word or by thought, saying:
'I have this offense; I shall confess it once the recitation of the precepts is finished.'"
"One should not create obstacles.
The same applies to doubt.
There was a certain residence where the bhikṣus did not know the poṣadha, nor did they know the poṣadha-karman.

When a bhikṣu who knows the Dharma, upholds the Vinaya, and understands the rules of discipline arrived, the other bhikṣus did not attend to him nor provide him with bedding and seats; that bhikṣu then departed.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should look after them well and provide them with bedding and requisites.
If you do not, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
At a certain residence, the entire Saṃgha had committed an offense, yet they did not know which category of offense it belonged to.
A bhikṣu who was learned in the Dharma, upheld the Vinaya, and understood the Vinaya-rituals arrived there. One bhikṣu among them went to him and asked:
"We have committed such and such an act; to which category of offense does this belong?"
He replied, "It is such-and-such an offense.
Then [the other] said to him:
"Regarding this residence, the entire Saṃgha has committed such-and-such an offense.
He then confesses his fault before that bhikṣu.
Having confessed, he returns and says to the other bhikṣus:
"We have previously committed such-and-such offenses; we should together repent so as not to defile our practice of the holy life and suffer for a long night."
The bhikṣus spoke with anger, saying,
"Why did you speak such words to us? They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Monks, you should confess your transgression before those monks who know the Dharma; it is not that you should not speak at all.
However, you should not approach people to speak; to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.”
At that time, Śāriputra went to the dwelling place of the group of six bhikṣus and, seeing that they were transgressing the precepts, said to them:
"Do not commit such offenses!
The group of six bhikṣus then provoked him and asked:
"What should be done? What should not be done? Thus he troubled him throughout the entire night.
Śāriputra reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha rebuked the group of six bhikṣus in various ways:
"You foolish men! An elder bhikṣu has compassionately instructed you; why do you, on the contrary, harass and provoke him throughout the entire night?"
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is not that one should not instruct; rather, one should not go about instructing others.
Only when someone has committed an offense and recognizes their own transgression should one then instruct them."

At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were traveling through the human realm, revered as teachers by the fourfold assembly, kings, ministers, śramaṇas, and brahmins. They arrived at the residence of a certain bhikṣu, where various donors, for the sake of the two of them, made offerings to the Saṃgha, providing robes and gifts for the monastery attendants;
they also received together the value of a *kṣaumapāla* (woolen garment), worth twelve thousand gold coins, which was announced three times:
"Whoever needs it, let him take it."
Since no one took it, they returned it to the donor.
At that time, the bhikṣus in the assembly gradually traveled back to where the Buddha was. As was his custom, the Buddha greeted the bhikṣus with words of comfort and then asked:
"Did Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana travel about with sufficient provisions?"
He replied, "It is very abundant!
World-Honored One!"

Furthermore, he saw another extraordinary event: the community of monks had collectively obtained a piece of *kambala* cloth worth twelve thousand gold coins. Although they called out three times to offer it to the bhikṣus, no one took it, so they returned it to the donor.
At that time, there were two mahallaka bhikṣus who, hearing this from no great distance from the Buddha, one of them said:
"Those elders are foolish!"
"We shall not only lose our own gains, but will also prevent the donors from obtaining great merit.
If I were there, I would surely take it for them.
Another person then said:
"I am the senior elder; I should take [the portion]!
Thus they fell into dispute.
Having seen this, the Buddha spoke a verse:
"You two *mahallakas*, do not remain among that assembly;
because there is no dispute here, these precious robes shall be returned to their original owners.
The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.

At that time, Upāli, together with those who upheld the Vinaya, traveled about and arrived at the dwelling place of the bhikṣus. For those for whom a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence), *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), or *adhyeṣaṇā-karman* (act of subordination) was appropriate, he performed them all;
for those for whom a *parivāsa* (probation), *mānatva* (penance), *mūlāpakarṣa* (reduction of the period), or *āvarhaṇa* (restoration) was appropriate, he performed them all.
If a boundary should be dissolved, it shall be dissolved;
if it should be established, it shall be established.
If it is appropriate to perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of instructing bhikṣuṇīs, the formal act of instruction shall be performed.
Being unable to accept the instruction and admonition, they should undergo the formal act of releasing the instruction and admonition (*an-avavāda-vinaya-karman*).
When the other monks heard of this, they thought:
"These monks who uphold the Vinaya have come; they will surely cause us much doubt and remorse."
She then took up her bedding, closed the door, and departed from that dwelling.
Furthermore, when the bhikṣuṇīs saw Upāli, they scolded him in anger, saying:
"It is because this bhikṣu constantly asks the World-Honored One whether these precepts should be observed by the two-fold saṃgha or by a single-fold saṃgha."
"The Buddha has then ordered that this be maintained by the two divisions of the Saṃgha; because of this, I have been subjected to much hardship and distress.
Among the bhikṣus whom Upāli had brought with him, there were some who returned first. After the Buddha questioned them according to his usual practice, he asked again:
"In the places where Upāli traveled, was the provision of offerings abundant?"
He replied, "It is not enough.
He asked again:
"Why is this? [The Buddha asked. They answered the Buddha in full, explaining how the bhikṣus had abandoned their dwellings and how the bhikṣuṇīs had reviled them.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned those bhikṣus:
"Is it truly so for you? They replied, "It is truly so."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked them in various ways: “You are all foolish!
"If you do not show respect to a bhikṣu who upholds the Vinaya, whom then should you respect?
Having rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish for the bhikṣus the first rule of training."
"If a bhikṣu hears that a bhikṣu who upholds the Vinaya is coming, he should not avoid him and depart; rather, he should sweep and sprinkle the area, and prepare the dwelling and bedding.
If he hears that the visitor is about to arrive, he should go out half a yojana to welcome him;
if there is some doubt or difficulty, he must certainly go to the gate."

If there is a bhikṣu who upholds the Vinaya, one should carry his robes and requisites for him, provide water for bathing, supply towels for wiping his hands and feet, prepare bathing implements, offer post-midday drinks, and request him to preach the Dharma.
If one asks with a genuine desire for understanding, the bhikṣu who upholds the Vinaya should answer in accordance with the Dharma;
if one asks out of a desire to provoke or annoy, he should not answer.
On the following morning, he should provide them with the morning meal and *tambula*, followed by the midday meal.
One should act as a petitioner for the host and request that they remain for the rains retreat;
furthermore, one should act as a petitioner for the donor of robes and provide such offerings. If one does not do so, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.
At that time, on the day of the *poṣadha*, the World-Honored One sat in the open air surrounded by the bhikṣus, who stood before and behind him. He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Be silent; now it is time for the *poṣadha*, and we shall recite the *Prātimokṣa*."
A certain bhikṣu rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The bhikṣu Garga has recently fallen ill with insanity; sometimes he comes and sometimes he does not.
Furthermore, he does not remember whether he came or did not come, and because of this, he neglects the communal affairs of the Saṃgha.”
"Now he does not come again!
The Buddha said,
"Send one bhikṣu to call him here!"
Having received these instructions, he went to summon him; however, though he searched everywhere, he could not find him. He returned and reported this to the Buddha, who said:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to perform the formal rite of a white-two-karmavācanā for one who is insane from a distance."
A certain bhikṣu addressed the assembly:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!

This bhikṣu so-and-so is afflicted by madness; he sometimes comes and sometimes does not come, nor does he remember whether he came or did not come, and because of this, he neglects the communal affairs of the Saṃgha."
The Saṃgha now performs the formal act of *kṛtaka* (insanity) for [Name] from afar, so that he may carry out the affairs of the Saṃgha whether present or absent.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, please listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is afflicted with madness... [and so on]... such that he does not currently participate in the affairs of the Sangha."
"Whichever elders approve, let them remain silent;
if you do not approve, speak.
The Sangha has finished performing the formal act of insanity for so-and-so."
"Because the Saṃgha remained silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Later, having recovered, he requested the lifting of the *karmavācanā*; he reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to resolve this by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation).
The monk who has recovered from his illness should go before the Saṃgha, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and say:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], previously suffered from madness; sometimes I would come and sometimes I would not, nor did I remember whether I had come or not.
The Saṃgha has already performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for me regarding my madness."
"I am now cured; I beg the Saṃgha to revoke the *unmattaka-karman* (the formal act for one who is insane).
Thus he begs three times.
A single bhikṣu should then announce as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, was previously insane; he would sometimes come and sometimes not, nor did he remember whether he had come or not.
The Saṃgha has performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for one who is insane upon him."
Now that he has recovered, he requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *kṣiptacitta-karman* (the formal act for one who is insane);
the Saṃgha now grants him the lifting of the *kṣiptacitta-karman*.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience.
The motion is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, was previously afflicted by madness... [and so forth] ...the Saṃgha now grants him the lifting of the formal act for madness."
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has finished lifting the *unmattaka-karman* (the formal act for one who is insane) for the bhikṣu so-and-so.
“Since the Saṃgha remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
At that time, on the day of the Poṣadha, the World-Honored One sat in the open air surrounded by the bhikṣus, who stood before and behind him. He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Be silent, all of you; now we shall perform the *poṣadha* and recite the precepts.
A certain bhikṣu rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The bhikṣu named so-and-so is ill and has not come."
The Buddha said,
"You should have one bhikṣu bring it here.
The bhikṣus did not know how to bring it and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Teach them to lean on a staff and have others support them;
if they are unable to do so, carry them away using their robes."
They immediately followed the instruction and carried him there.
Because of the physical exertion, his illness became even more severe, and some even died.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should take the *pāriśuddhi* (declaration of purity) and bring it here.
In this regard, there are cases where it is called "giving the *pāriśuddhi*" and cases where it is not;
there are cases where it is called "receiving the *pāriśuddhi*" and cases where it is not.
Some may be said to have received the transmission of the *śuddhaka-icchā* (the desire for purity),
while others may not. Those who are said not to have received the transmission of the *śuddhaka-icchā* are those who give it to a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā.

One may give the *śuddhikāma* (desire for purity) to those with deranged minds, distracted minds, minds impaired by illness, persons who have been expelled, persons who have been suspended, persons who have confessed their offenses, or persons residing in a different boundary.
If one does not perform the formal proclamation three times according to the Dharma, saying:
"I now give you my desire for purity; you receive my desire for purity. When the Sangha performs its business according to the Dharma, please announce my name and cast the voting tally on my behalf."
In all such cases, it is not termed "giving the desire for purity" (śuddhikāmatā). Conversely, it is termed "giving the desire for purity.
One who does not receive the desire for purity is as follows:

If one acts contrary to the Dharma, does not know the other person's name, or [commits any of the aforementioned faults], as described above, none of these are termed "receiving a pure desire" (*śuddha-kāma*).
Conversely, if one acts otherwise, it is termed "receiving a pure desire."
Regarding the one who is said to "come having brought pure desire":
if a bhikṣu who has brought pure desire comes to the *poṣadha* assembly, yet then falls asleep, or becomes insane, or has a distracted mind, or a mind impaired by illness;

or if the Saṃgha has performed against him the *karmavācanā* for not seeing an offense, the *karmavācanā* for not relinquishing evil and false views, or the *karmavācanā* for not confessing a transgression.
If one transforms into a person with both sexual organs, a eunuch, or becomes rootless;
or if one forgets to speak [the consent], these are also termed "bringing pure desire.
If one falls asleep or forgets and does not speak, one commits the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If one falls asleep along the way, or even forgets to convey it, in all such cases one cannot be said to have brought a pure *śuddhika* (declaration of purity).
Furthermore, there are sick bhikṣus who are unable to speak with their mouths to declare a pure *śuddhika*.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"One should give one's presence and pure desire (śuddhaka-icchā).
The bhikṣus did not know how to give their presence and pure desire, so they reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If one raises a hand, raises a finger, shakes the body, shakes the head, or even just raises the eyes, it is termed 'the body' and 'pure desire'."
Furthermore, there were sick bhikṣus who were unable to personally convey their *śuddhika-icchā* (the desire for purity). They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"The entire assembly should go to the place where the sick person is. The bhikṣu who recites the precepts should sit in the center and recite the precepts, while the sick bhikṣus are made to face the one reciting the precepts."
Furthermore, there were some sick bhikṣus who were unable to turn toward the person reciting the precepts, so they sat or lay down with their backs turned.
When this was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"One should perform the poṣadha outside the boundary; one must not perform a separate assembly's poṣadha within the boundary."
At that time, on the day of the recitation of the precepts, the World-Honored One sat in the open air surrounded by the bhikṣus, who stood before and behind him. He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Be silent; now we shall perform the poṣadha and recite the precepts."
A certain bhikṣu rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The bhikṣu so-and-so has been seized by government officials and was unable to come.
The Buddha said:
"A single bhikṣu should be sent to explain the reason for this and request that they return for the poṣadha; if they agree, it is well.
If they do not agree, one should tell the layperson to step aside briefly so that you may obtain their pure consent (śuddhaka-icchā); if you obtain it, it is well.
If you do not obtain it, you should say: "
"Let the entire Saṃgha come to this bhikṣu for the poṣadha. If they can do so, it is well;
if not, they should go outside the boundary to perform the poṣadha, for one must not perform the poṣadha separately within the boundary as a distinct group.
There was a forest hermitage where the bhikṣus gathered on the fifteenth day for the uposatha and the recitation of the precepts.
At that time, some bandits arrived; when the bhikṣus saw them, they stopped and did not recite the precepts.
The bandits asked,
"Why do you remain silent? He replied:
"What we have spoken should not be heard by laypeople," they said.
The bandits asked again,
"Is what you have spoken not the word of the Buddha?"
He replied, “Yes. He asked again:
"If these are the words of the Buddha, who would not wish to hear them?
You have gathered here now surely because you wish to discuss matters that are detrimental to us!
Having said this, they struck [the monks] and seized their robes and bowls.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, if any bhikṣus see bandits approaching, they should immediately recite other sūtras so that [the recitation] is not interrupted."

At that time, there was a king named Udayana who was well-versed in the science of physiognomy. He had a queen named Candraprabhā, whose beauty was exquisite and whose singing and dancing surpassed all others.
Later, she performed a dance before the king atop a high pavilion.
The King saw the signs of death within a year; observing them closely, his heart was troubled and his countenance was displeased.
The Queen perceived this and addressed the King, saying:
"Is my dancing not beautiful?"
"Why are you not pleased? The king said,
"There is no need to ask me!"
The lady questioned him insistently up to three times; the king, having no other recourse, related the matter in full.
The lady said to the king, "If it is truly so, I pray you grant me permission to leave the household life!"
The king said, "I hold you in deep respect and love; we shall not be parted even in death. Our remaining joys are but a few days away—how can we be separated while still alive?
The lady spoke again to the king:
"Having been stained by worldly glory for so long, I have become deluded and obscured regarding the path of practice; in this brief span of life, I encounter nothing but suffering.
I pray that you will surely show compassion and grant me permission to fulfill my wish to leave the household life."
The king said, "You are young and have practiced the Way; your insight and discernment are clear and decisive, so you will surely be reborn in heaven.
If we meet again, I shall fulfill your wish."
The lady said, "If this vow is fulfilled, I swear not to break my promise!
She was then permitted to leave the household life.

Thereupon, he took his leave and departed. Before long, while practicing the Way, he attained the fruit of *anāgāmin* and immediately passed away to be reborn in the Brahma Heaven. There, he thought to himself:
"That I was able to leave the household life is due to the King's grace; this debt of gratitude is heavy and must be repaid, for it must not be neglected."
He immediately descended and stood in the air above the royal palace, saying to the king:
"The Lady Candraprabhā is none other than myself; because I previously made a pact with you, O King, I have come now to fulfill that promise."
The king said, "I do not know you, O Deva; please manifest your true form.
He immediately transformed back into his former shape and stood before the king.
Seeing that the King’s attachment was deep, he wished to draw near him, but then flew up into the void and said to the King:
"Why does Your Majesty still indulge in these sensual desires?"
Desire is impermanent, suffering, empty, and impure; if one contemplates this meaning, one may attain liberation.
If it is not so, one will inevitably fall into the three miserable realms, from which it is truly difficult to extricate oneself!

Upon hearing these words, the king’s mind became immediately supple and gentle; he then abdicated the royal throne to his crown prince, left the household life to study the Way, and dwelt beneath the trees in the mountain forests on the outskirts of the city.

Seeing that his father had left the household life but was not departing far away, the Crown Prince constantly feared he might change his mind and regret his decision, returning to seize the throne; thus, he always wished for his father, the King, to go far away to another land.
Then the bhikṣu Rāja thought to himself:
"I have received the Buddha's teaching yet have not seen the Buddha; I shall now go there to pay homage to the World-Honored One.
Having had this thought, he set out.
At that time, the Prince, together with the various brahmins, saw him depart from the forest while atop a high tower, and said to the new king:
"The King Bhikṣu has now departed!"
The Crown Prince was delighted.
The Bhikṣu King had forgotten his sitting mat; after a short while he remembered it and immediately went back to retrieve it.
The Brahmins spoke again to the new king, saying:
"The King-Bhikṣu has returned; could it be that something has happened?
The Crown Prince, struck with terror, immediately commanded his attendants:
"Go quickly and kill him!"
"Kill every single one of those śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas!
He further commanded:
"If they fear death, they may employ many stratagems; be careful not to fail to kill them and then come to see me!"
Having received these instructions, he went at once and said,
"The new king has commanded me to kill the bhikṣu! The bhikṣu asked:
"Why did you kill me? He replied, "Because the bhikṣu has emerged from the forest and returned, I feared he would seize my throne; for this reason, I killed you."
The bhikṣu King said:
"I do not covet the royal throne; I was merely returning for a moment to retrieve my sitting mat which I had forgotten.
Why, on this account, am I to be put to death?"
The messenger spoke again:
"I have received the King's repeated command:
'He will surely fear death and employ many stratagems; be careful not to return to see me without having killed him!'"
"How can I now return empty-handed?
The Bhikṣu King spoke again:
"I have not yet obtained what I sought in leaving the household life; please grant me a brief respite and wait until the shadow of that tree arrives."
The messenger listened to him.
He then applied himself diligently to contemplation and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
When the shadow of the tree arrived, the messenger spoke again, saying that the shadow had already reached him; the bhikṣu replied once more:
"I have not yet fully attained what I sought by leaving the household life; may you grant me further respite so that I may wait for one more shadow.
The messenger granted him leave once more.
In this manner, after four such occasions, he attained the four fruits of śrāmaṇya and then spoke to the messenger:
"You may do as you wish; go back and tell your king: 'I have no craving for the royal throne; I returned only because I forgot my sitting mat.
If you kill me for this, you will be killing your father and killing an Arhat—consider that you will suffer great misery for a long night!'"
Having spoken thus, he went to his death.
After the executioner had killed him and returned to the king’s presence, the king saw him from afar and immediately felt remorse.
Upon his arrival, the king asked:
"Have you already killed him? He replied, "I have!"
The king asked again,
"What did my father, the King, say at the time of his death?
The messenger sobbed and answered him in full detail as it had occurred.
Upon hearing these words, blood issued from the king’s mouth, and he entered the great Avīci Hell in his physical body.

At that time, King Bimbisāra and his neighboring kingdoms, having previously heard the instruction to slaughter all the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas, feared they might enter their own territories; thus, the king commanded his staff-bearers to guard the bhikṣus, and the staff-bearers, having received the command, did not leave their posts for a moment.
At that time, there were five hundred bhikṣus staying at a certain residence in Rājagṛha. On the fifteenth day, they gathered and said to him, "Please step aside for a moment;
we wish to perform the poṣadha ceremony.
The staff-bearer replied:
"We have received the royal decree that we may not depart for even a moment; how could we dare openly disobey the Great King's command?
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If they are unwilling to leave, one should simply recite the preface of the *Prātimokṣa* and then say:
'The remainder is as the Sangha has heard before.
One should perform the *poṣadha* in this manner; one must not fail to perform the *poṣadha*."
At that time, when the bhikṣus assembled on the day of the poṣadha to recite the precepts, the group of six bhikṣus quarreled and would not cease; thus, they were unable to recite the precepts.
When King Bimbisāra arrived, the dispute was temporarily settled, but after he departed, they resumed fighting and were again unable to recite the precepts.
Not knowing what to do, they reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If there is a situation such as that of King Bimbisāra, where monks encounter danger or difficulty and the fighting has temporarily ceased, one should then recite the introduction to the precepts."
When the introduction to the recitation of the precepts has been concluded, one should say:
"The remainder is as is commonly heard by the Saṃgha.
One should perform the poṣadha in this manner; one must not fail to perform the poṣadha.

When the Saṃgha was about to perform a formal act (karmavācanā) during the Poṣadha ceremony, the group of six bhikṣus accepted the "desire for purity" (śuddhika-icchā) from others, yet they failed to appear among the assembly and instead departed beyond the boundary, intending to cause the Saṃgha’s formal act to fail.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The saṃgha’s formal ritual (karmavācanā) is valid;
however, one who receives the pure consent (śuddhika-kāma) from another commits a duṣkṛta offense."
At that time, the bhikṣus were always reciting the precepts in brief. The junior bhikṣus said, "Venerable sirs!
Recite them in full; we have never heard them before."
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I do not permit the constant abbreviated recitation of the precepts; however, there are ten causes and conditions under which the abbreviated recitation of the precepts is permitted:
first, when there are persons of high status present."
Second, there are ferocious beasts;
third, there are venomous insects;
fourth, the ground grows wild grass.
Fifth, the ground is covered with thorns;
sixth, there are holes inhabited by venomous snakes;
seventh, illness.
8. Darkness; 9. mud on the ground;
10. cramped seating.
These are called the ten causes and conditions.
If one is still able to obtain the five kinds of recitation of the precepts, it is well; if not, one should say:
"Now, on the fourteenth or fifteenth day, during the time of the *poṣadha*, each of you should together rectify body, speech, and mind;
do not be negligent! This, too, may be called *poṣadha*.
"One should perform the *poṣadha* in this manner; one must not fail to perform the *poṣadha*.
There is a certain residence where, while the recitation of the precepts (*pravāraṇā*) is taking place, more bhikṣus arrive—whether they be more numerous, equal in number, or fewer.

Furthermore, there is another residence where, having completed the recitation of the precepts, before anyone has risen and departed, more bhikṣus arrive—whether they be more numerous, equal in number, or fewer.

Furthermore, there is another residence where, after the recitation of the *Poṣadha* has been completed, some monks have departed while others have not yet departed, and then more monks arrive—whether they be many, equal in number, or few.

Furthermore, there is another residence where, after the recitation of the *Poṣadha* has been completed, all the monks have departed, and then more monks arrive—whether they be many, equal in number, or few.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If, while the precepts are being recited, another bhikṣu arrives—whether he be more numerous or equal in number—you should perform the poṣadha and recite the precepts once again."
If there are few, they should listen to the subsequent precepts.

If the recitation of the precepts has already concluded and no bhikṣus have yet risen, and another bhikṣu arrives—whether there be many or an equal number—they should perform the poṣadha and recite the precepts once more;
if there are few, they should kneel on their right knees within the saṃgha and declare their purity.

If, after the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* has been completed, some bhikṣus have risen and departed while others have not yet risen and departed, and more bhikṣus arrive—whether they be equal in number or more numerous—one should perform the *poṣadha* and recite the *Prātimokṣa* once again.
If there are fewer, one should seek reconciliation with the bhikṣus already present and perform the *poṣadha* and recite the *Prātimokṣa* again; if this is achieved, it is well.
If it cannot be achieved, one should go outside the boundary (*sīmā*) to perform the *poṣadha*; one must not perform separate *poṣadhas* within the same boundary.
"If, after the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* has been concluded, all the bhikṣus have risen and departed, and another bhikṣu arrives, it shall be treated in the same manner.
This applies whether the assembly consists of resident bhikṣus, or if resident bhikṣus arrive, or guest bhikṣus arrive, or both resident and guest bhikṣus arrive;
or if the assembly consists of guest bhikṣus, or if guest bhikṣus arrive, or resident bhikṣus arrive, or both guest and resident bhikṣus arrive.

If resident monks have assembled, or if resident monks arrive, or if resident monks arrive, or if visiting monks arrive—whether they are numerous, equal in number, or few—even until all the monks rise and depart, it is all as described above.

There was a certain residence where, at the time of the *poṣadha*, the bhikṣus gathered intending to recite the precepts. They saw strange rope beds, robes, and bowls, yet they did not see any bhikṣus.
Without considering whether there were bhikṣus present or not, the bhikṣus proceeded together to recite the precepts.
There was a certain residence where, at the time of the *poṣadha*, the bhikṣus gathered intending to recite the precepts; they saw foreign rope-beds, robes, and bowls, but did not see any bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves: "There are no bhikṣus here."
He then recited the precepts.

At one residence, when it was time for the *poṣadha*, the monks assembled with the intention of reciting the precepts; however, they saw foreign couches, robes, and bowls, yet no monks were to be seen.
The monks thought to themselves: "Whether there are monks here or not, we shall simply recite the precepts."
He then recited the precepts.

At a certain residence, when it was time for the *poṣadha*, the monks gathered and intended to recite the precepts; however, they saw strange rope-beds, robes, and bowls, yet they did not see any monks. The monks thought to themselves:
"A monk must have departed from or disappeared from this place."
They recited the precepts with the intention of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
At a certain residence, when it was time for the poṣadha, the bhikṣus gathered and intended to recite the precepts; they saw foreign rope-cots, robes, and alms-bowls, but did not see any bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves: "There are bhikṣus here!"
Without seeking or searching for them, they proceeded to recite the precepts.
At one residence, when it was time for the *poṣadha*, the bhikṣus gathered with the intention of reciting the precepts; they saw strange rope beds, robes, and bowls, but no bhikṣus were to be seen.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves,
"There is a bhikṣu here! Though they searched for him,
they could not find him, and so they recited the precepts.

There was a certain residence where, at the time of the *poṣadha*, the monks gathered intending to recite the precepts. Seeing an unusual rope bed, robes, and bowls, yet not seeing any monks, the monks thought to themselves:
"There must be monks here!"
When they sought them out and found them, they recited the precepts together.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"First, second, third, and fifth—these four modes of reciting the *Poṣadha* all involve faults; the *karmavācanā* is not accomplished, and one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The fourth case also involves a fault; the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) is not accomplished, and one commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
The sixth case involves no fault; the formal procedure is not accomplished, but there is no offense.
The seventh case involves no fault; the formal procedure is accomplished, and there is no offense.
If the resident bhikṣus have assembled, yet no resident bhikṣu is seen, no visiting bhikṣu is seen, and no resident-visiting bhikṣu is seen;
if the visiting bhikṣus have assembled, yet no visiting bhikṣu is seen, no resident bhikṣu is seen, and no resident-visiting bhikṣu is seen;
if the resident-visiting bhikṣus have assembled, yet no resident-visiting bhikṣu is seen, no resident bhikṣu is seen, and no visiting bhikṣu is seen.
The cases of having faults and being without faults are all as described above.

There was a certain residence where, at the time of the *poṣadha*, the bhikṣus assembled; they heard the sound of a bhikṣu coughing, or sniffling, or shaking his robe, yet they did not form the thought:
"There is a bhikṣu here," or "There is no bhikṣu here."
Then they recited the precepts.
Even at a certain residence, when the monks had assembled for the *poṣadha*, they heard the sound of a monk sneezing, sniffling, or shaking his robe, and they thought: "There is a monk here!"
Having sought them out, they recited the *Prātimokṣa* together.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha’s response regarding whether there was an offense or no offense was also entirely as stated above.
There was one bhikṣu who, having received the *śuddhaka-icchā* (the desire for purity) from another bhikṣu, performed the *poṣadha* with that one bhikṣu;
there were two bhikṣus who, having received the *śuddhaka-icchā* from two bhikṣus, performed the *poṣadha* with those two bhikṣus;
and there were three bhikṣus who, having received the *śuddhaka-icchā* from three bhikṣus, performed the *poṣadha* with those three bhikṣus.
There were many bhikṣus who received the pure desires (*śuddhaka-kāma*) of many other bhikṣus and performed the *poṣadha* ceremony.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"None of these should be done!"
"Now I allow a large number of bhikṣus to assemble, while a small number of bhikṣus may come bearing the *śuddhaka-icchā* (the desire for purity).

At a certain residence, a group of bhikṣus assembled, intending to perform the *poṣadha* and recite the precepts. They saw bhikṣus from another residence and perceived them as belonging to their own community (*sāmantaka-saṃjñā*).
Having seen them, they neither remembered nor questioned them, and then proceeded to recite the precepts.

There was a residence where a group of bhikṣus assembled, intending to perform the uposatha and recite the precepts. Seeing bhikṣus from another residence, they perceived them as being of the same residence;
having seen them, they remembered [the distinction] but did not inquire, and then proceeded to recite the precepts.

There was a residence where a group of bhikṣus gathered, intending to perform the uposatha and recite the precepts. Seeing bhikṣus from another residence, they perceived them as belonging to their own community;
having seen them, they recalled [the rule], inquired, and recited the precepts together.

There was a residence where a group of bhikṣus had gathered, intending to perform the poṣadha and recite the precepts. They saw a bhikṣu from another residence; they were uncertain as to whether he belonged to their own boundary, yet they had no doubt that he was a bhikṣu.
Without reflecting or inquiring, they proceeded to recite the precepts.

There was a certain residence where a group of bhikṣus gathered, intending to perform the uposatha and recite the precepts. Seeing a bhikṣu from another residence, they were uncertain as to whether he belonged to their boundary, yet they had no doubt that he was a bhikṣu. Remembering him but not asking, they proceeded to recite the precepts.

There was a certain residence where a group of bhikṣus gathered, intending to perform the uposatha and recite the precepts. Seeing a bhikṣu from another residence, they had doubts regarding the boundary but no doubts regarding his status as a bhikṣu; thus, by recollecting and questioning him, they recited the precepts together.

There was a residence where a group of bhikṣus had gathered intending to recite the Prātimokṣa. Seeing a bhikṣu from another residence, they harbored doubt regarding that bhikṣu but no doubt regarding the boundary (sīmā). Without remembering him or questioning him, they proceeded to recite the Prātimokṣa.

There was a certain residence where a group of bhikṣus gathered, intending to perform the uposatha and recite the precepts. They saw a bhikṣu from another residence; they had doubts regarding that bhikṣu, but no doubts regarding the boundary. Without reflecting or inquiring, they proceeded to recite the precepts.

There was a residence where a group of bhikṣus had gathered, intending to perform the uposatha and recite the precepts. Seeing a bhikṣu from another residence, they were doubtful regarding his status as a bhikṣu, though they had no doubt regarding the boundary (sīmā). Having reflected and questioned him, they recited the precepts together with him.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“If there are six defects, the karmavācanā is not established, and one commits a duṣkṛta offense.”
"In these three cases, there is no fault; the *karmavācanā* is accomplished, and there is no offense.
The same applies to those living together.
A visiting bhikṣu says it is the fourteenth day, while the resident bhikṣus say it is the fifteenth day.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"The visiting bhikṣus should follow the resident bhikṣus."
There were no resident bhikṣus, and the visiting bhikṣus themselves acted differently from the aforementioned cases; not knowing what to do, they reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Those who arrive later should follow those who arrived first."
When visiting bhikṣus arrived at one time, they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"You should ask the bhikṣus of the local area.
If there are no bhikṣus in the local area, you should ask the government officials for the number of days and follow that."

At that time, various bhikṣus went from a monastery where bhikṣus resided to a monastery where bhikṣus resided to perform the *poṣadha*; they went to a monastery where no bhikṣus resided to perform the *poṣadha*; they went to a monastery where both bhikṣus and non-bhikṣus resided to perform the *poṣadha*; they went to a monastery where quarreling bhikṣus resided to perform the *poṣadha*; and they went to a monastery where bhikṣus who had split the *saṃgha* resided to perform the *poṣadha*.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If on the day of the poṣadha one goes to the four places first, it is a duṣkṛta;
if one goes to the one place last, it is a sthūlātyaya."
At a certain residence, on the day of the *poṣadha*, the monk Upananda served as the senior elder (*sthavira*); when the community of monks requested him to recite the precepts,
he replied, "I have forgotten them."
The bhikṣus said, "If you have forgotten,
why did you sit in the place of the senior monk?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“The senior monk (sthavira) should recite the precepts;
if he does not, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
The bhikṣus did not know up to what point one was considered a senior monk, so they reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Those above whom there is no one else are all designated as *sthavira* (elders).
When the bhikṣus forgot [the precepts] during the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, they reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"A bystander should provide the instruction; if they still forget, they should be instructed again; if they forget a third time, another person should be appointed to continue the recitation in sequence, but one must not recite it repeatedly."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus engaged in quarreling during the uposatha night, obstructing the Saṃgha’s recitation of the precepts.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"If it is possible to proceed with the recitation of the precepts and those who have risen are still few, you should reconvene and recite the precepts."
If those who have arrived are many or constitute a quorum, they should remain; it is permitted to postpone the *poṣadha* until the following day.

Whether they are reciting the Vinaya, preaching the Dharma, engaging in discussion, or receiving abundant offerings, if there is no time to recite the precepts, it is permitted in all such cases to defer until the next day.
The bhikṣus did not first invite someone to recite the precepts, and because of this delay, the recitation of the precepts was postponed.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should first invite someone to recite the precepts."

At that time, the monks first recited the precepts and afterwards performed various formal acts (*karmas*). The group of six monks departed as soon as the recitation of the precepts was finished; they did not join the Saṃgha in harmony to perform the formal acts, and thus the formal acts they performed were not in accordance with the Dharma.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should first perform the various *karmas*, and only then recite the precepts; by doing so, one shall hold the Sangha together so that they do not depart."
At that time, the bhikṣus all recited the precepts together and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"You should not recite the precepts together; one person should be requested to recite them."
There was a bhikṣu who recited the precepts using a melodic, chanting voice. When this was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"They should recite them directly.
At that time, during the poṣadha ceremony at a certain residence, Upāli was the senior elder (sthavira), and he proclaimed:
“Today the Saṃgha is performing the Uposatha on the fifteenth day and reciting the Prātimokṣa; those bhikṣus who have not come have declared their *chanda* and *pariśuddhi*.
What shall the Saṃgha do now?
What business shall it perform for the sake of these bhikṣus?”
The bhikṣus replied:
"Bhikṣu So-and-so should be subjected to the karma of censure, the karma of banishment, the karma of dependence, the karma of formal accusation, and the karma of subordination."

"A certain bhikṣu should be granted parivāsa, mānatva, mūlāpakarṣa, and ābhīkṣṇaka. Upāli said, "I do not know the karmavācanā. Upāli replied, "I do not know the formal procedure. Upāli said, "I do not know the ritual. Upāli said, "I do not know the rite. Upāli said, "I do not know the ceremony. Upāli said, "I do not know the performance. Upāli said, "I do not know the execution. Upāli said, "I do not know the application. Upāli said, "I do not know the implementation. Upāli said, "I do not know the enactment. Upāli said, "I do not know the performance of the ritual. Upāli said, "I do not know the performance of the rite. Upāli said, "I do not know the performance of the ceremony. Upāli said, "I do not know the performance of the performance. Upāli said, "I do not know the performance of the performance of the rite. The bhikṣus asked: "If you do not know, why did you ask the Saṃgha and the bhikṣus what they were doing?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“The Elder should recite the precepts; the one who upholds the Vinaya should perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).

At that time, some bhikṣus listened to the recitation of the precepts without showing respect, such as by tucking their robes over one shoulder, placing their hands on their hips, wearing leather sandals, covering their heads, lying down, or leaning against something.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You must show increased respect!
You must not listen to the recitation of the precepts with your robes tucked up behind your back, nor while reclining or leaning against something; those who violate this commit a *duṣkṛta* offense!"

On the day of the *poṣadha*, there was a bhikṣu who slept soundly; only after the recitation of the precepts had concluded did he startle awake and say, "The Saṃgha has assembled, let us recite the precepts together.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not sleep at all during the daytime.
Furthermore, there were various monks serving as *karmadāna* (officers) who, being unable to sleep, became exhausted and could find no physical ease.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to sleep in a secluded place; however, you should inform a bhikṣu who is a close acquaintance:
'I am sleeping in such-and-such a place; if there is any business for the Saṃgha, please call for me!'"
Again, there was another bhikṣu who fell asleep during the recitation of the precepts; only upon waking did he say to the other bhikṣus, "Why have you not recited the precepts?
The bhikṣus asked him:
"What do you remember? He replied,
"I fell asleep."
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should not fall asleep while the precepts are being recited; one who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."

At a certain residence where the *poṣadha* was being observed, the resident bhikṣus were reciting the precepts in a secluded place. When visiting bhikṣus arrived, they did not know the location [of the assembly].
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there is no obstacle, one should not recite the precepts while avoiding a secluded place."
There were some bhikṣus who did not know when the time for the recitation of the precepts had arrived. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“The senior monk (upādhyāya) should know when the time has arrived; he should instruct the junior monks to sweep the area, arrange the seats, prepare the voting sticks (śalākā), and provide lamps.”
The bhikṣus entrusted their affairs to one another for even minor matters. They reported this to the Buddha, who said:
"I do not permit entrusting one's affairs to others for minor matters.

The bhikṣus then wished to adorn the poṣadha hall by hanging silk streamers and scattering flowers; they also provided the Saṃgha with post-midday drinks and offered them clothing and other requisites.
Furthermore, wishing to praise the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha with verses, he informed the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"I grant permission for all!"
"If there are various meritorious deeds to be performed, one should do them in a timely manner.
