The bhikṣus wished to make the walking path high; they reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Allow the ground to be leveled.
As they practiced walking meditation in pairs, the path was repeatedly damaged. They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to plaster it with white lime; I also allow you to spread cloth or *pāṭala* grass upon it."
During a great assembly, there were many people but few rooms, and the bhikṣus had no place to stay.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there is space within a room large enough to accommodate one's knees, I allow you to spread your robes on the ground to sit upon, leaving the center clear."
Once the bhikṣus were living in the same room, they began to disturb one another.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should separate them with a cloth screen; you are also permitted to construct a cave."
The bhikṣus sat leaning against the walls; when the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled them, saying:
"Are these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, old men who have left the household life, or are they simply lacking in dignified decorum?"
"Why do you sit leaning against a wall?
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"You should not sit leaning against a wall!"
There were some elderly and sick bhikṣus who, being unable to support themselves, took a bundle of grass and leaned against it while sitting, thereby defiling the interior of their rooms.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not lean against a bundle of grass; I allow the making of a meditation bench and a meditation belt."
The bhikṣus made meditation belts that were too wide; they reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "They should not exceed eight finger-widths in width.
The bhikṣus then made meditation belts that were too narrow; they reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not reduce it to less than five finger-widths.
The bhikṣus again made meditation belts of variegated colors and informed the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"They should be made of a single color."
"If it is a variegated color, you should wash it until it becomes a neutral (badara) color, and only then shall you be permitted to keep it.

At that time, the Elder Kāśyapa obtained a garment; he wished to make it into an antaravāsaka, but it was too long, and he wished to make it into either a saṃghāṭī or an uttarāsaṅga, yet it was too short for both. He repeatedly pulled and stretched it.
The Buddha went to his room and saw him, asking,
"What are you doing? He answered the question by relating the matter in detail.
The Buddha said:

"If it is insufficient, one should have three long pieces and one short piece; if it is still insufficient, two long pieces and one short piece are permitted; if it is still insufficient, one long piece and one short piece are permitted; if it is still insufficient, one may affix additional strips to form leaves."
The Elder Kāśyapa obtained another robe, but it was too small to be made into the three patched robes (tricīvara).
He informed the Buddha about this, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to make a patchwork saṃghāṭī and an uttarāsaṅga, but the antaravāsaka may be made as a plain (unpatched) garment."
When there was a large assembly, the lay devotees offered robes as alms.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Please listen and accept [this request].
Those laypeople wished to receive a ritual blessing (paritta).
They informed the Buddha of this matter.
The Buddha said,
"You should perform a prayer of blessing!
The bhikṣus did not know how to perform the prayer of blessing, so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"You should have the *karmadāna* offer a blessing.
Not knowing where to place it, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should perform the formal procedure of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* as previously prescribed, and place it in the central room.
Not knowing who should guard it, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should appoint a single bhikṣu to guard [the robes] by means of a formal motion and one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman), as previously described.
The bhikṣus then appointed an ignorant bhikṣu, who could not distinguish between good and bad robes.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One who possesses five qualities should not be appointed as a guardian of robes:
one who follows favoritism, ill will, delusion, or fear, and one who does not know the quality of the robes."
The bhikṣus divided [the robes] in a noisy place; they lost their robes, and the bhikṣu who was guarding the robes incurred a bad reputation.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should divide them in a quiet place."
At the time the robes were being distributed, a visiting bhikṣu arrived.
An established bhikṣu asked him, "Where were you on such-and-such a day? He replied:
"In such-and-such a place.
The bhikṣus said, "On the day we obtained our robes, this bhikṣu was within our boundary; therefore, the distribution of the robes is not valid."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If on the day one obtains the robe, there is a monk present and one perceives him as a monk, the distribution of the robe is not accomplished, and one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*;
if there is doubt regarding the presence of a monk, it is likewise."
If there is no bhikṣu, yet one has the perception that there is a bhikṣu, and they divide the robe-cloth, they incur a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if there is no bhikṣu and one suspects there is one, it is likewise.
If there is no bhikṣu and one has the perception that there is no bhikṣu, and they divide the robe-cloth, there is no offense.
At that time, some bhikṣus lay upon the monastic bedding without wearing an undergarment; it became soiled and impure.
Furthermore, another bhikṣu lay upon the monastic bedding without an undergarment and, stretching out his legs, stepped through and tore it.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"In order to protect the body, protect the robes, and protect the monastic bedding, I allow you to keep a single mat to spread upon the monastic bedding."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, because the Buddha had not permitted them to lie directly upon the monastic bedding, spread out pieces of cloth several inches wide over the monastic bedding.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The width and length [of the covering] should be the same as those of the bedding."
The bhikṣus fell asleep without maintaining mindfulness and emitted semen, soiling their single-layered mats.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should spread a sitting mat upon the single-layered mat."
There were some bhikṣus who were troubled by bedbugs; they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to separately prepare a wide and long single-layered mat to spread out, with its edges hanging down one foot on each of the four sides of the bed."
At that time, Upāli asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
How many kinds of robes should one receive and maintain?”
The Buddha said:
"One should accept and maintain the three robes;

furthermore, one should accept and maintain the undergarment, the outer cloak, the rain-bathing robe, the wound-covering robe, the mosquito net, the cloth for spreading on the walking path, the cloth for warding off fleas, the single-layered spread, the sitting mat, the thigh-protector, the knee-protector, the head-protector, the body-wiping cloth, the hand-wiping cloth, the face-cloth, the needle and thread case, the bowl bag, the sandal bag, and the water-strainer. All such robes or items resembling robes should be accepted and maintained."
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
You constantly praise for us few desires and contentment; we take great delight in this.”
"We pray that you will allow us to go naked!
The Buddha said,
"You foolish people!"
"If one wishes to adopt the ritual practices of non-Buddhists, the offender commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense!

There were some bhikṣus who addressed the Buddha, saying they wished to make garments from human hair, deer skin, sheepskin, bird feathers, horse mane, yak tails, or from grass, tree bark, and leaves.
The Buddha said:
"Foolish man! You wish to perform the rituals and laws of the non-Buddhists; none of the rituals and laws of the non-Buddhists may be performed. To perform them constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense."
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“We pray that you will permit us to wear the *saṃkakṣikā* (undergarment) inside and the *pāṭa* (outer robe) as an upper garment.
The Buddha said:
“Foolish man! You wish to adopt the ritual observances of a layperson; one who commits this offense incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
There were some bhikṣus who wished to wear a tunic (*saṃkakṣikā*) underneath and a cotton robe (*kārpāsika*) over it.
Some wished to wear *soma* cloth or variegated cotton garments;
some wished to wear finger-rings, paint their eyebrows and eyes, or wear multicolored leather sandals.
They informed the Buddha of this, and the Buddha said:
“Foolish man! This is the conduct of laypeople; none of the conduct of laypeople may be performed. One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
A certain bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:
“We pray that you will allow us to wear robes of pure blue, yellow, red, white, and black!
The Buddha said:
“Robes of pure black are to be worn by women who have recently given birth; for one who violates this, it is a *pāyattika* offense.”
"For the other four colors, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from cold headaches; they reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"I allow you to cover [the head] with a robe, and I also allow you to make a cap; stop when it becomes warm."
There were some bhikṣus who entered villages without wearing their saṃkakṣikās, leaving their chests exposed. When the women saw this, they laughed and mocked them.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "You should not do so!"
"When entering a village, one should wear the saṃkakṣikā; whoever violates this incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Some bhikṣus wore their saṃkakṣikās, but they were blown to the ground by the wind. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should fasten it with a belt."
There were some bhikṣus working on high up, while women were below them; seeing their bodies, the women laughed and mocked them.
The bhikṣus felt ashamed and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"When working, it is permitted to take your robe behind you, pass it through the fork of your legs, and gather it in front."
At that time, Bhaddali, knowing that the place where the offerings for the *vassa* (rainy season) retreat had not yet been distributed, went there and said:
"Why do you not distribute them quickly?
If they are not distributed, there may be dangers such as being gnawed by insects, or damage from water and fire."
"If there is a portion that can be used by yourselves, you may give it to your disciples or use it for performing meritorious deeds.
The bhikṣus then divided [the goods], whereupon Bāḍhananda said,
"You do not distinguish between the noble and the base."
The bhikṣus said, "If you can distinguish them well, divide them for us and take a portion for yourself as well.
He then divided them accordingly.
He took what he had obtained and went elsewhere; this happened not just once.
Having acquired heavy garments, he returned to his residence. When the bhikṣus saw him, they praised him, saying:
"You possess great merit!"
"I have obtained such a robe.
He replied, "It was not brought about by merit; it was simply acquired through skillful speech at various places of residence during the rainy season retreat!"
The bhikṣus censured him in various ways, saying,
"How can one dwell in a single place for the rainy season retreat yet receive a share of offerings from various locations?
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Baddhananda:
"Is it true that you did so? He replied:
"It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways, saying:
"I have always taught that one should have few desires and be content; why do you now accept so much and never feel satisfied?
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should not observe the rains retreat in a single location while receiving a share of the offerings for the retreat from various places. Whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!"
At that time, the bhikṣus entered the village wearing only their upper and lower robes. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do so; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."

There was a bhikṣu who entered a village wearing his robe backwards. When the other bhikṣus saw him, they said to him, "What difference is there between wearing a robe backwards and wearing one that has not been cut according to the prescribed pattern?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do so; one who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

There were some bhikṣus who, before entering or after leaving a village, had their robes snagged and torn by grasses and trees, and dust had entered the folds of the fabric; they wished to put them back on but did not dare.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"In order to protect the robes, I allow you to wear them turned inside out when entering or leaving a village.

There were some bhikṣus who dyed their plain robes to create stripes, while others sewed leaf-patterns onto their robes, or gathered the fabric to form leaf-shapes, or made the leaves point upward on one half and downward on the other.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do so; those who violate this commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There were some bhikṣus wearing robes of variegated colors; they reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not do so; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
There were some bhikṣus who, during the rainy season, wore their robes inverted, causing water to seep into the layers and ruin them.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not wear [the robe] upside down during the rainy season; if it is not raining, one may do as one pleases.
At that time, some bhikṣus had extra robes, bowls, or other items which they wished to give to the Saṃgha. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There are nine ways of receiving gifts, all of which are permitted for giving to the Saṃgha:"
First, giving obtained through a specific realm;
second, giving obtained through a specific requirement;
third, giving obtained through a specific limit.
Fourth, gifts received by the Saṃgha;
fifth, gifts received by the present Saṃgha;
sixth, gifts received by the Saṃgha of the rainy-season retreat.
Seventh, receiving offerings from the two divisions of the Saṃgha;
eighth, receiving offerings through instruction;
ninth, receiving offerings from individuals.
Regarding the gift to those within a boundary: the donor says,
"I give this to the Sangha within this boundary."
This is called "alms obtained from a specific boundary" (*sīmā-labdha-dakṣiṇā*).
Regarding "alms obtained by agreement":

during the rainy season retreat (*varṣāvāsa*), the community of monks residing in different boundaries makes a mutual agreement that whatever alms are obtained at a single location shall be shared equally among them; this is called "alms obtained by agreement."
Regarding "receiving a gift with restrictions":
it is when the donor says,
"Give this gift to such-and-such a person."
This is called "a gift obtained for a specific limit.
Regarding "a gift obtained for the Saṃgha":
when a donor gives to the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha should know the object given and dispose of it as appropriate; this is called "a gift obtained for the Saṃgha."
"Gifts obtained by the *saṃgha* present" refers to when a donor gives directly to the *saṃgha* face-to-face; this is called "gifts obtained by the *saṃgha* present.
"Gifts obtained by the *saṃgha* during the rainy-season retreat" refers to:
The donor says: "I give this to the community of monks observing the rains retreat.
This is called the community observing the rains retreat receiving a gift.
Regarding the distribution of offerings to the two assemblies of monks:

when a donor gives to both the assembly of bhikṣus and the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, if there are more bhikṣus and fewer bhikṣuṇīs, or if there are more bhikṣuṇīs and fewer bhikṣus, they should all divide it equally.
If there are bhikṣus but no bhikṣuṇīs, the bhikṣus should divide it among themselves entirely.
If there are bhikṣuṇīs but no bhikṣus present, the bhikṣuṇīs should divide it among themselves;
this is called a gift received by the two-fold saṃgha.
Regarding the instruction for receiving gifts:
The donor instructs the monks to act in such a manner and use [the gift] in such a way; if they share it accordingly, this is called "obtaining a gift through instruction.
Regarding those who receive the gift: the donor says:
"I give this to so-and-so"—
this is called "a person receiving a gift.
Furthermore, there are five ways of receiving a gift:

"Gifts given to the Buddha and the Saṃgha; gifts given to the Buddha and the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha; gifts given to the Buddha and both divisions of the Saṃgha; gifts given on behalf of another; and gifts from a long-standing invitation to the Saṃgha.
At that time, a certain śrāmaṇera passed away.
The bhikṣus did not know how to dispose of those items and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If they were given to someone during his lifetime, they should be given to that person."
"If it was not given away during his lifetime, the present Saṃgha should divide it.
There was a monk of little renown who passed away, leaving behind upper and lower robes as well as non-robes.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If it was not already given away when he was alive, the Saṃgha present there should divide it."
"If someone has already given [an item] to another when it was produced, but that person has not yet taken it away, the Saṃgha should grant it to them by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
A bhikṣu should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
A certain bhikṣu has passed away here; whatever he possessed during his lifetime, whether robes or non-robes, the present Saṃgha should divide among themselves, and now we give it to [Name].
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus:
'Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!'"
A certain bhikṣu has passed away here; whatever he possessed during his lifetime, whether it be robes or non-robes, the present Saṃgha should divide among themselves, and we now give this to [Name].
"Whichever elders approve, let them remain silent;
if they do not approve, let them speak.
The Sangha has finished bestowing the robe upon [Name]."
The Saṃgha has consented by remaining silent;
this matter is thus upheld.
There was a monk of great renown who was supported by kings, ministers, and the masses; when he passed away, his possessions were exceedingly numerous.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If it was previously given to someone while [the donor] was alive, you should grant it by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman)."

If, at the time of death, there are items—whether divisible or indivisible—that have not yet been given away, such as *pāna* cloth, *soma* cloth, *karpāsa* cloth, or *kośeya* wool five finger-widths long; or a *saṃghāṭī*, an *uttarāsaṅga*, an *antarvāsaka*; or lower garments, a *śāṭī*, a single-layered mat, an undergarment, a cloak, or a sitting mat; or a needle-case, a water-strainer, a bowl-bag, a sandal-bag; or large and small bowls, a door-latch, and so forth—such items as these which are divisible, the present Saṃgha should divide among themselves.

Whether it be brocade, damask, woolen cloth, felt, or *kūrcaka* (hair-cloth) exceeding five finger-widths; whether it be a rain-bath robe, a wound-covering robe, a mosquito net, a walking-meditation mat, a single-layered mat for warding off bedbugs, or a bed, couch, or stool;
with the exception of large and small earthen bowls and earthen water-jars, all other earthenware vessels;
and with the exception of large and small iron bowls, door-hooks, nail-clippers, and needles, all other iron implements.
Except for copper *khandaka* bowls and copper *tāra* containers for medicinal eye-salves, all other copper vessels;
as well as items such as umbrellas and mendicant staffs—such objects as these are indivisible and should belong to the communal use of the Saṃgha.

There were certain bhikṣus who had received offerings for the rainy season retreat but had not yet divided them; among them, some passed away, others returned to lay life, some became followers of external paths, some went on long journeys, some became śrāmaṇeras, some received the full ordination again, some underwent a change of sexual organs, and some had their organs destroyed.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"If one who has received offerings during the rainy season retreat passes away before they have been distributed, and if that person had already given them away while alive, one should grant them to the intended recipient through a formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*."
If it was not previously given away when [the robe] arose, the present Saṃgha should divide it.
The same applies if one returns to secular life, becomes a non-Buddhist, travels far away, undergoes a change of sexual organs, or if the organs cease to exist.
"If one becomes a śrāmaṇera, [the gift] should be shared with the śrāmaṇeras.
If one subsequently receives the full ordination, it should be shared with the fully ordained bhikṣus.

There were certain bhikṣus who, during the retreat, had not yet received the retreat offerings; whether they passed away or their faculties changed, the same applies when the offerings are received later.
It was the same for the bhikṣuṇīs.
At that time, while the saṃgha had received offerings for the rainy season retreat but had not yet distributed them, Tissa caused a schism in the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If property is acquired before the Sangha has been split, it should be divided equally.
If property is acquired after the split, it should be divided according to the distribution of the offerings."

There were certain bhikṣus whose Saṃgha within a shared boundary had been split. Later, wishing to perform various formal acts (karmas) and to confer full ordination upon others, they did not know what to do and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"If the Sangha has already been split, even if they are within the same boundary, it is permitted to perform *karmavācanā* and carry out monastic affairs; this does not constitute the offense of acting in a separate assembly.
There was a certain residence where a single bhikṣu lived. During a time that was not the *varṣā* retreat, he received a robe intended for the Sangha and thought to himself:
“The Buddha has taught that four or more persons constitute a *saṃgha*; I am now alone, so I do not know what to do.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“You should receive and maintain it, or perform a *pariśuddha-dāna*, or give it to another person.”
If it were not so, other bhikṣus who arrive should share it together.
If there is a dwelling place for bhikṣus and a gift intended for the Saṃgha is obtained outside of the rainy-season retreat (vassa), and no bhikṣus are present, the bhikṣuṇīs should divide it.

If there is a residence for bhikṣuṇīs where, during a time other than the *varṣā* retreat, robes are obtained as an offering for the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, and if no bhikṣuṇīs are present, the bhikṣus should divide them.
If a bhikṣu dies at a bhikṣu’s residence outside of the rainy-season retreat (varṣā), and there are no other bhikṣus present, the bhikṣuṇīs should divide [the inheritance].
If a bhikṣuṇī dies at a bhikṣuṇī’s residence outside of the rainy-season retreat, and there are no other bhikṣuṇīs present, the bhikṣus should divide [the inheritance].
It is likewise with all offerings received during the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat).
There was a disciple of a non-Buddhist who had gone forth within the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya; his kinsmen all spoke thus:
"Why have you abandoned our path to Arhatship to go forth among the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas?"
"I must go back and retrieve it! He further said,
"If he hears of this, he might perhaps flee."
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, do not break their *anvāraṃbha* (rainy-season retreat); if you go to fetch it at that time, you will certainly obtain it without doubt.
When that bhikṣu heard this, he did not know what to do and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I permit you to break the rains retreat and depart.
That bhikṣu then traveled from one residence to another, not knowing where he should receive his share of the offerings for the rains retreat. He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If one has resided for many days in a place, one should receive one's share from there.
There were two bhikṣus traveling together on a road; one bhikṣu fell ill, and while the other was attending to him, he passed away.
The bhikṣu who had attended to the sick person took his robes and bowl and went to the Buddha’s presence, reporting the matter to him.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:

“Attending to the sick is extremely difficult; I now authorize that one’s three robes and bowl be bestowed upon another through a formal act consisting of a motion and two proclamations (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).”
A bhikṣu shall announce: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Bhikṣu So-and-so has passed away;
his three robes and bowl are now present and should be divided by the Saṃgha, but they are now being given to the attendant who nursed him."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus as a formal motion:
'Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!'"
"A certain bhikṣu has passed away; his three robes and alms bowl are now present and should be distributed by the Saṃgha, yet we shall now give them to the attendant who cared for him.
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak."
The Sangha has already granted the robe and bowl to the bhikṣu so-and-so;
the Sangha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.

There was a certain bhikṣu who was indolent; from the beginning he did not assist in communal affairs, nor did he attend upon his upādhyāya or ācārya. When he fell ill, there was no one to look after him; his body was fouled by excrement and urine, becoming impure, foul-smelling, and filthy.
The Buddha, while inspecting the rooms, saw him; he personally bathed him, washed his clothes, removed all impurities, and helped him lie upon the bed, comforting him by his side:
"Do not be afraid!"
"You shall certainly not pass away with this life.

Having heard this, that bhikṣu was filled with joy. The Buddha further taught him various sublime dharmas, whereby he became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Ānanda:
"Why is there no one to look after the bhikṣu in such-and-such a room?
Ānanda answered the Buddha in full detail regarding the matter, and the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"What you have done is contrary to the Dharma!
Monks have no parents; if they do not look after one another, who will look after you?
From now on, I allow monks to look after those who are ill."
The bhikṣus did not know who should attend to the sick, so they reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"A disciple should attend to his preceptor (upādhyāya), and a preceptor should attend to his disciple."
"Ācārya, it is the same for one who shares the same Upādhyāya and Ācārya.
There was a visiting bhikṣu who was ill; he had no Upādhyāya, no Ācārya, no fellow disciples, and no one to look after him.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"One should first exhort a single person to look after it. If there is no such person, one should appoint a person in turn each day. If they are unwilling, they should be dealt with according to the Dharma."
At that time, the bhikṣus vied with one another to go and look at him, thereby disturbing and troubling the patient.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "You should not do so!"
"Two or three people should go together to attend to whatever is appropriate for the patient's care.
At that time, it was difficult for the attendant to obtain medicine, yet the patient refused to take it, thereby obstructing and neglecting their practice of the Path.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There are five conditions that make it difficult to care for a sick person:

being unable to moderate one's food intake; being unwilling to take medicine appropriate for the illness; being unwilling to describe the symptoms of the illness to the caregiver; not following the caregiver's instructions; and being unable to constantly contemplate impermanence."
There are five things that prevent one from being able to nurse the sick:
not knowing the medicine appropriate for the illness;
and being unable to obtain food suitable for the illness.
They are unable to preach the Dharma to the sick to instruct, benefit, and gladden them;
they loathe the excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva of the sick;
they attend to them for the sake of profit, rather than with a heart of compassion.

There were certain attendants who, whether acting on behalf of the patient or for their own private purposes, departed; after they had gone, the patient passed away, and others took possession of his robes and bowl.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not give it to just anyone; it should be given to the one who has attended to the patient until the end.
There was once a bhikṣu who was ill, and there were many people attending to him.
The bhikṣus did not know how many people were entitled to receive the robe, so they informed the Buddha about this.
The Buddha said:
“If a bhikṣu passes away, the robe should be given to two persons:”
To bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras,
even if they be one's parents or brothers, [the robe] should not be given.
If a bhikṣuṇī has passed away, one should give her robes to three persons:
"Bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇerīs.
Then the bhikṣus divided the goods of the śrāmaṇeras who had attended to the sick, giving one-third to the śrāmaṇeras.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "It should be distributed equally.
There was a bhikṣu who had passed away who had previously made a formal gift of his robes to the bhikṣus; however, the bhikṣus were unwilling to return them.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If those [items] were originally given by someone who was not a relative, out of a kind intention, they should all be returned.

At that time, after Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had completed their *pravāraṇā*, they were traveling about with their attendants, followed by many bhikṣus from their shared retreat and neighboring residences.
When the laypeople saw this, each of them thought,
"I shall offer an *an-ga-nyi* (summer retreat robe) for the Saṃgha on behalf of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
They immediately made the offerings, and [the monks] obtained a great deal.
The bhikṣus at that place where the gift was received said to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana,
"Let us divide these robes together. They replied:
"We have not entered the same *varṣā* retreat; we can only obtain food, but we have no share of these robes.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should divide them equally among yourselves."
At that time, after Udayin and Bhaddāla had completed their *pravāraṇā*, they were also traveling about with a large number of bhikṣus.
When the laypeople saw them, they said:
"If a bhikṣu has observed the rains retreat at our residence, we shall give this robe as an offering."
The acquisitions were also many, and those visiting bhikṣus asked to share them;
he replied, "These have been given to the bhikṣus who are observing the rains retreat within my boundary; they cannot be given to you."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should not divide it among yourselves.

At that time, there was a merchant who, carrying *cīvara* (woolen garments), came from the country of Pāri to Kauśāmbī. Having heard that the Buddha had appeared in the world and possessed great majestic power, and that his disciples were likewise so, he brought a large quantity of *cīvara* robes as an offering to the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus said,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept kṣauma garments.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I shall listen and receive it.
Again, he separately offered some to the Elder, who also did not dare to accept it, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to separately accept *kambala* robes."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I also permit you to receive [the precepts] separately. At that time, Visākhā said:

"If you reside in the dwelling I have prepared for you, you should wear and use my three robes, undergarments, cloak, rain-bathing robe, wound-covering robe, single-layered mat, bedbug-preventing cloth, and mosquito net; you must not wear or use the robes of others."
The bhikṣus thought that this belonged to the Saṃgha of the four directions and did not dare to wear it directly against their bodies.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If the donor is present, I allow you to wear it directly against the body."
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who offered their robes, bowls, and other belongings to the bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus did not dare to accept them.
The bhikṣuṇīs said, "Where else shall we seek a field of merit?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to accept them according to your own preference.
At that time, the bhikṣus obtained robes with cotton cloth for the warp and *kambala* wool for the woof, yet they did not dare to accept them.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I permit you to accept them.
At that time, in Śrāvastī, there were people who worked with *kambala* wool; seeing the bhikṣus wearing *kambala* robes, they spoke to them, saying:
"The robes worn by the Venerable One, if washed and pounded so that the nap appears, will have an exceptionally fine and bright pattern.
The bhikṣus did not dare to do so and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to wash and pound them; if you do not know how, I allow you to hire someone."

There were some bhikṣus who were washing and treading *kambala* woolen cloth in an open space. When the white-robed laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled them, saying, "These bhikṣus are exactly like the masters who tread *kambala* wool!"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"One should tread upon it in a secluded place.
When they wished to cut the edge of a *kambala* (woolen garment) but did not know with what to do so, they reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"You should make scissors.
When the white-robed laypeople saw the bhikṣus wearing robes woven with variegated-colored thread, they criticized and reviled them, saying:
“What distinguishes the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, from the people of the world?
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“One should not wear robes woven with multicolored threads; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense.”
There was a woman whose children died as soon as they were born. Later, she gave birth to a son and took him to the bhikṣus, seeking a monastic robe for him to wear.
The bhikṣus did not dare to give it to him, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I permit you to give it to him."
There was a certain monk of little learning who had no robes; when several women begged for them, he could not give them any.
They said, "We shall provide the material ourselves; dye it for us."
The bhikṣus did not dare to dye them, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I allow you to dye them.
At that time, the parents of Piṅgalavatsa were poor; they wished to offer him robes for his support, yet they did not dare to do so.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a person were to carry their father on the right shoulder and their mother on the left shoulder for a hundred years, even while discharging excrement and urine upon them, and were to provide them with the most exquisite worldly food, clothing, and offerings, they still could not repay even a moment’s worth of their kindness."
"From this day forward, I permit all bhikṣus to provide for their parents with all their heart and for as long as they live.
If one fails to provide such support, one shall incur a grave offense!
— *The Five-Part Vinaya*, Scroll 20.
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, Fascicle Twenty-one.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Jibin during the Song Dynasty,
together with Zhu Daosheng and others.
The Fifth Section of the Third Division: The Rules on Robes (Cīvara-vastu). At that time, the Śākya kingdom still adhered to its ancient custom of not intermarrying with those of any other clan.
King Prasenajit, coveting their lineage and relying on the strength of his army, dispatched an envoy to declare:
"If you do not grant me a marriage alliance, I shall destroy your kingdom."
The Śākyas deliberated together:
"By what means may we avoid his cruelty while not violating our country's ancient customs? They all said:
"It would be fitting to select a fine maidservant of beautiful appearance, most exquisitely adorned in worldly finery, and known as a member of the Śākya clan, and bestow her upon him.
Following this deliberation, they immediately provided King Prasenajit with the full ceremonial rites to escort her away.
Later, he gave birth to a son whose countenance was exceptionally outstanding. The king commanded the various physiognomists to establish a name for him based on his physical characteristics.
The physiognomists said, "The King originally obtained his mother through his majesty; according to this meaning, he should be named Vaidūrya."
When he reached the age of eight, the king, wishing to provide him with an education, had this thought:
"Among all arts, archery is the most excellent; within the realm of Jambudvīpa, only the Śākya clan possesses it."
When the Buddha was a bodhisattva, he shot an arrow for one yojana and another for one krośa; Śakramāna shot for one yojana, while those of the lowest skill did not fall short of one krośa.
"I shall have my son go to study under his maternal uncle!
He then commanded the sons of the great ministers to attend upon the Prince, and to request from Śākyamuni the art of archery.
At that time, the Śākyas had newly constructed a great hall and made a solemn agreement:
"We shall first offer it to the Buddha and his disciples; only thereafter shall we occupy it."
Prince Vaidūrya entered the pleasure grove with his retinue to sport there. When the Śākyas saw him, they spoke with angry indignation:
"You low-born son of a slave! We do not consider you a worthy field of merit!"
"How is it that the World-Honored One has dared to take his seat in front of us before we have even entered?
Prince Virūḍhaka was filled with great resentment and commanded a man, saying:
"Keep this in mind; when I become king, report this to me at once!"
He then departed immediately.
Later, the Śākyas excavated the earth of the hall and replaced it with new ground; thereafter, they invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to partake of a meal therein and preached the sublime Dharma.

Having mastered the art of archery, Prince Vaidūrya returned to the city of Śrāvastī; among the youth, he immediately succeeded to the royal throne, and those with whom he had previously studied were all appointed to high-ranking positions.
The minister who had previously received the instruction then addressed the king, saying:
"Does Your Majesty remember when the Śākyas reviled you at such-and-such a time? The king said:
“I remember! The minister spoke again, saying:
“If we do not report this now, what more do you wish to wait for?”
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately arrayed his fourfold army and went forth to wage war against the Śākyas.
When the World-Honored One heard of this, he sat down by the roadside beneath a shadeless śiṃśapā tree.
The king saw the Buddha from afar, descended from his carriage, and approached on foot. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
There are many fine trees; for what reason do you sit beneath this tree that provides no shade?”
The World-Honored One replied, “The joy of the protection of one’s kinsmen.
Knowing the Buddha’s intention and out of compassion for the Śākyas, the king immediately turned his army back; he did this a second time as well.
The minister again addressed the king as he had before, and the king immediately prepared his carriage to go and attack the Śākyas.
However, the Buddha, knowing that the Śākyas' karmic retribution from past lives was unavoidable, stayed behind and did not come out.

When the Śākyas heard that King Virūḍhaka was coming to invade their kingdom, they also arrayed their fourfold army and went out to meet him in battle. At a distance of one yojana, they shot arrows at him; some passed straight through his ears, others cut off his hair, shaving it completely away until not a trace of beard or mustache remained, and all his weapons were simultaneously shattered and destroyed, yet without wounding his flesh.
King Virūḍhaka asked his attendants,
"How far is it from here to the Śākyas? They replied:
"Retreat one yojana from here.
The king, greatly terrified, said:
"If such is the case even before the vanguard has engaged, our army will be utterly defeated once we come into contact with them!"
"It would be better to return to our own country; it would be fortunate if we could ensure our own survival.
At that time, one of the ministers said:
"The Śākyas all observe the five precepts; they would rather lose their own lives than ever harm a living being."
"Your Majesty, simply advance your army; do not worry about defeat or loss!
The King immediately followed this advice and commanded his troops to move forward.
The Śākyas returned to the city, closing the gates to defend themselves. King Virūḍhaka sent a messenger to say:
"If you open the gates immediately, there shall be those who escape;
if I capture the city through assault, not a single person shall be spared.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana, hearing that King Virūḍhaka intended to attack Śrāvastī, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I pray that the Buddha will allow me to manifest an iron cage and enclose that great city!
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
“Although you possess supernormal powers, how could you possibly alter this karmic retribution resulting from fixed causes and conditions?”
The Buddha, based on this principle, spoke these verses:
"Whether karma be black or white, it never decays;
though long deferred, it must inevitably arrive, and one shall experience its results right here before one's eyes."
Neither in the sky nor in the midst of the sea, nor by entering into mountain clefts,
can one find a place where one may escape the calamities of past karma;
for one is led by the force of retribution, whether near or far, deep or hidden.
"They will naturally enter therein; wherever they go, there shall be no lack of resolve.

At that time, the Śākyas, seeing the enemy army's great strength, were divided: some said to open the gates to accept their surrender, while others said to hold fast and defend to the death. In this state of indecision, they cast lots together, following the majority.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas was among the crowd at the gate; he took up the voting sticks seven times, and as the sticks for opening the gate were in the majority, the gate was immediately opened.
Once King Virūḍhaka had gained the city, he issued an order to his three armies:
"Kill every member of the Śākya clan; however, be careful not to harm anyone who is not of the Śākya clan!"
When the three hundred million Śākyas heard this, they all took up reeds and cried out,
"I am a Śākya who holds a reed!
The gatekeepers believed them and released them, allowing them to depart.
Thereupon, Śreṇika Bimbisāra went to King Virūḍhaka; as the king regarded him as his maternal grandfather, he addressed him, saying:
"Grandfather! What boon do you seek?"
He replied, "I pray that you no longer kill my kinsmen!
The king said:
"This cannot be obtained; let us seek another boon!
He spoke again:
"I pray that from the moment I submerge into the water until I emerge, you will allow all those who come out during that interval to go free; whoever emerges shall no longer be killed."
King Vairāṭa thought to himself, "It is but a brief moment beneath the water; why should it not be possible?
He then granted his permission.
Śreṇika then untied his hair, submerged it in the water, and tied it to the roots of a tree in the water, whereupon he did not emerge again.

The king, wondering why he had been gone so long, sent someone into the water to look for him; they saw that he was already dead, with his hair tied to the roots of the tree, and reported this to the king.
The king then sighed in admiration, saying,
"You are truly able to disregard even your own life for the sake of your kin!
He immediately issued a proclamation to the three armies:
"If there be anyone else who kills a member of the Śākya clan, he shall be punished according to military law.
At that time, the bhikṣus heard that King Virūḍhaka was slaughtering the people of the Śākya nation, and they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“King Virūḍhaka is foolish!
Seven days from now, he shall suffer the consequences of his crime against the student, and his entire retinue, great and small, shall likewise lose their lives.”
Upon hearing these instructions from the Buddha, King Vairāṭa thought to himself, "The Buddha does not speak in vain; while other sufferings may still be endured, I fear only being burned by fire!

He immediately boarded a boat with his retinue and entered the Ayiravatī River. When the seven-day period arrived, the waters suddenly surged in a violent flood, whereby they were submerged and all died at once.
The remnants of the Śākyas, stripped bare to the flesh, went to where the bhikṣus were and said:
"We are of the Śākya clan; we are the kinsmen of the World-Honored One."
"We pray for a small amount of clothing!
The bhikṣus did not dare to give it to them, thinking:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to give clothing to the Śākyas."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to give them. Later,
there were five lay followers (*upāsaka*) who observed the five precepts and, having been robbed, came to the bhikṣus to borrow robes.
The bhikṣus did not dare to lend them, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to lend the robes of upāsakas.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Listen: if it is returned, you should take it back;
if it is not returned, then give it away.”
At that time, because of a gift for the sake of the rains retreat, Upāli’s brother, Bhadanta, entered the rains retreat at two locations.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
“He should receive half a share from each location.”
At that time, while the bhikṣus were traveling on the road, they did not gather up their robes; the robes dragged along the ground, becoming soiled and torn.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do so; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
"You should make a bag to contain it.
The bhikṣus made bags that were too long and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "You should not do so!"
"The front should reach as far as the navel, and the back as far as the waist.
The bhikṣus made robe-bags out of expensive materials and informed the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said, "You should not do so!"
"One should use coarse materials to make them.

While some bhikṣus were traveling on the road, they sought someone to carry their robes, or they themselves carried others' robes; as a result, they either lost their own robes or lost those belonging to others.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "You should not do so!
If you hire someone to carry your robes, you must first show them to him."
"If one carries clothes for others, one should take them out and inspect them.
The bhikṣus placed the clothes inside bags and sewed their openings shut; consequently, when they wished to retrieve them, it was difficult to do so.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do so! You should make a belt and fasten it."
"If it is not for constant use, sewing it is also permitted.
The bhikṣus placed their kṣauma and kārpāsa garments in one place together, where insects were born and gnawed them to ruin.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should place cotton between the *kambala* and the *kṣaumā*, and then insert within it various insect-repelling fragrances such as *kuśīra*, *nābhi*, and *haricandana*."
Later, when the bhikṣus took up the robes, they did not recognize them. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should mark them with a name and make a sign.

If a bhikṣu has deposited a robe for twelve years and does not come back to claim it, the Saṃgha should assemble and appraise its value; it shall then be used for the sake of the Saṃgha of the four directions."
"If that bhikṣu returns later and uses property belonging to the Saṃgha from the four directions to repay it, it would be well if he does not accept [the current gift].
At that time, Ānanda received the offered robe but had no need for it; he accepted it on behalf of Śāriputra and immediately sent a bhikṣu to deliver the robe to him.
That bhikṣu thought to himself:
"Śāriputra has received many offerings, yet I have no robes.
I shall now take them by means of consent!"
He then put it on. Later, he became doubtful and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Although he received it for him, he has not yet relinquished it."
If one takes and maintains [an object] from a bhikṣu with whom one has reached an agreement, it is not a proper taking and maintaining;
if one takes and maintains [an object] from a bhikṣu who has already received it, this is a proper taking and maintaining.
Ānanda, having obtained a waist-belt that he did not need, accepted it for Aniruddha; he then sent another bhikṣu with it, saying:
"This belt now belongs to Aniruddha."
That bhikṣu also reflected as before and subsequently gave rise to doubt.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Since he has already stated that it belongs to Aniruddha, it is considered already relinquished."
If one takes possession with the consent of the bhikṣu to whom it is given, that is a proper taking of possession;
if one takes possession with the consent of a bhikṣu who is capable [of giving], that is not a proper taking of possession.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not wear undergarments but wore the monastic robes directly over their bodies; they became soiled and filthy, and were gnawed by rats.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do this; whoever violates this rule commits a duṣkṛta offense."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus made undergarments for themselves that were either the same size as a saṃkakṣikā or like a nirvāṇa-saṅghāṭī.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "You should not do so!"
It should be performed in three ways:
the superior method is to cover from the head down to the ankles, spreading the left hand to cover them so that they are completely concealed;
the middling method is to cover from the head down to the mid-calf, extending the left arm to cover it as far as the wrist.
The lower robe should cover from the head down to the knees; when spread out to cover the left arm, it should reach about half an elbow.

However, the bhikṣus did not use their inner robes to cover their right shoulders, but instead wore the monastic outer cloak over them; consequently, it became soiled and filthy, and was gnawed by rats.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should not do so!

There were some bhikṣus who, while receiving the scriptures or when paying their respects to their preceptors (upādhyāya) and teachers (ācārya), wore the monastic cloak (saṃghāṭī) with one shoulder bared, causing it to hang down to the ground.
Sometimes, when rising to walk at night, they were unable to lift [the robes] properly and left them lying on the ground, where they became soiled with mud and dirt.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When receiving the scriptures or paying respects, you should bare one shoulder and lift [the robe] so that it is clear of the ground."
"When rising at night, you should gather up and fold the outer robe so as not to let it become dirty.
The bhikṣus wore the saṃghāṭī robe, and when it became torn, they did not mend it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be repaired.
Not knowing who should perform the repair,
the Buddha said:
"If [these items] are used during the four months of winter or the three months of summer, they should be repaired.
There were some bhikṣus living in forest hermitages who, when departing, did not put away the monastic bedding, causing it to rot and decay.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be entrusted to a village.
If there is no place to entrust it, you should return to being the owner of the dwelling."
"If there is fear or apprehension, and the people of the village all move away, one should likewise transport [the bedding] to a place of safety.
However, because the bhikṣus did not look after their bedding while departing, it became scattered and lost.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"You should follow them and look after them.
Once they had reached a place of safety, those monks neither gave them rooms to stay in nor allowed them to settle their belongings in rooms.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should give them to all.
If the former location is no longer established, one should use them right there where they currently reside."
"If it is later restored, one should bring back the remainder;
if it has been completely exhausted with nothing left, the bhikṣus at that location should give a small or large portion from their own supplies.
There were some bhikṣus who used bedding and furniture belonging to this room for use in that room.
The owners of the various rooms rebuked him, saying:
"How can you take the property of my room and use it in another room?
This is precisely taking what is not given!"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "One should not do so!

There were some visiting bhikṣus who wished to pay their respects to their teachers and receive instruction in the sūtras; they took the bedding and requisites from their own quarters to those [teachers'] rooms, but the resident bhikṣus would not allow it.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should first speak to the bhikṣu of the original room; if he consents, it is well.
If he does not consent, one may nevertheless take it with him."
"If they travel far away from there, they should be sent back to their original rooms.

There were some bhikṣus who, wearing the saṃghāṭī robes, entered the heated bathhouse and the kitchen, entered the midst of the Saṃgha for meals, or went to relieve themselves nearby, where they were smoked out and soiled with mud.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should not do so!
There were some sick bhikṣus who needed to wear [the robe] while going to various places, yet they did not dare to do so; they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If you have an illness, you are permitted to wear them while traveling to other places, provided you protect them well.
However, you must not wear them while voiding excrement or urine."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, wearing their upper and lower robes and carrying pieces of cloth five fingers wide, entered a village without their three robes.
When the other bhikṣus saw this, they asked them:
"Has the World-Honored One not prohibited entering a village without wearing the three robes?"
The group of six bhikṣus then showed them pieces of cloth, saying,
"These are our three robes.
The elder bhikṣus rebuked them in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: "It is true."
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"One must not do so; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta*.
From now on, it is permitted to make three robes—superior, middling, and inferior—in the dimensions of an undergarment.
At a certain monastery, the Saṃgha obtained cloth suitable for distribution, yet one bhikṣu took it to the boundary altar (*sīmā*) and took possession of it alone.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This should not be done; one who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
The present Saṃgha should divide [the property]."

There was an elder bhikṣu traveling through the countryside with a group of bhikṣus; among them were both guests and residents, and they obtained a small amount of cloth to be distributed, which was insufficient for distribution.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The resident bhikṣus should say to the visiting bhikṣus: 'Elders!'"

"This robe is too small to be divided. If the visiting bhikṣu says, "Take it all and give it to me," [the resident bhikṣu should respond: "I cannot do so. If he insists, saying, "I will take it back later," [the resident bhikṣu] may give it to him. If he does not insist, he should not give it. If he gives it anyway, he commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If the visiting bhikṣu says, "Take it all and give it to me," and the resident bhikṣu gives it to him, there is no offense. One should take it;
however, if he says,
"I will not give even a single thread," [one should not take it].
"Then it should be divided among us.
It was the same when a visiting bhikṣu spoke to a resident bhikṣu.
There was a bhikṣu who took a shroud from a burial mound; the owner of the mound lost his garment and went to inquire about it.
"Who has taken my shroud from the burial mound? Someone replied,
"The bhikṣus have taken it!"
He then rebuked him in anger, saying, "The bhikṣus have stolen the robes of my ancestors!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not take them!
However, if the village has moved away and they remain there later, you are permitted to take them with the intention that they are *pāṃsukūla* (rag-robe) materials.
There were also bhikṣus who took banners and canopies from within shrines; the case was treated in the same manner.
There were some bhikṣus who went to a place of battle to take the clothes of the dead; the soldiers rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣus wish for us to kill many people!"
When the elder bhikṣus heard of this, they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "One should not do so!
There were some bhikṣus with few acquaintances who wished to go to a battlefield to take the clothes of the dead, but they did not dare to go.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I permit you to take [the requisites] after the soldiers have departed.

There were some laypeople who, after the soldiers had left, went to collect the remains of their kinsmen's corpses; they saw that all the dead bodies had been stripped and flayed, such that they could no longer be recognized, and they spoke with reproach:
"How is it that a bhikṣu strips my kinsman of his clothing?
If he has any clothes, they should be recognized.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When no one is watching, take it.
This was also the case when taking robes at the place where someone had been killed.
Some bhikṣus took the robes of the deceased and, without altering them, kept them as their own bhikṣu robes.
When the laypeople saw this, they said,
"This is the clothing of our own kinsmen!
and they began to weep.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should quickly dismantle it to make robes for the bhikṣus and keep them;
if it is an iron vessel, you should quickly fashion it into large or small bowls, door-hooks, or whatever other items are required."
There was a very wealthy family whose property thieves plundered but could not carry away entirely; they left some behind, hidden among the refuse.
Later, wishing to retrieve it, they did not dare to approach during the day, but instead waited and watched from afar.
There was a bhikṣu who, while gathering discarded rags, arrived at a place where goods were stored; seeing the corner of a garment protruding, he took it.
From afar, a thief said to him:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"Do not take my things.
When the family that had been robbed heard this, they recognized him as the thief, bound him, and sent him to the authorities; the authorities then executed him.
While being bound, the thief spoke these words:
"If this bhikṣu had not taken my robe, how could he have recognized me?
This bhikṣu has killed me; it was not that man!
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If it is heavy when lifted, one should not take it.

There were some bhikṣus who walked while looking at the ground in the streets and alleys; when laypeople saw them, some said they were searching for money, while others said they were searching for discarded rags (pāṃśukūla).

A disciple of a non-Buddhist teacher wrapped some money in a cloth and placed it on the road; when a bhikṣu saw it, he picked it up and then said to the crowd, "These bhikṣus are indeed searching for money."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not take articles wrapped in cloth from the streets.
There was a bhikṣu who, for the sake of clothing, went to a cemetery and saw a newly deceased woman with a casket before her head.

The bhikṣu thought it was an empty box, so he took it and brought it back. Upon arriving at his dwelling and opening it to look inside, he saw various articles for adorning the body; not knowing what to do with them, he reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "When taking [an object], one should first open it and inspect it; if one takes it without inspection, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There were some bhikṣus traveling on a road with non-Buddhists who were killed by bandits.
The bhikṣu then took that garment and made it into a bhikṣu’s robe without altering its color.
When other non-Buddhists saw this, they said, "This is the robe of our kinsman; the bhikṣus must have killed him to take it!"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not accept it!
If you have already accepted it, you must immediately dye it to change its color and make it into a bhikṣu’s robe."
There were some bhikṣus who had few desires and were contented, and they did not accept robes offered by householders.
The householders made this deliberation:
"By what means can we cause those bhikṣus to accept the robes we offer?"
While it was being torn apart and burned, he placed it here and there in the streets and alleys; then, waiting for him to enter the village, he said:
"Look to your left and right; if you see anything, take it."
They then acted according to their deliberation.
When that bhikṣu saw this, he thought to himself:
"We do not accept robes as gifts from householders; these must surely have been made for us by the lay devotees."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should take it while maintaining the perception that it is refuse.
A certain bhikṣu passed away, and the bhikṣus laid him out in the central courtyard without covering him with robes; his body was exposed, and his male organ became engorged.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled him, saying:
"The Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya), for they have caused the male organ to become so large.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not leave it exposed to the elements; it should be covered with a robe. Whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
A certain corpulent bhikṣu passed away, and the bhikṣus placed his body upon living grass. His fat oozed out and spread about, killing the living grass.
The various non-Buddhist practitioners saw this and criticized them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim to practice loving-kindness; how is it that they now injure and kill living beings?
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not place [the body] upon living beings; it should be buried, or burned by fire, or placed upon a stone.
A certain bhikṣu was swept away and killed by water, and his robes and bowl remained hanging from the branch of a tree within the boundary.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they thought, "This has entered within the boundary of the Saṃgha; it belongs to the Saṃgha," and so they did not dare to take it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to take it as *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) material."

The bhikṣus did not know how many kinds of paṃsukūla (rag-robe) there were, so they informed the Buddha about this. The Buddha said: "There are ten kinds of paṃsukūla: discarded old clothes from when a king ascends the throne;

clothes from a cemetery; clothes covering a grave; clothes from a street; discarded old clothes from a newly married woman; clothes worn by a woman to manifest her virtue at the time of her marriage; clothes from a woman who has recently given birth; clothes chewed by cattle; clothes gnawed by rats; and clothes burned by fire."
At that time, the bhikṣus wore brightly colored robes, which the white-robed laypeople criticized and rebuked. They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"One should not wear brightly colored robes; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
There was a bhikṣu who kept a rain-bathing robe that was less than five cubits in size. He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A rain-bathing robe must not be less than five cubits; whoever violates this incurs a pāyattika offense."
At that time, because various laypeople had shaved the heads of their sons and daughters during the retreat, they offered robes to the Saṃgha.
Having accepted them, the bhikṣus wished to divert the offerings for the purpose of the retreat.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do so! This is called 'giving according to the specific circumstance'; it should be divided among the present community of monks. One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
There were certain bhikṣus who, without relinquishing the three robes they had previously received, accepted other robes;
they then performed the ritual of pure gifting (*viśuddhi-dāna*) for their former robes or gave them away to others.
Later, remembering this, they informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is called 'receiving again,' and it is also called 'pure giving' or 'giving to another';
however, if one does not relinquish [the original], one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

At that time, some bhikṣus had robes subject to forfeiture (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*) which they had neither relinquished nor confessed. These were then consumed by fire, swept away by water, plundered by thieves, or lost and ruined. Not knowing what to do, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"This is indeed called 'renunciation,' yet you must still perform the confession for a *pāyattika* offense.
At that time, the bhikṣus kept robes without having performed the ritual of pure donation (*viśuddha-dāna*). They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not do so; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
At a certain monastery, the community of monks received a gift of brocade.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do with it and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"It should be accepted!
It may be used to adorn a stūpa, or for the purpose of constructing a stūpa, or for the use of the Saṃgha."

At a certain monastery, the Saṃgha wished to divide the robes; however, there was a bhikṣu of few desires who did not accept his share, yet required a waistband, a meditation belt, a cap, and a water-strainer.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“One should give it!
When they had given it and he asked for it again, they reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When distributing items, one should first ask:
'Will you accept this portion?
If they say they will, it should be given to them equally."
"If you say you need a waist-cord or the like, you should be given one-third;
if you ask for more, it should not be given.
There was a bhikṣu who possessed a *kuśeya* robe, while the Saṃgha of the four directions possessed a *saṃghāṭī*. He wished to trade with them, but the bhikṣus did not dare to give it to him.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to exchange it!
If the price of the *kusā* grass is high, the Saṃgha should give the bhikṣu double the amount."
If the price of the saṃghāṭī is high, the bhikṣu should give double the amount to the Saṃgha;
if he is poor and has no means to give double to the Saṃgha, yet he is certainly one who has few desires and is content, it is also permitted for him to give it away.
The same applies to other garments.
At that time, the bhikṣu Revata suffered from cold feet and requested from a certain brāhmaṇa a *kambala* garment to wrap around his feet. Having made the request, he felt doubt:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept forbidding us from requesting garments from those who are not our relatives; I do not know what to do."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"In view of such circumstances, I allow you to beg for those robes that ought to be worn and maintained: namely, the calf-protecting robe, the thigh-protecting robe, the head-protecting robe, and the towels for wiping the hands, face, and body."

At that time, the bhikṣus took robes from the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha of the four directions, from stūpas, and from those who were not in agreement with them, treating them all as if they were in agreement.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not do so!"
One may perform the formal act of taking consent from one's preceptor (upādhyāya), an ācārya, a fellow preceptor or ācārya, or from disciples and those who share the same intention.
There were certain bhikṣus who, while still alive, made dispositions regarding their robes and belongings, saying:
"After my death, I shall give these robes and belongings to so-and-so; these robes and belongings shall be used in such and such a manner."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This should not be done! One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
"Where there is no giving, there is no taking; where there is no using, there is no using.

At that time, Ānanda frequently went in and out of the house of the Malla Luī. Later, when he was not there, [Luī] took a costly *karpāsa* cloth with his consent. Subsequently, Ānanda felt doubt and regret, thinking:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to take robes from laypeople with their consent."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I also permit you to take robes from a layperson with their consent.
At that time, the bhikṣus were separated from their rain-bathing robes and did not know what clothing they should wear when it was time to bathe.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There are five causes and conditions by which one may be exempt from the rain-bathing robe:
when it is not raining; when there is no suspicion of rain; when not crossing water; during mealtime or when ill; and when the robe has not yet been finished."
"There are five causes and conditions by which one may retain one's *saṃghāṭī*:
during rain, when there is doubt about rain, while crossing water, during illness, and while work is not yet finished.
At a certain residence, the Saṃgha wished to divide the robes, but some visiting bhikṣus arrived; because the portion for the resident bhikṣus would have been small, they did not wish to divide them.
They reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"Even if there is only enough for one waist-cord, it should be divided accordingly; if it is too little to be divided, one should perform a formal act of two announcements (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) to give it to a monk who has no robes."
A single bhikṣu shall announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This saṃgha has obtained cloth, or perhaps not cloth; it is now bestowed in its entirety upon the bhikṣu so-and-so."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus as a formal motion (jñapti). 'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"
"Does this monk receive the robe, or is it not a robe, or even if he does not consent? Speak!
The Sangha has already given the robe to the bhikṣu so-and-so;
the Sangha consents, because of their silence."
"Thus shall this matter be upheld.
The Leather-Work Rules, the Sixth Section of the Third Division of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī.
At that time, Mahākātyāyana was dwelling in Mount Parvata in the country of Āśmāparānta.

In that country there was an elder named Śramaṇa Koṭīkarṇa, who had faith and delight in the Buddha-dharma and constantly provided for the bhikṣus. Having seen the Dharma and attained its fruit, he received the three refuges and the five precepts, and regularly entered the saṃghārāma to listen to and receive the teachings of the Dharma.
At that time, the śramaṇa Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa thought to himself in a secluded place:
"As the Buddha has said, those who live at home are stained by attachment and cannot extensively cultivate the holy life;
those who have left the home life are without attachment, just like space."
"What if I were now, within the unconditioned Dharma, to shave off my hair and beard, leave the household life, and study the Path?
Having thought this, he went to Kātyāyana at dawn, prostrated with his head at the teacher's feet, and fully declared his thoughts, desiring to seek ordination and receive the full precepts.
Kātyāyana said, "It is indeed as you say that those who live at home are stained by attachment;
however, for one who has left the household life, observes ascetic discipline, purely cultivates the holy life, sits alone beneath a tree, and always eats but one meal a day."
"You were originally wealthy and lived in comfort; this matter is extremely difficult.
Having heard this, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa returned to his home.
This happened three times, and seeing that his resolve was sincere, [the Buddha] allowed him to go forth.

In that country there were no groups of ten monks; thus, after spending six years as a śrāmaṇera, Kātyāyana used his supernormal powers to assemble a group of ten from another country and conferred the full ordination upon him.
Having received the precepts, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa thought to himself:
"I have heard of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, yet I have not yet had the honor of seeing him; I shall now go to pay my respects to the World-Honored One."
Having reflected thus, he went to where Kātyāyana was, prostrated himself at his feet, and requested permission to go to the Buddha.
Kātyāyana said, "Excellent! I rejoice in your decision."
"You should know that it is now the proper time to inquire after the World-Honored One’s health on my behalf.
Furthermore, I submit these five matters to the Buddha:

First, in the country of Aśmāparāntaka there are no groups of ten monks; although Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa served as a *śrāmaṇera* for six years, he was unable to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). Kātyāyana used his supernormal powers to assemble a sangha from other countries, and only then was he able to receive it. I pray that the World-Honored One will permit the reception of full ordination in this country even when the quorum of ten is not met!"
Furthermore, as this country has much sand, gravel, and thorns, we pray that you will permit the bhikṣus of this country to wear leather sandals with thick soles!
Moreover, as the people of this country all spread skins upon the ground to serve as seats and bedding, we pray that you will permit the bhikṣus of this country to spread skins upon the ground!
Furthermore, the people of this country bathe every day; please permit the bhikṣus of this country to bathe every day as well!

Moreover, there is a bhikṣu who has sent a robe to a bhikṣu in another region; before the robe arrives, another bhikṣu says to the one to whom it was sent, causing that bhikṣu to give rise to doubt, fearing he may commit the offense of possessing an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*). Please dispel this doubt for him!
Thereupon, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa received the instruction and departed.
Having reached the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and conveyed his preceptor’s greetings.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Ānanda, spread out bedding for this visiting bhikṣu!
Ānanda thought to himself:
"Because the Buddha wishes to stay overnight with this bhikṣu, he has me prepare the bedding."

He immediately prepared a bedding within the Buddha’s chamber. The Buddha and Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa stayed together in the same room; during the first watch and the middle watch of the night, they remained silent and spoke no words.
When the final watch arrived, the Buddha thought to himself:
"This son of noble family has his deportment well-restrained; I shall cause him to preach the Dharma."
