He then said to him, "You may preach the Dharma.
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa received these instructions and immediately preached the *Ṣoḍaśārthavargīya Sūtra*. Having finished speaking, he remained silent.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! Is the speech of the people in that country all like this?"
He replied, "There is one who surpasses me.
He asked again:
"Why have you stayed in that country for so long without coming to see me?
He replied, "I have long known the faults and perils of desire; however, due to certain causes and conditions, I was unable to come sooner."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Seeing the faults and afflictions of the world, One should personally act in accordance with the Dharma;
The wise do not delight in evil, While those who do evil do not delight in the good."
Thereupon, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa thought to himself:
"The Upādhyāya has instructed me to inform the Buddha of these five matters; now is the very time to do so.
He then informed the Buddha accordingly.
When the night had passed, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed Yaśas:
"You should further explain the five dharmas that Kātyāyana reported.
Yaśas then explained them once more.
After the Buddha had praised in various ways having few desires and being content, as well as praising the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, it is permitted that in the country of Aśmaka-āpāṇḍu and in all border regions where there are few bhikṣus, five who uphold the Vinaya may confer full ordination;
it is also permitted in places with sand, stones, and thorns to wear leather sandals with thick soles."
It is also permitted, where leather is available, to make leather bedding and mats;
it is also permitted, where bathing is required, to bathe every day.

If a bhikṣu sends clothing to a bhikṣu in another location, even if the recipient bhikṣu has already heard of it, he does not incur the offense of possessing extra robes as long as the clothing has not yet entered his hands.
At that time, the bhikṣus made leather sandals of various shapes and various colors.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"I do not permit the making of leather sandals of different shapes or different colors; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
There were some bhikṣus who made leather sandals from horse hide, elephant hide, and human skin.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I do not permit you to make them!"
"If one uses human skin, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if horse or elephant skin, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, Upananda frequently went to a certain cowherd's house; he put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to that dwelling.
He had a spotted calf; when Upāli (Bhadanta) gazed at it intently, the thought arose in him that he wished to obtain its hide to make a sitting mat.
The owner asked him, "Why do you gaze so intently at this calf?"
He replied, "This calf has a lovely dappled color; it would be quite suitable for making a bedding mat.
He then addressed [the Buddha], saying:
“The Venerable One has always looked after my household; how could I begrudge a single calf and not give it to you?
He then slaughtered the calf in front of its mother and gave it to him.
Having received it, Upāli (Baddhananda) took it back to the monastery, while the mother cow followed behind, lowing piteously as she pursued him.
The bhikṣus asked,
"For what reason does this cow low piteously and follow you? He replied:
“I do not know! He asked again:
“This ox pursues you, yet it does not pursue others; how can you say you do not know?”
He then answered by relating the matter in full.
The bhikṣus censured him in various ways and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned Upananda:
“Is it truly so? He replied, “It is truly so.”
"World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you are not permitted to keep any kind of leather!"
Later, the bhikṣus required small pieces of leather but did not dare to use them. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to use small pieces of leather to make articles."
There were some bhikṣus who, returning from outside, stepped onto the monastic bedding barefoot, leaving it muddy and unclean.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to wear leather sandals when entering and leaving."
There was an elderly and sick bhikṣu traveling along a road with companions through a dangerous area; because he walked slowly, he could not keep up with them.
His companions said to him, "Venerable sir, walk quickly so that you do not fall victim to robbers!"
They replied, "We are old and sick; we cannot walk!
Their companion said:
"There are here elephants, horses, mules, donkeys, camels, carts, and oxen that can be ridden.
The bhikṣus did not dare to do so and reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit elderly and sick bhikṣus to ride them, provided they do not ride female animals."
There were some laypeople who offered a leather carriage to the Sangha, but the bhikṣus did not dare to accept it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to accept it."
"Remove the skin and replace it with another cloth.
There were some laypeople who offered a leather carriage specifically to the Elder, but he did not dare accept it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is also permitted to receive [the meat] privately; the skin shall be removed according to the aforementioned rule.
Some senior and elderly bhikṣus who were ill wished to enter a village riding in a carriage, but they did not dare to do so.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit it.
Not knowing whom to have carry him, he reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Have a *kappiya-kāraka* carry you.
There were some bhikṣus in a place of fear who wished to cross a body of water but had no boat.
A cowherd was driving his cattle across the water, and they spoke to him, saying:
"One may grasp the cow's tail.
The bhikṣus did not dare to do so, and they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Listen, you may grasp [it].
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus grasped the tails of female oxen while crossing water, and they prodded their sores with their hands.
When this was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"It is not permitted to cross water by grasping the tail of a female animal.
There were some bhikṣus who wished to cross water, yet there was no animal available to grasp; not knowing what to do, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to bind grass and wood to make rafts.
From now on, I permit the bhikṣus to possess flotation bags made from either sheepskin or oxhide."
"Both individual monks and the Saṃgha of the four quarters should keep [these items].

While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, King Bimbisāra ruled over the two kingdoms of Magadha and Aṅga, which contained forty-two thousand villages; among the local elites there, none were without faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.

Except for the son of a householder named Śrona in the city of Campā, who possessed a great fortune of two billion coins and was thus called by his contemporaries "Śrona Two-Billion," this person had enjoyed pleasure since birth; his hands and feet were soft and supple, and fine hair grew upon the soles of his feet.
King Bimbisāra thought to himself:
"Within my realm, there is only Ekaśṛṅga who has not yet placed faith in the Buddha-dharma; how should I cause him to believe and rejoice?"
"If I were to go there myself, they would be greatly terrified;
if I were to summon them, they would surely give rise to suspicion and fear.
It is only right that I send word to the sixty eminent families of the city of Campā to come and witness the prince’s wedding; through this meeting, I shall instruct them in the Dharma."
Having thought this, he immediately summoned him.
At that time, his kinsmen all addressed the king, saying:
"Viśvantara has never trodden upon the ground; hair grows beneath his feet like the hair on a person's crown, so he is unable to come in person."
"I pray that Your Majesty will grant a special reprieve for this one person!
The King said, "He may ride upon an elephant, a horse, or a carriage."
He replied, "His body is extremely delicate; he would not even be able to endure it.
The king said:
"Now that the prince is to be married, we must certainly meet him; let your kinsmen all come as they please!
The kinsmen deliberated together:
"We must only dig a canal to allow boats to pass, traveling several *li* per day so that it may not be laborious; thus shall we respectfully fulfill the King's command!"
They then escorted him together to Rājagṛha. His kinsmen addressed the king, saying:
"Viśāṃpati has now finally arrived; we pray that you will grant permission for him to follow the family rites!"
The king asked, "What is your family custom? She replied:
"Spread a robe upon the ground and carry him away by lifting him up. The King said, "So be it!"
He immediately ordered a seat to be spread;
furthermore, he had a fine, soft garment spread out as a cushion and bade him sit upon it.
The king then asked:
"Is it true that hair grows on the soles of your feet?
He replied, "It is indeed so."
"Great King! The king said,
"I wish to see him."
He replied, "I wish for a trustworthy person to examine it!
The king said:
"I wish to see for myself.
He replied, "I pray you,
allow me to stretch out my feet!"
The king said, "So be it!
and immediately extended his feet to show them to the king.
Just as he had heard, the radiance dazzled the king’s eyes so that he could not look at it steadily; struck with a sense of wonder, he thought to himself:
"In my kingdom has been born such a person of great merit!"
Looking around to his left and right, he saw that there were previously three great lay devotees (gṛhapati), with Viśākhā making four.
He asked them:
"Each of you possesses how much wealth to have attained the status of a lay devotee?"
The first person said,
"I have one billion three hundred million coins.
The second person said:
"I have fourteen hundred million," said the third person.
"I have fourteen hundred million, and also a priceless mani-jewel."
Viśāṃpati said: "I have twenty koṭis, as well as five hundred maṇi-jewels and a single maṇi-jewel couch.
The king asked Viśāṃpati:
“From whom did you obtain this? He replied,
“This treasure was not part of my father’s remaining wealth, nor was it acquired through my own efforts.”
"I was sleeping on the high tower, and upon waking, he was already before me.
When the king heard these words, his sense of wonder redoubled.
He further thought to himself:
“The merit of this person can only be known by a Buddha; no one else is able to comprehend it.
He then immediately prepared his carriage and went to where the Buddha was, prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet and addressing him, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"From where did these two billion five hundred mani-jewels and one mani-jewel bed come?
The Buddha said,
"This person was previously in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where he had five hundred celestial maidens with whom he shared the deepest mutual affection."
As they were being born there, the celestial maidens all wondered, "Where has our lord, the deva-son, been reborn?

Observing with their divine eyes, they saw that he had been born here. Each took a *maṇi* jewel and the precious couch upon which he had previously lain, transformed them to match his current body, placed them before him, and departed.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, the king paid his respects, withdrew, and gathered sixty eminent leaders of the city of Campā, saying to them:
“I now appoint Viśāṃpāyana as the foremost householder of that city; you all shall honor him.”
He further addressed Koṭivimśa and the sixty others, saying:
"I have been your king, governing you with the Dharma, and have already provided you with benefits in this present life."
"Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is at Vulture Peak Mountain; each of you should go there to seek the benefit of future lives.
Having received these instructions, they all departed.
At that time, the Elder Sāgata was walking up and down on a flat rock in the mountains when the householders arrived at his location and said to him:
"Venerable One!
Please inform the Buddha on my behalf that Bimbisāra of Campā and sixty householders wish to pay their respects to the World-Honored One.
Sāketas vanished from the flat rock before the householders and reappeared before the Buddha, reporting everything to him in detail.
The Buddha said, "You may go on ahead and prepare a seat upon the flat rock; I shall follow shortly after.
Having received these instructions, he vanished before the Buddha and reappeared by leaping onto the flat rock in front of the assembly of lay devotees, where he prepared a seat for the Buddha.
The Buddha, maintaining his usual dignified demeanor, followed behind on foot.
The lay devotees thought to themselves:
"This bhikṣu possesses great supernormal power; he emerges from and enters into this flat rock as easily as if he were entering water."
They all paid him respect together, yet they remained arrogant toward the World-Honored One.
Once the World-Honored One had arrived and taken his seat, it was according to the constant law of all Buddhas:
first to cause them to give rise to a heart of joy, and only then to preach the Dharma.
The Buddha said to Sāketā, "Rise and fan the Buddha!
He received the instruction and rose to fan him; in a brief moment, he manifested various supernatural transformations, just like Uruvilvākāśyapa.
Still remaining before the Buddha, he prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and addressed him, saying:
“The Buddha is my Great Teacher; I am the Buddha’s disciple.
Having said this three times, he returned once more to his original seat.
Thereupon, the lay devotees thought to themselves:
"If even the supernatural power of a disciple is such as this, how much more so that of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha!"
He then turned his mind toward devotion and looked up with reverence.

The Buddha preached various sublime dharmas for him, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening him; from the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, he attained the pure Dharma-eye while still seated, and received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
Viśāṃpati rose from his seat, went barefoot before the Buddha, and prostrated himself in salutation;
the Buddha then smiled. Sāgata thought to himself:
"For what cause and condition does the Buddha smile?"
Having reflected thus, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha:
"By what cause and condition do you now manifest a smile?
The Buddha spoke to Sāgata:
"From twenty koṭis and ninety-one kalpas ago, it is only now that my feet have first trodden upon the ground.
He asked again,
"By what causes and conditions, for twenty koṭis and ninety-one kalpas, did your feet not tread upon the ground?"
The Buddha said:
"In a past age, there appeared in the world a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Vipaśyin.
His father, the King, governed a city twelve yojanas long and seven yojanas wide, which was populous, peaceful, prosperous, and joyful."
That Buddha was accompanied by a great assembly of sixty-eight thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats residing there; the king invited the Buddha and the saṃgha to eat in his palace every day.
At that time, there was a man in the great assembly named Subīṣa who, together with the multitude, went to the king's presence and said:
"Your Majesty is now performing various meritorious deeds; we pray that you will allow us also to participate in them!"

The king said, "Currently, the community of the Buddha's disciples numbers sixty-eight thousand; I fear you will not be able to provide for them, and might instead cause further distress to the Sangha.
They replied to the king once more:
"I am capable of accomplishing this myself; I pray you will grant me your permission!
The King said, "Excellent!"
Still fearing that it might not suffice, he ordered food to be prepared as usual,
saying, "If they are not provided for fully, you must supplement it with this.
Thereupon, the people prepared offerings that surpassed even the King's own food.
In this manner, for many days, the food prepared by the king was no longer provided.
It was then the turn of Subhadra to prepare the offerings; he had people excavate the road and fill it again with fine, soft soil, which he then plastered with fragrant mud.

On both sides, he erected eighty jeweled pillars, placing various colored *maṇi* gems upon their capitals, hanging multicolored banners, and stretching multicolored canopies that completely covered the road at every point. Various kinds of beverages were also set out along the path.

Within his home, he prepared sixty-eight thousand seats, with one bhikṣu seated upon each; he provided each with five hundred cauldrons of soup as an offering, and bestowed upon each bhikṣu two pieces of karpāsa cloth and a pair of leather sandals.
Furthermore, he built a single dwelling for the Saṃgha of the four quarters, and the bedding and mats spread upon the floor were all exquisitely fine.
The one who was Viśākha at that time is now Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa.
"From this point forward, the blessings he receives among devas and humans will be equal and without distinction.
If you do not see me now, my feet shall not even touch the ground.
At that time, Viśvantara knelt on his right knee and addressed the Buddha:
"I pray that you will grant me permission to leave the household life and receive full ordination!
The Buddha said,
"Have your parents given you their permission?"
He replied, “No. The Buddha said:
"If my parents do not grant their permission, I shall not be able to leave the home life. He replied,
"I shall return home and inform my parents."
The Buddha said,
“Excellent! Now is precisely the right time.”
Thereupon, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and returned to the city of Campā, where he said to his mother:
"I now wish to leave the household life to study the Way."
The mother said,
"Stop, stop! For what reason do you wish to leave the household life?"
I have only you; even in death I would not wish to be parted from you, so how could I bear to be separated while alive?
Now my wealth, treasures, servants, fields, and houses are beyond measure; you may enjoy them at will to perform meritorious deeds and experience the pleasures of the five senses.
After he had entreated her as many as three times, she finally granted her permission.

He prostrated at his mother’s feet, circumambulated her three times to the right, and returned to the Buddha’s presence. There, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, knelt on his right knee, and said to the Buddha:
“My mother has given her consent; I pray that you will allow me to go forth and receive full ordination!”
The Buddha said:
"Come, bhikṣu! Go forth and receive full ordination; cultivate the holy life extensively."
"I have well expounded the Dharma, which can exhaust the source of suffering!
As he spoke these words, two billion hairs fell from his head and beard of their own accord; the saṃghāṭī robe was upon his body, and the alms bowl was in his hand.

Not long after he had gone forth, he practiced walking meditation with such diligence in the Śītavana charnel ground that his feet were wounded and bled; crows followed him, pecking and swallowing the blood.
Then, Viśvantara thought to himself:
"Among the disciples of the Buddha, there is none who excels me in diligence, yet even now I have not attained the exhaustion of the source of all suffering."
"My family is fortunately possessed of much wealth and treasure; I could return to secular life and joyfully perform meritorious deeds.
The Buddha, knowing his thought, descended from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and saw crows pecking at and swallowing his blood.
He asked Ānanda,
"For what reason is there this blood, which crows are vying with one another to peck at? He replied:
"Viśāṃpati was walking here and his foot was wounded, drawing blood.
The Blessed One then went to where he was and asked Viśāṃpati,
"Did you truly have such a thought?"
He replied, "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"I now ask you; answer me as you please.
When you were living at home, were you skilled at playing the lute?"
He replied, “Excellent! He asked again:
"When the strings of a lute are too tight, is the tone pleasant? He replied, "No, it is not."
He asked again,
"When the strings of the lute are loose, is the tone harmonious? He replied:
"Not good! He asked again, "What would be good?"
He replied, "Neither too tight nor too loose; only then will it be good.
The Buddha said:
"It is likewise within my Dharma: through what cause can one attain the Way by being either too lax or too urgent?
If one practices diligence with moderation, one will exhaust suffering before long."
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, Viśāṃpati attained the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya) without remainder right there at the place of walking meditation (caṅkrama).
Because Viśāṃpati’s feet were wounded and injured, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now permit Viśāṃpati to wear single-layered leather sandals.”
Viśāṃpati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I renounce two billion coins, five hundred maṇi jewels, one maṇi jeweled couch, twenty noble ladies, and countless court maidens.”
"If I were to wear single-layer leather sandals, people would criticize me, saying:
'Having renounced such wealth and treasures, he still greedily accepts and wears single-layer leather sandals.
World-Honored One, if you permit all bhikṣus to wear them, I shall wear them."
The Buddha then praised having few desires and being content, praised the precepts, and praised the observance of the precepts; having done so, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to wear single-layered leather sandals."
There were some bhikṣus who wore double-layered leather sandals. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This is not permitted; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus wore leather sandals while walking back and forth in front of and behind their upādhyāyas and ācāryas, and other bhikṣus likewise followed their example.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not wear leather sandals in the presence of one's upādhyāya or ācārya; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
There are circumstances under which it is not an offense to wear leather sandals in the presence of one’s *upādhyāya* or *ācārya*:
if the ground is covered with thorns, if the ground is covered with grass that pricks the feet, if the ground is covered with sand and gravel, when one is ill, or when it is dark.
At that time, the bhikṣus were wearing sandals made of gold, silver, ivory, and stone.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled them, saying:
"These bhikṣus are like kings and high ministers; though they constantly preach few desires and contentment, they now indulge in extravagance without restraint!"
"There is no conduct of a śramaṇa!
You have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they rebuked him in various ways and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"From now on, I do not permit the wearing of sandals such as those mentioned above; anyone who violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense!"
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī.
There was a dwelling place that was low-lying and damp; when leather sandals were worn there, they became putrid and maggots were born within them.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Listen, monks: sandals made of *pāṭala* grass, *kāśī* grass, *mṛdvīkā* grass, *kuśa* grass, and so forth, are permitted.
When the monks put them on, water leaked out from beneath and soaked their feet.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to use raw leather as the inner lining.
There were some bhikṣus who wore wooden sandals and wooden clogs; while walking within the monastery, they made noise and disturbed the bhikṣus who were practicing meditation.
Furthermore, there was another bhikṣu who, wearing wooden clogs, suffered from diarrhea and stepped on and killed a snake at night.
He reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, because of this incident, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"From now on, I do not permit the wearing of wooden clogs or wooden sandals; anyone who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
"It is permitted to wear leather sandals at three places that are not used for walking about:
at the place for defecating, at the place for urinating, and at the place for washing hands and feet.
There were some bhikṣus who wore leather sandals stuffed with cotton; they reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should not be done; one who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
There were some bhikṣus whose big toes were chafed by the nose-piece of their leather sandals. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to insert a soft material into the nose-piece."
There were some bhikṣus whose heels had cracked; they reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to apply bear fat and wrap them with bear skin.
At that time, Pilindavatsa was always walking with single-minded concentration and did not notice that he had stepped on his own toes until they were broken.
The Buddha saw this and addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit the bhikṣus to wear *pūras* (shoes).
The bhikṣus made the soles of their shoes very deep, and the laypeople criticized and reproached them, saying:
"The leather boots worn by this bhikṣu are like our own shoes.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not make the soles too deep; they are permitted to reach up to the ankles."
There were some bhikṣus who made sandals like boots; the laypeople criticized them as described above.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The front [of the sandals] should be open."
There were some bhikṣus who wore painted leather sandals.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not wear them; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
"If you obtain them, I allow you to dye them a discolored color and wear them.

At that time, Revata was traveling among the people in the country of Daṭhabba when he encountered cold snow that caused his feet to become frozen and damaged. He returned to the Jetavana, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha asked,
"Why is your foot like this?
He answered in full detail regarding the matter.
The Buddha asked,
"Do the people of that country have anything to which they are attached? They replied:
"The people of that country wear fur boots and leather sandals.
After the Buddha had praised in various ways having few desires and knowing contentment, and having praised the precepts and the observance of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit those in snowy and cold countries to wear fur boots and leather sandals."
"If there is anything else in that country that you feel attached to, you are permitted to wear it as you please.
There were some bhikṣus traveling through snow and cold whose feet became frostbitten.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to use ghee, salt, and bear fat for ointment, and to make boots from bear skin.
There were some bhikṣus traveling on the road who did not know what to use to carry their provisions.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to use bags made of sheepskin, oxhide, deerskin, or cotton cloth.
There were some bhikṣus who used them to store food, which became soiled; they reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be washed clean.
The bhikṣus then washed the leather bags, but they rotted and became infested with worms. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not wash leather bags; rather, they should be wiped and scrubbed on the inside. If they become clean, that is well;
if they remain unclean, they should not be kept.
There were monks dwelling in forest hermitages who kept leather mats; when wild beasts caught the scent of them, they came and killed those monks.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"In forest hermitages (āraṇya), one should not keep leather mats.
One should take them to the village dwellings to serve as mats for ladders and pathways."
There was a bhikṣu following behind the Buddha who had been pricked in the foot and was unable to walk.
When the laypeople saw him, they said to him:
"Venerable One!..."
"The Buddha has already gone far away; why do you not travel more swiftly?
He replied, "Thorns are piercing my feet, so I cannot walk."
The laypeople asked, "Can you wear this cloak?
The bhikṣu did not dare to put it on, so he went before the Buddha and informed him.
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to wear them.
A certain bhikṣu found a leather sandal among the graves, yet he did not dare to take it.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to take them.
There were some bhikṣus who obtained sandals made of various shapes and colors and from various kinds of leather, yet they did not dare to take them.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"With the exception of human, horse, and elephant hides, it is permitted to take the rest;
provided that their original shape and color are destroyed. If the shape and color cannot be destroyed, they must be kept within the monastery and may not be taken outside."
There were some bhikṣus who, having obtained new leather sandals, did not dare to accept them. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to accept them.
You should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) put them on and walk seven paces; only then may you wear them yourself."
There were bhikṣus whose leather sandals, boots, and shoes were worn out, yet they did not know whom to ask to repair them.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should borrow someone to repair them."
"If there is no one else, a bhikṣu may repair [the items] himself; he is also permitted to keep large and small awls, large and small knives, and thread for sewing leather.
There were some bhikṣus who repaired leather sandals and other such items for bhikṣus who held wrong views. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not work for such persons; one should work for those who possess a sense of shame and desire to train in the precepts."
The bhikṣus did not know what object to use to store their leather tools, so they informed the Buddha about this.
The Buddha said,
"I allow you to store them in a leather bag."
The Mahīśāsaka Vinaya, Volume 21–22,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśa during the Song Dynasty.
Translated together with Zhu Daosheng and others.
Section Seven of the Third Division on Medicines. Regarding medicines: The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣus were afflicted by autumnal diseases. The Buddha, while walking through the quarters, saw them and had this thought:
“Worldly people consider ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar to be medicines; I shall now permit the bhikṣus to consume them.
On this matter, he assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
“From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to consume the four kinds of medicine: ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar.”
The bhikṣus consumed ghee that was bitter and foul-smelling.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to boil it thoroughly; you may boil it yourself or have someone else boil it."
"If there is no pure ground, it is permitted to boil [the ghee] on impure ground.
When the bhikṣus consumed the ghee, they experienced nausea and were about to vomit.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should clear the mouth with whatever is suitable, such as *harītakī*, *āmalaka* fruit, honey, garlic, or flour.
There was a bhikṣu who contracted a fever and ought to have taken ghee, but when the bhikṣus went to beg for it on his behalf, they could not obtain it; instead, they obtained milk.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) prepare the ghee, boiling it until it is cooked and free from the smell of food; it may then be accepted and consumed for seven days."

There was a bhikṣu who suffered from a wind-disorder (vāta) and required oil for his treatment. Although the other bhikṣus sought it on his behalf, they could not obtain oil, but instead obtained sesame seeds.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should have a *kappiyakāraka* (a lay attendant) press the oil so that it is free of any odor of food; having received it, one may consume it for seven days."
There was a bhikṣu who contracted a fever and required rock honey as medicine. Although the bhikṣus begged for it on his behalf, they could not obtain it, but instead obtained sugarcane.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should have a *kappiyakāraka* (pure person) prepare rock honey from it; provided it has no flavor of food, it may be accepted and consumed for seven days."
The bhikṣus did not know when it should be considered cooked.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When you lift it with a ladle and pour it out in a continuous, unbroken stream, it is cooked."
There were some bhikṣus who suffered from wind-related illnesses and required the fat of oxen, donkeys, camels, or sturgeon for their treatment.
When these bhikṣus went begging for these items and could not obtain them, they instead received four kinds of fatty meat.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) should boil it; one should collect the oil and re-boil it.
If it is boiled at the proper time, re-boiled at the proper time, and strained at the proper time, yet received at an improper time, it must not be kept overnight for consumption."
"If it is boiled at the proper time, decocted at the proper time, strained at the proper time, and received at the proper time, it may be consumed for seven days.
There were some bhikṣus who contracted autumnal diseases and required the consumption of medicinal roots.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The use of all root medicines is permitted; fruit medicines are likewise.
There were some bhikṣus who contracted autumnal illnesses and required the use of herb medicines; they reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"All medicinal herbs are permitted for consumption.
A certain bhikṣu suffering from a wind disorder required to induce perspiration; he informed the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said, "I permit you to do so."
There was a bhikṣu with a wind-disorder who required the consumption of various red and white salts; he informed the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to consume them.
There was another bhikṣu with a wind-disorder who required the compounding of urine, oil, ash, and fermented grain-liquor (kaṣāya) to rub upon his body.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to blend [the ingredients] and rub it on.
There was a bhikṣu who suffered from scabies and wished to treat it; he reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Regarding legal proceedings:
there was a bhikṣu suffering from an abscess who needed to incise it with a blade and apply medicine.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:"
“Listen. There was a bhikṣu suffering from a foot ailment who required a bear-skin boot and bear fat for an ointment;
furthermore, he required flour, snake skin, bear fat, and ghee, which were to be placed inside a bitter gourd and soaked therein.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit it for all.
There was a bhikṣu with an abscess in a private part, and a physician incised it with a knife.
As he passed by the Buddha’s dwelling, the physician informed the Buddha, saying,
"The blade has already reached the anus.
The World-Honored One looked at it and said:
"This is a place difficult to guard; if an ordinary person were to die here, one would lose a great benefit.
From now on, it is not permitted to use a blade to break open the private parts; whoever violates this commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense."
There was a bhikṣu who contracted a fever while traveling; the Buddha said:
"He should take emetic and purgative medicines to relieve himself, moderate his food intake, and eat according to his illness."
There was a bhikṣu who suffered from eye disease, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to prepare medicinal ointment for the eyes.
At that time, Revata consumed rock honey at an improper time, and Aniruddha said to him:
"Is it not the case that one should eat only at the proper time? I saw when they were making stone honey that they pounded rice and put it inside.
He immediately became doubtful and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Aniruddha:
"You said that you saw them making stone honey (śarkarā), putting pounded rice into it. Why did they do so?"
He replied, "The ritual procedure ought to be thus.
After the Buddha had praised fewness of desires and contentment in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“If from now on one prepares medicine in this manner, it is permitted to take it at improper times.
Then the Elder Upāli asked the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!
"If *kālabhojana* (medicines taken at the proper time) and *akālabhojana* (medicines taken at improper times) are combined for consumption, at what time should they be taken?
The Buddha said, "They should follow the rules for *kālabhojana*; they must not be taken at an improper time."
"The seven-day medicine and the lifetime medicine are also like this.
He asked again,
"If non-time medicine and seven-day medicine are combined for acceptance, at what time should they be taken?"
He replied: "One should take it from among the non-timely medicines (akālabhaiṣajya), but it must not be consumed after having been kept overnight.
It is the same for life-long medicines (yāvajjīvika)."
He asked again:
"If the seven-day medicine and the lifetime medicine are to be received together, for how long should they be taken? He replied:
"One should take seven-day medicine; it must not be consumed for the duration of one's life.
8. On the Rules of Eating: The *Pañcabhāga-vinaya*, Third Division, Part Eight, on the Rules of Eating. The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, the five bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One! Where should we eat?”
The Buddha said,
"I permit you all to go for alms.
They then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"What vessel should be used?
The Buddha said,
"The use of the bowl is permitted."
At that time, the bhikṣus received non-glutinous rice porridge through alms-seeking, yet they did not dare to accept it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to accept food as you please."

At that time, when the bhikṣus went on their alms-rounds, they obtained various kinds of rice, or various kinds of cakes, or various kinds of parched flour, or various kinds of cooked wheat and beans, or various kinds of roasted barley and glutinous rice, or various kinds of soups, or various kinds of fermented grain-liquor and sauces, or various kinds of salt, or various kinds of meat, or various kinds of fish, or various kinds of milk and curd, or various kinds of vegetables;
or they obtained various kinds of roots, such as lotus roots, and so forth;
or they obtained various kinds of stalks, such as sugarcane, and so forth.
If they obtain various fruits, such as mangoes or coconuts, they must not dare to accept them.
When this was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"I permit you all to accept and eat them according to your own discretion."
The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī.
At that time, there was a famine and alms-food was difficult to obtain. The bhikṣus took their food and placed it elsewhere, only to lose it, whereupon they thought:
"If the World-Honored One would permit us to eat together and stay overnight in one place, we would not suffer such hardship."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to eat together and stay overnight in one place.
Later, when the bhikṣus prepared food in another location and lost it, they thought to themselves:
"If the Blessed One would permit us to prepare food at our residence, we would not suffer such hardship.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to prepare food at your residence."
The bhikṣus hired people to prepare food, giving them both wages and food, yet those people stole again. They then thought:
"If the Buddha would permit us to prepare our own food, we could avoid this expense."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to prepare food yourselves.
Once the bhikṣus had begun preparing food themselves, they sought people to hand it to them and then demanded wages for their labor, thinking as follows:
"If the Blessed One would allow us to carry food ourselves, rather than seeking someone to be hired to deliver it, we could avoid this expense.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to carry food yourselves, provided that you do not seek someone who has been hired to deliver it."
The bhikṣus obtained wooden fruits, but there was no one to hand them over. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to take and eat them with the thought that they are like wood.
The bhikṣus obtained fruits from a pond, but there was no one to hand them over. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen and receive it from the pond water.
When the bhikṣus wished to eat fruit but had no *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to prepare food) to purify it, they informed the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"Listen, first remove the core, and then eat it.
While the Buddha was at Vaiśālī, the World-Honored One suffered from a wind ailment; Ānanda personally cooked medicinal gruel and offered it to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Who cooked this medicine? He replied:
"This was cooked by me.

The Buddha said to Ānanda, "I previously permitted the bhikṣus to eat food prepared together, food prepared at their place of residence, food they prepared themselves, and food they received while carrying it themselves. Do you still employ these practices today?"
He replied, “I still use it.
The Buddha said:
"What you have done is contrary to the Dharma!
I permitted this during the time of famine; how can you still employ this practice now?
From this day forward, whoever violates it commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!"
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī and asked Ānanda:

"I previously permitted the bhikṣus to take wood-fruits with the thought that they were mere wood, to receive pool-fruits directly from the water, and to eat fruits that had been purified by a non-purifier after first removing the pits. Do you still practice these methods today?"
He replied, “I still use it.
The Buddha said:
"What you have done is contrary to the Dharma!
I permitted this during times of famine; why do you still employ this practice now?
From this day forward, whoever violates it commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!"

At that time, there was a female lay follower (upāsikā) in the city of Śrāvastī named Subhī, who had faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma, had realized the Dharma and attained the fruit [of the path], and had taken refuge in the Triple Gem; she constantly invited the entire community of monks to provide them with medicinal broth and medicine.
At a later time, he came to enter the monastery and saw a bhikṣu who had taken emetic medicine.
He asked him,
"Venerable sir!..."
"What do you require now? He replied,
"I am exhausted from vomiting and purging, and I long to eat meat."
He said, "Venerable sir! I shall deliver it tomorrow; please accept it!"
Thereupon, he returned home and sent a man early in the morning with money to purchase meat.
On that day, King Prasenajit had issued a decree:
"Whoever kills [a living being] shall be punished with a heavy penalty."
He was unable to purchase it and returned to report the matter as such.
[The King] gave him more money and ordered him to search for it everywhere, saying:
"Do not calculate the price; even if it costs one coin, if you find something the size of one coin, you must buy it."
Still, he could not be found.
The upāsikā thought to herself:
"I gave my word yesterday; if I do not find him, he may perhaps pass away."
He then took a sharp knife, entered the house, cut the flesh from his thigh, gave it to a maidservant to cook, and sent it to the bhikṣu.
When the bhikṣu received it and ate it, his illness was immediately cured.
Then, when the husband returned from his journey, he did not see his wife coming or going, entering or leaving;
he immediately asked, "Where is Subhadrā? She replied:
"There is an illness within," he said.
He immediately entered and asked,
"What is the nature of your ailment and suffering?"
The wife answered him fully regarding the matter.
Her husband said,
"I fear that for this illness of yours, there is no possibility of recovery!"
"Furthermore, before I die, you should invite the Buddha and the Sangha to partake of a midday meal tomorrow.
The wife said, "Very well!"

He immediately instructed his son-in-law to invite the Buddha and the Sangha; prostrating himself at their feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying, "I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will honor me with a meal tomorrow.
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent. He returned home and prepared many exquisite foods throughout the entire night.

At dawn, the seats were spread out and a messenger was sent to announce that the time had arrived. The Buddha, surrounded by the assembly of monks in front and behind, went to her house and sat upon the prepared seat.
The son-in-law personally offered water for washing, but the Buddha did not accept it, saying:
"Call the upāsikā Subhaddā and have her come out!"
He immediately sent someone to say,
"The World-Honored One calls for you. He replied:
“Please convey my greetings to the World-Honored One on my behalf; I am too ill to come out.
He reported this to the Buddha, yet the Buddha still called for him.

This was repeated three times until he was carried to the Buddha’s presence on a cloth stretcher. Upon seeing the World-Honored One, his sores were immediately healed and his flesh returned to its former color, whereupon he conceived a sense of rare wonder:
"I have such a Great Teacher and fellow practitioners of the holy life!
he thought, and with great joy and exultation, he personally served the food.
When the meal was finished, he offered water for rinsing the mouth, took a small seat, and sat before the Buddha.
The Buddha spoke verses of sympathetic joy for him, just as he had spoken for Vairaṭṭha, and further expounded various sublime dharmas;
having instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened him, he returned to his own dwelling.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked that bhikṣu:
"What did you eat yesterday? He replied:
"Eat meat," he said.
He was asked again:
"Is the meat delicious?"
He replied, "Delicious! The Buddha said:
"You foolish person!
Why did you eat human flesh without asking?
From this day forward, eating meat without asking constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense!"
"If one eats human flesh, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
There were some bhikṣus who ate elephant meat; whenever King Prasenajit’s elephants died, he would invariably send them to the various spirits and deities.
Because the śramaṇas were eating elephant meat, he then began killing all the elephants.
A bhikṣu sent a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) to fetch some meat and bring it back; when the laypeople saw this, they criticized and reviled him, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, eat no meat that they will not consume; they are worse than crows!"
"How can you consume such impure and foul-smelling filth and enter my house?
You have no conduct of a śramaṇa; you have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have done so? They replied:
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
After the Buddha had rebuked him in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From now on, eating elephant meat is a *duṣkṛta* offense!
The same applies to horse meat.
When the various bhikṣus ate lion, tiger, leopard, and bear meat, the wild beasts caught their scent and subsequently killed the bhikṣus.
When the laypeople saw this, they asked,
"Why is it like this? Someone said:
"By eating the flesh of those very species," he rebuked [the monk], and even as before, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, to eat these four kinds of meat constitutes a duṣkṛta offense!"
The bhikṣus ate dog meat, and when the dogs caught the scent, they followed after them and barked.
When the laypeople saw this, they asked,
"Why do the dogs bark specifically at the bhikṣus?"
Someone said, "It was because he ate dog meat.
He then rebuked him, and even informed the bhikṣus as described above.
"From now on, eating dog meat is a *duṣkṛta* offense!
When the bhikṣus ate snake meat, the laypeople criticized and reviled them.
The Dragon King Svayambhū, having transformed himself into human form, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated, and said:
"We dragons possess great supernormal powers and wander through the world assuming various forms and colors.
Now that these bhikṣus eat snake meat, perhaps it was a dragon that harmed the bhikṣu."
"I pray that the Buddha will establish a rule that the bhikṣus shall not eat snake meat!
The Buddha expounded various sublime dharmas for him, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him; having done so, he sent him back to his own dwelling.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the bhikṣus and informed them with the words of the Dragon King Śubhavasu:
"From now on, to eat snake meat is a duṣkṛta offense!"
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, a householder invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha. The elder bhikṣus asked the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”
"If a person invites the Saṃgha, whom exactly are they inviting?
The Buddha said,
"Those who are correctly directed and correctly proceeding— they are all already invited."
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Such people as these exist everywhere—in the four directions and even in the heavens. Might we not be committing the offense of eating separately from the community?"
He then did not dare to go.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one separately invites four or more persons within the boundary, it is called eating in a separate group."
"If one accepts an invitation in succession, there is no offense.
A bhikṣu who had received an invitation thought to himself:
"There are also bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās within this boundary; will I not be committing the offense of eating separately from the community?"
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one invites the Saṃgha, it should consist of two groups for the meal:
bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras."
"If one invites the two assemblies of monks, it shall be a meal for the five groups:
bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs.
There were some ordinary bhikṣus practicing meditation who thought to themselves:
“As the Blessed One has said:
‘If one invites the Saṅgha, those who are correctly proceeding and correctly directed are all included in that invitation.
Now I am but an ordinary person, not yet correctly proceeding or correctly directed; will I not be taking food that was not given?”
They reported this to the Buddha, who asked those bhikṣus,
"Have you not gone forth for the sake of liberation? They replied:
"I am seeking liberation.
The Buddha said:
"When you invite the Sangha, the noble ones and those practicing meditation should all eat."
There were some ordinary bhikṣus who recited the sūtras and thought to themselves, "I am not one who practices dhyāna.
They also gave rise to doubts as described above and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"The reciter of the sūtras should also eat.
Then, some ordinary bhikṣus who assisted with various communal affairs thought to themselves:
"I am not one who practices seated meditation or recites the sūtras."
Again, as before, they harbored doubts and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Those who assist in the communal affairs should also eat.
He then addressed the bhikṣus:
"When inviting the Saṃgha, all members of the community except those who have violated their precepts should eat.
While the Buddha was traveling through the town of Aṇāpinḍada, a high minister there named Bhadra invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha, having prepared many kinds of delicious food and drink.
On the following day at mealtime, he prepared a seat and announced:
"The food is ready; may the Noble One know the time.
At that time, the bhikṣus had already accepted invitations for a previous meal and were all fully satiated.
The Buddha, surrounded by the great assembly before and behind him, went to his house and took his seat; the good young minister personally served the food, yet none of the bhikṣus were able to eat.
The minister said:
"Why do you not eat as much as you please?
Is it because you think there is too little food?"
"Is it because the food does not please your palate?
The bhikṣus replied, "The food is not unpalatable, nor do we say it is insufficient; however, we have already eaten our fill this morning, and for that reason, we are unable [to eat more]."
That minister then spoke with resentment:
"How is it that, having already accepted my invitation, you have eaten your fill elsewhere?
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If you have already accepted an invitation from another, you may drink rice gruel so thin that it does not form characters when written;
if you obtain thick gruel or solid food, you should say to the host:
'I have already accepted an invitation elsewhere; you may give this to others.'"
At that time, the Buddha was traveling together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, proceeding from Rājagṛha toward Vaiśālī.

Between the two kingdoms, there was an elder of Rājagṛha named Hastibhadra, who was traveling from Vaiśālī with five hundred wagons. Seeing from afar that the World-Honored One’s countenance was extraordinary, like a mountain of gold, he felt a heart of joy and approached the Buddha. Prostrating his head at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I have some stone honey that I wish to offer to the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus.
The Buddha accepted it by remaining silent, and he then personally distributed it himself.
The bhikṣus did not dare to accept it, and they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha praised fewness of desires and contentment, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to eat when hungry and to drink water mixed with it when thirsty."
The householder distributed a single jar of rock honey throughout the entire assembly of the Buddha, yet it was still not exhausted. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have distributed this single jar of rock honey throughout the entire assembly, and there is still a remainder. To whom else should it be given?"
The Buddha said, "You may place it upon ground where no grass grows, or in water that contains no insects.
He then followed these instructions and placed it in water free of insects; immediately the water boiled violently, smoke rose up, and it made a sound like iron being cast into water.
The elder was terrified and returned to report this to the Buddha.

The Buddha expounded various sublime teachings for him, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening him—namely, the discourse on giving, the discourse on morality, and the discourse on rebirth in heaven;
he explained how sensual desires are a source of affliction, how household life is a burden of defilement, and how renouncing the world is free from attachment.
Next, he taught him the Dharma that all Buddhas constantly proclaim:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Immediately upon that seat, he became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.

The Buddha proceeded further on his journey and came upon a craftsman whose daughter was skilled at making soup. She invited the Buddha and the Sangha, offering them soup alone as their meal for the afternoon.
The bhikṣus did not dare to eat, saying,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to take soup as our meal.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Listen, you may eat as a subsequent meal with the intention of doing so.
The Buddha gradually traveled on until he reached Vaiśālī and stayed at the Multi-storied Lecture Hall by the Monkey River.

There was a general named Siṃha who was a disciple of the Nirgranthas; hearing that the Blessed One had come to travel in this city and possessed great renown, being titled the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, he exclaimed:
"Excellent! I wish to see such an invitation to the Buddha!

He immediately prepared his carriage and set out. From afar, he beheld the World-Honored One’s countenance, exceptionally sublime like a mountain of gold. He approached the Buddha's dwelling, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Buddha preached various sublime Dharmas to him, including the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; immediately upon these words, he attained the pure Dharma-eye while still seated.
Rising from his seat, he knelt with his right knee on the ground and addressed the Buddha:
"I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will deign to accept my humble meal tomorrow!"
The Buddha accepted this by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, the general returned home and commanded his market buyers:
"Purchase all the dead meat available here, regardless of whether it is expensive or cheap."

Following these instructions, he purchased everything and prepared various kinds of fine food throughout the night. In the early morning, he arranged the seats and went in person to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is ready; may the Holy One know the time."
The Buddha, surrounded by the community of bhikṣus before and behind him, went to his house and sat upon the prepared seat.
The general served the food with his own hands, filled with joy and without distraction.

At that time, when the Nirgranthas heard that General Siṃha had invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha and prepared an abundance of delicacies, they conceived feelings of jealousy. They immediately went through the streets and alleys, crying out with all their might:
"General Siṃha has betrayed his teacher and acted without righteousness; he now serves the śramaṇa Gautama and slaughters oxen and sheep with his own hands to provide offerings."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they did not dare to eat. General Siṃha knelt on one knee and said to the Buddha:
“These Nirgranthas have slandered the Buddha for a long night; as for me, even unto the end of my life, I shall never intentionally kill.”
"I pray that you command the bhikṣus not to harbor any suspicion, but to eat their fill at their own pleasure!
The Buddha then told the bhikṣus:
"Eat as much as you wish."
When the meal was finished and the water for washing had been offered, he took a small seat and sat before the Buddha.
The Buddha recited the verses of rejoicing for him as before, after which he rose from his seat and departed.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"There are three kinds of meat that must not be eaten:
that which is seen, that which is heard, and that which is suspected.
'Seen' means seeing it killed for one's own sake;..."
"Regarding 'hearing' [of the slaughter], it means hearing from a trustworthy person that the animal was killed for one's sake;
regarding 'suspecting,' it means suspecting that it was killed for one's sake.
If one has neither seen, nor heard, nor suspected [the slaughter for one's sake], this is considered pure meat, and one is permitted to eat it according to one's inclination."

If [meat] has been killed for the sake of a bhikṣu, it should not be eaten by that bhikṣu or a śrāmaṇera; however, it is permitted for a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇerī, an upāsaka, or an upāsikā to eat it.
The same applies if it has been killed for the sake of a bhikṣuṇī, an upāsaka, or an upāsikā.

At that time, people from the kingdoms of Magadha, Aṅga, Kāśī, Kośala, Vṛji, Malla, and Sūma, having heard that the Buddha had appeared in the world possessing great majestic power and that his disciples were likewise so, all came and gathered like clouds in the city of Vaiśālī.

In every household within the city, seven-jeweled chariots, horses, and retinues were already so densely packed that there was no room for another; the remaining twelve thousand vehicles could not be accommodated within the city and were stationed outside its walls.

All vied with one another to offer seasonal food, non-seasonal food, seven-day food, and lifelong food to the Buddha and the Sangha; these were piled up in the courtyards until they formed great heaps, sprawling in disorder and covered in dust and mud, where birds and beasts gathered to devour them.
The World-Honored One, while walking through the quarters, saw this and asked Ānanda,
"For what reason are these foods and drinks discarded in the middle courtyard?
He answered in full detail regarding the matter.
“There is no place of safety, which is why this has come to pass.
The Buddha praised having few desires and knowing contentment, and addressed the bhikṣus:
“I now authorize that a central room be designated as a pure place for storing food through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement).”
A bhikṣu shall announce: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This certain room is now designated as the pure place for the Saṃgha’s meal."
"If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha listen with patience.
This is the motion. "Venerable Sangha, listen!"
Now, this [specific] room is designated as the pure place for the monks' meal.
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has already designated such-and-such a room as the pure place for the Sangha’s meal;
since the Sangha consents by remaining silent,
this matter is thus upheld.
After the Sangha had finished eating, the bhikṣus would cook soups and porridge within the hall and prepare medicinal decoctions.
Before and after meals, and during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, there were the sounds of knives and cutting boards, men and women, and the barking of dogs.
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"For what reason are there these various sounds in the room?
Ānanda answered fully according to the facts, and the Buddha rebuked him in various ways, saying:
“How should one prepare food and compound medicines within the monastery’s pure food-storage area?
From now on, anyone who violates this shall commit a *duṣkṛta* offense!

While the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha, the bhikṣus fell ill during the autumn season. In order to prepare medicinal decoctions and dietetic foods according to their ailments, they entered the villages both at the proper time and at improper times. Consequently, they encountered calamities from water and fire, as well as bandits; they faced dangers to their robes and bowls, dangers to their holy life (*brahmacarya*), and dangers to their very lives.
There was a weaver who built a house along the road and wove there. Seeing the bhikṣus entering the village at both the proper and improper times, he said to them:
"If you have anything to do, you may do it here; if you wish to leave anything behind, you may leave it here as well."
The bhikṣus did not dare to do so and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I permit you to construct a *śuddhasthāna* (pure house) in the residence of a layperson.
However, they subsequently caused a disturbance for the host, interfering with his weaving work.
The weaver thought to himself:
"I originally built this house for the purpose of weaving; now that I am unable to weave, I shall instead offer it to the Sangha as a pure dwelling."
He immediately gave it as an offering to the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus, regarding this as a building belonging to the Saṃgha, did not dare to prepare food or compound medicines within it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to prepare food within a 'pure house' (śuddhāvasatha) dedicated to the Saṃgha.
There were some bhikṣus who had newly constructed a dwelling but did not yet have a pure house for the Saṃgha; not knowing what to do, they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If one constructs a new dwelling place, one should first designate a certain area as pure ground (śuddhasthāna), and then food may be placed therein.
Until the *karmavācanā* has been performed, a bhikṣu must not enter it until the dawn light appears."
At a certain residence, the resident bhikṣus had long since departed, and the later-arriving bhikṣus did not know which buildings were considered "pure dwellings" (śuddhāvasatha).
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If a place has been empty for twelve years, I allow the bhikṣus to designate it as a pure dwelling at their own discretion."

There was a certain residence that lacked a purified dwelling for the Saṃgha and had not yet reached twelve years of age; a monk arrived later and did not know where to establish a purified area (śuddhasthāna). He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If there is a place where people do not come and go, or a location that does not require use, one should temporarily designate it as a pure place.
There were some bhikṣus who placed food inside a pure house, and it was stolen by someone.
They reported this to the Buddha, who said:
"One should perform the *karmavācanā* for a central room to establish it as a pure place (*śucisthāna*).
There were some bhikṣus who wished to perform the *karmavācanā* for the interior of a single room's wall to establish it as a pure ground (*śuddhabhūmi*).
They informed the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said,
"I permit it.
There were some bhikṣus who wished to perform a formal ritual (karmavācanā) on a single room, including the area where the roof water drips, to designate it as pure ground (śuddhasthāna).
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit it.
There were some bhikṣus who wished to perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) in the middle courtyard to designate it as a pure area (*śuddhasthāna*).
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit it.
There were some bhikṣus who wished to perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to designate a corner of a room or half a room as pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*).
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit it.
There were some bhikṣus who wished to consecrate a wooden shelf as a pure place for storing food.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is not permitted!
One must rely upon the ground; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
There were certain bhikṣus who wished to perform a formal ritual (karmavācanā) to designate the upper story of a multi-storied building as a pure area (śuddhasthāna).
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This is not permitted; whoever violates this incurs a duṣkṛta offense."
There were some bhikṣus who wished to perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) regarding the area beneath a multi-storied building, as well as to formally designate it as a pure place (*śuddhasthāna*).
They informed the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"I allow it."
There were some bhikṣus who wished to perform a formal act (karmavācanā) to designate a vehicle as a pure place.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This is not permitted; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
There were some bhikṣus who wished to extend the formal ritual (karmavācanā) to include the interior of the monastery grounds as a purified area (śuddhasthāna).
They informed the Buddha about this, and the Buddha said:
"I allow it."
"A *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) should be performed. One bhikṣu should announce:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!"

This dwelling place is shared for communal residence, communal *poṣadha*, and communal receipt of offerings; the Saṃgha now demarcates it as a pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*), with the exception of such-and-such a place.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen.
The announcement is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This is one residential area, with the exception of such-and-such a place."
"Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has finished demarcating this as a pure ground."
The Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.
The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, there was an elder named Munda in the city of Vādi, who possessed great merit; his wife, son, daughter-in-law, as well as his male and female servants, all likewise possessed great merit.
When the elder entered the granary, grain rained from the sky and ceased only after he had emerged;
when his wife took the rice vessels and distributed them among those inside and outside, they were refilled as fast as they were taken, never becoming exhausted;
and when his son grasped the golden purse and poured out the coins, they flowed forth without end.
The daughter-in-law took out one *shu* of rice and obtained enough for the food of everyone inside and outside the household for one month, yet it was not exhausted;
whenever her slave plowed, he would always form seven furrows;
and when her maidservant ground half a *liang* of unguent to smear upon the house both inside and out, it likewise did not diminish or run out.
When people from the four quarters heard of this, there were none who did not come to see it.
King Bimbisāra, having heard of it as well, also wished to go and view it; without first issuing instructions to his attendants, he suddenly arrived at the house with his retinue.
When the elder heard that the king had arrived, he immediately went out to welcome him; seeing the king, he paid his respects, saying:
"Welcome, Great King! We pray that you will deign to visit us. The king asked:
"Did you hear that I was coming before?
He replied, "I did not hear it!"
The king said, "My army is vast; it cannot be supplied all at once! The elder replied:

"I myself shall provide for the King and his ministers; my son shall provide for the Crown Prince; my wife shall provide for the ladies of the inner palace; my male and female servants shall suffice to provide for all the soldiers; and grain and fodder shall likewise suffice to provide for the army's elephants and horses."
"I pray that you will deign to visit us!
When the King arrived at his house and was seated, he said:
"I have heard that the elder, his wife, son, daughter-in-law, servants, and maidservants all possess great merit; I now wish to see them all."
He replied, "I dare not conceal anything!

The king immediately ordered the rice in the granary to be removed and the surrounding area swept and sprinkled clean; he then had a throne spread out and invited the king to enter and sit. Only then did he enter the granary, whereupon the five grains spontaneously rained down from the sky, leaving the king in great wonder and admiration.

Furthermore, wishing to see the power of his wife’s merit, he took a vessel of rice and placed it before her; she took some and distributed it until the entire host of soldiers was fully satisfied, yet it was not diminished.

Furthermore, wishing to demonstrate the power of his son’s merit, he immediately ordered a golden bag to be seized and filled with gold. He presented it to the King and the great assembly, saying that they might all take as much as they desired; yet the gold was never exhausted.

Furthermore, wishing to witness the power of his daughter-in-law’s merit, he immediately ordered a *droṇa* of rice to be brought out; it served the king and the great assembly for an entire month without being exhausted.
Furthermore, wishing to witness the power of his slave’s merit, he immediately ordered him to plow, and seven furrows were instantly completed.

Furthermore, wishing to witness the power of that maidservant’s merit, he immediately commanded that half a *liang* of fragrant ointment be ground; its scent was heard within half a *yojana* without distinction, and even after it had been smeared over the entire assembly, there was still not enough to go around.
The king and the great assembly, beholding the power of his merit and virtue, could not help but praise him in admiration, and they immediately returned to the palace.

At that time, the World-Honored One, together with a great community of bhikṣus numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty, was traveling through the human realm and arrived at the city of Vaḍḍha. When the elder Puṇṇa heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had now come and was staying beneath the Āmra grove, he wished to go out to welcome him, prostrate himself before him, and inquire after his well-being.
When the various non-Buddhists heard this, they went to him and said:
"Do not go out to welcome the śramaṇa Gautama; rather, the śramaṇa Gautama should come to see you! Why is that?..."
Your merit surpasses that of others; among all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, kings, and householders, there are none who would not come to your door.
Having heard this, the householder’s mind was set at rest.
Later, he again thought:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has been here for some time now, yet he has not come to see me; his path must surely be superior."
"For what reason do you remain here and not go to pay your respects?

He then prepared his carriage and departed the city. From afar, he beheld the World-Honored One’s countenance, exceptionally sublime like a mountain of gold. He proceeded to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha taught him various sublime dharmas, from the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, until he attained the pure Dharma-eye while still seated upon his mat.
He then rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will accept my invitation for a meal tomorrow!"
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
The householder returned home and prepared many kinds of delicious food and drink. At the time for the meal the following day, he went in person to inform the Buddha:
"May the Holy One know the time!"
The Buddha, surrounded by the community of monks in front and behind, went to the house and sat down upon the seat.
The elder personally served the food with his own hands; when the meal was finished, he offered water for washing, and then the members of his household, both great and small, sat before the Buddha.

The Buddha preached various sublime dharmas to him, from the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, until he attained the pure Dharma-eye and received the three refuges and five precepts.
The elder addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
My wife, my son, my daughter-in-law, and my male and female servants all say,
"This is due to our own merit.
But in truth, whose power is it?
“We pray that the Buddha will explain this! The Buddha said,
“You all share in this merit!”
He asked again,
"In what way do they coexist? He replied:

“Formerly, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a weaver. The weaver had a wife; the wife had a son; the son had a wife. Their household consisted of exactly one male slave and one female slave, and they all ate together at one time.”
A pratyekabuddha came to him for alms, and the weaver said, "Eat yourselves; take my portion and give it to him!
His wife said:
"Take my portion and give it to him!
The son, and even the servants and slaves, all said the same.
The Pratyekabuddha said:

"You have all already set aside your portions for me; since you have fulfilled your good intentions, you may each give me a small portion so that your own food remains sufficient and I, too, shall be satiated."
Thereupon, he reduced his own portion by one spoonful, which filled the other’s bowl.
Having received the food, the Pratyekabuddha ate it and then manifested various supernatural transformations in the midst of the air before departing.

Those people, at the end of their lives, were reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; when their lifespan there was exhausted, they were reborn above in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, proceeding in turn up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. After seven such cycles, they were reborn again by virtue of their remaining merit.
"The weaver and his family at that time are none other than you yourselves!
Thereupon, the householder addressed the Saṃgha before the Buddha, saying:
"I now invite the entire Saṃgha to receive boundless offerings; whatever you may require, in whatever measure, at whatever time, please take it from me."
The bhikṣus did not dare to accept it, thinking to themselves:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept unlimited offerings.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen; you may receive [the requisites] according to your wish.
There were some bhikṣus who wished to travel far and requested provisions for the journey. The elder then dispatched people to deliver gold, silver, coins, and goods to them.
Having arrived at their destination, they had acquired a great abundance of goods;
the messengers returned and reported, "The provisions we brought are now in great surplus.
The elder said to them:
"I have already given this as an offering; it should not be taken back.
