You may take it and go to the monastery to offer it to the Sangha.
He then gave it to the Sangha.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I allow the monastery attendants (śrāmaṇera) to receive [the money] on behalf of the Saṃgha and exchange it for items required by the Saṃgha; the bhikṣus should not handle such affairs."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One departed from the Gabled Grove and traveled among the people.

The elder Puṇḍarīka followed behind with provisions for a meal, intending to provide them in a desolate place where no one else was present: he brought twelve hundred and fifty elephants, twelve hundred and fifty cows, and twelve hundred and fifty bulls; furthermore, five hundred carts were laden with various kinds of fine foods.

Having arrived at the place where they were to halt in the wilderness, they prepared everything throughout the night; then, on the following morning, they spread out a seat for a bhikṣu beneath the shade of one elephant and a seat for the World-Honored One beneath the shade of the largest elephant.
When the time arrived and it was announced that the meal was ready, the bhikṣus did not dare to sit, thinking to themselves:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to sit under the shade of living beings.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen and sit!
Once the assembly was seated, the elder first ordered one person to milk a cow and give it to a bhikṣu. The bhikṣus did not dare to accept it, thinking to themselves:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to drink warm cow's milk."
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to drink.
After he had drunk, the elder personally served the food with his own hands; when the meal was finished, he offered water for rinsing and sat before the Buddha.
The Buddha recited for him verses of sympathetic joy, just as he had done for Vīraka;
he further expounded various sublime dharmas.
Having instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened him, he returned to his home.
The Buddha and the great assembly rose from their seats and departed, traveling gradually northward toward the dwelling place of the Jaina matted-hair ascetics.
When the Jainas heard that the Buddha, having renounced his Śākya clan, had become a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, and would arrive that evening, they thought to themselves:
"In the past, those sages who practiced the holy life did not eat after midday, though they drank various non-timely beverages."
That is to say:
mango juice, rose-apple juice, wood-apple juice, *pālevata* fruit juice, grape juice, *kūla* fruit juice, sugarcane juice, and honey juice.
“The Śramaṇa Gautama should also drink this; I shall prepare it in advance so that when he arrives, I may serve it.

Having finished the preparations, he went out with five hundred disciples to welcome the World-Honored One. Seeing the World-Honored One from afar, his countenance was exceptionally sublime, like a mountain of gold; his joy increased all the more. He approached the Buddha’s presence and stood before him to greet him, saying: “Welcome, Gautama!”
"Please come and sit in my house.
The Buddha then went to his home and sat down with the bhikṣus in order.
The brahmin then brought down some non-timely gruel (vikāla-pāna), but the bhikṣus did not dare to accept it, thinking to themselves:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted me to drink non-timely beverages.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to drink them!"
The bhikṣus asked again,
“For what reason did the Buddha obtain permission to drink?
The Buddha said:
"When thirsty, you shall have a drink.
The brahmin then thought again:
"I should now prepare the food of the seers for the śramaṇa Gautama and his followers to provide for tomorrow."
He then prepared meals of millet, sorghum, foxtail millet, panicled millet, and *kuśaka* rice.
When it was time for the meal the following day, he announced that the food was ready.
The Buddha and the great assembly took their seats together, and the brahmin personally served them food with his own hands.
The bhikṣus did not dare to eat, thinking to themselves:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to eat the food of the rishis."
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to eat.
When the meal was finished and the water for rinsing had been offered, he took a small stool and sat before the Buddha.
The Buddha recited for him verses of sympathetic joy, just as he had done for Vīraja;
he further expounded various sublime teachings.
Having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him, he rose from his seat and proceeded toward the village of Āmra.
At that time, there were two barbers, father and son, who had both gone forth as monastics. Hearing that the World-Honored One was about to arrive, they deliberated thus:

"These householders do not respect the Triple Gem; if the Buddha comes here, surely no one will provide us with gruel. We should work together to shave the heads of people and take their wages to provide for ourselves."
Having deliberated thus, they set out immediately and obtained the materials to prepare the gruel.
At dawn, they invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha; once the monks had finished eating, the Buddha asked the two bhikṣus, "How did you manage to prepare this gruel?"
He reported the matter to the Buddha in full detail, and the Buddha rebuked him in various ways, saying:
"What you have done is contrary to the Dharma!
How can you hire yourself out to shave the heads of laypeople?"
"From now on, if a barber goes forth as a renunciant, he is not permitted to keep a razor; anyone who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
When the Buddha arrived at the town of Pāpā, the Malla warriors of Pāpā heard that the Buddha was coming and immediately deliberated together, saying:
"If we do not go out to welcome him, we shall each be fined five hundred gold coins."
They all came out, both great and small, to welcome the World-Honored One; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Buddha preached various sublime dharmas for them, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them. They then invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to observe the summer retreat for four months, and the Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
When the Mallas knew that the Buddha had accepted [the invitation], some individuals prepared food for one day, others for two days, and so on up to ten days;
some two people together prepared food for one day, and so on up to ten people together preparing food for one day;
some provided only the morning meal, some made only rice gruel, and some made only *tambula* (sweetened milk-rice).
At that time, there was a man named Rauruka, who had been a close friend of Ānanda during his days as a layman;
he asked the bhikṣus, "Where is Ānanda now?"
He replied, "Ānanda,
out of reverence for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, is currently standing behind the Buddha.
He then went to where Ānanda was, prostrated at his feet, and stood back.
Ānanda said, "I am greatly delighted to see you welcoming the Buddha! He replied:

"I have not come out of respect for the Buddha; rather, my kinsmen made a mutual agreement that if I do not go out to welcome the Buddha, I shall be fined five hundred gold coins. It is for this reason that I have come!"
Having heard this, Ānanda was filled with despondency:
"How is it that my own kinsman does not revere and have faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha?
He immediately went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
“World-Honored One, I pray that this person may have faith and reverence for the Buddha’s Dharma!
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“It will not be difficult for this person to have faith in the Buddha; do not harbor any anxiety!”
The Buddha, having suffused his entire body with a mind of loving-kindness, entered his chamber and sat down with the door closed. Later, Luī,
longing for the World-Honored One as a calf yearns for its mother, saw many bhikṣus walking up and down on the open ground and asked,
"Where is the Buddha?"
The bhikṣus pointed out, saying:
"He is in that large room with the door closed; you may go there slowly, clear your throat, and knock on the door.
Out of compassion for you, the World-Honored One will open it for you."
Immediately, as he had spoken, the door opened. Once Ruci had entered, he cupped his hands to support the Buddha’s feet, announced his name, and prostrated himself in homage.

The Buddha preached various sublime Dharmas for him—teaching, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him—namely, the discourse on giving, up to the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

Thereupon, he became free from dust and defilement, attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, and having seen the Dharma and realized the fruit, he received the three refuges and the five precepts, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus will always accept my offerings, and not accept invitations from others.
The Buddha said:
"All those who are practitioners have this aspiration; I have already accepted their invitations for the four months of the summer retreat, so there is no vacancy.
He thought to himself:
"What gift is there that the Buddha has not yet accepted, such that I might not lose the opportunity to serve as a field of merit for them?"
"I have not yet seen anyone provide *khādaniya* (solid food).
He then prepared it and brought it at the time of the meal.
The bhikṣus did not dare to accept it, thinking to themselves:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to eat *khādaniya* food at the proper mealtime.
They reported this to the Buddha,
and the Buddha said:
"Listen to the distribution of food!
At that time, Visākhā, mother of Migāra, established a fixed limit for her alms-giving to the Saṅgha, saying:
"At such-and-such a time, take such-and-such an amount."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to accept it!
There were some lay devotees who invited the bhikṣus to accept offerings according to their own wishes.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not accept offerings made during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; furthermore, a donor should not give gold, silver, precious objects, or women to the Saṃgha."
"If a bhikṣu approves of such a gift, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if he accepts it, he must be dealt with according to the Dharma!
There were some laypeople who invited the Saṃgha in succession.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"They should be appointed in succession to accept invitations.
The bhikṣus did not know who should be appointed and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One bhikṣu should be appointed through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) to serve as the person designated to accept the invitation.
Then, one bhikṣu should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha now appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to act as the person authorized to accept invitations.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen."
[The motion] is thus announced. "Venerable Sangha, listen!
The Sangha now appoints the bhikṣu so-and-so to act as the person authorized to accept invitations."
"Whichever elders consent, let them remain silent;
whoever does not consent, let them speak.
The Sangha has finished appointing the bhikṣu so-and-so as the person authorized to accept invitations."
"Because the Saṃgha remains silent,
this matter is thus upheld. Thereupon,
the bhikṣus appointed an ignorant bhikṣu who did not know the proper sequence.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not appoint an ignorant bhikṣu.
If there are five qualities, one should not appoint him: [the list of five qualities follows]."
"Driven by desire, anger, delusion, or fear, they do not know whether [a patient] has recovered or not.
There were some laypeople who regularly prepared food to send as offerings to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to receive it!"

There were some laypeople who, having newly completed a dwelling, a heated room, and a bathhouse for the Sangha, prepared food and drink for the gift of the dwelling and sent bhikṣus to go and receive them.
Not knowing who should go to fetch it, they reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"The bhikṣu who resides in that room should go to fetch it.
This occurred while the Buddha was staying in the city of Vaiśālī.
At that time, there was a famine, and because alms-food was difficult to obtain, the brahmin bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"If the World-Honored One would permit us to plant fruit trees, we could satisfy our hunger."
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to plant them.
Once the fruit had ripened into seeds, the bhikṣus, fearing that they had planted with their own hands, did not dare to eat them.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to eat them according to your preference.
Some bhikṣus climbed onto trees to grasp the fruits, testing whether they were raw or ripe.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "One should not reach up to touch fruit on a tree.

There were some bhikṣus who saw fruit falling onto ground that was not pure; they had someone gather it into one place and let it remain overnight, not knowing what to do. They reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If one does not know whether the ground is pure or impure, one is permitted to eat;
if one knows it is an impure ground, one should not eat."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus took the best fruits first and ate them, while the other virtuous bhikṣus received none.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) to appoint one bhikṣu as the fruit-distributor; if there are many fruits, they may be eaten at will."
The group of six bhikṣus sent monastic fruit to laypeople, who then requested it from other bhikṣus.
When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"One should not send monastic fruit to laypeople; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
Some laypeople came into the monastery and, seeing the fruit, asked the bhikṣus for it; the bhikṣus did not dare to give it to them, whereupon the laypeople immediately criticized and rebuked them.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"It should be given. At that time,
the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī.
At that time, there was a famine, and because it was difficult to obtain almsfood, the brahmin bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"If the World-Honored One would allow us to grow vegetables, we could satisfy our hunger during times of scarcity."
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit it.
All of this is as explained above regarding the planting of fruit.
If a layperson grows vegetables on land belonging to the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha requires them, they may request them up to three times.

When the bhikṣus had the *kappiyakāraka* (pure man) wash vegetables in an impure place, and before the task was finished, the dawn had already appeared; they became doubtful and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"There is no offense."
The bhikṣus had no kappiyakāraka (pure attendant) and did not know who should distribute the food for the Saṃgha. They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should receive it himself and then distribute it."
There were wooden vessels used for serving food that became greasy and unclean; when these were scrubbed with tiles or stones, they damaged the monastic utensils.
When this was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"One should not scrub them with tiles or stones; rather, one should wash them with boiling water and ash."
There were jars of ghee, oil, and honey that required covering, yet no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible) was present.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should use a new cloth to cover them, ensuring that the hand does not come near."
The jar was overturned suddenly, and there was no *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) available to set it upright.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should set it upright yourself, provided that you do not allow the vessel to leave the ground."
There was a bhikṣu who, out of anger and resentment toward another, took a jar of ghee and placed it on impure ground overnight, intending that the other would no longer be able to eat it.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"For that [resentful] bhikṣu, it is impure; however, the bhikṣu who is the owner of the ghee may eat it."
"If he carries them onto impure ground, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
Some bhikṣus transported food and drink by boat, but there was no *śuddha-puruṣa* (pure person) to steer the vessel or row it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things allowable), I permit a bhikṣu to drive a vehicle himself or row a boat himself.
At that time, the Saṃgha was transporting rice by cart, and a certain brāhmaṇa threw a handful of impure rice into the cart.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If it can be separated, remove it;
if it cannot be separated, remove a handful."
A wild fox stole a bhikṣu’s butter jar and placed it on impure ground, where it remained overnight.
Not knowing what to do, he reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to eat it; there is no offense.
Suppose there is a fruit tree whose roots are in impure ground while its branches cover pure ground;
a bhikṣu, also being on impure ground, places food and drink upon the branches of the tree and leaves them overnight.
Not knowing what to do, they reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "A branch attached to the root constitutes impure ground; it must not be eaten."
There was a fruit tree whose roots were in pure ground while its branches covered impure ground;
a bhikṣu, also being in pure ground, placed food and drink upon the branches and left them there overnight.
Not knowing what to do, they reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to eat; there is no offense."
There was a fruit tree whose roots were situated on both pure and impure ground, and whose branches covered both pure and impure ground;
a bhikṣu was also situated on both pure and impure ground, and its fruit fell onto both pure and impure ground and remained there overnight.
Not knowing what to do, they reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"This was not done by a bhikṣu; you may all eat it without committing an offense."
There was a monk who took earth from pure ground to build a house on impure ground;
he placed food inside it, considering it to be pure.
When this was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"It is said: 'One relies on the site as pure; if it is impure, one must not eat there!
A certain bhikṣu took earth from an impure site to build a house on a pure site, yet he did not dare to place his food within it."
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense in eating such food.

There was the meat of deer and other animals that had died after being swept away by water; as there was no *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle pure things) to collect it, the bhikṣus entered the water and took it themselves.
Not knowing what to do, they reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Once you have reached the shore, have a lay attendant cut away the portion grasped by the bhikṣu's hand; the remainder may be eaten without offense."
At a certain monastery, the resident bhikṣus obtained a great quantity of mangoes; having eaten their fill, they gave the remainder to a lay attendant.
The next day, the attendant prepared a soup with it and offered it to the bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus did not dare to eat it.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one did not originally intend to eat it again, all such eating is permitted and constitutes no offense.
There were some bhikṣus who, at the time of eating, did not share their food with those who had received nothing.
The laypeople criticized them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, eat like cats and wildcats; they do not share with one another.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one distributes [the food] among the *parivāsa* monks, or even fails to give it to a single person, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

A certain brāhmaṇa entrusted some parched grain (*saktu*) to a bhikṣu; the bhikṣu kept it on impure ground overnight. When the brāhmaṇa came to retrieve it the next day, he distributed it among the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣu, having already placed [the food] on ground that was not pure, did not dare to accept it.
He reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Originally, these were *pāyasa* (milk-rice) for laypeople; there is no offense in accepting and eating them.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
"Even if it is something I have prescribed, if it is not considered pure in other regions, you must not use it."
"Although this was not established by me, it must certainly be practiced in other regions; all must practice it without fail.
9. The Rules for the Kaṭhina Robe. *Pañcavargīya-vinaya*, Third Section, Part Nine: The Rules for the Kaṭhina Robe. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, if any of the bhikṣus required any one of the three robes, they would take it from the Saṃgha.
On one occasion, Ānanda’s robe was worn out, and the bhikṣus said to him,
“Venerable One!...”
"One may take materials from among the Sangha to make it.
He replied, "The World-Honored One does not permit the keeping of extra robes; I cannot complete the work in a single day, and I fear I would incur the offense of possessing an extra robe."

Furthermore, a bhikṣu well-known to the community of Pāṭaliputra came to Śrāvastī; however, because he arrived one night late for the later retreat, he did not reach it and instead observed the retreat at Sāketa.

When sixteen days of the *varṣā* retreat had passed, they carried their heavy robes and braved the mud and rain to reach the Buddha’s dwelling. They prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
It is the constant custom of the World-Honored One to greet visiting bhikṣus, saying:
"Was your *varṣā* spent in harmony? Was almsfood easy to obtain? And were you not fatigued on the road?"
He replied: “The rains retreat was harmonious, and we did not lack for almsfood.
However, encountering mud and rain on the road while carrying heavy robes, we were utterly exhausted.”
The bhikṣus also reported the matter concerning Aniruddha to the Buddha.

The Buddha convened the community of bhikṣus for two reasons; having praised those with few desires and contentment in various ways, and having praised the upholding of the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to accept the kaṭhina robe."
By receiving the kaṭhina robe, one does not incur offenses regarding five matters:
eating in a group apart from the community, eating repeatedly, entering a village without informing other bhikṣus, keeping extra robes, and staying overnight separated from one's robes.
If a donor offers *kaṭhina* cloth to the Saṃgha, it should be given to those among the bhikṣus who have few robes by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
One bhikṣu should announce:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!..."
The Saṃgha has obtained these kaṭhina robes and now bestows them upon the bhikṣu [Name].
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This kāṭhina-cloth has been obtained by the Sangha; it is now given to the bhikṣu so-and-so.
Those elders who consent, remain silent;..."
If you do not approve, please speak.
The Sangha has finished bestowing the *kaṭhina* robe-cloth upon the bhikṣu [Name];
the Sangha approves, as it remains silent.
"Maintain this matter thus.
Once that bhikṣu has received it, he should wash, dye, beat, and sew it on that very day; it is well if he can accomplish it alone.
If he cannot complete it, the Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) to appoint one bhikṣu, or two, three, or even many bhikṣus to assist him.
A single bhikṣu shall announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
We now appoint the bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so to assist the bhikṣu so-and-so in making robes."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall announce as follows. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
I now appoint the bhikṣus So-and-so and So-and-so to assist the bhikṣu So-and-so in making his robe.
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
The Saṃgha has already appointed the bhikṣus so-and-so and so-and-so to assist the bhikṣu so-and-so in making his robe;
the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent.
Thus this matter is upheld.

When the robe-making is finished, the monk who was given the items by the Saṃgha should take the robe to the assembly, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, kneel with his right knee on the ground, and announce:
"The Saṃgha has obtained these *kaṭhina* cloth materials; they have already been washed, dyed, beaten, and sewn, and have been properly prepared."
"May the Saṃgha accept this as a *kaṭhina* robe.
Having made this formal announcement (*jñapti*) in this manner, he should again rise and display it to the entire community of monks.
The bhikṣus should respond, saying:
"Elder! We rejoice;
we share this with you. Thereafter, the Saṃgha should accept it through a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman), and one bhikṣu should proclaim:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This kāṭhina-cloth has been obtained by the Saṃgha; it has been washed, dyed, beaten, and sewn, and has been properly prepared. We now accept it to be made into a kāṭhina robe."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus as a formal motion. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Sangha has obtained these *kaṭhina* cloths; having washed, dyed, beaten, and sewn them, and having completed the work according to the Dharma, we now receive them to make the *kaṭhina* robe.
"Whichever elders consent, remain silent;
if you do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has finished accepting the *kaṭhina* robe."
"Because the Saṃgha has remained silent,
this matter is thus upheld.
The bhikṣu to whom the robes and requisites were given by the Saṃgha should then go on a round, saying:
"This robe has already been accepted by the Saṃgha to be made into a kaṭhina robe.
Each of the bhikṣus should say:
"This robe has already been accepted by the Saṃgha to be made into a kaṭhina robe; this constitutes a proper acceptance."
"Whatever merit exists herein belongs entirely to me.
Within this, there are those who have successfully received the kaṭhina robe and those who have not.
The non-fulfillment of the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) occurs as follows: if the washing, dyeing, beating, or sewing is not performed according to the Dharma;

if the robe is too small or too large; if it is a garment of brocade or fine silk; if the acceptance is undertaken before the *pravāraṇā* ceremony has concluded; if one is motivated by a craving for gain and offerings; or if one intentionally intends to relinquish the five matters—none of these constitute a valid acceptance.
Conversely, this establishes the acceptance [of the *kaṭhina*].
There are eight matters by which one loses the *kaṭhina* robe:

first, the expiration of the time; second, the loss of the robe; third, hearing of its loss; fourth, departing to a distant place; fifth, the severance of hope; sixth, the robe exiting the boundary; seventh, a person exiting the boundary; eighth, relinquishing it through a formal motion and double proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
There are two causes and conditions by which one may not receive the *kaṭhina* robe:
first, when the making of the robe is not yet finished; second, when one abandons the residence and departs.
There are thirty days for receiving the *kaṭhina*, and there are likewise thirty days for relinquishing it.
If one receives the *pūrvavarṣā* (early rains retreat) on the sixteenth day of the seventh month, it is relinquished on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month;

if one receives it from the seventeenth day of the seventh month through the fifteenth day of the eighth month, it is relinquished from the sixteenth day of the eleventh month through the fourteenth day of the twelfth month.
If one accepts [the robe] on the sixteenth day of the eighth month during the later retreat, it must be relinquished by the fifteenth day of the twelfth month.
If the period for robes has ended, one should relinquish it through a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
A single bhikṣu should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha now relinquishes the kaṭhina robe."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus as a formal motion:
'Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!'"
The Sangha now relinquishes the kaṭhina robe.
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has finished relinquishing the kaṭhina robe;
the Sangha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.
The Mahīśāsaka Vinaya, Volume 212 (part of Volume 23),
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśa during the Song Dynasty.
Translated together with Zhu Daosheng and others.
Part Four: The Method for Settling Disputes. Chapter One: The Method for Settling Disputes. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, the bhikṣus were fond of engaging in mutual strife and litigation against one another.
Bhikṣus dispute with bhikṣus; bhikṣus dispute with bhikṣuṇīs; bhikṣuṇīs dispute with bhikṣuṇīs; bhikṣuṇīs dispute with bhikṣus.

At that time, Channa supported the bhikṣuṇīs against the bhikṣus; thus, disputes that had not yet arisen arose, those already arisen were increased and expanded, those not yet extinguished were not extinguished, and those already extinguished arose once more.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked them:
"Is it true that you have done so?
They replied: [Yes].
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
"What you have done is contrary to the Dharma and does not accord with the Path!
Having rebuked them thus, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, if bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs quarrel, or if they even abandon a bhikṣu to side with a bhikṣuṇī, all such acts constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense."
There are four kinds of disputes:
first, verbal; second, regarding instruction.
"Third, the offense;
fourth, the matter.
"On account of these matters, I have established for the bhikṣus seven methods for settling disputes, so that whenever a dispute arises, it may be resolved and extinguished."
Where the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) should be granted, grant the *saṃmukhavinaya*;
where the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) should be granted, grant the *smṛtivinaya*;
where the *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement for one not insane) should be granted, grant the *amūḍhavinaya*.

Where a confession of one's own accord (*pratijñākāraka*) should be granted, grant a confession of one's own accord; where a verdict by a majority (*yadbhūyaiṣīya*) should be granted, grant a verdict by a majority;
where a covering with grass (*tṛṇaprastāraka*) should be granted, grant a covering with grass.
"You should apply the *yebhuyyasika* (decision by majority) procedure; you should apply the *yebhuyyasika* procedure. What is meant by a dispute over speech?

It is when monks dispute with one another, some saying it is Dharma and others saying it is not Dharma; that it is Vinaya and others saying it is not Vinaya; that it is an offense and others saying it is not an offense; that it is a grave offense and others saying it is not a grave offense; that it is a residual offense and others saying it is not a residual offense; that it is a coarse offense and others saying it is not a coarse offense; that it is cleared by a formal act (*kamma*) and others saying it is not cleared by a formal act; that it was spoken by the Buddha and others saying it was not spoken by the Buddha; or that it was established by the Buddha and others saying it was not established by the Buddha.
Because of this, they give rise to anger and further revile one another;
this is called "dispute over words" (*adhikaraṇa-vivāda*). What is meant by "dispute over instruction" (*anuśāsana-adhikaraṇa*)?
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu, saying:
"Do you remember having committed a pārājika?
Do you remember having committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa, sthūlātyaya, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, duṣkṛta, or dubbhāsita?"
That bhikṣu does not rejoice in it nor accept it, and because of this, a dispute arises.
This is called a dispute concerning instruction (*anuśāsanī-vivāda*). What is meant by a dispute concerning an offense (*āpatti-vivāda*)?
If a bhikṣu commits an offense ranging from a pārājika down to a mere bad speech, or if he engages in quarreling and mutual abuse, giving rise to evil actions of body, speech, and mind—
this is called a dispute arising from an offense.
What is meant by "dispute over matters" (*adhikaraṇa-vivāda*)?
It refers to the various activities regularly performed by the Saṃgha—namely, all *karmas* and whatever actions are undertaken—which give rise to dispute.
This is called a dispute over matters.
Upāli asked the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By how many matters are disputes extinguished?”
The Buddha said: "It is settled by means of the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence) and the *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (decision by the majority).
He asked again:
"How is it extinguished? He replied:

"If a bhikṣu disputes with another bhikṣu regarding what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, up to what was prescribed by the Buddha and what was not prescribed by the Buddha, and the Saṃgha settles the matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha's teaching; [then it is extinguished]."
"If he says, 'This is the Dharma; this is the Buddha's teaching,' and accepts it and endures it, this is called settlement by *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence).
What is meant by "in the presence"?
There are three kinds of "presence":
presence of the Saṃgha, presence of the person, and presence of the Vinaya.
What is meant by the presence of the Saṃgha?
The assembly of the Saṃgha gathered together is called the presence of the Saṃgha.
What is meant by the presence of the persons?
When one is present before the person with whom one is disputing,
this is called "presence of the person" (*pudgala-sammukhatā*).
What is meant by "presence of the discipline" (*vinaya-sammukhatā*)?
One should extinguish [the dispute] by means of whatever Dharma, whatever Vinaya, and whatever teaching of the Buddha it may be appropriate to use for its extinction.
This is called "extinction in the presence of the Vinaya" (vinayapratyakṣa).
If, after it has been thus extinguished, it is raised again, one incurs a pāyattika offense.

Furthermore, if a dispute over speech is settled in this manner, the monks involved in the dispute are dissatisfied. They hear that in another residence there is one monk, or two, or three, up to an entire community, who is intelligent and wise, understands the Prātimokṣa, and thinks:
"It would be well to go and settle this matter; we should go and settle it."
One should first explain the matter in its entirety to the monks within that assembly who are learned in the Dharma, and only thereafter request the gathering of the Saṃgha.
Once the Saṃgha has assembled, one should say to them:
"Depart for a moment; we shall deliberate together on your case."
Once that bhikṣu has departed, the Saṃgha should deliberate together:
"If that bhikṣu speaks truthfully and seeks for us to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, we shall together settle it in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya;
if that bhikṣu does not speak truthfully, we shall not be able to settle this matter in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya."
Those monks engaged in that dispute should also deliberate together, saying:

"If the Saṃgha, in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, establishes a limit such that our matter shall be settled today, tomorrow, or the day after, we shall fully recount the beginning and end of the matter before the Saṃgha and entrust the Saṃgha to settle it."
Having arrived among the Saṃgha, he related the matter in detail from beginning to end. If the Saṃgha were to speak in two ways—
some saying, "It should be so," or others saying:
"One should not do so!

That bhikṣu should go to the Saṃgha day after day, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, prostrate at the feet of the Saṃgha, and kneel with his right knee on the ground, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], intentionally emitted semen and committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which I have not concealed.
I have requested from the Saṃgha the practice of mānatva for six nights, and the Saṃgha has already granted me the practice of mānatva for six nights.
"I have now practiced *mānatva* for several days; such-and-such days remain. May the Venerable Sangha take note.
After six nights have passed, one should request *ābhāhana* from the Sangha, saying:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!..."
I, bhikṣu [Name], intentionally emitted semen, thereby committing a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which I have not concealed.
I requested from the Saṃgha a six-night period of *mānatva* practice, and the Saṃgha has already granted me this six-night *mānatva*.
"I have completed the six-night *mānatva* penance; I now request *ābhāna* from the Saṃgha.
May the Saṃgha grant me *ābhāna*!
Thus he requested three times.
A single bhikṣu should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so intentionally emitted semen, thereby committing a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which he has not concealed."
He requested from the Saṃgha the practice of *mānatva* for six nights; the Saṃgha had already granted him the practice of *mānatva* for six nights.
Having completed those six nights of *mānatva*, that bhikṣu requested *ābṛhaṇa* (rehabilitation) from the Saṃgha.
The Sangha now grants the *āpattipratideśana* (rehabilitation) to [Name].
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha listen and grant its consent.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, intentionally emitted semen... [and so forth]... the Saṃgha now grants so-and-so an āpattipratideśanā (formal act of rehabilitation).
Those elders who consent, remain silent;..."
"If you do not approve, please speak.
Thus a second and third time. "The Saṃgha has completed the *āpavarga* (rehabilitation) for the bhikṣu so-and-so; [it is approved by those who agree,] and it is thus silent."
The Saṃgha granted him forbearance because he remained silent.
"This matter is thus upheld.
There was a bhikṣu who intentionally emitted semen, thereby committing a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense; having concealed it for one night, he did not know what to do and questioned the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus did not know [what to do] and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:

"I now authorize the Saṃgha to perform a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) to grant this bhikṣu the practice of a single night’s separate residence (*parivāsa*)."
The bhikṣu who has committed the offense should go before the Saṃgha and make this announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], intentionally emitted semen and committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which I concealed for one night. I now request from the Saṃgha the parivāsa (probation) for one night."
"I request that the Saṃgha grant me the practice of separate residence for one night.
Thus he requests three times.
A single bhikṣu should then announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, intentionally emitted semen and committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which he concealed for one night. He now requests from the Saṃgha the parivāsa (probation) procedure for one night."
Now the Saṃgha grants such-and-such a person the rite of a one-night separate residence.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen and grant its consent.
This is the motion.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, intentionally emitted semen; therefore, the Saṃgha now grants so-and-so the disciplinary procedure of *parivāsa* for one night."
"Whichever elders approve, remain silent;
whoever does not approve, speak.
Thus a second and third time.
"The Saṃgha has already granted the bhikṣu so-and-so a one-night parivāsa;
the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld."

When that bhikṣu has completed his one-night parivāsa, he should request from the Saṃgha the practice of mānatva, up to and including ābhāṣaṇa; the Saṃgha shall likewise grant it to him as described above.
There was a bhikṣu who intentionally emitted semen, thereby committing a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. Without concealing it, he requested from the Saṃgha that he be granted the practice of mānatva.
During the six nights [of the probation], he committed another offense, likewise without concealment, and not knowing what to do, he questioned the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus did not know [how to proceed] either, so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:

"I now permit that bhikṣu to again request from the Saṃgha the practice of *mānatva*; the Saṃgha, moreover, should grant that bhikṣu the practice of *mānatva* through a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*)."

When that bhikṣu has completed the six-night practice, he should again request from the Saṃgha the performance of the original *mānatva*; the Saṃgha should also grant it to him by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
That bhikṣu further requests of the Saṃgha, saying:

"I, bhikṣu so-and-so, previously intentionally emitted semen and committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which I did not conceal; I requested from the Saṃgha to perform mānatva, and the Saṃgha granted me the performance of mānatva."
During those six nights, I committed further offenses, which I did not conceal; I now request from the Saṃgha that I again undergo the *mānāpya*.
May you grant me the *mānāpya* once more!
Thus he requested three times.
A single bhikṣu, according to his words of request, should grant it through a formal motion followed by three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
When those six nights have been completed, he should again request from the Saṃgha to undergo the original six-night *mānatva*, saying:
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], previously intentionally emitted semen, thereby committing a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, which I did not conceal;
I requested from the Saṃgha to undergo the mānatva penance, and the Saṃgha granted me the mānatva."
During those six nights, I committed further offenses, yet I did not conceal them;
I again requested from the Saṃgha to undergo six nights of *mānatva*.
Having now completed those six nights of *mānatva*, I now request from the Saṃgha to undergo the original six nights of *mānatva*.
"I request that the Saṃgha grant me the original six-night *mānatva*.
Thus he should beg three times.
A single bhikṣu should, according to these words of request, grant it by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

When that bhikṣu has completed the six-night *mānatva* penance for his original offense, he should request *ābhāhana* (rehabilitation) as described above, and the Saṃgha should grant it to him as described above.
There was a bhikṣu who intentionally emitted semen, committing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, and concealed it for one night; the Saṃgha granted him a one-night *parivāsa* (probation).
While in that state, he committed another offense and likewise concealed it for one night; not knowing what to do, he questioned the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus also did not know, so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:

"I now permit that bhikṣu to again request from the Saṃgha one night of separate residence (parivāsa), and the Saṃgha should likewise grant him one night of separate residence through a formal act of jñapti-caturtha-karman."

"When that one-night *parivāsa* has been completed, he should again request from the Saṃgha the original one-night *parivāsa*; the Saṃgha, moreover, should grant it to him by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
That bhikṣu then requested from the Saṃgha another one-night *parivāsa*, saying:
"I, the bhikṣu [Name], previously intentionally emitted semen, thereby committing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which I concealed for one night."
"I requested from the Saṃgha a one-night parivāsa, and the Saṃgha granted me a one-night parivāsa.
During that period, I committed another offense and concealed it for one night;
I now again request from the Saṃgha a one-night parivāsa."
"I pray that the Saṃgha will further grant me a separate residence for one night.
Thus he requests three times.
A single bhikṣu should, according to these words of request, grant it to him by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).
When he has completed that one-night *parivāsa*, he must again request from the Saṃgha the original one-night *parivāsa*, saying:
"I, bhikṣu [Name], previously intentionally emitted semen, committing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, which I concealed for one night;
I requested from the Saṃgha a one-night *parivāsa*, and the Saṃgha granted me a one-night *parivāsa*."
I committed another offense therein and likewise concealed it for one night;
I again requested from the Saṃgha a parivāsa of one night, and the Saṃgha granted me a parivāsa of one night.
"I have already completed one night of separate residence; I now request from the Saṃgha the original one-night separate residence.
May the Saṃgha grant me the original one-night separate residence!
Thus he requested three times.
A single bhikṣu should grant it to him by means of a formal motion followed by three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman), according to the words of his request.
Once that bhikṣu has completed the initial one-night parivāsa, he should, as before, request and undergo the six-night mānatva.
Having completed the *mānatva*, he should again request *ābhāṣaṇā* as described above, and the Saṃgha should all grant it to him by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* as described above.

There was a bhikṣu who intentionally emitted semen, committing a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, and concealed it for one night; the Saṃgha granted him a one-night *parivāsa* (separate residence) as described above.
If he commits another offense therein and likewise conceals it for one night, the Saṃgha shall again grant him a further *parivāsa* of one night as described above.
When that period is completed, the Saṃgha shall again grant him the original *parivāsa* of one night as described above.
When the probation (parivāsa) was completed, the Saṃgha again granted him six nights of penance (mānatva) as before.
While undergoing that, he committed another offense, which he did not conceal; the Saṃgha again granted him six nights of penance (mānatva) as before.
When those six nights have been completed, the Saṃgha again grants him the *mānatva* of the original offense as described above.
When that has been completed, they then grant him the *ābhāṣaṇa* as described above.
If a bhikṣu commits one saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, or even many, and conceals them for two nights, or even for many nights;
if the Saṃgha grants him parivāsa, it shall be calculated based on the longest period of concealment, and he shall be granted parivāsa according to that number of days.

If the Saṃgha has granted a period of parivāsa (probation) and he subsequently commits another offense during that time, if he concealed it, the Saṃgha should grant him a further period of parivāsa according to the number of days;
if he did not conceal it, the Saṃgha should grant him a mānatva of six nights as prescribed above.
When the further *parivāsa* has been completed and the *mānatva* has been completed, the Saṃgha should again grant him the original *parivāsa* as described above.
When the original *parivāsa* has been completed, he should be granted the six-night *mānatva*.
If he commits another offense during that period, the Saṃgha should again grant him six nights of *mānatva*.
When that has been completed, the Saṃgha should again grant him the original *mānatva* as described above, and thereafter grant him *ābhāṣya* (rehabilitation) as described above.
There was a bhikṣu who committed two saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, concealing both for one night;
he then informed the Saṃgha that he had committed one offense, concealed for one night, and the Saṃgha granted him a parivāsa of one night.
When the night's separate residence was completed, remorse arose in his mind:
"I have actually committed two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses; why did I say I committed only one and concealed it for one night?"
He returned to the midst of the Saṃgha and said:
"I have indeed committed two saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, both concealed for the same night.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen; let him be granted another night of separate residence.

That bhikṣu should fully recount the aforementioned matter and request it three times; then, one bhikṣu should grant it to him through a formal motion followed by three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman), using the exact words of the request.
There was a bhikṣu who committed one saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and concealed it for two nights;
he informed the Saṃgha that he had concealed it for only one night, and the Saṃgha granted him a parivāsa of one night.
When the one-night separate residence was completed, remorse arose in his mind:
"I actually concealed [the offense] for two nights; why did I say one night?
He returned to the Saṃgha and informed the monks of the matter. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen, the Saṃgha shall grant him another night of *parivāsa*.
That bhikṣu should fully recount the aforementioned matters and request it three times; the Saṃgha, according to his request, shall grant it by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

There was a bhikṣu who committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and concealed it; he then left the order, but later went forth again and received full ordination, on that very day confessing his previous offense.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should grant him the parivāsa probation for the number of days he concealed [the offense] prior to his time as a renunciant."
There was a bhikṣu who committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense; without concealing it, he left the monastic order before having performed the mānatva penance.
Later, after returning and receiving full ordination again, he concealed it.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should follow that bhikṣu’s seniority in receiving the precepts and grant him *parivāsa* according to the number of days since his ordination.
Suppose a bhikṣu commits two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses—one concealed and one unconcealed—and then leaves the monastic order;
Afterwards, having received the full ordination (*upasampadā*), if he conceals again what was previously unconcealed,
or ceases to conceal what was previously concealed,
it shall be according to the number of days that the preceding monk concealed [the offense], up to the day he left the religious life.
If the concealment occurs later, the period of *parivāsa* (probation) shall be calculated from the day he receives the precepts again.
If a bhikṣu commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and conceals it, then renounces the order;
after subsequently receiving the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) again, he conceals it once more.
One should grant the *parivāsa* (probation) according to the number of days that the offense was concealed before and after by that bhikṣu.
If a bhikṣu commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense but does not conceal it and then renounces the monastic life;
If, after later returning and receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), he likewise does not conceal [the offense], the Sangha should grant him six nights of *mānatta* penance.

If a bhikṣu commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense while acting as a śrāmaṇera, or when his mind is deranged, distracted, or impaired by illness, or if the Sangha has performed against him the formal act (*karman*) of "not seeing the offense," the formal act of "not repenting," or the formal act of "not relinquishing evil and false views," all cases are explained as being like those concerning one who has left the religious life.

If a bhikṣu commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and knows its number—whether it be one offense or various offenses—and having concealed it, he leaves the order; or, after later receiving full ordination again, he no longer conceals it;
or, having previously not concealed it, he leaves the order and later, after receiving full ordination again, he conceals it;

or, having previously half-concealed and half-not concealed it, after receiving the precepts again, he no longer conceals what was previously concealed, but further conceals what was previously not concealed.
If both the prior and subsequent [offenses] were concealed, one shall perform the *parivāsa* (probation) as previously described.
If neither the prior nor the subsequent [offenses] were concealed, one shall perform the *mānatva* for six nights, also as above.
If one becomes a *śrāmaṇera*, or even performs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of not relinquishing evil and heterodox views, it is likewise.

If a *bhikṣu* desists from the path (*pravrajyā*) while undergoing the period of separate residence (*parivāsa*), and later returns to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), he should calculate the number of days previously spent in separate residence and simply add them to the current period, so that the original period of separate residence is fulfilled; this is also the case for other such instances.
If one becomes a śrāmaṇera, or even if the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of not relinquishing evil and false views has been performed, it is likewise.
If a bhikṣu ceases his practice while undergoing *mānatva* and later returns to receive full ordination again, the calculation of the days is likewise;
the same applies to the original *mānatva* period.
If one becomes a śrāmaṇera, or even if the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of not relinquishing evil and false views has been performed, it is likewise.
If a bhikṣu has completed the *parivāsa* penance, or completed the original *parivāsa*, but has not yet been granted the *mānatva* before leaving the order;
if he later returns and receives full ordination again, he should be made to perform the *mānatva*.

If one has completed the *mānatva* penance, or completed the original *mānatva*, but has not yet been granted the *ābhāṣaṇa*, and subsequently receives the full ordination (*upasampadā*) again, one should grant the *ābhāṣaṇa*.
If one becomes a śrāmaṇera, this applies likewise even until the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of not relinquishing evil and false views.
If a bhikṣu commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, knowing the number of times he committed it and knowing the number of days he concealed it;

he requests from the Saṃgha, in accordance with the Dharma, the period of separate residence (*parivāsa*); he requests from the Saṃgha, in accordance with the Dharma, the *mānatva*; he requests from the Saṃgha, in accordance with the Dharma, the restoration to the original status (*mūlāpakarṣa*); and he requests from the Saṃgha, in accordance with the Dharma, the rehabilitation (*ābṛhaṇa*).
If the Saṃgha grants [the matter] entirely in accordance with the Dharma, this person is said to be pure;
if even one item is granted by the Saṃgha not in accordance with the Dharma, this person is not said to be pure.
There were two bhikṣus who committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense; one bhikṣu knew he had committed it, while the other did not know he had committed it, yet both concealed it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The one who knew he had committed the offense should be granted the parivāsa probation."
"If one does not know that they have committed an offense, they should be granted *mānatta*.
The same applies whether they remember it or do not remember it.
There were two bhikṣus who committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and concealed it."
One bhikṣu forms one perception;
another bhikṣu forms a different perception, such that one says it is a pārājika offense while the other says it is a sthūlātyaya, or even down to calling it a mere evil speech.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one forms the perception of unity, he should be given the *parivāsa* (probation);
if one forms the perception of difference, he should be given the *mānatva* (penance)."
There were certain bhikṣus who, while undergoing the *parivāsa* (probation), or while undergoing the *mānatva* (penance), or while undergoing the *ābhāṣaṇa* (rehabilitation), passed away.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, saying:
"Did he pass away while fully endowed with the precepts?"
"Did they pass away having broken the precepts?
The Buddha said,
"All were fully endowed with the precepts."
There was a bhikṣu who had committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, but he did not know the number of offenses nor did he remember how long he had concealed them.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Grant him the parivāsa probation starting from the time he remembers having committed the offenses."
Doubt is also like this.
There is a bhikṣu who conceals [an offense] from all people;
there is a bhikṣu who conceals it from that person but does not conceal it from this person.
There was a bhikṣu who concealed [his offense] in this land but did not conceal it in that land.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha,
and the Buddha said:
"Concealing all things is what is meant by 'concealment.
If one conceals [faults] from one's preceptor (upādhyāya), teacher (ācārya), or those toward whom one feels reverence, it is not called concealment;
if one conceals them from other people, it is called concealment."
If, in this land, one conceals something because it is known by many people and one does not wish for them to know, it is not called concealment;
if one conceals it in that other land, it is called concealment.
The Mahīśāsaka Vinaya, Volume 23;
The Mahīśāsaka Vinaya, Volume 24. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśa during the Song Dynasty.
Translated together with Zhu Daosheng and others;
Part Four, Section Two: The Lower Portion of the *Karmavācanā* (Ritual Procedures). The Buddha was staying in the city of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had transgressed a precept but did not know which one he had violated. He spoke about this to the other bhikṣus.
Some of the bhikṣus said that he had committed an offense, while others said that he had not.
Those who said he had not committed an offense spoke to him, saying:
"You have not violated the precepts."
Having heard this, he then conceived the thought that he had not violated the precepts.
To those who had indeed violated them, he said:
"You have violated the precepts; you should recognize your own fault and repent."
"Do not defile the holy life, do not betray the faithful offerings of others, and do not suffer for a long night!
That bhikṣu replied, "I have committed no offense; why should I see my own fault and repent?"
It was said that those bhikṣus who had violated the precepts were subjected to the formal act of *ajñapti-karman* for not acknowledging their offense.
Once they had been suspended (*ukkhepanīya*), they entered the city of Kauśāmbī to seek allies, saying:
"I have committed no offense; those bhikṣus insist that I am guilty and have performed the *ajñapti-karman* against me for not acknowledging my offense, but this constitutes an invalid formal act."
"Venerable sirs!
You should rescue me in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya!
He then went to the bhikṣus outside the city and sought assistance from them as he had done above.
Upon hearing this, all the bhikṣus joined together to assist them.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the Saṃgha had already been split, rose from his seat and went into the midst of the assembly of bhikṣus who were assisting the suspended bhikṣu, saying to them:
"You must not speak such words as to say that this bhikṣu has committed no offense."
If that bhikṣu has not actually committed an offense and yet has been accused, you should still say to him:
"You should recognize your own fault and repent. He will then think thus:

"If I say that I do not see my offense, the Saṃgha shall perform the formal act of 'not seeing an offense' against me; they shall not dwell with me, nor shall they participate with me in the Uposatha, the Pravāraṇā, or any other affairs of the Saṃgha."
"You should not engage in such disputes, which cause the Saṃgha to be discordant and live in separation, giving rise to all manner of defilements.
You must fear this matter and should cause that person to recognize their own fault and repent!"
When the Blessed One had finished speaking this, he went again to the assembly of bhikṣus who were censuring others and said to them:
"You must not forcibly bring up the offenses of others!
If they have actually committed an offense, the Saṃgha should tell them to see the offense for themselves."
If he should say,
"I have no offense that can be seen," the Saṃgha should nevertheless deliberate:

"If we were to perform the *ajñapti-karman* of 'not seeing one's offense' against them, and not dwell with them, nor participate with them in the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, or any monastic affairs, this would lead to disputes and mutual reviling, causing the Saṃgha to be discordant, to live separately, and to give rise to various defilements."
“You all should fear this matter; set it aside and do not raise it!
Although the bhikṣus heard the Buddha’s words, they still did not cease their quarreling; they then shouted insults at the meal and struck one another.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"One should not revile one another, nor should one raise their voice over food; those who violate this commit a *duṣkṛta* offense!
If they strike one another, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense!"
Although the bhikṣus heard the Buddha’s words, they still did not cease their dispute and proceeded to perform separate monastic acts (saṃghakarma) within the boundary.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:

“If the Saṃgha has already been split, and they perform separate formal acts (karmavācanā) within the boundary that are in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, these are also called accomplished karmas.”
Why is this? Because the two groups hold divergent views and do not dwell together.
There are two kinds of non-dwelling:
"There are those who become *asamvāsa* (those who do not live in communion) by their own action, and there are those with whom the Saṃgha, through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), renders *asamvāsa*.
Although the bhikṣus heard these words of the Buddha, they continued to dispute without ceasing.
The Buddha again addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do not engage in mutual strife or contention, nor slander one another, nor revile one another.
You should dwell together in harmony in one place, blending like water and milk, and jointly propagate the Teacher’s instruction."
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
May you dwell in peace and security!”
"Although the Buddha is the Lord of the Dharma, we shall know it ourselves.
The Buddha stopped them three times, but the bhikṣus answered as they had before.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus again:
"In the distant past, there was a king in Kosala named Dīghāvu; his domain was small and his army was weak.

His neighbor, the king of Kāsi named Brahmadatta, ruled over a vast territory with a powerful and flourishing host. Gradually he encroached upon and seized [Dīghāvu’s lands], until he finally swallowed up his kingdom."
King Brahmadatta obtained a minister from King Dīrghāyu, whom he favored greatly and entrusted with the affairs of state.
At that time, King Dīrghāyu, being naked, took his wife and became a brahmin, going to live in the house of a potter in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
The wife suddenly had this thought:
"I wish that at the time of sunrise, amidst the battle of the fourfold army at the crossroads, I might drink the water from the sharpening of swords.
Having thought this, she said to the king:
"If this wish is not fulfilled, I shall die right here.
The king said,
"This cannot be accomplished!"
"The illness you now suffer will surely lead to your death; there is no doubt.
He then spoke further to his wife, saying:
"If Brahmāda hears of this and learns where I am, he will certainly bind me hand and foot, beat the donkey-drum, and tear my body into five pieces!"
"You may wait a moment; I shall go in secret to question a former minister regarding the meaning of this matter.
Having spoken, he went at once and questioned him in full detail.
The former minister replied:
"I must see the lady; I shall examine her for myself.
He then went to where the lady was, and seeing her from afar, he bared his right shoulder, prostrated himself with his head at her feet, and three times addressed her, saying: "Lady!"
"Now you carry a son of great merit and virtue; the royal lineage of the Kingdom of Kosala shall have its successor!
He further said to the king, "Tomorrow morning, I shall cause the lady’s wish to bear fruit."
Having spoken thus, he returned to where Brahmadatta was and said:
"Does Your Majesty know?

Such a star has appeared; you ought to assemble the fourfold army and, at dawn when the sun first rises, engage in battle in two arrays at a crossroads, all whetting their blades, in order to avert this calamity."
"If it is not done so, there will surely be great misfortune!
King Brahmadata said, "Then you may do as you please."

Thereupon, the minister immediately ordered the fourfold army to be arrayed; at dawn, when the sun first rose, the two forces met for battle at the crossroads, and all began sharpening their blades. He secretly had the lady stationed in one place and gave her the water used for sharpening the blades.

The lady immediately drank it, and the child grew within her womb. When the months were complete, she gave birth to a son whose countenance was exceptionally marvelous; he was named Changsheng (Long Life).
When he reached the age of ten, his father said to him:
"Brahmadatta has invaded and seized our kingdom. It has been a long time since I fled with your mother to this place, and you have now grown to maturity."
"If they were to hear of this, father and son would surely perish together at once.
You must go far away; do not dote upon your parents!
Changsheng wept bitterly, prostrated at his parents' feet, circumambulated them three times, and departed.
In his cultivation of the arts—calculation, writing, archery, charioteering, the taming of elephants and horses, and music—he excelled beyond all others.
He devoted himself particularly to elephant trainers, mastering every technique of elephant training.
"Long-life King was formerly a barber; later, he served as a barber for Brahmāda.

When he went to that place seeking to have his hair shaved, Brahmāda recognized him immediately. Fearing he might be hidden away, [the king] questioned him thoroughly regarding his residence and where he had fled to hide, and reported this to Brahmāda."

Having heard this, Brahmada immediately ordered them to be seized; he had the husband and wife bound back-to-back and, beating a donkey-bleating drum, caused the proclamation to be made throughout the streets and alleys, and at the crossroads, they were to be divided into five parts.
Upon receiving these instructions, he immediately captured him.
Hearing this, Changsheng went to the side of the road; having seen him, his heart was shattered within, and he thought to himself:
"The enmity between father and son is such that they do not share the same heaven or earth."
"How can I now endure this? The sincerity of even a common man is sufficient to evoke a response! I shall rather give up my life to avenge this shame.
Thus he spoke, intending to sacrifice his very life to repay his grievance.
Seeing him from afar, his parents knew that he must harbor thoughts of seeking revenge; they then spoke aloud to him alone, like madmen:
"Do not look at the long, nor look at the short!"
To repay enmity with enmity provides no means for the enmity to cease;
to repay enmity with virtue, the enmity comes to an end!
To act in accordance with the hearts of one's parents is what is called a filial son.
"To follow one's feelings and indulge one's will is not what I call the Way!
At that time, those who witnessed it all said that King Changshou was speaking madly out of fear.

Only Changsheng heard and deeply grasped his father’s intent; he disciplined himself to serve him with reverence, and though his own emotions were momentarily stilled, although he was internally shattered, he showed nothing of it outwardly.
He immediately restrained himself and returned to the elephant trainer’s quarters, yet he still did not forget his methods for seeking revenge.
Later, while in the elephant stable at night, he played the lute; its sound was clear and harmonious.
Upon hearing this, Brahmāda immediately asked,
"Who in the stables is capable of doing this? They replied:
"A certain elephant trainer has a disciple; this was his playing.
He immediately summoned him and ordered him to play again. Having heard it, he thought to himself:
"Since I became king, I have never heard such a thing!"
He then placed his full trust in him, keeping him constantly by his side.
Later, the king arrayed the fourfold army and set out for a hunt with his court ladies, ministers, and the crown prince.
The troops scattered in all directions, vying with one another to pursue the deer.
Changsheng was then driving the king’s chariot, having escaped three *yojanas* ahead of the army without anyone noticing him.
The King, his body utterly exhausted, said to Changsheng:
"I wish to lie down for a short while; can you protect me? He replied:
"O King, sleep in peace; I shall protect you.
The king then stayed beneath the tree and fell asleep with his head resting upon his [the yakṣa's] knee.
The sword that protected the king’s person then spontaneously drew itself forth and stood before the long-lived one.
Upon seeing him, Changsheng immediately thought to himself:
"This king harbors a great enmity toward me; how could I not take advantage of this encounter today!"
He immediately rose and seized his sword, intending to cut off the king’s neck, but then he thought again:
"The kindness of one's parents exceeds that of heaven and earth; at the moment of death, they instructed me:
'Do not see their long [faults], nor see their short [merits]!'"
"To repay enmity with enmity provides no means for enmity to cease!
How could I now go against this instruction?
He immediately returned the sword and resumed his attendance at the bedside as before.
The king was suddenly startled awake, and Changsheng asked him, "Why are you startled? He replied:
"I dreamed that Prince Jīvaka took up a sword, intending to take my life!
Jīva said, "In this desolate wilderness,
by what cause or condition could there suddenly be a Prince Jīvaka?"
"It must be that the mountain deity is merely terrifying the King!
Your Majesty, simply rest in peace; do not harbor any anxiety!
Thus he spoke three times.
When the king finally fell asleep, Changsheng again thought to himself:
"My parents, at the time of their death, instructed me most earnestly: 'Repay enmity with virtue, and only then will that enmity come to an end!'"
"In the past, how did my three desires oppose you?
From this day forward, I shall resolve to serve Your Majesty as if you were a kinsman, and never again give rise to even a hair’s breadth of harmful intent.
Having formed this thought, the king awoke and was greatly delighted.
Changsheng asked,
"For what reason are you so greatly joyful? He replied:
"I dreamed that Prince Changshou wished to treat me as a kinsman and no longer harbored any intent to harm me; for this reason, I am greatly rejoiced.
Thereupon, Changsheng addressed the king, saying:
"Prince Changshou is none other than myself. Since Your Majesty harmed my parents, my resolve was to kill you."
"By reverently repeating the final testament three times, Your Majesty has avoided [punishment];
yet this mind is difficult to guard, and it may well arise again later.
I pray that Your Majesty will consider this and not leave room for future regret!"
The king said:
"I have acted without the Way, while you, father and son, cherish benevolence.
How could I now harbor any schemes or anxieties?"
"You have granted me my life; I swear I shall not betray you!
He then immediately returned to his army and assembled his ministers to deliberate together:
"If we capture Prince Jīvaka, how should we punish him?"
Some said: "One should cut off his hands and feet! Others said:
"One should cut off their ears and nose!
some said; "One should mince them with an axe! others said.
Or someone said:
"It should be roasted on a wooden spit!
The king then pointed and said:
"This person is none other than Prince Jīvaka; he has granted me my life, and I must now repay him with my own life.
None of you shall harbor any evil intentions toward him!"
Thereupon, he returned to the palace and gave his daughter to him as a wife;

with his left hand holding a golden basin and his right hand holding a golden pitcher, he poured water over the hands of Jīvaka, and having returned to his own country, he once again became the King of Kosala.
"The neighboring kingdoms remained in harmony for many successive generations.
He then addressed the bhikṣus:
"Even when kings and people of the world have provoked such great enmity, by not dwelling upon it, they instead become close and friendly."
"You have left the household life to seek the path of the unconditioned; how is it that over such a trivial matter you engage in mutual strife and thereby lose the great benefit?
You should abandon this mindset and return to harmony, blending like water and milk, so that together you may propagate the Master's teaching and dwell in peace and happiness."
The bhikṣus spoke again to the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
May you dwell in peace and security!”
“Although the Buddha is the Lord of the Dharma, I know this myself.
Still refusing to desist, the Buddha then ascended into the void and spoke this verse:
“Mutually reviling one another with evil words, In the end, there is no superior Dharma.”
When the Saṃgha is split into two factions, it is invariably due to these matters.
Even those who have severed bones, taken human life, plundered cattle, horses, and wealth,
or sowed the enmity that destroys nations and exterminates clans— such as these can still achieve reconciliation.
It is like two pieces of wood rubbing together; both produce fire that consumes them, spreading to everything it reaches.
The anger of the foolish is just like this. If you revile one another and persist in holding onto that resentment without letting go, [you will suffer the same fate].
Enmity and calamity find no way to cease; day and night their roots and shoots grow.
When faced with various harsh words and insults, if one can refrain from retaliating, this forbearance will not breed further resentment, and existing enmity will naturally be eliminated.
"If one seeks to remove hatred with hatred, hatred will never come to rest;
by not dwelling on hatred, it is naturally removed—this is the most courageous and steadfast.
Having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One immediately used his supernormal power to fly to the village of Pāṭali and stayed beneath a *bhadrapāla* tree, without any attendants.
At that time, there was a great elephant who was troubled by the herd; whenever he wished to drink water, the elephant calves would stir it up before him until it became turbid;
and whenever he wished to eat grass, those calves would graze right in front of him, trampling and defiling it.
The elephant thought to himself:
"I am now beset by this herd of elephants; it would be better for me to withdraw.
Having thought this, he immediately departed, whereupon he constantly obtained clear water and fine grass as he gradually made his way toward the Bhadrapāla forest.
Seeing the Buddha, they were filled with joy; they fetched water for the Buddha and cleared the grass from around him.
Because these two elephants had distanced themselves from the pleasures of the crowd and likewise delighted in tranquility, the Buddha spoke this verse:
"The two dragons are of one mind, Both weary of the afflictions of the multitude."
"Having already abandoned all solitary wandering, I now delight in this empty forest.
After the Buddha had spoken these verses, he departed from the Bhadrapāla Forest for the city of Śrāvastī and stayed at the Jetavana Monastery.

At that time, laymen and laywomen, kings, ministers, elders, householders, non-Buddhists, śramaṇas, and brahmins made offerings, paid homage, showed respect, and offered praise to him; they bestowed upon him abundant food, drink, and clothing. Yet the World-Honored One remained unattached, just like a lotus flower.
At that time, the upāsakas of the city of Kauśāmbī all spoke thus:
"We have now lost a great benefit because the World-Honored One does not remain here due to the bhikṣus' fondness for quarreling."
"We must employ skillful means to cause him to depart.
Thereupon, they made a pact among themselves not to speak with him again nor provide him with food or clothing.
Those other bhikṣus also spoke these words:
"Because of our own transgressions, we have caused the Blessed One to abandon us and depart.
We should now go together to the Buddha's presence and bitterly repent for our faults!
Thereupon, they put on their robes, took up their bowls, and went to where the Buddha was.

At that time, hearing that the monks who had been quarreling had arrived, Śāriputra went together with five hundred monks to where the Buddha was. Prostrating at his feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The quarreling monks from Kauśāmbī are now coming; how should we receive them?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
