"You should listen to the words of those two groups; if they are in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught, you should treat them well and associate with them as companions."
He asked again:
"World-Honored One!
How many matters must be present for one to know that another’s speech is in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught?"
"By how many matters does one know that his speech is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha?
The Buddha said:
"If he accomplishes fourteen things:"
To speak of the Dharma as non-Dharma, or even to say that what was established by the Buddha was not established by the Buddha—this is non-Dharma, non-discipline, and not the teaching of the Buddha.
"If it is contrary to the above, that is the Dharma, that is the Vinaya, and that is the teaching of the Buddha.

At that time, when Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī heard that those quarreling bhikṣus had arrived, she went together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated herself at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“The monks of Kauśāmbī who are quarreling have now arrived; how should we receive them?

The Buddha said, “You should listen to the words of those two groups. If they are in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught, you should receive them well.”
One should seek five matters from monks who act in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teachings:
a bhikṣuṇī must, every half-month, request from a monk who acts in accordance with the Dharma a person to provide her with instruction;
and a bhikṣuṇī must observe the summer retreat (varṣā) in a place where there is a monk who acts in accordance with the Dharma.

When the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) is concluded, one should request [the confession of] offenses regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected from a bhikṣu who acts in accordance with the Dharma.
Once a *śikṣamāṇā* has completed two years of training in the precepts, she should receive full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) within the assembly of both orders of monks and nuns.

If a bhikṣuṇī commits a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), she should perform the *mānatva* penance for half a month within the assembly of both orders; having performed the *mānatva*, she should seek absolution from the offenses before twenty members each from the two assemblies.
"If there are other matters for the community of bhikṣuṇīs, they should seek out a bhikṣu who acts in accordance with the Dharma.

At that time, when the householder Anāthapiṇḍada heard that those quarreling bhikṣus had arrived, he went together with five hundred upāsakas to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"The bhikṣus from Kauśāmbī who have come here to settle their dispute—how should we receive them?

The Buddha said, "You should listen to the words of those two groups; if they are in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught, you should accept their instructions."
As for receiving them with respect and making offerings to them, one should treat them all with complete equality. Why is this?
It is because, for example, if genuine gold is broken into two pieces, no difference can be found between them.
Viśākhā Mātṛ and five hundred upāsikās went to where the Buddha was and addressed him; the Buddha’s reply was likewise as before.
At that time, Ānanda saw those monks who had been quarreling enter the city of Śrāvastī, and he went to inform the Buddha:
“Those quarreling monks have already entered; how should I prepare the bedding for them?”
The Buddha said:
"One should give them a peripheral room;
if that is insufficient, give them a central room."
"One must not allow that Elder to be without a place to stay!
Ānanda, having received these instructions, immediately prepared a seat for him to dwell in.
At that time, the monk who had been subject to the formal act of suspension thought to himself in a secluded place:
"Am I indeed guilty? Or am I without guilt?
Have I been subject to formal suspension?"
Is the formal act of suspension invalid? Is the *karmavācanā* performed according to the Dharma,
or is it contrary to the Dharma?
"I shall now carefully reflect upon this in accordance with the Sūtras and the Vinaya.

Having reflected, he recognized that he was guilty, that he had been formally charged, and that the *karmavācanā* had been performed according to the Dharma. He then went to where the companion bhikṣu was staying and said to him:
"I have already seen my own fault!"
"Venerable sirs!
Please seek reconciliation for me and revoke the previous *karma*.
The bhikṣus then took him to the place where the bhikṣu who had been subjected to the *adarśana-āpatti-karman* was staying and said to him:
"This bhikṣu has already recognized his own offense; we pray that you will revoke the previous *karma* for him!
Thereupon, the Saṃghas of both divisions took the suspended bhikṣu to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"This bhikṣu has committed an offense; it is not that he has not committed one.
He has been subject to the formal act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma); it is not that he has not been so suspended."
"The *karmavācanā* has been accomplished and is not unaccomplished.
The Saṃgha should now revoke the previous *karmavācanā* and perform a second *jñapti-dvitīya-karmavācanā* to bring about reconciliation.
That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha, prostrate at the feet of the Saṃgha, and say:
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], have had the *saṃgha* perform the formal act of *adṛṣṭāparādha-karman* against me.
I now submit to the *saṃgha* and repent; I beg for the lifting of this *adṛṣṭāparādha-karman*."
"May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, release me!
Thus he should say three times.
Then one bhikṣu should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

These bhikṣus previously engaged in mutual quarreling and verbal abuse, some claiming [the other] had committed an offense while others claimed he had not; some claiming he was subject to *ukkhepanīyakamma* (suspension) while others claimed he was not; some claiming the *kamma* was valid while others claimed it was invalid. Now these bhikṣus themselves see that they have committed an offense, and do not claim they have not;
they acknowledge they are subject to *ukkhepanīyakamma*, and do not claim they are not."
The *karmavācanā* is accomplished and not unaccomplished.
The Saṃgha now intends to lift the *ajñapti-karma* for not seeing one's offense and to restore harmony.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen.
The motion is thus stated:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
These bhikṣus previously quarreled with one another, and so forth, until they have now returned to harmony."
"Whichever elders consent, let them remain silent;
whoever does not consent, let them speak.
The Sangha has finished performing the *karmavācanā* for the monk so-and-so to lift the formal act and restore harmony."
The Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.
The Buddha said:
“Once the *karmavācanā* is concluded, one should immediately perform the *saṃgha-sāmaggī-poṣadha* together with them.
At that time, Upāli asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!”
“How many qualities must a bhikṣu possess to be entitled to raise a formal charge?
The Buddha said, “As it was explained in the section on the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.”
The Buddha was staying at the country of Campā, dwelling by the side of the Ganges River, not far from Rājagṛha.
At a certain residence there was a bhikṣu of the Kāśyapa clan who served as the *karmadāna* (steward), and he made this vow:
"May many bhikṣus from the four quarters come to assemble here, so that the upāsakas and upāsikās may, because of this, perform much meritorious virtue!"
That dwelling place was spacious and vast, and subsequently his aspirations were fulfilled.

At that time, many learned bhikṣus arrived at that residence; the bhikṣu Kāśyapa went out to meet them, prostrated and inquired after their well-being, carried their robes and bowls for them, prepared bathing requisites, and provided post-meal drinks.
On the following day, he offered them both morning and midday meals, as well as robes, continuing in this manner for many days.
The visiting bhikṣus deliberated together, saying:
"This bhikṣu possesses a sense of shame and modesty and practices the holy life; he wishes for us to dwell here for a long time.
We should indeed observe the rains retreat here."
Having deliberated thus, they immediately lived together.
Later, the bhikṣu Kāśyapa thought to himself:

"These visiting bhikṣus have rested from their exhaustion and know the location of the village; I cannot continue to exhort and convert people every day to provide them with both morning and midday meals."
Having thought this, he stopped.
The visiting bhikṣus resented him and further deliberated:
"This bhikṣu wishes for us to leave early; he is certainly an evil bhikṣu, devoid of shame and remorse, and does not cultivate the holy life!"
"We shall perform the formal act of *karma* against him for not acknowledging his offense.
Having deliberated thus, they together censured him.
Then, the bhikṣu Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"Am I guilty of an offense?
Am I free from offense? Have I been subject to the formal act of suspension?"
Is the formal act (kamma) of suspension invalid?
Is the formal act valid? Or is it invalid?
"The World-Honored One is currently by the banks of the Ganges; I shall go there to consult him, and whatever instructions he gives, I shall respectfully carry out.
Having thought this, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went to where the Buddha was. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha comforted him, saying:
"Where have you come from?
Have you not lacked almsfood, and are you not weary from the road?"
He replied, "I have not lacked for alms, nor am I weary from the road.
Not far from Rājagṛha there is a residence; I was serving as its *karmadāna* (steward) and have come from there."
He then related the entire sequence of events, from beginning to end, to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "You have committed no offense; no fault is to be seen."
"You may now return and dwell there with a peaceful mind.
Kāśyapa accepted these instructions, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him to the right, and withdrew.
When the visiting bhikṣus saw that he had departed, they again deliberated together, saying:
"We have acted improperly!
Why did we suspend this pure and blameless bhikṣu?
We should go together to the Buddha's presence, repent our transgression, and eliminate our offense."
When the rains retreat and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony were concluded, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha greeted him, saying:
“Was there no lack of almsfood? Were you not weary from the journey?”
"In what place do you dwell during the retreat? He replied,
"Alms-food is not lacking, and the roads are not wearying."
"Not far from the city of Rājagṛha, there is a residence where we have entered the rains retreat.
The Buddha asked, "In that residence,
did you perform the formal act of *karma* of 'accusation for not seeing an offense' against those bhikṣus?"
He replied, "I did. He asked again:
"By what matter was he censured?
He replied, "There was no matter."
The Buddha rebuked them in various ways, saying:
"What you have done is contrary to the Dharma!
You should not commit such evil deeds!"
"How does one perform the formal act of *karma* for charging a pure and blameless bhikṣu with not seeing his offense?
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We were foolish to have committed these deeds; we all feel remorse and now come to repent.
We only pray that you will compassionately accept our confession!
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
“If a bhikṣu performs various *karmas* on account of no grounds, those *karmas* are all invalid.

There were certain bhikṣus who, from a distance, performed the *karman* of censure, the *karman* of banishment, the *karman* of dependence, the *karman* of accusation, and the *karman* of subordination;
furthermore, they performed from a distance the acts of separate residence (*parivāsa*), the period of initial reparation (*mūlāpakarṣa*), the penance (*mānatva*), and rehabilitation (*ābṛhaṇa*).
Furthermore, they established boundaries from afar and dissolved them from afar;
they also released those persons appointed by the Saṃgha from afar, and further appointed from afar those members of the Saṃgha who had not yet been appointed.
The bhikṣus reported these matters to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:

"If one performs the *karma* of reprimand at a distance, up to and including the *karma* of appointing a person not yet appointed by the Saṃgha at a distance—all these are *karmas* that do not accord with the Dharma; the *karma* is not accomplished."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus performed an improper *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), up to and including a *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), outside the boundary.
Having completed these acts, they entered within the boundary and said to the bhikṣus:
"We have performed the *tarjanīya-karman*, up to and including the *pratisāraṇīya-karman*, against such-and-such bhikṣus outside the boundary."
"Venerable sirs! You should listen so that this formal act (*karmavācanā*) may be accomplished according to the Dharma.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:

"If a bhikṣu performs any of the five kinds of illegal *karmans* outside the boundary—up to and including the *karman* of appointing someone whom the Saṃgha has not authorized—even if he returns and tells the bhikṣus within the boundary to listen so that the *karman* may be accomplished, none of them are valid."
At that time, the bhikṣus performed the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) for one another: one bhikṣu with one bhikṣu, and so on up to one bhikṣu with many bhikṣus;
two bhikṣus with many bhikṣus, and likewise for all others.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"All these *karmavācanā* procedures are invalid; they incur the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
The Buddha spoke again:
"If one performs a *karmavācanā* (formal act) by proceeding directly to the formal motion without first making the announcement, the *karmavācanā* is not valid;
if one states what should have been stated first after stating it later, or states what should have been stated later before stating it earlier, these are also all invalid;
and if, at the time of the *karmavācanā*, there is someone entitled to raise an objection who does not agree, it is also invalid—in all such cases, one commits the offense of *duṣkṛta*."
At that time, the bhikṣus performed a karmavācanā using other methods and other rules.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The karmavācanā is not valid."

At that time, the bhikṣus performed illegal *saṃghakarma* with a divided assembly, illegal *saṃghakarma* with a united assembly, legal *saṃghakarma* with a divided assembly, and legal *saṃghakarma* with a united assembly.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. On account of this, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"I do not permit three kinds of karmavācanā; I permit only the karmavācanā performed in accordance with the Dharma through harmonious assembly!"
There are five kinds of formal acts (*kamma*):

an unlawful act performed by an incomplete assembly; an act resembling the Dharma performed by an incomplete assembly; an act resembling the Dharma performed by a complete assembly; and a lawful act performed by a complete assembly.
What is an illegal *karmavācanā*?

It is when those who ought to attend do not attend, those who ought to delegate their authority do not delegate it, and there are persons entitled to raise objections who do not consent, yet the *karmavācanā* is nonetheless forcibly carried out.
One should perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation), yet they only made the motion without performing the *karman*;
or they only performed the *karman* without making the motion;
or they made the motion twice without performing the *karman*.
Regarding the *jñapti-karman* (motion) and the *karmavācanā* (proclamation):
one should perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations), yet if one only performs the motion without the three proclamations;
or if one only performs the three proclamations without the motion.
This is called an illegal *karmavācanā*.
What is meant by a *karmavācanā* performed by a separate assembly?

It refers to performing a *karmavācanā* by force when those who ought to have come do not come, when those who ought to have given their consent (*anuśrāvaṇā*) do not give it, and when those entitled to raise an objection during the *karmavācanā* do not agree.
This is called a formal act performed by a separate assembly (*bhinnasaṃgha-karman*). What is meant by a formal act that resembles the Dharma but is performed by a separate assembly?
It refers to cases where those who ought to come do not come, and those who ought to grant their authorization (*anujñā*) do not grant it.
If, in the case of a *jñapti-dvitīya* or *jñapti-caturtha* *karmavācanā*, the formal motion (*jñapti*) is performed after the *karmavācanā*;
or if, at the time of the *karmavācanā*, those entitled to raise an objection do not agree, yet the *karmavācanā* is nonetheless forcibly carried out—
this is called a *karmavācanā* that resembles the Dharma but is performed by a separate assembly.
What is a formal act of concordant semblance?
It is when those who ought to come have come, and those who ought to give proxy have given proxy;
yet, in the case of a *jñapti-dvitīya* or *jñapti-caturtha* formal act, the formal act is performed first and the motion (*jñapti*) is made afterwards.
If, at the time of a *karmavācanā*, there are those entitled to raise an objection who do not do so,
this is called a concordant *karmavācanā* that resembles the Dharma.
What is a *karmavācanā* that is in accordance with the Dharma?
Those who ought to come have come; those who ought to be entrusted with the matter have been entrusted. At the time of the *karmavācanā*, those entitled to raise objections do not object.
Whether it be a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* or a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, in all cases one first makes the formal announcement (*jñapti*) and subsequently performs the *karman*.

This is called a *karmavācanā* (formal act) performed according to the Dharma. Suppose, when a formal act of censure is being carried out against a bhikṣu in an illegal manner, there are seven persons in the Saṃgha who dispute it: one says, "This is an illegal *karmavācanā*"; one says, "This is a *karmavācanā* performed by a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*)"; one says, "This is a *karmavācanā* that resembles the Dharma but is performed by a separate assembly"; one says, "This is a *karmavācanā* that resembles the Dharma and is performed by a harmonious assembly (*saṃgha*)"; one says, "This is a *karmavācanā* performed according to the Dharma and by a harmonious assembly"; one says, "The *karmavācanā* has been validly accomplished"; and one says, "The *karmavācanā* has not been validly accomplished."
Among these seven persons, two speak according to the Dharma:
namely, those who declare that it is an illegal *karmavācanā* and that the *karma* was not validly performed.

This also applies to cases where a *bhikṣu* is subjected to a *tarjanīyakarman* by a separate assembly (*nānāsaṃgha*), a *tarjanīyakarman* by a separate assembly that resembles the Dharma, or a *tarjanīyakarman* by a harmonious assembly (*saṃghasāmagrī*) that resembles the Dharma.
When a formal act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) is performed against a bhikṣu in accordance with the Dharma, there are seven types of speech, two of which are in accordance with the Dharma.
These refer to a formal act that is both in accordance with the Dharma and performed through a harmonious assembly, thereby constituting a validly accomplished karman.
The *karman* for expulsion, the *karman* for dependence, the *karman* for charging with an offense, and the *karman* for subduing the mind are also like this.
Suppose there are monks who engage in quarreling and dispute; the other monks deliberate thus:
"This monk is fond of quarreling and frequently creates trouble."
"We should rather unite and perform a formal act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) against him in accordance with the Dharma.
They then united and intended to perform a formal act of censure in accordance with the Dharma;
however, they instead performed an improper formal act of censure, and thus the formal act was not validly accomplished.
This applies even to the case where they instead perform a formal act of censure that merely resembles the Dharma (a *sādharmya-samagrī-jñapti-caturtha-karman*), which is likewise invalid.
Those bhikṣus then move to another residence, where the bhikṣus of that other residence deliberate thus:
"This bhikṣu is fond of quarreling; those bhikṣus performed a formal act of censure that merely resembled the Dharma, and thus the formal act was not validly accomplished."
"We would rather perform a formal act of *tarjanīya-karman* (reproval) against him in accordance with the Dharma and in harmony.
Thus, they intended to perform a formal act of *tarjanīya-karman* in accordance with the Dharma and in harmony, yet instead they performed an illegal *pravāsanīya-karman* (banishment);
even when they instead performed a legal *pravāsanīya-karman*, the formal acts were all invalid.
This applies even up to the case where they perform the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against one another; it is also like this.
There was a bhikṣu who engaged in evil conduct and defiled families.
The other bhikṣus deliberated thus:
"This bhikṣu has committed evil deeds and defiled families.
We should unite and perform a formal act of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) against him in accordance with the Dharma.
Thus they intended to perform a formal act of expulsion in accordance with the Dharma, yet instead they performed an improper formal act of expulsion, and the formal act was not accomplished.

This applies even to the case where they perform a formal act of reconciliation (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) that resembles the Dharma, such as a *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), which is likewise [invalid].
That bhikṣu then moves to another residence, and the bhikṣus at that other residence deliberate thus:
"This bhikṣu has committed evil deeds and defiled families."
"The monks have performed a formal act of concordance that resembles the Dharma for him, yet the formal act was not validly accomplished.
We should rather perform a formal act of expulsion against him in accordance with the Dharma."

They then intended to perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) of expulsion in accordance with the Dharma, but instead performed an unlawful act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*), and thus the formal act was not accomplished.
This continued until they instead performed a lawful act of dependence, yet all such formal acts remained unaccomplished.
Even up to the formal act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*), it is likewise.
There was a bhikṣu who was foolish and lacked wisdom, repeatedly committing offenses.
The bhikṣus deliberated thus:

"This bhikṣu is foolish and lacks wisdom; he repeatedly commits offenses. We should rather join together to perform for him a formal act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*) in accordance with the Dharma.
Thus they intended to perform a formal act of dependence in accordance with the Dharma, yet instead they performed an improper formal act of dependence, and the formal act was not accomplished.
This applies even to the formal act of reconciliation (*sāmagrī-karman*) performed in a manner resembling the Dharma;
it is the same in all such cases. That bhikṣu then moved to another residence, where the bhikṣus of that residence deliberated thus:
"This bhikṣu is foolish and lacks wisdom; he repeatedly commits offenses."
Those bhikṣus performed a formal act of dependence that was a semblance of the Dharma and lacked true harmony; thus, the formal act was invalid.
We should rather perform for them a formal act of dependence that is in accordance with the Dharma.

He then intended to perform a formal act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*) in accordance with the Dharma for him, but instead performed a formal act of accusation (*codanā-karman*) that was contrary to the Dharma; thus, the formal act was not accomplished.
This continued until he instead performed a formal act of accusation that was in accordance with the Dharma; yet even then, the formal act was likewise not accomplished.
This applies even up to the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), which is likewise.
Suppose there is a bhikṣu who has committed an offense, yet does not recognize the offense, does not repent for it, and does not relinquish his evil and heterodox views.
The bhikṣus deliberated thus:
"This bhikṣu has committed an offense, yet he does not recognize his fault, does not repent, and does not abandon his evil and false views.
We should rather unite and perform a formal act of *karma* to reprove him in accordance with the Dharma."
They then intended to perform a formal act of accusation (*karmavācanā*) in accordance with the Dharma, yet instead performed an improper act of accusation; thus, the formal act was not accomplished.
This continued until they instead performed a formal act of accusation that merely resembled the Dharma and was carried out in concord; it was likewise [invalid].
That bhikṣu then moved to another residence, where the bhikṣus of that residence deliberated thus:
"This bhikṣu has committed an offense; he does not acknowledge his offense, does not repent, and does not relinquish his evil and false views."
Those bhikṣus have performed a formal act of suspension for resemblance to the Dharma (dharmābhāsa-samagrī-ukṣepa-karman), and thus the karman was not validly accomplished.
We should rather perform a formal act of suspension that is in accordance with the Dharma (yathādharma-ukṣepa-karman).

They then intended to perform a formal act of *karma* (karman) for the purpose of censuring [the offender] in accordance with the Dharma, but instead performed an improper *karma* for the purpose of making him submit; thus the *karma* was not accomplished.
This continued until they instead performed a proper *karma* for the purpose of making him submit, yet even this *karma* was likewise not accomplished.
Even down to the formal act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*), it is likewise.
There was a bhikṣu who addressed laypeople with harsh and abusive speech.
The bhikṣus deliberated thus:
"This bhikṣu has used coarse and evil speech to revile the laypeople; we should unite and perform a formal act of reconciliation for him according to the Dharma.
Thus they intended to perform a formal act of reconciliation according to the Dharma, yet instead they performed an improper formal act of reconciliation, and the formal act was not accomplished.
This applies even to the case where they instead perform a formal act of reconciliation (*saṃvāsanīya-karman*) that resembles the Dharma;
it is the same in all respects. When those monks move to another residence, the monks of that other residence deliberate thus:
"This monk used coarse and evil speech to revile the laypeople; the formal act of reconciliation resembling the Dharma performed for him was invalid."
"We would rather perform a formal act of reconciliation (*tassapāpiyasikā*) in accordance with the Dharma.

Thus, they intended to perform a formal act of reconciliation in accordance with the Dharma, but instead performed an improper formal act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*), and the formal act was therefore invalid.
Even when they instead perform a formal act of reprimand (*tarjanīya-karman*) according to the Dharma, the karman is likewise not accomplished.
This applies equally even when they instead perform a formal act of accusation (*ukṣepaṇīya-karman*).
There are five kinds of saṃgha:
a saṃgha of four bhikṣus, a saṃgha of five bhikṣus, a saṃgha of ten bhikṣus, a saṃgha of twenty bhikṣus, and an immeasurable saṃgha of bhikṣus.
Regarding a community of four bhikṣus:
with the exception of the *karmavācanā* for receiving the precepts and the *karmavācanā* for the removal of offenses, all other *karmas* may be performed together.
Regarding a community of five bhikṣus:

In China, with the exception of the *karmavācanā* for receiving ordination and the *karmavācanā* for expiation of offenses, all other *karmas* may be performed collectively. In border regions, with the exception of the *karmavācanā* for expiation of offenses, all other *karmas* may be performed collectively.
Regarding a community of ten bhikṣus:
with the exception of the *karmavācanā* for expiation of offenses, all other *karmas* may be performed collectively.
Regarding a community of twenty bhikṣus:
all formal acts (karmas) may be performed together by them.
If a formal act is performed by a community of four bhikṣus, and the fourth person is not in accordance with the Dharma or the Vinaya, the formal act is not accomplished and the Saṃgha is at fault.
Upāli asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One,
if someone should rebuke the Saṃgha during a formal act of discipline (karmavācanā), [what should be done]?"
"Who is censured?
Who is not censured?
The Buddha said:
"If one who has received the *karmavācanā* rebukes [the offender], it does not constitute a valid rebuke;
if a bhikṣu rebukes from behind a wall, it does not constitute a valid rebuke;
if a bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī rebukes, none of these constitute a valid rebuke."
"If a bhikṣu of the same boundary reproaches [the offender], such that even the person sitting beside him hears it, the reproach is considered accomplished.
There are three kinds of persons to whom the lifting of a *karmavācanā* (formal act) should not be granted;
if it is granted to them, the lifting is not accomplished.
What are the three?
If a bhikṣu commits an offense but does not recognize it as such;
or if a bhikṣu ought to repent for an offense but is unwilling to do so.
If a bhikṣu should abandon evil and false views, yet is unwilling to abandon them—
this is the third. If something has not yet been performed for him, it should be performed;
If the *karmavācanā* has already been performed for them, it is called a "well-performed *karmavācanā*.
If the opposite is the case—that is, if the *karmavācanā* has not yet been lifted—then it should be lifted;
if it has already been lifted, it is called a "well-lifted [karmavācanā]."
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there were two bhikṣus, one named Paṇḍaka and the other named Rohiṭa, who delighted in quarreling with one another and also incited strife among others;
they caused disputes to arise where none had existed before, and once arisen, they caused them to increase and spread.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked those two bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you did so? They replied: [Yes].
"It is truly so,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha rebuked him in various ways:
“You foolish man! What you have done is contrary to the Dharma; you ought not to have committed such an evil deed!
Having rebuked him thus, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, if there is such a bhikṣu, the Saṃgha should perform a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against him.

If he does not desist, the Saṃgha should, according to the specific case, perform a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) to impose a further penalty upon him."
"If there are three factors, one should perform the *karma* of censure against them:
they themselves engage in strife and further incite others to strife, doing so not just once but repeatedly.
Furthermore, there are another three factors:"
If one associates with evil friends, keeps company with wicked people, and delights in committing evil oneself, one should also be subjected to the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure).
Furthermore, there are three other conditions:

if one violates the higher training in ethics (*adhiśīla*), violates the higher training in view (*adhidṛṣṭi*), or associates with and conforms to the ways of laypeople (*avadātavasana*), one should also be subjected to the *tarjanīya-karman*.
There are three ways in which a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) is invalid:
censuring someone from a distance when that person should be present;
and failing to ask the Saṃgha:
They did not ask, "Should the *karma* of censure be performed against him?
nor did they cause the person to be censured to confess his own transgression, instead failing to have him speak for himself.
Furthermore, there are three ways in which a *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act) is not valid:
performing a *karmavācanā* that ought to be done in the presence [of the assembly] without being present;
and performing it with an illegal separate assembly.
One should cause him to confess his own faults, rather than allowing him to speak for himself.
A bhikṣu who has received the karma of censure (kukkucca-kamma) should properly conform to the Saṃgha.
What is meant by "properly conforming"?
One should not ordain others;
one should not confer the full precepts upon others;
one should not act as a formal preceptor for others.
One should not keep a śrāmaṇera;
one should not serve as the person who distributes voting tallies, nor should one accept such a position even if appointed by the Saṃgha;
one should not instruct bhikṣuṇīs, nor should one accept such a task even if appointed by the Saṃgha.
One should not accept any assignments made by the monastic community;
when performing communal duties, one must not speak;
and one must not revile other bhikṣus.
One must not rely on the power of a king, nor rely on one's own strength, nor rely on the power of kinsmen; one should rely solely on the power of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
One should repent and reproach oneself, not oppose the will of the Sangha, and seek the lifting of the *karmavācanā*.
Those two bhikṣus later became properly submissive to the Saṃgha; they repented, reproached themselves, and sought the lifting of the *kukkuṭaka-karman* (reproachful formal act).
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The Saṃgha should grant them the lifting [of that karman] through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations)."
That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha, prostrate at the feet of the Saṃgha, and three times request the lifting of the *tajjanīya-karman*.
A single bhikṣu should then announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so by name, delights in quarreling and strife, causing discord between this party and that;
he brings about quarrels that have not yet arisen and increases those already arisen.
The Saṃgha has previously performed the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against him; if he does not desist, his offense shall be further aggravated.

So-and-so has already properly submitted to the Saṃgha, repented, and taken responsibility for his transgression, seeking the lifting of the *karmavācanā*. The Saṃgha now grants him the lifting of the *karmavācanā*.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen.
[The motion] is thus announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is fond of quarreling and disputing... [omitted] ...the Saṃgha now grants him the lifting of the *karmavācanā*."
"Whichever elders approve, remain silent;
whoever does not approve, speak.
Thus a second and third time.
“The Sangha has completed the lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman* against the bhikṣu so-and-so;
the Sangha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.”
At that time, not far from the city of Śrāvastī, there was an Āmalaka grove.
Beside that grove lived an elder named Citta, who had faith and devotion in the Buddha-dharma and constantly provided for the bhikṣus.

In the Āmalaka grove there was a bhikṣu named Sudharma, who had long resided there as the *karmadāna*. Whenever the householder Citta invited the Saṃgha for food and clothing, or offered various goods, he would first inform him.
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were wandering through that forest together with five hundred bhikṣus. When the elder heard of this, he went out himself to welcome them.

Upon their arrival, he prostrated with his head at their feet and withdrew to stand to one side. After they had preached the sublime Dharma to him, instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening him, he said:
"I pray that you will accept my offering of food for visiting bhikṣus tomorrow!"
He accepted it in silence.
Knowing he had accepted, he returned home and went to the place where the bhikṣu Sudharma was, saying to him:
"I have invited Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana for tomorrow's meal."
"Venerable sir!
You too should come and eat.
The bhikṣu Kalyāṇadharma thought to himself:

"This wicked elder’s mind is already ruined; in the past, whenever he invited the Saṃgha, he would first inform me, yet now he has invited Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and five hundred bhikṣus without letting me know!"
Having thought this, he said,
"I shall go tomorrow.
The elder returned home and spent the entire night preparing various kinds of fine food, ensuring that no delicacies known in the world were lacking.
At dawn, the seats were laid out and the Bhikṣu Śubhadharma arrived; seeing what had been prepared, he noted that rare delicacies were all provided.
Since the household pressed oil for their livelihood, he said to them, "You have every variety of flavor, yet you lack one thing: sesame cakes."
Having heard this, the householder spoke with indignation:
"Venerable Sir!
You who harbor many treasures of the Dharma, yet utter such evil words!"
He then spoke a parable for them:

"In the past, there was a merchant who carried a hen from the north to the kingdom of Pāpīyasī. In the kingdom of Pāpīyasī there were no roosters; she mated with a crow and laid eggs. Once the chicks had hatched and grown, they became large birds that could neither produce the cry of a cock nor the call of a crow."
"Now, Venerable Sir, you who possess such great treasures of the Dharma have uttered these wicked words.
Upon hearing this, the Bhikṣu Saddharma became resentful and said, "The householder has insulted me so bitterly; why should I remain here any longer?"
"Now you must depart for afar!
The elder spoke again:
"Venerable sir, do not be angry; please remain here for a while!"
"I shall provide you with food and clothing as is my custom.
Thus he spoke a second and a third time, yet [the monk] still refused to stay.
The elder asked:
"Venerable sir!
Where do you wish to go? He replied:
"I wish to go to where the Buddha is.

The elder said, "If you reach the Buddha's presence, I pray that you will inquire after the World-Honored One’s health on my behalf and relate this matter in full detail, without adding or omitting anything!"
He replied, "So be it!
Thereupon, the elder,
having prepared the seats, went to inform [the Buddha] that the time had come and the food was ready.
Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the great assembly surrounded him and went to that house, where they took their seats.
The elder personally served the food; when the meal was finished, he provided water for washing and sat on a small stool before them.
Having taught him various sublime dharmas to instruct, benefit, and gladden him, [the Buddha] rose from his seat and departed.

After the meal, the bhikṣu Sudharma returned to the forest; he put on his robes, took up his bowl, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and reported in detail to the World-Honored One everything that the householder Citta had said.
The Buddha then rebuked him, saying:
"You foolish man! How can you address that elder with such base and contemptuous words?"
He then assembled the community of bhikṣus on account of this matter and addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, you should perform the formal act of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for such bhikṣus as these to express their submissiveness and apologize to that layperson."
A bhikṣu shall announce: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so has addressed a layperson with contemptuous speech. Now the Saṃgha shall perform the *karmavācanā* for him to adopt a humble attitude, in order to apologize to that layperson."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus as a formal motion:
'Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!'"

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has addressed a certain layperson with contemptuous words. The Saṃgha now intends to perform the *karmavācanā* for him to adopt a humble attitude and apologize to that layperson.
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
Thus for the second and third time.
"The Saṃgha has completed the *karmavācanā* for the bhikṣu so-and-so to perform the act of humbling himself;
the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent."
"Maintain this matter thus.

Furthermore, one should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one subsequent proclamation) to appoint a bhikṣu to accompany that bhikṣu to apologize to the layperson (*avadātavasana*).
One bhikṣu should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha now appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to accompany the bhikṣu [Name] in offering his apologies to the layperson.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and hear this."
The motion is thus made. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha now appoints the bhikṣu so-and-so as an attendant to the bhikṣu so-and-so to offer apologies to the layperson."
"Whichever elders approve, let them remain silent;
whoever does not approve, let them speak.
The Sangha has appointed the bhikṣu [Name] as an attendant for the bhikṣu [Name], and the formal leave-taking from the layperson is now concluded."
"Because the Saṃgha has remained silent,
this matter is thus upheld.
That bhikṣu should take the bhikṣu appointed by the Saṃgha and go to take the hand of the layperson, apologizing and saying:
"I previously addressed you with base and lowly speech; I now repent this transgression.
Please accept my repentance!
If he accepts it, that is well.

If he does not accept [the confession], the monk appointed by the Saṃgha should lead that monk to a place where he is within sight but beyond hearing, and instruct him to perform a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) confession, saying:
"I, the bhikṣu So-and-so, addressed coarse and evil speech to the layperson So-and-so; I have committed a *duṣkṛta* offense and now confess it before you, Venerable Sir!"
Thus it was said a second and a third time.
Thereafter, the bhikṣu appointed by the Saṃgha returned alone to the layperson’s place and said:
“The Saṃgha has already disciplined that bhikṣu, and I too have re-disciplined him; you may now accept his confession of transgression.”
Thereafter, that bhikṣu should again come forward and offer his apologies to the layperson as before;
he should then properly submit to the Saṃgha, as explained in the section on the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure).
Once he has properly submitted to the Saṃgha, repented his transgression, and taken self-reproach, he should request the lifting of the *karmavācanā*.
The Saṃgha should grant him the lifting of the *karmavācanā*; the procedure for this *karmavācanā* is also as described above.

Fifth Division: 1. The Method for Dividing the Saṃgha. In the first part of the Fifth Division, "The Method for Dividing the Saṃgha," at that time, Devadatta had this third thought:
"Now that I have divided the saṃgha of the śramaṇa Gautama, I shall attain great renown, and everyone will say:..."
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great supernormal powers, yet Devadatta is able to break his Saṃgha.
Having thought this, he spoke to his followers—Aśvajit, Punarvasu, Varṣākāra, Lohitya, Kokālika, Khaṇḍadravya, and Samudradatta.
Among that assembly, Tripuṣṭa was the most highly intelligent;
he said to Devadatta, "The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great majestic power; how can his saṃgha possibly be split?"
He replied: "I shall declare five rules before the Saṃgha that I shall observe for as long as I live:
first, not to eat salt;..."
2. Not consuming ghee or milk;
3. Not consuming fish or meat, for if one consumes them, wholesome dharmas will not arise;
4. Begging for food, for if one accepts invitations from others, wholesome dharmas will not arise.

Fifth, during the eight months of spring and summer we shall sit exposed to the dew, and during the four months of winter we shall dwell in grass huts; if we accept the shelter of others' houses, the wholesome Dharma will not arise.
The people of both Magadha and Aṅga all believe in and delight in ascetic practices; if we practice these five dharmas, our followers will surely be many, which will be sufficient to destroy them.
Having heard this, Tripusṭa also thought that he could obtain half of the Saṃgha from the Buddha and spread his fame far and wide; he then immediately followed him.
At that time, Devadatta had a lay disciple named Hośudatta who constantly made offerings to him.
Devadatta then spoke to him as well, and he likewise gave his consent.
Thereupon, on the day of the fifteenth-day *poṣadha*, Devadatta spoke of the aforementioned five matters before the Saṃgha; he distributed voting sticks himself and proclaimed:
"Those who accept and delight in these five dharmas may take this stick."
At that time, five hundred bhikṣus all took up the voting sticks (śalākā), with the sole exception of Ānanda and one bhikṣu who was a srotāpanna.
At that time, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the various great arhats were all not present at that poṣadha assembly.
When Devadatta had finished distributing the voting sticks, he immediately performed the *poṣadha* ceremony in harmony with five hundred bhikṣus.

Ānanda and a certain bhikṣu who was a srotāpanna, having not received a stick, departed at once and went to where the Buddha was; they prostrated themselves at his feet and reported these matters to the Buddha.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"It is easy for good people to meet together; it is difficult for evil people to meet with the good.
It is easy for evil people to meet together; it is difficult for good people to meet with the evil."
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, having heard of this matter, went to where the Buddha was.
Seeing them from afar, the Buddha greeted them with a sigh of welcome: "Welcome, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana!"
"You all may go among the followers of Devadatta and bring back five hundred bhikṣus.
The two received these instructions, prostrated at his feet, and departed.
At that time, the srotāpanna bhikṣus who had followed Ānanda saw Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana leave, and they immediately began to weep.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu,
“For what reason are you weeping? He replied:
“Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana are the foremost disciples of the Buddha.
They have now gone among the followers of Devadatta; fearing that they may learn his teachings, I weep for this reason.”
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu,
“Stop and do not weep!
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana shall soon return with five hundred bhikṣus.”
Thereupon Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana went to that assembly.
When Svāgata saw them from afar, he ran to Devadatta and said:
"Now the foremost disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, are coming; they may well break the resolve of the bhikṣus."
"Do not speak with him, nor allow him to sit!
However, Devadatta considered his own five points to be the Way; he did not accept their words, nor did he take them to heart.
When Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had arrived, Devadatta said:
"Welcome, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana!
Please take these seats."
He said: "If a person possesses wisdom, they will accept and practice what they have never heard before.
You were formerly the foremost disciples of the śramaṇa Gautama; would it not be excellent if you were now to become my foremost disciples?"
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana remained silent and did not answer.
Devadatta, believing that his words had been accepted, immediately imitated the Buddha’s usual practice and addressed Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana:
"You may preach the Dharma to the assembly; I have a slight backache and shall attend to it myself."
He then folded his saṃghāṭī robe into four layers and used it as a pillow; lying on his right side with one foot resting upon the other, he did not maintain mindfulness before him.
In a short while, he fell into a deep sleep, turned onto his left side, and let out a cry that startled people.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana manifested various supernormal powers as he had done on previous occasions.
Śāriputra preached various sublime Dharmas, excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, with excellent meaning and excellent phrasing—the characteristics of the holy life.
Upon hearing this, five hundred bhikṣus immediately became free from dust and defilement while seated, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.
Having seen the Dharma and realized the fruit, they said to one another:
"Let us rise and return to the presence of the Buddha."
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana immediately rose from their seats and returned to the Buddha’s presence together with five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, Svāti kicked Devadatta with his toe and reviled him, saying,
“Slave of the Śākyas, rise!”
"Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana have taken the bhikṣus away by other means!
Devadatta started up in alarm and reviled them, saying,
"These are bhikṣus of evil desire!"
"Having first conceived a benevolent thought, how is it that you have suddenly given rise to an evil mind and used skillful means to take my bhikṣu away?
He was then seized by great terror, and warm blood gushed from his nostrils; he immediately fell alive into the Great Avīci Hell.
After Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I wish to have these five hundred bhikṣus receive the full ordination again.
The Buddha said,
"There is no need to receive it again!"
Why is this? Because these five hundred bhikṣus were deluded, they took up the voting sticks with the notion that it was the Dharma.
Now, I permit the Saṃgha only to order them to perform the *sthūlātyaya* repentance.
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha,
“How marvelous, World-Honored One! Devadatta,
having imitated the Buddha, has fallen into such a place of suffering.”
The Buddha said:
"Devadatta did not only imitate me and fall into hell in the present;
in the past as well, he once imitated me and fell into a place of suffering."
Maudgalyāyana asked again,
"What was that matter? The Buddha said:

“In a past age, there was a pond in a secluded place. A great elephant entered the pond to take lotus roots, which he washed clean and ate; thus his physical strength and vitality were fully restored.”
Furthermore, there was another elephant who also imitated him by taking lotus roots; he ate them without washing them and thereby contracted a disease, eventually passing away.
On account of this matter, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Do not imitate the Great Dragon; the Great Dragon is not to be imitated."
"Because he sought to emulate the great dragon, he ate mud and suffered the pain of death.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"That great elephant was my own self."
The one with the different appearance is Devadatta.
Because he imitated me in the past, it led to his death;
now, by imitating me again, he undergoes this great suffering.
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha:
“How marvelous, World-Honored One!
Devadatta heard the Dharma from the Buddha, recited the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma, and attained the five supernormal powers.”
"How is it that you have, on the contrary, become arrogant toward the World-Honored One?
The Buddha said, "Not only in this present life; in the past as well, you heard the Dharma from me and were arrogant toward me."
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha,
saying, "What is the matter?
The Buddha replied:
"In a past age, there was an elephant trainer who was extremely skilled at taming elephants, and the king provided him with very generous support.
At that time, a certain man went to his place and said to him:
'Teach me how to tame elephants; I shall be your disciple.'"
The elephant trainer then instructed him, withholding nothing at all.
Once the man had mastered this, jealousy arose within him; he went to the king’s presence and said, "What that man knows does not surpass my own!"
"How is it that while you provide for him, he remains far behind and cannot catch up?
The king immediately summoned the elephant trainer and asked:
"Between you and your disciple, who is superior?"
He replied, "I pray that you will grant me seven days to demonstrate the method of taming elephants.
The king immediately granted his request.
During those seven days, the elephant trainer further trained the elephants:
when told to advance, they retreated;
when told to retreat, they advanced.
When told to sit, it stood;
when told to stand, it sat.
It was thus trained through such contrary instructions.
When the seventh day arrived, he performed the art of taming elephants before the king together with his disciple.
At first, the two were indistinguishable from one another.
The king asked the disciple:
"Do you have any other qualities? He replied, "No!"
He asked that teacher again:
"Do you have any other teachings?
The teacher replied:
"It exists! The king said,
"Then show it at once."
He then did exactly as instructed, and the elephants all followed him.
Thereupon, the king realized for the first time that his disciple’s previous words had been false; he spoke with anger, saying:
"How could you deceive me to my face?"
The elephant trainer addressed the king, saying:
"This man was my disciple; I previously instructed him without withholding anything.
Yet, before he had fully mastered it, he treated me with contempt."
I shall now provide an analogy; I pray that Your Majesty will listen!
Once upon a time, there was a man who, during the last month of spring, wore a single-layered leather sandal. As the ground grew hot and the leather became dry, it bit into and tore his foot.
Intending to protect his foot, he instead caused himself further injury.
"I am also like this: I first instructed my disciples, desiring their benefit, yet they instead brought about harm.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as a person wearing leather sandals, Intends originally to protect his feet,"
When one suffers from feverish agitation, one instead turns back to harm oneself;
so too do the foolish and evil people of the world, who do not acknowledge the kindness shown to them,
yet having learned a craft from a teacher, they instead slander and deceive him.
The Buddha said:
"That elephant trainer was I myself! That disciple was Devadatta!"
"Life after life he has studied under me, yet he instead treats me with contempt.
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha,
"How rare it is, World-Honored One!"
"Śāriputra once preached the Dharma and shattered Devadatta’s assembly.
The Buddha said, "Not only in this present life; in the past as well, he once preached the Dharma to shatter that assembly."
He asked again,
"What are the details of this matter? He replied:
“In a past age, there was a master archer named Kauṇḍinya.
A man came to study the art of archery from him, and for six years he instructed him, saying:
‘You should hold the bow in this manner, and strike the arrow in this manner.’”
However, he had not yet taught him the method of releasing the arrow.
Later, the disciple thought to himself:
"I have spent six years learning how to grasp the bow and notch the arrow, yet I have never once released one; I shall try releasing it now."
He then released an arrow that pierced a large tree and passed right through into the ground.
When his teacher heard of this, he asked,
"Have you already released the arrow?"
He replied, "I have released them.
He asked again:
"Where did you shoot? He then pointed to the tree he had shot.
The teacher said:
"You have already mastered archery!
I am the first, and you are the second.
He spoke further, saying:
"At such-and-such a place, five hundred bandits have cut off the road, and no one dares to pass through it.
You should go and destroy them to clear the way; you will achieve great merit!"
He immediately gave him a carriage drawn by a horse and a beautiful woman, as well as a golden bowl and five hundred arrows.
Thereupon, the disciple mounted the carriage with the woman, took up his wish-fulfilling bow, and girded himself with the five hundred arrows; having received these instructions, he departed.
It so happened that he encountered those bandits who were dividing their spoils, and they had stationed scouts on the main road.
The patrol officers saw them from afar and rushed to inform the bandit leader.
The leader said to his men, "In all our time as bandits,
we have never before seen anyone traveling alone with such a beautiful woman on this road."
"He must be brave and fearless, not intimidated by powerful enemies; we should allow him to pass without disturbing him!
That man then stayed in one place and ordered his wife to take a golden bowl to the robbers' location, where she was to beg for food in his name.
All the bandits were enamored with his wife and, moreover, coveted the golden bowl; they immediately deliberated, saying:
"The woman’s beauty is such as this, and the golden bowl is like that!
How can we allow her to depart?"
The bandit leader spoke again:
"He must have calculated that he has nothing to fear, which is why he dares to do this.
For now, we should endure and restrain ourselves; be careful not to invite disaster!"
Upon hearing this, the bandits gave her a bowl filled with fine rice.
Carrying the food back, the woman was sent again with these instructions:
"When you divide the goods, give me one share!"
The bandits were greatly incensed and said: "Who is this person?
How dare he, as a single man, treat our great multitude with such contempt!"
"We must kill him together; do not harbor this shame!
The bandit leader spoke to her as he had before, and she immediately shared her portion with him again.
When the woman returned with her share, he sent word to her once more, saying:
"You may fight with me; we shall not let each other off.
The bandits spoke again:
"This man treats us with increasing contempt; we can no longer endure it!"

The bandit leader tried to dissuade them with reasoned exhortations, but they would not stop; driven by fierce anger and forgetting their peril, they united their strength and went to attack that man.
That man then discharged a single arrow and killed one person;
with four hundred and ninety-nine more arrows, he killed four hundred and ninety-nine people.
One arrow remained, intended for the bandit leader; however, as they sought further opportunities to strike one another, they could find none.
The man then had his wife stand naked before the bandit leader.
The bandit leader’s mind was thrown into confusion; because of this, he released his hand and immediately killed him again.
Thereupon, his wife spoke these verses:
"Though he possessed keen arrows and a bow, Never once did a single shot go astray."
"The slaughter and injury are already so chaotic;
how can you not feel remorse? The man replied in verse:
"I possess this wondrous skill; my bow and arrows respond to my heart and hand."
Whenever I killed one, I felt immediate joy; for what reason should I now feel remorse?
I originally traveled this path to eliminate enmity and harm for others, disregarding my own body and life to achieve a reputation for valor and strength.
The Buddha said:
"That master archer was none other than myself;
that disciple archer was Śāriputra."
The five hundred bandits were these five hundred bhikṣus;
the bandit leader was Devadatta.
In the past, Śāriputra defeated that host of bandits with each individual arrow.
"Now, with a single teaching of the Dharma, he has broken the assembly of Devadatta.
Maudgalyāyana again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!"
Devadatta reviled him, saying,
"Evil-desire bhikṣu!
and immediately fell into the great hell with his physical body still intact.
The Buddha said,
"Not only in this present life, but in the past as well, he once suffered great pain in his physical body due to harsh speech.
He asked again:
"What was that matter? He replied:
"In a past age, by the waterside of a forest pond, there were two geese who formed a close friendship with a tortoise."
Later, when the water in the pond had dried up, the two geese deliberated thus:
"Now that this pond's water has run dry, our dear friend will surely suffer great distress!
Having finished their discussion, they spoke to the tortoise, saying:
"This pond’s water has dried up; there is no way for you to cross.
You may take hold of a piece of wood, and we shall each take hold of one end, carrying you to where there is great water."
"When you are holding the wood in your beak, you must be careful not to speak!
He then immediately took it in his beak.
As they passed through a village, the children saw him and all said:
"A crane is carrying off the tortoise!
A crane is carrying off the tortoise!
At this, the tortoise spoke with anger:
"What business is that of yours? [he asked].
Thereupon, the wood slipped from his grasp, fell to the ground, and he died.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse on account of this:
"When a man is born, an axe is held within his mouth; it is that which hews his own body, arising from his evil speech.
To praise those who deserve condemnation and to condemn those who deserve praise—thus one brings calamity upon oneself and shall never find joy."
If one quarrels over wealth and profit, this evil is not yet great;
but to harbor an evil mind toward the Buddha—this is truly a great evil.
There are a hundred thousand āpāyika hells, and thirty-six nīraya hells.
"One who harbors evil intentions toward a worthy person shall fall into this hell.
The Buddha said,
"That turtle was Devadatta!"
"In the past, because of angry speech, you brought upon yourselves the suffering of death;
now, by again reviling with anger, you shall fall into the great hells.
He then addressed the bhikṣus:
“If I had seen even a hair’s breadth of wholesome dharma in Devadatta, I would never have predicted that he would fall into the great hell to suffer for one kalpa.
It is like a person who has fallen into a great pit of excrement; if someone wishes to rescue him, they cannot find even a hair’s breadth of clean place to grab hold of.”
"I observe Devadatta, and he is likewise.
He further addressed the bhikṣus:
"I do not see any other dharma that destroys a person's aspiration for the unsurpassed path as much as fame and gain."
The reason Devadatta caused a schism in the Saṃgha was due to gain and offerings.
Devadatta brought about the schism by accomplishing eight unrighteous factors:
gain and lack of gain, fame and lack of fame, honor and dishonor, delighting in evil, and following evil associates.
Upāli asked the Buddha,
“In what way is one said to have ‘caused a schism in the Saṃgha’?
The Buddha replied:
“There are four matters that constitute a schism in the Saṃgha:
preaching the five dharmas, distributing voting sticks oneself, taking up voting sticks, and performing separate monastic acts within the same boundary.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'the Saṃgha is not in harmony, yet it is not split'?
The Buddha said:
"If a king assists in splitting the Saṃgha, causing the Saṃgha to be in disharmony, yet it is not split."
If a minister, an upāsaka, an upāsikā, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī, or even one bhikṣu up to seven bhikṣus assist in causing a schism in the Saṃgha, it is likewise.
If one performs monastic affairs without consulting the Elder, this constitutes a lack of harmony, yet it does not constitute a schism in the Saṃgha;
the same applies to not eating together, sitting separately during meals, or engaging in quarreling and verbal abuse.
"It is when eight bhikṣus within a single boundary divide into two groups and perform monastic affairs separately that it is called 'schism.
He asked again, "In this case,
who is it that causes the schism?"
The Buddha said,
"It is the one who acts as the master.
He asked again:
"Who, having fallen into the great hell for an entire kalpa, cannot be saved?
The Buddha said:
"The one who acts as the master."
He asked again:
"Does every person who causes a schism in the Saṃgha suffer the torments of the great hells for an entire kalpa?
The Buddha said:
"It is not necessarily the case that all must undergo the suffering of the great hells for one kalpa.
There are eight types of persons who, by causing a schism in the Saṃgha, undergo the suffering of the great hells for one kalpa:
those who, regarding what is Dharma as Dharma, declare it to be non-Dharma;..."
If it is not the Dharma, yet perceiving it as not the Dharma, one says it is the Dharma;
if it is the Dharma, yet perceiving it as not the Dharma, one says it is the Dharma;
if it is not the Dharma, yet perceiving it as the Dharma, one says it is not the Dharma.
If a thing is Dharma or non-Dharma, yet one perceives it as Dharma and speaks of it as non-Dharma;
if a thing is Dharma or non-Dharma, yet one perceives it as non-Dharma and speaks of it as Dharma;
or if a thing is Dharma, yet one has doubt regarding it being non-Dharma and speaks of it as Dharma.
If one has doubt regarding what is Dharma and speaks of it as non-Dharma;
or if there are six types of persons who cause a schism in the Saṃgha yet do not fall into the great hells to suffer for an eon:
those who, regarding what is Dharma, perceive it as Dharma and speak of it as such.
If it is non-Dharma and one perceives it as non-Dharma, one declares it to be non-Dharma;
if it is Dharma and one perceives it as non-Dharma, one declares it to be non-Dharma;
if it is non-Dharma and one perceives it as Dharma, one declares it to be Dharma.
"If a thing is legal (*dharma*) or illegal (*adharma*), if one perceives it as illegal, one says it is illegal;
if a thing is legal or illegal, if one perceives it as legal, one says it is legal.
2. On the Rules for Bedding and Furniture (*Śayanāsana-vastu*). The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, Fifth Division, Part Two: On the Rules for Bedding and Furniture. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha.

At that time, the bhikṣu Aṭṭhi was attending upon the Buddha at his side. Later, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food, proceeding with dignified and orderly deportment while keeping his eyes fixed upon the ground.
A certain householder saw him and thought to himself:
"I have never seen anyone like this before.
He then went up to him and asked:
“Who are you? Whose disciple are you?
Under whom have you gone forth?”
"Whose Dharma do you practice?
At that time, the Buddha had only recently attained enlightenment, and everyone in the world called him the Great Śramaṇa.
He replied:
"My name is Aṭṭhaka; the Great Śramaṇa is my teacher.
I have gone forth under him and practice his Dharma.
Having heard this, the householder exclaimed:
“It is truly marvelous!
That one who possesses such majestic deportment would leave the great śramaṇa to go forth and practice his dharma.
He asked again:
“Where do you currently dwell?
He replied, “The forest hermitage,
mountain crags, beneath trees, open spaces, and among burial mounds— these are my dwelling places.”
Upon hearing this, the elder felt redoubled joy and exclaimed:
"Your deportment is so dignified and refined; your teacher alone is already superior, yet you have further taken up residence in such a place as this!"
He asked again,
“What kind of bedding did you spread? He replied:
"Kāśika grass, kuśa grass, babhruka grass, muñja grass, tree leaves, and so forth, down to sand and soil—all these are my bedding."
Having heard this, the elder felt even greater joy and reverence, and exclaimed:
"You are truly able to maintain such fewness of desires.
He then asked again:
"If I were to build a dwelling for you, Venerable Sir, would you be able to use it? He replied,
"The World-Honored One has not yet permitted us to accept and use such dwellings."
He further said, "Venerable One!
You may report this to the Buddha; I shall also report it myself."
Aṭṭhika silently accepted his words.
After the meal, he returned to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and reported this matter to him.

The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus; having praised fewness of desires and contentment, praised the precepts, and praised those who uphold the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to accept the gift of dwellings.

Later, that elder came to where the Buddha was; seeing from afar the World-Honored One’s countenance, exceptionally sublime like a mountain of gold, he felt inward joy and reverence. He went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Buddha taught him various sublime dharmas, from the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, until he attained the pure Dharma-eye while still seated. Having seen the Dharma and realized the fruit, he received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I wish to construct a dwelling to offer to the bhikṣus; I pray that you will accept it!
The Buddha granted his silent consent.
Knowing that the Buddha had consented, the elder rose from his seat, went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and departed.
On that very day, sixty rooms were constructed;

furthermore, food and drink for the distribution hall were prepared, with all the family members joining together to provide them. There was nothing among the world’s rare delicacies that was not fully prepared. Some were splitting wood, some were drawing water, some were cooking, some were sweeping the ground, some were sprinkling the floor with fragrant liquid, some were arranging the seats, some were scattering flowers, and some were preparing the high throne.
At that time, there was an elder in Śrāvastī named Sudatta who lent three hundred thousand gold coins to the people of Rājagṛha, with whom they had an annual debt settlement.
The elder used to travel one yojana to welcome them and provide a great feast, but he could no longer manage to go out.
Sudatta had this thought:
"Could it be that he has encountered royal peril, or danger from water, fire, thieves, humans, or non-humans, and for that reason does not come to welcome me?"
Having arrived, he went first to his house and saw that various kinds of delicacies had been prepared;
he asked, "Are you preparing for a wedding or a festival?
Or have you invited the King?"
He replied, "It is not for a wedding or a festival, nor have we invited the King.
He asked again:
"Why have you prepared such wonderful food and drink? He replied,
"A Buddha has appeared in the world with great majesty and virtue, and his disciples are likewise so."
"I have invited him today and have therefore prepared this offering; it is for this reason that I was unable to go out to meet him!

Sudatta said, "I too have heard that a Buddha shall appear in the world, titled Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat."
"Is the one you have now invited a Buddha,
or is he not a Buddha? He replied:
"It is the Buddha! He asked again, "Where is he now?"
The householder then bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, pointed his right hand toward where the Buddha was, and said,
"The Buddha is in that place."

Having heard this, Sudatta was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He bared his right shoulder, prostrated toward the Buddha from afar, and three times cried out, "Namo Buddhāya. Throughout the night he meditated on the Buddha until, utterly exhausted, he fell asleep.
His spiritual friends from past lives acted as divine protectors for him, and the spirits formed this thought:
"We shall cause this elder not to spend a single night before he is able to see the Buddha."
Immediately, the night became bright.
Sudatta, thinking that the sun had already risen, rose and proceeded toward the city gate; the city gate opened of its own accord.
Once he had passed through, the gate closed by itself, and suddenly it returned to darkness.
Sudatta was terrified and thought to himself,
"Was I not driven mad just now? The deity,
knowing his thoughts, immediately spoke this verse:
"Now is the time to approach the Buddha; if one takes even a single step, its benefit exceeds the gift of a thousand pieces of gold, which neither elephants nor horses can equal.
He spoke again:
"Do not fear, do not be terrified!
Press forward, press forward!
In a moment you shall see the Buddha."
Having heard this, Sudatta’s fear was immediately dispelled; he then stepped forward and saw from afar that the World-Honored One’s majestic bearing was extraordinary, like a mountain of gold.
The World-Honored One saw him and praised him, saying:
"Welcome, Sudatta! Hearing this, Sudatta was filled with joy.
"The Buddha alone knows the names given to me by my parents.

He prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and the Buddha preached various sublime Dharmas for him, including the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Thereupon, while still seated, he attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Having seen the Dharma and attained the fruit, he received the three refuges and the five precepts, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will accept my invitation for the summer retreat in the city of Śrāvastī."
Thus he requested three times, and the Buddha remained silent each time;
only upon his fourth request did the Buddha address him, saying:
"If a dwelling place is free from clamor, secluded and soundless, it is there that the Buddhas should observe the summer retreat."
The householder said to the Buddha,
“I understand, World-Honored One!
I pray that you will appoint one bhikṣu to manage this undertaking for me!”
The Buddha asked,
"Whom do you now desire? She replied:
"I wish to obtain Śāriputra.
The Buddha then said to Śāriputra,
"You may go at once to manage this matter for me."
Śāriputra accepted the instruction and departed.
At that time, the aforementioned elder went to the Buddha in person early in the morning and said, "The meal is prepared; may the Holy One know the proper time."
The Buddha, accompanied by the community of bhikṣus, dressed in his robes and carrying his bowl, proceeded surrounded by them before and behind to the house, where they sat down in order.
The elder served the food with his own hands; when the meal was finished and the water for washing had been offered, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I offer this garden and its dwellings to the Sangha of the four quarters.
The Buddha accepted by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had accepted, he took a small seat and sat before the Buddha.
The Buddha then spoke these verses of sympathetic joy and blessing:
"To ward off wind, cold, and heat, And to obstruct all evil beasts;
To shield against rain, dew, and dust, And likewise to remove the affliction of mosquitoes and gadflies."
"By giving to those who uphold the precepts, who practice meditation, recite the Dharma, and explain its teachings—
if one hears and understands their meaning, one shall reach the end of the source of all suffering.
Having spoken these verses, the Buddha further expounded various wonderful Dharmas.
Having instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them, he returned to his own abode.
Thereupon, the householder Sudatta led Śāriputra back to the city of Śrāvastī, proclaiming at every village they passed:
"The Buddha has appeared in the world with great majesty and virtue; his disciples are likewise so."
"I have already requested him to enter the rains retreat at Śrāvastī.
You all should together prepare his lodgings, repair the roads and bridges, and arrange the offerings in advance to await the World-Honored One."
When those people heard this proclamation, they knew that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was about to pass through there; they were all greatly rejoiced and respectfully heeded his words.
Once the elder Sudatta had arrived at Śrāvastī, he thought to himself:
"Where is the most excellent place suitable for building a vihāra?"

"Only this Jeta Grove in the city has such lush and beautiful fruit trees; its waters are pure, with flowing springs and bathing pools, and it is fully supplied with fragrant flowers. You should purchase it and have it developed."
Having thought this, he went to that place and said, "I wish to purchase this grove; would you be willing to sell it? He replied:
"If you can cover the ground with gold coins so that there is no space left uncovered, only then shall we proceed together.
Sudatta then covered the ground with gold coins.
Jeta said:
"I spoke this parable not with the intention of bargaining.
Sudatta replied again,
"If you stated this as the price, how can you now seek to recede from the agreement!"
As they disputed and quarreled, the matter was eventually brought before the authorities. The officials adjudicated according to the law and awarded it to Sudatta.
Jeta asked Sudatta, "For what reason did you not spare your gold and jewels when purchasing this grove?"
Sudatta replied, “The Buddha has appeared in the world with great majesty and virtue, and his disciples are likewise so.
I have already invited him to observe the rains retreat here; therefore, I have exhausted my resources without any sense of stinginess.”
Jeta spoke again:
"If you will allow me to give the garden another name, calling it the Jeta Grove Monastery (Jetavana-vihāra), then I shall bestow it upon you. Sudatta said:
"Excellent! he said, and immediately ordered people to spread gold coins upon the ground to measure the site for the tree, filling every gap until it was level.
