Śāriputra then measured out the grounds with a cord to construct a place for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), a lecture hall, a heated bathhouse, a kitchen, a bathing house, and various other chambers, ensuring that all were appropriately arranged.
At that time, the various rooms were not properly plastered, and wind, dust, snakes, and rats damaged the monks' bedding and disturbed the bhikṣus.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"I allow you to apply mud to both the interior and exterior surfaces, as well as to the ceilings."
The Saṃgha should maintain various tools for building houses, such as axes, chisels, knives, saws, mattocks, spades, ladders, and scaffolds;
it is also permitted to apply lime, plaster, and paint, and to construct windows, doors, panels, bolts, locks, and door-latches.
"It is not permitted to carry it at one's waist like the handle of a knife; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There were some bhikṣus who, while engaged in manual labor, had their bodies soiled with dust and required bathing.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to bathe.
Since there was mud at the bathing place, the Buddha said:
"Listen: the ground may be paved with bricks, and wooden planks may be used for beds.
There were some bhikṣus who, having found bedding and rope-cots among the burial mounds, did not dare to take them.
The Buddha said:
"Listen. If it is too large, it should be cut down.
At that time, between the two cities of Rājagṛha and Śrāvastī, there was a dwelling place which laymen had offered to the bhikṣus, yet no one lived there.
The Buddha said, "I permit white-robed laypeople to invite a *māmātṛ* (steward) to remain and look after [the monastery], providing whatever is required.
At that time, the various residences had no fences or enclosures; cattle and horses would charge through them, damaging the walking paths (*caṅkrama*).
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to build a fence around it and dig a moat.
Yet the oxen and horses still managed to enter.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to plant thorny brambles to serve as a fence.
Yet even then, oxen and horses would still be able to break through them.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to build walls, whether by piling bricks or using clay tiles, and to cover them with grass or roof tiles.
I permit you to construct gatehouses, and I also permit you to build them in two stories; I permit you to make them with double doors."
There were some bhikṣus who, while inside their rooms, chewed tooth-sticks, washed their hands and faces, and washed their feet, thereby dampening the ground and ruining the Sangha’s bedding.
The Buddha said: "You should not do so!"
There were some elderly and sick bhikṣus who, during the cold season, were unable to go out to wash. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to use a basin and a jar to catch the water.
There was a dwelling where dust was rising; the Buddha said:
"One should plaster the ground and spread each of the ten kinds of robes over it, one by one.
There were some junior bhikṣus who had already washed their feet; when a senior bhikṣu arrived later, he drove them away before they had finished washing their feet.
The Buddha said, "If those of lower rank have already washed [their feet], you should allow them to finish.
There were some bhikṣus who practiced walking meditation (caṅkrama) in the open air; when it rained, their robes became soaked, which caused them to abandon their walking meditation.
The Buddha said, "I permit you to construct a cloistered walkway.
There were some bhikṣus who walked in the courtyard; when it rained, the ground became damaged and their feet were soiled.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to build steps and paths by piling bricks and stones.
There were some monasteries where there was no water; the Buddha said:
"I allow you to dig a well or construct a pure pool.
The bhikṣus wished to make bedding mats to spread upon their beds; the Buddha said:
"I allow you to make them using any of the ten kinds of cloth, and to stuff them with wool, camel hair, cotton, or even soft grass."
The bhikṣus made mats that were excessively thick. The Buddha said:
"A maximum thickness of eight finger-breadths is permitted.
It is permitted for the Saṃgha to make them, for the Saṃgha of the four quarters to make them, or for individuals to make them privately."
When the Sangha’s bedding and requisites were damaged, they did not know what to do.
The Buddha said:
"A person should be appointed to repair and wash them."
At that time, the bhikṣus were distributing the monastic bedding daily. The Buddha said:
"This should not be done! I allow you to distribute the bedding on the final day of spring."
At the beginning of summer, when the time for entering the rains retreat arrived, the group of six bhikṣus selected fine rooms and excellent bedding to dwell in.
The Buddha said: "You should not do so!"
"A formal motion with a second proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) should be made to appoint one bhikṣu as the distributor of bedding.
The appointed bhikṣu should mark the bedding to identify which room it belongs to, and then distribute it according to the order of seniority."
If there are those who are senior and of good standing, the *upādhyāya* (preceptor) must provide them with [a seat];
if they do not require it, then it should be given to those sitting below in order.
If there are bhikṣus who arrive later, they should be settled according to their seniority in the proper sequence.
From there, they proceeded one after another to the lower quarters; if the junior monk had no room, they stopped.
The bhikṣus wished to make new rope beds and wooden beds.
The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to make it.
If there is no skilled craftsman, it is also permitted for a bhikṣu to make it himself.
Ten kinds of thread are permitted; one may make a cord from each individual thread."
There were some bhikṣus who wished to store their rope beds; the Buddha said, "I allow you to store them.
There were some bhikṣus who walked or stood upon their rope beds, and the ropes broke.
The Buddha said:
"One should not walk or stand upon a rope bed.
There were some bhikṣus who were short of stature; they wished to take down or lift clothing from a shelf, but could not reach it.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to fix your mindfulness before you and take it while standing on the thigh of a rope bed.
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who sat upon storage rope beds; their menstrual blood stained them, becoming impure and causing the bedding to rot and decay.
The Buddha said,
"A bhikṣuṇī should not sit upon a storage-rope bed.
There were some young śrāmaṇeras who, while staying on a storage-rope bed, urinated and defecated, soiling and ruining it with impurities.
The Buddha said:
"Even a novice monk should not stay on a storage cord-bed.
There were some bhikṣus who, while on high beds, received the sūtras and inquired about their meaning.
The Buddha said,
"Those who receive the scriptures and inquire about their meaning should all sit in the lower seats.
At the dwellings of the bhikṣus, weeds grew in the courtyards.
The Buddha said,
"I allow that a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) be made aware [of the situation].
Dust and dirt in the room defiled the beds and bedding.
The Buddha said,
"I allow you to make whisks according to your preference and use them to fan yourselves.
At the time of a great assembly, many bhikṣus arrived while the dwellings were large but few in number, so there was no place for them to stay.
The Buddha said:
"In the dwelling quarters, arrange the bedding in successive order until there is sufficient space for each person; once it is full, stop.
If one wishes to screen oneself with a robe from the front, each person is permitted to do so."
"If it is sufficient, that is well;
if it is insufficient and there is vacant space outside, you are permitted to build a hut. The resident bhikṣus should construct it for you.
Once the hut was built, after the Great Assembly had concluded, it was consumed by fire, and the flames spread to the residence.
The Buddha said:
"After the great assembly has concluded, one should dismantle [the dwelling] and depart.
If the resident bhikṣus are reluctant and do not permit its dismantling, the visiting bhikṣus should simply entrust it to the resident bhikṣus and leave."
During times of heavy rain, the bhikṣus had no place to assemble.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to construct a large hall."
During the cold season, the bhikṣus gathered together and suffered from the cold.
The Buddha said,
"I allow you to construct a heated hall."

At that time, Śāriputra was overseeing the construction of a new great hall for the mother of Viśākhā. She brought grain and rice to offer as alms to the Sangha of the four quarters, but the bhikṣus did not dare to eat it.
The Buddha said:
"If it is prepared for the Sangha of the four directions, it is permitted that they eat it at will.
There were some bhikṣus who, having returned from begging for alms, offered them to the Sangha of the four directions, but did not know who should eat them.
The Buddha said:
"One who works for the Sangha of the four directions may eat.
There were dwellings that had fallen into ruin, yet the bhikṣus did not repair them.
The Buddha said:

"One should exhort and convert them through the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) for both monastics and laypeople; those who wish to undergo treatment should be allowed to do so.
Then, a single bhikṣu makes the proclamation:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
A certain room is dilapidated and there is no one to repair it; so-and-so wishes to repair it.
The Saṃgha now grants him permission to do so."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience.
This is the motion. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
"A certain room is dilapidated; let the present Sangha now have it repaired.
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak."
The Sangha has finished repairing the cell of [Name], which was previously damaged;
the Sangha consents by remaining silent.
This matter is thus upheld.
"If one wishes to inscribe the name 'the room of the donor so-and-so,' it is permitted to do so.
The same applies to bedding and requisites.

At a certain residence, the area was flooded by a great deluge; each of the bhikṣus moved their own bedding and requisites from their rooms, but there was a room where no bhikṣu resided and no one took charge of its belongings, so they were submerged and rotted away by the water.
Later, when the householder donor who owned the room saw this, he rebuked the bhikṣus in anger, saying:
"Why have you alone caused the bedding in my room to become soaked and rotted by water?"
The Buddha said:
"If there is a danger of water or fire, you should raise a loud cry and strike the *gandī* bell, so that the entire Saṃgha may join together to assist in lifting [the vessel]."
"If there is even one person who does not assist in lifting [the body], they shall incur the offense of *duṣkṛta*!
At that time, Rāhula went to the village of Nāla, where he was deeply revered and trusted by a certain upāsaka, who built a dwelling for him.
When the construction of the dwelling was finished, Rāhula had some minor business and traveled among the people.
At that time, Ānanda went to that village, and the lay devotee (upāsaka) there again offered the dwelling to Ānanda.
Rāhula returned and ordered Ānanda to leave. Ānanda said:
"Although you were given it first, you gave it back to me after you had gone; therefore, it is my room."
Thereupon, they went together to that lay follower’s place and asked,
"Whose room is this for certain? He replied:
"Although I previously gave this to Rāhula, Rāhula abandoned it and departed.
At a later time, I gave it again to Ānanda; therefore, it should belong to Ānanda's room."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"It is not only in this present life that this upāsaka has acted thus; he was likewise so in the past!"
The bhikṣus asked again,
"What was the matter? The Buddha said:
"In a past age, there was a king named Bharu.
Within his realm lived two rishis: one named Rāhula, who always delighted in sitting meditation;
the other named Ānanda, who was widely learned and fearless."
That king had previously seen Rāhula and held him in great esteem, so he built a dwelling for him.
Once it was completed, the king went away to wander among the people.
Later, Ānanda arrived; the king also held him in high regard and consequently bestowed upon him the very dwelling he had previously constructed.
When Rāhula returned from his alms round, he had Ānanda come out and said,
"This is my room! Ānanda spoke as he had done before.
"This is my room!
They went together to the king's presence and asked,
"Whose room is this for certain?"
He replied, "Although I previously gave it to Rāhula, Rāhula abandoned it and left.
I subsequently gave it to Ānanda; therefore, this must be Ānanda’s room."
At that time, the devas, nāgas, and spirits all spoke these words:
"This king acts contrary to the Dharma!
How can he first bestow a dwelling upon Rāhula and later seize it away to bestow it upon Ānanda?"
"I shall now destroy their retinue!
They immediately went together to the royal palace and killed the king's attendants by throwing stones at them.
On account of this matter, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"The King’s giving was without distinction of priority; the seers contended over it, which incited the wrath of the spirits and brought about his own destruction along with his retinue.
To act according to the dictates of attachment is not praised by the wise."
"Therefore, you should abandon craving and joyfully speak in accordance with the Dharma.
The Buddha said:
"That seer Rāhula is none other than the present Rāhula."
"The seer Ānanda is now this Ānanda; the king is now this upāsaka.
Thus he addressed the bhikṣus.
"From now on, it is not permitted to accept a dwelling previously offered by another; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
At that time, the Buddha was traveling through the human settlements of the Kosalā country with a great community of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, heading toward the village of Khānumata.
There were five bhikṣus who had long resided there; hearing that the Buddha was coming with a great assembly, they consulted together, saying:
"In that multitude are Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; they will surely trouble us."
"We would rather divide these dwellings, lodgings, bedding, and garden fruits into five portions, making each our own private property.
Having thus deliberated, they divided them.
When the Buddha and his assembly had arrived, the bhikṣus went to them and said, "Open your rooms and spread out bedding; we must stay here.
The five bhikṣus replied:
“The Buddha is the Lord of Dharma; we should open the first room for him to dwell in.
As for the other places, we have already divided them all; they are our private property and no longer belong to the Saṃgha.”
"You may go into the village yourself and seek a place of rest according to your acquaintances.
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, having no place to stay, took up residence for the night beneath the eaves of the Buddha’s dwelling.
The next day, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus for this matter and addressed them:
"There are five kinds of property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four quarters that must not be guarded as private property, must not be sold, and must not be divided."

What are the five? First, the dwelling site; second, the rooms and buildings; third, necessary articles; fourth, fruit trees; and fifth, flowers and fruits. All Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, and Bhikṣus have a share in these. Whether they guard them, sell them, or divide them among themselves, they all commit the offense of sthūlātyaya.
After those five bhikṣus had divided the dwelling place, the Saṃgha later gathered from the four directions and divided it once more.
Subsequently, other guest bhikṣus arrived and said, "Open a room for us; we shall dwell therein."
The bhikṣus who had arrived previously said:
"We have come from the four directions; this is our portion.
We have already divided it among ourselves; it no longer belongs to you."
"You may go into the village and seek a place where you can settle.
The later-coming bhikṣu then went into the village to seek a residence, and the laypeople said,
"Venerable One!..."
"Why do you not stay in the monastic quarters that exist there, but instead come here?
The bhikṣus then returned toward the monastic quarters; by the time they arrived, it was already dark, and they were killed by a tiger on the road.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. On account of this, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"Did I not previously state that there are five kinds of property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions, which cannot be guarded as private property, cannot be sold, and cannot be divided?"
"How could you guard the monastery quarters for the Saṃgha and refuse them to the bhikṣus who arrived later, thereby causing them to be harmed by a tiger!
Having rebuked him in these various ways, he further said:
"Whether one guards, sells, or distributes property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions, it is all a sthūlātyaya offense!"
There were some bhikṣus living on the seashore where timber was difficult to obtain and there was nothing with which to build a house.
Since there were many large fish bones there, they wished to take them and use them [for construction].
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to do so.
The bhikṣus were troubled by the stench of fish bones.
The Buddha said, "I permit you to plaster it with fragrant mud.

There were some bhikṣus who were engaged in constructing a dwelling for the Saṃgha; when they had finished, visiting bhikṣus arrived, and as these visitors were the senior monks (sthaviras), they drove the original builders out and took possession of their rooms.
He spoke with anger:
"I have labored hard in my management, yet instead I find no peace.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen, manager: you may stay as long as you please.
The bhikṣus then granted him this for an extended period. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should measure the amount of labor performed; at most, he may be permitted to stay for twelve years."
"You should grant it to him by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
A single bhikṣu proclaims:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, acts as the manager; the Saṃgha now grants him a room according to his preference for a stay of several years.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen.
The motion is thus made: "Venerable Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, acts as the manager; the Sangha now grants him a dwelling of his choice to occupy for a certain number of years."
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has granted this bhikṣu so-and-so the right to dwell in whichever room he prefers for a certain number of years. This matter is concluded.
"The Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent;
this matter is thus upheld.

There were some bhikṣus who made wooden beds and rope beds and placed them in their rooms; they either plastered the floors or performed minor repairs, and then requested permission to dwell there at their own pleasure.
The Buddha said:
"One should not seek [to dwell there].
If the labor expended in repairing the dwelling is at least one-third complete, it is permitted to request permission from the Saṃgha to reside there as one pleases."
The Mahīśāsaka Vinaya, Volume Twenty-five;
The Mahīśāsaka Vinaya, Volume Twenty-six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśa during the Song Dynasty.
Translated together with Zhu Daosheng and others.
Section Five: Miscellaneous Dharmas. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣus were eating from the same vessels as laypeople; their hands touched one another, and they had to wash them repeatedly.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not eat from the same vessel as a layperson.
There was a bhikṣu who went to the home of a relative, and the relative said:
"We are not others, nor are we impure; why may we not eat together?
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to eat together while maintaining mindfulness directed toward the food before you, provided that your hands do not touch one another."
There were bhikṣus eating together with laypeople; because their bowls were small, their hands touched one another.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to eat while holding the bowl with the left hand."

The bhikṣus greeted one another at various times: when eating, during the monastic meal, while drinking gruel, while eating fruit, while walking in meditation (caṅkrama), when not wearing the three robes, in the dark, and when not speaking together; they even greeted one another in private out of anger.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"At such times, one must not pay obeisance; whoever violates this incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
Furthermore, there are five types of persons to whom one should not pay obeisance:

The *karmavācanā* of censure (*tarjanīya*), the *karmavācanā* of banishment (*niḥsaraṇīya*), the *karmavācanā* of dependence (*nissaya*), the *karmavācanā* of accusation (*pravrājana*), and the *karmavācanā* of submissiveness (*pravāsanīya*).
Furthermore, there are five who should not be saluted:
one who has been suspended (*ukkhittaka*), one with whom one may not speak (*asaṃvāsika*), one undergoing the *mūlāpatti-pārivāsa*, a bhikṣuṇī, and a śrāmaṇera.
Furthermore, there are five types of persons who should not be saluted:
those with a deranged mind, those with a distracted mind, those with a diseased mind, laypeople, and followers of external paths.
Furthermore, there are five other types of persons who should not be saluted:
Parivāsa (probation), mānatva (penance) to be performed, the performance of mānatva, the restoration of the original status (*pūrvakalpa*), and *ābhāṣaṇa* (rehabilitation).
There are five who should be venerated:
the Buddha, the Pratyekabuddha, a senior monk who acts in accordance with the Dharma, the upādhyāya, and the ācārya.
At that time, some bhikṣus grew their hair long; their minds took no delight in the Path, and some returned to secular life or became followers of external paths.
Laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"We, the laypeople, grow our hair, and these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do the same."
"What is the difference?
It is merely that he wears robes of dyed, discarded color that have been cut and pieced together!
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should not cultivate long hair; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
The bhikṣus shaved their hair in places where food was prepared, as well as in the lecture halls and heated rooms. They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should not be so! However, if one is old or ill and cannot endure the cold, I allow them to stay in a heated room.
At that time, the bhikṣus shaved their hair according to seniority; they reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no need to follow the order!
If there is an urgent matter, it is permitted to shave first;
if there is no urgent matter, those who have already washed shall shave first."
There were some bhikṣus who shaved their hair here and there throughout the courtyard without sweeping it up.
When this was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"One should shave in a single location; once shaved, one should sweep it up and dispose of it by placing it in water, in fire, or burying it."
"If there is no barber, it is also permitted for a bhikṣu who is capable of shaving to do so; it is also permitted to keep a razor.
There were some bhikṣus whose nose hairs were long, and the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to keep tweezers to pull them out."
The bhikṣus then made tweezers out of gold and silver. The Buddha said: "This should not be done!
I allow the use of copper, iron, ivory, horn, bamboo, or wood, with the exception of lacquer wood."
There were some bhikṣus whose ears were blocked by obstructions. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to keep ear-pickers; the rest is as stated above.
There were also some bhikṣus who had food lodged between their teeth, which caused them to have foul breath.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to keep a tooth-pick.
The rest is as stated above.
At that time, King Bimbisāra thought to himself:
"What is there that I have not yet given as an offering to the Saṃgha?
He reflected thoroughly and found that he had given everything except for items used for cleaning the teeth.
He then filled a cart with [food] and offered it to the bhikṣus as a meal provision.
The bhikṣus did not dare to accept it, so they reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I permit you all to accept it."
The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Soma. He himself fashioned a clay mold for a bowl to serve as a model for the future, and ordered a potter to fire it.
The potter then made many more and fired them together. Upon opening the kiln door to inspect them, he saw that they had all become golden bowls. Terrified, he said:
"This is the supernatural power of the Great Śramaṇa!"
"If the King hears of this, he will surely say that I possess much gold and treasure," [the man] thought, and he took them and buried them.
The Buddha again caused them to be burned, and they all turned into silver bowls; yet again, [the man], being terrified, buried them.
The Buddha again caused it to be burned until it became a copper bowl, its color a fine blue like that of the Jambu tree; he gave it to the bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus did not dare to accept it.
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to keep one.
There was a bhikṣu whose bowl was broken, and he traveled about without a bowl.
The Buddha said:
"You should seek another bowl;
if you are able to make one yourself, I permit you to do so."
There were some bhikṣus who burned their alms bowls until they were red; the Buddha said, "They should be fumigated.
There were also some bhikṣus who kept alms bowls made of gold, silver, the seven precious substances, ivory, copper, stone, or wood.
The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣus are like kings or high ministers; they constantly preach few desires and contentment, yet now they keep such fine alms bowls."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"From now on, I do not permit you to keep the aforementioned bowls!"
"If one keeps gold, silver, or even a stone bowl, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if one keeps a wooden bowl, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Ukara who had a daughter who habitually ate from a white-bronze bowl.
After she had gone forth, she continued to use her former utensils for almsround.
The laypeople criticized and reviled her, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, use copper bowls; they cannot be distinguished from the non-Buddhists."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The use of non-Buddhist copper bowls is not permitted; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense!
I allow the use of three kinds of bowls:"
"iron bowls, earthenware bowls, and *sumana* flower bowls.
At that time, the Licchavis of Vaiśālī obtained sandalwood bowls and deliberated together:
"To whom should these bowls be given?"
Some said: "It should be given to the World-Honored One. Others said:
"It should be given to Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha.

Many people wished to give it to the Blessed One; since the majority prevailed over the few, they filled their alms bowl to the brim with white honey and *modaka* cakes, presented it to the Blessed One, and said:
"We have obtained this bowl together and offer it to the Blessed One."
"I only pray that you will compassionately accept them!
The Buddha accepted the joy-balls and returned them to him in his bowl, saying:
"This is the bowl of a non-Buddhist, which the Buddha does not keep.
They further deliberated together, saying,
"We offered this bowl to the World-Honored One, but the World-Honored One did not accept it."
"I would rather use this now to give as an offering to the Sangha.
Having deliberated thus, he immediately took his bowl and went to the monastery to offer it to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus did not dare to accept it and reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Listen! Break it for use as incense.
Later, the Licchavis obtained another bowl made of ox-head sandalwood; they placed it atop a high standard and proclaimed:
"If there is anyone with supernatural power who can take it, give it to them.
At that time, Piṇḍola addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"The World-Honored One has declared you to be foremost in supernormal powers; why do you not take it?"
He replied, "You also possess supernormal powers; you may go and fetch it yourself.
He then immediately took it and offered it to the Sangha.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do and reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to accept it, break it up, and use it as incense."
At that time, the four great śrāvakas—Kāśyapa, Maudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, and Piṇḍola—deliberated together:
"In the city of Rājagṛha, there are those who do not have faith in or delight in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; we should join together to cause them to believe and take delight."
Having deliberated thus, they surveyed the surrounding area, both near and far, and saw only the elder Bhadrika and his sister, who did not have faith in or delight in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha.
Three Śrāvakas asked:
"Are you able to convert Bhadrika?"
Piṇḍola said, "I can transform her sister.
That householder then constructed seven layers of gates and provided three types of musical performances.
When he was about to eat, his seven apertures were all closed, and he performed a single musical piece with each morsel of food.
At that time, Anuruddha went before him to beg for alms, and the householder asked,
"From which direction did you enter?"
He replied, "I entered through the gate.
The elder then questioned the gatekeeper:
"Why did you allow a beggar to enter?
He replied, "The gate was closed as usual; I saw no one enter."
The householder then placed a piece of hemp cake into his bowl and said,
"Go away! If you have anything else, you should make food of it."
Having received it, Anuruddha departed immediately.
Later, at mealtime, Kāśyapa again went before him to beg; the exchange of questions and answers was as before.
Afterwards, he asked the gatekeeper:
"Why did you listen again as a beggar forced his way into my door?
He replied, "The door was closed as usual; I saw no one enter."
The elder again placed a piece of fish into his bowl and said to him,
"Get out! If you have anything at all, you should take this as your food."
After Kāśyapa had departed, his wife asked him,
"What do you think? Do you suppose this bhikṣu came to beg because he was unable to obtain food?"
He replied, "So it is! The wife said:
"Do you recognize the bhikṣu who came before? He replied, "I do not."
The wife said: "His name is Aniruddha;
he is the son of the Śākya clan who has renounced the palaces of the three watches and the pleasures of the five desires to leave the household life and study the Way."
He asked again:
"Did you recognize the bhikṣu who came later? He replied:
"I do not know him," the wife said.
"He is the son of the great clan of the Māṇava Piṅgalāyana; he has renounced nine hundred and ninety fields, houses, and oxen to leave the household life and study the Way."
"Out of compassion for you, I have come merely to beg for alms!
When the elder heard his wife’s words, he felt a deep sense of reverence and submission within his heart.

Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana flew into the air and preached the Dharma for him, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; immediately upon these words, while still seated, the elder became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Having seen the Dharma and attained the fruit, he immediately received the three refuges and the five precepts.
From that time forward, he constantly provided for the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and various non-Buddhist practitioners.
Then the three śrāvakas said to Piṇḍola:
"We have already transformed Baddhika, causing her to gain faith and joy; you should now go and, next, transform her elder sister."
Thereupon, at dawn, Piṇḍola dressed himself, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food; he arrived at the house in due course.
At that time, the elder’s sister was personally making *maṇḍaka* cakes; seeing Piṇḍola suddenly appear, she immediately lowered her head and closed her eyes.
Piṇḍola also gazed at the bowl with single-minded concentration and said:
"I shall certainly not give it to you!"
"Focus your mind on the bowl; what do you wish to have?
Then Piṇḍola emitted smoke from his body.
He spoke again:
"Even if smoke issues from your entire body, we will still not give it to you!
Piṇḍola then set his whole body ablaze.
He spoke again:
"Even if my entire body were ablaze with fire, I would still not give it to you!
Piṇḍola then soared into the air.
He spoke again:
"Even if you fly up into the void, I will still not give it to you!
Piṇḍola then hung upside down in mid-air.
He spoke again:
"Even if you were hanging upside down in mid-air, we would not give it to you!
Piṇḍola thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has not permitted us to force ourselves upon others to beg."
He then departed.
Not far from Rājagṛha there was a large rock; Piṇḍola sat upon it and, together with the rock, flew into Rājagṛha.
When the people in the city saw this, they were all struck with great terror; fearing that the stone would fall to the ground, there was no one who did not flee.
When it reached the top of the elder’s sister’s house, it stopped there and would not move on.
Upon seeing this, he was seized with great terror; his heart trembled and his hair stood on end. Joining his palms, he said:
"I pray you, grant me my life! I shall return the stone to its original place and provide you with food."
Pindola then took the stone, returned it to its original place, and stood before him.
The elder’s sister thought to herself:
"I cannot give him this large cake; I shall instead make smaller ones to give him."
He again made a small pellet, which grew larger;
this happened three times, each time becoming greater than before.
Thereupon, he thought to himself:
"I intended to make them small, but they all turned out large instead.
I shall now simply give him one cake. He then handed over a single cake;
however, the cakes became linked together, even extending to the vessel itself, which also became attached to them.
He grasped the vessel with his hand, and his hand became stuck to it; he then said to Piṇḍola:
"If you require cakes, I shall give them all to you; I do not begrudge even the vessel."
"Why do you need me, such that you keep your hand upon the vessel and do not let it go? He replied,
"I have no need for the cake or the vessel, nor do I need you."
"The four of us deliberated together to deliver you and your younger brother.
While the other three have already converted your brother, it is for this reason that I must deliver you!"
He asked, "What do you wish for me to do now? He replied:
"Sister, you may wear this head-dress and follow me as I offer it to the Buddha and the Sangha.
She then put on the head-dress and followed Piṇḍola. Piṇḍola immediately transformed his appearance so that they all passed through other gates, allowing people to see them.

Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he personally served the Buddha and the one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus with his own hands until they were all fully satiated, yet there was still some left over.
Taking it with him, he went to inform the Buddha:
"With these few cakes I offered to the Buddha and the one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, they have all been fully satiated, yet there is still some that remains."
"Now, where should this be placed?
The Buddha said,
"It may be placed on ground where no grass grows, or in water that contains no insects."

The woman then placed it into water free of insects; the water boiled and made a sound like hot iron being cast into a small amount of water. She was immediately struck with terror, and her hair stood on end.
Returning to where the Buddha was, she prostrated herself at his feet and sat down to one side.

The Buddha expounded various sublime Dharmas for him until he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; he then received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, provided for the fourfold assembly, and sought the Way no differently than his younger brother.
The elder bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked Piṇḍola:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I do not permit the manifestation of supernormal powers; to manifest them is a duṣkṛta offense.

At that time, King Bimbisāra possessed an āmra grove that was lush and beautiful throughout the three seasons. He constantly offered its flowers and fruits to the bhikṣus, who took as much as they required.
The bhikṣus then ate those fruits; they ate them before meals and after meals, never failing to consume them at any time;
some took full bowls away with them, while others ate half and threw the rest on the ground.
Later, a messenger was sent from a neighboring kingdom; the messenger addressed the king, saying:
"I have heard that Your Majesty possesses a mango grove that flourishes throughout the three seasons.
I pray that I may see its fruit!"
The king then ordered them to be brought.
At that time, the bhikṣus ate them all, and they informed the king of this.
The king’s ministers on his left and right together censured him, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of satiety; though the King has no regrets, the recipients themselves should have exercised restraint.
How is it that they have eaten up all the fruit from a single garden?"
When the elder bhikṣus heard this, they reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked them:
"Is it true that you did so?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
After the Buddha had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, eating unclean fruit is not permitted; if one eats it, it is a duṣkṛta offense!
There was a householder who invited the saṃgha to eat fruit, and the bhikṣus sent someone to clean each piece individually.
The sun eventually passed midday, so that they were no longer permitted to eat.
He then rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas are just like small children; they have people clean each individual fruit until it is no longer possible to reach the midday meal."
"What shall I now do with these various fruits?
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There are five kinds of seeds:"
There are five kinds of seeds: root-seeds, joint-seeds, node-seeds, fruit-seeds, and seed-seeds.
If one eats fruit, it must be purified through the five methods of purification for the śramaṇa:
purification by fire, purification by knife, purification by birds, purification by injury, and purification by immature seeds.
If eating roots, one should also perform the five kinds of purification according to the śramaṇa dharma:
peeling, cutting, breaking, washing, and fire-purification.
If eating stalks or leaves, one should perform three kinds of purification according to the śramaṇa dharma:
There are purification by cutting, purification by fire, and purification by washing.
When performing purification, one should perform a collective purification; if one item within a single heap or a single vessel is purified, it is called collective purification.
There was a bhikṣu who wished to kindle a fire in the bathhouse and was splitting firewood when a snake emerged from a hole in the wood and bit his foot, whereupon he died immediately.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"That bhikṣu was harmed by the snake because he did not know the names of the eight kinds of snakes, did not direct a mind of loving-kindness toward them, and did not recite incantations."
The eight kinds of snakes are:
the Tīraka snake, the Takṣaka snake, the Elāpattra snake, the Śaṅkhapāla snake, the Kambalāśvatara snake, the Vāsuki snake, the Gautama snake, and the Nanda and Upananda snakes.
The one who subdues the serpent with mantras says:
"I have compassion for all the dragon kings, both in the heavens and in the world;
by means of this compassionate mind of mine, may all their venomous hatred be extinguished."
"By the power of my wisdom, I shall use it to destroy this poison;
whether it be a poison of flavor or a poison of no-flavor, it shall be shattered and sink into the earth.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"If that bhikṣu protects himself with this mantra, he will not be harmed or killed by venomous snakes.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who was bitten by a snake; the other bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should use this mantra to recite over him so that he may attain peace and safety."
Having received these instructions, he went and recited the incantation, and the man was immediately cured.
Furthermore, there were monks who were bitten by snakes in various places; they reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to employ incantations and treat them as appropriate."
At that time, the bhikṣus consumed many rich foods, which increased their various ailments.
Jīvaka went to the Buddha’s dwelling early in the morning, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
“Now these bhikṣus eat many rich foods, which increases their various ailments.
I pray that you will allow them to bathe in a bathhouse to eliminate this affliction!
The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, recounting Jīvaka’s words, addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I permit the bhikṣus to construct bathhouses for the purpose of bathing therein to alleviate illness.
Some bhikṣus bathed naked, rubbed and massaged one another, and likewise left the bathhouse naked.
The laypeople criticized them, saying, "These śramaṇas are all like the Nirgranthas; they possess neither the proper decorum nor the right conduct.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this, assembled the community of bhikṣus. After rebuking them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From now on, I allow you to wear a bathing robe; naked bathing is not permitted!
Nakedness and rubbing against one another are each a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There were some bhikṣus who, while bathing, went outside and rubbed their backs against walls and trees; upon returning to the water to rinse themselves, they wounded and bruised their bodies.
The Buddha said: "You should not do so!
I allow the use of grape skins, *mālū* bark, soap-nut powder, and other such substances for removing dirt."
The bhikṣus distributed the soap powder and other items according to their personal acquaintances. The Buddha said, "They should be distributed equally.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Upananda wore his outer robe backward and crawled on all fours in the darkness to terrify the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"You should not do so. If one wears the outer robe backward or crawls on all fours, it is an *dukkaṭa* offense."
The bhikṣus suffered from the heat inside their rooms and wished to wear their saṃkakṣikās draped over their shoulders.
The Buddha said,
"I permit this within the rooms."
There were some bhikṣus who had no pillows when they slept. The Buddha said, "I allow you to make pillows.
There were some bhikṣus who suffered from lice. The Buddha said:
"Listen, pick it up.
The bhikṣus picked it up and placed it inside the room, returning it to within their robes.
The Buddha said:
"Listen: they were being gathered outside the rooms.
When the bhikṣus gathered them in the water during the rains, the Buddha said:
"They should be gathered in discarded refuse and lifted up with a compassionate mind."
There were some bhikṣus who suffered from fleas. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to spread your bedding on the ground and sweep them away;
if they are within mats or cushions, I allow you to remove them by exposing them to the sun."
There were some bhikṣus who suffered from bedbugs; the Buddha said, "I allow you to remove them and seal the cracks with mud.
There were also some elderly and sick bhikṣus who suffered from the cold and wished to light a fire inside their rooms.
The Buddha said,
"In cold weather, lighting a fire is permitted.
The bhikṣus then lit fires, which scorched their floor mats and smoked out the rooms.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to build a fire-pit outside the house and burn there; once the smoke has cleared, you may enter.
The bhikṣus did not know with what materials to construct it.
The Buddha said:

"I permit [stoves] to be made of copper, iron, clay, or stone; I permit monks and the Saṃgha of the four quarters to possess them privately; furthermore, I permit one to construct a fire-pit on the ground."
The bhikṣus drank from their bowls after midday.
The Buddha said:
"One should not drink from a bowl after midday."
"It is permitted to make separate drinking vessels; they may be made of copper, iron, or clay.

A certain bhikṣu, having completed his summer retreat in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, arrived at the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī and went to the Buddha's presence. Prostrating with his head at the Buddha's feet, he said to the Buddha:
"In this country people drink rice gruel, whereas in that country they drink parched grain porridge."
"I pray that you will permit the bhikṣus to drink flour-mash and gruel in the early morning.
The Buddha said,
"I permit them to drink it."
When the bhikṣus required salt while drinking, the Buddha said:
"I permit you to keep salt; I permit the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha of the four directions, and individuals to keep it; I permit you to make vessels for scooping salt."
The bhikṣus then fashioned the forms of sentient beings, or made human hands holding salt-spoons.
The Buddha said:
"I do not permit the making of these various forms."
At that time, the laypeople set out food on platters and offered it to the bhikṣus; the bhikṣus did not dare to accept it, whereupon the laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are unable to receive offerings!"
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to receive it [in the hands].
There were some bhikṣus who drank gruel from their bowls; because it was so hot, they could not hold them.
The Buddha said,
"I allow you to make separate vessels for drinking rice gruel.
The bhikṣus suffered from the weight of carrying their food.
The Buddha said,
"I allow you to place stools.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus fashioned stools with legs of various shapes.
The Buddha said, "I do not permit this.
When the bhikṣus went to the houses of laypeople, the laypeople served food on tables with legs of various shapes; the bhikṣus did not dare to eat.
The Buddha said:
"It is permitted for laypeople to receive [the *kaṭhina*], but they are not permitted to store it themselves.
The bhikṣus required the *kaṭhina* to be spread.
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to possess [containers] made of copper, iron, clay, or stone.
There were some laypeople who brought rice gruel to the bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus did not know where to place it for distribution.
The Buddha said:
"I permit the making of basins and bowls, provided they are fitted with rings and handles.
When serving gruel, one should ask: [Is there enough?]"
"Is there another patient who needs rice gruel?
If there is none, it should first be given to the patient.
At that time, Visākhā wished to have the community of monks cook rice gruel at her residence; the Buddha said:
"Listen. The bhikṣus did not know where to place the rice.
The Buddha said:
"It should be placed upon a grass mat.
Regarding the grains within the rice, they did not know what to do with them.
The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to keep mortars and pestles, and to have a *karmadāna* winnow the rice.
[The monks] did not know with what object to winnow the rice.
The Buddha said:
"Listen: you are permitted to keep winnowing baskets.
The bhikṣus required cauldrons.
The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to possess [ladles], made of copper, iron, clay, or stone.
The bhikṣus required ladles.
The Buddha said:
"It is also permitted to do so; with the exception of lacquer trees, all other woods are permitted for use.
A sick bhikṣu desired fine gruel.
The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things allowable) perform the task;

if there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, it is permitted for a bhikṣu to wash and heat the vessel, add water, and have the *kappiya-kāraka* soak beans and rice in it, after which the bhikṣu may light the fire."
"When the gruel is cooked, receive it from a lay attendant and give it to the patient.
The bhikṣus had so much rice that they had no place to store it.
The Buddha said:
"Listen: prepare one room with fine clay, sweep the floor clean, and settle there.
When the rice was exhausted, the bhikṣus remained; they smelled the odor of the rice.
The Buddha said:
“Listen: the ground was smeared with fragrant clay.

While the Buddha was traveling through the human realms in the kingdom of Kosala, accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty great bhikṣus, he arrived at the brahmin village of Todeyya. There, beneath a sāla tree by the roadside, he spread out a seat and sat down to rest; then, the Buddha smiled.
Ānanda thought to himself:
"The Buddhas do not smile without cause; there must surely be a reason for the Buddha’s present smile.
He then bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"Ānanda! In a past age, there was a king named Jinmei (Gimbi). He had a daughter who, at the time of her birth, was naturally adorned with a golden flower garland. The king immediately assembled his ministers to deliberate on what name she should be given, and they all said:"
"You should consult the Brahmin physiognomist.
He immediately commanded that all the physiognomists assemble and have them bestow names upon him.
The physiognomists said:
"This girl was born wearing a natural golden flower garland; she should be named Mālinī. Thus she was named.
The king cherished her deeply and, having inquired throughout the kingdom, selected girls born on the same day as her to serve as her attendants.
At that time, there were five hundred women in the kingdom who were born on the same day as [the king]; their names were all recorded so that they might serve him.
When they had grown up, the king commanded the five hundred brahmins whom he supported to provide for them, saying:
"You should act as I do, preparing five hundred pots of soup every day and serving it to them according to their preferences."
The woman then provided offerings for the brahmins exactly as commanded.

When the meal was finished, she immediately took five hundred women and traveled in a chariot drawn by four horses to amuse herself in gardens and pavilions, going from garden to garden and from pavilion to pavilion, doing so every single day.
"At that time, Kāśyapa Buddha was residing in a certain park. Whenever the charioteer arrived at the park where the Buddha resided, he would turn the carriage around and not enter.
The woman asked the charioteer:
'There is no garden within my kingdom that I have not entered; for what reason do you always avoid this park?'"
He replied, “In this place there is a shaven-headed śramaṇa named Kāśyapa; it is not appropriate to see him, and for that reason I did not enter.
The woman said:
“The śramaṇa Kāśyapa—what concern has he with human affairs?
You may simply turn the carriage around and enter this garden to visit him.

They immediately turned the carriage around and entered as far as the road allowed; then, proceeding on foot into the garden, they saw from afar that the countenance of the Buddha Kāśyapa was extraordinary and sublime, like a mountain of gold.
Having seen him, he gave rise to a heart of joy and approached the Buddha’s presence, prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrawing to stand to one side.

The Buddha preached various sublime dharmas for him, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; until, having realized the Dharma and attained the fruit, he received the three refuges and the five precepts.
He rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
Not long after he had left, he thought to himself:
"I have always provided five hundred pots of soup twice daily to five hundred brahmins; they are not fields of merit and should not receive such offerings!"
"It would be better to prepare even more exquisite food and drink to offer to the World-Honored One Kāśyapa.
Having thought this, she gave orders for it to be prepared and sent offerings every day.
At that time, when the brahmins heard that Mālinī had become a disciple of the Buddha Kāśyapa and was providing him with superior delicacies, they conceived feelings of jealousy and deliberated thus:
"We must employ a stratagem to kill this girl together.
At that time, King Kalmāṣapāda experienced eleven kinds of dreams during the night: he dreamed that a tree four finger-widths tall immediately bore flowers;
he dreamed that those flowers immediately bore fruit; [and so forth].
He dreamed that while a calf was plowing, a large ox stood watching;
he dreamed that three cauldrons were cooking rice side-by-side, yet the rice from the two outer cauldrons leaped into one another without falling into the central one;
and he dreamed that a camel with two heads was eating grass.
He dreamed that a mare turned around to drink the milk of her own foal;
he dreamed that a golden bowl traveled through the air;
and he dreamed that a wild fox urinated into the golden bowl.
He dreamed of a monkey sitting upon a golden bed;
he dreamed of selling gośīrṣa sandalwood that was like withered grass;
and he dreamed that the center of the water was turbid while the four edges were pure.
At dawn, he assembled his various ministers and related his dream in detail, inquiring of them:
"What kind of dream is this?
The ministers replied:
"One should question the brahmin physiognomist.
He immediately summoned him and questioned him.
The brahmins then thought to themselves:
"We intended to kill this girl, and now we have found her!
they said, and then addressed the king:
"This dream is inauspicious!"
"Either he shall lose his kingdom, or he shall meet his end.
The king asked again,
"Is there any expedient by which one might escape this calamity?"
He replied, "There is!
But it is beloved by the king; he will certainly not allow it to be used."
The king said, "Speak! The physiognomist replied:

"King So-and-so, such-and-such an elephant, such-and-such a horse, such-and-such a great minister, and such-and-such a great Brahmin shall take five hundred bulls, five hundred buffaloes, five hundred heifers, five hundred young bulls, five hundred rams, five hundred castrated rams, and Princess Mālinī along with her five hundred attendants; seven days hence, they shall be slaughtered at the crossroads to sacrifice to the gods, and this calamity may then be extinguished."
"If this is not done, this calamity cannot be avoided!

When the king heard this, he believed it and immediately issued an edict to prepare for it; he then summoned his daughter and told her the matter in detail, granting her six days to fulfill whatever she desired.
The woman said to the king:
"I do not at all begrudge my death.
I pray that on the first day, you and the people of the city—men and women, great and small—shall go together to the dwelling of Kāśyapa Buddha."
The king immediately granted his permission.
Thereupon, he summoned all those within the city, who surrounded him from front and back as they proceeded to the place where Kāśyapa was.

The Buddha expounded various sublime Dharmas for them, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them; eventually, they realized the Dharma and attained the fruits [of the path], receiving the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
"I pray that on the second day, I may go to the Buddha's dwelling together with the king’s ministers;
I pray that on the third day, I may go to the Buddha's dwelling together with the princes;
and I pray that on the fourth day, I may go to the Buddha's dwelling together with the princesses."
"I pray that on the fifth day, you may go with the King’s consort and court ladies to the Buddha’s dwelling;
and on the sixth day, I pray that you may go with the King to the Buddha’s dwelling.
The King granted all these requests, and they all perceived the Dharma and attained the fruits [of the path]. They received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, as described above.
Having attained the fruit, the king asked Kāśyapa Buddha about his eleven dreams:
"What is the karmic retribution for these dreams?
The Buddha said:
"These eleven dreams pertain to the future, not to the present!
As for the dream of seeing a small tree bearing flowers:
in a future age, there shall be a Buddha appearing among people with a lifespan of one hundred years, named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
At that time, people’s hair would turn white at the age of thirty;
those who saw flowers in their dreams would immediately bear fruit [as sons]. At that time, people of twenty years of age would already have given birth to children.
As for the dream of seeing a calf plowing while the great ox stands watching:
it means that at that time, the children will take charge of the family affairs, and the parents will no longer possess autonomy.
As for the dream of seeing three cauldrons cooking rice simultaneously, with the rice from the two side cauldrons leaping into one another but not falling into the central cauldron: [it signifies...]
At that time, the wealthy gave gifts to one another, while the poor received nothing.
Dreaming of a two-headed camel eating grass signifies that at that time there will be ministers who,
having already consumed the king’s stipends, further seize the property of the people.
As for the dream of seeing a mare drinking the milk of her foal:
at that time, after the mother has given her daughter in marriage, she instead turns around and seeks food from her.
As for the dream of seeing a golden bowl traveling through the void:
At that time, the rains will not fall according to the seasons, nor will they be widespread.
As for the dream of seeing a wild fox urinating into a golden bowl:
at that time, people will marry only for the sake of wealth, without selecting their ancestral lineage.
As for the dream of seeing a monkey sitting upon a golden bed:
at that time, the king governs by unlawful means, being tyrannical and unrighteous.
As for the dream of seeing ox-head sandalwood sold at the same price as rotten grass:
At that time, the śramaṇas of the Śākya clan, out of greed for gain and offerings, preached the Dharma to laypeople.
They saw in a dream that the center of the water was turbid while the four edges were clear;
this signifies that at that time, the Buddha-dharma will first perish in the central lands, while it instead flourishes in the borderlands.
The Buddha said, "The significance of the King's eleven dreams is as follows; there shall be no ill omen for Your Majesty’s person.
Thereupon, while still upon his seat, the King issued a decree to his ministers: "Whatever offerings were intended for the sacrifice to the gods, I now bestow them all as a gift of fearlessness."
"From this day forth, I would rather lose my own life than intentionally kill a living being, much less a human being!
I shall not intentionally harm even insects or ants, much less women or other people!"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"After that Kāśyapa Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, his king erected for the Buddha a stupa of gold and silver, half a yojana in length and breadth and one yojana in height;
it was constructed with bricks of gold and silver placed alternately, and it still remains within the earth today."
The Buddha then brought forth the stupa to show it to the fourfold assembly; the entire-body relics of Kāśyapa Buddha remained as solemn and intact as they had been originally.
On account of this matter, the Buddha took a lump of clay and spoke this verse:
"Though one were to obtain Jambūnada gold, And the profit of hundreds and thousands of precious jewels,"
"It would not be as good as taking a single lump of clay and building a stūpa for the Buddha.
Having said this, he returned it to its original place.
The Buddha then used four lumps of clay to plaster over the spot where the stūpa had disappeared.
The one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus also each applied four handfuls of clay.
Thereupon, those bhikṣus wished to erect a stūpa for Kāśyapa Buddha upon the plastered site.
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to rise.
They then rose together.
At that time, the first stūpa was erected upon the ground of Jambudvīpa.
Thereafter, the bhikṣus desired to erect stūpas for the arhats, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
The Buddha said: "I permit that there are four kinds of persons for whom a stūpa should be erected: the Tathāgata, an noble disciple, a pratyekabuddha, and a wheel-turning monarch.

The bhikṣus wished to build open-air stūpas, roofed stūpas, and wallless stūpas; they wished to construct niches and images within, railings without, and dew-receptacle basins; they wished to erect pillars of copper, iron, stone, or wood before the stūpas, topped with various animal figures such as elephants and lions; and they wished to plant trees to the left and right of the stūpas.
The Buddha permitted them all.
At that time, the various non-Buddhists also built stupas for themselves and made various offerings; when the people saw this, they conceived faith and joy.
The bhikṣus then had this thought:
"If the Buddha would permit us to offer various kinds of worship to the stūpas, the multitude would likewise give rise to faith and joy.
The Buddha granted this permission.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus themselves sang and danced as an offering to the stūpas.
The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"Laypeople dance and sing, and these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do the very same.
What difference is there between us?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not personally perform songs and dances as an offering to a stūpa; however, it is permitted to have others do so on his behalf."
"It is permitted for bhikṣus to praise the Buddha themselves and to offer flowers, incense, banners, and canopies at the stūpas.
When the bhikṣus were begging for alms and obtained flowers, they did not dare to accept them. The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are unworthy of receiving offerings, nor do they wish to make offerings at the stūpas."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
“I permit you to receive it.
They did not know where to place it.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to make three kinds of bags:
a flower bag, a food bag, and a water-strainer bag."
There were some bhikṣus who went about gathering flowers themselves, traveling from one village to another;
outside the villages, they were plundered by bandits.
The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas are exactly like garland-makers or their disciples.
The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted to go outside the village to gather flowers."
The bhikṣus offered flowers strung together with cords, and the laypeople rebuked them as described above.
The Buddha said:
"You should not offer them strung together; rather, you should scatter them for offering."
"If there are withered petals, those that are green on the outside may all be plucked away; by rubbing the stem three times with the hand, the flower will naturally open beautifully.
The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the bhikṣus grew their nails long; they gave rise to a mind of attachment and did not delight in practicing the holy life (brahmacarya), eventually leading some to return to secular life or become followers of external paths.
The laypeople criticized them, saying:
"These śramaṇas are like those who indulge in sensual desires; they groom their hands and nails, lacking any sense of renunciation.
Once, a bhikṣu with long nails entered a village to beg for food; a woman saw him and called out to him, inviting him to engage in sexual intercourse.
The bhikṣu said, "I am a renunciant; I do not do such a thing! The woman said:
"If you do not follow me, I shall bring ill repute upon you.
He then tore at his own clothes with his claws, wounding his flesh,
and cried out loudly:
"A bhikṣu forcibly pulled at me; though I did not comply with him, he immediately seized me, tearing my clothes and wounding my flesh.
When the crowd came to look, some believed it and some did not.
Those who believed said, "This bhikṣu has long nails; he must have committed this act.
Those who did not believe said:
"This woman has always been ill-behaved; she is merely slandering the bhikṣus!
They all joined in censuring him, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu keep such long nails?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I do not permit you to grow your nails long; anyone who violates this incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
I permit you to keep a nail-cutter, with one end fashioned as an ear-scraper."
There were some bhikṣus who dyed their nails red, and the laypeople criticized and rebuked them.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do so; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
At that time, the bhikṣus were making robes for the sake of ornamentation.
The Buddha said:
"I do not permit making robes for the sake of ornamentation; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
There was a bhikṣu guarding the monastic quarters who, because a bhikṣu bringing food arrived late, climbed a tree to look for him; he fell from the tree and broke his ribs.
The Buddha said:
"Climbing trees is not permitted; one who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
There were some bhikṣus who needed to climb trees for minor reasons.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to climb them, but you must not go higher than the height of a man."
There were some bhikṣus who wished to take dry branches from the tops of tall trees for firewood.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to take them by means of a ladder, but you must not climb the tree."
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus who encountered dangers from water, fire, wild beasts, or bandits; wishing to climb trees, they did not dare to do so and consequently fell into distress.
The Buddha said:
"In the face of such perils, I permit you to climb as you wish."

There were two bhikṣus traveling together on a road who did not possess water-strainers. Becoming thirsty and wishing to drink water, they saw insects within it; one bhikṣu drank, while the other did not drink and died.
The monk who had drunk water went to where the Buddha was and reported the matter to him.
The Buddha said, "That monk possessed a sense of shame and remorse; he was thus able to maintain his precepts until death."
"From now on, I do not permit traveling without a water-strainer; anyone who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
There were some bhikṣus who wished to travel to a nearby location, but as they lacked water-strainers, they did not dare to go.
The Buddha said, "I permit you to travel within half a yojana without a water-strainer.

Later, there were two bhikṣus traveling together on a road; one bhikṣu had a water-strainer while the other did not, yet they would not lend it to one another, and they became extremely parched with thirst.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Did I not previously prohibit traveling more than half a yojana without a water-strainer?
If one has no water-strainer, it is permitted provided there is a corner of a robe that can be used to strain the water."
"When intending to travel, one should think of using a water strainer.
It is also permitted to keep a water-straining tube.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus made them out of gold, silver, and precious gems.
The Buddha said: "You should not do so!
I allow you to make them using copper, iron, bamboo, wood, tile, or stone."

"Regarding the ten kinds of households from whom robes may be accepted: fine cloth must be used for the edges; the use of *pāṃsukūla* (rag-robe) material is not permitted. One who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, Śāriputra suffered from a wind ailment, and there was a *harītakī* fruit placed at the foot of his bed.
When Kokālika arrived, he was driven away by the Elder Śāriputra.
Śāriputra immediately avoided him, forgetting his harītakī fruit.
When Kokālika saw this, he said to the bhikṣus:
“The World-Honored One praises Śāriputra for having few desires and being content, yet now he stores up what we do not possess.
When Śāriputra heard this, he thought to himself:
“How can I fall into such censure over such a trivial matter?”
He then took it and threw it away.
The bhikṣus said to him,
"Venerable One!"
"This medicine is required for my wind ailment; do not discard it, you may take it back!
He replied, "Because of this trivial thing, you have caused my fellow practitioner of the holy life to fall into such suspicion and reproach."
"I have already discarded it; I shall never take it up again!
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra, it is not only now that he has discarded this medicine and refused to take it again; in a past life as well, he was just like this.
Long ago in the past, there was a black snake that bit a calf and then returned to its hole.”
There was a mantra-practitioner who, using a mantra for a black ram, sought to summon [the snake] out of its hole, but was unable to make it emerge.
The practitioner then lit a fire before the calf and recited the mantra over it; it transformed into a fire-bee that entered the snake’s hole, burning and stinging the black snake.
Unable to endure the pain, the snake then emerged from its hole.
The ram used its horns to scoop the snake up and place it before the incantation-master, who said to it:
"Go back and lick the poison; otherwise, you shall be cast into this fire!"
The black snake then spoke in verse:
"Once I have spat out this venom, I shall never draw it back in;
if the time for death arrives, I will end my life and never turn back."
"Upon this, he did not withdraw his venom but threw himself into the fire.
The Buddha said,
"The black snake of that time was Śāriputra."
"In the past, even when undergoing such suffering of death, you did not refrain from taking poison; how much less would you now take up medicine that has been discarded?
From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to keep medicine."
The group of six bhikṣus then accumulated a great quantity of medicines, whereupon the laypeople criticized and reviled them, saying:
"Are these śramaṇas intending to act as physicians,
or do they intend to engage in trade?"
They claim for themselves that they have few desires and are content, yet they lack satiety!
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“One should not store medicine in great quantities!”
"It is permitted to keep various kinds of medicinal herbs, one *āḍhaka* each.
If there is a chronic illness, it is permitted to keep more as required.
There were some bhikṣus who had no knives; they used pieces of bamboo and reed to cut their robes, but the robes became damaged.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to keep a knife for cutting [garments].
Thereupon, the bhikṣus made large knives; when bandits arrived, they were able to use them to harm the bhikṣus.
The Buddha said:
"I do not permit the making of large knives; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
I permit [knives] one finger-width in length, with a blade on one side and a handle made of wood—excluding lacquer trees."
The bhikṣus received needles but did not dare to accept them; the Buddha said, "I allow you to receive and keep them.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus kept many of them.
The Buddha said:
"One should not keep many.
I permit you to keep three needles; any others should be given away as pure gifts."
At that time, the monastery of Ānanda in Vaiśālī was low-lying and damp; it was infested with mosquitoes and gadflies and was sweltering and hot, which caused the bhikṣus great distress.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to keep fans and fly-whisks."
The bhikṣus used horsehair to make whisks, which killed insects.
The Buddha said:
"I do not permit the use of horsehair to make whisks; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
There were some bhikṣus who placed their bowls on the ground while filled with food, and they overturned them.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to make bowl-stands using copper, iron, ivory, horn, clay, stone, bamboo, or wood—excluding lacquer trees."
"Even tying grass beneath it is permitted.
There were some bhikṣus whose bowls became cracked and peeled from the fuming; the Buddha said:
"They should be fumigated again."
The bhikṣus provided food for the laborers without measuring the amount; even when there was plenty, they still became angry.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to keep measures such as the *dou*, *hu*, *sheng*, and *he*."
"Whether for the Sangha, the Sangha of the four quarters, or for private use, it is permitted to keep [these items];
there should also be a reserve store.
The bhikṣus hired laborers, but when they did not give them ghee, oil, honey, or rock sugar in proportion to their work, the workers became angry even though they had received much.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to keep scales, as was previously stated.
At that time, the bhikṣus were learning to write, and the laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
“Why do the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, not diligently recite and study?
What is the use of learning writing?
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Learning to read and write is not permitted.
Later, when the bhikṣus were assigned their turn for communal duties, they did not know how to record them and thus forgot their assignments.
The Buddha said:
"Listen to and study the scriptures, but do not listen to [other things] that cause one to neglect their practice.
When the bhikṣus wished to learn incantations for bees, snakes, and other poisons,
the Buddha said:
"Listen and learn.
Some bhikṣus kept fields, houses, and shops, which led the laypeople to criticize and reproach them, saying:
"We keep fields, houses, and shops because we have the burden of wives and children; [why do you monks do the same?]"
"The various bhikṣus are also like this.
How are they any different from me?
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"None of these are permitted to be kept; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
There were some laypeople who offered fields, houses, and shops to the Saṃgha, but the bhikṣus did not dare to accept them. Consequently, those laypeople rebuked and criticized them, saying:
"These bhikṣus are not worthy of receiving offerings!
[The monks] reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow the Saṃgha to receive them, provided that a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) is made aware of it."
There were some bhikṣus who went to pay their respects to the non-Buddhist teachers such as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and Maskarin Gośālīputra.
The Buddha said:
"You should not pay them visits; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
The bhikṣus practiced various forms of divination, whereupon the laypeople criticized them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, cannot even purify their own views; how then could they know of future events?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is not permitted; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense.
The bhikṣus then studied spells for deluding people, and the Buddha said:
"It is not permitted; whoever violates this commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense!
The bhikṣus studied the incantations for raising the dead, and the Buddha said:
"It is not permitted; whoever violates this commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense!"
The bhikṣus asked diviners and physiognomists, wishing to know for themselves whether their fortunes were auspicious or inauspicious.
The Buddha said:
"This is not permitted; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
When the laypeople saw the bhikṣus reciting secular texts, they criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not have faith in or delight in the holy life; they have abandoned the Buddha’s sūtras and precepts to recite secular texts!"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "It is not permitted!
There were some bhikṣus who engaged in debate with non-Buddhists; being ignorant, they felt ashamed and thought to themselves:
"If the Buddha had permitted us to read and recite non-Buddhist texts, we would not have incurred this disgrace.
The Buddha said,
"I permit the reading of non-Buddhist texts for the purpose of subduing the followers of external paths."
"However, you must not follow the views of the scholars.

There were some bhikṣus who kept many small copper vessels; the laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying, "These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, keep so many of these utensils; how are they any different from us?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I do not permit the keeping of many small copper vessels; one who violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense.

There were two brothers who were brahmins and reciters of the Chāndogyopaniṣad; later, they went forth into the True Dharma and, hearing that the bhikṣus were reciting the sūtras incorrectly, they criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"Venerable sirs!

Having been ordained for so long, you do not know the speech of men or women, the singular or plural forms, the present, past, or future tenses, nor the long or short vowels, or the light or heavy syllables, yet you recite the Buddha’s scriptures in such a manner!"
The bhikṣu heard this and felt ashamed.
The two bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was and reported the matter to him in full detail.
The Buddha said:
"You may recite and chant according to the local dialects of the country, but you must not deviate from or lose the Buddha’s intent!
