It is not permitted to render the Buddha’s words into the language of external scriptures; anyone who violates this commits a *sthūlātyaya* offense!"
There were some bhikṣus who entered a village without tying their lower garments; they fell to the ground and were exposed, whereupon the women laughed at them, and they felt ashamed.
The Buddha said:
"I do not permit entering a village without tying one's lower garment; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
"I allow you to possess a waistband.
The bhikṣus made waistbands that were too long, wrapping around the waist four or five times.
The Buddha said:
"One should not listen for more than two or three turns.
The bhikṣus made their waistbands too wide; the Buddha said:
"The width is permitted to be at most four finger-breadths, and it shall not be less than one finger-breadth."
The bhikṣus made [the robes] using variegated-colored threads. The Buddha said:
"It is not permitted! It is permitted to use a single color according to one's needs."
There were some bhikṣus who entered a village wearing light clothing; the wind blew and their bodies were exposed, causing the women to laugh and them to feel ashamed.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to make fastenings for your robes and hook them together."
"One should use copper, iron, ivory, horn, bamboo, or wood to make hooks, with the exception of lacquer trees;
one may even make a strap and fasten it.
The bhikṣus wore their robes in a single layer, and the lower parts were easily damaged.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to wear robes in reverse order, with hooks, buttons, and belts attached both above and below.
There were some bhikṣus who, when reciting mantras, did not consume salt and did not sleep on beds, saying:
"Homage to the Bhagavān.
He gave rise to doubt:
"Could it be that I am following a divergent view and accepting the teachings of another teacher?"
They reported this to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "The nature of divine spells is such; you must simply not follow their views."
At that time, the bhikṣu Maitrībala said to the Malla son Udayin,
"The bhikṣu Dhava has committed adultery with your wife.
Upon hearing this, Udayin immediately questioned Dhava.
"Is it truly so? Dova did not answer. Luyi then said:
“Dhāva, having committed an act of lust, was ashamed and had no words with which to answer me.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

“I authorize you to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for the purpose of overturning the bowl (*pātra-nyubja*) for Ulkāmukha, the son of the Malla; henceforth, no one at all shall enter his house again.”
A single bhikṣu should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Malla son Rūpa has falsely slandered Dabba by claiming he had sexual intercourse with his wife."
The Saṃgha now performs the *kapāla-āvṛti* (bowl-covering) karmavācanā against him; no one at all shall go to enter his house.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Malla son, Rāṣṭrapāla, has falsely slandered Dharmaruci by claiming he had sexual relations with his wife.
The Saṃgha now performs the *pātra-nyubja* (inverted bowl) karma against him; no one at all shall go or enter his house."
"Whichever elders approve, let them remain silent;
whoever does not approve, let them speak.
The Sangha has completed the *pātra-nyāsa* (bowl-inversion) *karmavācanā* against Ulūka, the son of a Malla."
The Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.
If the Saṃgha performs the *pātra-āvarta* (turning-over of the bowl) karma against someone, none of the fourfold assembly shall have any dealings with them or engage in speech.

There were some bhikṣus who, having had a minor dispute with certain upāsakas, performed the *pātrāvarṇa* (bowl-covering) karmavācanā against them. The Buddha said: "One should not perform the *pātrāvarṇa* karmavācanā against a white-robed layperson on account of a minor matter; rather, it should be performed only when eight conditions are fulfilled: 1. They do not respect the Saṃgha. 2. They do not respect the Dharma.

3. They do not respect the Vinaya. 4. They do not respect the preceptors (*upādhyāya*). 5. They do not respect the teachers (*ācārya*). 6. They do not respect their fellow practitioners (*sabrahmacārin*). 7. They do not respect the elders among the bhikṣus. 8. They do not respect the teachings they have received. If these eight factors are present, then one should perform the *pātrāvarṇa* karmavācanā. If they are not present, one should not. If one performs it when they are not present, one commits an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*)."

If an upāsaka, in the presence of bhikṣus, disparages the Triple Gem and the precepts; if he wishes to bring harm to the bhikṣus, creates an ill reputation for them, seeks to seize their dwellings, or commits offenses against bhikṣuṇīs.
"These are the eight.
Ānanda had been close friends with Udayin during his time as a layman. The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Go to Udayin's place and say to him:"
"The Sangha has already performed the *kapāla* (inverted-bowl) rite against you.
Ānanda, having received these instructions, went to his door, where the gatekeeper announced: "Ānanda is outside."
He said, "Let him enter. Ānanda spoke, saying:
"I shall not enter your gate again.
When Elapattra heard this, he hurried out and asked,
"Why have you suddenly stopped entering my gate?"

He replied, "The Sangha has already performed the *pātra-āvṛtti* (the ritual of overturning the bowl) against you; none of the fourfold assembly may come and go with you or converse with you. Luyi said:
"If it were as you say, you would be killing me!
She fainted and fell to the ground. Ānanda said:
"Arise! Go and apologize to Dhāva; the Saṃgha shall grant you the lifting of the *pātra-nyāga* (the bowl-banishment).
Luī immediately rose from the ground, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I truly did not see Dabba having an affair with my wife; it was Mātṛceṭa who told me, and I merely believed his words.
The Buddha said, “You should offer an apology to Dabba, and the Saṃgha shall grant you the lifting of the *pātrānāmi* (upturned bowl) karmavācanā.”
Having received these instructions, he went at once to Dabba’s place, prostrated himself with his head at the elder’s feet, grasped them with his hands, and said:
“Out of my own folly, I believed the words of others and slandered you, O Venerable One.”
"I pray that you will accept my confession!
The bhikṣu Dhava immediately accepted it for him.
Having offered his apologies, Elavila returned to the Buddha's presence and said:
“I have already finished declining the bhikṣu Ṭhapa.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“I allow the Saṃgha to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to release him.”

The Malla son, Rauruka, should go before the Saṃgha, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, prostrate at the feet of each member of the Saṃgha one by one, kneel with palms joined, and make this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!..."

The Malla son of the Ikṣvāku clan, Dharmaruci, falsely slandered me, saying that he had committed adultery with my wife; consequently, the Saṃgha performed the *pātra-nyubja* (inverted bowl) karmavācanā against me, forbidding all four assemblies from coming to or going from my home.
I have already finished apologizing to the *ḍomba*; I now properly comply with the Saṃgha and request from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *pātra-nyāsa* (the bowl-covering) *karmavācanā*.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, lift it for me!
Thus he requests three times.
A single bhikṣu should then announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

The son of a Malla from the village of Elavaddana falsely slandered Dabba Mallaputta by claiming he had sexual relations with his wife. Consequently, the Sangha performed the *pātra-ovaddhana* (bowl-inversion) ritual against him, prohibiting all four assemblies from coming to visit or conversing with him.
I, [Name], having already apologized to the *karmadāna*, have requested from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *pātra-nyāga* (the bowl-covering) *karman*. The Saṃgha now grants this lifting.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Malla son Rauruka has falsely slandered Dabba; now the Saṃgha grants him absolution from this.
Those elders who consent, remain silent; [those who do not, speak]."
Those who do not approve, speak.
The Sangha has finished performing the *kapāla-uddharaṇa-karman* (the ritual for lifting the overturned bowl) for Lu-yi Li-shi-zi;
because the Sangha approves by remaining silent.
"Maintain this matter thus.
There were some upāsakas who, having become slightly angry with or resentful toward the bhikṣus, no longer showed them respect or faith.
The Buddha said:
"An upāsaka should not, on account of some minor matter, fail to show respect and faith toward a bhikṣu.
Even if a bhikṣu has accomplished eight qualities, one should still not fail to show him respect and faith:
disparaging the Triple Gem and the precepts;..."
They wish to bring harm to the upāsakas;
they seek to bring ill repute upon the upāsakas;
they wish to seize the dwellings of the upāsakas.
"To regard what is unrighteous as righteous and thus deceive the upāsakas—
this is the eighth. Furthermore,
if an upāsaka becomes angry with a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu should not go to his house."
"If the entire village is hostile toward the bhikṣus, a bhikṣu should not go to that village.
At that time, Baddhananda was carrying an umbrella, wearing leather sandals, and walking along with a bag for his bowl slung over his shoulder and a staff carried across it.

There was a lay follower who was walking behind with a disciple of a non-Buddhist teacher; seeing them from afar, he thought they were the non-Buddhist and said to the disciple, "Look at how your teacher walks along the road, lacking any dignified deportment."
The disciple of the non-Buddhist said:
"You all see those who lack dignified deportment and assume they are non-Buddhists;
yet this person is truly a son of the Śākyas."
The two men argued with one another and subsequently made a wager.
When they pursued [the monk] and questioned him, he was indeed a śrāmaṇera.
Having lost the wager, the upāsaka felt great shame and remorse.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I do not permit one to perform such a ritual while traveling on a road; anyone who violates this incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense!
There were some bhikṣus traveling on a road who, upon receiving an umbrella for the sake of a stūpa, did not dare to accept it.
The lay devotees criticized them, saying, "These śramaṇas,
sons of the Śākyas, do not wish to make offerings to the stūpa!
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen! You must not maintain your conduct according to the deportment of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
There were some elderly and infirm bhikṣus who required staffs and carrying-bags to hold their alms bowls while begging for food.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to request it from the Saṃgha.
That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha and make this request:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, the bhikṣu [Name], am old and infirm; I now request from the Saṃgha permission to carry a staff and use a net-bag to hold my alms bowl while begging for food.
May the Saṃgha grant me this!"
Thus he requests three times.
The Saṃgha should deliberate whether it is appropriate to grant it or not: if he is truly not aged or infirm, it should not be granted;
if he is truly aged or infirm, it should be granted by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
A certain bhikṣu announced:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so is aged and infirm; he now requests from the Saṃgha permission to use a staff and a net-bag to carry his bowl while begging for alms. May the Saṃgha grant him this."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience.
This is the motion. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so by name, is aged and infirm... [as before] ...the Saṃgha now grants him this.
Which elders consent, let them remain silent;
those who do not consent, let them speak.
The Sangha has already granted permission for the bhikṣu so-and-so, who is aged and infirm, to beg for alms while leaning on a staff and carrying his bowl in a net-bag;
the Sangha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.
There were some bhikṣus who wished to keep staffs and carrying bags.
The Buddha said:
"One should possess a staff and a carrying bag only if one has been designated by the formal act (karmavācanā) of the Saṃgha."
"If there is a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative, it is also permitted to keep [the robe] as belonging to her.
There were some bhikṣus who, while begging for alms in the rain, ruined the color of their robes.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to hold the umbrella until you reach the gate, at which point you should set it on the ground; once you have received the alms-food, you may take it up again and depart.

There were some bhikṣus who, having returned from begging with their umbrellas, placed them in the heated hall, the lecture hall, or the dining area; the dripping water moistened the ground and turned it into mud.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to build a house to house them, provided they do not obstruct one another.
There were some bhikṣus who wished to privately construct covers; the Buddha said:
"I permit its construction!
Its dimensions may be made according to one's preference; it may be constructed of wood, except for lacquer trees;
and whether covered with leaves or grass, I also permit each of the ten kinds of cloth to be used as a covering."
The Sangha, the Sangha of the four quarters, and individuals are all permitted to keep [these items]; it is also permitted to keep one extra as a precaution.
There was a bhikṣu who suffered from eye disease; the Buddha said:
"I permit the application of eye medicine and nasal irrigation, the rubbing of oil and ghee upon the crown of the head, and the rubbing of salt and ghee upon the soles of the feet."
The bhikṣus did not know with what materials to make a nasal irrigation tube.
The Buddha said:
"With the exception of lacquer trees, one may make it from other bamboo, wood, copper, iron, ivory, or horn."
There was a bhikṣu named Gopī who would invariably chew his food after having finished his meal.
When the other bhikṣus saw this, they suspected he was committing the offense of eating at an improper time, and they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, “Monks!

This bhikṣu was constantly born among cattle for five hundred previous lifetimes; due to the remaining karmic retribution, he has now been born among humans, and whatever he eats does not digest unless he first chews it like a cow.”
"From now on, there shall be no offense for belching at such times as these.

There were some bhikṣus who lived depending upon the Saṃgha, or lived depending upon the Saṃgha of the four quarters, or lived depending upon a stūpa; they received no instruction, being foolish and ignorant, and were unable to train in the precepts.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I do not permit one to dwell depending upon the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha of the four directions, or a stūpa; anyone who violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense!
I permit dependence upon a senior monk (sthavira) or a bhikṣu who acts according to the Dharma and is able to provide instruction and admonition."

At that time, the bhikṣus slept under the same cover, their bodies touching one another, which gave rise to defiled and attached thoughts, and they no longer took pleasure in practicing the holy life.
The Buddha said:
"I do not permit sleeping under the same cover; whoever violates this incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense."
If there is no clothing to cover them, it is permitted for them to wear different undergarments while using the same upper garment to cover themselves.
If the dwelling is cramped and they do not know one another, it is permitted for them to sit on the same bed, but they must not sleep;
if they sleep, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At a certain forest hermitage, a wild fire was about to arrive, and [the monks] did not know what to do.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Go and extinguish it!"
Having received these instructions, he went to extinguish it but was unable to do so; he returned and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Speak to the fire deity in my name, saying:..."
“The World-Honored One wishes for you to extinguish it.
Having received these instructions, he went and spoke [to the fire], and the fire was immediately extinguished.
He returned and informed the Buddha, who said:
“Not only in this present life does the fire extinguish upon hearing my name;
in a past life, there was an island in the ocean that was constantly burned by fire for seven years.”
In the thickets upon that island, a pheasant had hatched a chick. Seeing the fire approaching, its parents abandoned it and fled.
Thereafter, the chick spread out its wings and feet toward the fire deity and spoke this verse:
"I have feet, yet I cannot walk; I have wings, yet I cannot fly."
"My parents have abandoned me; I only pray that you will save my life!
The Fire God then replied with a verse:
"That which is born from an egg is not what I seek, yet now you beg it of me."
"I shall now bestow upon you a space of one fathom on each of the four sides.
The Buddha said:
"The young pheasant at that time was none other than myself."
The Fire God is the present Fire God.
Previously he extinguished fire for me, and now he has again extinguished it for me.

When a wildfire approaches, one should strike the *gandī* or call out for the monks to assemble together. One should have a *karmadāna* (lay attendant) cut the grass on both sides and burn it back toward the fire, then douse it with water and earth, and extinguish it by beating it out with wet clothes.
In certain monasteries, banners and canopies that had been abundant within the stupas were discarded in the courtyards, where they lay scattered about and were trampled underfoot.
Laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying, "These śramaṇas have no regard for the property of others; they have ruined these offerings."
"This is not the Dharma of a śramaṇa!
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Except for the stupas of Buddhas and pratyekabuddhas, it is permitted to use the surplus property of other stupas for the sake of the Saṃgha of the four directions."
"If this stupa requires [funds] later, take property belonging to the Sangha of the four directions and restore it.

At that time, the bhikṣus ate raw and cooked garlic; they ate it before meals and after meals, at all times without exception, and even ate it on an empty stomach, so that their dwellings became foul-smelling.
When laypeople entered the quarters and smelled the odor, they criticized them, saying:
"The dwellings of these śramaṇas smell of garlic, just like a kitchen.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is not permitted to eat garlic without a valid reason!
If one eats it for a valid reason, one must not walk or stand upwind from the bhikṣus.
A certain bhikṣu ate garlic for a minor reason; when the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, he did not dare go to listen.
The Buddha asked,
"For what reason have you not come to listen to the Dharma? They replied:
“The World-Honored One does not permit one to eat garlic and then walk or stand upwind from the bhikṣus; this is why I did not dare.
The Buddha rebuked that bhikṣu in various ways:
“You foolish man! What you have done is contrary to the Dharma!”
"Out of greed for foul-smelling filth, you have lost the benefit of the immeasurable flavor of the Dharma!
Having rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I do not permit the consumption of garlic on account of minor causes; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
A bhikṣu who has consumed garlic should properly conform to the other bhikṣus.
To "properly conform" means that for seven days he must not enter the heated room, the lecture hall, the dining hall, the bathhouse, the latrine, another’s cell, a village, or pass by a stūpa.
After seven days, bedding that should be shaken out shall be shaken out;
that which should be washed shall be washed;
and that which should be aired shall be aired.
Those who should be fumigated with incense shall be fumigated.
One should sprinkle and sweep the interior of the room and plaster its inside thoroughly.
Having personally washed one's clothes and bathed one's body, one may then enter.
At that time, the bhikṣus kept large copper pots. When the laypeople saw them, they asked, "Whose vessel is this? Someone replied:
"Those bhikṣus have given their permission," he said,
and then he reviled them, saying:
"These śramaṇas are just like the ministers of a king!"
"What is the use of keeping this large copper cauldron?
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you are not permitted to keep large copper cauldrons!"
"If one keeps more than one *śu* [a measure], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, the bhikṣus urinated here and there, making the places foul-smelling and impure. The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no rules of dignified conduct!"
"Urine has no fixed place; its location is foul and impure.
There was a bhikṣu who urinated in an improper place. A spirit seized his male organ and dragged him to a secluded spot, saying:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"One should urinate in this place.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I do not permit urinating indiscriminately. One should establish a designated place in a secluded spot; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
There were visiting bhikṣus who did not know where the place for urination was;
the Buddha said, "I allow you to ask the resident bhikṣus.
There were also bhikṣus who were elderly or ill and unable to reach the place for urination; the Buddha said:
"Listen, you are permitted to keep a vessel for urine.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus placed the urine vessels inside their rooms where they were foul-smelling.
The Buddha said:
"One should not wear it inside the room.
After the bhikṣus wore it outside the room, evil insects entered within.
The Buddha said:
"If one must defecate inside a room, one should seal the opening securely;
if it is placed outside the room, fill it completely with water.
There were some bhikṣus who defecated in various places, and the laypeople criticized them as described above.
The Buddha said:

"You should not do so! I allow you to dig the ground in a secluded place to construct a latrine house, covering it above and providing upper and lower passages as well as railings; when the latrine is full, it should be cleared out."
"If insects are born [there], you should dig a pit and place them there;
if they have not yet been born, place powdered yeast in the latrine pit, and the insects will not arise.
There were some bhikṣus who did not chew tooth-sticks; their mouths smelled foul and their food was not digested.
There were some bhikṣus who, while conversing with a senior elder, found his breath foul.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should chew willow twigs!"
"There are five benefits to chewing *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks):
they aid digestion, eliminate cold and heat disorders, improve the sense of taste regarding saliva, prevent bad breath, and clarify the eyes.
Some bhikṣus went about chewing wood [indiscriminately], whereupon the Buddha said:
"There are five kinds of wood that should not be chewed:
lacquer trees, poisonous trees, *śyāmā* trees, *mātuluṅga* trees, and *bodhi* trees; all others are permitted for chewing."
At that time, the bhikṣus wished to adorn the place for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to adorn it until the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā* day.
During the night, they recited the Dharma-sūtras and chanted gāthās, but they did not know who should perform these duties.
The Buddha said,
"One who is capable should be appointed.
However, the bhikṣus declined on the pretext of minor illnesses and were unwilling to preach the Dharma or chant the sūtras.
The Buddha said:
"One should not decline to preach the sutras or chant the gāthās on account of a minor illness.
When various evil beasts came into a dwelling place, the Buddha said:
"Listen for the sound of drums, wooden clappers, loud shouts, and the lighting of fires.
When venomous insects entered a dwelling place, the Buddha said:
"They should be taken up and discarded far away."
The bhikṣus grasped them with their hands, and their hands were stung.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to hold them with an object and carry them away in a jar.
At a certain residence, they did not close the doors and lost their robes and bowls.
The Buddha said:
"You should make a lock and key such that others do not know how to open it.
Śāriputra suffered from wind-disorder (vāta), and King Prasenajit said to him:
"One should fumigate the nose with a dried frog.
[The monks] did not dare to use it.
The Buddha said:
“Listen and take heed.
A bhikṣu wished to dye his robes, and the Buddha said:
“I allow you to use roots, stalks, flowers, leaves, and bark for dyeing.”
There was a bhikṣu who wished to dye his kṣauma cloth;
the Buddha said, "I allow you to use the śiśapa tree, the khadira tree, and the walnut tree for dyeing."
The bhikṣus then dyed their robes a pure black. The Buddha said, "One should not make robes of pure black.
Nanda possessed the thirty-two marks; although he did not equal the Buddha, when the bhikṣus saw him from afar, they took him for the World-Honored One and would always rise for him.
Nanda felt ashamed and did not know what to do;
he reported this to the Buddha, who said,
"I permit Nanda to make his robes with characteristics different from those of the Buddha's robes."

There were some bhikṣus who, having undertaken the twelve dhūta practices of an araṇyaka, did not relinquish them, yet they dwelt among people, accepted invitations, and even accepted dwellings and other such things.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Each and every one of these is a *duṣkṛta* offense!
I allow [monks] to stay near a village, even as far as one *krośa*."
"If you cannot do so, you must all abandon it.
There were some bhikṣus who made offerings to spirits and deities; the Buddha said:
"You should not do so; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
"One must not construct a stūpa for spirits or for the teachers of non-Buddhist paths; it is the same in these cases.
There were some bhikṣus who, having constructed a stūpa for spirits, the spirits then took up residence therein.
Later, when they were destroyed, the spirits became angry.
The Buddha said:
"Once something has been made, its destruction is not permitted; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
There were some bhikṣus who defecated or urinated inside shrines dedicated to spirits, or circumambulated them counter-clockwise before departing, which provoked the anger of those spirits.
The Buddha said:
"You should not do so; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
"If the road goes to the left, you may follow it.
Some bhikṣus carved wood into the shapes of male and female figures, birds, and beasts;
they also made various kinds of toys and gave them to laypeople's children.
The Buddha said:
"One should neither perform nor give [these things]; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
There was a bhikṣu who sang and danced himself and taught others to sing and dance.
"One makes music oneself and teaches others to make music.
The Buddha said:
"This should not be done; one who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."

The *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, Fascicle 26, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kasmīra in collaboration with Zhu Daosheng and others during the Song dynasty. Section Four: The Dharma of the Four Modes of Deportment; Part Five of the Division on Deportment. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, there was a brahmin renunciant who was excessively fastidious about cleanliness; he loathed his own excrement and urine, and while using sharp toilet grass, he cut and wounded his flesh, causing blood to soil his robes and the bedding of the Sangha.
The bhikṣus rebuked him in various ways, saying:
"Since you yourself loathe even the sight of excrement and urine, how can you possibly attend to the illnesses of the bhikṣus?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Using toilet grass is not permitted.
At that time, some bhikṣus went to the latrine naked; the laypeople criticized and reviled them, saying:
"These bhikṣus look exactly like the Nirgranthas!"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not go to the latrine naked!
To go to the latrine naked is an *āpatti* of *dukkaṭa*."
There was a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who lived far from a latrine; when he had an urgent need for defecation, he could not wait until he reached it.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If you truly cannot endure it, I allow you to look in the four directions; provided there is no one about, you may go."

There was a monk who had already entered the latrine first. Later, another monk entered the latrine without maintaining mindfulness; he did not snap his fingers nor cough, but went straight in and bumped against him.
The first monk felt ashamed and resentful, while the second monk apologized for his regret.
Furthermore, there was a case where the entering monk snapped his fingers, yet the monk already inside the latrine made no sound, so the newcomer entered nonetheless and caused resentment.
They both reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not defecate with a distracted mind!
To defecate with a distracted mind is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
I now establish for the bhikṣus the initial rules of training regarding the use of the latrine and so forth; herein, a bhikṣu should train throughout his entire life.
If he does not so train, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

"When a bhikṣu goes to the latrine, he should maintain single-minded attention and look ahead, behind, and to his left and right. Upon reaching the front of the latrine, he should cough and snap his fingers to alert those inside—whether human or non-human—and the occupant of the latrine should likewise snap their fingers and cough."

Once you have entered the latrine, you should again look behind, before, to the left, and to the right, and look up into the space between the rafters to see if there are snakes, vipers, or venomous insects.
You should not thrust your robe against the two sides of the door; rather, you should fold it up neatly.
Settle yourself with a single mind; do not cause it to move forward or backward so as to soil the upper part of the latrine.

If there is already filth present, or if you have soiled it yourself, you must attend to the matter: it must be washed if it needs washing, wiped if it needs wiping, and cleared of weeds and impurities if they need removing. Only after doing so should you depart.
Lower your robe slowly and protect it so that it does not become defiled.
When going to the place for urination or the place for washing after defecating or urinating, you should act in this same manner.
"When using water, you should first examine whether there are insects in the water or not."
One must not use excessive water, yet it must suffice for the task at hand.
When scooping water with a vessel, one should do so with extreme care and gentleness;
one must not allow the vessels to strike one another, thereby causing them to break or be damaged.
If the water is exhausted, one should take more until it is full.
If there is an urgent matter, one must certainly take enough for a single person to use, covering the opening with one's hand before departing.

There were some bhikṣus who sat in meditation, slept, dyed and sewed robes, received the scriptures, or practiced walking meditation near the latrines, thereby obstructing other bhikṣus from using them.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"One should not do so!
There were some bhikṣus whose dwelling places were so narrow that they could not avoid the latrines.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If the dwelling is narrow and small, I allow you to cover it with clothing or other items so that they do not obstruct one another.
There were some bhikṣus who chewed tooth-sticks while on the latrine; the other bhikṣus despised them for this, and it also obstructed others from using the latrine.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "One should not do so!
There were some bhikṣus who chewed tooth-sticks beside the latrines; the Buddha said:
"This should not be done either!
There were some bhikṣus who, having finished chewing their tooth-sticks, stuck them on the hooks on the walls of the latrines, thereby damaging the robes of other bhikṣus or injuring their flesh.
The Buddha said, "You should not do so!
When the bhikṣus had finished chewing their tooth-sticks, they placed them at the base of the trees; the tree spirits became resentful and angry.
The Buddha said,
"You should not do so! There were some bhikṣus who, having finished defecating, had no object with which to wipe themselves clean, and thus they soiled their bodies and robes.
The Buddha said,
"I allow the use of toilet grass.
The bhikṣus then used bamboo splinters and reed fragments, which wounded and damaged their flesh.
The Buddha said:
"One should not use articles made from communal property as toilet grass; rather, one should shave off the sharp edges.
With the exception of lacquer trees, all other types of wood are permitted for use."
The bhikṣus made the toilet grass too long, or too short, or too coarse, or too fine.
The Buddha said:
"It should be made to be of medium length."
When the bhikṣus had finished using the toilet grass, they threw it into the toilet hole.
The Buddha said:
"You should not do so!"
The bhikṣus scattered the toilet grass on the ground in a disorderly manner. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to use a vessel to hold it.
When it is full, whoever sees it should remove it and place it in a pit, or instruct that it be burned with fire."
The bhikṣus washed after defecating or urinating and their hands became soiled.
The Buddha said,
"I allow you to wash them thoroughly using ash, earth, or cow dung."
After the bhikṣus had finished washing away their excrement and urine, they scrubbed the walls with their hands, thereby damaging them.
The Buddha said:
"One should not scrub the walls; one should scrub and wash them with bricks or stones."
The bhikṣus used ash, soil, and cow dung on the ground, making it filthy.
The Buddha said:
"They should be contained in vessels."
There were some bhikṣus who made tooth-sticks too long. The Buddha said:
"You should not do so! The maximum length permitted is one span (vitasti)."
There was a bhikṣu who, while chewing a short tooth-stick, saw the Buddha and, out of reverence, swallowed it. Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he was kept free from harm.
The Buddha said:
"One should not do so!"
"It should be at its shortest as long as five fingers; it should also not be too coarse or too fine.
The bhikṣus did not stay in one place while chewing the tooth-sticks, but defiled the ground everywhere.
The Buddha said, "You should not do so!

There was a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who stayed in one place and chewed tooth-sticks; because the road was distant, it hindered his alms-round and caused him to lose the offerings received by the Saṃgha.
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus dwelling in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka) are permitted to chew tooth-sticks with a single-minded focus.
There were some bhikṣus who chewed tooth-sticks while standing at the edge of a well.
The Buddha said, "You should not do so!
There were some bhikṣus who, having finished using their tooth-sticks, did not rinse them; insects ate them and died.
The Buddha said:
"You should not do so! After you have finished using it, wash it thoroughly before discarding it."
There were some bhikṣus who lacked tooth-sticks. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to cut away the portion already used and keep the remainder for further use.
A certain bhikṣu kept his tooth-sticks in a leather bag for holding sandals; the sandals' filth defiled them.
The Buddha said,
"You should use other materials for holding [the tooth-sticks].

There were some bhikṣus who chewed tooth-sticks in the heated bathhouse, the lecture hall, the dining hall, or at the place where food was prepared, as well as in the presence of their upādhyāyas, ācāryas, and senior monks (sthaviras).
The Buddha said, "You should not do so!
There were some bhikṣus who were ill; when their upādhyāyas, ācāryas, or senior elders came to attend to them, they did not dare to chew tooth-sticks in their presence.
The Buddha said,
"It is permitted when one is ill.
When the bhikṣus chewed tooth-sticks in the presence of laypeople, the laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, are only diligent in cleaning their teeth.
The Buddha said, “You should not do so!”
The bhikṣus then did not dare to chew tooth-sticks in the presence of any laypeople. The Buddha said:
"This should not be so! One should not chew [tooth-sticks] in the presence of noble laypeople."
There were some bhikṣus who chewed tooth-sticks in front of non-Buddhists; they too were rebuked as above.
The Buddha said:
"One should not do so either!"
The bhikṣus then did not dare to chew tooth-sticks in the presence of any of the non-Buddhists, whereupon they said again:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, show us respect; they do not dare to chew tooth-sticks in our presence."
The Buddha said:
"You should not do so! If one is capable of causing benefit or harm to the Buddha-dharma, one should not chew [betel] in front of them."
The Buddha said, "I have established for the bhikṣus the initial rules of training regarding the use of the latrine and so forth; these should be observed for as long as life lasts.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went on almsround who did not maintain mindfulness before him. Having entered another's house, he failed to remember the way out and emerged from a different location, where he saw a woman inside the room lying on her back, naked.
Having seen this, he was terrified and fled away in great haste.
When the master of the house returned and saw that the bhikṣu had fled in terror, he thought to himself:
"There must certainly be some trouble or offense within my house!"
He immediately looked inside the house and saw his wife lying on her back, naked; thinking that she had already consorted with the bhikṣu, he hurriedly pursued him, saying:
"Wait a moment!"
"You have performed such and such deeds in my house.
The bhikṣu replied, "Do not speak such words!"
"I am a bhikṣu; according to our dharma, I do not commit such evil.
The man did not believe him, beat him nearly to death, seized his robes and bowl, and then released him.
Once that bhikṣu had returned to the monastic quarters, he related the matter in detail to the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reprimanded him in various ways, saying:
"How is it that you do not maintain mindfulness before you when entering another's home, such that you do not remember the way out?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Now, for the sake of bhikṣus who beg for alms, I establish these rules for beginners, which should be practiced for as long as one lives;
if you do not practice them, it is a duṣkṛta offense!
A bhikṣu who begs for alms should rise early with a single-minded focus, descend from his bed, put on his leather sandals, take up his inner robe, and shake it out to remove the dust.
The waistband is also treated in this manner.

Having put on the lower robe in a neat and orderly fashion, measure one span upward from below the heels; fold the left side over the top, make two folds on each side, and make two folds at the back, where the cord should be drawn through and tied.
One should take up the leather sandals for traveling slowly and must not put them on incorrectly.
One should single-mindedly take up the saṃghāṭī robe and the alms bowl.
When washing the bowl, one should kneel cross-legged; one must not stand.
If washing an iron bowl, it is permitted to hold it one foot above the ground;
a *soma* bowl, four finger-widths above the ground;
and a clay bowl, between these two.
Once washed, one should not place it in a dangerous location, nor should one place it where objects might fall upon it;
one must not leave it unwiped, but should instead set it out in the sun to dry.
One should place drinking water in the shade and wash-water for the bowl in the sun.
When departing, one should maintain single-minded concentration.
If it is necessary to close the door, one should place the bowl between one's feet and then close it; the bolt and key should be concealed so that no one sees them.

Not far from the village, on a level and even piece of ground where there was fine, soft grass, he placed his bowl upon it, shook out his saṃghāṭī and his inner and outer robes, and put them on neatly and properly.

Holding his robe with his left hand and carrying his alms-bowl in his right, he should walk with his head slightly bowed, looking ahead, properly observing the characteristics of the streets and alleys, and skillfully discerning the features of others' gates and doorways.
Upon reaching the gate-chamber, one should snap one's fingers, cough, or knock to make a sound, so that those within—whether human or non-human—may know of one’s arrival.
Once inside the gate, one should deliberate upon where it is appropriate to stand. If someone says, "Venerable sir, please come in! [one should enter].
"Then, one should enter with a single-minded focus.
If someone offers food, one should not accept it while standing over the food;
if a woman offers food, one should not converse with her, should not gaze intently at her, and should not observe signs of quality or defect in the food."
If one household provides enough, that is well;
if not, go to other households until you have enough and then stop.

Having received the food, exit the village and move away from people. You should set down the bowl on the ground, remove your saṃghāṭī robe, shake it to remove dust, and if it is soiled with mud, wipe it clean. Then fold it back up and place it over your shoulder.
Returning to his dwelling, he opened the door and entered, placing his robe and bowl in their usual positions. He shook out his leather sandals and wiped them clean;
then, with a single-minded focus, he washed his feet, dried them thoroughly, and put on his sandals before proceeding toward his room.
Having opened the door and entered, he should place his robes and bowl in their proper places.
If he wishes to apply oil to his feet, he is permitted to apply it only to the soles.
He should sweep the dining area clean, spread out a sitting mat, fetch pure water, and prepare a towel for wiping hands and feet.
If there are already raw or cooked vegetables, fermented grain vinegar, salt, or sauces in the residence, one should receive them in advance and store them in one place.
One should wash and prepare the vessels for surplus food; when measuring the food and finding that there is a surplus, one should first reduce the portion and place it therein.
If one sees an elder returning after carrying food, one should rise to welcome him, take his robe and bowl and place them in the elder's usual spot, and say:
"Your robe and bowl are here!"
To remove their leather sandals, those with soil on them should place them outside the door.
When the time arrives, the *kīṭaka* (wooden gong) is struck, or an announcement is made for the assembly to sit.

Once they have assembled and are seated, [the server] first distributes the vessels containing abundant food; if there is a surplus, one should reduce it and place it therein, and if there is a deficiency, one should take from elsewhere until it is sufficient.
Thereafter, the vegetable sauce is served.
If a bhikṣu arrives later while the meal is being eaten, one should offer him water; or, if water is offered, he may take food from the vessel containing the remaining food.
If he does not accept the water, it is understood that he has already finished eating.

When the assembly has finished eating, one should collect the sitting mats, sweep the ground, remove the refuse and discard it far away, wash clean the vessels that held the surplus food, cover them and place them back in their original positions, and then lift up the water jar.

First, one should go to the quarters of the Upādhyāya and Ācārya and perform whatever duties are required; thereafter, returning to one’s own room, one should engage in recitation, seated meditation, or walking meditation, using a pure mind to eliminate all hindrances and entanglements.
Furthermore, the Upādhyāya and Ācārya must not detain their disciples for trivial matters.

If the preceptor or the ācārya is about to preach the Dharma to the fourfold assembly, the disciple should sweep the place of preaching, spread out the sitting mats, prepare the water jar, and provide a towel for wiping hands and feet.
If there is non-timely beverage (*vikālabhojana*), it should be strained clean and placed in one spot.
When the preaching of the Dharma is finished, one should return and put away the sitting mats and other belongings.
If the *upādhyāya* or *ācārya* requires to bathe, one should prepare the bathing requisites.
If cold water is required, take cold water;
if warm water is required, provide warm water.
Once the teacher has entered the bathhouse, one should announce:
"Do you need to enter? If it is necessary, then enter;
if you do enter, you should remain behind [the teacher].
When the teacher goes out, one should assist him;
if he needs to return to his room but cannot go, one should carry him on one's back or lift him up with one's robe.
If he requires non-time [unseasonal] drinks, one should provide them.
If one is to call for a certain bhikṣu, one should call for him.
If a lamp is required, one should light it if there is no lamp.
When serving a drink, one should announce:
"Drink this; it has already been thoroughly strained.
At night, one should ask the teacher:
"Must I stay here overnight?"
If he says it is needed, then stay;
if he says it is not needed, you should return to your room and practice the path as described above.
At dawn, you should go to inquire after his well-being.
"Did you sleep peacefully?
One should seek for him food before and after [the meal], as well as rice-gruel and *pāyasa*.
If there is any among the Sangha, one should request a portion for him.
If there is a place where [the teacher] is invited next, one should also request a portion for him.
If the teacher wishes to enter a village, one should ask him what he requires and provide him with either light or heavy robes.
If the teacher says:
"If you follow me," one should indeed follow. Upon arriving at another's house,
if one is unable to enter the gate, one should not harbor resentment.
If one enters the gate and does not obtain a seat, one should not feel resentment; rather, one should stand behind the teacher.
If a donor offers food, one should accept it; if one does not obtain any, one should likewise not feel resentment.
If the teacher has leftover food and gives some to one to eat, one should likewise not feel resentment.
If one is preaching the Dharma in the home of a layperson, one should not speak in a confused or disorderly manner;
if the teacher utters vulgar or unskillful words, one should cause him to become aware of them.
When the teacher returns, one should follow him back as one would when walking on the path above.
This is the initial training rule for forest-dwelling bhikṣus regarding alms-gathering, which they should observe for as long as they live.

At that time, many bhikṣus were observing the summer retreat at a single residence; once the retreat had been formally entered, there was no one to assist them in preparing the morning meal, the afternoon meal, or the rice-gruel and *tambula*.
During the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), the bhikṣus were extremely short of food; once the *pravāraṇā* ceremony was concluded, they departed.
After they had left, the resident bhikṣus spoke to the lay devotees (*upāsaka*), saying:
"You should give rise to a heart of joy and celebration! Such and such excellent bhikṣus have resided here for the retreat!"
The laypeople said: "If that is so!
We have not given it well."
"You all act as my companions; why have such and such virtuous bhikṣus come here and not informed me?
I have always invited them from afar, yet I could never manage to receive them;
but now that they have come of their own accord, I am unable to provide for them!"
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went to another residence and said to the resident bhikṣus:
"Open our room doors and spread out bedding for us!
They then settled there.
One of the six groups of bhikṣus entered first; failing to maintain mindfulness before him, he was bitten and killed by a snake falling from above.
The other bhikṣus wept and were filled with distress.
The elder bhikṣus went quickly to question him, and he answered according to the facts.
The elder bhikṣus rebuked him, saying:
"How could you enter an empty room without maintaining mindfulness before you?"
The bhikṣus reported the foregoing matter in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I shall now establish for visiting and resident bhikṣus the rules for beginners, which should be studied for as long as one lives;
if one does not study them, it is a duṣkṛta offense."

If resident bhikṣus hear that visiting elder bhikṣus are traveling through the countryside and will soon arrive here, they should repair the dwellings, shake out the mats and bedding, air the bedding utensils, sweep the interior of the rooms, level the ground in front of the rooms, set aside pure water in one place, and prepare towels for wiping hands and feet.
If one hears that [a guest] has arrived, one should go out to meet them and have a junior monk take their robes and bowl.

Once they have entered, one should prepare a seat for them, provide water for washing the feet, wash their feet, and offer a towel for wiping the hands and feet as well as a cloth for the leather sandals.
If a visiting senior monk has many robes and a large retinue, one should provide him with two rooms.
One should then ask:
"What kind of undergarments do you have?"
"According to whether they are of superior, middling, or inferior status, provide them with appropriate robes and bedding.
If a visiting bhikṣu is ill, he should be given a room near the latrine.
If he requires bathing, provide him with the necessary bathing implements."
If they require non-timely beverages, these should also be provided.
One should spend the entire night gathering for them and preaching the Dharma.
At dawn, one should prepare for them the morning meal, the afternoon meal, as well as rice gruel and *tambula*.
Please remain for the summer retreat (*varṣā*) and exhort all people to provide offerings.
When those visiting bhikṣus wish to enter the monastery, if they have previously tucked up their robes, they should lower them.
If one has previously tucked up the waistband, one should not do so again.
If one has previously placed the robe over the head, one should lower it onto the shoulders.
Having removed the leather sandals, shake them out and wipe them clean; then, wrap them in leaves of grass and carry them inside.
Having entered, he should sit in one place and rest for a short while.
He should ask the resident bhikṣus:
"Which is the room of the senior elder?"
Once you know where he is, you should go to pay him homage, inquire after his well-being, and converse with him.
If it is early in the day, you should pay homage to the stūpa.
Having paid homage to the stūpa, you should then pay homage to the various elders in order.
Then, having washed one's hands and feet, one should ask:
"In this residence, who is the person assigned to distribute the bedding for the Saṃgha?"
Having understood this, he went to inquire:
"I am so many years old; do I have a share of a dwelling?
If the other says there is, he then says:
"Give it to me. If he gives it, one should further ask:
"Has anyone previously lived in this room?"
If you say there are none, you should go before the door of the room and first throw a tile or stone into the room to listen for any sound.
If there is a sound, you should not enter;

if there is no sound, you should open the door and stand aside from it. If nothing comes out, only then should you enter, wait a moment until your eyes are clear, and inspect the room thoroughly. You should press down on the bed with a staff and look under the bed at the ground to see if there are any poisonous insects.
Gradually open the window.
If it is early in the day, one should take out the bedding, shake it out, and sun it.
If there was no bedding previously, one should go to the monk who distributes bedding and request some.
If one obtains a bedding to take, one should further ask:
"What is feared in that room during the first watch of the night?
What is feared during the middle watch and the last watch?"
If they say, "I fear forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka) during the first watch of the night," one should ask:
"What plan should I make?
If one answers:
"One should protect oneself in this manner."
One should partake of it.
It should be done likewise during the middle watch and the last watch of the night.
Furthermore, one should ask:
"Is there food in this room?
"At what time do they prepare the meal in this village—early or late?
"In which street did the Saṃgha perform the *śikṣādattaka-karman* for the family?"
"In which alley did the Saṃgha perform the *pātra-āvartana* (bowl-turning) ritual against him?
In which alley is there a vicious dog?
In which alley are there prostitutes, elderly maidens, and widows?"
"In this place, where is the place for the poṣadha?
When is the poṣadha held?
Where is the place for drinking congee?"
"What place is a place for eating?
If there is any monastic business therein, all should go quickly and must not linger.
This is the initial training rule for visiting and resident bhikṣus, which should be observed for as long as one lives.

The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. At that time, many lay devotees invited the Saṃgha for a meal. Among the bhikṣus, some were putting on their robes and about to go for the meal; some had already returned and were taking off their robes; some were carrying their bowls and about to go; some had already returned and were washing their bowls; some had just left the monastery; some had already returned and were just entering; some had just finished eating; and some were just about to eat.
The laypeople criticized them, saying:
"Even other outsiders know to accept invitations together and eat at the same time;
yet these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, act contrary to any sense of discipline!"
"We do not know who has already eaten and who has not yet eaten.
When the elder bhikṣus heard these various reproaches, they reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Now, for the sake of the elder bhikṣus, I establish these preliminary rules for eating which should be studied for as long as one lives;
if one does not study them, it is a duṣkṛta offense!
If a layperson invites the Saṃgha, the bhikṣu who regularly enters and leaves that layperson's home should inform the elder on their behalf."
The Elder should instruct all the bhikṣus, saying:
"Now we shall accept the invitation of the donor so-and-so.
You must all assemble together and maintain proper dignified conduct.
He also dispatched the host’s attendants to escort the bhikṣus, instructing them in advance to inform [the assembly] of their arrival.
If it was early in the day and the meal had not yet been prepared, and the *upādhyāya* (senior elder) needed to go elsewhere, he was permitted to take one bhikṣu with him;
however, they must return promptly and may not delay until the time for the assembly has passed.

Upon entering the door of a house where they are invited, they should all maintain mindfulness directed toward the present, knowing their respective seats and leaving space for those who have not yet arrived.
If there is a corded bed that lacks cords, one should cover it with a robe; if a bhikṣu does not know this and sits down, he may overturn it, exposing his body and feeling shame.
The Buddha said, "When you wish to sit, first press down with your hand, and then sit.
There were some bhikṣus who sat on rope beds that had been spread out; they sat so forcefully that the beds tore and broke.
The Buddha said:
"One should first lift the mat and spread it wide, and only then sit.
When a donor offers water, one should ask:
“Is there a water-receptacle?
If there is one, one should not let the water fall upon the ground;
if there is none, one should not let the water collect in one place until it turns to mud.
If one obtains roots, stalks, leaves, or fruits but does not know how to eat them, one should wait for those around to eat first, and only then consume them.
There was a bhikṣu who began eating before the food had been distributed to all; a layperson criticized him, saying:
"These bhikṣus do not wait for their turn; they eat as soon as they get food, worse than small children!"
The Buddha said:
"It should not be so! One must obtain them in equal portions; only then may you eat."
In some places where the Saṃgha was large, the Elder did not know when the food had been distributed equally.
The Buddha said:
"One should loudly announce the *saṃghabhadra*."
When the bhikṣus had finished eating, they departed in silence.
The laypeople criticized them, saying:
"When other non-Buddhist practitioners have finished eating the food of others, they all depart after reciting blessings."
The śramaṇa Śākyaputra remained silent and said nothing; the donor did not know whether he was pleased or not.
The Buddha said, "The elder should depart after having offered a blessing."
The bhikṣus departed without waiting for the elders.
The Buddha said:
"I allow eight persons, including the elders, to wait for one another; the rest may proceed as they please."
In a certain monastery, Śāriputra was the senior-most elder and Rāhula was the junior-most.
When the host who had invited them served the meal, he gave the ghee-soup to the senior-most elder, the oil-soup to the next elder, and the *takra*-soup to the junior-most.
After his meal, Rāhula went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
The Buddha asked Rāhula, “What did you eat today?”
Rāhula then replied with a verse:
“Those who eat oil possess strength; those who eat ghee possess a fine complexion.
If one eats a gruel of dried dregs, one has neither strength, let alone a fine complexion!”
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Today we have eaten *zékū* soup.
After the meal, Śāriputra went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha asked Śāriputra:
"What did you eat today? He replied:
"He ate his meal with ghee soup.
The Buddha rebuked him, saying,
"Your eating today was improper!"
"How is it that the senior bhikṣus eat ghee, the middle-ranking bhikṣus eat oil, and the junior bhikṣus eat *ze-ku* (a type of medicinal paste)?
Śāriputra remained silent and did not answer; he then went to a secluded place and vomited up all the food.
The Buddha said:
"From now on, when you receive an invitation, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should say to the host:
'Give everything; give equally.'"

"If a donor brings food, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should instruct the junior monks (navaka bhikṣu) to sweep the dining area, spread out seats, fetch pure water, and bring out the vessel for leftover food."
Whatever is required must all be prepared and provided.
When the time arrives, one should announce it, or strike the *gandī* bell, to cause everyone to assemble together for the meal.
If the host is slow in preparing the food, one should urge them to hasten so that the meal does not miss its proper time.
This is the initial rule for a senior elder regarding the time of eating, which should be observed for as long as one lives.
At that time, there was a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who was indolent; he did not take water for drinking, nor water for washing his hands and feet, nor water for use by the latrine.
At that time, a large group of forest-dwelling bandits went to seek drinking water, and [the monk] replied, "There is none.
They further requested water for washing their hands and feet, as well as water from near the latrine, and he replied:
“There is none either.
He then said to the bhikṣus, “You śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, always possess three kinds of water; for what reason do you have none now?”
He replied, "I did not take it; therefore, there is none.
The thief spoke again:
"Now, simply give me water; I will not come again!
His answer was also as before.
He asked once more:
"Why is there no water? He replied,
"Because people were lazy, they did not store water."
The bandits then seized his robes and bowl, beat him nearly to death, and departed.
Furthermore, there was a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who could not distinguish the stars; some bandits stayed the night with him and said to the bhikṣu, "We shall sleep for a short while;
when dawn approaches, please tell us."
After the bandits had slept for a short while, they asked the bhikṣu whether it was early or late.
The bhikṣu said,
"It is still early!"
Thus he asked three times; though the night had already turned to dawn, he still said it was early.
When the pursuers of the thief arrived and seized him to take him away, the thief spoke with anger:
“If a bhikṣu had told me the time, I would not have slept until dawn.
Now that he has been caught by this [creature], he is indeed a bhikṣu!
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha in full detail, and the Buddha said:
"Now, for bhikṣus dwelling in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka), I establish these rules for beginners, which should be studied for as long as life lasts;
if one does not study them, it is a duṣkṛta offense!

A bhikṣu dwelling in a forest hermitage should be well-acquainted with the characteristics of the four directions, should be well-versed in appropriate timing, should be able to distinguish the constellations and know the early or late seasons, should keep track of the days of the month and the half-months, and should also record the years, months, and days."
For what benefit should one know the characteristics of the four directions?
It is so that, by knowing the direction from which an enemy approaches, one may avoid them.
For what benefit should one skillfully understand the appropriate timing and circumstances?
When bandits approach, one should reflect thus:
"Is it appropriate to flee and hide?
Or is it appropriate to rise and welcome them?"
"Is it appropriate to preach the Dharma for them,
or is it appropriate to make offerings?
Having understood what is suitable for their capacities, one should act accordingly.
For what benefit should one skillfully know the lunar mansions?

One should know the appearance of the stars in the first watch of the night, the appearance of the stars in the middle watch of the night, and the appearance of the stars in the last watch of the night; thereby one may know for oneself whether it is now time for sleep or now time for practicing the Path.
Furthermore, if bandits should question one, one will be able to tell them the time of day.
If one is captured by bandits and released upon being taken away, one may discern the path for returning by observing the stars.
For what benefit should one properly know the number of days in a month and a half-month?
It is so that, knowing the day of the *poṣadha* has arrived, one may go into the village to seek confession and perform the pure *poṣadha*.
For what benefit should one skillfully know the number of years, months, and days?
If it is the spring season, one should know how many days have passed so that one may enter the summer retreat (*varṣā*);
and during the retreat, one should know how many days have elapsed.
When the time for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony arrives, one should go into the village to seek confession and perform the *pravāraṇā* in a state of purity.

If it is a bhikṣu dwelling in the forest (*āraṇyaka*), he should prepare a place for washing his feet beneath a tree on level ground, arrange the items for washing, keep water for washing, and sit in his regular seated position.
If someone comes, one should greet them with joy.
If a thief asks for water, one should remove one's leather sandals, wash one's hands clean, and hold up the water to give it to him;
if he asks whether the water is cold or warm, one should answer him as appropriate.
If a lay follower (*upāsaka*) asks for water, one should act in the same manner.
If an outsider comes to ask for water, and they are capable of either harming or benefiting the Buddha-dharma, one should also act as described above;
if they are incapable of doing so, one should simply put on leather sandals, take up the water with both hands, and give it to them, ensuring that they do not say:
"Bhikṣus show me respect.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who returned from begging for alms in a village; he did not cover the bowl, and an owl’s urine fell into it. The bhikṣu ate it without realizing it and subsequently contracted the disease of consumption (yakṣman).

Furthermore, there was another bhikṣu who also returned from begging for alms in a village; he had not covered the bowl with his hand when a *kruñca* bird flew over the bowl carrying a snake, dropped the snake, and it fell into the bowl.
Although the bhikṣu removed the superior rice, he died after eating the inferior rice.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If you wish to eat within the village, you are permitted to stay and eat.
If you wish to carry [the food] back, you should cover the bowl.
There were some elderly and sick bhikṣus who, having gone for alms, returned carrying their bowls with their hands trembling.
The Buddha said,
"I allow you to make a netted bag to hold your bowl and hang it from your armpit.
Some bhikṣus hung their bowls under their arms, and sweat flowed out and soiled them.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to wrap it in a hand-towel and take it back.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had returned from begging for alms; while in a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka), he was pursued by bandits, and he thought to himself:
"If this bhikṣu does not give me even a single morsel of food, I shall kill him!
Having arrived at his dwelling, he saw the thief coming from afar and invited him to eat.
After the bandits had eaten, they said:
"How extraordinary! You have now attained great merit;
you have given us our lives and further granted us yours."
He then recounted his previous reflections.
That bhikṣu reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu carries food to a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka) and someone comes there, he should give them the food."
If no one comes, he should wait a short while;
if after waiting for a long time no one has come, the bhikṣu who is hungry may first eat half;
if still no one has come, he may eat another half.
"Finally, one should leave behind a single morsel.

There were some forest-dwelling (*āraṇyaka*) bhikṣus who, having finished their meal, ate everything until nothing remained; when bandits came and begged for food from these bhikṣus, they had no food to give them.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit bhikṣus dwelling in forest hermitages to store food.
If food is difficult to obtain, bhikṣus from the village should provide it."
"If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things permissible), you are permitted to carry it back yourself; place it as you wish on either pure or impure ground.
Some bhikṣus carried food back to their *āraṇyaka* (forest) dwellings themselves and placed it on impure ground. When thieves did not come to beg for it, they did not know what to do.
The Buddha said:
"One should give them to a laborer, a garden keeper, or a śrāmaṇera.
"If a bhikṣu dwelling in the forest requires jars, basins, or other utensils, the bhikṣus of the village should provide them."
"If bedding and seating are required, these should also be provided.
On the path traveled, there may be trees or grass that obstruct the bhikṣu’s progress or hook and tear his robes.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to weave grass into a garment and wear it outside the path, or to cover it with some other material.
I also permit you to tie it back onto the branches of a tree."
When binding together grasses and wood, the branches broke and the leaves fell.
The Buddha said,
"If it was not intentional, there is no offense."
There was a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who came out in the early morning; dew had moistened his robes and ruined their color.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to wear them high [on the shoulders], and I also allow you to shake off the dew with a staff."
"When approaching a village, you should return to the monastery, put on your robes according to the Dharma, and place your staff and alms-bowl in one spot; when returning, take them back with you.
There was a forest-dwelling (*āraṇyaka*) bhikṣu who required earth to make mud.
The Buddha said:
"If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person), it is permitted to take earth from a crumbling bank;
if there is no earth from a crumbling bank, it is permitted to sprinkle water on the ground, crush grass and spread it upon it, trample it to form mud, and then take it for use."
There was a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who, when departing, did not lift up the monastic rope-beds, wooden beds, or bedding; consequently, they rotted or were burned by fire.
The Buddha said:
"One should gather them and place them in one location, lock the door, hide the door-latch in a place sheltered from the rain, mark it, and then depart."
"If other bhikṣus go there, you should tell them where it is hidden.

At that time, the bhikṣus were making robes without stretching the cloth; they cut it as soon as they measured it, so that the robes were sometimes too long, sometimes too short, and sometimes crooked, and thus could not be completed.
They sought more material, but could not obtain any.
Furthermore, there were some bhikṣus who always wore only a single robe, wearing it both while staying in their dwellings and when entering villages.
There were also some bhikṣus who used their three robes to wrap fruits, gourds, grass, wood, leaves, and cow dung.

There were some bhikṣus who used their alms bowls to sweep away refuse, to hold leftover food, to hold beverages taken after midday, or to hold incense and medicine; furthermore, they would leave them out without washing them, place them in the sun, set them on the ground, or leave them in dangerous places.
The bhikṣus all reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I now establish for the bhikṣus the initial training rules regarding robes and bowls, which should be practiced for as long as life lasts;
if one does not practice them, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
"If a bhikṣu obtains new cloth, he should first wash it, spread it out to measure it, and then cut it. Having cut it, he should sew it;
having sewn it, he should dye it and hang it up to dry, turning it over."
Once dyed, it should be spread upon the ground; if one wishes to hang it, loops should be attached at the top and bottom.
As for the *saṃghāṭī*, it should be kept according to the rules for the *saṃghāṭī* and must not be used to wrap other items.
The same applies to the *uttarāsaṅga*, the *antarvāsaka*, and all other robes that are to be worn; they should be cherished and protected as carefully as one's own thin skin.
One should hold the alms bowl according to the rules for the bowl; one must not treat it as described above, but guard it carefully as one would one's own eyes.
*Pañcavargika-vinaya*, Fascicle 27 and Fascicle 28, by the Mahīśāsaka school.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Song Dynasty, together with Zhu Daosheng and others. Part Five:
The Fifth Section on Prohibiting the Poṣadha. Regarding the Prohibition of the Poṣadha: The Buddha was staying at the banks of the Gaṅgā River in the kingdom of Campā.

At that time, on the fifteenth day of the observance (poṣadha), the World-Honored One sat in the open air surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus; he gazed upon the entire community of monks and remained there in silence.
When the first watch of the night had passed, Ānanda rose from his seat, went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The first watch has already passed, and the assembly has been seated for a long time.”
"I pray that you will recite the precepts for the bhikṣus!
The World-Honored One remained silent, and Ānanda returned to his seat.
When midnight had passed, he again made this request, and the Buddha likewise remained silent.
During the latter part of the night, he spoke again, saying:
"The dawn is about to appear, and the assembly has been seated for a long time.
We pray that you will recite the precepts for the bhikṣus!"
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"If the assembly is not pure, the Tathāgata does not recite the precepts for them.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"Who in this assembly is impure, such that the World-Honored One speaks these words?
He then observed everywhere and saw a certain bhikṣu sitting near the Buddha who was not a bhikṣu yet claimed to be a bhikṣu;
he was not a śramaṇa yet claimed to be a śramaṇa.
Not practicing the holy life, they claim to practice the holy life;
having accomplished evil dharmas, they conceal their offenses and do not abandon their wrong views.
He immediately rose from his seat, went before them, and said:
"The Tathāgata has already seen you!
Depart, be gone, and do not remain here!
Having said this, he took him by the arm, led him outside the gate, and returned to sit in his original place.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"How strange, Maudgalyāyana!
This is unprecedented!"
"This foolish person does not recognize his own transgression, yet causes others to pull him by the arm and lead him out.
Thereupon, Ānanda rose again from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“The assembly is already pure.
Please recite the precepts for the bhikṣus!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"From this day forward, you yourselves shall recite the precepts together; I shall no longer be able to preach them for the bhikṣus.
Why is this? If the assembly is not pure and the Tathāgata preaches for it, the head of that person who has violated the precepts shall split into seven pieces."
He further addressed Ānanda:
"The great ocean possesses eight marvelous qualities, because of which the asuras delight in dwelling within it.
What are these eight?"
The great ocean gradually deepens;
its tides do not exceed their limits;
and it does not harbor corpses overnight.
As the hundred rivers converge, they no longer bear their individual names;
as the myriad streams all return to them, there is neither increase nor decrease.
They produce various treasures such as true pearls, maṇi-jewels, coral, lapis lazuli, white jade, gold, silver, and crystal.
Beings of great bodies all dwell within it;
they share the same salty taste.
This is the eighth.
This True Dharma of mine is likewise thus, possessing eight unprecedented qualities in which all the bhikṣus together take delight.
What are these eight?
They are: gradual regulation, gradual instruction, and gradual training.
My disciples never dare to transgress the precepts I have established;
should they commit an offense, they are inevitably expelled and not permitted to remain overnight.
Those from various backgrounds who leave the household life all abandon their original surnames and style themselves as Śākyaputrīya śramaṇas.
Sons and daughters of good family, those who have left the household life mostly attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder, yet there is neither increase nor decrease;
there are various treasures of the Dharma, namely the four foundations of mindfulness, up to the eightfold noble path and all other factors conducive to enlightenment;
and there are great beings—arhats, those progressing toward arhatship, up to stream-enterers and those progressing toward stream-entry—who dwell within the True Dharma.
"If there are those who enter, they share the same flavor of liberation.
This constitutes the eight [factors].
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus committed an offense but did not repent, yet they performed the *poṣadha*; other bhikṣus also emulated them.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This should not be done; one who commits such an offense incurs a duṣkṛta.
Even so, the bhikṣus continued to commit offenses and did not repent during the poṣadha ceremony. The Buddha said:
"One should abide in the *poṣadha*.

There were some bhikṣus who abided either before the *poṣadha* had been performed, or after it had already been completed; all such cases of abiding in the *poṣadha* are as explained in the section on abiding in the *pravāraṇā*.

6. The Rules for Parivāsa (Separate Residence). In the sixth section of the fifth division of the *Pañcavargika-vinaya*, concerning the rules for parivāsa: At that time, bhikṣus who were undergoing parivāsa ordained śrāmaṇeras, conferred full ordination upon them, acted as their preceptors (*upādhyāya*), and kept them as śrāmaṇeras.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do so! Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu undergoing parivāsa who accepted the veneration of another virtuous bhikṣu and ordered him to carry his robes, bowl, and leather sandals.
The Buddha said,

"You should not do so! Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu undergoing parivāsa who, seeing a bhikṣu acting in accordance with the Dharma approach, hid himself away, fearing that his own status as one under parivāsa would be known.
The Buddha said,
"You should not do so! Furthermore,
there was another bhikṣu living in separate residence who invited the Saṃgha for a meal, but then returned to eat in his own private quarters.
The Buddha said:
"You should not do so! You should receive the food while standing below the great bhikṣus."
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu undergoing parivāsa who walked in front of a bhikṣu who was acting in accordance with the Dharma.
The Buddha said: "This should not be done!"
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu undergoing parivāsa who wished to go to the house of a layperson together with a bhikṣu who was practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
The Buddha said: "You should not do so!"
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus undergoing parivāsa who either committed the original offense again or committed other secondary offenses.
The Buddha said:
"This should not be done!"
