Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu living in parivāsa who did not put on his robe before a bhikṣu who was acting in accordance with the Dharma.
The Buddha said: "You should not do so!"
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu living apart who constantly wore his three robes while working, so that they became stained with mud.
The Buddha said:
"You should not do this!"
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus undergoing separate residence who sat on the same bed as bhikṣus who were living in accordance with the Dharma, or they sat upon fine beds themselves.
The Buddha said: "This should not be done!"

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu living in parivāsa who walked in meditation alongside a bhikṣu who was practicing in accordance with the Dharma, or occupied a superior place for walking in meditation.
The Buddha said: "This should not be done!"
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu undergoing parivāsa who accepted the Sangha’s appointment to recite the precepts and chant the sūtras.
The Buddha said: "This should not be done!"

Furthermore, there were bhikṣus living in seclusion who performed various formal acts (karmas), namely: the act of censure (tarjanīya-karman), the act of banishment (pravāsanīya-karman), the act of dependence (niśraya-karman), the act of accusation (pratisāraṇīya-karman), and the act of subordination (pratisamharaṇīya-karman).
The Buddha said,
"You should not do so! Furthermore,
there was a bhikṣu living in separation who conversed with a bhikṣu who was acting in accordance with the Dharma.
The Buddha said,
"You should not do so! Furthermore,
there was another bhikṣu living in separate residence who wished to preach the Dharma to the fourfold assembly.
The Buddha said,
"It should not be so! Furthermore,
there was a bhikṣu undergoing parivāsa who did not remember the number of days, months, half-months, or years he had spent in parivāsa.
The Buddha said, "You should know this.

Furthermore, there were bhikṣus living apart who, in the presence of bhikṣus acting in accordance with the Dharma, wore their robes tucked up at the back, placed their hands on their hips, wore leather sandals, covered their heads, or draped their robes over both shoulders; they either sat or lay down [in such a manner].
The Buddha said,
"None of these should be done!
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu undergoing parivāsa who did not comply with the rules for a bhikṣu undergoing parivāsa.
The Buddha said:
"You should not do so! Furthermore, there were bhikṣus living in isolation who did not inform incoming visiting bhikṣus, nor did they inform departing bhikṣus.
The Buddha said,
"One should announce it.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu undergoing separate residence who announced it to the Saṃgha every day.
The Buddha said:
"One should announce it at the time of the poṣadha;
if one is performing mānatva, one should announce it every day."
Furthermore, there was another bhikṣu undergoing parivāsa who wished to travel far away and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"He should complete the relinquishment [of his status] and then depart."
One should perform the relinquishment in this manner,
saying to a single monk who is acting in accordance with the Dharma:
"Venerable Sir, please listen!..."
"I now renounce the practice of separate residence; I shall practice it again later.
Thus he should say three times.
If he does not renounce it and departs, then upon seeing a bhikṣu on the road, he must immediately declare his separate residence.
As various monks undergoing *parivāsa* (probation) were on the road, they spoke at length about their probation. Seeing them, some laypeople said:
"What offense has this monk committed that he must repent?"
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not speak at length on the road; one should simply say:
'Venerable sir!'"
"I, bhikṣu so-and-so, am practicing the *parivāsa* (probation) dharma; [I have already spent] so many days, with so many days remaining.
Venerable Sir, please bear this in mind!
If that bhikṣu abandons the *parivāsa* and goes to another place, he should request the Saṃgha there to undergo the *parivāsa* once again.
That Sangha should grant him the practice of *parivāsa*;
if they do not grant it, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Furthermore, there is a monk undergoing *parivāsa* who, having received the *parivāsa* discipline, goes to dwell in a place where no other monks reside, and during that period of *parivāsa*, commits another grave offense.
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu undergoing parivāsa must not dwell alone in one place, nor should he commit further evil offenses; those who do so commit a duṣkṛta offense!
Furthermore, there were certain bhikṣus undergoing parivāsa who, after receiving their probationary status, went to dwell in the company of bhikṣus who did not act according to the Dharma.
The Buddha said:
"It should not be so! If there is even a single bhikṣu who abides in accordance with the Dharma, he may stay; one who violates this incurs a duṣkṛta offense."
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu undergoing parivāsa who lived in the same room as a bhikṣu who was acting in accordance with the Dharma.
The Buddha said: "This should not be done!"
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu undergoing parivāsa who bathed in the same bathing hall as a bhikṣu who was living in accordance with the Dharma.
The Buddha said: "This should not be done!"

It is permitted to carry firewood into the bathhouse, wash the bathhouse, and sweep it; one should prepare ash and earth, as well as bathing powder, and arrange beds and seats. One may remove the robes and leather sandals of the bhikṣus and massage their bodies with oil, performing these services for those who accept them.
Furthermore, there were bhikṣus undergoing the parivāsa probation who bathed together in a communal bathhouse.
The Buddha said:
"I permit it."
"However, you must provide him with his necessities in due order.
A bhikṣu living in isolation has three things that are most inferior:
he walks at the very rear of the great bhikṣus; he is given the lowest bedding and seats; and he is given the lowest dwelling.
A *parivāsa* (probationary) bhikṣu returns to his original status in three circumstances:
when the Saṃgha receives offerings, at the time of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, and during the distribution of alms bowls.
There are eight matters by which a *parivāsa* bhikṣu loses the status of probation:
Not informing others when departing for another location;
not informing an incoming bhikṣu;
and not informing when departing oneself.
He departs without informing others;
he dwells alone in a secluded place;
and while in a state of separate residence, he commits another grave offense.
Sleeping in the same room as a bhikṣu who is in accordance with the Dharma;
failing to leave and stay apart when traveling a long distance, and failing to inform a bhikṣu encountered on the road.
One also loses the *mānatva* penance through these eight matters:
Except for when one dwells alone in a single place, if one performs [the rite] among a sangha of fewer than twenty members, the remaining seven [cases] are as described above.
7. The Method of Subduing (Vinaya-dharma). The Fifth Division of the Pañcavargika-vinaya, Part Seven: The Method of Subduing. At that time, the Elder Upāli asked the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!”
"Does Sudinna, son of Kalandaka, commit a pārājika offense?
The Buddha said,
"In all initial instances, there is no offense."
He asked again,
"Is a bhikṣu staying in an araṇya (forest hermitage) guilty of an offense?
The Buddha said:
"An offense! There was a bhikṣu who, while suffering from insanity, committed sexual intercourse. Once his madness had subsided, he became doubtful and questioned the Buddha about it.
The Buddha said:
"Those who are insane do not commit offenses; the same applies to those with distracted minds or minds impaired by illness.
Sūndarananda, the son of the Vṛjis, did not relinquish his precepts yet engaged in sexual intercourse; he later raised this question with the Buddha.

The Buddha said: "It is an offense! There was a bhikṣu who engaged in sexual intercourse with a woman possessing both sexual organs; there was a bhikṣu who engaged in sexual intercourse with a woman whose two orifices were joined; there was a bhikṣu who engaged in sexual intercourse with a eunuch; there was a bhikṣu who engaged in sexual intercourse with a man; and there was a bhikṣu who engaged in sexual intercourse with a young child. Later, they all gave rise to doubts and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"All have committed an offense!
There was a bhikṣu who engaged in sexual intercourse with a young girl, and the girl died immediately.
Suspecting that he had committed two *pārājika* offenses, he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If one commits sexual misconduct, it is a *pārājika*; if the woman dies, it is a *sthūlātyaya*."
There was a bhikṣu who made a wooden female figure and engaged in sexual intercourse with it; later, he questioned the Buddha about this matter.
The Buddha said:
"If semen is emitted, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
"If it does not emerge, it is a sthūlātyaya.
The same applies to a clay or painted image of a woman.
There was a bhikṣu who engaged in sexual intercourse with an elephant; later, he questioned the Buddha about this matter.
The Buddha said:
"It is an offense! It is the same for all animals."
At that time, there was a foolish female lay follower (upāsikā) in Rājagṛha who held this view:
"Giving through sexual desire is the foremost gift.
She then invited the bhikṣus to receive it from her, and the bhikṣus said:
"Sisters! You should not do so;
this was prohibited by the Buddha!
The women spoke again:
"Lying down while walking constitutes an offense; standing while walking is not called an offense.
The bhikṣu then followed those words.
Later, he questioned the Buddha about this, and the Buddha said:
"If he commits [the offense] while seated and walking, with the courtesan on his back;
or if the woman moves while the bhikṣu does not move— it is likewise."
At that time, there was in Śrāvastī a foolish and faithful female lay disciple named Sukhāvatī who held this view:
"To give the gift of sexual desire is the foremost gift."
She then invited the bhikṣus to accept it as an offering, but the bhikṣus said:
"Sister, you should not do this;
this is what the Buddha has prohibited!"
The woman spoke again:
"Three places constitute an offense: the cleft of the thighs, the navel, and all other parts do not count as an offense.
The bhikṣu then followed her words.
Later, he questioned the Buddha about this matter, and the Buddha said:
"If the impurity is emitted, it is all *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is not emitted, it is all *sthūlātyaya*."
At that time, in a forest hermitage, there was a bhikṣu who was sleeping soundly in the open air. A woman saw him and committed sexual intercourse upon him.
When the bhikṣu woke up, he saw his body defiled by impurity and saw the woman depart from between his legs; filled with doubt, he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha asked,
"Do you experience pleasure? He replied:
"I did not accept it.
The Buddha said, "There is no offense; [you are blameless]."
"To fall into a deep sleep in the open air is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The same applies to sleeping with the door of one's room open.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who fell into a deep sleep in the open air, and a woman committed sexual intercourse upon him.
The bhikṣu woke up; when he emerged [from his state], he experienced pleasure and developed a doubt, so he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"An offense!"
In Vaiśālī, there was an arhat bhikṣu who had contracted a wind disorder (*vāta-roga*), causing his entire body to become rigid and stiff.
His attendant placed him on the open ground and entered the village to beg for food.
A woman came and engaged in sexual intercourse with him.
After the intercourse was completed, the bhikṣu’s male organ remained as stiff and erect as before. The women said:
"This is a heroic man.
She then smeared him with fragrant ointments, bound his hair with a floral garland, prostrated before him, and departed.
When the nurse returned, she saw that his body was defiled by impurities and thought to herself:
"This bhikṣu does not cultivate the holy life and has violated the pure precepts; I shall remain for his uposatha!
He further thought:
"The World-Honored One does not permit staying for the uposatha of a sick bhikṣu; I shall wait until he recovers."
After he had recovered from his illness, [the other monk] remained for the *poṣadha* ceremony and said to him:
"While you were previously ill, you violated the precepts! He replied:
"At that time, I was ill; my body was stiff and rigid, and I was unable to control myself, yet this does not constitute a violation of the precepts.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "This bhikṣu has already attained arhatship.
Due to a wind-disorder (vāta-roga), his body was stiff and rigid, and he was unable to control himself."
"Because he did not experience pleasure, there was no offense.
However, the monk who tended to the patient committed a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) by leaving him in the open air.
At that time, there was a monk who inserted his male organ into another monk’s mouth; subsequently, both gave rise to doubt and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If the one who inflicts the wound acts in jest, it is a sthūlātyaya;
if the recipient does not act in jest, it is a pārājika."
If the recipient acts with intent to joke, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if the one who pricks does not act with intent to joke, it is a *pārājika*.
If both act with intent to joke, both commit a *sthūlātyaya*.
"If both engage in lewd behavior, both commit a *pārājika* offense.
At that time, some bhikṣus bathed together with laypeople in a bathhouse; the laypeople observed their physical forms and described them to other women.
Furthermore, when their bodies touched, they gave rise to minds of defiled attachment, which ultimately led them to return to secular life or become followers of external paths.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "You should not do so!"
"If one bathes together with a layperson in a bathing house, it is a thullaccaya.
There was a mahallaka bhikkhu who, in a dream, engaged in sexual intercourse with his former wife.
Having awakened, he left his cell and cried out in a loud voice:
"I am no śramaṇa! I am no son of the Śākya!
When the bhikṣus asked him the reason, he replied:
"I committed sexual misconduct with my former wife.
He asked again,
"Where is your former wife now?"
He replied, "In my native village. He asked again:
"Did he come here? Or did you go to him? He replied:
"He does not come, and I do not go.
He asked again,
"How then can one engage in sexual intercourse?"
He replied, "I engaged in sexual intercourse while dreaming.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense;
however, if one falls asleep without maintaining mindfulness before oneself, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
There was a bhikṣu who stood while urinating when a dog came and bit his male organ; he became doubtful and questioned the Buddha about it.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense [for the act itself], but to urinate while standing constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
A bhikṣu should not keep such animals in his dwelling; one who does so commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!"
There was a bhikṣu whose male organ was long; with a lustful mind, he inserted it into his own anus. He developed doubts and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"An offense!"
There was a bhikṣu whose body was weak; he inserted his male organ into his own mouth, and it was likewise with another.
There was also a bhikṣu practicing dhyāna when a māra-maiden came before him.
A bhikṣu, seeing her, gave rise to a mind of lustful attachment; unconsciously, he rose and seized her.
The woman then fled, and the bhikṣu also ran after her.
When she reached a dead horse and disappeared into it, the bhikṣu committed sexual intercourse upon the horse. He immediately felt remorse and spoke of it to the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow the Saṃgha to perform the formal procedure of a *pārajika* through a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) against that bhikṣu.

That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha, remove his leather sandals, bare his right shoulder, prostrate at the feet of the Saṃgha, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and make the following formal announcement:
"I, bhikṣu [name], having committed an act of sexual misconduct, immediately felt remorse and did not conceal it; I now request from the Saṃgha the *pārājika* karmavācanā.
May the Saṃgha grant me the *pārājika* karmavācanā!"
Thus he requests three times.
A monk who knows the Dharma should then announce:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having committed an act of sexual misconduct, immediately felt remorse and did not conceal it; he has requested from the Saṃgha the *pārājika* karma.
The Saṃgha now grants him the *pārājika* karma.
"If it is the time for the Sangha and the Sangha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus:
'Venerable Sangha, please listen!'"
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed sexual misconduct... [and so forth] ...the Saṃgha now performs the *pārājika* karmavācanā against him.
Those elders who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
Thus it was said a second and a third time:
"The Saṃgha has completed the *pārājika* karma against the bhikṣu so-and-so;
the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent."
"Maintain this matter thus.
The Buddha said:
"That bhikṣu must not, for as long as he lives, give food to a mahābhikṣu; rather, he shall receive it from a *kappiyakāraka* (pure person) himself."
"If, during the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, or when performing various *karmas*, those who come do so well;
if they do not come, there is no offense for either party.
A bhikṣu who had engaged in sexual intercourse with a celestial maiden (*devī*), a nāga maiden (*nāgī*), or an asura maiden (*asurī*) raised a doubt and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "In all cases, they have committed an offense.
There was a bhikṣu who went to another's place where food was being prepared and took a bowl of soup; he developed doubts and questioned the Buddha about it.
The Buddha asked,
"With what intention did you take it? He replied:
"By means of a thieving mind.
The Buddha said:
"If the value is five coins, one commits a pārājika offense; [if less than that, it is a sthūlātyaya offense]."
"If it is less than five coins, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
It is the same when one enters another's garden and takes a fruit or a vegetable with the intent to steal.
There was a bhikṣu who had been stripped by bandits; having recovered his robes and belongings through a dispute, he developed doubts and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "There is no offense.

Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who was robbed by bandits; once he had fallen into their hands or they had already taken [the goods], he later pursued them and recovered [the property]. He then gave rise to doubt and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha asked,
"Have you relinquished the robe in your mind? He replied:
“Not yet relinquished.
The Buddha said:
“If it has not been relinquished, there is no offense; once it has been relinquished, one commits an offense.”
There was a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who saw a wild boar running toward him with an arrow in its body. They spoke among themselves, saying, "Do not mention that you have seen it!
A hunter soon arrived and questioned the bhikṣu:
"Did you see the pig I shot?
He replied, "Where is there a pig?"
"Whose pig is this? There is no pig.
Later, he had this thought:
“I said there were no pigs; will I not incur the offense of concealing a pig?
He raised this doubt with the Buddha, and the Buddha said, “There is no offense.”
"If there are such causes and conditions for using other words to interrupt a question, there is no offense in any case.
There was a forest-dwelling bhikṣu who saw a hunter catch a live deer, tie it up, and depart; out of compassion, the bhikṣu released it, and having developed a doubt, he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
However, one should not release [the creature] by means of another's property; whoever does so commits a *duṣkṛta*."
"Releasing all other sentient beings with a mind of compassion is also like this.

There was a bhikṣu who saw a *kruñca* bird carrying meat in its beak as it flew away; he playfully pursued it to make it release the meat, and having given rise to a doubt, he questioned the Buddha about it.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
However, one should not employ skillful means to cause another to lose [their property] in a way that is of no benefit; to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense!"
A certain bhikṣu saw another’s ox walking along the road; with the intent to steal, he drove it away, but immediately regretted it and abandoned it. A doubt arose in him, so he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense [of pārājika], but you have committed a sthūlātyaya offense.”
There was a bhikṣu who saw an object being swept away by the current; with the intent to steal, he seized it. Doubt arose within him, so he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If its value is five coins, it is a pārājika offense."
A certain bhikṣu, not far from the Jeta Grove, saw another man plowing a field and said to him, "This is the saṃgha’s field; do not plow it!
The plowman thought to himself:
"The bhikṣus have great power; if they were to bring a lawsuit against me, I might lose my property.
Thinking thus, he stopped and did not plow.
The bhikṣu returned to Jetavana and asked the bhikṣus:
"Whose field is this? The bhikṣus replied,
"It is the field of a certain lay devotee."
He then raised a doubt with the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
However, if one employs a stratagem in an unbeneficial manner with the intent to cause loss, it is all *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing)."
At that time, the group of seventeen youths had been plundered by bandits, and their parents were weeping in distress.
When Pilindavatsa saw them while on his alms round, he asked them the reason for their grief, and they answered him in full detail.

Pilindavatsa immediately entered meditative concentration and observed that the thieves had taken them to an island in the Āciravatī River; he then used his supernormal powers to retrieve them and placed each one upon the upper story of their respective family’s house, saying to their parents, "Do not weep any longer!"
"Your children have now all returned home and are playing on the upper story of the multi-storied pavilion.
Later, he questioned the Buddha about this, and the Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
"One incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
There was a bhikṣu who, for the sake of gain and offerings, falsely increased his own age to make it greater than that of others.
Later, he questioned the Buddha about this matter, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense [for the well itself], but lying through falsehood incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
In a certain residence, a monk shared a well with a layperson (*avadātavasana*).
The layperson took water with a thieving mind (*steyacitta*), and the monk likewise, with a thieving mind, had this thought:
"Why have I alone not taken much? Before he had taken anything, he gave rise to this doubt and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If one takes another's water with a value exceeding five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika* offense.

There was a bhikṣu who stole another's robe at that place when its value was five *kārsāpaṇas*, but brought it here to sell for less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, thinking he had not committed a *pārājika* offense.
Śāriputra raised a doubt with the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If its value at the place of origin was exactly five māsakas, it is a pārājika offense.
If it was not worth five māsakas at that place, but was sold for five māsakas upon arriving here, it is a sthūlātyaya offense."
There was a bhikṣu who stole another’s Buddhist sūtras, claiming they were the Buddha’s own words and thus not an offense.
Later, he questioned the Buddha about this matter. The Buddha said:
“If one calculates the value of the paper, brush, and labor of transcription, and it amounts to five coins, it constitutes an offense.”
At that time, there was a householder in Kauśāmbī who had seen the Dharma and attained the fruit; he constantly provided for the bhikṣus.
The householder and his sister each had a son, and the two of them together regularly made offerings to the Elder Ācāra Bhikṣu.
When the elder was about to pass away, he showed the location of his treasure store to the bhikṣu Acchuta and said to him:
"After my death, if one of those two sons has faith and joy in the Buddha-dharma and is always without attachment toward the bhikṣus, you may show this treasury to him."
Having spoken thus, he drew his last breath.
Later, the bhikṣu Acchuta examined the two sons; seeing that the son was upright while the nephew was faithful and devoted, he spoke to the nephew and enabled him to obtain the treasure store.
Upon hearing this, the son immediately went to where Ānanda was and asked,
"To whom should my father’s inherited property belong? He replied:
"It should belong to my son.
He then said to Ānanda,
"My father’s treasure-store has been given to me by the bhikṣu Acchola, the son of my paternal aunt."
Ānanda immediately went and said to Acchola, "You are not a śramaṇa; you are not a son of the Śākya! Acchola replied:
"I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya clan!
We may rely upon the sūtras and vinaya ourselves to collectively adjudicate this matter. Ānanda said:
"This matter is already settled; why is it necessary to rely on the Sūtras and Vinaya?

At that time, all the elder bhikṣus were followers of Ānanda and assisted him. Consequently, the two groups of Ānanda and Āśvalāyana became separate and no longer lived in harmony; for six years they did not observe the summer retreat together, nor did they perform the *poṣadha* or *pravāraṇā* ceremonies at their respective residences.
The fame of this reached far and wide, penetrating even to the Brahma Heaven.
At that time, Rāhula was traveling through the city of Kapilavastu, where all the women of the Śākya clan came out together to welcome him. They recounted the matter in detail, saying:
"How is it that not long after the World-Honored One entered Nirvāṇa, the Saṃgha has remained in discord for as long as six years?"
"We wish to reconcile them, but we do not know the skillful means. Rāhula said,
"I shall instruct you so that they may be reconciled."
Ānanda soon arrived, and all the infants came to embrace him;
yet when he set them down on the ground, they would inevitably cry.
Ānanda would then invariably ask:
"Why do you not take him? You should answer:
"If the Elder unites with Ācchu, only then shall we take the child!"
"By this expedient means, we may bring about their reconciliation.

Ānanda arrived shortly thereafter; the five hundred Śākya women took their children and went out to meet him, placing them all before Ānanda on the ground, whereupon the children immediately began to cry loudly.
Ānanda said, "Why do you not take him up?
They answered in unison:
“If the Elder reconciles with Aciravata, we shall then take this child back!
Ānanda, moved by these words and pitying the infant, said:
“Sisters, take the child; I shall reconcile with him.”
He then convened the Saṅgha, and Upāli asked Ānanda:
"In how many ways does a bhikṣu take what is not given such that he is no longer a śramaṇa and no longer a son of the Śākya?"
He replied: "There are three kinds:
taking it oneself, instructing another to take it, and sending someone to take it."
He asked Ācūla again:
"Did you take it yourself, or did you instruct someone else to take it, or did you send someone to take it? He replied:
"No," he replied.
He then asked Ānanda again,
"What fault did the bhikṣu Acchola commit?"
Ānanda said: "Acchuda is without fault; it was my own mistake!
Thereupon, Ānanda made a proclamation throughout the Saṃgha:
"This was my fault; Ācāra is without transgression.
He then confessed to Ācāra and reconciled with him.
There was a bhikṣu who was originally a thief, and he said to the other bhikṣus:
“Let us go together to that village to fetch some goods.
The bhikṣus followed his words and went ahead to fetch them.
Later, those bhikṣus gave rise to doubts and questioned the Buddha:
“I have thus instructed another to steal; do I incur a *pārājika* offense?
The Buddha said, “You do not incur [a *pārājika*], but you commit a *sthūlātyaya* offense.”
There was a bhikṣu who took clothing from another’s covered grave, banners atop a grave, clothing from among graves, or items within a shrine—things protected by others.
He became doubtful and questioned the Buddha. The Buddha said:
“If one takes what another has not yet relinquished in mind, and its value is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is all a *pārājika* offense.”
"Even though the objects within a temple have no owner, they are likewise protected by the officials.
There was a bhikṣu who, out of anger toward another, burned that person's house, or burned their fields, grain, and property.
He raised a doubt with the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense of the full category, but he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
It is the same when, out of anger, one destroys the property of another."
A certain bhikṣu found a bag containing a thousand taels of gold inside a rat's burrow; taking it with the intent to steal, he became doubtful and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "It belongs to the rats; you have committed no offense."
"One incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
If one seizes the property of birds or beasts with the intent to steal, it is likewise.
There was a bhikṣu who, at a meal, ate another's portion without permission; the other asked:
"Who will eat my portion?
He replied, "I shall eat it!"
He became angry and, having developed doubts, questioned the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If it was not with the intent to steal, there is no offense. One should not arbitrarily agree to eat another's portion; one who does so commits a *duṣkṛta*."
There was a bhikṣu who engaged in gambling and won articles belonging to others; he developed doubts and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "There is no offense [against the precepts], but you have incurred a duṣkṛta (wrongdoing)."
There were two bhikṣus who, having agreed with one another, exchanged their robes; later, they became angry and slandered each other, claiming that the other had stolen them.
They developed doubts and questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense."
"One must not arbitrarily agree to wear another's robe; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!

At that time, Bhadanta was traveling along a road with some merchants. Upon reaching a customs checkpoint, the merchants borrowed a bag from Bhadanta, secretly placed a highly valuable pearl inside it, and returned it to him; Bhadanta did not notice.
Having passed through the frontier gate, he searched for the pearls in his bag,
and Baddhālaka said, "I did not take your pearls. The merchant said:
"You truly did not take it; I merely borrowed your bag earlier and placed the pearls inside!
He then returned the pearls to him.
The man gave rise to doubts and questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
If you wish to exit the pass and borrow an item from someone, once it has been returned, you should shake it out and inspect it; to do otherwise constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.”
At that time, a disciple of the bhikṣuṇī Caṇḍasumana went to her teacher’s donor’s house and falsely said:
“My teacher is ill and requires a medicinal gruel made with three kinds of herbs.”
Having received it, she ate it herself outside.
Later, the women of the household went to inquire after her,
saying, "Auntie, has your illness improved?"
He replied, "I am not ill at all; why do you ask me?
and then he related everything in detail.
The teacher said to his disciple,
"You have stolen my porridge! He replied:
"I truly did not steal; I took it only with the consent of my preceptor!
He raised this doubt before the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one does not have the intent to steal, there is no offense."
"To intentionally speak falsehood, one incurs the offense of *pāyattika*.
A certain bhikṣu saw that the master’s field was without water; he diverted water belonging to another to irrigate it, and being filled with doubt, he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If it is worth five coins, one commits an offense.
There was a bhikṣu on high ground who threw a robe down to a bhikṣu on low ground; both gave rise to doubt and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If one throws [an object] with the intent to steal, it is a pārājika offense;
if one takes it without the intent to steal, it is a sthūlātyaya offense."
If one throws [the object] without the intent to steal, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one takes it with the intent to steal, it is a *pārājika*.
If both acts are done with the intent to steal, both constitute *pārājika*.
"If both lacked the intent to steal, both are guilty of sthūlātyaya.
There was a bhikṣu who, with the intent to steal, traded for an item belonging to the Saṃgha; he became doubtful and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"A transaction worth five *kārsāpaṇas* constitutes an offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who threw a stone at a snake; it struck a person by mistake and killed him. He gave rise to doubt and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"With what intention did you do this? He replied,
"I intended to throw it to kill the snake."
The Buddha said:
"If a person dies, there is no offense; if one throws a snake [at someone], one commits a *duṣkṛta*.
There was a bhikṣu who killed a macaque; because it resembled a human, he gave rise to doubt and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"To take the life of an animal constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
There was a woman whose husband was away on a journey; having conceived through an illicit liaison, she requested an abortifacient from a bhikṣu whom she regularly supported.
The child died with her, but the mother did not; she gave rise to doubts and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"It is an offense."
If one intends to cause an abortion and the mother dies while the child does not, one commits a sthūlātyaya;
if both die, one commits a pārājika;
if neither dies, one commits a sthūlātyaya.
"Pressing the abdomen to induce an abortion is likewise [a grave offense].
There were certain bhikṣus who did not delight in practicing the holy life (brahmacarya), yet they did not renounce the path; instead, they returned to lowly and base occupations.
At one time, one of them threw himself from a high place to seek death, but he fell upon a person below; that person died, while he himself did not.
He gave rise to a doubt regarding the Buddha, and the Buddha asked,
"With what state of mind did you do this? He replied:
"I wish to fall and die myself.
The Buddha said, "If he dies, there is no offense; [if you die, there is an offense]."
"If one employs means to commit suicide, it is all *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
There were two bhikṣus who previously harbored mutual resentment; later, while traveling together on a road, they struck each other, and one of them subsequently died.
He gave rise to a doubt regarding the Buddha, and the Buddha asked,
"With what state of mind did you do this? He replied:
"An angry mind. The Buddha said: "If there was no intent to kill, there is no offense; [otherwise, there is an offense]."
To become angry with another bhikṣu incurs a pāyattika offense.
From now on, it is not permitted to walk together on a road with one who has been angry with you until you have mutually apologized; anyone who violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense.
There was a bhikṣu who struck and killed a ghost; having developed a doubt, he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "He has committed a sthūlātyaya.
There was another bhikṣu who intended to kill one person but mistakenly killed another; having developed a doubt, he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense [of pārājika], but one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.

At that time, various bhikṣus, for the sake of gain and offerings, praised others in various ways for their accomplishment in morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Yet he secretly used them for his own adornment, which gave rise to doubt regarding the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If one speaks of such things without clarity, as you have done, it constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense."
In Vaiśālī there was a great tree named Nyagrodha, whose shade could cover five hundred chariots.
When the bhikṣuṇī Puṣpā saw it, she said to the other bhikṣuṇīs:
"When I was in the heavens, the flower I wore behind my ear was as large as this tree."
The bhikṣuṇīs, deeming this impossible, rebuked her in various ways:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī claim for herself that she has attained superhuman states?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There truly are such flowers in the heavens; the Bhikṣuṇī Huasè has spoken the truth and has committed no offense.
As for the bhikṣu Piluṭasika, five hundred boils broke out upon his body; the boils were so festering and putrid that they could not be looked upon.
The bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, went to pay their respects; having seen him, she laughed.
The bhikṣuṇīs rebuked her, saying:
"How can you lack a heart of compassion? Seeing a bhikṣu in such a state, you instead laugh at him?"
Puṣpacitrā replied, “In a past life,
this bhikṣu was a great king named Vijaya, and at that time I was his chief consort.”

That king forcibly took five hundred young maidens and ruined their present lives; because of these causes and conditions, for countless hundreds of thousands of millions of years he fell into the great hell, where he was scorched and boiled by bitter poisons, and as a residual retribution, he now suffers from these five hundred boils and sores.
The bhikṣuṇīs, deeming this impossible, rebuked her in various ways:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī claim for herself the attainment of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma)?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"That bhikṣu is indeed so! Puṣpacitra speaks the truth; he has committed no offense.
Then the Elder Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus:
"I saw a lotus flower at Lake Anavatapta, as large as a chariot wheel.
The bhikṣus did not believe him, saying that he was making false claims regarding the attainment of superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*).
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There truly were such flowers; Maudgalyāyana spoke the truth, and there is no offense.
There were other bhikṣus who falsely claimed to have attained superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), speaking as follows:
"I possess the causal conditions of karmic retribution, as well as the divine eye, the divine ear, and the knowledge of others' minds.
Later, he questioned the Buddha about this, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense [of pārājika], but you have incurred a sthūlātyaya offense."
There were certain bhikṣus who falsely claimed to have attained superhuman states, saying:
"I have attained the divine eye, the divine ear, and the knowledge of others' minds; all my outflows are exhausted."
Later, he questioned the Buddha about this, and the Buddha said,
"It is an offense.
There was a brahmin who invited the Sangha for a meal and said:
"Venerable Arhats, please come and sit down to eat.
When they had finished eating,
he said, "Arhats, please depart."
The bhikṣus, having given rise to doubts, questioned the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If a person praises themselves of their own accord, there is no offense in any of these cases.

There were some bhikṣus who, for the sake of gain and offerings, remained composed in their sitting, rising, walking, standing, and speech, desiring to manifest the appearance of one who has attained the Path so that others would know it.
Later, they questioned the Buddha about this, and the Buddha said:
"Such manifestations of these portents all constitute the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
There were some bhikṣus who, as their lives drew to a close and they were destined to fall into hell, saw all the various signs of hell and beheld the henchmen of Yama standing before them.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who was destined for rebirth in heaven; he saw all the celestial palaces, heard the sounds of music, and saw devaputras and apsaras speaking to him from before him.
He told everyone about this, which gave rise to doubts, so they questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "This was a manifestation of an auspicious sign; it was not a falsehood, and there is no offense."

There were certain bhikṣus who originally intended to speak of other matters, but later unintentionally spoke of superhuman states (uttaramanuṣyadharma). They became doubtful and questioned the Buddha about it.
The Buddha said:
"Since this was not their original intention, they do not commit an offense; however, they incur a sthūlātyaya offense."
There were certain bhikṣus who said to laypeople:
"If anyone stays in your room, they will all accomplish such and such dharmas of the Path.
Later, they themselves went to stay there and gave rise to doubts; they questioned the Buddha about this, and the Buddha said:
"Employing such means as these constitutes an offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
There were certain bhikṣus who, having claimed for themselves superhuman attainments (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), intended for humans to hear them but non-humans heard them instead;
or they intended for non-humans to hear them but humans heard them instead."
Furthermore, if one intends for humans and non-humans to hear [the words], yet they do not hear them, all such persons give rise to doubt and question the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"All have committed a sthūlātyaya offense."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana said to the bhikṣus,
"The wife of such-and-such a layman shall give birth to a son.
When she was about to give birth, it was changed to a daughter.
When King Prasenajit was at war with King Ajātaśatru, Maudgalyāyana said,
"King Prasenajit shall be victorious," yet the result was otherwise.
Later, they gathered for battle once more, and again said,
"King Ajātaśatru shall be victorious. Yet once more, it was not so.
The bhikṣus rebuked him, saying:
"How can you falsely claim to have attained superhuman states?
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“As Maudgalyāyana said, one should simply observe what is before and not what is behind!
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who scratched his private parts; impurity was discharged, and he gave rise to a doubt and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha asked,
"With what state of mind did you do this? He replied:
"From beginning to end, there was no intention to leave.
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
"If one intends to emit [semen] and it is emitted, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if one intends to emit it but it is not emitted, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
The same applies to bathing with warm water or warming oneself by a fire, if impurity is emitted."
There was a bhikṣu who, while recollecting an act of sexual desire, emitted impurity; he gave rise to doubt and questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "With what state of mind did you do this?"
He replied, "I recall that while engaging in sexual intercourse, impurity issued forth of its own accord.
The Buddha said:
"No offense; however, to recall having engaged in sexual acts constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
There was a bhikṣu who intentionally used his body to press against his garment to discharge semen, yet he claimed it did not constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
He questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"In such a case, if the monk emits semen, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa;
if he does not emit it, it is a sthūlātyaya."
A certain bhikṣu emitted semen while near the image of a woman; having developed a doubt, he questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "If one emits semen, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa;
if one does not emit it, it is a sthūlātyaya."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who struck a woman’s body with his elbow, and another bhikṣu who pulled a woman with the hook of his alms-bowl.
They developed doubts and questioned the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Both have committed a sthūlātyaya.”
"If one seizes her garment, or pulls at her cord or staff, it is likewise.
There was a bhikṣu who, while a woman was on a bed, in a boat or carriage, or upon a tree, shook her with a lustful mind.
They raised a doubt with the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If monks act in such a manner, they all commit a sthūlātyaya offense.
At that time, there was a woman wearing a blue garment; when a monk saw her, he spoke to her, saying:
"Sister! You have agreed to [the color] blue.
She raised this doubt with the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one utters such evil words based on [another's] physical form, it is the same in all such cases.
At that time, there was a husband and wife who were quarreling and living in discord; a bhikṣu went to reconcile them.
A doubt arose regarding the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If the marital bond has already been dissolved and they reunite, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa;
if it has not been dissolved, there is no offense."
The Mahīśāsaka Vinaya, Volume 28 and Volume 29,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśa during the Song Dynasty.
Translated together with Zhu Daosheng and others.

8. The Fifth Division, Part Eight: The Dharma for Bhikṣuṇīs. At that time, the World-Honored One was returning to Śrāvastī; before reaching the city of Kapilavastu, he stayed beneath a nyagrodha tree.

King Śuddhodana went out to welcome him; seeing from afar that the World-Honored One’s countenance was extraordinary, like a mountain of gold, he stepped forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and spoke this verse:
"When the physiognomists prophesied at your birth, I heard it and paid my first respect;
When the tree bent, I bowed my head; Now that you have attained the Way, I pay these three prostrations."
Having spoken this verse, he withdrew to sit on one side.
The Buddha taught him various sublime Dharmas, until he realized the Dharma and attained the fruit [of the path].
Rising from his seat, he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that you will grant me ordination and the full precepts.
The Buddha then observed him and saw that if the king were to leave the household life, he would have nothing further to attain; thereupon, he said to the king:
"Do not be negligent!
You shall naturally attain this sublime Dharma in due course.
Thereupon, he requested to receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
After he had received the five precepts, the Buddha further expounded various sublime dharmas for him, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him; the king then returned to his residence.
Once the king had entered the palace, he made a proclamation three times in the courtyard:
"Those who wish to go forth in the True Dharma and Vinaya of the Tathāgata are permitted to do so."

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, having heard this proclamation by the king, was immediately surrounded by five hundred Śākya women, preceding and following her. Carrying two new garments, she went to where the Buddha was, prostrated herself at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I have personally woven this robe; I now offer it to you, and pray that you will graciously accept it!
The Buddha said, "You may give it to the Sangha; you shall obtain a great reward!"
He reported this again as before, and the Buddha said:
"You may give it to the Saṃgha; I am included within the number of the Saṃgha.
He reported this again as before, and the Buddha said:
"I shall receive one portion and offer it to the Saṅgha with that one portion.
Having thus received the instruction, she offered it to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
Gopikā then addressed the Buddha again:
“May it please you to allow women to go forth in the Buddha’s True Dharma and receive full ordination!
The Buddha said:
“Stop, stop! Do not speak such words!”
Why is this? Because in the past, none of the Buddhas permitted women to leave the household life.

Yet these women, relying solely upon the Buddha, shaved their heads and donned the saffron robes while remaining at home; through diligent and energetic practice, they attained the fruits of the Path.
"The future Buddhas will also be like this.
I now permit you to take this as the Dharma!
Gautamī made her request three times as before, and the Buddha likewise refused her three times.
Thereupon Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī wept bitterly, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew.
The Buddha, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, was traveling through the human world from Kapilavastu.
Gautamī and five hundred Śākya women shaved their own heads, donned saffron robes, and followed behind him weeping, constantly staying wherever the World-Honored One had stayed overnight.
The Buddha gradually traveled on until he arrived at Śrāvastī and stayed at the Jeta Grove. Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and five hundred Śākya women were weeping at the gate.
When Ānanda went out in the morning and saw them in such a state, he immediately asked the reason for it. They replied:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"The World-Honored One does not permit women to leave the household life and receive full ordination; it is for this reason that we grieve for ourselves!
We pray that you will petition him on our behalf, so that we may fulfill our aspiration!"
Ānanda immediately returned, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, and reported everything in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha stopped Ānanda as previously described.
Ānanda spoke to the Buddha again, saying:
“Not many days after the Buddha was born, his mother passed away.
Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī nursed and raised the World-Honored One until he reached adulthood; how can one fail to repay such great kindness?”
The Buddha said, "I also have great kindness toward Mahāprajāpatī; because she relied upon me, she came to recognize the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and gave rise to reverent faith."

If a person relies upon a spiritual friend and gives rise to faith and reverence for the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, one could not repay that person even by providing them with clothing, food, medicine, and all necessities for the rest of one's life!
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If women go forth from home and receive full ordination, can they attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa path?
The Buddha said:
"I can attain it! Ānanda said:
"If one attains the four paths, World-Honored One!"
"Why do you not permit her to go forth and receive full ordination?
The Buddha said, "I now permit Gautamī to receive the eight rules that must not be transgressed; this shall constitute her going forth and obtaining full ordination."
What are the eight?
A bhikṣuṇī should, every half-month, request from the community of bhikṣus a person to provide instruction;
a bhikṣuṇī should not observe the summer retreat (varṣā) in a place where there are no bhikṣus.
When the bhikṣuṇīs perform the *pravāraṇā*, they should request from the assembly of bhikṣus the three matters regarding offenses seen, heard, or suspected;
a śikṣamāṇā who has completed two years of training in the precepts should receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) within the community of both orders;
a bhikṣuṇī must not revile a bhikṣu, nor may she speak of a bhikṣu’s breaking of the precepts, his breaking of dignified conduct, or his breaking of right view in the homes of laypeople.
A bhikṣuṇī may not accuse a bhikṣu of an offense, whereas a bhikṣu may reprove a bhikṣuṇī.

If a bhikṣuṇī commits a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), she must undergo the *mānatva* penance for half a month within both divisions of the Saṃgha; having completed the half-month *mānatva*, she must seek absolution from twenty monks of each division.
Even if a bhikṣuṇī has been ordained for a hundred years, she must nevertheless pay homage to, rise to greet, and welcome a bhikṣu who has only recently received the precepts.
Ānanda, having received these instructions, immediately went out and said to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
“Listen attentively!
I shall speak what the Buddha has taught.”

Gautamī adjusted her robes once more, prostrated herself from afar at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and listened with a single-minded focus as Ānanda related everything as above. Gautamī said:
“It is just as when young men and women, being pure and clean, take delight in bathing their bodies and putting on new, clean clothes.”

If someone were to bestow upon him garlands of *campaka* flowers, *vārṣika* flowers, *utpala* lotuses, or *atimuktaka* flowers, that person would rejoice and, taking them with both hands, place them upon his head.
"I now receive the World-Honored One’s Dharma teaching upon the crown of my head, and it is likewise so.
He further said to Ānanda:
"I pray that you will enter once more on my behalf to inform the World-Honored One, saying: 'I have received the eight dharmas upon the crown of my head!'"
Among these eight matters, I wish to request one boon: may it please be granted that bhikṣuṇīs pay homage to bhikṣus according to seniority!
How can a bhikṣuṇī who is a hundred years old pay homage to a bhikṣu who has only recently received the precepts?
Ānanda again reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha told Ānanda:
"It is impossible that I would permit bhikṣuṇīs to pay homage to bhikṣus according to their seniority."
Women have five obstacles:
they cannot become Śakra, Lord of Devas; Māra, King of Devas; Brahmā, King of Devas; a Cakravartin, Holy Wheel-Turning King; or the Dharma King of the triple world.
If women had not been permitted to leave the household life and receive full ordination, the Buddha’s True Dharma would have remained in the world for a thousand years;
now that their leaving the household life has been permitted, it shall be diminished by five hundred years.
"It is just as if a household has many women and few men; you should know that such a family will not last long before its decline.
He further addressed Ānanda:

"If women had not gone forth from home to receive full ordination within my Dharma, then after my parinirvāṇa, the upāsakas and upāsikās would have carried the four requisites and followed behind the bhikṣus, saying: 'Venerable sirs, please accept these robes, bowls, bedding, and medicines.'"
"Venerable One!
Out of compassion for me, please accept my offerings.
If he sees him as he is leaving the gate, he should then take him by the arm and say:
"The Venerable One has been kind to me; I beg you to sit for a moment so that I may find peace!
If they encounter one another on the road, they should all loosen their hair, brush the bhikṣu’s feet, and spread it out for him to step upon.
"Now that permission for ordination has been granted, this matter is almost exhausted!
Having heard this, Ānanda wept with grief and resentment, and said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I did not hear of this before, nor did I know this Dharma, when I requested permission for women to go forth and receive full ordination.
Had I known it beforehand, how could I have made three requests?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do not weep any longer!
It is because Māra has obscured your mind that you are acting thus."
"Now, I permit women to go forth and receive full ordination; they must comply with what I have established and must not violate it.
They must not arbitrarily establish rules regarding what I have not established!"
Ānanda then went out and related the Buddha’s teaching in detail to Gautamī.
Gautamī rejoiced and practiced accordingly; she immediately became a renunciant and received full ordination.
She spoke again to Ānanda:
"Regarding these five hundred Śākya women, how should they now receive full ordination?
I pray that you will petition [the Buddha] once more on their behalf!"
Ānanda immediately informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"I permit the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī to act as her preceptor; she shall receive the full ordination through the formal procedure of a fourfold proclamation (jñapti-caturtha-karman) within an assembly of ten bhikṣus."
"One may perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for three people at one time; it must not reach four.
Once the ordination had been received, Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī, together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated herself at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"How should we put on our robes?
The Buddha said,
"In accordance with the rules for bhikṣus."
He asked again,
"What shall we eat? and he replied:
"Listen to the request for alms.
He spoke again:
"What is the *poṣadha*?"
He replied, "I permit the separate *poṣadha*; every half-month, one should request from the community of monks a person to provide instruction.
He further said:
“How does one enter the rains retreat? He replied,
“It is permitted to enter the three-month rains retreat under a roof.”
He asked again,
"How is the *pravāraṇā* performed? He replied:
"Listen to the separate *pravāraṇā*.
Go among the community of monks and request [the confession of] offenses seen, heard, or suspected.
He further addressed them:
"How should the kaṭhina robe be received?
He replied, "It is permitted to receive it for a period of four months by means of a formal motion and a second proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman)."
He asked again,
"How is it that you keep leather? He replied:
“Listen; you may wear leather sandals while traveling.
He further asked:
“How are disputes to be settled?”
The Buddha said, "I allow you to extinguish the four types of disputes by means of the seven methods for settling disputes.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs did not first bestow the two-year training upon their disciples before conferring full ordination; consequently, the disciples were foolish and ignorant, unable to train in the precepts.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do so; one who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
It should be done in this way:"

First, for two years he was instructed not to kill living beings; for two years not to steal; for two years not to engage in sexual misconduct; for two years not to speak falsely; for two years not to drink intoxicants; and for two years not to eat at improper times.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who acted as a matchmaker and committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Not knowing what to do, she reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha, on account of this matter, assembled the two divisions of the Saṃgha and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen as the two assemblies of monks perform the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to grant that bhikṣuṇī a half-month period of *mānatva*.
That bhikṣuṇī should go before the Saṃgha, bare her right shoulder, remove her leather sandals, prostrate at the feet of the two assemblies of monks, and say:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"
I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], having acted as a matchmaker, have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. I now request from the Saṃgha a half-month period of mānatva.
May the Saṃgha grant me a half-month period of mānatva!
Thus he requests three times.
A single bhikṣu should then announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so acted as a matchmaker and has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense; she requests from the Saṃgha a half-month of mānatva.
The Saṃgha now grants her a half-month of mānatva.
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience.
This is the motion. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so acted as a matchmaker, thereby committing a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense; she has requested from the Saṃgha a half-month period of mānatva.
The Saṃgha now grants her a half-month period of mānatva.
"Whichever elders approve, remain silent;
those who do not approve, speak.
Thus it was said three times.
“The Saṃgha has already granted the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so the half-month *mānatva*;
the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.”

Once the Saṃgha has granted her the *mānatva* penance, she should rise at dawn to sweep and sprinkle the various rooms of the bhikṣuṇīs’ residence, plaster and repair the walls and floors, fill all water receptacles, and perform whatever tasks are to be done.
Furthermore, whether visiting bhikṣuṇīs arrive or resident bhikṣuṇīs depart, she must announce these matters to them as well.
Furthermore, she should go to the dwelling place of the bhikṣus accompanied by another bhikṣuṇī; whatever needs to be done there, she should perform it all as described above.
If visiting bhikṣus arrive or if bhikṣus depart, she must also announce these matters.
When the sun is about to set, she should return to the dwelling place of the bhikṣuṇīs.

After they had practiced in this manner for half a month, they sought the *karmavācanā* for the removal of offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*) from among twenty members of each of the two assemblies, according to the rules for *bhikṣus*.
At that time, the *bhikṣuṇīs* did not pay homage to the *bhikṣus*, and as there was no one to instruct them, they remained ignorant and foolish, unable to train in the precepts.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha rebuked them, saying:
"I have previously taught the eight dharmas that must not be transgressed: a bhikṣuṇī of a hundred years' standing must pay homage to a bhikṣu who has only recently received the precepts."
"Why do you not pay homage now?
Having rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I authorize the bhikṣus to pay homage to their elders in the order of seniority."
All bhikṣuṇīs pay homage to all bhikṣus and also pay homage to one another according to seniority;
śikṣamāṇās pay homage to all bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs and also pay homage to one another according to seniority;
śrāmaṇeras do likewise.
"Śrāmaṇerīs should pay homage to all bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇeras, and likewise pay homage to one another according to seniority.

There were bhikṣuṇīs who, while at a higher position, paid homage to bhikṣus at a lower position; some paid homage from behind the bhikṣus, some from the side, some grasped their feet with their hands, and some knelt upon the ground to pay homage.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"None of these should be done!
I allow a bhikṣuṇī to stand neither too close nor too far from a bhikṣu, with palms joined and head bowed, and speak as follows:"
“Homage. At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs had long hair, so the Buddha said:
“You should request a woman to shave it for you.”
If there are no women, it is permitted to have a man do it;
however, he must not be alone, nor must he be allowed to hold her. There must be another bhikṣuṇī companion present to hold her, and only then may he shave her.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs received the sūtras from other bhikṣuṇīs but were unable to memorize them.
Furthermore, there was another bhikṣuṇī who received a single *pātimokkha* from a bhikṣuṇī but could not master it even after many days.
Later, she received [the teachings] from a bhikṣu and immediately attained them.
She reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow bhikṣuṇīs to receive the sūtras from bhikṣus."
If there are coarse or harsh words within a sutra, one is permitted to write it down and transmit it;
if one does not know how to write, one is permitted to transmit it with a screen or partition between them;
if there is no screen or partition, one is permitted to transmit it while facing away from one another.
There were certain bhikṣuṇīs who performed the poṣadha together with the bhikṣus; seeing a bhikṣu commit an offense, they wished to bring it to his attention.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Bhikṣuṇīs must not perform the poṣadha together with the bhikṣus."
"Every half-month, one bhikṣuṇī should request a bhikṣu from the community of bhikṣus to act as her instructor.
The bhikṣus were unwilling to go and request this for them. The Buddha said:
"I allow bhikṣuṇīs to provide offerings [to the bhikṣus], such as alms-bowl bags, water-strainers, waist-bands, fragrant oil, food before the meal, and food after the meal."
Whether the *poṣadha* had not yet been performed and he made the announcement, or whether the *poṣadha* had already been performed and he then made the announcement, the Buddha said:
"It should not be done in that way!
When the monks who have not come are being announced for their confession of purity (*pāriśuddhi*), one should rise from one's seat, stand before the Saṃgha, and announce as follows:"
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The harmonious community of bhikṣuṇīs at [Name] Vihāra prostrates at the feet of the harmonious community of bhikṣus and requests a person to provide instruction."
If the Sangha has already appointed a person to provide instruction, the Elder should reply:
"Receive it from the bhikṣu so-and-so.
If the Sangha has not appointed anyone, but there is someone capable of preaching the Dharma, he should reply:
"Go to such-and-such a bhikṣu and receive [the instruction].
If there is still no one available, one should reply:
"There is no person here to provide the formal instruction, nor is there anyone capable of preaching the Dharma."
"May you all not be negligent!
On the following day, the bhikṣuṇīs should come and ask:
"Has the request for instruction of the bhikṣus been completed, and has it been reported to the Saṃgha?"
This bhikṣu should transmit the words of the elder and speak to them.
There were certain bhikṣuṇīs who observed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony together with the bhikṣus.

When these bhikṣuṇīs wished to go to a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*) to attend the *pravāraṇā* of the bhikṣus, they encountered robbers, water, or fire on the way, facing threats to their lives, threats to their holy life (*brahmacarya*), or threats to their robes and bowls.
Furthermore, they waited upon one another and delayed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:

"A bhikṣuṇī must not perform the *pravāraṇā* together with a bhikṣu; she should perform the *pravāraṇā* separately. She should request from the community of bhikṣus [the confession of] offenses regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected."

At that time, there were no bhikṣus in the village. The bhikṣuṇīs went to the forest hermitage (āraṇyaka) to request [the confession of] offenses regarding what was seen, heard, or suspected; however, either because the road was too distant or because those bhikṣus did not act as mediators, they were ultimately unable to make their request.
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow bhikṣus dwelling in forest hermitages to go to the village for the sake of the bhikṣuṇīs' invitation for criticism (pravāraṇā) and to bring about their reconciliation."

"The bhikṣuṇīs should first assemble the community for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; thereafter, they shall appoint a bhikṣuṇī to go before the community of bhikṣus and request [the confession of] offenses regarding what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
Having arrived, she should bare her right shoulder, remove her leather sandals, and pay homage from afar to the feet of the Saṃgha.
Thereafter, entering among the Saṃgha, she joins her palms, bows her body, and says:
"The harmonious community of the bhikṣuṇīs at [Name] Vihāra pays homage at the feet of the harmonious community of bhikṣus."
"We, the community of bhikṣuṇīs, being in harmony, request the venerable saṃgha to perform the *pravāraṇā* and speak regarding our faults seen, heard, or suspected.
Thus they requested three times.
Then the bhikṣus spoke to the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī:
"You do not have a preceptor; therefore, you have not accomplished the going forth or received full ordination.
He then became doubtful and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"When you received the eight rules that must not be transgressed, you had already gone forth and received full ordination."
There was a bhikṣuṇī who enticed a bhikṣu, saying:
"I am of noble lineage, my deportment is complete, and I possess all the qualities of a woman.
Desiring to serve that bhikṣu, she gave rise to a mind of defiled attachment; no longer finding joy in the Path, he eventually returned to secular life.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī must not seduce or mock a bhikṣu; one who violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."

There were some bhikṣuṇīs who came to the dwelling place of the bhikṣus; some had their chests and ribs exposed, while others had their thighs and calves exposed. When the bhikṣus saw them, they gave rise to minds of defiled attachment and no longer took pleasure in the Path, eventually leading them to return to secular life.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This should not be done! From now on, it is not permitted for bhikṣuṇīs to enter the dwelling place of bhikṣus!"
Since she was not permitted to enter, she received no instruction; being ignorant and lacking knowledge, she was unable to train in the precepts.
She reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣuṇī who acts according to the Dharma permits her entry, you should also summon her."
Since she would not come when called, the Buddha said:
"If she does not come when called, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense!
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs did not speak with the bhikṣus; as there was no one to instruct them, they were ignorant and lacked understanding, unable to train in the precepts.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“This should not be done; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense!
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Uccā repeatedly committed offenses, and the community of bhikṣuṇīs performed the *ajñapti-karman* of "not seeing the offense" against her, whereupon she wept and said:
“I am foolish; the Saṃgha has performed the *ajñāna-āpatti-karman* against me, and I have further committed a grave offense therein!
I pray that the Saṃgha will revoke this *karman* for me!”
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"One should not perform the lifting of the *karmavācanā* for her; rather, one should perform a formal motion and a second *karmavācanā* to appoint a bhikṣuṇī as a companion, so that they may speak together and act together."
A single bhikṣuṇī shall announce:
"May the community of nuns listen!
We now appoint the bhikṣuṇī So-and-so to be a companion to the bhikṣuṇī Uppalavaṇṇā, to converse with her and to dwell together with her."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus as a formal motion.
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen!"
I now appoint the bhikṣuṇī [Name] to accompany the bhikṣuṇī Ucchā as her companion for conversation and shared conduct.
Those of you, venerable ladies, who approve, remain silent;
those who do not approve, speak.
The Sangha has already appointed the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so as a companion for the bhikṣuṇī Ucchā;
the Sangha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.
There was a bhikṣuṇī whose menstrual flow had occurred, staining her feet and robes;
when she entered a village to beg for food, the laypeople saw this and reviled her.
The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣuṇī is menstruating, she is not permitted to enter a village to beg for food.
She is permitted to store provisions, and it is also permitted for her to have a disciple beg on her behalf;
if she has no disciple, she is permitted to wear a menstrual cloth while begging for food."

There were daughters of noble families who had gone forth as nuns but did not wear shawls to cover their shoulders; when laypeople saw their shoulders and arms, they mocked them together, causing all the women to feel shame and embarrassment.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to wear the shoulder-covering robe (saṃkakṣikā)!

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs gave the full ordination (upasampadā) to their disciples who had not completed the two-year period of training in the precepts and whose conduct was not in accord with the rules.
The Buddha said:
"It should not be done so; one who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
From now on, it is permitted to assemble a group of ten only after having obtained the consent of the *upādhyāya* and the *ācārya*."

Upon arriving at the place for receiving the precepts, one should lead the person about to receive them to a location where they are within sight but beyond earshot; there, the preceptor (upādhyāya) should seek out a ritual master (karmavācanācārya) and an instructor (anuvādacārya).
Having obtained [the candidate], the *karmavācanā* master should perform the formal act (*karma*) to instruct the instructor, commanding them to go outside and announce:
"May the noble community of nuns listen!
So-and-so seeks to receive full ordination from So-and-so; So-and-so shall serve as the instructor."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus.
The instructor should first perform this initial rite by asking the upādhyāya:
"Has this person seeking full ordination completed two years of training?
Are their robes and bowl complete?
If they say they are not complete, one should tell them to make them so.
If they say they possess it, one should further ask:
"Is this your own property,
or is it borrowed?"
If he says he is borrowing it, one should tell the owner to relinquish it;
only then should one go to the person who wishes to receive the precepts and say:
"Do not be afraid; in a moment, I shall place you in a high and superior state!"
If he is not already familiar with them, he should slightly open his robes to examine whether there are any obstacles to the method of receiving the precepts.
He should then ask:
"Which of these are your saṃghāṭī, uttarāsaṅga, antarvāsaka, aṃsavastra, and snānaśāṭikā?"
If he does not recognize [the offense], one should speak to him so that he recognizes it.
Next, one should give him the robe and bowl as explained in the section on bhikṣus.
Furthermore, one should say to him:
"Listen, [Name]! Now is the time for speaking the truth. I shall now question you; if something exists, you should say it exists; if it does not exist, you should say it does not exist.
Women have such diseases as these:..."
Do you have any such grave illnesses as leprosy, white leprosy, consumption, insanity, carbuncles, fistulas, or glandular swellings?
Are you not in debt?
Are you not another's wife?
Has your husband given his permission?
Is she not subject to the state?
Is she not a slave?
Is she a human being?
Are you a woman? Are your female organs complete? Are you not a eunuch?
Are you not a barren woman?
Are you not one whose two channels are joined?
Does your menses flow?
Have you not gone out frequently?
Have you completed two years of training in the precepts?
Have you already sought a preceptor?
"Does your father and mother permit it?
Do you wish to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*)?
As I have now asked you, so shall the Sangha ask you later; you should likewise answer them."
The instructor should return and stand before the Saṃgha, declaring:
"I have finished my questioning!
The *karmavācanā* master should then address the Saṃgha, saying:
“Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
So-and-so seeks to receive full ordination from So-and-so; So-and-so has already completed the preliminary inquiries. We now authorize her to be brought forward.
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent and listen.”
“Thus it is declared.
The preceptor should go and bring [the candidate] back, instructing him to prostrate at the feet of the Saṃgha.

Once he has prostrated, he should be led before the *karmavācanā* master and instructed to kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms toward the *karmavācanā* master, and request from the Saṃgha the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The instruction is as follows: "I, [Name], seek full ordination from the preceptor [Name];
I now request the Sangha to grant me full ordination, with [Name] as my preceptor."
"The Saṃgha has rescued me out of compassion!
Thus he requests three times.
The Preceptor then returns to his seat, and the Karmavācanā Master should address the Saṃgha:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from so-and-so;
he requests the Saṃgha for full ordination, with so-and-so as his preceptor."
I now ask about various difficult matters within the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience.
This is the formal announcement.
One should say to him:
"Listen! Now is the time for truthful speech. I shall now question you; if something exists, say that it exists; if it does not exist, say that it does not exist."
...up to "...Do you wish to receive the precepts?"—
all as asked above. Having asked as above, the *karmavācanā* master should further proclaim:
“Venerable Sisters, may the Saṃgha listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from so-and-so;

she has requested the Saṃgha for full ordination, declaring that she is free from all obstacles, has completed two years of training, possesses the five robes and bowl, has already sought out a preceptor, and has received permission from her parents; she desires to receive full ordination.”
The Sangha now confers the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as the preceptor.
If the time is ripe for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent and listen.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
“Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
So-and-so seeks to receive full ordination from So-and-so.
… [and so on] … “The preceptor is So-and-so.”
"Whichever of you, sisters, approves, remain silent;
whoever does not approve, speak.
Thus it was said a second and a third time.
“The Sangha has already conferred the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as the preceptor;
the Sangha consents by remaining silent.
This matter is thus upheld.”
The preceptor and the ācārya should then assemble a community of ten bhikṣuṇīs and lead the candidate for ordination into the midst of the bhikṣu saṃgha.
Standing at a slight distance before the bhikṣu karmavācanā master, with both knees touching the ground, she should request the full ordination.
The *karmavācanā* master should instruct him, saying:

"I, [Name], seeking full ordination from the preceptor [Name], have already received full ordination within a single assembly; I am pure and free from all obstacles; I have completed the two years of training; my robes and bowl are complete; I have sought a preceptor; my parents have given their permission; I have not committed a grave offense; I wish to receive full ordination;
I now request the Sangha to grant me full ordination, with [Name] as my preceptor."
"The Saṃgha has rescued me out of compassion!
Thus he requests three times.
