Having requested three times, the *karmavācanā* master should announce:

"Venerable Sangha, listen! This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from so-and-so. He has already received full ordination within one assembly; he is pure and free from obstacles; he has completed two years of training in the precepts; he has performed what was previously required to be done; his robes and bowl are complete; he has requested a preceptor; his parents have given their permission; he has not committed a grave offense; and he desires to receive full ordination.
He now requests the Sangha for full ordination, with so-and-so as his preceptor."
The Sangha now confers the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as preceptor.
If it is the proper time for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent and listen.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from so-and-so. ...
[and so on] ... “The Saṃgha now grants full ordination to so-and-so, with so-and-so as preceptor.”
"Whichever elders approve, let them remain silent;
those who do not approve, let them speak.
Thus it was said a second and a third time.
“The Sangha has already conferred the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as the preceptor;
the Sangha consents by remaining silent.
This matter is thus upheld.”
Furthermore, one should say:

"Listen, [Name]! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has proclaimed the eight pārājika rules. If a bhikṣuṇī commits any one of these rules, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan."
No one shall engage in sexual misconduct, even to the extent of looking at another man with a mind of lustful attachment.
If a bhikṣuṇī engages in sexual intercourse, even with an animal, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī; she is no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.
"Throughout this life, you must not violate these!
If you can uphold them, you should say: 'I can!'"
“Stealing is forbidden in all cases, even down to a blade of grass.

If a bhikṣuṇī, whether in a village or in an open space, steals another’s guarded property worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more than five *kārsāpaṇas*, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor a daughter of the Śākya clan.”
"In this regard, you must not commit any violation for as long as life lasts!
If you can uphold this, you should say: "I can!"
“Under no circumstances shall one kill any living being, even down to an ant.

If a bhikṣuṇī, whether it be a human or a being resembling a human, should herself take life with her own hand, provide a weapon, instruct another to kill, encourage death, or praise death, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī; she is no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.”
"In this regard, you must not commit any violation for as long as life lasts!
If you can uphold this, you should say: "I can!"
"No one shall speak falsely, even in jest.

If a bhikṣuṇī, though lacking any superhuman qualities herself, claims to possess various dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, meditative attainments, or [the fruits of] the path, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī; she is no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan."
"Within this, you must not commit any violation for as long as life lasts!
If you can uphold this, you should say: "I can!"
“Under no circumstances shall one associate with men.
If a bhikṣuṇī, her mind overcome by lustful desire, touches a man’s body from below the hair to above the knees;

or if a man performs such touching, she must not accept it—whether by pressing, pinching, lifting, lowering, grasping, or pulling—then she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.”
"Throughout this life, you must not commit [these offenses]!
If you can uphold them, you should say: "I can!"
“Under no circumstances may one dwell or converse with a man.

If a bhikṣuṇī, her mind transformed by lustful desire, should receive a man—whether by taking his hand, or taking hold of his robe, or agreeing to travel together, or traveling alone with him, or dwelling alone with him, or conversing alone with him, or sitting alone with him, or by drawing her body close to his—if she commits these eight acts, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor a daughter of the Śākya clan.”
"Throughout this life, you must not commit [these offenses]!
If you can uphold them, you should say: "I can!"
“None shall follow the words of a bhikṣu who acts contrary to the Dharma.
If a bhikṣuṇī knows that a bhikṣu has been formally charged by a harmonious Saṃgha of bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma,
yet she follows that bhikṣu.”
The bhikṣuṇīs said to them:
"Sisters! This bhikṣu has been formally accused by the harmonious Saṃgha of bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma."
"Do not comply with this! If,
despite being admonished in this way, he persists and does not relinquish his position,
he should be admonished a second and a third time.
If, upon the second and third admonitions, she abandons this matter, it is well;
if she does not abandon it, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī and no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, one must not commit an offense!
If one is able to uphold it, they should say: "I am able!
One must not conceal any grave or evil offenses committed by others.
If a bhikṣuṇī knows that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a pārājika offense,
and at a later time— whether that other bhikṣuṇī has left the order, died, gone away, been suspended, or changed her sex— she speaks to the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"I previously knew that this bhikṣuṇī had committed a pārājika offense."
"To not inform the Saṃgha and not speak of it to others is to be neither a bhikṣuṇī nor a daughter of the Śākya clan.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit such an offense!
If you can uphold this, you should say:
"Yes! The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are truly skilled at employing parables to manifest actual facts:
it is just as when the eye of a needle is broken, it can no longer be used for sewing."
It is just as when a person dies, they can never again be reborn with that same body;
it is like the heartwood of a tāla tree that has been cut off, which neither sprouts nor grows;
it is like a stone that has been shattered, which cannot be joined back together again.
"If a bhikṣuṇī violates any one of these eight rules, it is impossible for her to regain the status of a bhikṣuṇī.
Furthermore, you should say to her: "Listen, [Name]!"
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has proclaimed these eight rules that must not be transgressed; you must not transgress them for as long as you live.
A bhikṣuṇī should, every half-month, request from the community of bhikṣus a person to provide instruction;
a bhikṣuṇī should not observe the rains retreat in a place where there are no bhikṣus.
When the bhikṣuṇīs perform the *pravāraṇā*, they should request from the assembly of bhikṣus the three matters regarding offenses seen, heard, or suspected;
a śikṣamāṇā who has completed two years of training in the precepts should receive full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) within the dual assembly of monks and nuns;
a bhikṣuṇī must not revile a bhikṣu, nor may she speak of a bhikṣu’s violation of dignified conduct, violation of the precepts, or violation of right view in the homes of laypeople.
A bhikṣuṇī should not accuse a bhikṣu of an offense; a bhikṣu may reprove a bhikṣuṇī.

If a bhikṣuṇī commits a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), she must undergo the *mānatva* penance for half a month within both assemblies of the Saṃgha. Once the half-month *mānatva* has been completed, she must seek absolution from twenty monks of each assembly.
Even if a bhikṣuṇī has been ordained for a hundred years, she must nevertheless pay homage to, rise in greeting, and welcome a newly ordained bhikṣu.
Furthermore, one should say:

"Listen, [Name]! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has declared these four reliances (*niśraya*). For as long as life lasts, you shall rely upon them when going forth and receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*)."
"Relying on rag robes, one leaves the household life and receives full ordination.
If you can do so, you should say: "I can!"

“If one obtains extra robes—whether cotton cloth, *kambala* woolen cloth, *kośeya* silk cloth, *kṣauma* linen cloth, *kṣomika* cloth, *vāsana* cloth, *āhana* cloth, *gautaka* cloth, or hemp cloth—one should accept them.”
“By relying on the practice of begging for alms, one leaves the household life and receives full ordination.
If you are able, you should say: “I am able!”
“If one obtains long-term food—whether it be food for the Saṃgha, food before the meal, food after the meal, or food offered by invitation—one should accept it.
One leaves the household life and receives full ordination based upon coarse and inferior bedding.”
If one is able, they should say: "I am able!
If one obtains a long-lasting hut, a multi-storied building, a large or small room, or a square or round house, it should be accepted.
"One who relies on inferior medicine may go forth and receive full ordination.
If one is able, one should say: "I am able!"
"If one obtains an excess of ghee, oil, honey, or rock sugar, it should be accepted.
One should then say: "Listen, [Name]!
You have already completed the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for receiving full ordination;
the *karman* has been performed according to the Dharma. The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas constantly make this aspiration:
"When shall we obtain a human body, leave the household life, and receive full ordination?"
"You have now attained this; it is like a person receiving a royal throne—your reception of the bhikṣuṇī-dharma is likewise.
You should be patient, easy to converse with, and easy to instruct!"
"You should train in the three precepts, extinguish the three poisons, transcend the three realms, and realize the fruit of Arhatship.
As for anything else you do not know, your Upādhyāya and Ācārya shall explain it to you."
At that time, there was a courtesan named Paṅkadhā who had gone forth in the True Dharma and Vinaya; she wished to go to a forest hermitage (āraṇyaka-vihāra) to receive full ordination (upasampadā).
When the bandits heard this, they intended to lie in wait along the road to seize her; the woman, having also heard of it, did not dare to go.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to confer the full ordination (upasaṃpadā) from a distance by means of a formal motion followed by three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman)."

The preceptor and the instructor first assembled a community of ten bhikṣuṇīs to complete the conferral of the precepts upon her; having done so, they placed the recipient of the precepts in one location.
Then, leading the community of ten bhikṣuṇīs to a forest retreat (āraṇyaka), they all prostrated at the feet of the bhikṣu-saṃgha.
The *karmavācanā* master requests the precepts from the Saṃgha, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
So-and-so seeks to receive full ordination from So-and-so; [he requests it from you]."

Having already received full ordination within one assembly, being pure and free from obstacles, having completed two years of training, having performed all preliminary duties, being fully equipped with robes and bowl, having sought out a preceptor, having received permission from one's parents, and not having committed any grave offense—one now desires to receive full ordination;
today, before the Sangha, one begs for the conferral of full ordination, with [Name] as preceptor.
"May the Saṃgha rescue and deliver me out of compassion!
Thus he requests three times.
The *karmācārya* monk should then perform the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the threefold proclamation (*karma*) according to the above wording of his request.

Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the instructor (*ācārya*), leading the assembly of ten bhikṣuṇīs, return to the original place where the ordination was to be received. They call the candidate for ordination, instructing her to prostrate at the feet of the Saṃgha and to kneel with palms joined before the presiding master of the *karma*.

The *karmācārya* shall explain to him the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* performed by the Saṃgha; having caused him to listen, he shall then fully explain, as above, the eight *pārājika* dharmas, the four *aupamya* dharmas, the eight *anatikramaṇīya* dharmas, and the four *niśraya* dharmas, up to: "As for anything else you do not know, your *upādhyāya* and *ācārya* shall explain it to you."
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who wore brightly colored garments as ornaments.
Laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs resemble courtesans; they wish to seek out men!"
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This should not be done; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense.
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who painted their eyes, and the Buddha said:
"It must not be done; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who suffered from eye ailments and required painting [of their eyes]; the Buddha said:
"For those who are ill, painting is permitted."
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who walked ahead of the bhikṣus; the Buddha said, "This should not be done;
whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense.
There were also some bhikṣuṇīs who, seeing a bhikṣu coming from afar, stood still and did not dare to move forward, thereby obstructing his almsround.
The Buddha said, "If they are traveling a long distance, I allow them to go in front.
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who, while walking in front of the bhikṣus, sniffed at odors and spat on the ground. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done; one who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who sat in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), and their menstrual blood flowed out and soiled their heels, leading people to see it and criticize them.
Furthermore, there was another bhikṣuṇī who sat in the full-lotus posture, and a dung beetle entered her female organ, whereby she became ill.
She informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"All bhikṣuṇīs should sit with their legs folded one over the other; if they sit in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka), they should extend one leg across the other. Any who violate this commit a duṣkṛta offense."
There was a householder who wished to exchange his dwelling with a bhikṣuṇī, but the bhikṣuṇīs did not dare to do so.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to exchange dwellings."
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who sewed their robes by stretching them out like the method used for sewing leather boots.
The Buddha said: "You should not do so!"
"If robes become shrunken or curled, it is permitted to place a girdle [on them].
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who, in their dwelling places, urinated and defecated here and there, making them foul-smelling and filthy.
The Buddha said:
"You must not do so; whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta*.
You should construct a latrine.
The bhikṣuṇīs dug deep pits for their latrines and placed aborted fetuses inside them. When a scavenger saw this, he reviled them, saying:
"These people constantly praise the renunciation of desire, the thought of desire, and the fever of desire;
yet they practice those very acts themselves, fearing that others might discover them, even casting their fetuses into latrines."
"Why do you not abandon the religious life and enjoy the five desires?
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not construct latrines that are too deep."
"Listen very closely: fold your hands at one cubit [from the mouth] and keep your mouth small.
Some bhikṣuṇīs placed fetuses in bowls and bags and discarded them in the early morning.
At that time, King Prasenajit had affairs on his borders and dispatched an army to campaign against them. Among those who had faith and devotion to the Buddha-dharma, there were some who thought:
"I should first provide food for the renunciants, and only then depart."
He immediately dispatched a messenger to search for her; upon encountering that bhikṣuṇī, he invited her to return and accept a meal offering.
The bhikṣuṇī said, “You go on ahead; I shall follow after you.”
He then earnestly entreated him, and by force brought him back;
when they came out and set down the food from beneath the bowl, they saw the infant fetus, whereupon he rebuked him in various ways, saying:
"These people constantly preach compassion and the protection of sentient beings, yet now they have personally killed their own child."
"You lack the conduct of a śramaṇa and have destroyed the dharma of a śramaṇa!
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣuṇī sees a bhikṣu while begging for food, she should take out her bowl and show it to him."
The bhikṣuṇīs then all took out their bowls and tilted them sideways to show [the emptiness], thereby obstructing their alms-round.
The Buddha said:
"Simply show it roughly enough to let them know it is empty."
A certain bhikṣuṇī gave birth to a son and did not know what to do.
She reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement) to appoint a bhikṣuṇī as her companion."
A single bhikṣuṇī should announce within the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs:
"May the noble saṃgha listen!
This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has given birth to a son; we now appoint the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so to attend upon her."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus as a formal motion (jñapti). 'Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen!'"
This Bhikṣuṇī so-and-so has given birth to a son; we now appoint the Bhikṣuṇī so-and-so to accompany her.
Those of you, Venerable Sisters, who consent, remain silent;
those who do not consent, speak.
The Sangha has already appointed the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so as a companion for the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so;
the Sangha consents, as it remains silent.
This matter is thus upheld.
Two bhikṣuṇīs holding a child gave rise to doubt; the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
Two bhikṣuṇīs sleeping together with a child gave rise to doubt; the Buddha said:
“There is no offense!
Thus he adorned the child and they sang together.
The Buddha said:
"You must not do so! It is permitted to bathe them and give them milk to suckle.
If they are weaned from the embrace, you should give them to a bhikṣu to ordain as a novice."
"If you do not wish for her to go forth, you should give her to your relatives; let your relatives raise her until she has grown up.
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who, when invited by the saṃgha of bhikṣus, did not go in the proper order.
The Buddha said:
"It should not be done thus!
You should appoint them in succession to go."
There were certain bhikṣuṇīs who entered a village without fastening their lower robes; they fell to the ground and their bodies were exposed.
The Buddha said:
"They should fasten them with a waist-cord."
They made the waistband excessively long; the Buddha said, "I allow it to wrap around the waist once.
They made the waistband excessively wide; the Buddha said:
"Make it very wide, as wide as one finger.
[They] made a multi-colored waist-cord. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done thus!"
"Listen to this single rule:
There were certain bhikṣuṇīs who entered a village wearing light clothing; the wind blew and their bodies were exposed.
The Buddha said:"
"Listen: [the bowl] should be secured with hooks and loops above and below, fastened with a belt.
When daughters of noble families who had gone forth were carrying their bowls while begging for food, they held them with their hands.
The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to make a net-bag to carry the alms-bowl while begging for food.
[The monks] hung it under their armpits, where it became soiled with sweat and dust entered it.
The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to make a bowl-covering cloth.
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who practiced sorcery with the intent to kill living beings.
The Buddha said:
"If one practices sorcery (*gūdha*) with the intent to kill sentient beings, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
likewise, if one performs incantations to raise the dead with the intent to kill sentient beings, it is also thus."
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who kept various kinds of multicolored robes, and the white-robed laypeople criticized and reviled them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs look exactly like courtesans!"
The Buddha said, "It should not be done;
one who violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There were monks who had food from the previous day's meal, while the bhikṣuṇīs had no food; yet the monks did not dare to give it to them.
The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to give [food] without offense.
It is likewise for a bhikṣuṇī who gives food that has been kept overnight to a bhikṣu."
There were some bhikṣus who went to the dwelling place of the bhikṣuṇīs, but there was no *kappiya-kāraka* (one who makes things permissible) to hand over the food.
The Buddha said:
"When there is no *kappiya-kāraka*, it is permitted for a bhikṣuṇī to hand over food to a bhikṣu; there is no offense."
"It is likewise for a bhikṣu who gives food to a bhikṣuṇī.
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who engaged in the sale of intoxicants, and many people criticized and reviled them.
The Buddha said:
"You must not do so; one who violates this commits a sthūlātyaya offense!
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who kept fields, plow-oxen, and slaves, and personally supervised their cultivation.
The laypeople criticized and rebuked them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs are even looking after plowing fields themselves; how are they any different from us?
The Buddha said:
"One should not look at it oneself; one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) know it.
Whoever violates this commits a *duṣkṛta* offense!
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who exhaled air, and many people reviled them.
The Buddha said:
"This should not be done; one who violates this incurs a sthūlātyaya.
There were certain bhikṣuṇīs who kept courtesans and sat at market stalls to lease them out.
Many people censured him.
The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; whoever violates this commits a sthūlātyaya."
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who pressed oil for sale, and many people criticized and rebuked them.
The Buddha said, "You should not do so; whoever violates this commits a sthūlātyaya offense."
There were some bhikṣuṇīs who played by hopping on one foot, and many people criticized and rebuked them.
The Buddha said:
"You should not do so; whoever violates this commits a duṣkṛta offense."
"Playing by hanging oneself from a rope is likewise [a grave offense].
When a fire broke out at the dwelling place of certain bhikṣuṇīs, the Buddha said:
"One should strike the ghaṇṭā or call for an assembly; everyone shall together extinguish the fire by scattering earth, pouring water, or using water-soaked clothing to douse it."
At that time, a large number of lay devotees invited the community of bhikṣuṇīs for a meal.

The bhikṣuṇīs rose early in the morning, donned their robes, and took up their bowls, but only upon arriving at the house of the invitation did they inquire about seniority among one another; consequently, the appointed time passed.
The lay devotees criticized and rebuked them, saying: "These bhikṣuṇīs are exactly like brahmin women!"
They asked one another how much scripture each had mastered; the one with the most was considered the greatest.
[The host thought,] "I have now prepared this offering, but the time for the meal has already passed.
What should I do? He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When a large assembly gathers, it is permitted for eight senior monks (*sthavira*) to inquire about their relative seniority and sit according to order;
the remaining persons may take their seats as they obtain them.
*Pañcavargīya-vinaya*, Fascicle 29 and Fascicle 30, Mahīśāsaka.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Song Dynasty, together with Zhu Daosheng and others. Section Five:

The Compilation of the Dharma by the Five Hundred; Part Nine: The Compilation of the Dharma by the Five Hundred. At that time, not long after the World-Honored One had entered *nirvāṇa*, Mahākāśyapa was at the Gabled Hall on the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats, with the sole exception of Ānanda.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Formerly, I was traveling from the kingdom of Pāpīyas toward the city of Kauśāmbī;
midway between the two kingdoms, I heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had already entered parinirvāṇa. At that time, my heart was bewildered and confused, and I could not compose myself."
The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās of the various villages—some lame, some leaping—rolled upon the ground, all wailing in grief and lamenting his swift and rapid passing:
"The world is now empty; the Eye of the World has been extinguished!"
At that time, Upananda had previously been traveling there and stopped the crowd, saying:
"That elder always says:
'One should practice this; one should not practice that.'"
"One should study this; one should not study that.
Only now have we been liberated from this suffering!
We may act as we please, no longer subject to any constraints.
"Why are you all weeping together?
When I heard these words, my grief and distress redoubled. Although the Buddha has entered *nirvāṇa*, the *vinaya* remains present; we ought to encourage one another and compile it together.
Do not allow Upananda and his like to establish separate factions and thereby destroy the True Dharma.
All the bhikṣus approved this as excellent and addressed Kāśyapa, saying:

"Ānanda has constantly attended upon the World-Honored One; he is wise and of vast learning, fully upholding the Dharma-piṭaka. He should now be permitted to be included among those who compile the Vinaya."
Kāśyapa said, “Ānanda is still on the stage of training; he may yet follow after desire, hatred, delusion, or fear. You should not permit him [to enter].
At that time, Ānanda was in Vaiśālī, constantly preaching the Dharma day and night for the fourfold assembly. As people came and went, it was almost as if the Buddha were present.

There was a Vajjian bhikṣu sitting in meditation on that upper terrace; because of this noise and disturbance, he was unable to practice the various liberations and samādhis, and he thought to himself:
"What should Ānanda do now while still on the stage of training? Is he doing what ought to be done, or is he doing nothing?"
Yet he constantly remains amidst the clamor and bustle, and speaks much.
Having entered meditative concentration and observed this, he saw that there was something yet to be done.
He then thought again:
"I shall now preach the Dharma of wearying detachment for him, so that through this he may attain awakening.
He then went to Ānanda and spoke these verses for him:
"Sitting in a quiet place beneath a tree, The mind inclines toward Nirvāṇa; The mind inclines toward Nirvāṇa;"
"Do not be negligent in your meditation; what is the use of speaking so much?
The bhikṣus also said to Ānanda, "You should quickly attend to what must be done!"
"Mahākāśyapa now wishes to compile the Vinaya, yet he does not permit you to be included among those in this assembly.

Having heard the verse spoken by the Bhikṣu of the Vaṅga clan, and having also heard that Kāśyapa would not allow him to be among those compiling the Vinaya, Ānanda practiced walking meditation and engaged in contemplation with diligence throughout the first, middle, and last watches of the night, hoping to attain liberation, yet he was unable to do so.

As the latter part of the night drew to a close, his body was utterly exhausted and he wished to lie down for a short while; before his head had even reached the pillow, his outflows were suddenly exhausted.
When the bhikṣus learned of this, they immediately informed Kāśyapa:
"Ānanda attained liberation last night; you should now permit him to be included in the count of those who compile the Vinaya."
Kāśyapa consented immediately; thereupon, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"How much food, drink, bedding, and seating are required to provide for those who have gathered for the *saṃghabhedaka-vinaya*?"
Seeing that Rājagṛha alone was sufficient to provide for their needs, he announced among the Saṃgha:
"Five hundred Arhats from this assembly should go to Rājagṛha for the rains retreat; no one else is permitted to go!"

Having established this regulation, five hundred arhats arrived at Rājagṛha; during the first month of the summer retreat, they repaired their dwellings and bedding, and during the second month, they practiced and sported within the various dhyānas and liberations.
After three months, they gathered together in one place, whereupon Kāśyapa addressed the Saṃgha, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I shall now inquire regarding the meaning of the Vinaya among the Saṃgha concerning Upāli."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus.
Then Upāli also addressed the Saṃgha, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I shall now answer the Vinaya principles concerning Kāśyapa.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen."
“Thus it was announced. Kāśyapa then asked Upāli:
“In what place did the Buddha establish the first precept?”
Upāli said, “In Vaiśālī. He asked again:
"By whom was it established? He replied,
"It was established because of Sudinna Kalandaputra."
He asked again:
"By what matter was it established? He replied:
"To engage in sexual intercourse with both [a woman] and her mother. He asked again:
"Are there two rules established for this?"
He replied, "There was!
There was a bhikṣu who engaged in sexual intercourse with a macaque."
Kāśyapa asked again:
"In what place was the second precept established? He replied:
"In Rājagṛha. He asked again: "On account of whom was it established?"
He replied, "Because of Dhanika.
He asked again:
"For what reason was this rule established? He replied,
"Because they stole King Bimbisāra’s timber."
Kāśyapa asked again:
"Where was the third precept established? He replied:
"In Vaiśālī. He asked again: "On account of whom was it established?"
He replied, “It was because of many bhikṣus.
He asked again:
"For what reason was it established?
He replied, "Because they were taking each other's lives."
Kāśyapa asked again:
"In what place was the fourth precept established? He replied:
"In Vaiśālī. He asked again: "On account of whom was it established?"
He replied, "It was because of the bhikṣus from the Vālukāmukha River.
He asked again:
"By what matter was it established?
He replied, "Falsely claiming to have attained superhuman states."
After Kāśyapa had thus questioned regarding all the *vinaya*, he proclaimed within the Saṃgha:
"This is the *vinaya* of the bhikṣus; this is the *vinaya* of the bhikṣuṇīs; together they are named the *Vinayapiṭaka*."
Kāśyapa addressed the Saṃgha again, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I now wish to inquire regarding the meaning of the Sūtras from Ānanda within this Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen,
I shall speak thus.
Ānanda also addressed the Saṃgha, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I shall now explain the meaning of the Kāśyapa Sūtra.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and hear me."
"Thus it was reported. Kāśyapa then asked Ānanda:
"In what place did the Buddha preach the *Ekottarika-āgama*?"
In what places were the *Daśottara-sūtra*, the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*, the *Saṃgīti-sūtra*, the *Sāmaññaphala-sūtra*, and the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* spoken?
Which sūtras were spoken because of the bhikṣus?
"What sūtras have been spoken with bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devaputras, and devakanyās as the interlocutors?
Ānanda answered, repeating everything exactly as the Buddha had spoken.
After Kāśyapa had thus questioned regarding all the sūtras, he proclaimed within the Saṃgha:
"These are the long sūtras; they shall now be compiled into one collection named the Dīrgha Āgama.
These are neither long nor short; they shall now be compiled into one collection named the Madhyama Āgama."

These are miscellaneous discourses spoken for the sake of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, sons of gods, and daughters of gods; now collected into one section, they are called the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
These are discourses that proceed from one dharma up to eleven dharmas; now collected into one section, they are called the *Ekottara Āgama*.
All other miscellaneous discourses are now collected into one section, named the *Kṣudraka Piṭaka*; together, these are termed the *Sūtra Piṭaka*.
We have now completed the compilation of the Dharma. From this day forward, that which has not been prescribed by the Buddha must not be arbitrarily prescribed;
and that which has already been prescribed must not be violated.
"As the Buddha has taught, you should study it with care.
Ānanda spoke again to Kāśyapa, saying:
"I have heard this directly from the Buddha:"
"After my parinirvāṇa, if you wish to abolish the minor precepts, I permit their abolition.
Kāśyapa then asked: "What do you consider to be the minor precepts?"
He replied, "I do not know. He asked again:
"Why do you not know? He replied,
"I did not ask the World-Honored One."
He asked again: "Why did you not ask? He replied:
At that time, the Buddha’s body was in pain, and he feared it would cause him further distress.
Kāśyapa rebuked him, saying:
"You have committed a *duṣkṛta* offense by failing to inquire about this matter."
"You should see your own faults and repent! Ānanda said,
"Venerable Sir!..."
It is not that I lack reverence for the precepts, nor that I did not wish to inquire about this matter;
it was only for fear of disturbing the World-Honored One that I did not dare.
Within this, I saw no sign of transgression, yet out of respect and faith in your great virtue, I shall now repent my error.
Kāśyapa again rebuked Ānanda, saying:
"When you sewed the saṃghāṭī for the World-Honored One, you pressed it down with your toes; this constitutes a duṣkṛta offense, and you should likewise acknowledge your fault and repent!"
Ānanda said, “It is not that I lack respect for the Buddha; it was because no one was holding the heel-strap that I pressed down with my foot.
Within this matter, I did not perceive any sign of transgression, yet I have deep faith and reverence for the Venerable One; I now confess my fault!”
Kāśyapa further rebuked Ānanda, saying:
"You requested the World-Honored One three times to allow women to go forth in the True Dharma; you have committed a *duṣkṛta* offense and must likewise acknowledge your fault and repent!"
Ānanda said: "It is not that I lack respect for the Dharma; however, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī nurtured the World-Honored One until he attained great renunciation and achieved the Great Way."
This merit ought to be requited; therefore, I have made this request three times.
Within this matter, I also do not perceive any sign of transgression; out of reverence and faith in the Venerable One, I now confess my fault!
Kāśyapa again interrogated Ānanda, saying:
"When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he manifested a sign and said to you:
'If there be one who has attained the four bases of psychic power, and wishes to remain for a kalpa or even longer than a kalpa, they may do so.'"

"The Tathāgata has accomplished immeasurable meditative dharmas; thus, three times have I manifested signs and spoken to you. Yet you did not request the Buddha to remain in the world for one kalpa, or even more than one kalpa. You have committed a duṣkṛta offense; you should likewise recognize this fault and repent!"
Ānanda said: "It was not that I did not wish to entreat the Buddha to remain for a long time; rather, the evil Māra Pāpīyān obscured my mind, and for this reason it came to this!
Within this matter, I do not see any sign of transgression, yet out of reverence and faith toward the Great Virtuous One, I now repent."
Kāśyapa again rebuked Ānanda, saying:
"In the past, the Buddha requested water from you three times, yet you did not provide it!
You have committed a duṣkṛta offense; you should also acknowledge this fault and repent!"
Ānanda said: "It was not that I did not wish to offer it!
At that time, five hundred carts were crossing upstream, which had made the water turbid and not yet clear; fearing it might cause illness, I did not offer it."
"In this matter, I also do not perceive any transgression; out of reverence and faith toward the Venerable One, I shall now repent my error!
Kāśyapa again interrogated Ānanda, saying:
"You have committed a *duṣkṛta* offense by allowing women to pay homage to the relics first; you too must recognize your fault and repent!"
Ānanda said: "It was not that I wished for women to pay homage to the śarīra first; I feared that by the time of sunset they might not be able to enter the city, and for that reason I permitted it."
"In this matter, I did not perceive the characteristics of an offense; yet out of reverence and faith in the Venerable One, I shall now repent my transgression!
Out of reverence and faith in Mahākāśyapa, Ānanda immediately performed the repentance for six *duṣkṛta* offenses before the assembly of monks.
Kāśyapa again interrogated Ānanda, saying:
"If we consider the *śaikṣa-dharmas* to be minor rules (*kṣudrānuśaṃsa*), other bhikṣus will say that even up to the four *pratideśanīya* rules are likewise minor rules;
if we consider the four *pratideśanīya* rules to be minor rules, other bhikṣus will further say that even up to the *pāyattika* rules are likewise minor rules."
If we consider the *pāyattika* rules to be minor precepts, other monks will then say that even the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules are likewise minor precepts.
"In an instant they have become four kinds;
how can they be fixed? Kāśyapa spoke again:
"If we, not knowing the characteristics of the minor precepts, were to arbitrarily abolish them, the various non-Buddhists would say this:"
"The Dharma of the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, is like smoke: while the Master was present, all that he established was practiced;
but after his parinirvāṇa, they are unwilling to learn it again."
Kāśyapa again proclaimed among the Saṃgha:
"We have finished compiling the Dharma. That which was not prohibited by the Buddha should not be arbitrarily prohibited;
that which has already been prohibited must not be violated."

“As the Buddha has taught, you should study it with care. At that time, the Elder Pūraṇa was in the south. Together with his retinue, he arrived among the assembly in the time it takes to bend and extend one’s arm and said to Kāśyapa:
“I have heard that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa and that all the elder bhikṣus have gathered here to discuss the Vinaya; is this indeed so?”
Kāśyapa replied: "Virtuous One!
It is indeed so."
Pūraṇa said, "Let us discuss it further!
Kāśyapa then discussed it again as before.
Having finished his discourse, Pūraṇa said to Kāśyapa:

"I have heard directly from the Buddha that it is permissible to eat food stored indoors, food cooked indoors, food cooked by oneself, food carried by oneself, food received from others, fruit picked by oneself, food received directly from a body of water, and to eat fruit that has been purified by removing the pits when no one is available to purify it."
Kāśyapa replied: "Venerable sir!
As for these seven-strip robes, when the Buddha was in Vaiśālī during a time of famine when alms were difficult to obtain, he temporarily permitted them."
"Subsequently, he immediately prohibited four more rules there; then, upon arriving at Śrāvastī, he again prohibited three.
Pūraṇa said, "The World-Honored One should not prohibit what he has already permitted, nor permit what he has already prohibited."
Kāśyapa replied: "The Buddha is the Lord of Dharma and possesses mastery over the Dharma.
What fault is there in his revoking a prohibition after it has been established, or re-establishing a prohibition after it has been permitted?"
Pūraṇa said, "I can endure other matters, but I cannot practice these seven points!
Kāśyapa again proclaimed this among the Saṃgha:
"If that which has not been prescribed by the Buddha is not to be arbitrarily prescribed;
and if it has already been prescribed, one must not violate it.
One should diligently study according to what the Buddha has taught."
At that time, the bhikṣu Chanda of Kauśāmbī was causing trouble for the Saṃgha and would not live in harmony with them.
A certain bhikṣu, having completed his summer retreat, went to where Kāśyapa was and reported the matter in full.
Kāśyapa said to Ānanda, "Go to Kauśāmbī and,
in the name of the Buddha and the Saṃgha, carry out the *brahmadaṇḍa* rite to punish them.
Accepting the mission, Ānanda set out together with five hundred bhikṣus.
When Channa heard that Ānanda had arrived with five hundred bhikṣus, he went out to meet them and asked Ānanda:
"For what reason have you come here?
Do you perhaps intend to do me some harm?"
He replied, "I wish only to benefit you! Chandaka said:
"How will this benefit me? He replied,
"I shall now, by means of the words of the Buddha and the words of the Saṃgha, perform the *brahmadaṇḍa* rite to punish you!"
He then asked, "What is called the Brahma-vihāra rite? He replied:
“Regarding the Brahma-altar rite: no bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās shall come and go with you, nor engage in conversation with you.”
Upon hearing this, Channa fell to the ground in a faint.
He said to Ānanda, "Is this not what is called killing me? Ānanda replied:
"I have personally heard from the Buddha:
'You shall attain the Way from me!
Arise, and I shall preach the Dharma for you."
He immediately rose to listen.

Ānanda taught him various sublime dharmas, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening him; thereupon, he became free from dust and removed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena.

When the Dharma and Vinaya were being compiled, the Elder Ājñātakauṇḍinya was the first presiding elder, Pūrṇa was the second, Vāṣpa was the third, Tayagautama Kāśyapa was the fourth, Bhadragautama Kāśyapa was the fifth, Mahākāśyapa was the sixth, Upāli was the seventh, and Aniruddha was the eighth; there were exactly five hundred arhats, neither more nor less, and for this reason it is called the "Compilation of the Dharma by Five Hundred."

10. The Seventeen Rules of the Fifth Part of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* on the Council of Seven Hundred. One hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bhikṣus of the Vṛji clan in Vaiśālī first initiated ten unlawful practices (*adharma*):
first, the practice of storing salt and ginger together as pure;
second, the practice of eating by pinching food with two fingers as pure.
3. Purity through eating while seated again;
4. Purity through eating beyond the village boundary;
5. Purity through mixing ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar with curdled milk.
Sixth, drinking *jāluga* liquor is pure;
seventh, making a sitting mat of any size at will is pure;
eighth, practicing what was previously practiced is pure.
9. Seeking permission for purification;
10. Purification through accepting and keeping gold, silver, and money.

Those bhikṣus would regularly, on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month, fill their alms bowls with water and gather where many people were assembled. Holding the bowls before them as an auspicious sign, they would entreat people to offer alms.
At that time, whenever laypeople—men and women, old and young—passed by, they would point to the water in the bowl and say:
"There is auspiciousness within this!
You may give [these] robes, bowls, sandals, and the price for medicine."
To those who wished to give, they gave;
to those who did not wish to give, they rebuked them, saying:
"A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, should not accept or possess gold, silver, or money!"
"If someone were to give it to you of their own accord, you should not even look at it; why then do you now go about seeking such alms?
At that time, the Elder Yaśas Kākaṇḍaka-putra was in the multi-storied lecture hall by the side of the Monkey Pond, and he said to the bhikṣus:
"Do not seek alms in this manner!"
"I have personally heard from the Buddha that if one seeks alms through unrighteous means or bestows gifts upon those who seek them unrighteously, both incur transgression!
Having spoken thus to the bhikṣus, he further addressed the laymen and laywomen, both young and old:
"None of you should make such offerings!"
"I have heard directly from the Buddha that if one seeks alms through what is not the Dharma, or gives alms to one who seeks them through what is not the Dharma, both incur guilt!
After those bhikṣus had received gold, silver, and coins, they said to Yaśas:
"Venerable One!..."
"You may accept this portion.
He replied, "I will not accept a portion of alms obtained through unlawful means!"
He spoke again, saying:
"If you do not accept it yourself, you may give it to the Sangha. He replied:
“Since we have not accepted [the robe], how can we give it to the Saṃgha?
Thereupon, the bhikṣus, because Yaśas had previously instructed the laypeople in such a way as to revile them, performed the *jñapti-karman* of subordination against him.
After the *karmavācanā* had been performed, Yaśas said:
"I have heard directly from the Buddha that if the Saṃgha performs a *vinayātisāra-karman* against one, they should appoint one bhikṣu as a companion to apologize to the lay followers."

The bhikṣus then performed a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one proclamation) to appoint a bhikṣu as a companion for Yaśas. Yaśas led him to the residence of a layperson (*avadātavasana*), where he happened upon five hundred upāsakas gathered in one place. He then said to them:
"Gentlemen, you should know this: what is the Dharma, I declare to be the Dharma;
what is not the Dharma, I declare to be not the Dharma."
"This is the Vinaya; I declare this to be the Vinaya.
This is not the Vinaya; I declare this to be not the Vinaya.
This is the Buddha's teaching; I declare this to be the Buddha's teaching."
"It is not the Buddha's teaching; I say it is not the Buddha's teaching.
What I previously said caused the lay followers (upāsakas) to become angry, and now I come to apologize!
All the lay followers were greatly astonished and said:
"Venerable Sir! When will you speak to us of what is Dharma,
what is Vinaya, and what is the Buddha's teaching, so as to provoke our anger and cause us to come and offer our apologies?"
Yaśas spoke further to the people, saying:
"At one time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Jīvaka-āmra-vana in Rājagṛha.
At that time, King Bimbisāra and his various ministers gathered at the palace gate and held this discussion:"
"Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, ought to accept, store, and use gold, silver, and precious gems, and engage in their trade.
At that time, there was a great minister among the assembly named Mukhamaṇḍika who said to the people:
"Do not propose such a matter; śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, ought not to accept, store, or use gold, silver, and precious gems, nor engage in their trade."
He then went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter, saying:
"In what I have said, is there perhaps no error or transgression?
The Buddha said:
"What you have said hits the mark exactly! Why is this?
I have always taught that a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, should not accept, store, or trade in gold, silver, or precious gems."
Again he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will send word to the multitude so that they may know this is not an error!
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! He then addressed Zhujì:
"For example, the sun and moon, when obscured by the four veils of smoke, clouds, dust, and asuras, are neither bright nor pure."
Śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas likewise have four kinds of obscurations:
some do not sever their craving for sensual desire and engage in sexual conduct;
others are addicted to wine and food and are unable to abandon them.
Some exclusively engage in wrong livelihood to sustain themselves;
some accept and store gold, silver, jewels, and pearls, and use them for trade.
If a person regards the five desires as pure, that person likewise regards the acceptance, storage, and trade of gold, silver, jewels, and pearls as pure.
If a person considers it pure to accept, possess, or trade in gold, silver, and precious gems, that person considers the five desires to be pure.

If a person has left the household life and received full ordination under me, yet considers it pure to accept, possess, or trade in gold, silver, and precious gems, you should know that this person certainly does not believe in my Dharma and Vinaya.
Although I have always said that if one needs a vehicle, one may seek a vehicle, and if one needs a person, one may seek a person— permitting the seeking of whatever things are required—
I have never allowed the acceptance, possession, or use of gold, silver, or precious jewels for the purpose of trade.
After Yaśas had said this, he spoke again:

“I previously declared that this is the Dharma and that is not the Dharma, this is the Vinaya and that is not the Vinaya, this is the Buddha’s teaching and that is not the Buddha’s teaching, and this was spoken by the Buddha and that was not spoken by the Buddha.”
The upāsakas said: "Among these words, we have no lack of faith or delight.
Now, in Vaiśālī, there is only the Venerable One who is a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas."
"We pray that you will accept from us these four requisites for life-long support!
Having thanked the lay devotees, Yaśas returned with the monk sent by the Saṃgha to the monastery.
The Bhikṣus of the Vṛji asked the messenger-bhikṣu,
"Has the bhikṣu Yaśas already apologized to the upāsakas? He replied:
“I have already declined!
However, all the laypeople believe his words and all say:
‘Now, there is only the Venerable One in Vaiśālī!’”
"Since he has already invited us to provide the four requisites for the rest of his life, there is no further benefit for us in this matter.
The Bhikṣus of Vaṅga then reported that Yaśas had previously instructed the other bhikṣus to revile the Saṃgha, thereby committing a *pāyattika* offense.
He said, "You must recognize your transgression and repent! Yaśas replied:
"I have no offense that can be seen; why then should I repent?
The Bhikṣus of Vaṅga then gathered together, intending to perform the *ajñapti-karman* (formal act) of "not seeing the offense" against him.
Thereupon, Yaśas used his supernormal power to fly to the kingdom of Pāpīyasī.

At that time, there were sixty bhikṣus in the city of Pālī who were all forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka), practitioners of the three robes, alms-gathering, rag-robes, constant sitting, and open-air sitting; they were fully endowed with the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, and were all disciples of Ānanda.
They all flew together toward Vaiśālī.

When Yaśas saw this, he placed his robe and bowl in mid-air as if they were resting on the ground; he then exchanged greetings with that bhikṣu and fully explained the ten kinds of unrighteous conduct of the Vṛji bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sir!..."
"We should together discuss the Vinaya rules to extinguish this matter, lest the Bhikṣus of Vaḍḍha cause the True Dharma to perish!
Those bhikṣus should not harbor resentment in their hearts, desiring instead to work together to extinguish [the dispute].
Furthermore, there were thirty bhikṣus from the village of Pāṭalī who possessed virtues equal to those mentioned above; they too were disciples of Ānanda and resided in the kingdom of Mathurā.
Yaśas consulted with these sixty bhikṣus, saying:
"If we can obtain those thirty bhikṣus to join us, we will surely be able to extinguish that evil matter in accordance with the Dharma."

Having deliberated thus, they flew together to where that bhikṣu was and related everything as stated above; he, too, did not oppose them in his heart, desiring to join them in extinguishing [the fire].
Furthermore, there were thirty bhikṣus from the village of Pāṭalī who possessed virtues identical to those mentioned above; they were also disciples of Ānanda and resided in the village of Alabī.

Yaśas again joined with ninety others and held the same discussion as before, going to their location and explaining everything as previously stated. They, too, were of one mind and desired to join in suppressing [the heresy].

At that time, the elder Subhūti was on Mount Arbuda. Yaśas again joined with one hundred and twenty people to deliberate as previously discussed, and they went to his location to explain the matter in full detail as before; he also concurred in heart, wishing to join them in its destruction.
At that time, the Elder Revata was in the city of Kauśāmbī; he had attained the samādhi of loving-kindness and possessed a large retinue.

Yaśas, together with one hundred and twenty-one others, also deliberated as previously discussed and went to his location, reporting everything as described above. He likewise agreed in heart, wishing to join them in eradicating [the schism].

At that time, the bhikṣus of the Vṛji clan, hearing that Yaśas had gone to where Revata was at Kauśāmbī, loaded a boat to the brim with saṃghāṭī robes, alms bowls, and all other necessary items, intending likewise to go there to trade goods and seek assistance.
Among his companions on the ship was a Vinaya-master named Sālaṇa, who reflected privately:
"Are the Bhikṣus of the Vajjī acting in accordance with the Dharma?
He then examined their conduct according to the various sūtras and vinayas and found that they were not acting in accordance with the Dharma.
Then a deity in the air proclaimed three times:
"So it is, so it is! The conduct of the Vajjian bhikṣus is unlawful, just as you have seen!"
The bhikṣus of the Vajjī clan arrived at Kauśāmbī; they all went together ashore to where the Elder Revata was and said to him:
"We have brought many requisites for śramaṇas to offer to the Venerable One."
"I pray that you will accept it!
He replied, "My robes and bowl are complete; I have no further need for them!"
He spoke again, saying:
"If you do not require much, I pray that you accept a small amount! He replied:
"I have already prepared my robes and bowl; I cannot violate the Dharma by accepting [offerings] for your sake!
Upāli had a disciple named Dharma who constantly attended him. The Bhikṣus of the Vṛji clan then went to his place and said to him:
"We have requisites required by a śramaṇa; if you lack anything, you may take it from us!"
He replied, "I have everything I need; I lack nothing.
The Bhikṣus of the Vṛji clan spoke again:
"When the Buddha was in the world, if people came to offer gifts to the Buddha and the Buddha did not accept them, he would have them given to Ānanda, and Ānanda accepted them all.
Once Ānanda had accepted them, it was as if the Buddha himself had accepted them."
Upon hearing this, Bodhidharma accepted one item from each of them.
Having accepted it, he asked:
"For what purpose do you insist on giving me these items?"
He replied, "I wish for you to speak on my behalf to your preceptor, asking him to assist me with his power so that Yaśas does not cause the destruction of our Dharma and Vinaya.
Then Dharmadatta went to the preceptor’s quarters and said:
"Upādhyāya, you should assist the Bhikṣus of the Vṛji.
He replied, "They practice the ways of those who act contrary to the Dharma; I will not assist them!"
Dharma replied again,
"I pray that you will deliberate further!
He answered, saying:
"You now urge me to assist those who act contrary to the Dharma; you are not my disciple!
From this day forth, do not remain by my side, nor shall I ever again speak with you!"
Dharma, filled with shame and fear, went to where the bhikṣus of Vaṅga were.
They all asked him,
"Does your preceptor have any intention to assist us?"
He replied, "There is none!
It has merely caused me now to be reproached by you and to undergo the penalty of being excluded from conversation."
The bhikṣus of the Vajjī clan asked him,
"How many years old are you now? He replied:
"Twenty years old," he said, "and yet your age and virtue are such as this!"
"How can you bear to perform this act of *pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman* (formal exclusion through refusal of speech)? Thereupon, the Elder Revata thought to himself:
"If I were to settle this matter here, the person who committed the offense will surely initiate it again. I should now go together with them to where the matter originated and settle it there."
Having reflected thus, he went together with the great assembly to the city of Vaiśālī.

In that city there was previously a bhikṣu named Sarvagāmin, who was the foremost among the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, in Jambudvīpa; he had attained arhatship, possessed the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, and was also the greatest disciple of Ānanda.
Outside the monastery, Yaśas said to Revata,
"You may go to the Elder’s room, spread out bedding,
and stay the night," and he related the preceding events in detail.
"I shall also pay my respects to the Elder in the early morning.
Once the group had entered the monks' quarters, that Elder prepared bathing requisites and provided post-midday gruel.
Upāli went alone to the room of the senior elder, spread out his bedding, and stayed there for the night. During the night, Upāli thought to himself:
"Even this senior elder, Sarvakāmin, who is weak and old, still exerts himself so strenuously that he sits in meditation throughout the entire night."
"What is appropriate for me now to obtain peaceful sleep?
Sarvakāmin also thought to himself:
"This visiting bhikṣu is utterly exhausted from his journey, yet even after bathing he still sits in meditation and practices the Path throughout the entire night."
"How can I now obtain a peaceful sleep?
The two men pushed each other aside and consequently sat in meditation throughout the entire night.
When the latter part of the night arrived, everyone went to ask Līlavatī:
"In which concentration have you spent much of this night?
He replied, "My nature is largely characterized by loving-kindness; tonight, I have spent much time in this concentration."
Sarvagāmin said, "This is a coarse concentration.
He asked again:
"Are you an arhat? He replied, "I am."
Revata asked Sarvakāmin repeatedly, "Elder,
in what meditative concentration have you been dwelling much this night? He replied:
"I am by nature fond of the contemplation of emptiness; tonight I have frequently dwelt in this samādhi.
Revata said, "This is the practice of great beings. Why is that?"
"The emptiness samādhi is the dharma of great beings.
He asked again, "Is the Elder an Arhat?"
He replied, "It is so!
After the final watch of the night had ended, the bhikṣu Yaśas went before the cell and snapped his fingers; the senior monk opened the door, and he entered at once to pay his respects.
After exchanging greetings, Revata asked Sarvakāmin:
"Is it pure for salt and ginger to be mixed and kept overnight? He replied:
"This matter should be questioned within the Saṃgha;

for if it were questioned of me alone, I fear that those who do not act according to the Dharma would regard me as partial, and would not allow me to be counted among those who deliberate upon the Vinaya."
Thereupon Revata immediately assembled the Saṃgha, intending to discuss the Vinaya;
however, as there was much confused talk, he addressed the Saṃgha, saying:
"Today we wish to discuss the Dharma of the Vinaya together, yet there is much confused talk, so that no resolution can be reached."
"Both sides should each seek out four persons; the Saṃgha shall perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to appoint them as the presiding judges.
The Bhikṣus of the Vṛji first sought out four persons:
the first was named Sarvakāmin, the second Revata, the third Asoka, and the fourth Sumana.
The bhikṣus of the town of Pāṭaliputra also sought out four men:
the first was named Svāti, the second Śāradvatīputra, the third Dīrghakeśa, and the fourth Vatsala.
Once the elders had been appointed by the Saṃgha, they deliberated together:
"In what place is it secluded, quiet, and level, where we may collectively discuss the Vinaya?"
He then surveyed them all and saw that only the park offered by the woman Vīrā was excellent.
Revata then sent his disciple Dharma there to arrange the seats, instructing him:
"If the Elder arrives, you must withdraw at once!"
Having received the command, they immediately spread out the seats, and the elder monks arrived and sat down in order.
Thereupon, Revata asked the elder Sarvakāmin:
"Is it pure for salt and ginger to be kept overnight together?"
He replied, "Impure! He asked again:
"In what place was it established? He replied, "In Rājagṛha."
He asked again:
"By whom was it established? He replied:
"It was because of a certain forest-dwelling bhikṣu.
He asked again,
"What offense did he commit?"
He replied, "One commits the offense of *pāyattika* for eating food kept overnight. Revata said:
“This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Buddha!
The conduct of the Vajjian bhikṣus is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the teaching of the Buddha!”
"Now, I cast one tally. Revata asked again:
"Is it pure to eat food by pinching it between two fingers?"
The Elder asked:
"What is meant by 'purifying food by picking it up with two fingers'? Revata replied:
"A bhikṣu, having already finished his meal, obtains more food and eats it by pinching it with two fingers.
He replied: "It is impure!"
He asked again:
"Where was it enacted? He replied:
"In Rājagṛha. He asked again: "On account of whom was it established?"
He replied, "Because of Upananda. He asked again:
"What offense have you committed? He replied,
"I committed the *pāyattika* offense of eating food without performing the ritual of leaving food remaining."
Revata said: "This is the Dharma! ... up to: it is not the Buddha's teaching!"
"Now I cast the second tally.
Sitting to eat after [the meal has been] purified, and eating after crossing a village boundary to purify [the food], are also like this.
He casts the third and fourth tallies.
Revata asked again:
"Are ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar pure when mixed with curd?
The Elder asked:
"What is meant by 'clarified butter, oil, honey, and rock sugar mixed with curd is pure'?
Revata replied, "It is to drink them at a time other than the prescribed mealtime."
He replied, "It is impure. He asked again:
"In what place was it established? He replied, "In Śrāvastī."
He asked again:
"By whom was it established? He replied:
"It was because of Kāḷudāyin.
He asked again,
"What offense did he commit?"
He replied, "One commits a *pāyattika* offense for eating at an improper time. Revata said:
“This is the Dharma! … and so on, up to: it is not the Buddha’s teaching!
Now, the fifth tally is cast.”
Revata asked again: "Is it pure to drink *jaḷoga* liquor? The Elder asked:
"What is meant by 'jalogi liquor'?
Revata replied, "It is wine that has been fermented but is not yet mature."
He replied, "It is impure. He asked again:
"In what place was it established? He replied, "In Kauśāmbī."
He asked again:
"By whom was it established? He replied:
"Because of Śākya. He asked again:
"What offense has been committed?"
He replied, "Drinking alcohol is a *pāyattika* offense. Revata said:
"This is the Dharma! ...
up to: it is not the Buddha's teaching!
Now the sixth tally is cast down."
Revata asked again: "Is it pure to make a sitting mat (niṣīdana) of any size one pleases? He replied:
"It is impure! He asked again:
"Where was it prescribed?"
He replied, “Śrāvastī. He asked again:
"By whom was it established? He replied,
"It was established because of Kālodāyin."
He asked again,
"What offense have you committed? He replied:
"You have committed a *pāyattika* offense. Revata said:
"This is the Dharma!"
"Even it is not the Buddha's teaching!
Now, the seventh tally is cast. Upāli asked again:
“Is practicing what was previously practiced pure?
The Elder asked, “What is meant by ‘practicing what was previously practiced’?”
Revata said, "It was done while I was still a layperson. The Elder said:
"Sometimes there is that which may be practiced,
and sometimes there is that which may not be practiced. Revata said, "This is the Dharma!"
"...it is not even the Buddha's teaching!
Now, the eighth tally is cast down. Revata asked again:
"Is the request for permission heard?
The Elder asked: "What is meant by 'requesting permission'?"
Revata said, "Perform the *karmavācanā* separately first, and then come to seek the consent of others. He replied:
"It is impure! He asked again:
"Where was it prescribed?"
He replied, "In the kingdom of Campā.
He asked again:
"By whom was it established?
He replied, "It was established because of the group of six bhikṣus."
He asked again,
"What offense have you committed? He replied:
"Follow the formal procedure (karmavācanā). Upāli said:
"This is the Dharma!"
"It is not even the Buddha's teaching!
Now, the ninth tally is cast. Upāli asked again:
"Is it pure to accept and keep gold, silver,
and coins? He replied,
"It is not pure!"
He asked again:
"Where was it enacted? He replied:
“In Rājagṛha. He asked again: “On account of whom was it established?”
He replied, "Because of Nanda and Upananda.
He asked again:
"What offense have you committed? He replied,
"I have committed the offense of accepting, possessing gold, silver, and money, which is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
Revata said: "This is the Dharma! ... up to: it is not the Buddha's teaching!"
"Now I cast the tenth tally.

Having finished the questioning, they returned together and reconvened the entire assembly. Within the great multitude, Revata again questioned each person one by one, as above, regarding "Sarvakāmin," casting one tally up to the tenth tally.
Thereupon Revata proclaimed:
"We have finished our discussion on the Vinaya rules. That which was not ordained by the Buddha must not be arbitrarily ordained;
that which has already been ordained must not be contravened."
"As the Buddha has taught, you should study this with diligence.
At that time, among the assembly of those who upheld the Vinaya, the first elder was named Sarvakāmin, with one hundred and thirty-six years of seniority;
the second elder was named Revata, with one hundred and twenty years of seniority.

The third elder was named Sambhūta and the fourth elder was named Yasas; both were one hundred and ten years since their ordination. There were exactly seven hundred arhats, neither more nor less; therefore, this is called the "Council of Seven Hundred for the Compilation of the Dharma."
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Wufen lü), Scroll Thirty. Compiled by the Kasmirian Vinaya Master Buddhayaśas, a member of the Mahīśāsaka school!

He arrived in Yangzhou in the seventh month of the autumn of the first year of the Jingping era of the Great Song dynasty. In the eleventh month of winter, Wang Lian—the Prince of Langye and Imperial Secretary of the Jin—along with the bhikṣus Shi Huayan and Zhu Daosheng, requested that he produce this translation.
The Buddha-translator Shi personally held the Sanskrit text, while the Śramaṇa Zhisheng of Yutian served as the translator; by the twelfth month of the following year, the work was fully completed.

Having examined the principles and returned to the essence of the text, I have preserved its conciseness and completeness; though I may not have exhausted the ultimate source, I hope there will be no major errors.
May this [merit], like dust and dew, augment the vastness of mountains and seas, and be bequeathed to ten thousand generations as those who share the same boat!

Recorded by Lin: Regarding the birth of a monk; the present-life outflows; the mind’s division into evil speech; the matter of the Malla wrestlers; the robe of the mother; the nun’s washing of old clothes;
whether dyeing, beating, or weaving them into robes for one's own use; and the time of the flower garland and the ewe.

If one spreads out wool with the hands; if one accepts the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of five or six words for the sake of receiving the *ārāmika* (monastery attendant) precepts; if one stays overnight beyond two nights;
if a *śrāmaṇera*, a female water-carrier, a *bhikṣuṇī*, or a *bhikṣu* [acts in such a way]; if one travels together on a road with a *bhikṣuṇī* who has made a prior appointment until sunset;
or if one travels by boat from this village to that village with a *bhikṣuṇī* who has made a prior appointment, or if one boards [a vehicle].

Regarding water or descending into water: except for the occasion of crossing directly over [a river] while receiving food to eat; except when a donor has previously resolved to provide a set number of meals or robes;

except during times of festivals or gatherings; except for food taken into the mouth; except for the *mūrdhaja* (top-knot) initiation; except when another bhikṣu gives rise to doubt or regret and departs after granting his consent (*chanda*);
except at the time of an invitation; except for a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*); except for concealing a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; except for slandering a fellow bhikṣu.

the practice of consciousness-training, the training in increasing wisdom, daily dwelling, the arising of lust, not going to see or hear,
